Tired of massive space battles, shooting at at yet another zombie infestation or fancy spaceships that only exist in loading screens?  Well then Conan: Exiles might be the change of pace you're looking for.  Based on the award-winning universe of Robert E. Howard's Conan the Barbarian Conan: Exiles sets you loose as an unnamed exile in a gods-forsaken wasteland with literally nothing.  Depending on how you set up the game you may not even have the clothes on your back!  Fight, explore and survive in numerous environments making use of the hundreds of items available.  Level up by killing, exploring and crafting and if you're feeling really decadent you can build your own palace.
The Good:
HUGE Map.
You aren't stuck with just a tiny part of a map that you have to be level gajillion to travel beyond.  Nor or are you forced to unlock specific portions of it.  In Conan: Exiles you can literally go where ever your heart desires.  Granted you might get killed if you♥♥♥♥♥♥off the wrong bad guys but Conan: Exiles is surprisingly forgiving in that regard.  Unlike many other survival games exploration is actually encouoraged because you can earn exp just for finding some new landmark you've never found before.  All you really need are the very basics of survival equipment and you can go anywhere on the map your heart desires.  Just be patient, there's no fast travel in Conan: Exiles so your avatar is going to be hoofing it for quite a while.
Home Sweet Home:
Building a home base for you and your friends is a surprising amount of fun.  With the latest update creating good looking and creative homes is also quite satisfying.  Gone are the days when you had to put up with certain designs because of a lack of appropriate pieces.  Funcom has done a great job of giving you the tools you need to make that dream home (complete with murderous archers and cauldrons of bubbling oil) a reality.
Gorgeous atmosphere:
Everything about Conan: Exiles is beautiful.  From the amazing and varied landscapes to the lovely musical scores to the transition from day into nighttime the entire game is a feast for the senses.  The armors in the game are well crafted and actually look like something you could wear into battle.  The weapons as well are really diverse and well rendered.
You don't just have three of the same axes that are different colors, each weapon looks unique and is wonderfully well done.  Thankfully, the team has gone to great effort to create different kinds of weapons for different kinds of players.
Gone are the days when everyone runs around carrying the exact same, max level sword (or those days will be gone once the combat system is finalized).  The art team really deserves the credit for making Conan: Exiles as appealing as it is.
The Bad:
Still a lot of bugs:
Compared to many other notable early access titles Conan: Exiles seems to suffer from far too many bugs and glitches.  Combat also feels way out of balance.  Fixing these issues is quite the grind, I get that but with the game's official release date being May of 2018 the game simply feels too unstable for where it is.  Thankfully, Funcom has heard the feedback and is in the "optimization stage" of development and is focused on squashing bugs.  If all goes well this complaint will largely be gone by launch.
Unbalanced Land:
No, you don't HAVE to be level 60 to travel into the frozen north but if you aren't you won't be able to do much other than smile and wave at the locals.  For a map of this size it's pretty surprising how tightly divided up the NPCs seem to be.  Leaving the southern river with tier one gear is possible with enough skill but novice players will feel the pain of leaving their dismembered corpses littering the land.  While it makes sense that different camps require levels of skill to assault the level jump required for some of them seems far too steep.  Even the critters you have to fight seem to have really high difficulty spikes depending on where you go.
Too much of not enough to do:
The current journey log is great but it stops too soon and even having that there are often times you wander around in your tier six armor (or completely nude if you're like me) wondering: "Okay, now what?  Do I assault the same Darfari camp for the umpteenth time or do I try to fight the boss in the Dregs and get killed AGAIN?"  Leveling up can become quite the grind and once you pass level 30 it gets really painful.  So much so that the reward you get for hard work almost doesn't seem worth it.  Trying to find new and exciting challenges can really difficult and because there's no fast travel traveling to find them can become quite a chore by itself.
The Nitpicky:
Not enough variety in the character generator:
Not that the game really needs it since there are no cut scenes but still, being able to create a unique character is the core of any role playing game.  While the generator does provide several options and more are on the way it still seems like everyone looks pretty much the same save for hair and skin tone.  The ability to dye your armor sets creates more personalization than the character generator but then perhaps that's the point?
Item descriptions are quite vague:
Most of the items I pick up in game (this is especially true of the food) have only a story description but no real explanation of the what kind of (if any) in game mechanic they provide.  Does this food give me a buff?  How much hunger/thrist does this provide?  Does this stuff I picked up do anything other than glow?  I've been quite shocked to find out this item I've been throwing away actually had a use so many times it's pretty infuriating.
Overall, Conan: Exiles is a good game entry to the survival game genre.  It's pretty rough and requires a lot of polish but the game has come a really long way in the nearly a year it's been in early access.  Many fans of the original works of Robert E. Howard have enjoyed the game and even his family have thrown out their full support.  While it has a long way to go the progress made so far give me hope that once this game is finally finished it'll be a worthy entry to the Conan universe.

It is one of those games that is more a visual novel than anything. (Though I would say it's more than that, it's an entire experience.) There are a million little stories told through the characters. Bizarre stories always, sad stories most of the time, always feeling like they're maybe on the edge of some deep meaning. And the dialogue options allow you to take a part in this story telling and guide what happened to the characters. The latest chapter especially allows more freedom, I think, in what happens and what scenarios you experience that gives a greater sense of freedom that the other chapters. I enjoyed this change. It makes a difference if I can decide if my characters are making a mushroom stew or playing cards. Honestly, I wish I could convince everyone to play this game with an open mind, but if I can convince even one person to play who might fall in love with it then I will be very happy.

Stay a while, and listen! Once upon a time, I used to hate Warframe. Of course, that wasn't always the case. In fact, it enraptured me when I first started playing several years back, when Warframe first released onto Steam. That high dropped fast when I hit a proverbial wall; the game was a nightmare to play solo, getting around to anywhere felt like a chore, and I've got a horror story involving Kubrow eggs that would've turned quite a few people away from the game. It left a really sour taste in my mouth.
But then something happened: on the spur of a friend, who was gathering their clan back together, compounded with my current dilemma of not having sweet FA to do with myself, I went back to Warframe very recently, a few weeks ago in fact. I went in expecting to be ejected back out by how off-putting everything felt, but when I got back into playing..
I was having
It felt remeniscent of when I first started playing, in a way that the game wasn't able to capture with me ever since. Things became more streamlined, a lot of mechanics that irked me got switched up dramatically, and the recent content with the Plains of Eidolon has brought a much-needed new zest. The momentum feels far less like I'm driving off a cliff, and more like I'm running over everything in my way. It's been quite the interesting turnaround.
tl:dr at the bottom.
Warframe is a game that prides itself on the joys of murdering hordes of enemies in style. There's a reason the game is called 'Fashionframe' by its community, and there's really no evading why: everything you see is bleeding with flair and personality, from your arsenal of weaponry to the Warframes to even the enemies and planets you encounter. There is really no better way to describe the aesthetic other than "They really know how to make space ninjas look cool."
There's no mistaking that graphics like Warframe's is gonna take a pretty decent computer to run smoothly, even on minimum settings; at least a considerably strong graphics card and a motherboard that isn't going to light on literal fire. That said, Warframe surprisingly doesn't require that much processing power, and the graphics are very easily customizable to give mercy on computers at the lower end of the spectrum.
The main plot gives you the gist of what you have to know: You are a Tenno, part of a society of warriors who don powerful suits that envelop their body, refining them into tools of elegant destruction: the titular Warframes.
The story, and the whole game, begins with a mysterious object being hoisted out of the ground by the Grineer, a militarized race of would-be conquerors. The Grineer go about forcing their find open to see what's inside; surprise, it's you, the player! After a short sequence that doubles as a tutorial, you meet the Lotus, a woman who aids and guides Tenno, and your annoying but trusty companion Ordis, an AI that JUST. WON'T
After introductions are done, you're thrust out into your planet-hopping adventure of sticking it to the Grineer, among a bunch of other crises that crash head-long into the plot every so often.
The fun of Warframe's lore is that while you're left with questions, you're always given just enough to know what's going on. As you progress through different questlines, which leaves you meeting a colorful B-cast and travelling to many different locations, you start to learn the broader strokes of the game, like the Orokin, the Void, and the three-way conflict between the Grineer, the Tenno, and the Corpus (a race of salesmen, as best as I can explain it) as a mysterious Infestation spreads.
A lot of people describe the game as an endless loot-and-shoot, and they're not far off the mark; it's a point of argument that you'll usually be setting your own goals in terms of what you're doing, what to do next, and you have to do to reach that point. Never will there be an idle moment, as there
be something you should or will be doing to increase your power. I'll try to keep this brief, if I can.
Essentially, your Warframe is the baseline of what you can do, and you alter its powers the more you play the game. Once upon a time, you automatically started with Excalibur, a sword, and some guns; now, you can select between a few Frames for which one you start with, as well as Mk-1 weapons you'll be carting around for the foreseeable future. Be careful how you pick your equipment, because you'll be stuck with it a while; I had the fate of starting with the bow and fists, both turned out to be awkward to use.
In terms of matchmaking for PvE, you have options between solo and public matches, as well as friend and invite-only settings. Solo play is far more viable than it used to be, but you might sometimes run across a tight spot with certian missions. Never be afraid to let other players lend you a hand.
As for general gameplay, you'll be seeing a theme of mission types over random maps using pre-built 'rooms' to serve as a layout. The mission types are fairly varied, but the main theme is that there's an army, there's you, and there will be slightly less of that army by the time you're done.
Throughout playing, it's important to learn the system of movement; Warframe is infamous for its fast pace and ecclectic map design, taking advantage of the variety of mechanics that you'll be using to your advantage. Originally, the movement was a lot more clunky, and it was hard to keep a good momentum. Now, you'll be making use of double jumps, slides, wall grabs, so-called 'bullet jumps,' abilities, and mods in order to speed through the map like a maelstrom of Space-Ninja steel.
Speaking of, Mods are decidedly one of the most important elements of the game: powerful cards that slot into your equipment, increasing stats and even drastically changing their properties. The system is pretty extensive, and would take more words than I'm allowed for this review.
Another important element of the game is crafting; you'll be finding a ton of materials and blueprints as you play, and you'll be using both to create new and more powerful equipment. (And I'd suggest making new weapons fast, those Mk-1 weapons are weaker than their regular variants. Helpful advice.)
The community in Warframe is pretty frickin' massive, which is to be expected in a Free-to-Play title. But more than that, they're an astonishingly reserved and helpful bunch. You'll rarely outright see any toxicity aside from the occasional oddball player in a public lobby, as there's a shockingly healthy stream of updates and support by the devteam, the likes of which I rarely saw when I was first playing.
Warframe is
so much so, I've had to omit a lot of stuff while writing this, like Void Relics, Syndicates, the Conclave, and the Plains of Eidolon expansion. But feel comfortable at least giving this a try; coming from someone who was once turned off of Warframe, I can safely say that it's won me back. The dev team obviously cares about this game's future, and I can greatly appreciate that. Play it. It looks fun, it feels fun, and running around as a neon-pink ninja with a sword the size of a small spaceship is an invocative enough image just typing, let alone thinking about it.

As with many Paradox titles, Crusader Kings II belongs to the rather small genre of Grand Strategy Games. Unfortunately, this also proves to be one of the deciding points of purchase--to anyone who has not taken the time to watch and understand the scale on which the game takes place, the game may appear intimidating. Factor in the time investment into building a virtual, medieval empire, as well as [attempting] management of the hundreds of AI below, above, and beside the player, and the heart of even a dedicated strategy gamer may falter.
Warnings aside, however, Crusader Kings II is--hands down--one of the finest of Paradox's titles, as well as one of the greatest games I have had the privilege of playing, managing to blend traditional Grand Strategy elements with the scale of character development and management matched by at least a (further) traditional tabletop RPG. To clarify, the player is a ruler, and manages their character's development through a series of decisions that may lead to any number of events: love, trysts, marriage, rivalry, friendship, heroism, murder, and--maniacally, in the most literal sense of the word--madness. Whether or not you invest in the expansions (highly recommended), you will always be guaranteed a plethora of storytelling options, ideas for lore (being a writer, especially important), and chances to shape Europe in your image. But will you?
Needless to say, this is indeed a highly recommended title!

What a fantastic journey. Every once in a while, you get incredibly hyped for that next game that's about to come out... and every so often, that very game delivers on the hype. This game ultimately did that for me, and I'm almost sad that the journey is now over (unless I start another new game). Starting each category at 10 points.
Visuals: starting at +10
================
The game's graphics look fantastic. There is a vast amount of polished detail in each and every environment. The developers didn't leave anything out. Even areas you may only explore once, if only for a couple of minutes, got all the same polished details as areas that you'll be spending hours upon hours inside of. Brilliant, long, hard work went into sewing the fields of this game's visuals, and the developers are reaping the fantastic benefits of that hard work. Well done.
+ No real cons here. I never had any screen tearing and rarely saw any seams throughout the world.
Final score: 10/10
Sound/Music: +10
=============
For anyone who has read my past reviews, you'll know I use the word "weight" a lot when it comes to sound effects. This "weight" means that for each and every major sound effect in the game, there should typically be some kind of "impact" behind them. It doesn't have to be a big "boom" for that to work. It can be the sounds of butterfly wings flapping in the wind (which would be incredibly hard to hear), or it can be a loud thunderbolt. Either way, whichever object or environment a sound effect has been stuck in/onto, it has to have a strong feeling behind it. This is not easy to explain, but let's just say that Divinity Original Sin 2 pulls it off extremely well.
+ All abilities sound effects, even ones that are as simple as throwing a dagger, feel heavy. There is strength behind them. No ability is left out, nothing is in the "filler" category. Excellent.
+ Music appears to be orchestra, and it's great. Battle music pumps you up. "Majestic" music calms you down, and provides a sense of relief behind it. It all sounds fantastic.
+ Pre-final battle music setup is excellent (only those who've played the game will understand).
+ Great voice work across all characters, both major and minor.
Final score: 10/10
Performance: +10
=============
Overall, the game runs well.
+ When everything is working, it performs at 60 FPS, constantly.
+/- Long long load times between regions. I mark this as neither a plus or a minus due to the fact that once you're loaded in, there are no load times whatsoever. The game loads everything upon entry (this is why is takes so long).
- Bugs bugs and more bugs. Nothing game breaking fortunately. A common theme when it comes to Larian Studios games. The good news is, most bugs are extremely minor. Quest bugs WILL be contracted, inhibiting you from actually completing a quest. Other quest related bugs include 1) actually completing a quest, but it never leaving your quest log. 2) you have option A and option B to choose from. You chose option A, but the game will say you chose option B. -1
- Certain battles have frustrating situations where a turn will not end immediately, forcing you to wait for up to 5-10 minutes at a time for each turn to finally end (even though nothing is happening). This will hopefully be patched in the near future. It was not patched in this playthrough. -1
- Game will crash every now and then. -1
- Strange lag issues in regards to certain spells (such as blood storm). These lag issues will persist until the specific spell (or spells) animations have completely ended, sometimes several turns after being cast. -1
Final score: 6/10
Story: +10
========
You are a source wielder. You've been captured and you're about to sent to what would closely resemble a "prison island" to serve out your remaining days. It's time to escape! This is where the adventure begins.
+ Premade characters all have an actual personality that you will love or hate. It will slowly be fleshed out as the story progresses, whether for better or for worse. Whichever character you pick (or don't pick, you can make your own too) will still have their main story attached, but you get to make a plethora of extra decisions behind them that will ultimately influence their endgame personality. So don't be afraid to pick the premades (you can also edit their classes and appearances).
+ Relevant in-game choices that will affect the endings.
+ Special endings for certain characters are available.
- Some scenes would have a far greater impact if it wasn't simply reading text. A few animations here and there wouldn't hurt, especially behind big scenes (that would normally be a cutscene vs an interactable scene). -1
Final score: 9/10
Gameplay: +10
===========
Gameplay hinges upon building your starting character with either physical, magical, or ranged damage types (ranged being both physical and magical, depending on if you're an archer or a mage). You'll run around and collect lots of loot, sell the loot, buy better loot; craft items, scrolls, and potions; learn a vast amount of abilities and even craft secret "hidden" abilities; there is plenty to do here, and you will be busy, all while having fun (hopefully).
+ Respec any time once you hit Act 2, for free. This will actually probably enrage some players, because they want to feel the weight of locking in their choice of permenant abilities (i.e. Diablo 2). Respecing for me on the other hand was the greatest thing to ever happen in this game. I started as a Battlemage, switched to a full time mage, and then later switched to a mostly full-timer tank/DPS with certain mage support abilities attached. I had another character start as a full healer and supporter, who later stayed as a full healer supporter, but also had fire and ice abilities to help in combat, if they couldn't do anything else. You can experiment to your heart's delight. So get past Act 1, then indulge in the world of change!
+ You can play as a skeleton, with facial hair.
+ Various unique abilities for each race are well implemented and can provide extra benefits to playing a certain class with a certain race (such as a thief/assassin with an undead, due to getting a free skeleton key to unlock any chest provided you have high enough Thievery skill. No need to buy lockpicks!)
+ Crowd control in this game is just as fantastic as it was in the first game, with a vast amount of new CC abilities (like sleeping).
+ The addition of Armor and Magic Armor is also fantastic, providing you with protection against CC abilities of both the physical and magical aspects until that chosen armor is depleted (unless you have Glass Cannon).
+ Playing with friends is a lot of fun.
+/- Some talents in the game feel wholly useless (Demon and Ice King), while others feel overpowered. I mark this as plus or minus simply because you can respec at any given time. It would only benefit to take certain "less useful" talents to quick specific areas of the game, then respec again back to whatever you were originally with. That being said...
- I played the game on Tactician mode (which is basically hard mode) and having a slightly higher fire resistance or slightly lower ice resistance never really made that big of a difference. The enemies in this mode having such incredibly strong physical or magical abilities would typically negate your armor too too quickly, and 15% out of 100% is just not very helpful. Leadership was a much better option, and also freed up the "wasted" talent points. These less useful abilites are what you would call "filler". -1
Final score: 9/10
Overall: 8.8/10 (44/50 = 0.88)
=====================

TL;DR: Pick this game up, its free so you have nothing to lose but time.
I will start off by naming pros and cons then expand on them further.
Pros:
-Free to play without being pay to win
-Nice and generous community
-Gameplay
-Plenty of content
-Grindy (this is personal preference)
-Top notch customization
Cons:
-Can be limiting if you dont put in coin (but not that limiting, I'll explain later)
-The gameplay loop can get repetitive
-Time gates
Pros explained
------------------------------
It is Free to play yes, and it is done, well, right! There are no Pay to win aspects, the game rewards you for paying money but not in an unhealthy way. The way buying things works is you pay for the premium currency and you can either outright buy weapons and warframes or buy cosmetics. The Need to buy or pay money isnt in your face and you can actually work around buying currency by trading meaning you can get paid items without forking up coin.
The community here is super generous and very kind, players and devs included. Many are willing to help you through missions, teach you the ropes, offer up information and tips. Ive even heard a few freiends tell me people have bought and gifted entire warframes and vaulted Prime warframes too.
The gameplay is unlike any other, think mirors edge meets destiny. It is awesome. The gunplay feels great, you get a HUGE variety of weapons. Every Frame feels unique and has great abilities. Its just fun, I dont know how to explain it much more than that. Go look up some gameplay videos, youll see what I mean.
The game is VERY grindy, thats what this game is, if you dont enjoy grinding, this game isnt for you, simple. You grind so you can grind better. There is no endgame because the endgame is whatever you want it to be. You are very unlikely to run out of things to grind for unless you have a few thousand hours under your belt tbh.
The customization is the best int he genre and one of the best in games. You can really make your Frames your own. You can give them your own personality and spin. Its so nice seeing everyone creations.
Cons explained
---------------------------
The game isnt super in your face with microtransactions but its a F2P game and t gives off that vibe in some cases. You have to pay for extra weapon slots, Warframe slots and it timegates you on crafting. This isnt all bad though, these things are super cheap and since trading uses premium currency you just need to farm certain mods and sell them. The market it booming so its not super hard to sell, but it can be overwhelming for some.
So do I reccomend this game? Hell freaking yeah! Its one of if not the best F2P game out there. If my praise hasnt convinced you then the Plains of Eidolon will. PoE was a FREE update that feels like a completely new game. Added a HUGE new open world map, lots of new items, missions and enemies. Along with one fo the most epic feeling fights Ive ever played, on par with Shadow of Collosus bosses.
Digital Extreams clearly care about this game, you can feel the love they have put into it, the passion in the game is real. If they continue ont he route they are on Warframe will continue to not only grow but will cement itself in gaming history.

I like it.  It's like XCom meets Heroes of the Storm.
You have the turn-based combat of Xcom with the Hero selection and abilities of HotS.
Simultaneous action selection (preperation/dash/blast/movement) mean you have to anticipate the enemy team's actions, and it cuts down on waiting for the turn phase to complete drastically.  You only have to wait 20s in Co-Op and PvP mode before the next turn.  AI only mode means you get a whole 60s, if you're trying to learn a character or get a feel for the game.
My only concern is if the entrence fee is going to gate the game from a large playerbase.  It is, after all, a predominately PvP arena-like game, and you need a large base of players to keep queue times short.  I'm a bit curious why they didn't go for a F2P model, and offer a hero pack at $20 to start.  [shrugs]
I'm going to enjoy this free weekend and decide to risk the investment over it, but I highly recommend everyone interested to get your feet wet for free while you can.

This is a good game and a solid simulator. However, after a while the territory 'shrinks' It does not take that long to explore the highway aspect of the states currently in the game. This game needs more states to drive through, it would be very cool if the continental US (plus Alaska) was completely available in the game. How about the Coq in Canda, that would be cool indeed. The game sorely needs territory expansion. I would also suggest a greater variety of trucks available in the game, currently 2 makes is kind of limiting, and this is probably due in large part to licensing issues. I would suggest the developers just make up a couple of new brands of trucks, there is no harm in doing that (add an option for the purists to disable this.) The game developers need to keep the DLC affordable, it is not feasible to spend hundreds of dollars on this or any game with the cost of continually purchasing DLC. I bought this game on sale for an excellent price and recommend waiting until it is on sale again.
Personally I think this is a great game and I have very few complaints. Additionally I have found very few bugs as well. Sometimes the AI crashes vehicles into your truck, but it is uncommon enough that I can forgive this occurence, save often. One other occasional flaw is that traffic will stack up on an on ramp, less common on an exit ramp, this also happens on roads, and it can be impossible to continue the current game, I usually revert to a previous save when this happens. The scenery is excellent and there are enough AI vehicles in the environment to give it a realistic feel and make it challenging. I have a list of suggestions for another review post at some point in the future, to increase the re-playability of the game and its dynamicism.
The 'compression' of time is done well as it would be totally unacceptible for a 14 hour delivery to really take 14 hours (some of us work and have kids so gaming time is minimal), the developers have handled time compression gracefully. My oldest son prefers the European Truck simulator, I have not played that but he feels it offers a greater variety of options, so that is a path to consider as well. Some jobs, in particular, heavy/oversize loads are impossible to park (in a realistic sense they would never depart or arrive at the chosen locations) and this can be a bit frustrating if one wants to maximize experience points, but at least you can opt not to park the trailer in these cases (the experience point hit is minimal compared to the experience points derived from completing the rest of the job perfectly.) Perhaps it would be nice to see wage versus time in addition to wage versus miles, for example the speed restriction in California, I am in favor of keeping this restriction but having the option to view wage versus time might allow one to better optimize chosen loads to transport.
Overall this is a great game, worth picking up if you like big trucks (and personally I like big trucks, Peterbilt and Kenworth), you will not be disappointed, that is if you like simulation games to begin with. This is a one of a kind game the likes of which you will not find elsewhere, where else can you cruise in a big rig... You will want a PC that can shove a little, I play this on a high performance laptop with no issues (12 GiB of RAM, NVIDIA 965M with 4GiB VRAM, i7 6700HQ, and an SSD) , the game is reasonable optimized, so I would not expect the performance per some hardware specification to improve significantly in the future. I give it a 7.5 out of 10. More territory, at a reasonable price, would instantly increase this to 9 out of 10.

I'll admit, I first got this after the Overwatch open beta ended, and I was craving more of the same. At first glance it might seem similar if you ignore ALL the information about the game. Fortunately, it was an entirely different game, and has become one of my absolute favorite surprises in a long time.
This is a turn based tactics competitive strategy game. First to five kills, 4v4, but you can make custom games which change up that formula. This a purely PVP game, with no PVE aspect (unless you play with bots). You move on a grid and on each turn you have twenty seconds to decide what to do. Within that time frame, you can see your team mate\'s moves but not the enemies. After the twenty seconds, all turns play simultaneously in a specific order of operations. It ends up playing like a very animated game of chess. Your whole team may plan to attack one person, but before the attack phase is the dash phase, and if that enemy dashes all your teams attacks will still play out, each one missing the shot. Which could place them in a bad spot, or maybe another enemy accidentally dashes into someones line of fire and gets killed.
The strategy of the game is not the abilities or perfectly placed shots, but correctly guessing your opponents next move or two. This is not a twitch game, which is refreshing. I'm not against twitch games. I've played those my entire life and they are my favorite genre. But this is a nice change of pace. Seeing your team mate's choreographed moves executed as planned and out-smarting the entire team is one of the best experiences I've had in a competitive game in a long time.
I cannot get enough of this game even in this state and I sincerely hope it does well once it comes out.  It needs more players. No pay to win. Microtransactions are only for cosmetics and taunts. Free updates and characters for everyone. This scratches an itch I never knew existed.
[Edit] They have added a free mode, similar to other games with a couple free freelancer rotations and some other restrictions. They actually removed some of the loot box restrictions upon feedback from the community. They have been very active in adding new freelancers since release. I remember at least five new freelancers from when I got the game, with another one just being teased around the corner. Their community support has been phenomenal.

As usual I don't rate games unless they are released fully and I only rate them for their genres they represent.  So here goes :)
8 out of 10 Simulator Rating.  This game does put you into the feel of being behind the wheel of a Truck or heavy ground vehicle.  you get all the feelings of Driving up a hill with a heavy load, Shifting to make it through situations, Dealing with oversized vehicles in undersized roadways.
6 out of 10 Exploration Rating.  This game has a huge map which expands with each state they add.  Though I did get the feeling of being trapped in some areas (IE being unable to go down a road that you see cars coming from).
5 out of 10 for Its Modded Multiplayer.  The Main game is about running the simulation with AI vehicles which to me perform too predictably and are way to numerous.  Get the Free Multiplayer mod and you can play without AI's and deal with Real Players.  Still needs a lot of work though since I believe Voice Coms need to be drastically improved and a way to just talk in proximity to others is required.
3 out of 10 Expanding your vehicle and customization.  It does have a lot of Modded support but in the main game I found that you reach a point where your creativity in choosing parts for your truck ends.  It ends up being just a paint job change every so often or driving different vehicle sizes.
2 out of 10 Modifications.  I am not really into heavily modding my gameplay so I do feel that if a Feature is Modded and Popular it should already be in the main game.
Overall a very enjoyable game if you like to challenge yourself in doing a run quicker or with less Accidents :)  Graphics are Decent and with full simulation of all the AI's or even with a bunch of players the game runs pretty smoothly.
I am still reviewing and playing the game so I might have new Ratings later.
About 1 and a half weeks of play and at the time of this review almost 90 hours of play time.

31 hours in about 2.5 days of ownership.
The game needs some work, obviously, it's still early access. There are places that are unfinished, the Thrall system needs more work, like maybe ordering Thralls to gather for you and fight with you when they follow you instead of having to tell them to stop following you first. Perhaps a way to free Thralls who act like NPC allies. (Conan was, after all, aware that slavery was a necessary evil, still a liberator rather than a Thrall keeper himself, so a way to 'free' Thralls and have them join you would be a nice 'fluff' touch to the game.) I would suggest a way to free 'thralls' captured by NPC exiles and freeing captive 'dinner' from the cannibals as nice way to implement this.
The game is awesome, and if they stopped work on it, I would still be playing it as is. But single and co-op play is fun, and there's enough content to keep you busy, though without more factions and 'raiding' between NPC factions, the game risks getting very stale.
Still, go far, so good.

I’ve bought Conan Exiles on day one and as you can see by the amount of hours I played this game, I like it a lot.
Until now I haven’t reviewed the game but now here it is.
Although the game is still in development, I can already recommend this game to those interested in a single-player survival game who like crafting, building, exploring, etc. in a fantasy game world.
I guess this game is mostly known for its multiplayer, but I’ve played it in single-player only.
There are no quests, there is no campaign. But the game world feels and sounds alive.
From the moment you start the game in the hot desert, you’re free to go in any direction you want and do whatever you want. You’re trying to survive, gather resources, craft tools and items, and try to get out of the desert.
When you reach the oasis alongside the river, you think you’re safe. But here another aspect of survival kicks in: you’re attacked by monsters and/or other exiles (NPC’s). You try to fight them off or run away to find a safe place. During this, you get to admire the great graphics and game world, the beautiful water, the detailed textures of the sand on the river bank, trees swaying in the wind and impressive vistas of rocks, mountains, etc.
But you don’t got too much time to enjoy the views, because you’re getting thirsty and hungry. You need to go hunting for food and drink water, build a campfire to cook food, etc. So you need to go craft, gather resources, etc. This is where the game really shines. The blending of survival, crafting, gathering materials, and then building structures.
The possibility of building crafting stations, houses, walls, towers and other structures is awesome. You can basically build an entire city, a place of civilization in the middle of a brutal and lawless land.
This combined with the ability to capture NPC’s (thralls) and put them into your crafting stations, on your walls and in your city, is really amazing. Not only is it fun, it also increases your economy/production and helps levelling up your character. At the moment, it’s not really necessary to defend your settlement with captured NPC’s in the single-player game because your settlement won’t get attacked by NPC’s (unless you attack an NPC-camp and the NPC’s follow you to your settlement). As I understand, raids on your settlement by NPC’s is a possible addition to the game in the future (known as “The Purge”).
The game world is filled with places to discover and see, but the existing dungeons (caves, ruins, etc.) in the game could be improved upon. And some more/better rewards for exploring dungeons would be a nice addition. It is very possible this will be added to the game or improved upon in the future. I really enjoyed the dungeon known as “The Dregs” that was added to the game.
When the game just came out, the combat with monsters and NPC’s wasn’t very fun I think personally. But the combat has improved during development and I lowered the game difficulty thanks to the added difficulty-options. These things made combat more fun.
Other things worth mentioning are the great music, the sandstorm, notes you can read left by other exiles in the game world and funny things like climbing trees, jumping off cliffs or♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off dangerous wildlife like rhino’s and elephants.

I have the actual physical Card Game as well.  So already my review may be a bit biased because of that fact.
This game is Star Realms based on a card game of the same name.
It is mostly a 2 player game but can be played by more players.
This version starts as free and allows the user to play with the core game against the AI and has some campaign solo missions available for the user as well.
To play online though you will need to get what they call is the Full version.  Fairly inexpensive but lets you play online.
The game does have a hot seat play option called pass.
Right now i do not see any options to play multiplayer and co-op.....so thats not something available yet
The game has the full artwork from the game and its interface is not too bad.
In addition for more content that you can get....yuo can purchase some of the expansions for star realms.  I say some....as the only ones available are the original gambits and the differing crisis expansions....and nothing else.
I am not too surprised....as I asume the AI would not be able to handle the cosmic gambits nor the 4 updates....as those offer special mission cards and co-op play missions and combined faction cards...that not be able to be handled by the AI too well.
The music is ok....and can be repetitive...however it does change a bit as you play and i felt it was not too annoying.  Though like with many things some users may not feel the music is very good at all.
The graphics onthe steam version are not too bad either....however running this at 4k or more you will start to see the textures dont look as good on their resize.
The game also advertises on the start page, i actual find that form of advertisement to be fairly good....as it shows things available that might interesting from the company but also since its a menu it doesnt matter inthe slightest.
My only gripe so far...is that i feel sometimes the computer cheats....and very blatently....like for example....you start with supposedly 8 scouts and 2 vipers....the computer will show the right cards ion its draw pile....but when it starts it will give itself extra cards.
First turn you are supposed to only have 3 cards in your hand....computer will sometimes play 4 of them.
To give good examples of the extra card things....i have been hit onthe computer's turn....with 5 vipers.......another time....the computer played 3 scouts a blob homeworld and a blob dreadnought......on its turn when it should have had no cards except the scouts and vipers.
So aside from that....its a fun game to play...i recommend it for those who like strategy card games.

To start with the start menu, it looks like a bad science-fiction shooter from 1995. In the free version of the game, you can only play games against brainless AI. For the so-called full version, you get to play online against fellow star realms freaks (otherwise they wouldn't be playing this game), but you have to pay an extra $ 4 to get all campaign missions and cards.
To give you a few examples of the flaws:
- You can't enter a game before your first turn begins.
- There is no timer to see how much time you have left in your turn. When time runs out you first have to check your game history before realising you lost.
- You have to discover how the ranking system works by yourself. I only discovered how the ranking system works after 2 months of playing.
- You can only see the turn of your opponent after he played all of his cards. There is no effort done on dynamic gameplay.
- The "next game" button does not work properly. To switch between games, you have to leave the current game and enter your other game.
Unless you are a big fan of the original board game, avoid this game at all costs.

The S.T.A.L.K.E.R series will always be one of my favorite FPS's. The game is scary, fun, difficult (but in a good way), and, IMO, has the best atmosphere in a game I've ever experienced. You get a certain feeling when playing this game that is hard to find in others, it's a feeling hard to describe. It also has that Russian charm, with all the characters speaking in thick russian accents and living completely off of a diet of sausages and vodka. It's also got a lot of replayability.
In addition, the game also has one of the most devoted fanbases I have ever seen, right next to the Half-Life fanbase. Despite the last game (Call of Pripyat) being released way back in 2009, the fanbase still survives and even thrives off of fan films, a whole bunch of super well-made and extensive mods, art, MEMES, and users simply sharing the experiences they've had playing the game. I guarantee you'll be having a lot of fun with this game, even after you're done playing.
Oh, and did I mention mods? Boy, are you in for a treat when it comes to mods. S.T.A.L.K.E.R has an amazing modbase. Even now, mods are still being made. Call of Chernobyl, Misery, Autumn Aurora, and so many others, all free and made by professionals. There are also a whole lot of upcoming mods, including a multiplayer mod.
Sadly, the game suffers from Half Life syndrome. S.T.A.L.K.E.R 2 was in development but was quickly canceled due to a whole bunch of complex issues GSC Game World had to face. But GSC has made a comeback, having recently released Cossacks 3. So things are looking up for S.T.A.L.K.E.R!
So, yeah, you should totally get this game. Now get out of here, S.T.A.L.K.E.R.

Around October last year, my best friend convinced me to buy a couple of games in the Steam autumn sale, called The Legend of Heroes Trails in the Sky, and its sequel, Trails in the Sky SC, which was just localized. It took me a few months to get to actually playing and completing them due to various reasons, but now that I did (and stayed up till 6 in the morning to finish SC), I have one thing to say. It was all so, SO worth it.
Where do I even start? The story is an amazing example of tricking you into thinking it's a run of the mill JRPG, when it's anything but. It's an intricate, deep, well-thought out and wonderful story, with some of the best world building I've ever seen. (NPC's with their own stories isn't something you come across every day.) The characters are so charming, lovable, well-written, and so well-developed, including even the villains, which honestly feel more like well-intentioned extremists at times rather than outright villainous. The OST is simply marvelous, whether it be boss battle themes (like the one down here) or emotional tracks, it all fits so well and sounds amazing. Sure, the game looks outdated at first glance, but it sure as heck doesn't feel that way, and the battle system is quite easy to grasp, especially if you're not used to turn-based games.
Overall, Trails in the Sky was one of the best video games I've experienced in quite a while, and it was worth every minute and so worth buying. It was awesome and amazing, and I can't recommend it enough.

This is a simple but honest game that can put you through quite a test. With a simple premise of 'don't get hit' for as long as possible you're treated to hordes of nightmarish enemies.
The game starts benign enough before demanding a true FPS "in the zone" mindset. Enemies will inevitably spawn faster than you can slay. Different foes with different behaviors will test your ability to react and prioritize targets. Devil Daggers soon becomes a chaotic exercise of spatial awareness and crowd control. Victory is in extending your time alive, leaving a feeling of accomplishment (or maybe "I can do better") as the game ejects you on death to the scoreboard and you reset to begin anew.
If there was a benchmark for FPS skill, it would be Devil Daggers, and this benchmarking tool is very cheap with plenty of replayability...if you're willing to try and try again to extend your time by another five more seconds.

As with many Paradox titles, Crusader Kings II belongs to the rather small genre of Grand Strategy Games. Unfortunately, this also proves to be one of the deciding points of purchase--to anyone who has not taken the time to watch and understand the scale on which the game takes place, the game may appear intimidating. Factor in the time investment into building a virtual, medieval empire, as well as [attempting] management of the hundreds of AI below, above, and beside the player, and the heart of even a dedicated strategy gamer may falter.
Warnings aside, however, Crusader Kings II is--hands down--one of the finest of Paradox's titles, as well as one of the greatest games I have had the privilege of playing, managing to blend traditional Grand Strategy elements with the scale of character development and management matched by at least a (further) traditional tabletop RPG. To clarify, the player is a ruler, and manages their character's development through a series of decisions that may lead to any number of events: love, trysts, marriage, rivalry, friendship, heroism, murder, and--maniacally, in the most literal sense of the word--madness. Whether or not you invest in the expansions (highly recommended), you will always be guaranteed a plethora of storytelling options, ideas for lore (being a writer, especially important), and chances to shape Europe in your image. But will you?
Needless to say, this is indeed a highly recommended title!

(Note: I've been playing this game directly on Glyph since very early beta, but just got it on Steam, so the "Time Played" amount listed above is not accurate.)
An online multiplayer turn-based tactical game isn't a genre you'd really expect to work that well, but somehow Atlas Reactor pulls off a miracle and merges these elements in such a natural and seamless way as to make you wonder why nobody's done anything like this before.
In some ways, it's a lot like a MOBA. There's an extensive list of heroes, which each fit into different roles, and you choose one to play. You're matched up into a team of four (or you can gather a group of friends to build a team of your own), and face off against an opposing team. Everybody has 20 seconds to enter their moves simultanious, and then you watch how they all resolve. The first team to get 5 kills wins.
The 20 second time limit and simultanious turn resolution keeps everything moving quickly despite being turn-based. It averages maybe 40 seconds total per turn, with no more than 20 turns per match. The 20 seconds is enough to keep you on your toes, but is almost always enough time if you're paying attention and know your powers.
One of the places where it breaks from most MOBAs is that it's very easy to learn all your powers and customization options. Every character has 5 powers, and each power has a set of modifers that can be applied to them to tweak them to your play style. These tweaks are applied between matches, so you have time to read them and choose properly, and when you initially pick a character is generally has some pretty reasonable defaults if you just want to jump into the game. You can also choose three extra powers, called "catalysts", which can be used once per match. The selection of available catalysts are the same for all characters. All of this together provides just enough customization to be interesting, while not being overwhelming.
The tactical system during a game is also brilliant. The turn is divided into 4 phases: prep, dash, attack and move. Every power triggers on one of the first three phases. Prep powers tend to be buffs or traps (or sometimes debuffs). Dash powers tend to be powers that involve some amount of special movement. Attack phase powers can be anything, but are most often attacks. The movement phase is when you do movement.
This means much of the tactics is about predicting what the enemy will do. For instance, if you choose an attack power on them, and they dash out of the attack's area, the attack will miss. Unless you can correctly predict where they're dashing to, and attack that position instead. Or, you can use a prep power to lay down a trap that they'll hit with their dash. So much of playing this game effective is getting into the mind of your opponent and guessing what they'll do.
This is honestly one of the most solid competitive multiplayer games I've ever played. Highly recommended.

Edit #2: I've changed my review back to positive. This is due to two factors. One being that the player population has increased to a degree that the level of elitist toxicity has been greatly diluted. The second is that the developers have added integrated Discord functionality into the game, allowing easy access to coordinated team/group voice chat without having to use the Atlas Reactor Fan Discord.
The devs have really made something very unique and special with Atlas Reactor.
Edit: What I was hoping wouldn't happen to this game is already happening. In addition to the generally unpleasant behavior you can experience in any multiplayer game, the cliquish behavior of many of the most experienced players deserves special mention.
Throwing tantrums, throwing game matches, treating new players horribly, supporting all these behaviors as long as it is from someone in their clique. It's all just very ugly, and extends to the moderation on the official Discord server. The moderation being very lax on some people but unforgiving on others that aren't part of the usual crowd.
The situation is unfortunate, particularly since the population of the game is so small. There is no avoiding these people, as would be possible in a game with more players. So, the gameplay itself is still great, but I have finally found putting up with the increasing toxicity in a very small pool of players to not be worth it. Your mileage may vary.
.............................................................................................................................................
There's currently nothing else out there like Atlas Reactor. Other turn-based strategy PvP games are either card-based or are only 1v1 with each player controlling a whole team, such as Aerena or Banner Saga: Factions.
Even though the game is currently in Early Access, the base game play is rock solid. The 20-second duration of the decision phase creates a sense of urgency and tension and keeps match durations reasonable. You can sit down for a single-match bite-size play session of around 20 minutes.
The developers have been taking player feedback into account as they continue to build upon the solid foundation and have been making measured balance adjustments. Two new Freelancers and a new arena map have been added since Beta began and there are many more of both in the pipeline.
If you dig turn-based strategy games as well as team-based PvP then Atlas Reactor is all win. While also having zero P2W.

So this game has been an enormous favourite of mine for more than a decade now, I think, and before late 2013, I didn't even have the full version. If the shareware is the best game ever, what is the full version then? Well, it is a million times better. This package has the 20+ masterfully desinged levels of the original game, but also two extra episodes that are actually friggin great (instead of a complete butchery of all the things that made the base game good *cough* looking at you Quake 2). As good as Duke and Blood are, SW is the absolute undeniable and undisputed godgame of not only Build engine, but the entire genre of FPS.
Pros and Cons.
Cons.
Slightly wonky hitboxes on enemies. Otherwise there are no cons.
Pros.
Shadow Warrior has the greatest gameplay and control of any FPS game ever. Especially now since this Redux runs extremely smoothly and perfectly.
It has the greatest level design of the genre, ever. The levels are never maze-like or confusing, and they're packed with secrets that are fun to find and highly rewarding.
It has the greatest weapon and item selection in the history of games. Every gun and item has its use for different situations and enemies, none (except the smoke bomb) feel worthless, ever.
It has the greates ENEMY design of the entire genre, of all time. Every enemy feels like a threat and is capable of killing you, but none are overpowered or have cheap attacks you can't avoid with some master level ninja skills. They look great, they sound sick, and they're extremely varied. You also get some nice big boss ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s to deal with.
Speaking of sound, SW's sound effects, music and ambience are a huge part of the experience, being possibly the best in the entire genre. John Galt does amazing voice work as the protagonist Lo Wang, a man not to mess with, but one with a very immature sense of humor.
A masterful veteran like me can complete the game on "No pain no gain" mode without problems, but very much worth mentioning is also the fact that SW is always fair, even on the hardest difficulty. You will always be able to kill enemies without taking damage if you're quick enough, unlike in many other games, where hit-scanning enemies feel artificially tough and unfair. SW also very rarely spawns monsters right in front of your unexpecting face, which is how FPS games should be like. Even the SW reboot violates this rule with its stupid "arena fights" that are put into the game in a lack of better ideas for level design. I like the game, but compared to the original piece of art, it moves like a pregnant yak (to quote master Wang himself)

Probably not worth the full $20 price tag, but I thoroughly enjoyed it.  Watching the city buses smash into one another as the bridges fell apart was always worth a chuckle.
In simple construction mode it's possible to beat every mission in a single sitting (if you can dedicate most of a day off to that sort of thing).  This isn't a game you'll really go back to more than once or twice.
The user interface could also use a little work.  Sometimes you end up building pieces that don't quite touch and immediately fall apart once you start the simulation.  It's workable, but not great.
There's also one achievement that I think may be impossible in the game's current state.  The way a lot of people are achieving Wood Bridge Master is with a glitch.  I spent over an hour trying every design I could think of to no avail, but I never entered advanced construction mode either.  It may be possible, but I seriously doubt it.
As one reviewer noted, each simulation can yield different results.  If you get really close and don't want to redesign anything, you might be able to complete it by trying the simulation a few times.  I once had a bridge pass even though it was hanging by a thread after the final train went over it.

The S.T.A.L.K.E.R series will always be one of my favorite FPS's. The game is scary, fun, difficult (but in a good way), and, IMO, has the best atmosphere in a game I've ever experienced. You get a certain feeling when playing this game that is hard to find in others, it's a feeling hard to describe. It also has that Russian charm, with all the characters speaking in thick russian accents and living completely off of a diet of sausages and vodka. It's also got a lot of replayability.
In addition, the game also has one of the most devoted fanbases I have ever seen, right next to the Half-Life fanbase. Despite the last game (Call of Pripyat) being released way back in 2009, the fanbase still survives and even thrives off of fan films, a whole bunch of super well-made and extensive mods, art, MEMES, and users simply sharing the experiences they've had playing the game. I guarantee you'll be having a lot of fun with this game, even after you're done playing.
Oh, and did I mention mods? Boy, are you in for a treat when it comes to mods. S.T.A.L.K.E.R has an amazing modbase. Even now, mods are still being made. Call of Chernobyl, Misery, Autumn Aurora, and so many others, all free and made by professionals. There are also a whole lot of upcoming mods, including a multiplayer mod.
Sadly, the game suffers from Half Life syndrome. S.T.A.L.K.E.R 2 was in development but was quickly canceled due to a whole bunch of complex issues GSC Game World had to face. But GSC has made a comeback, having recently released Cossacks 3. So things are looking up for S.T.A.L.K.E.R!
So, yeah, you should totally get this game. Now get out of here, S.T.A.L.K.E.R.

Kentucky Route Zero is the most bewitching, intriguing, thought-provoking, and simply beautiful piece of interactive media I've come across in years. Many criticisms have been levelled against the protracted development time, which is both a weakness (unclear communication) and strength (opportunity to revisit, the release of interludes) of the episodic nature of the game. Now that 4 out of the 5 planned Acts have been released, it's a perfect time to pick it up and dig in. With the recent release of Act IV, it's clear how much care and detail has been put into each successive release - including a major revamping of the engine. Small choices and decisions from each Act carry through in unexpected ways, combining exponentially to create both subtle and major changes in each playthrough. The writing is simply great, too - probably the finest example of Telltale-style narrative choice out there. Every option you don't pick adds flavor to the world, its characters, and their motivations.
The game opens up a few times each Act, letting you explore the roads of Kentucky and the mysterious roads & rivers beneath it. Tons of hidden encounters and locations can be found in these parts, completely missable if you choose to rush through. Many places can be revisited, with some surprising changes to be found. It's really a joy to replay and uncover these secrets, choose different paths in conversations, pick up on new threads and connections each time. The game's themes of memory, loss, debt, place, identity...are really embedded everywhere you look. I get a kick out of all of the references and influences, too: historical, architectural, artistic, early poetic computation, stagecraft and set design - not pretentious, just added depth & flavor.
A Few Situations You Might Encounter Playing Kentucky Route Zero:
- Performing recorded found sounds at a theremin concert on a houseboat.
- Playing a text adventure simulating the creation of the archaic supercomputer you're playing it on.
- Picking mushrooms on an artificial island of cypress trees.
- Exploring a museum of domeciles, mostly inhabited.
- Touring a subterranean whiskey distillery underneath a church burial ground.

Despite my gushing, Warframe is not perfect. The new player experience is trying to say the least. And thats after several years of improvements.  If you have fun doing the tutorial stuff, or can at least see the potential in the game, please use the in game chat options to find help whenever you get stuck. I havent done too much of a deep dive into the PC community, but if its anything like the PS4 community for the game, will be just as friendly and supportive of new players,  having had to deal with the new player experience themselves. Keep an open Wiki on hand as well, you'll need it. Also, despite the myriad bug fixes present in each update, there are still a pretty large number of bugs in the game, mostly annoyances, nothing game breaking or progress negating. The Plains of Eidolon update is hugely ambitious, and just a little undercooked in my opinion. The game tries to funnel you, the new player, to this area ASAP, but seems to limit the amount of things that are doable at lower level. Conversely, the rewards dont really seem good enough to attract more accomplished players to participate. It also included a rework of the much maligned 'Focus' system of progression.
But thats another of Warframes fails: systems placed on systems bolted onto systems. Its not THAT bad, but it gets a little cumbersome keeping track of it all, especially if youve taken an extended break from the game; you may feel lost upon return.
Still, an immensely fun, rewarding excperience that should at least be sampled if youve any interest in Destiny, or the soon to be new kid on the block: Anthem. Which looks to have 'borrowed' quite liberally from many of warframes core ideas, but thats another story....

Why people love this game so much is beyond me!
Everything bad that can happen, when a series of PC-games sets foot on console-territory for the first time, actually happens here. To see that, you only need to compare it to its own prequel, Morrowind. In nearly every category, except the technical ones, it’s a regression.
The main problem for me is the gameworld: outside of the cities, it feels and looks more like generated by a computer than handcrafted by a designer. This is even worse in the dungeons. There are a few kinds of them like elven ruins, abandoned strongholds or natural caverns, but in their kind, they all look the same. Also, most of the time they are filled only with random enemies and random loot. Exploring them is pointless because of that. Wherever you go, you won’t find anything unique. All this and the very „clean“ graphical style leads to a lifeless, sterile, generic and random world. It is by far the worst open world I ever saw in a game.
This is NOT a matter of personal taste, this is a simple immersion-killing fact! But nobody gives a damn.
The other big problem here is the Level-Scaling-System: wherever you go, you will only meet opponents that are adjusted to your current level. Always! This means, that there are neither high-level-regions where you are completely lost at the beginning, nor enemies, that your hero crushes between his thumb and index finger later in the game.  Your hero gets stronger on paper, but you simply don’t feel it.
This is a very big flaw and it also kills the immersion! But again, nobody gives a damn.
There is a long list of other, smaller problems, but I will leave them out, because they are not gamebreaking for me or they are just peculiarities of the TES-series, that will – like war – never change. ;)
This site goes into detail:
There is exactly 1 positive thing, I can say about Oblivion: It has a good overall quest-design.
That’s it!
There is one word, I already used earlier in this review, which sums it up and perfectly describes Oblivion:
RANDOM!
You are walking through a random world, exploring random dungeons, fighting random enemies, picking up random loot. Not to forget the random main storyline! The randomness of this game surpasses every Open-World-RPG I ever played in my life. And that were much. For the biggest part, Oblivion is soulless and made without love.
Why people don’t see this, or why they don’t care, is something I will never understand!

If you have an electric guitar laying around and wouldn't mind learning how to play, this is a great way to start.
I've been teaching myself for about five years now and purchased Rocksmith on the grounds of learning some songs I have a hard time finding tabs for online. Though I wanted to jump to the hardest difficulty to get a 100% accurate tab instead of every other note in a song, the game insists on taking it easy and adding difficulty as you play along and presumably get better.
I'm a bit stubborn so I was a little unsure about this at first- but this is how improvements are made. You PRACTICE. So as I played, I noticed songs gradually start adding more notes as opposed to the simple starting fragments. This system works great. There's also tons of little games to sharpen certain skills.
The best feature in my book, strangely enough, became the settings for all the amps. As the owner of an amp with just-alright sound settings, having a ton of new sounds and effects to work with was awesome. I have actually found myself: plugging the guitar into my computer to fire up the game, selecting an in-game amp setting, then plugging my headphone jack into the aux. on my amp, and using Rocksmith as my new amp at the volume of my real amp.
Rocksmith is a valuable asset for someone who already plays guitar as well as those interested in giving it a go. Give it a try!

Atlas Reactor was a godsend to me. I love video games, especially games like LoL, but they're always just a smidge too fast for my reaction time. I excell at games where I can take just a second to think before I make a choice, and Reactor has mastered this in the best way possible. Simultaneous turns! Not only does it give you a window of time to calculate a move, think about what your opponent is doing, and try to predict their dash/move phase, it keeps the game moving at a still rapid pace. This takes a lot of the mechanical skill of moving your fingers lightning speed away, and increases the ability to play a good head game. Like a very fancy game of chess.
The characters are diverse, no two are exactly the same. Every role (support, frontline, firepower) are all very fun to play. Normally I shy away from support/tank roles, favoring DPS, but each character has a way to be a firecracker. The art is stylized in a very fun and interesting way, and the voice acting is on fleek.
The future is bright for this game. Log in, try it out, and stay for a wild ride.

Fantastic and unique Online Multiplayer game. Has a handful of modes, though I tend to play TDM and Conquest. (There's also DM, and some sort of Tag.... maybe another mode I'm forgetting).
The gameplay is pretty straight-forward and simple, Drive around shoot people. You have a secondary fire and primary fire. There is one type of pick-up the fully replenishes both.  There's also Health and a type of Over-Shield pick-up.  There's a red rocket pick-up but I'm still not entirely clear on what it does. Simple fun gameplay.
Where it gets interesting is customization. You earn points as you play , (always at least one point for participation per match, and then points for Kills, and base captures in certain modes, as well as points for the winner/ winning team).  I find you earn points at a very good rate, generous. You then use the points to buy new parts that change your tank in really fun ways I find.
But there are countless parts so even with generous points it'll take a while to unlock them all. There are various types of "Propulsions" , Chassis, Turrets, Main Weapons and Support weapons. The propulsions alone have several types , each with 3 weight classes that determine speed and armor. Legs that stick to walls and ceilings so you can climb around, Hoverpads that let you drive on water (both of these let you strafe (with Q and E).  Then there's tank treads that can't strafe but still let you turn on a dime, and wheels for speed but no dime-turning.
The weights vary in armor greatly, as well as speed. I never found an opponent way too armored up for me (a light fast tank) to kill. But in those scenarios I did have to use my speed to gain advantageous positions and avoid their attacks.
I could go into more but I feel like this sums it up. Its simple, but creative and fun. I am having a blast playing it. And have yet to figure out how they make money in the game (???)

First time I encountered a bridge building game was back in the time when Pontifex and later Bridge Construction Set came out. Messing with physics was intriguing even though the game stressed out my old hardware beyond its limits. Looong did I hope that a modern version of such game would appear and there Bridge Project hit the target. After all, it's the same developer. They've gone up with the size from 32 MB (Pontifex) to 511 MB (Bridge Project). New maps to play, more decent graphics, perhaps a bit more casual feel to it but still, the essense is there.
The basic interface is simple. Select the material to use, click on a joint and draw the piece where you want it to be. Simple mode helps you out quite a lot adding blocks, mirroring blocks and adding cross beams to support the structure. You can get far with it and be happy to see how the vehicles cross your newly built bridge.
However, the most facinating part of the game is to scrap the simple mode and go expert. How far can you strip down the bridge and make it withstand the stress from the vehicles without it falling apart? To build a bridge with least number of elements, as light as possible, and with lowest budget is where you compete with yourself and globally with other players. The game has in-built global leaderboards where you can check out how well the best ones have done it.
And this is where the interface gets in the way of the fun. You use the mouse to control pretty much everything (in addition to some keyboard shortcut keys). The left mouse button is for selecting and building, the middle button lets you dolly the camera, zoom works with mouse scroll, and the right button is for turning the camera and selecting the items for deletion.
Unfortunately the last one simply doesn't seem to have any logic to it. The mouse pointer, humangous arrow, seems to be little off at all times. And despite of which item is highlighted on screen when mouse pointer is on it, the right click either selects another item or it simply turns the camera! Why?!? Why can't I select an item with LMB and then hit delete key from keyboard? That's how every other software works. No, here you need to find a specific spot of an item somewhere and then right click on it and select delete option. More often than not I was unable to find the correct spot and I ended up restarting the map instead. The cables seemed to be the worst. Using the separate select mode makes selection much easier and then even the delete key works. But why is it a separate mode? Fortunately space bar is the shortcut.
The game is fun and it'll keep me playing it trying to best myself over and over again. If you're into semi-realistic physics simulation and construction then you probably will like the game. However, if you're easily irritated by cloggy interface then I'd recommend testing the game before purchase. Chronic Logic offers a free demo on their website with limited number of maps to try it out.

I won't bother to play the 5th episode... if it ever comes out. I'm putting this in my steam category reserved for games to never look at again. Along side several permanently broken and forgotten titles, some kickstarters that were never finished, but released anyways, and the Worms series.

I would firmly recommend this game to anyone who wants to beef up their skills with the actual physical card game. If you're looking for a quick way to get familiar with cards and strategies, there's none better than jumping into the deep end with this game. By the time you've played through a few campaigns, you'll have gotten an excellent feeling for the "flow" of the game and you'll bust through your RL games with no problems.
But avoid the hard campaign mode, for god's sake. What turned out to be difficult missions in the normal difficulty setting mutate into unwinnable nightmares. Just about the only way you can win some of them requires the hand of god to descend from heaven and bless your chances of turning up the precise cards you need, whilst sabotaging the AI opponent at the same time.
Why, let's start a match off. Terrific, I start with two vipers and one scout and can't buy jack while the AI strolls into the trade row with pocketloads of money. Oh, you really needed that card there? Well guess what, the AI is forcing you to discard one of your scouts and now you can't afford it. Oh great, the AI just bought that card to MOCK you. Now it's discarding its own cards and buying EVERYTHING you wanted. Phew, the cards just got freshly reshuffled, perfect and clean.... God damnit, all the ones you need to use NOW are at the bottom! Oh no, now the computer is synergizing... sweet mother of god, the synergizing... and by the time you're even remotely close to a hair's breadth of winning, the AI grabs you by your skull and piles on thirteen thousand damage points and you're throwing your computer against the wall.

Guitar Hero Who? Man, this game blows that out of the water. Want to really learn how to play guitar? This is the real deal. And for $10...what a steal! You still have to have a real guitar and pick and you have to get the USB cable to plug into your guitar...but man! what a great learning tool.
I already knew some chords and songs, so picking this up didn't have a huge learning curve. But if you've never picked up a guitar before, this might be a bit of a challenge. But the payoff is, you will learn how to really play the songs in the game and real chords and progressions that you can use to train your fingers to play many other songs.
The real beauty of this game though come in 2 forms. The first, is that it turns your computer into an amp. As you progress through the game, you earn amps, guitars, and effects pedals. Then, when you just want to practice outside of the journey or mini-games, you have multiple effects and amps to tweak your sound.
The second, and most important, is that this game adjust the difficulty in REAL TIME! It is awesome. It senses, mid-song, if you are struggling, and then tones down the difficulty. And, if you are doing well, it slowly increases the difficulty while you are in the middle of playing. If it senses that it bumped up the difficulty too much, it takes it down a notch. Watching this happen mid-song makes what could be a frustrating experience into a very satisfying one. Some songs have easier riffs than others, and to be rewarded for your effort is awesome.
Pick this game up and then go look at the library for some DLC. I have added 2 songs to my list of songs from the DLC, and it makes the game that more fun to be able to play along with songs I really enjoy.

Undoubtedly, the BEST Paradox game out there. If you are interested in trying this genre, CK2 is the best place to start. Granted, I think the whole world owns this by now (given the frequent sales) but in the off-chance you don't, ignore every baby who complains about DLC. The devs released a full-fledged game, period. They then released DLCs to enhance the game. If you want them, buy them; if not, you don't have to. I own most of them, because I love the game (hence the high hours, most of which were offline and not recorded so double or triple my current hour count).
Pros+
Alternate History - Ever wondered what it would be like to restore the Roman Empire? Or, what if William the Conqueror had failed? This game allows for almost any imagining of what might have been.
Complex diplomatic/economic system - I honestly can't think of a comparison for the diplomacy or economics. There are a LOT of factors that influence both and decisions can be costly.
Story - Who would have thought that constructing a story around a made-up person would be so much fun? Or that there would be any sort of buy-in for an inbred, dwarf ruling over England? At times it's hilarious; at others maddening as you watch your hard-fought gains taken away by luck or genetics. Love it!
Cons-
There aren't any; maybe graphics, but if you're into this type of game you already knew that.
BUY THIS GAME!!! Buy the DLC if you want it, but don't post something here bashing them for caring about paying themselves and doing extra work on the game. That's pure stupidity.
