I have been looking for an "old school" RPG for a long time along the lines of Baldur's Gate.
This game reminds me of what I fondly remember those games to be. The games I used to play weren't as good as this, so I must be getting senile in my dotage.
Pro:
Character Creation. This is the first time I really wanted to play a non-human character. In older games you would get the same old Tolkien-esque non humans to choose from that in the end were just humans with different stat caps. The non-human characters in Divinity 2 actually give a whole other way to roleplay your campaign; from special abilities that shall we say, might be a little too gastronomically challenging for squeamish players to ones that add a delightfully morbid sense of humor to the game. Time to break out of our "humans only" team leader habits.
Tutorial. The first third (or so) of the game can be considered a tutorial for how to maximize your party's effectiveness. Much better than simply throwing you in a training room and showing the basic button clicks to make a fight happen.
Graphics/Art. I'm usually not overly concerned with every game having absolutely jaw dropping graphics to be entertaining. That being said, Divinity 2 is gorgeous. The attention to artistic detail has led me to walk into more than one trap while admiring the art on the walls.
Story. I'm not going to go into a great level of detail here, I want you to discover the story yourself. What you get however manages to balance what we expect from a fantasy RPG while adding new elements that keep you guessing whether you really are the hero or not.
Side Quests. Plenty to do there to take up all of your free time. One feature I really enjoyed is that there isn't always a good solution, and that solution might have repercussions down the road you did not expect. No Mass Effect Paragon system here folks.
Cons:
Learning curve. After the tutorial adventure the difficulty can seem to ramp up very quickly, I found this to be primarily due to the sheer amount of customizability you have available to you. Be patient, save often.
Pathing. Sometimes your party does not like you and wants to go sightseeing when you are clicking on the next objective. Keep an eye on where they are going.
Divinity 2 is a fantastic game that shows you don't have to go to the AAA publishers to have a memorable experience. Give it a try and gnaw on a couple of dismembered arms for me.

Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is an excellent game with a few things you need to keep in mind.
The game itself:
If you're sick and tired of the generic-as-hell First Person Shooter with bland mechanics, why not try a first person game that focuses on melee combat and some archery instead? Wanna play a game with gritty, gory melee action? You're all set. Different game modes? You're all set. A game that requires skill? You're all set, to some degree.
The gameplay is very fun and enjoyable. It gives you the gritty, gory combat you would expect from a game like this which should leave you satisfied. You can slice off people's heads with the sheer power of a zweihander. You can smash people's faces like a watermelon with a maul, or if you're one of those annoying♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥who like to get on a melee fighter's nerves, you can frustrate the living♥♥♥♥♥♥outta them with archery.
There are three melee classes and only one archer class. Melee classes are: vanguard, knight, and man-at-arms. The vanguard may very well be the most common class on this game, most often played by people who either were too awful at the game to learn the mechanics of the other two classes, or by skilled players who like to make use of long range weapons. The vanguard hits like a truck, provides decent armor, has decent mobility, and has long range melee weapons. You can see why he is the most common melee class used on this game.
Of course, if you want to apply more skill in this game, there's always the knight!*cough cough* ballerina dancing with mauls *cough cough*
Basically, the knight is used by players who, for the most part, prefer a class that can take the most hits. He also has weapons which are very effected and very high damage, but they require more skill. People who use the knight as their main class of choice want a more complex playstyle. Other types of players who use the knight are the dimwitted dip♥♥♥♥♥ who think that the most authentic, realistic method of fighting involves bringing a messer or maul and spinning it around from awkward angles like a complete retard. Knights take tons of damage, but tend to be fat asses and are slow as a result. Their weapons aren't ranged like the vanguards, so they have to close the distance a bit.
Then there's the man at arms, the class with the second-weakest armor (very weak, but no as weak as the archer), but also possessing very fast speed and quick, short-range weapons. People who use the man at arms are either masters at melee, or clueless dip♥♥♥♥♥ who don't know how to use his full potential. This is the melee class that is the most difficult to learn (which is why I don't play as him), but when mastered, chances are you will curb-stomp the other classes. This is because people who know how to use the man-at-arms know that his main purpose is to be an extremely annoying piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥that you somehow can't hit no matter how hard you try, and when he hits you, he does it when you least expect it. That's how you play as this class. Either that, or you can use this class how most people, including me, use him, which is just running around your opponent, hoping to dodge him, but then you somehow run into a sword and get yourself pwned.
The last class, which is hated by all Chivalry players who only use melee, is the archer. He has the weakest armor and can get killed in one hit by a powerful weapon, so you'd probably think he'd be the puniest class (which he is), but he's not as harmless as you'd think. An archer's ranged weapons include crossbows and javelins, to name a few. Archers have earned their reputation as extremely annoying ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s by attacking melee fighters who are caught in a fight with another meleer. They also attack meleers from behind, where they least expect them, or they camp in secluded areas, waiting for an unexpecting meleer to jump in their trap. Their ranged weapons are very powerful. Now, you might think you could beat the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of an archer in melee (which is mostly true), but keep in mind that skilled players can use the archer's melee similar to a man at arms, which is by using footwork and forcing the player to hesitate.
So yeah, that's basically the combat gameplay right there, but now on to the cons!
The cons:
1) If you thought that the combat on this game would be simple and straight forward, think again. Chivalry is a game where fighters can twist their spines around like pretzels (without any injury at all), spin around, and land a hit on you, even when you thought you perfectly blocked that strike. Is it annoying? Yes, but most of the people who have played this game a long time do it. The people who have 1,000+ hours on this game are, for the most part, going to use strikes from awkward angles to kill you in seconds. You would think you'd be able to block them, even when you saw how slow the strike was, but think again. Players who fight like this know the combat animations very well, and they are able to predict the weapon's range of damage. It doesn't matter if you think moves like these would be realistically impossible, because the game mechanics don't give two flying ♥♥♥♥♥ about realism.
2) As mentioned before, blocking tends to be useless when you need it against players who fight in such a strange way.
3) The Chivalry community tends to get whiny and ♥♥♥♥♥y about these things called feints. You see, on Chivalry, being able to use dragging, ballerina dancing, and a bunch of other bat♥♥♥♥♥♥crazy moves that allow the player to hit you from odd angles, therefore rendering your blocks useless, is something that is considered the norm. If you use feints, which are meant to trick a player into thinking you're going to strike them with a specific move, allowing you to disrupt their blocking rythm and use a completely different strike when they're open, then you will be seen as a heretic among the community for exploiting the game mechanics. Yes my friend, that's right! People will start whining about how big of a scrub you are for using feints, and they are the very people who exploit the game's combat animations to land hits that completely ignore your parries.
Dragging the mouse to slow down attacks or speed them up to hit your opponent? Good. Feinting to hit your opponent? Bad. I don't get why it is that way since feinting is a means to the same end.
With all that aside, the game is still pretty awesome.

This game could actually be decent if work would be put into this, more work than already put in. The game is very glitchy, but it does have the potential to be a good $5 shooter game that people would actually play. If the creator wouldnt make this too much as a joke it would be decent.
Here are a few flaws that could be fixed fairly simply:
The double jumping mechanic:
This mechanic of the game is very glitchy. The double jumping is a good idea, it is just that if you hold shift while double jumping and you move in a certain direction, it may have the chance of zooming you across the map. Doing so leads to another problem:
Unfair fall damage:
Fall damage honestly shouldn't be in this game, it would honestly be much more enjoyable to play if fall damage was not a factor into playing the game. Many times I find myself double jumping, then proceed to falling and loosing about 25 HP, even though the height difference from me jumping to landing is very minimal.
Water:
There is no swimming in this game. Water is literally just a texture. You can jump in to the water, though there will be no signs that you actually are in the water, just simpally getting rid of fall damage in the water and make you a bit slower would actually make water useful.
The Glitches (Maps mostly):
The maps have some flaws, incliding getting trapped and random places, having odd hitboxes, weird fall damage (already covered), and etc. These can be fixed by overall smoothing the map, but I am no game designer so I honestly wouldn't really know how. The other glitch is the buildings, they can with the double jump mechanic be sent into, and you are just in the building. This is similar to the Minecraft X-Ray exploit where if you put a block over your head, you can see ores and such. I dont know if that still exists, I haven't played minecraft in a few years. But having houses and doors that can be opened to have access to the houses would be nice.
This may sound like I am complaining about the whole game, but the creator of this has the right idea into making a decent amount of money with it. This game may sound like a joke: "Noob Squad", but as I have said many times now, this game DOES have potential. For that I will reccomded this game in hopes that the creator will fix these glitches that I have pointed out so the game can be more enjoyable to play.
NOTE: I did not pay for this game, my friend gifted it to me, but personally, I feel that it is worth a dollar.

The first thing I can say is that the game uses a simple concept, and has very interesting details.
The real reason I really enjoyed playing this game is that the execution is spot on when it comes to all little things.
The main mechanic of the game consists of combat phases. This RPG style mechanic allows players to plan one (or more) actions to be executed during the turn and a move. The sequence of execution is particularly clear (Prep , Dash, Blast and Move). This simple mechanic allows for a lot of depth in the gameplay as it introduces the notion of outplay.
Prediction is as important as your actions in this game, which is what makes it an interesting game (and the execution is spot on, allowing for serious outplay and bluffs).
The idea of a simultaneous turns makes the game pace particularly not slow as one would expect. The "decition" phase, where you plan your move, is pretty on point with the 20s timer and the resolution phase (spectating the outcome of the turn) is also very well executed that it is entertaining to watch.
And here is where the details come to play, the freelancers (heroes/champions) all have quotes that mesh in really nice to add this interesting spectating feel.
The "taunt" mechanic is an example of the good little mechanics that are executed quite nicely. A taunt allows you to decide to play a short clip for everyone (friendlies and enemies) before you execute the ability for that turn (taunts are associated with abilities). Taunts act as a stylish bragging/confidence boost for instance taunting a prediction attack before it is executed adds much style to the basic mechanic. It is always nice to see someone taunt and miss their ability though. This adds a new dimension to the player.
There are other basic mechanics like cover/last seen but those are best found out after playing for a while and add some depth to the game.
Lastly, regarding the B2P model, I think the game is worth the money invested, very solid concept, splendid execution and most of the things can be crafted in game for no extra money.
TL;DR Great concept, perfect execution, worth the price tag. Interesting little perks and mechanics that add depth. Kept me playing for the entire time I have been trying it out, which is not very often for most games I play (and I played most MOBAs and MMOs and a lot of RPG and RTS games).
No excuses for bad latency, and you start outplaying from the very first turn.

In an age where turn-based games live in the shadows of the MOBA scene, Atlas Reactor proves they can make a comeback. That does mean, however, that you cannot undo actions like you could in normal JRPG's- but I feel this adds more to the strategic side of the game and becomes one of its strengths. I don't have many friends.. well I don't have many friends.. but I don't have friends who are into this type of game, but boy do they love to watch the gameplay. I was hesitant to pick up the game once it turned from F2P to P2P until I realized there really is no other game out there quite like this one. Will I enjoy it? Hell yeah. Is it a MOBA-killer? Not exactly. Is there room for improvement? Always- but that's what I'm most excited for, to see what else is in store for this game!

You can also change up the rules a bit to put a spin on the mayhem by customizing item drops, increasing the top speed, or running the courses in reverse for example.
With smooth gameplay, catchy music, and simple cartoony graphics, Speedrunners is definitely a must-have game for any fan of fast-paced side-scrolling platformers or anyone who enjoys competitive games in general. An outstanding example of a game that is easy to learn, but will take time to master.

The niche but well-regarded JRPG title, once exclusive to Japan, was finally ported and localized in the US in the form of a PSP release by XSEED games. It told the story of Estelle Bright and her adopted borther Joshua, as the two sought to become full time bracers as well as uncovering a mysterious conspiracy that would send their kingdom into chaos. The sequel to Trails in The Sky, SC(Second Chapter), after years of waiting and an additional year long delay, had had many fans hungry for a continuation of the story; a burning desire to return to its immersive world,  and the incredibly charming old-school RPG gameplay surrounding it. SC finally arrived in 2015 of October for PSP, Vita, and PC for digital download. It is a awesome and satisfying sequel to the first chapter. One thing I was disappointed about SC was that it takes place mostly in Liberl (again), and it felt repetitive to revissit the same places over again, just with replaced dialogue and cutscenes. But it didnt worry me too much, as the game does the most with what recycled resources there are.
Speaking of dialogue, this is perhaps my favorite part of the game: XSEED's awesome localization of the script. I dont know if the characters actually spoke like this in the original Japanese, but the way they speak in English is chock full of personality, quirkiness, and humor. The English version does a fantastic job of making each character's personality distinct. Just through their dialogue alone you could tell which character is which without looking at their portrait. Credit goes to both Andrew Dice and Jessica Chavez (and other people probably whose names arent mentioned), for pouring hundreds of hours translating the massive gigantic story. Trust me, this game is GIGANTIC.
To go off on a short tangent here, XSEED is a small but passionate Japanese localization company that does its best to bring awesome but not very well known franchises outside Japan to overshore. Because of the low sales of the games they localize, they are financially shaky. Not to mention they are translating the Legend of Heroes series' giant amounts of dialogue with little financial benefit in the end. I can not say this enough. PLEASE support the official releases of these titles in North America or elsewhere. We want XSEED to get credit where it's due. They are a tiny company but passionate about what they do, and they deserve whatever rewards they can muster. It's because of them we get to play this gorgeous series in English, with awesome personality-filled dialogue.
Trails in the Sky SC has an awesome story. Though a little on the cliche side, you will fall in love with almost every character. Gameplay allows for very personal customization options suited to your preferred playstyle for each character. It's fun immerse yourself in the world and go exploring. It's everything the traiditonal RPG purist or casual player will have fun with. Would I reccomend this game? Yes.

I'd leave a little summary of the plot, but the game does it so much better than I can ever do. Get. This. Game. And. Beat. It. This experience has been the metaphorical gold of Japanese Role-Playing Games.

Overall, Crusader Kings 2 is a pretty good game, and I would recommend it to anyone who is considering buying it. To give you some information about the game's strengths and weaknesses, I have written a list of some pros and cons of the game. I didn't cover everything (that list would be much longer), but these are a few I consider important when looking at CK2.
PROS:
1. There are so many mods for CK2, and most of them add something interesting or alter something in the base game that improves the gameplay.
2. With all expansion packs installed, you have a lot of options when it comes to things such as creating characters and playing the characters offered to you by the game.
3. The artwork is pretty good. During the loading screen, for example, the artwork, which are pictures that look like the colored windows in churches, fits the game's time period and tone.
4. It is fairly easy to mod the game yourself. I won't go into detail here, but simply put, all you have to do is copy files and folders, and change text (most of the time, anyways).
CONS:
1. When you try to use a mod, you might have to change the game version, or it won't work, as some mod creators aren't able to or don't keep up with game updates.
2. In order to get the full experience, you have to buy the dlcs, or your range of playable time periods and characters will be limited.
3. When it comes to modding the game, you have to be careful, as tiny errors can cause major problems, and might render the game unplayable.

200 hours later and I feel that I have to review this game.
In general, I enjoy stories with crazy twists and things going to places where I do not expect. Case in point: Novels like 9 Hours 9 Persons 9 Doors and Danganronpa 2, while they're not JRPG's definitely fulfill the crazy story criteria, and I love them.
Every now and then, I enjoy indulging in some generic "tropey" storytelling, as long as the execution is interesting enough for me to care. This is Trails in the Sky. This is also the moment that I'm telling you to start with the first game in case you're interested, simply because First Chapter and Second Chapter are one story, the Estelle & Joshua arc. Also, in case you played the first game and you didn't liked the story, you shouldn't really bother with the second. Contrary to the fans' belief, while the story does get better it doesn't get less generic and tropey, so if those points were your turn-off for the first game they will be your turn-off for the second one too.
Gameplay-wise here's what you'll expect: Turn-based combat, a magic system kinda similar to how FF7 materia work (you link Quartz together to use spells and you slot them in a certain way on an Orbment - the device where you place Quartz on - to use spells you couldn't use before), no random encounters but you can see the enemy roaming and choose to approach from behind (preemptive attack) or avoid him altogether, grinding is possible but really unecessary and discouraged. The game is OK challenging in normal mode, hard as steel in Hard mode and "you gotta be batshit insane to play this" in Nightmare (it's what I'm currently doing).
Although I already mentioned story elements, it's worth noting that the game is text-heavy. I mean REALLY text-heavy. Here's a
to understand. Now, I'm not saying that more means that you'll like it. I'm saying that reading dialogues in JRPG games shouldn't be an issue for you.
Last, but not least, the music. Fans complained that the first chapter lacked in the music department, which I have to agree given the kind of soundtrack people in Falcom are
of
. And oh they did, the absolute madmen.
All in all, a solid game if you don't mind generic stories (I don't believe that generic is inherently bad but that's just me) and turn-based combat, coupled with "Falcom-tier" soundtrack. I'm giving it 2 thumbs up because I got exactly what I expected and 200 hours and 2 playthroughs later I'm still enjoying it.
Trails in the Sky the 3rd is scheduled to be released in the West for the first time around spring 2017. Just adding that up. Also, the games "Trails of Cold Steel" that are currently available for Playstation 3 and Vita are part of the same saga, but the stories aren't related.

The combat system is just really imballanced, and the only way they seem to be able to cause a real challenge is by making your skills and abilities not work, or simply turn fights in to a grind fest. You can almost be assured that when you are in any kind of harder monster or boss fight none of you crowd control and generally things like speed down do not work. Also some bosses have bull skills like being able to kill your or phase you out of existance even if you have full guard. Also just like the first game if you accidently activate an S-Skill there doesn’t seem to be a way to deactive it, you have to use it.
-There are times where things go way too long between being able to save.
- If you thought the ending of the first game was tough, you ain’t seen nothing. I’m not sure who thought several hours of grinding boss fights at the end was going to be fun. If I hadn’t put like 120 hours in to the two games combined I would have bailed a long time ago, and almost did.
- The game is just anti fun. Rather than provide a good vehicle to tell a story instead you are stuck in a time sucking grindfest. If they had cut out like half the game, it could have been amazing.
TLDR;
I love parts of this game just like the first. It has a lot of the same flare, humor, good writing and great characters.
Too much asset reuse, boring bad quests, bad pacing, and crazy design dessisons just make the game anti-fun. If you value you sanity, do not play. The payoff is not worth it.

The combat, environment, NPCs (both voice acting and design) are far less homogenized in Skyrim. HOWEVER, this game has some great qualities from both. It has the RPG-style of Morrowind with the accessability of Skyrim; the immersiveness of Morrowind and the NPC inaction of Skyrim. While it may not scratch the D&D itch Morrowind does or dynamic, cinematic fun of an action game, like Skyrim, it almost does both at the same time.
It speaks volumes that this game can be the mediocre middle child of the Elder Scrolls franchise and still be one of the best games ever made. I recommend it (just, maybe not if you have already gotten used to the RPG of Morrowind or the non-derpy faces of Skyrim).

There's definitely a reason I abandoned this style of game a long time ago.
For a beginning player dance games can be very unwelcoming and this is no exception. Starting menus and searching for a room or knowing where to go is complicated to say the least. It's unlikely to find players who are new or who are willing to play with a new user. However, you can create your own room and practice solo. The brief tutorial for the actual dances is minimal and doesn't really prepare you for the speed of reaction you have to have to do well. Games start out very slow and become so full of moves that you don't have time it seems to properly complete and one misclick will surely cause you to miss the move completely. There doesn't seem to be much at all here to do with actually keeping time, rather it's just a matter of speed and accuracy.
Aside from this the game is simply dated. The graphics and art style have not held up well, but that is relatively expected from a game approaching 12 years since it's initial release. Character models are somewhere between chibi and manga style antimations. Initial character creation is very limited so don't expect a beautiful character straight from the beginning. That's not to say that there aren't items for customization later on, though.
Finally, the playerbase for this game seems to be severely lacking. Although I tried to find a game where players were actually at the game most were either completely silent and nonresponsive even when the room was full and waiting on them for start or there were heavy language barriers.
Overall, I can't recommend this game to a new player. I downloaded it because I remembered playing years ago and enjoying it but it just doesn't seem to have held up well over the years. If you're set on playing Audition Online my strongest advice to you would be to start the game with one (or a group) of your friends. Learn the game together and enjoy it with reliable active players. The game mechanics seem to all still function so going into the game with a group of people you know may be the key to finding something valuable in this game.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Call of Pripyat is more than simply a computer game, it's an experience. Never have I played anything more immersive and atmospheric than this to the point where I would not be surprised if you will begin to feel "The Zone" is an actual place. What is scary and perhaps even fascinating here, it nearly was. Had things just turned out differently on that faithful day back in 1986 Ukraine.
There is also still many areas, despite its age where this game put others to shame to this day. Where many other big budget titles have "suvival modes" or "survial aspects" about them this game actually doesn't kid around as it provides real and hard challenge. The Zone his a harsh and brutal place, yet rarely unfair. Another thing that definitely deserves mention here is the super realistic lighting system used in the game, both during day and night. With excellently beautiful god rays caressing the landscape during dawn and dusk, neither does it not shy away from as potraying shadows as truly dark. This, in combination with the dynamic weather system that has never been truly replicated anywhere else puts it in a league of its own.
Call of Pripyat is truly one of those gems where once you get in to it, you'll never want it to end and thanks to an excellent selection of user created mods "I Work Alone" or "Misery" with even more interesting projects in the works by the passionate community. Perhaps it doesn't have to.

The Good:
Its a fun Sonic Game.  If you played Sonic in the 90s then you should pick this up for the feels regardless of the cons that I will discuss below.  The music is amazing and the stages run around 5-7 mins a pop and are well designed.  If you aren't a Sonic fan then this is a purchase that you may or may not regret.  $25 CAD is a bit expensive imo for this game when you can grab something like DOOM for the same price.
The Bad:
There are a few bugs in the game.  In my playthrough, I died two times to two very different bugs, one being a soft lock and another where a piranha fish would latch onto me and I couldn't jump so I'd just drown with no chance to survive.  Hopefully these bugs get patched.  There were many documented on the console release via youtube and they are still present on the PC release after this two weak hiatus of waiting (not to patch the game, but to add DRM).  Bosses feel awkward in a sense that some are extremely easy and some are quite frustrating, the difficulty doesn't progress properly as some of the latter bosses are a joke meanwhile mid game bosses pose a challenge.  Aparently there is no controller support .... I have no idea how that happened but it's mind baffling!
The Ugly:
DENUVO has been found in the game.  I dont know if this effects performance or not since I do not own a console version however I have noticed at times some button presses are not responsive, however that may be intended or may be just me not use to playing Sonic on a Mechanical KB.  Overall, DENUVO is pi$$ing off the community (Lots of negative reviews) since we waited two weeks for SEGA to implement a DRM that will probably be cracked within 5 days.  It feels like SEGA took a giant $hit on the community and left a pi$$ stain for good measure.
Overall Verdict:
If bugs are fixed and DENUVO is removed like it should be (other game publlishers have removed it before), I'll give the game 9/10 and I will recommend it.
If bugs are not fixed and DENUVO remains, I would only recommend this game to Sonic Fans, otherwise, I do not recommend atm.
Lastly, if you are wondering:  Sonic&Knuckles w/ Sonic 3 attached > Sonic Mania.  I think the biggest gripe i have is that the latter part of the game kinda falls apart with regards to progression into a tangible story line.  The last stage doesn't feel right to me.  If some DLC is added to fix up some storyline then I can see SM=S&K3.

I'd always laughed at THOSE games. You know the ones. Guitar Hero, DJ Hero, Triangle Hero, Tamborine Hero, Kazoo Quest, etc etc. However a year ago I finally got up to date on the Donkey Kong rhythm platform game on the Gamecube. In this, you use bongos to control attacks, movement and jumping.. you really feel like a monkey, bashing away at those bongos.But anyway, that got me thinking how cool ACTUAL music is as a control/input/interface method for gaming. Then, I found out about this.
Unlike those lame Flute Quest Hero games, in this, you don't have a plastic flute or french horn or scratch turntable, but rather the actual musical equivalent. For this game, it is focused so far on guitar and bass. I am using a 7 string guitar, in a different  tuning to the game. My guitar was set up for this drop F tuning, so I was worried at first it might not like my guitar.. well, it wasn't an issue. There are stickers provided in the box that allow you to set the numbers of your frets via stickers on your guitar, so for me that was perfect, moving the frets up 2 spaces and ignoring my 7th/lowest string, I can play the game fine. Harmonics are a little tricky tho, but can always tune up for those tracks/parts..
In its essence, this is the best way to learn guitar. The best way for guitarists of any skill level to play along with other people's tunes, as well as for experienced guitarists to have a program with which to assess and further develop your existing skills.
The DLCs are great, a little bit of metal is available - Pantera, Lamb Of God and some oldies like Megadeath.. some indie rock like Pixies, but mostly this is about rock, new and classic.
There is a multiplayer aspect, but it's only local and you need to get two cables for it.. wondering if latency would increase due to extra guitar or bass input..
Also if you want to practice bass on a guitar, it has an octave pedal to 'emulate' bass on guitar. It's a pity there is no online multiplayer, but there is leaderboard scoring.
Not to mention there is an updated version RS2014 coming out in rOcktober, with support for different tunings (only found standard and drop D so far in the game).
There's a lot that could come to this game and a lot that is already in there so it's hard to describe everything. I dream of one day there being mod support for this title, or plugin/addon support by community producers. At the moment however there is a large range of DLC tunes you can purchase for $3.50 USD (in my region) each.. not a bad price to own a song, but also to have the tablature and a program to help you learn it :)
The latency is a bit of an issue at first, but once fiddling with the ini or game settings, you can get something reasonable.. seems to be somewhere around 30-200ms range depending on settings, but it can be worse if you don't follow the set up guides or have a cruddy PCI/PCI-E soundcard or a slow computer.
There's a lot to recommend about this game - support it and throw away any other music games you have that involve plastic. Why learn how to play a peace of plastic when you can play the real thing..
While it is harder to get into it, if you don't have an electric guitar or bass (obviously this is required for the game, but it doesn't mention it on the system requirements on the back, LOL!) it might be a bit of cost to buy one to play this.. but still, I think I would have learnt A LOT quicker when I started playing guitar 15 years ago, if I had've had this tool at my disposal then. The marketing is true - it IS the quickest and easiest way to learn guitar, I fully endorse that.
However if you are not sure guitar is for you, also if you are younger or have softer hands/skin, it might be worth starting out on a cheap nylon string acoustic before moving to steel string electric..

I know there must be a lot of people who appreciate this type of game and find it appealing from the get go but for me it has been nothing but grinding of teeth from the start. It's a text adventure with an abstract art to support the "narrative". If you enjoy poetry, going to modern art exhibitions and overall being "in and philosophical" with art world and have deep thoughts of how colour blue might taste like, this might be for you. In that case I also recommend movies like Mulholland Drive and Norwegian Wood. What comes to my personal tastes, these types of products just make me unreasonably angry. Yes I get the meaning behind symbolic meanings and "art is in beholders eye" I just don't agree they are good idea to have. Especially when it comes with cost of being a game.
I guess it comes down to having so few gameplay elements in it and being more of a interactive fiction. I never enjoyed walls of text, especially when I feel like it's absolutely meaningless what you do in the game and are just in for some weird art exhibition.
So far game has had few high points, but not nearly enough to survive past what can be described as computer demo-scene art from 90's.
/end of rant

Now, as with all games, there are pros and cons, so I'll go through a list with my pros and cons.
PROS:
-Great Story
-Amazing DLC (That includes all of it)
-Huge exploration factor
-A huge variety of enemies
-Better Dark Brotherhood and Thieve's Guild
-An amazing Mage's Guild quest line
-THE ARENA :D
-Tons upon tons of NPCs (and a lot of shops)
-A lot of great mods
-Becoming a Duke of Duchess in the Shivering Isles
CONS:
-Leveling system
-Horse Riding
-Guards will chase you to no end
-TROLLS
-Closing Oblivion Gates (I like doing this, but sometimes it does get annoying)
Don't let my playtime mislead you, by the way. I owned this game on the Xbox 360 and played at least 2 years worth of hours in it :D. Anyways, buying the game still rests in your hands. I cannot recommend this enough if you're into grand strategy like me.

As a big Twin Peaks fan, and a fan of most things the show has inspired, Kentucky Route Zero was on my radar for quite some time. I held off though because it was rumored to have been abandoned by the developers. Thankfully, that's not the case! 
There will be a total of 5 episodes and Episode 4 was just released this week. There was a long wait between Episodes 3 and 4, so long in fact that's why there are some recent negative reviews. With the advent of Episode 4, and the fact that it's currently 50% off, now is the perfect time to buy.
As far as the game itself, it has quickly become my favorite Point & Click game of all time. There is a lot of reading involved, but since the dialog is so clever and fascinating, it goes down like reading an excellent novel. The graphics are minimalistic, but the art style is unique; it's as gorgeous as any other game in my catalog. The minimalistic approach lets the player use their imagination to fill in the gaps in an already mysterious world.
Even when it's not on sale, the game is well worth every penny of the asking price. We can expect that Episode 5 won't take nearly as long to be released because the reasons for the prior delay are no longer factors. If you've been waiting for the perfect time to buy, DO IT NOW!

Atlas Reactor is definitely something different. It is confusing at first but each 'freelancer' has their own special unique abilities that really change up the game. There are three phrases in each round. Prep, which allows for freelancers to support and heal other allies, set traps etc. Dash which allows for freelances to latch onto enemies, or dash away from shots that will come in the blast phase. Blast which is where the majority of damage is lashed out with bombs and shots, and explosions and bites, etc.
Atlas Reactor has kept me busy during this free weekend with quick 15 minute games that I feel could be longer. The matchmaking system has some improving to do as I get matched up with some of the best players in the game when I am brand new and noobish. The sensation of hitting an enemy where you didn't think they would be is a great one too. Guessing is a big part of the game and the late-game is where the suspense is at its fullest.
I'd recommend it for $20. The other high-amount editions just include more skins so if you want to have those, you can. Can't wait to see when this game is completely finished.

Okay, so I wasn't really expecting this game to be really great when I got it. It was originally $20, but was on a 66% sale. I decided that I'd get it. It might be an entertaining puzzle game. Long answer short: it wasn't.
It isn't very entertaining. I mean, I guess it is what it says it is, but there isn't enough to it. There should be more creativity and imagination involved. There really isn't any. I was hoping that I would be able to build these large fancy bridges, but you only make simple ones.
The look of this game is only okay. The graphics look quite dated. It's not terrible, but it certainly isn't good. I'm also disappointed that it wasn't more entertaining to watch your bridge break. Instead, the pieces just detach and fall. There's no breaking apart, splintering, cracking, or whatever. All things considered, rather boring.
The controls are not the greatest either. Placing pieces is not very smooth. It feels like I'm playing an old game. Also, deleting a single piece is a pain. You right-click the piece to bring up the options for that piece (including deleting it), but most of the time, that menu doesn't show up.
My final complaint is the sound. First of all, the soundtrack sucks. I turned it off soon after I started the game. As for the other in-game sound, it sounds like I'm playing a game that's 20 years old. I'm not a game designer, but I'm pretty sure it is not that hard to have higher quality sounds for a game like this (which essentially consist of bridge-breaking noises, car horns, and annoying cheering). That reminds me, why did you find it necessary to add that stupid cheering after a car makes it across the bridge? This isn't a pre-school computer program.
Also, where is this workshop that it mentions? That was one of the reasons I got this. So that was also a disappointment. People probably could've added some interesting things to this game, but whatever.
Summary: This game is boring. There isn't enough creativity involved. The visuals are dated. The controls are not smooth enough when they work. The sound quality is awful. Overall, I would not even think about paying $20 for it. This game seems like it should be $5 dollars. The original price gave me a higher expectation, which it definitely did not come close to meeting.

This game was awesome when I first came into contact with it, from the vanilla game play to the mods that are supported and welcomed by the dev team, even so far as to have encorperated some of them into the updated versions of the game. It is awesome to see a game that is like that. With the promise of the games full release looming and the new content that is coming with that, I am excited about what the future of this game will be bringing.
About the game:
The building mechanics mirror many popular base building survival games; however, the building does come across as slightly more intuitive. The building can become tedious at times when there are too many surrounding or overlapping parts, but overall the building is easily a 7/10 in my opinion.
The graphics are amazing (if your computer can handle them), from the skin textures and the hair animations, to the clothing animations. The games graphics match every bit the standards that game are reaching these days and pushing them to their max.
The audio from battle music to ambient music is invigorating or relaxing depending on the area, the only thing that still needs a little work is the VOIP settings to more easily speak with others through the game. That being said, the way that voices interact with the environment around you (echoing off walls and such) is amazing.
I found the game to be fun, but some of the guns were too overpowered and the matchmaking was a little unfair. 10/10

After my first playthrough...
Play this game! I am serious, this was an amazing ride! I pumped about 4 hours into it so far through one playthrough, mainly because I wanted to explore, and I must say, those were my best 4 hours I spent with the little blue blur.
Sonic feels amazing to control, his movement is smooth and easy to direct and control, and although he might take a bit to slow down with no direct input, this can be resolved by holding the opposide direction, which is enjoyable to do. The level design takes direct advantage of Sonic's physics and controls and creates level design which rewards speed and quick action with extra goodies, to help you along, such as the super amazing shields. While there are no new shields, the fire shield, bubble shield, and eletric shield return in their full glory, each of their powers even providing useful level gimmics, such as the fire shield able to burn down certain objects for example. Some people have complained about instant death traps, but I honestly never found any that I could not easily avoid.
Each zone is bright and colorful, and this game is absolutely amazing. Incredible how a 2d retro-inspired game trumps big budget crap you commonly see shoved in your face these days. Unlike the baren, boring, ugly wargrounds of 3D monolith francises, Sonic Mania's zones are packed with color and detail. The animation is silky smooth, an aspect shared by the framerate, which stays at a constant 60fps even on my crappy computer, and each act looks a little bit diffrent, and I love this.
Just for the base game alone, no extras or anything else, buy and play this game. Everything about it is amazing, from gameplay, art, and music, it's a masterpiece. And I did not even mention the bonuses, but I'll leave this for you to find out.
Edit after longer play session: In my opinion, Sonic Mania still holds up. Yes, it may have a few problems here and there, such as some of the Blue Sphere stages being way too hard for their own good and it being hard to predict how Sonic will react to certain objects first time, but I still find it an enjoyable exprience. Is it better than Sonic 3? No, but it's pretty darn close, a little better than Sonic 2. Since the Winter Steam Sale might be coming... probably a good idea to pick up a copy of this, you won't regret it, if you like Sonic that is. If you don't... why are you here?

Kentucky Route Zero is truly the epitome of the quote "Every Frame a Painting". Beautiful, sad and thought-provoking, it's the kind of game you end up sitting in silence and thinking about long after you've finished playing. If you're anything like me you'll probably be screenshotting your way through your playthrough every chance you get; the cinematography and use of colour is just gorgeous and every move the camera makes works to frame the game's subjects in the most gorgeous and cinematic fashion possible (much like Shadow of the Colossus does)*. The attention to detail in the storytelling is simply breathtaking and the humour and references to media/information theory are v clever in their implementation (see: the Shannon-Weaver model).
If you enjoy stageplays, quietly weird fiction, and slow, thoughtful and intelligent storytelling then I definitely recommend this game. A wonderful example of Southern Gothic literature and excellent playwriting, it touches on themes such as debt, poverty, loss and being lost, and overcoming obstacles. The characters are diverse, sometimes quirky, often sympathetic, and always fascinating and engaging in their own rights. Having just finished Act IV last night in one sitting I'm left fairly heartbroken at its turn of events, but also hopeful that things will turn out okay in the end, even if the main players may not have much in the means of influence within the world of the game. Ben Babbitt's soundtrack is beautiful and adds perfectly to the ambience of the game, and the aliased style of the graphics are simple and minimalist (especially whilst traveling the Zero) and yet perfectly unique and fitting to the feel and tone of the game.
It's a multitude of things that make Kentucky Route Zero as enchanting as it is – it's a poem, it's a ghost story, it's a piece of art cinema;  it's a collection of vignettes on what it means to be lonely vs alone and the many different ways people may find it hard to fit into society. In my experience, it's best played late at night, when it's quiet both within and without – being in the right frame of mind is key to fully appreciating the game, but KR0 does a fine job of bringing you into that mood as soon as you start up the game anyway.
I'll finish here with a quote from a Tweet my friend (who gifted me the game) posted last night:
"He just wants to finish a delivery. She just wants answers about a family mystery. Things complicate, as they do. I hope they un-complicate."
So do I... so do I.
(*In case you haven't guessed by this point, I am, in fact, a Film Hons. grad and a filmmaker. haha)
This game would be better if I could build a wall, and get a small loan of a million gold.

This was a must-have game for anyone who has ever wanted to play the guitar; but it has been superceded by Rocksmith 2014.  This is only worth getting for the songs that you can import into RS2014, and there is the ADDITIONAL COST of getting the import-tool to do so on top of purchasing this game.
It requires an official Rocksmith Realtone Cable (and an electric guitar / bass) to play.  Unofficial cables can be used in conjunction with a patch, but this can cause problems.
Within 6 months of casual play I went from having absolutely no experience to mastering my first song; and I enjoyed pretty much every step along the way as the levelling system incrementally increased the difficulty to suit my level of ability.
It made practising a pleasure, which is crucial to developing your skills – more so than learning the numerous techniques that game teaches you and helps you to master.
The selection of songs is solid, and the vast amounts of DLC allow you to pick out some favourites to play.  This does, however, add to the cost a fair bit – and the fact that RS2014 charges to import the original game's songs to that version is pretty much charging you for the same content twice.  Thankfully that doesn't apply to the DLC songs.
The game does, unofficially, support custom (community made) songs; although these are of varying quality.
The game is an amazing technical achievement, and Ubisoft's usual nickel-and-diming doesn't detract from that.

"SC" is for the second chapter. If you haven't played the first, go find that one. It's excellent. You'll need the pair, btw.
As for SC, it's an overall improvement and a great closer of the story (as it is the second half).
The whole game system of the previous game is similar, but many improvements were made to the combat and a few expansions. Combat was made a bit faster due to shorter animations and enter/exits, some complexity was added here and there. One major improvement I loved was a lot of equipment has downsides so you have to debate over certain pieces for certain builds. Not just constant upgrades like the last game. The whole orb mechanic was overhauled and feels much better.
(SPOILER FREE) Story, for the most part, is very fulfilling and ties up well as a large part of the overall LoH larger series. If you enjoyed the First Chapter, you won't be dissapointed. Still a bit slow and sluggish in some areas (especially if you're going for all the side-quests and chests and such), but doesn't get too dull and pays off in the end.
Overall, the duo is an amazing set of JRPG games. Just amazing. If the combat (for the time) wasn't a bit dull and the story was a bit quicker, I wouldn't think for a second this wouldn't be considered a masterpiece of the RPG genre. As for now, it's close. Really close.
Side note: There's a small bug to watch out for if you're using a gamepad. Some menus in the final chapter couldn't be used with a gamepad, and it took me forever to find out via Steam forums that the mouse can be used to click on menu items when this happens. Duh, right? Stupid me. If this happens, remember the mouse!
Second side note: I had quite a few problems running the previous chapter, nothing game-breaking, but a few jolts. Many of those problems don't exist in the SC. I still get frame-stuttering in certain areas, but not as bad. Outside of that there's the final chapter menu/mouse problem. That's all. Pretty well ported this time.

Playing virtually any dynasty in this game, big or small, feels like trying to balance on top of a ball on top of another ball. Just when you hit that sweetspot your leader dies, and you fall and have like 30 seconds to have the new guy get up there and figure out how to not lose his balance or else it's game over; or atleast a gut-wrentching downsize.
If you bought the game and can't figure it out, play a small dynasty several times through. I've always been interested in Italian history so I played several games as the Duke of Ferrara starting in the late medieval era (1337ad) who controls only two counties. Starting in 1337ad makes it so your technology, baronies, temples and cities are universally well developed, meaning you can concentrate on learning the rules of medieval rulership and how they apply to the game and acheiving your goals for the playthrough. For your own game, try playing as a few different powerful leaders and then as a few weak ones so that you see the difference in player control over your realm.
I've now gone back to 867ad Italy, with the Duke of Tuscany, Adelberto Bonifazi. The king of Italy, a foreign invader from the Karling Dynasty of France is leige to the 5 major Italian duchies, and is moderately respected within Italy. Europe is divided from west to east by three different Karling Kings, and the throne of Italy is up for grabs within their house. It makes for fantastic storytelling of italian unification, or fragmentation (which is more consistant with the history books). Find any dynasty that tugs at your fairytale strings and you'll create the adventure yourself. You compile your own ruleset for winning, and you'll play again and again to get it 'just right'.
You are allowed to pick and choose from a wonderful list of histrorical characters from the 760's through the 1300's (more with DLC). You might even find yourself on wikipedia learning about how europe, northern africa and western asia used to work. Once you are briefly educated on succession laws, title claimancy, and holy war you'll be well on your way to taking Rome for the Byzantine empire and converting all Christians to Orthodox and thus resolving the great schism, or perhaps you'll begin as a small vassal, in control of a single county and have your progeny expand and reclaim The Holy Roman Empire. Or maybe you'll just want to keep a small duchy in Italy safe from foreign invasion generation after generation and keep your family safe at all costs.
It is at its core a sandbox game. You create the goals, you amend them, the world changes drastically, your position changes, there's an opening, the window closes, alliances are broken, new friends arrive at court to save the day, and eventually you forget what the original goal of winning was to begin with. You watch and contribute to the story as generations of genetic triumphs and failures are constantly bickering, warring, dieing, plotting, changing sides for no good reason, and are also generally trying to make sure you don't have a larger army than they do. Don't forget about all the neighbors, who are convinced that they would be better suited to rule in your lands than you are.
There are a thousand pitfalls to success in CK2 as there surely were in the more noble times, so always learn from your mistakes and try again. Use google. And always have enough gold to hire an appropriately sized mercenary army and pay them for 12 months. Always. Eight hour playthroughs that fall because of premature spending will remind you of that. Keep your neighbor rulers in the character watch list, keep a constant eye on beneficial marriages, and constantly scan the character find sheet for potential courtiers that would join your court and could serve as councilmembers. Remember that the safety of the family is top priority, so always be able to defend yourself, be it through your own army, your vassals or your alliance's, but never have a substantially smaller force than the neighbors or vassals. That will always spell game over.
And lastly, please try to remember at all times that those who cannot remember the past are doomed to repeat it.

Finally, a game comes along that has the potential to actually turn you into a rockstar. Well, maybe not literally, but Rocksmith can help you really learn songs. No more mashing colored buttons rhythmically on cheap toy controllers, because Rocksmith lets you use REAL GUITARS and BASSES to play along and learn songs. It reads the output of your instrument, so it knows if your playing the right notes or not at the right timing (provided you adjusted your latency properly).
This is incredible for noobs -- beginners just starting out who want to learn a few popular songs, because Rocksmith is less of a game and more of a gamified teaching tool. It tracks your progress, adapting to your apparent skill level mid song, so you'll see a few note fly on the screen at first, but if you play more notes, Rocksmith doesn't punish you, but instead decides to display more and more notes until the "real" guitar/bassline is finally revealed. Essentially, the game rewards you for being a better musician, the way it should be.
There are plenty of modes that teach techniques like string bending, double stops, hammer ons/pull offs, muting -- mainly through tutorials and games. These techniques are also used in songs, so they become as practical as they are entertaining.
Overall I'd have to say that Rocksmith is the best thing for beginners to learn songs beyond crappy online tabs, paying for lessons, books, "hot licks" DVDs or investing in software like Transcribe (which is excellent and I recommend to anybody remotely serious about learning music) to slow down tunes and learn piece by piece.

Atlas Reactor plays at a 20 second turn for all players, but that doesn’t necessarily mean all players play at the same pace. For some players, the games pacing may be to slow for them or way to fast when they first start playing the game. Matches tend to be played in a similar way that chess is played, you are meant to analyze what your opponent is doing to figure out your best way to outsmart them while your opponent does the same thing to you, the biggest difference is that you only control 1 piece which can perform multiple action in the game and you must cooperate with 3 other players. Being that this is a competitive game not everyone gets along very easily.
Basic breakdown though for how the game goes is combat is done simultaneously based on the phase of combat. This means all Prep abilities activate during the prep phase, all Dash abilities activate in the dash phase, all blast abilities activate in the blast phase, and all movement is done at the end of the blast phase. EVERYTHING happens at the same time in that phase but each lancer takes a turn, even if you die you still have that perfect op to take the other ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ down with you.

- The games learning curve will very based on a players experience with Turn-Based strategy games.

Chivalry Medieval Warfare...
Where do I begin?
This game has a basic concept with easily learnt controls with basic fighting to begin. Rank 1-15 servers introduce the idea of the balanced combat and allow you to try all 4 classes, The Honorable Knight which only spams the voice command 'come hither' while tanking more hits than any other class, The Vanguard who pokes people with sticks are wins by using a larger sword, The Man at arms who is squishy using speed and dodges to take down his prey, and worst for last, Cancer archers.
Rank 1-15 comes with a few hardships of fighting more experienced players over rank10 who know what they are doing but eventually you will catch on to the general game mechanics etc.
Unfortunatly many people with over 300 hours will create alternate accounts and reap these scrubby servers providing an unwelcomed experience for newcomers
Then comes the more difficult and frustrating part. The transition from rank 1-15 servers to the Big boy servers...
After rank 15 you cannot join the low level servers, this means that your enemies will be rank 15 and onwards, but since this game has been out for a while, many rank 40s and 60s will stomp on you with no remorse. My first encounter with a rank 50 was a quick nod to signify combat then I charged at him swinging my sword.
He ducked under it then 360 1shot me within half a second, decapatating me...
These phase from being the top of the low level server to being fauder for the high levels is quite difficult but learning how to become one of these monsters is all part of the game. I (while writing this review) have 400+ hours and have learned many of the strategys. I am able to take down rank 60s with hardship and slap about low levels. even with my large amount of playtime, people with 2k hours still are very difficult to take down and some low tatics are usually implimented.
Overall this game is fun and is good for consuming time without feeling bored. Even although it seems repetitive, It is still intriguing and exciting for me today. It can be a casual game with some people being friendly, forming huddles and spamming laugh getting attacked by an onslaught of tryhards but that is part of the fun. Learning about this game is fun, which weapon is the best, why does everyone hate feints, but one thing that a somewhat experienced person like myself should tell you... Don't be archer.
This Game is worth a play, even better with friends!

tl;dr: Are you looking for a great strategic turn-based experience? Buy this game.
Not looking for that? This might not be your speed.
Should you give this game a try if you have the option to? Absolutely.
As a player that has been playing this game since its Open Alpha I feel I can say that Atlas Reactor is a very unique turn-based MOBA that really sets itself apart from any other games in the MOBA genre. If you don't like turn-based combat then you should probably resume browsing for other games on Steam as this is not the game for you. With it's unique cast of characters a new player will be able to find someone that fits their playstyle. Healer (Support), Tank (Frontline), DPS (Firepower) this game has it all. From a happy-go-lucky ball of nuclear energy to a Cold Blooded shotgun totting killer, this game covers a whole spectrum of personalities that add to the fun.
The gameplay at it's core consists of 4 phases: Decision, Prep, Dash, and Blast. In this order in game it allows for many situations full of outplays that will seperate the skilled from the average. This makes the game fun as you can watch yourself grown and you can learn a lot from one match if you're paying attention. The gameplay never feels repetitive as every game allows for different team combinations and different decisions to change the experience.
The only problems right now is the small playerbase and the fact that queueing solo is not the best way to have a great experience. The queue times can be a bit long depending on the time you choose to play because of the smaller playerbase, but even then they aren't that long. I've never had a queue longer than 5 minutes. Queuing as a 4 man is easily the most enjoyable way to play this game which is a shame, but it's expected. Friends always make games better. Now if you don't have anyone in specific to play with you can join this
and find people in the community to play with!
The game is definitely worth a try and I would recommend it to anyone looking for a turn-based experience.
If you want a more indepth look at the game outside of watching streams you can read
article that I wrote about over 2 weeks ago that is a first look at Atlas Reactor. A few things have changed since then, but they don't make the article null.

It IS the best Sonic game ever made as many other pro reviewers have stated.
After about 8 hours of gameplay, I had completed the game. This game is absolutely the true sequel to Sonic 3 & Knuckles. Hands down.
Graphics are of course the sharpest the could be with the traditional art style of the Sonic Genesis series. Better than that though are the high frame animations, so much new life is given to these beloved characters and aside from that, it seems more story is allowed to be shown through intermediate cutscenes between levels, something that was non existent in the original Sonic trilogy.
Another place the credit definitely goes is the music. OH THE MUSIC. Nobody complains about the music because it's absolutely perfect.
All of these elements go along to take me back to an era in my childhood that I absolutely treasured and I'm so thankful to have felt it all again with Sonic Mania. Yes, if you have nostalgia for the genesis days, this will definitely bring you back.
Regarding gameplay and content though? Let me tell you about that with a small Q&A.
Q: Are these just the old levels with 2 or 3 original levels?
A: Nope. Every old level in this game is remastered and reimagined. It's like they pulled the best chunks out of the old ones, added new chunks and made them all make better sense with each other.
Q: Will I enjoy this without nostalgia goggles?
A: If you enjoy fast reflex platformers with beautiful style and excellent music, then Sonic Mania stands on it's own.
Highly recommend, it's the ESSENTIAL Sonic game now. Even the originals don't compare. Even I can take off my nostalgia goggles to admit that.

If you liked ETS2, you will like this game as well. Performance is much better and the game looks beautiful. A wide variety of (Western) American landscapes and minimal versions of cities make it fun to explore while making your deliveries. It is often worth to try alternative routes away from the direct highway connections to discover sights like the Grand Canyon or Yosemite Park.
Aside from that, the system of progress really stays the same for the tens of hours you might find yourself playing this game. After an initial phase of contract deliveries you start your own company and expand by buying new garages all over the country to employ drivers. Before I begin to review Shadow Warrior Redux, there is one bit of professionalism I need to clear up before we can continue: Go to hell Gearbox for removing the far superior versions of Duke Nukem 3D by General Arcade and the GOG original to resell Duke Nukem 3D, again, with worse audio than the 1996 version and charging $5 more than the Megaton Edition with no fan expansions, one new episode, and with zero discounts for previous owners. You can also go back to hell for threatening to sue the mod-tool creator for EDuke32 as well as making the new episode non-compatible for the mod which has kept the legacy of Duke Nukem alive for 20 years, not you.
With that business taken care of, let’s talk about how amazing the classic version of Shadow Warrior is as an old-school FPS that isn’t all fortune cookies and Wang jokes. It’s surprisingly a visionary game from the same Build engine as Duke Nukem 3D that predicted drivable vehicles/turrets, unique weapons like the sticky bombs and the katana, as well as having multiple functions for every weapon. The Redux is a technological marvel that should be the standard for rereleasing classic games with modern compatibility to preserve their legacy as well as being generous to offer the original DOS version for free. If any developer or publisher deserves praise for preserving the past of games, General Arcade and Devolver are deserving of your time and/or money to put as much effort into these classics.
Always remember Devolver Digital’s motto, “Tomorrow’s unethical business practices, today!”
Perhaps what remains as timeless as the game engine itself is Shadow Warror’s emphasis on character to sell its game much like Duke Nukem. Whereas Duke was a conglomeration of action movie hero tropes and quotes that played the references dead on, which never really seized his comedic value until The Birth episode and the fan-expansions like Life’s A Beach, Lo Wang himself embodies the status as a parody that goes beyond his obvious stereotype comedy. Jokes range from fortune cookie one-liners, secret locations with nerdy movie references and Lo Wang’s utter ego-obsessed personality that intentionally clashes with the amount of violence he causes on his enemies. In many ways, where the combat is the yin of Shadow Warrior the yang is the comedy of Wang himself.
Wang’s character is not limited to merely the comedy itself but also in the bizarre arsenal he has at his disposal. Whereas Duke Nukem and the DOOM marine used staples such as fists/legs, pistol, shotgun and rock-launcher, Lo Wang continues the same emphasis of weapon differentiation with more atypical weapons such as a katana, single/duel Uzis, a riot shotgun with single/burst fire, and a missile launcher that can fire standard, heat-seeking and nuclear explosives at enemies. On top of these weapons, Lo Wang also has equipment options that while not as effective as his weapons like the caltrops do make his options stand out. In this contrast, the uniqueness of his weaponry isn’t limited to cosmetic differences but mechanical decisions for the resources given to Lo Wang with enemies that challenge him much more than other enemies in the “DOOM-clone” era of FPSs such as exploding suicide bombers that may create phantoms or leaping Rippers. The result creates a game that not only relies on the comedy to add character but also the arsenal of Lo Wang to give him personality in gameplay.
This last point is something I think is often forgotten in modern FPSs as many modern shooters emphasize the standardized weapon selection, which isn’t necessarily required in every game, or they will offer a superfluous number of weapons with no mechanical changes other than firing rate, handling and ammo capacity. Perhaps this is one of many reasons why the Build-Engine Bros.—Duke Nukem, Lo Wang, Caleb from Blood—remains timeless despite their age or their limitations as character is perhaps the most important trait in FPSs that makes modern games like Halo and PREY (2006 & 2017) as beloved as the reverence for the Doom Marine.
Perhaps inspired by the levels of interactivity of the original DOOM, the Build Engine has perhaps the most sandbox-style appeal of old-school FPSs compared to the Unreal or Source engines of their landmark titles. DOOM was focused solely around its enemy placement and gunplay, offering exploration for secrets as the only means of interacting with the environment. The Build engine games, however, added more flavor to the formula by having tons of useless tat and interactable objects within the environments from simple pinball machines to remote-controlled bumper cars to add a greater sense of play with the non-linear maps of the Build Engine games.
If Hollywood Holocaust was Duke Nukem’s take on E1M1, the first level of Shadow Warrior is the embodiment of the Build Engine as Lo Wang can enter the building from multiple entryways along with shooting a garbage can as a platform to reach secret supplies, controlling a remote-controlled bumper car to get a key, and playing pachinko machines for fun as well as another secret. Sometimes the interactable objects do little else than make visuals and sounds play to entice you to mash the interact key with everything. While many of these means of interaction are optional, the sense of playfulness with the environment as distractions with some reward is something that makes these games feel more complex than their counterparts, and overtime with every game the emphasis has less put on these obtuse secrets and more on the level-design to never ruin their novelty.
Sandboxes is perhaps a more proper term to describe these levels as the mazes of DOOM were entrenched in the open-ended 2D limited by doorways that needed a certain means of progression. In the Build Engine games, verticality is another means of an entrance way encouraged by the level designers to reward players who learn the environments so well that they find exploits to reach the greater rewards without always going through the main doorway. Even when it comes to the helpfulness of drivable tanks and of usable turrets, they are never forced on the player but merely momentary distractions of carnage. Subtle differences like these leads to discovering the complex depth behind its simple gameplay that really displays how masterful of an FPS these games have become without sacrificing the pacing of handcrafted levels that have been replaced with open-worlds with little to no character in every corner of the map.
Now I think it’s important to note that Shadow Warrior is not a perfect game whatsoever beyond its simplistic narrative issue, and it’s mainly the result of its emphasis on difficulty. Enemies themselves are a limited, though adequate, roster with annoyances like the invisible ninjas that can blast fire like the summoners from DOOM 2 as well as the hornets that are absolute pets when you don’t have a smoke bomb. Damage is quite high on the default difficulty, which makes this one of the more challenge of Build Engine games, and sometimes the strangeness of the weapons can lead to the player suffering more hits than intended such as the wind-up time for the Nuke. There is also a larger emphasis on platforming and puzzle challenges beyond navigation and keys that can drag the pace down to a crawl with no action. As a whole, however, none of these minor issues ruin the experience as Shadow Warrior itself is as much of a time-honored classic as DOOM or Duke Nukem.
As wise master Wang once said, “It is better to have loved and lost than to have loved and got syphilis.” Or perhaps the saying of wisdom was rather, “Man who fart in church sit in own pew.”

Shadow warrior came out in 1997 and this is a remake-ish game with improved graphics and is easier to run on modern systems. You play as wang which is either a homage to old kung-fu movies or a walking stereo-type. The story isn't too important but the gameplay is an FPS and a really good one. You can also interact with the enviorment (a.k.a Duke Nukem) to find hidden refrences and one-liners. I love the weapons, the(very corny) jokes, the set pieces, this game is a blast. All your weapons are varied and have alternate fire modes giving you plenty of ideas to approach combat with enemies. Just simply put, this is a polished, well made game.
As I said the game has improved graphics but they are still the 2D in 3D-ish style game so it will look a bit dated but it does look much better than when it was on dosbox. The sound design is good but I can't get music to play aside from the title and credits which is odd, though, I don't know if thats my pc or the game. I also found it easy to get lost, not due to level design but odd placement for switches that open door's. The Boss battles are also easy, though the final boss most awesomely took a nuke to the FACE and didn't recieve much damage(still a cake walk though).
The wanton expansion pack add's more levels and it works fine. I don't think it's as good as the main campaign, as some design choices are very mixed to me. I didn't get lost quite as much as the first campaign but one section had me outside an airplane while in the air which was frustrating as you had to make jumps while wind was blowing you off the plane. I would also get crushed by doors, which is odd since this didn't happen in the main campaign. The sound track worked in these levels which is good(the tracks are good by the way with a nice blend of mid eastren influence). I should point out that the enemies are swaps of the enemies in the first campaign. Despite my complaints this is still a very solid expansion and worth playing.
The twin dragon expansion is my least favorite. This one lacked that passion you can feel in the other two campaigns. It did get rid of some of the issues from wanton destruction, but it was replaced with even worse design ideas. Some of the levels have invisible mines(nothing shows them to my knowlege) bad enemy placements, and over all just more trial and error than I liked. The gameplay is still here, but it's certainly the worst of the two expansions.
Overall yes I loved this game, it feels like a game that learned from the shooters that came before it. The expansions might not be as good as the main game, but this is totally worth playing. Two thumbs up.

The Far-East division of the Build trio is back in all it's gory, stupid, shiny, modern system friendly, DOSbox-less glory.
Presentation wise, well, it's a 90s Build engine game so it looks about as good (or bad) as they did back then, only this time, it runs on pretty much any resolution you can shake a stick at. I'm glad they put in a "Retro/Smooth" selector for the textures because personally, I'm not a big fan of "smooth" textures in source-ports of 90s classics, it loses its gritty charm. However, the game is somewhat unstable, mostly when you quickload, so save often (there's quicksave thank goodness), because it does tend to crash from time to time. Sound is also pretty decent, Lo Wang is my favourite of the three Build protagonists (the other two being Duke Nukem and Caleb from "Blood", for those that may not know) and the soundscape is good, but the game has a tendency to insanely boost some sounds like pain screams - it's a bit annoying at first but to be fair, I got used to it over time and it's not as noticeable. Some people also complain about the mouse aim being strange, but I don't know, I never felt that, maybe because I'm used to the way Build engine mouse movement behaves; besides, you can set X and Y sensitivity separately, so that should be that. One last thing - the crosshair is useless, because projectiles land a bit to the left of it. I was told this is a "flaw" inherent in the engine and I recommend simply turning the crosshair off and going with it.
Gameplay wise... what can I say, this game is 90s FPS gold, for some reason, I liked it more than Duke Nukem or Blood. Maybe it's the complex, multi-key hunt level design, the awesome weapons or maybe it's just Lo Wang's crude, unapologetic humour. Make no mistake, by today's standards, this game is offensive as all hell to East Asian cultures because Lo Wang is a walking Chinese action hero stereotype. But I think that it's done in a self-aware, tongue-in-cheek way that you can't really fault it. Just like Duke, who was making fun of roided-up, cocky white action heroes. You are thrown into these massive, non-linear levels with keys to find and bad guys to turn into flying meat. The enemy roster is varied and challenging. BTW, this game is pretty hard, unless you're weak like a baby's fart and play on anything lower than "Who Wants Wang" (Hard).
Thankfully, the weapons in this game are amazing to help speed up the extermination process. I think this is one of a select few FPS games in which the melee attack remains useful and powerful from start to finish, and it's simply a joy to slash enemies in half with a Katana while Lo Wang spouts classy one-liners such as "Oooh, sprit personarity!" or "You half a man you used to be!". The Shuriken and Sticky Bombs are pretty much useless (as weapons, you can use them as tools though), but the Uzi, Riot Shotgun, Missile Launcher, Grenade Launcher and Railgun are your go-to tools of Wanton Destruction (couldn't help myself). A lot of them have secondary or even tertiary firing modes, like the Guardian head, which is literally the severed head of an enemy type that shoots fire from its mouth in three different ways, the Rocket Launcher which fires heat-seeking missiles (provided you found a heat-seeker card) or even a goddamn nuke (provided you found the warhead), or the Riot Shotgun which fires either one blast or a burst of four consecutive blasts. Wang "like big wepen" indeed.
The expansion packs are decent, I enjoyed Wanton Destruction just a bit more than Twin Dragon, but they're both good and... well... expand the game experience (I know, I'm bursting with originality right now). Together they pretty much double the length of the original game.
Last and certainly not least, this game is, at times, ridiculously cheap during sales. I got it for 1€. One freakin' Euro, that's the price of like a cheap candy bar or something. If that's not value for money, I don't know what is. But even at full price, I'd still say it's worth it.
All in all, this game is great and it's a shame it got overshadowed (pun intended) by the games that came out around that time (mostly Quake), because it's an absolute classic. If you're on the verge, hesitate no more, grasshopper. "Who Wants some Wang?" You. You do.
