I had played guitar for a number of years and in a couple of bands, prior to when Rocksmith was released. Everyone is a bit different when it comes to learning music and/or an instrument. Some people actually do better learning this way than the traditional way. While the dlc's that come with the "game", (and I use the term loosely as I see it more as a learning tool), are great, but learning the scales and working on your techniques and fundamentals are necessary when you start playing more difficult pieces as well as music that's not available via Rocksmith.
Still, you do have techniques that you can work with in Rocksmith and there's plenty of videos on Youtube, guides on the internet, as well as videos and guides you can buy, be it via youtube or another route. Rocksmith is a great tool. It may not be the only tool you use, but that's a given with anything in life.
I would recommend this for guitarists that are intermediate level and above. For absolute beginners, I would recommend learning the fundamentals of guitar and at least understanding guitar tablature first. That is unless you just want to plink around with music, which you can certainly do. You could even learn the fundamentals later, after you've found that you wish to invest yourself into music/guitar later.

I went into this game not knowing anything about it and so not having any set expectations.
I came out of this game after completing two acts realizing I did not care enough about the world, story, or characters to go through more of the tedious "gameplay" to learn any more about them.
After the first couple minutes I was intrigued and curious as to where the game would go, it reminded me a little of a softer mix between Metro 2033 and maybe Silent Hill.
After Act I's lackluster conclusion that left me wondering what had even happened I had my doubts as to the cohesiveness of the world or the existence of a plot.
By the end of Act II I felt the game was constantly introducing new mysteries and oddities with no direction whatsoever and no plans to attempt to explain or justify them in any way. It reminded me only of the TV show Lost, but you realize it is going nowhere a whole lot quicker.
The game does something interesting with the dialog in that you establish your game world through it. You're given conflicting options to respond to someone's question and whatever you say is the truth of the world. It's a clever way to allow players to piece together their character's backstory slowly over the course of play.
I imagine this could be used to interesting effect within an RPG, but in this game all it means is that conversations later in the game just reference the things you said earlier as if to say "Hey, remember when you made a choice in this linear game pretending it has depth? I do!"
It's a pretty game, I like the art style and the smooth camera/scene transitions (in most cases), but games like this stand or fall on their story, and after two hours I am not sure I could care any less about this game's story.

Last instalment in S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series of games.
Game set in perviously unused locations in the Zone, with exception of part of town of Pripyat.
You play as Major Degtyarev, member of Ukrainian Special Forces, sent to the Zone to investigate mysterious crash of army helicopters sent to try and capture Wishgranter.
Gameplay is much less linear than in pervious Stalker games, but on other hand, game does not guide you by hand like in never titles, so it is sometimes easy to get lost or lose sense of what to do next.
Although game is (relatively) old, graphics are still very much presentable, and for example, in some instances game looks much better than say, Fallout 4. When you introduce various mods into it (yes, game is fully moddable, with huge depositories online for various improvements and/or changes), game simply looks amazing.
Although gameplay seems a bit more simplified than in pervious games, most of it is same. Shooting and ballistics play huge role in game, as well as weapon condition/ammunition types, so give it time to get used to it.
Stalker series of games always had very ''eastern slavic'' feel to them, simply because authors of game are from Eastern Europe, and are very good at translating look and feel of post-communism decay and changes.
Abandoned towns, villages, factories, overgrown roads, roaming wild animals, frequent weather changes, indescribable horrors and mutants, bandits and stalkers await all who enter the Zone.
But, once you are in, you will not want to leave.

A Virus Named TOM is a fast paced, grid-based action puzzle game. A famous and brilliant inventor is laid off from his corporate job after developing a series of revolutionary but unprofitable technologies. As revenge, this inventor creates TOM, a virus whose mission is to hack these technologies and bring havoc to the reputation of said company.
The core gameplay loop involves maneuvering a grid of rotating tiles to connect circuits while avoiding anti-viruses and other hazards. The game features quite a few puzzle mechanics, including time-limits, memory puzzles, timing puzzles and disjointed circuits.
Simply put, this game is decent, but definitely not worth the $10 asking price. I received this game in a bundle, and it served nicely as a quick distraction for a few hours. However the grid-based gameplay of connecting circuits together got stale very quickly, and it's very easy to find free online games that provide similar experiences.
Overall an okay but very forgettable game that shouldn't really be a contender for your wallet.

I've debated getting this game for a really long time and finally bought it over the winter sale.  I feel like I've been missing out on a great game.  Many of the poor reviews stem from poor interaction with real life people but it’s so hard to anticipate all the ways that someone can screw you over that it’s not fair to the developers to negatively critique the game based off of that.
This game has quickly become my favorite.  It’s true that there are a few bugs still but that’s what happens in early adoption of a game currently in development.
My brothers and I have different gaming styles.  One of them doesn’t like to build so much and the rest of us enjoy building as well as fighting, and we have been looking for a game that has both aspects in it so we can play together.  I really like how this game focuses on character development as well as building.  I think they did a great job in creating the combat style.  It’s a little glitchy sometimes.  The sword doesn’t always hit 100% and even after dodging, the thing you’re fighting still hits you, but overall fighting is pretty nice.  The attention to detail is impressive too, for example, when a tool breaks, the character will show an animation like shaking hands in pain, or brushing themselves off.  It’s these kinds of details that make it easier to get absorbed into the world.
One of the problems I have with many survival games is that it’s too easy to level and get to higher content.  While some people might not appreciate it, I quite enjoy that some things in this game take longer to get.  For example, one of the first crafting tables you can build requires lots of stone, wood, and hide.  It’s not too much that it feels like a huge grind, but it’s enough that it makes the game progression a more suitable pace for me.
Overall, I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys crafting games mixed with combat because I think the devs did a great job at creating a game that does both.

It IS the best Sonic game ever made as many other pro reviewers have stated.
After about 8 hours of gameplay, I had completed the game. This game is absolutely the true sequel to Sonic 3 & Knuckles. Hands down.
Graphics are of course the sharpest the could be with the traditional art style of the Sonic Genesis series. Better than that though are the high frame animations, so much new life is given to these beloved characters and aside from that, it seems more story is allowed to be shown through intermediate cutscenes between levels, something that was non existent in the original Sonic trilogy.
Another place the credit definitely goes is the music. OH THE MUSIC. Nobody complains about the music because it's absolutely perfect.
All of these elements go along to take me back to an era in my childhood that I absolutely treasured and I'm so thankful to have felt it all again with Sonic Mania. Yes, if you have nostalgia for the genesis days, this will definitely bring you back.
Regarding gameplay and content though? Let me tell you about that with a small Q&A.
Q: Are these just the old levels with 2 or 3 original levels?
A: Nope. Every old level in this game is remastered and reimagined. It's like they pulled the best chunks out of the old ones, added new chunks and made them all make better sense with each other.
Q: Will I enjoy this without nostalgia goggles?
A: If you enjoy fast reflex platformers with beautiful style and excellent music, then Sonic Mania stands on it's own.
Highly recommend, it's the ESSENTIAL Sonic game now. Even the originals don't compare. Even I can take off my nostalgia goggles to admit that.

CUTE, COMPLICATED JAPANESE GAME THAT MIGHT END YOUR FRIENDSHIPS
OK, not that serious, but competitive friends might get in for a fight! A mixture of Mario Party, trading cards and RPG, OJ is an addictive board game that seems too complicated at first, but after some time paying attention to what happens after reading the guide file, it becomes extremely funny!
Your objective is to clear tasks (caller "norma") before your opponents do. Whoever clear all levels of norma first, wins the game. Simple? Not so much! The board is filled with slots that will either benefit or trouble you, such as the drop slots, the bonus slots and people can even drop traps for whoever's coming! Not only that, but there are monster battles and a boss can either be summoned by a player through the use of cards or the game itself will place it there -- and they're not fooling around! Although the battles have a basis on chance, it's quite possible to follow a strategy so long as you know the character you're playing with. That is very important when fighting opponents, since they can be far more dangerous than regular mobs!
If you want to have some casual-yet-hardcore-competitive-fun with your friends, OJ is your game! I didn't find a single thing I don't like about it yet and the best part is that no one suffers netwrok delay (I'm in Brazil and I play with a friend on the US, so we do have issues with certain games). Worth the full price, even more worth it on sale. I didn't think twice before buying the 4-pack for half the price!

It conjures up images of pimple-faced nerds with bad haircuts sitting around an
with a two button joystick hacking away at
on a precious Friday night. Yeah, sure, that can be fun – but the medium has evolved dramatically from its fairly simplistic roots to what I would consider one of the highest forms of art. ‘Video games’ is an overly simplistic and even fairly derogatory term for something so complex and creative and beautiful that they have literally captivated the entire world. Many of us don’t simply play to ‘beat’ the computer or chase a high score, but to admire and be enveloped in some beautiful experience that has been created and put forth for us. In its rarest and most coveted form, it is candy for my brain; something I crave and cannot get enough of.
Art has layers of complexity, of course. For example a singer/songwriter wears two hats. They are both a poet and a singer. This is inherently more complex that just being a poet, with all else being equal. Creating a modern gaming experience that is exceptional really takes a delicate balance of it all – variables such as great music, artwork, technical and efficient programming skill, and of course a killer mechanic and conceptual design. You need the whole shebang in many cases. And perhaps the most important thing, in-fact the thing I value the most, is that there is little relationship between big budget titles and artistic success. I find most AAA titles to be quite sterile.
I don’t think I even need to list examples to get agreement on that point. In fact, it is arguable that some of the most risky and artistic gaming experiences could only be birthed from a single person or small team who had nothing to lose and everything to gain from putting their wonky, albeit sometimes brilliant, visions out there.
At the end of the day, the gaming experience is built by simply arranging zeros and ones in specific orders. Of course it works quite differently in reality, but that’s essentially it when stripped to its core. I’m not sure at which point video games made the jump from simply technical possibility to pure entertainment to something verging on art, but it certainly did happen. Games that really make you feel something, instead of just throwing an obstacle in your way such as finding a key to open the door. All I know is that one things most successful indie games have in common that many AAA title do not is pure where-it-on-your-shoulder heart and soul. Yeah it’s
, but it’s got
. And it sits you down and
and you are swept away and caught up.
Well, here’s to the indie titles with rough edges bubbled up from nothing but pure brilliant ideas that sent us forever into that love affair with modern gaming, never to return. My hats off to all the weird abstract shoestring-budget titles that dared to challenge gaming paradigms. And sure, there are casualties. Some titles fall from misinterpretation or even being too abstract. Perhaps missing the mark. Others fall for lack of funding, and overall lack of support. But perhaps in a sense they pave the way. They may be delicately priming our minds for something better; for the future.

Kentucky Route Zero has the most interesting dialogue system I have ever seen in a game. And not because it has particularly many choices or branching paths (though it certainly scratches the itch of dialogue tree decision-making), but because the dialogue system fluidly gives you information about the character you play as without a plot dump or exposition of their backstory. You don't learn anything about characters when you meet them, you learn it when you play as them. And when exactly you play as them is another interesting point, as what character you are controlling changes often once you meet the first other main character. And eventually you don't really control any one character, but rather you get to see what everyone in your party is thinking and choose one of their dialogue options. It's an interesting and effective way of learning about a main cast of characters that I've never really seen before. The visuals are absolutely gorgeous while running on a potato, because everything is solid colors and nothing in the environments needs to move much. Lots of pretty scenes and abstract imagery, in a nice rural setting. It's not usually something I bring up, but the audio design is such an important part of this game and done so well that it deserves praise too. I'm excited for acts IV and V, with act III being one of the most intriguing segments of a game I've ever played. If you're on the fence because all the acts aren't out yet, you should buy this. I don't want to spoil much more, but it's the best game I've played of it's genre, and this is probably my favorite genre of games. What's already here is great, and the developers are working hard to complete it.

Devil Daggers is a simple game: Survive as long as you can against endless waves of demonic monsters.
To start off with the obvious, the sound design is
, the game doesn't have any fast paced action music when in the arena, so you're left listening to the distorted cries of the hundreds of enemies swarming around you.
Each game lasts from anywhere from 50-500 seconds, and while there's not much content in the game, I have easily spent almost 100 hours in-game and could easily pull off 100 more, it's one of those games where you're always wanting to have just one more go at it until it's 4am and you can't physically focus on the screen long enough to keep playing.
Another great thing about the game is the controls, to a brand new player you will simply run and shoot, until you realize that there is much more to the game. Pulling off perfect bunnyhops will increase your speed, timing shotgun blasts with your jumps to launch yourself over enemies, after a while everything works together perfectly until you're gliding around the arena and through the smallest gaps between demons.
All in all Devil Daggers is one of those games that you can very easily get addicted to, staying up countless hours just to beat your score by at least a second or two. I definitely recommend this game to anyone who likes a fast-paced shooter that involves quick thinking and reactions!

There are precious few games that force the player into a sense of pure concentration at its best, where each death becomes little more than a foolish mistake between frantic bouts, and where one can become omnipotent through sheer intuiton and skill.
Devil Daggers is one of those games.
The game reinforces an almost Lovecraftesque vibe, as though you are a mere worm fighting for nothing in the face of the unknown, with each gem taken giving you a slightly deeper look into what should not be known, as you lose clarity in exchange for power through intuition. At its best this game is frustrating, terrifying, and is incredibly addictive in spades, and will leave you with an adrenaline rush and the need to fight for those extra few seconds for that high score.
The game runs exceptionally well, mostly due to its rendering style. The low-poly and low-resolution style is mesmerizing as legions upon legions of skulls dance across the screen, giving it a style not often seen nowadays. Another wonderful draw is the brilliant sound design, which is emphasized by the use of positional audio. There is little like knowing exactly what and where the enemy is merely by the use of sound.
All in all, I would highly recommend this game to anybody who enjoys FPS in its most distilled form, and can happily throw themselves at the game again when they fail against adversary, as death in Devil Daggers is not a question of
, but rather
.

Very good implementation of a great deckbuilder card game. The game engine is very elegant, and there are only a handful of "powers", so the cards are incredibly easy to learn and the game is easy to pick up. Each player starts with a basic ten card hand, with some 8 gold and 2 attack, and must choose cards to purchase from a common "deck row". This means the game is really about drafting the best cards to build an engine to help you first buy good cards ASAP, and then be able to access those cards for combinations that let you overcome the enemies defenses and KO them.  There are two types of cards: ships and bases. Ships leave play after you play them, while bases remain in play, giving you an ongoing benefit until your enemies destroy them. Some bases are "Outposts" and they protect your other base and you. There are four factions (red - machines, blue - trade federation, green - blob, and yellow - imperial) each with a different flavor. Many cards have "ally abilities" which trigger when two cards of the same faction are in play on your side at the same time. Additionally, many cards can be "scrapped" (removed from the game) to provide an additional benefit.  The variability in the trade row leads to a different challenge each time you play it.   The free game is fun, but if you play a bit, you'll soon find the easy AI to be too easy. It's totally worth the $5 to play the full version, which grants access to the more meaty medium and hard AI and online play, and also includes single player "missions", which are pretty fun and tell a story.

Just buy it and you won't regret it.
N.B.: Songs that play in-game during a match will inevitably get stuck in your head.

What a fantastic journey. Every once in a while, you get incredibly hyped for that next game that's about to come out... and every so often, that very game delivers on the hype. This game ultimately did that for me, and I'm almost sad that the journey is now over (unless I start another new game). Starting each category at 10 points.
Visuals: starting at +10
================
The game's graphics look fantastic. There is a vast amount of polished detail in each and every environment. The developers didn't leave anything out. Even areas you may only explore once, if only for a couple of minutes, got all the same polished details as areas that you'll be spending hours upon hours inside of. Brilliant, long, hard work went into sewing the fields of this game's visuals, and the developers are reaping the fantastic benefits of that hard work. Well done.
+ No real cons here. I never had any screen tearing and rarely saw any seams throughout the world.
Final score: 10/10
Sound/Music: +10
=============
For anyone who has read my past reviews, you'll know I use the word "weight" a lot when it comes to sound effects. This "weight" means that for each and every major sound effect in the game, there should typically be some kind of "impact" behind them. It doesn't have to be a big "boom" for that to work. It can be the sounds of butterfly wings flapping in the wind (which would be incredibly hard to hear), or it can be a loud thunderbolt. Either way, whichever object or environment a sound effect has been stuck in/onto, it has to have a strong feeling behind it. This is not easy to explain, but let's just say that Divinity Original Sin 2 pulls it off extremely well.
+ All abilities sound effects, even ones that are as simple as throwing a dagger, feel heavy. There is strength behind them. No ability is left out, nothing is in the "filler" category. Excellent.
+ Music appears to be orchestra, and it's great. Battle music pumps you up. "Majestic" music calms you down, and provides a sense of relief behind it. It all sounds fantastic.
+ Pre-final battle music setup is excellent (only those who've played the game will understand).
+ Great voice work across all characters, both major and minor.
Final score: 10/10
Performance: +10
=============
Overall, the game runs well.
+ When everything is working, it performs at 60 FPS, constantly.
+/- Long long load times between regions. I mark this as neither a plus or a minus due to the fact that once you're loaded in, there are no load times whatsoever. The game loads everything upon entry (this is why is takes so long).
- Bugs bugs and more bugs. Nothing game breaking fortunately. A common theme when it comes to Larian Studios games. The good news is, most bugs are extremely minor. Quest bugs WILL be contracted, inhibiting you from actually completing a quest. Other quest related bugs include 1) actually completing a quest, but it never leaving your quest log. 2) you have option A and option B to choose from. You chose option A, but the game will say you chose option B. -1
- Certain battles have frustrating situations where a turn will not end immediately, forcing you to wait for up to 5-10 minutes at a time for each turn to finally end (even though nothing is happening). This will hopefully be patched in the near future. It was not patched in this playthrough. -1
- Game will crash every now and then. -1
- Strange lag issues in regards to certain spells (such as blood storm). These lag issues will persist until the specific spell (or spells) animations have completely ended, sometimes several turns after being cast. -1
Final score: 6/10
Story: +10
========
You are a source wielder. You've been captured and you're about to sent to what would closely resemble a "prison island" to serve out your remaining days. It's time to escape! This is where the adventure begins.
+ Premade characters all have an actual personality that you will love or hate. It will slowly be fleshed out as the story progresses, whether for better or for worse. Whichever character you pick (or don't pick, you can make your own too) will still have their main story attached, but you get to make a plethora of extra decisions behind them that will ultimately influence their endgame personality. So don't be afraid to pick the premades (you can also edit their classes and appearances).
+ Relevant in-game choices that will affect the endings.
+ Special endings for certain characters are available.
- Some scenes would have a far greater impact if it wasn't simply reading text. A few animations here and there wouldn't hurt, especially behind big scenes (that would normally be a cutscene vs an interactable scene). -1
Final score: 9/10
Gameplay: +10
===========
Gameplay hinges upon building your starting character with either physical, magical, or ranged damage types (ranged being both physical and magical, depending on if you're an archer or a mage). You'll run around and collect lots of loot, sell the loot, buy better loot; craft items, scrolls, and potions; learn a vast amount of abilities and even craft secret "hidden" abilities; there is plenty to do here, and you will be busy, all while having fun (hopefully).
+ Respec any time once you hit Act 2, for free. This will actually probably enrage some players, because they want to feel the weight of locking in their choice of permenant abilities (i.e. Diablo 2). Respecing for me on the other hand was the greatest thing to ever happen in this game. I started as a Battlemage, switched to a full time mage, and then later switched to a mostly full-timer tank/DPS with certain mage support abilities attached. I had another character start as a full healer and supporter, who later stayed as a full healer supporter, but also had fire and ice abilities to help in combat, if they couldn't do anything else. You can experiment to your heart's delight. So get past Act 1, then indulge in the world of change!
+ You can play as a skeleton, with facial hair.
+ Various unique abilities for each race are well implemented and can provide extra benefits to playing a certain class with a certain race (such as a thief/assassin with an undead, due to getting a free skeleton key to unlock any chest provided you have high enough Thievery skill. No need to buy lockpicks!)
+ Crowd control in this game is just as fantastic as it was in the first game, with a vast amount of new CC abilities (like sleeping).
+ The addition of Armor and Magic Armor is also fantastic, providing you with protection against CC abilities of both the physical and magical aspects until that chosen armor is depleted (unless you have Glass Cannon).
+ Playing with friends is a lot of fun.
+/- Some talents in the game feel wholly useless (Demon and Ice King), while others feel overpowered. I mark this as plus or minus simply because you can respec at any given time. It would only benefit to take certain "less useful" talents to quick specific areas of the game, then respec again back to whatever you were originally with. That being said...
- I played the game on Tactician mode (which is basically hard mode) and having a slightly higher fire resistance or slightly lower ice resistance never really made that big of a difference. The enemies in this mode having such incredibly strong physical or magical abilities would typically negate your armor too too quickly, and 15% out of 100% is just not very helpful. Leadership was a much better option, and also freed up the "wasted" talent points. These less useful abilites are what you would call "filler". -1
Final score: 9/10
Overall: 8.8/10 (44/50 = 0.88)
=====================

I am a very picky gamer, so picky to the point that I'm not sure myself what constitutes as a game that I like - AND will invest large amounts of time in it. For the longest time my guilty pleasure has been League of Legends, and other than the occasional Visual Novels and incredibly interesting (but also short length) puzzle adventure games, there are tens of games that I never played more than a few minutes/hours.
Then came Atlas Reactor. I was a closed alpha tester then; having gotten a key from stream TheBlueMuzzy (Now AR's Community Manager, bless him) and decided that it looked to really fit my taste. To my surprise and delight, it verily did. Atlas Reactor is a Multiplayer Online Board Action (MOBA - But NOT that MOBA) featuring 4v4 simultaneous turn-based matches with a simple yet unbelievably addictive win condition - get 5 kills before 20 turns, or score the highest amount of kills.
During closed alpha its core gameplay has already been largely completed; a major reason why it was an instant love that I've sunk roughly 30-40 hours total into the game. Moreover, it has witty and funny characters such as the slightly insane Zuki (like seriously, for a time I couldn't match Tutorial Zuki with Terrorist Zuki in my head because Tutorial Zuki was actually sane), baby powder Quark, cigarette protagonist Lockwood (for god's love devs, PLEASE do not remove this cigar), OP b*itch Grey (at the time she can deal 600+ damage minimum EVERY GAME even in the hands of a newbie), boulder Rampart (he was so useless then he's like a mobile square of full cover), astronaut Garrison (c'mon, he totally looks like one), troll Grem, super adorable PuP (with 180 max HP then... good days), super standard healer Aurora, Big Bro Titus-Whose-Dash-Was-Better-Then-DEV-WHY-WHY-WHY, infinite healing Rask, Easy-to-die, hard-to-master Asana, and of course, my absolute favorite and eternal love, Nix. Even if the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s nerfed you, THEY STILL WON'T STOP US FROM 800 DAMAGE THE♥♥♥♥♥♥OUT OF OUR ENEMIES CORPSES, RIGHT LOVE?
Oh. Right, I totally forgot about that one completely insignificant and forgettable Free - does he even count as a Freelancer? Random Villager A will be a better name, right? - Helios-helios-elios-lios-os-os... also the dude who copyrights his jokes. He's so lame it's hilarious. More lines please, devs! Just so we can soak in his infinite self-depreciation and feel eternally warm on the inside!
Yep, the characters are the 2nd reason why I love AR so much. It's funny, but this is one game that you can replay the same maps 100+ times and not feel bored with it, kind of like how people spent years on Summoner's Rift and still rage at their teammates. The magic is here. Right now the store's a bit of a mess because the devs can't seem to decide what should be made in-game currency purchasable (NOTE: IT SHOULD BE 95% OF EVERYTHING, BECAUSE THE GAME'S MINIMUM $30 NOW) and whatnot, but there's no reason to believe that it can't be sorted out. Between the lines and dots of deception you kill your enemies to entertain Trusts and hope that one day, you can master your own destiny...

Video game mascots are one of the pinnacle inventions that brought the market back from the brink. For kids, it was a way for them to connect, to easily recognize out in the wild, and more importantly, allowed the arguments of who was better: Mario or Sonic? These conversations continued up to the fifth generation of the Playstation, Sega Saturn, and Nintendo 64. As time went on, these mascots seemed to fall back to the shadows (with the exception of Mario and terrible Sonic games), but there’s always something so charming about a main protagonist that resembles the characters on a cartoon. Chubby Pixel has braced an entry into the mascot platforming genre with Woodle Tree Adventures as a charismatic log, armed with a giant leaf, set to collect special apples and water droplets to give new life to his forest home.
Woodle Tree Adventures is a recreation of the popular 3D platformers like Super Mario 64, Spyro, and Croc. There are six worlds to explore (seven once you’ve collected 600 apples which means finishing the game) of all different atmospheres including wintry wonderlands, water ridden marshes, and bee infested honeycombs. Strapped with an ever growing bag, you’ll collect apples which will unlock new worlds.

Call of Pripyat shows its age and wears it well. Charming and exciting, even its quirks are endearing. It's the way I like my women, too. So, I was quickly enamored.

Despite many bugs, flaws and perhaps a slightly desolate and incomplete atmosphere, Call of Pripyat holds itself together with captivating gameplay. Challenging combat (on higher difficulties) requires careful consideration of one's equipment loadout. A fairly complex gear modification mechanic aids in this task, and ensures that a shabby AK-74u can become a bullet hose that can take down a charging bloodsucker before it gets within striking distance. But being able to detect the near invisible creature still remains an issue. As it's an open-world, non-linear game, exploration is a core element to gameplay. Without a fast travel system, one is left with the responsibility of getting from point A to point B quickly and safely. A gloomy landscape adds tension to travels, as does roving packs of wild dogs.
It is difficult to become bored with Call of Pripyat as there are many sidequests as well many Artifacts and item stashes to be found and plundered. Being able to navigate through the dangerous atmospheric anomalies separating the player from precious loot is a reward in itself (In addition to the valuable Artifacts!) In-game achievements also provide singular or recurring bonuses, which incentivizes their collection. The game can also be further expanded on with third-party content modifications. Which isn't to say that the game doesn't speak for itself. It can, and does.
A somewhat colorless landscape can become tiresome, and a plethora of glitches and development oversights can frustate a player. Questlines have branches depending on interaction with NPCs, which is not made immediately clear to the player. Access to a certain location of in-game popular legend is also quite tedious and it is unclear how the player can do this without consulting a guide (As of this writing I am unaware of any in-game hints to its location or how to get into it.).
Call of Priptyat became a favorite of mine very quick, and I recommend it to all who want a game with much depth of character.

This game is fantastic, but it is not for everyone. The gameplay is a hero-based, 4 vs 4, turn-based combat. Everyone inputs their moves, having 20 seconds to do so. Then, all the actions resolve simultaneously, according to a clearly defined priority list. So it is possible to dodge an attack that you know is coming, but if your opponent predicts your dodge, he can attack instead the new location you are moving to.  The maps are well made, the champ design is great, and the game has good art, music, and sound. Game balance is constantly evolving but is currently in a good place, where almost all characters are viable.
The unique feature about the turn based combat is that it is fully deterministic. There is no random chance for crit or miss, or random effects on skills, so the outcome of a battle fully depends on your ability to outplay your opponent.
There are three main ways of doing that: You can keep information hidden from your opponent by utilizing fog of war, predicting the moves your opponents will do and reacting to them, and making moves that are not predicted by your opponent. For example, if you know that all your opponents expect you to dodge to safety, they might not even attack you. What better time to stand still and unleash your strongest skill?
I've played over 100 hours of atlas reactor and the game is still very fresh. It's more fun playing in a group, so bring your friends or check out the free discord server and have fun!

I've been playing since Alpha Sneak Peak, so my Steam time is inaccurate. (My Steam key was given to me by Trion, but that's because I already owned Atlas Reactor.)
Atlas Reactor takes the turn-based gameplay of XCOM and throws it into a team arena, and tops it all off with a colorful, cyberpunk world.
If you like strategy games, you'll probably like this. Although it does still require you to be quick-thinking with time limits, but even post-surgery I was able to play without stressing (I didn't do well, but that's to be expected on all those meds).
As its still beta/early access, there's only 3 maps and 16 characters, only one game mode and no ranked play yet, but the gameplay is so solid that I'm loving it in spite of the option limitations.
Each character has their strengths and are all distinct from each other, with customization on secondary features on their abilities to make them play the way you want - and no one combination seems to be the best for anyone. There's no real team composition meta, either- sure, 1 frontliner, 2 firepower, and a support might seem optimal, but I've won games as and lost games to things like 3 frontliners + 1 support, or 3 supports + 1 firepower. So every match is going to play out uniquely.
There's also no RNG to get angry over. Abilities do fixed damage, moves happen in certain phases, all there is is your skill and ability to predict what the other team is doing, and communicate with your team on what to do.
Damn, what an action-packed classic.

If you haven't played Shadow Warrior, well then you missed something! You can play the classic one for free or consider buying the redux one at full price or discounted.
So, Shadow Warrior is a little fast paced-shooter where your goal is to make your way to stop the Zilla corporation from dominating the world. In order to do that you’ll need to come across many levels and in each level you need to find some more or less hidden keys or solving some puzzles.

"The Zilla Corporation is the most powerful of these conglomerates and will stop at nothing to achieve domination unseen by any other corporation in the world. Lo Wang, Zilla Corporation’s legendary Shadow Warrior, discovers this corruption and the dark powers being summoned to aid his employers in this quest for absolute power. As a man of honor, Lo Wang vows to battle these demonic forces with an arsenal of explosive weapons, his silent blade, and a razor-sharp wit."
So yeah your goal is to save the world from the Zilla Corporation several times!

Do not expect a lot from this redux, it's mostly tweaked graphics for higher resolution. But the game doesn't aged so much, which is good.

Like any FPS from the 90s area your goal is to reach the exit of each level and reach the final boss. To do so you need to make your way by killing every enemy you may encounter using only your katana and shuriken at the beginning but you'll progressively unlock a wide variety of deadly weapons ! And of course you can save your game at any time!
Adding to the weapons, ammunitions, health pack and armor pack, you'll also find several items you can use. This includes a portable medikit, caltrops (shuriken like but for the ground), a repair kit (to repair American-made machines), a poison gas and an item that make you invisible. Another good item are the fortune cookies which give you a true fun fact and an additional 50 HP to your health up to 200 HP.
In order to reach the exit you most likely need to find several keys, some are in plain sights and some are pretty well hidden. Sometimes you need to solve a puzzle instead: moving things, using machines or finding the right combination. And a few times you need to beat a boss instead. In my opinion bosses were much more aggressive and challenging in the main campaigns ant not at all in the bonus one.
You will come across huge amount of levels with most of the time hundreds of enemies to defeat! But don't worry Lo Wang with his skills, weapons and voice lines are here!  And each level is very different, except you may be tired after playing the game for more than 8 hours.
Anyway, in each level there is a fair amount of secret areas to find and sometimes a secret exit to play a secret level! Well they are most likely faster to finish but it's not that obvious as you may think because they are also enemies here! And the good thing is you can backtrack at any time during the level and you can also show the in-game tracking too.
After beating a level you'll have you score with your time.

The music is fine, you can play with it or mute it. The best part are the Wo Lang voice lines. You may not be tired of listening him over and over again.

They are all easily doable, only one will need a bit of practice which is a speed run of any level. But here again you can over use the save feature if needed, and the speed run is 1 minute long. (55 seconds or less to beat the speed run time)
The only tedious achievement is the one where you need to find most of the secrets area, but don't worry you don't need to find them all. If you die during the level and found any secret again it will count.
There are several achievements which are level related, so be sure to make a save at the beginning of every level in case you missed it. You can still use the level select cheat code but it seems it doesn't work for every level.

Oh Lord, I forgot to write a review!
More than 900 hours with the game open, and more than 500 hours of ingame action, and I somehow forgot about this part.
Well... it's good. Yeah. Very good.
The graphics are the high point. They might not be the most highly rendered or realistic of the games out right now, but the art style and love of design is very, very apparent. It reminds me of how much love was put into the Neogothic designs in Dark Souls -- yes, it's that gorgeous. Sweeping backgrounds, claustrophobic hallways, daunting shadows and scenic diasporas. The enemies, weapons, and warframes are all given depth and details that make them stand out... well, to be blunt, they usually stand out REALLY clearly... but because of how HIGHLY CUSTOMISABLE the color schemes of the weapons and warframes are, it can sometimes be hard to realize that the lovingly colored and outfitted player that you're staring at has a certain function he might fulfill in your group. Telling equipment and frames apart in the frantic fires of battle is tough as a box of nails, but in the down time there's plenty of pretty sights to admire.
The game mechanics are good bordering on great. There's an absolute plethora of weapons and "Warframes" (read: Character husks with individual, specialized powers) to be had, and each feels suitably unique in their application. The levels are mostly a series of semi-linear randomly connected dungeon tiles with very distinct styles and layouts, with the grand exception of the recently added "Plains of Eidolon" sandbox level of Earth. There's a slew of modes, but they mostly boil down to either "kill everything", "defend this/these", "hunt this mook" or "sneak here". Bosses are somewhat unique, with the most interesting of the bosses being those with environmental tricks -- Kela de Thaym, the Twin Queens, and the Teralyst come to mind. The biggest complaint to be had is that there's a grind involved in unlocks, and this brings up the most contentious aspect of this game.
It's free to play. Before you stop reading, though, hear me out. Everything that affects gameplay can be earned ingame, and the premium currency - platinum - can be garnered by earning and selling item parts and blueprints through the ingame trade chat (read: with other players!). The best use of that currency when you're a fresh player is on weapon and warframe slots so that you can keep the weapons and warframes that you actually enjoy. It's encouraged for you to sell the others since slots are limited.
Something that I noticed about myself when playing this: I started thinking after a while "man... putting that on my weapon would be super useful... and I have played for almost 100 hours, what's 10$ compared to that?"... I think that the model of free to play that's been developed here is NOT in any way disingenuous to the playerbase. There's nothing here that DEMANDS that you pay for a fair share of the gameplay. At no point did I feel it was necessary to put money into this game. I did it because it felt like DE had earned it. Trust me, you'll get your bang for your buck out of this WELL before you ever actually put any bucks down.
To top that off, understand that the PRIMARY focus of this game is COOPERATIVE PLAY. Most F2P games live or die by how they appeal to "whales", and this game is probably no exception. What this game does right however is that it does NOT hurt you if someone else spends their money - you're at no disadvantage by the game's own measures if you don't throw around dollars. It's all cosmetics or rate of play; if someone who's a big roller joins your team, then they will most likely just help you steamroll the objectives. Nothing here to tie your ego to your wallet, and no rich kiddies beating you into the ground because their own daddy was a trust fund baby. Just good 'ol mook annihilation.
If nothing else, just give it a shot. It might be a big download to just turn on for a glance, but I think anyone and everyone should give it a look.

If your looking for a great free to play game, then you have found one. Here are the pros and cons.
Pros.
AI.
Warframe is one of the few FtP games that has an extreamly intelligent AI system.
The AI will respond to their surrondings and any simuli they encounter (i.e. dead bodies, a sound, an arrow in the wall, their alllies stuck to the wall by multipul arrows, etc.)
Warframe also has an amazing stealth system, honestly, the best I've seen in any MMO. Enemies will usally only notice you if you are if their line of sight, or you fire a weapon that makes a loud noise, or if you do a flying kick into the back of their heads.
Levels.
Warframe has randomly generated maps, so no two levels will ever be the same, (that, or all the interior decorators have far too much time on thier hands.)
There is also a large variety of maps to choose from, including, but not limited to: desert, high tech ship, ice planet (tauntaun not included, please see the Lotus Help Desk for more information, thank you.)
Weaponry.
A large array of weapons for player to chose from allows any play style, from silent assassin, to loud explosive crowd control, and anything in between. Personaly, I mix the loud and quiet, for stealthy crowd control, silent but deadly.
Also recently, the devs have added weapon crafting to allow players to create more costomized weapons.
Warframes.
As the title say you are playing as warframes, powerful and sometimes unstoppable Tenno.
The number of warframes is always growing and there are improved (prime) versions of some warframes.
Each warframe is attuned to a certain element, power, or being. For example, the most well known warframe, Excalibur, uses swordsman/knight like powers, Ember on the other hand, has powers related to fire and heat.
Community.
The Warframe community is a, for lack of better words, diverse group of players. (Depending on set region and time of day.)
We range from casual players, to hardcore competition gamers.
Guilds can be classified as a sub-group to the community, if not, I don't see the point of guilds then. Thier are a large number of guilds in Warframe that many people are and can be part of. Guilds are a great way to connect with people who have similar ideas and want to be with likeminded individuals.
PVP.
PVP is a part of Warframe that I don't induldgue in too much, but it has been implicated very well by the D.E. team.
The PVP is composed of: a soccer like game (known as Lunaro,) team VS. team, or a free for all arena battles.
D.E. has made this game mode fair for all players by limiting weapons, warframes, and mods that are allowed in the PVP battles.
That basically handles all of the pros. Now for the cons. (Not conventions, but those are a real thing, and they are usually held in Canada.)
Cons.
Monetary System.
Warframe is based on the in-game currency known as "Platinum," or "Plat," as it is known as in-game.
You buy slots for weapons, warframes, companions, etc, with this plat. Without it you cannot keep and improve your arsenal.
The only ways obtain plat are, to spend real money, or trade hard-to-find components to other players for theirs.
The only good thing about obtaining plat is that when you log in for the first time each day, you have a chance of getting a plat discount of up to 75% off.
Grinding.
The game is mostly grinding. If you are used to the daily grind, then you will be fine with Warframe, if not, you can always pay plat for what you need in-game.
Other.
Beside the usual trolls, cheaters, and in general rude people (holding back to not be censored,) the working with other players can be a fun time as long as y'all are enjoying yourselves.
Conclusion.
If you have made it this far, then you have a good deal of patience and are willing to read before you play. Overall I would give Warframe a 12.6785049058230 out of 14.98549375639943847 so all-in-all a realy good game and a worthwhile play.

If I had to come up with a short phrase what this game is, I would say "This is Guitar Hero with REAL guitars!". Rocksmith is very good with teaching newcomers to guitar on how to actually play the guitar with it's very interactive User Interface, and it records how you are doing on each song you play. If you are doing good, it bumps you up a few notes, all the way until you reach 100% and you are playing note for note, chord per chord. It also has instructional videos on how to do certain techniques and then it has you doing that technique and it makes sure that you are doing the techniques properly.
Not only is this good for newcomers or beginners, but it is also useful for experienced and/or intermediate players! Especially when you are really busy and you don't have the time to practice as much, this game really brings you the motivation to want to practice as much as you used to before your busy schedual.
The Amp mode is very well thought out, and it very useful for people who want to create their own unique sound with different amps and pedals, without having to buy amps and a lot of different pedals.
If you are into guitar and you want a good way to learn guitar without having to pay a lot of money a week for lessons or you are looking for a good fun way to practice different styles of music, then I would say this is the game for you; and before I forget, you can also play bass guitars as well, and you can use ANY electric guitar and electric bass guitar.

Call of Pripyat shows its age and wears it well. Charming and exciting, even its quirks are endearing. It's the way I like my women, too. So, I was quickly enamored.

Despite many bugs, flaws and perhaps a slightly desolate and incomplete atmosphere, Call of Pripyat holds itself together with captivating gameplay. Challenging combat (on higher difficulties) requires careful consideration of one's equipment loadout. A fairly complex gear modification mechanic aids in this task, and ensures that a shabby AK-74u can become a bullet hose that can take down a charging bloodsucker before it gets within striking distance. But being able to detect the near invisible creature still remains an issue. As it's an open-world, non-linear game, exploration is a core element to gameplay. Without a fast travel system, one is left with the responsibility of getting from point A to point B quickly and safely. A gloomy landscape adds tension to travels, as does roving packs of wild dogs.
It is difficult to become bored with Call of Pripyat as there are many sidequests as well many Artifacts and item stashes to be found and plundered. Being able to navigate through the dangerous atmospheric anomalies separating the player from precious loot is a reward in itself (In addition to the valuable Artifacts!) In-game achievements also provide singular or recurring bonuses, which incentivizes their collection. The game can also be further expanded on with third-party content modifications. Which isn't to say that the game doesn't speak for itself. It can, and does.
A somewhat colorless landscape can become tiresome, and a plethora of glitches and development oversights can frustate a player. Questlines have branches depending on interaction with NPCs, which is not made immediately clear to the player. Access to a certain location of in-game popular legend is also quite tedious and it is unclear how the player can do this without consulting a guide (As of this writing I am unaware of any in-game hints to its location or how to get into it.).
Call of Priptyat became a favorite of mine very quick, and I recommend it to all who want a game with much depth of character.

Play along with the great selection of built in songs, maybe pick up some of the growing number of DLC songs or search around online for you favourite songs added in by modders!
The minigames are superb for building basic guitar skills, from moving your fingers around the fretboard to learning your basic scales. Sadly you won't be learning the Drums here but Rock Band already does a pretty nice job of emulating that so fear not drummers. Guitarists and Bassists need to pick this up though.

Atlas Reactor plays like a tactical miniatures game (think, "Infinity"), where each single character is controlled by a single person.
Turns are played out simultaneously, with four phases each (Prep, Dash, Blast, then Run). Each character has skills that activate at certain phases. While the actions of each phase are played out sequentially, they are done at the same time (if one character shoots another dead in Blast, the other character's Blast action still goes off). An action done in a previous phase can affect one done in a later phase (if one character stuns another the Blast phase, the other character's Run action doesn't occur). All choices are made during the initial Decision Phase (allied choices are normally shown). The decision phase has a 20 seconds timer (normally enough to think out choices, without becoming irritating to quick-thinkers).
This creates a game where success relies on predicting your opponent, cooperating with your team, and tracking you opponent's abilities are essential to success.
While the Tutorial explains the basics, it seemed lacking in explaining certain mechanics. It's recommended that a few Practice/AI games be played to gain familiarity.
So far, I haven't run into any major bugs.

I found Atlas Reactor to be a refreshing change of pace in online, multiplayer games. Although it can be compared to other "arena style" games like DOTA and League, I feel as though Atlas is a genre all of its own, mixing arena battle with a turn-based combat very XCOMesque.
The game currently has 16 "Freelancers" varying from support, to melee/tank "frontliners" and DPS "firepower". Each character has 5 unique abilities. Each ability falls under one of three types; prep, dash and blast. These types (Plus Move) take up the segments of a turn, each taking place during the turn in sequence. Prep abilities trigger first, followed by dash abilities or those abilities that allow your character to do a quick move on the board. The blast phase is the main combat phase that characters dish out their damage. Regardless of how much damage you have taken in the turn, every character gets to contribute to the turn meaning everyone uses their ability regardless of when in the turn they die. As the game progresses from turn to turn, characters battle each other for a 5 kill score with the winners coming out on top (and netting more xp and ELO, the ranking points system)
Account progression allows characters to earn ISO to purchase new character unlocks like skins, taunts, and special talent changes to abilities. The Season game mode allows you to earn loot boxes for the crafting minigame where you can make XP boosts (GG boosts) new background banners, titles and skins.
Overall the game, being in Beta, has room to grow. The foundation for a fun, competitive arena style game has opened up new directions for a world dominated by MOBA and I feel that Atlas, although NOT A MOBA has a place at the table to represent a unique and challenging experience for those familiar to them.

Loved the first one to bits, was so hyped for the sequel, didn't get into the early access as I didn't want to spoil the pleasure but bought the game soon after the official release. Played it with my gf via split-screen coop. The experience can be summed up with one word - a chore.
Pros:
- The narrator is awesome.
- The voice acting is decent, some characters are excellent.
- Some dialogues are smart and funny, mostly pet-pal related stuff.
- It's got dwarves in it.
- The co-op component is implemented in a very intuitive, user friendly way.
- The music is better than in the first game.
- IT'S GOT DWARVES IN IT! Other games take example.
- Character progression and itemization are OK.
- The game comes packed with various roleplaying options and features.
- The storyline is quite open, there is no good guys vs bad guys, it's not clear whether we (as a party) should be doing the things that we're doing. It's all grey area, sacrifice for the greater good sort of story but it's always up to the player to draw the line.
- The journal is a nice touch, way better than your usual quest tracker, unfortunately navigating it with a controller is a chore.
- The Game Master mode is pure gold.
Cons:
- The main story is terrible. Seriously, the first one wasn't that strong either, but at least it didn't treat itself overly seriously. The sequel is cheesy and plain stupid, but it's oh so serious about the plot. It feels like a third-grade fan fiction, or a tabletop RP game run by a weak but overly ambitious 14yo GM.
- The origin stories are weak, the characters in general are weak and not interesting. Couldn't care less.
- The pace of the game is uneven, often times you will find yourself wondering what's next, where should I go or why am I here in the first place? Unfortunately the game is designed in such a way, that even 1 level makes all the difference in the world. So if you wonder off the road or arrive in a certain place too early you will run into some tough, unfair fights. This was similar in the first game, but in the first game you could handle some tougher enemies by being creative and careful. Here's not the case due to terrible encounter design, shallow tactics and linear flow of combat. More below.
- The combat, the highlight of the title, the thing that kept me playing through the first game, is utterly boring. The encounter design is terrible. I loved the fights in the first one, the planning, the strategies, the enemies. Here 99% encounters feel like trash fights - all are virtually the same. Every enemy can fly, cast spells, teleport, shoot, heal etc. Usually your party gets ambushed with enemies popping out of the thin air. There's no preparation, no scouting, no positioning. CC, spell combos, buffs, debuffs, positioning etc all are next to useless - raw physical damage is the way to go most of the time. Boring.
- Some encounters are just plain stupid. Do not confuse stupid with difficult. The first game had some very difficult yet enjoyable and rewarding fights. Here it's just not fun, the enemies cheat all the time, the game can instakill you on random, the fights are long and tedious, sometimes there's a key component to a fight and if you don't know it you are bound to lose.
- You either fight a long, unfair, mostly boring battle you are very likely to lose, or... you can easily cheese the crap out of most encounters. Lame design.
- The bloody necrofire, seriously, it's ugly, it's overused, it's annoying, it's hard to see or select anything, yet it's up 80% fights.
- The game is riddled with bugs, nothing major so far (mainly UI and controller related stuff), but the little buggers take out another chip of enjoyment from this game. It's been in development for so long it's unacceptable.
- The UI for the gamepad is cumbersome, way too big. Cannot be scaled down.
- Loading screens are waaaaaay to long.
The first game was lighthearted and fun, the combat system was excellent, the encounters were very well designed and interesting. The sequel is a bloated mess, the story is overly serious yet very silly and childish, the combat system offers less variety, feels slower and unbalanced, the combat encounters feel uninspired, repetitive and boring. Beware of bugs. Been waiting for this game a long time but I sincerely regret spending money on it. It's big, it looks good, all the components look good on paper but it's just not fun to play. Going through the main story is a chore. Reading the dialogue is a chore. Fighting your way through boring fights is a chore. Exploring the world is a chore. There is a good game somewhere underneath, I guess some people will like it as it is. I didn't.
Verdict:
A chore.

An incredible pure-gameplay experience.
There is perhaps a modicum of a "story" here but it is basically a pure first-person-shooter gameplay experience and an adrenaline packed one at that. You step forward in the dark to grab the only thing you can see, a dagger and the experience begins. Sounds alert you to what direction you should be facing and you see a low-poly column in the distance. Suddenly it starts spewing out skulls. Kill them all, one hit and you're dead.
The action builds to a wonderful crescendo, the longer you last, the harder the game tries to kill you. At a certain point if you're like me you'll slip into a kind of zen, where you aren't actively "paying attention" but you are able to do quick, slight turns to knock a skull out of reality. The enemies have a wonderful gothic feel and the game keeps pulling you back even as it pushes you away with punishing difficulty. The goal? Live as long as you can and beat the others who have played. I have made it into the top 1000 players and I think that is the best I can hope for at the moment.
This game is worth whatever price is currently on it if you like FPS gameplay and challenging yourself.

The Good:
The story is as good if not better than the first game. It's basically a continuation but you see more of what's going on and you meet some new and interesting characters, Then beat the hell out of them.

The Bad:
It's so hard it's not funny. Later on in particular you need to arrive at the boss fights in good shape or you may as well not bother. This can be harder than it sounds.
There's a fair number of maze/wayfinding puzzle type missions. I'm not a fan. You might be. There's enough of them that I found it unimaginative/lazy. One in particular made no sense at all.
The gear and purchase options are just more of the same. Nothing really stands out or gives you a noticeable edge. The addition of food as a combat item is so you can survive rather than prosper. This is fine if you've got what you need. If you can't find or buy ingredient x it's just another frustration as you've then got to ID the monster and head back to wherever it is. Again, if you're not in good shape for whatever reason this can be a chore.
Overall I can't recommend this game. The effort vs. reward just doesn't stack up. Sure it's a decent story but you just don't feel any sense of progression as you work through it. The next wandering monster can maul you just as much if not more than the first. You know for certain that the next boss will have the upper hand and there's nothing you can do to counter it that makes much if any difference. In short, It's a slog and I want more than that from a game.

Frankly one of my favorite games in my library. A complete call back to the classic JRPGs of the mid-90s, Trails in the Sky easily belongs in the same category as Final Fantasy V, VI, and Chrono Trigger. It's got a well-detailed world, individual NPCs who almost all each have their own name (if they don't all), memorable music, fun characters, and an excellent storyline for the genre. Combat is turn-based with tiles, giving it the tactics sense where you position characters to avoid enemy attacks, and knock enemies around to maximize area attacks. If you think more JRPGs need to be on Steam, then get this game to say so.
As a side note, I level grinded for maybe 20 minutes total at the end of the game, so that really is 70+ hours of just gameplay, exploration, and side quests.
Edit: Nominated for the No Apologies Award because frankly I still listen to the soundtrack and get choked up by remembering certain moments.

In my review of Trails in the Sky First Chapter (FC), I felt inclined to refrain from mentioning any criticisms, largely because the only criticisms I had were nit-picky. I was full of praise as to how this game differs from any other JRPG I had played prior to the games in the Legend of Heroes series. As result, I purchased Trails in the Sky Second Chapter (SC) almost immediately after it was released on steam. In terms of gameplay and the overall mechanics in SC, they remain largely identical to FC and therefore there is no need to dwell on them in this review. I recognise that this review probably will not mean much to those who loved FC as it is likely they have already bought and finished SC. Likewise if you did not like FC, then I would be surprised if you are considering buying SC.
I can confidently say right off the bat that FC and SC together are among the best games I have ever played, with SC expanding on the greatness that was FC.
The consequence of playing and adoring FC is that I had extremely high expectations going into SC. Whilst those expectations were entirely met, this time around my review cannot be so clear cut as it was for FC. In order to review this game fairly and without bias, I intend to mention a noticeable flaw I identified because it would be ignorant to ignore it.
*No spoilers*
The story in SC is definitely a step up from FC, with enough plot twists to make you run around the room in excitement... I know I did. Every main character is developed from the first game in a meaningful way. Even Estelle develops from a largely clumsy, hilarious and enthusiastic person to a more mature... clumsy, hilarious and enthusiastic person.
Like FC, the story is split into a series of well-structured chapters, however in SC the game is separated into 9 different chapters rather than the 4 main chapters in FC. As expected the story neatly follows from FC. My main criticism of the game is based on the first 4 chapters. The problem with these chapters is that by chapter 2, the story gets largely predictable with the similar kind of occurrence happening in each chapter (I'll spare the details). Of course the predictability ends soon after the 4th chapter. This may not necessarily be a problem for many who have played SC, but it did get a tad repetitive, especially in conjunction with the side quests which do not vary that much. However, this is largely where my noticeable criticisms end and I appreciate this is largely a subjective criticism.
To this day, the 5th and 6th chapters of SC were... Some of the best segments of a game I have played in my entire life... And I have played a lot of games!
Although I will not describe the contents of those chapters, they were the most deeply engaging, emotional and thrilling parts of a game I have ever played, galvanizing anyone into adoring the game. I wish I could describe the details.
The ending of the game is satisfying. That is my greatest hope for any sequel of a JRPG. It is far too easy for games to conclude having left more questions than answers. Although there is a cliff-hanger which sets up the Third Chapter (TC), it is not the kind of cliff-hanger which leaves a lack of fulfilment and a taste of disappointment. As I mentioned to a friend, I would not mind if the Third Chapter is never localized... That’s not to say that when it is finished being localized I won't play it. I will buy it on the day it is released! Hell I will stay up all night with a countdown clock till its release! Nevertheless, what I am concluding is that the Second Chapter had a satisfying ending; it felt like the hours I had put into the game actually meant something significant in the end, rather than leaving a lingering anticipation for what happens next.
There is very little which can be said about gameplay other than it is almost identical to the First Chapter. In my review of FC, I mentioned the way in which gameplay differs from other JRPG's I am familiar with such as games in the Final Fantasy franchise. This difference remains the same in SC. The main new mechanic in SC is the ability to combine attacks with different characters (Chain attacks). They were a nice new addition to the game, but nothing revolutionary. If you loved the gameplay and the battle system in FC, then it follows that you should feel the same about SC.
The first thing I wanted to know when I bought the game is how the music would differ from FC. I have invested hours into listening to the music of FC outside of the game and I will probably spend many hours more listening to FC's OST. I can gladly say, the soundtrack in SC is a masterpiece - my favourites being: 'The Dream Continues,' 'Silver Will' and 'I Swear.' I do not recommend listening to any of the soundtrack before playing the game, solely because of the emotional effect they have within the game. None of the pieces are overused or underused. The first thing I did after finishing the game was search for the pieces on YouTube.
FC and SC felt like a dream. I say this as the two games felt like perfect games with very few flaws. Although I stated my noticeable criticism of SC, it is insignificant when looking at the overall standard of the game. The characters remain as funny as they were in FC, the story is brilliant, the music is sensational and the localization is without flaws. Only Aidios knows why this game is not as popular as it should be. I have always felt that it is the most well-made games which receive the least credit. I am now in the process of playing Trails of Cold Steel. As for the Third Chapter, I can only hope the dream continues.

I remember when I first saw A Virus Named Tom, and thought. "Wow that's so cool looking".  The graphics looked good, and the idea or a really good puzzler got me hyped for it.   I was so interested.    And now that I played it, I kind of wish I got a different game.
It's not that A Virus Named Tom is horrible.  It's well made, and the story is fun enough.  But the gameplay is just too annoying to be recommendable.
About half of the levels in this game are fantastic.  Like A+ puzzle solving, and interesting.  It's just the other half of the levels are some of the most annoying that I've played recently.  Some of them are just tedious, or monotonous.  And a few are just frustration filled.
The game plays a bit like pipedream where you have to make a path.  The difference is there's no time component to the game, and all the player can do is rotate the squares.  This works well.  And while the control scheme is a little annoying, it works.   In fact it's kind of fun.
The other side of the game is that it takes a lot to make a game out of that idea.  With Pipe Dream there's a huge time component.  With A Virus Named Tom the game gets into a number of other ideas.  While there's a time component for score, the majority of A Virus Named Tom is played with enemies, or other annoyances to slow down the player.
The two big complaints I have for the game is the mystery blocks, and the twitch gameplay.  In the second set of levels you start finding these mystery blocks.  This isn't awful at first, but they reuse those mystery blocks entirely too much.  Eventually when you get to the third set of levels they start to disappear, but overall, they are some of the most annoying  blocks in the game.   The issue with them is that the player must either remember the board, the pattern they need, or just fiddle with the blocks until they work.  It's a pointless exercise.  While some levels like that could be interesting, they come TOO often, and aren't very fun gameplay elements.  If they flashed every 5 seconds it might be useful, instead it's just a full mystery the entire time.
The second issue that's quite annoying is about half the levels have enemies.  Most of the time this is fine, you just have to keep spatial awareness.  However quite a few times these enemies move too fast, or are there just to test your twitch gameplay.    You have to react too fast.  If this is a puzzle game, it shouldn't take that much control and just is annoying.  If this is a twitch gameplay, where is that action for the rest of the game.  Those are some of the worst designed levels that I've seen.  I like the game mind you, I just hate those twitch levels.
I loved the look of A Virus Named Tom when I first saw it, I thought it looked interesting, but now that I've played it (on ps3 and PC) I have to say, I'm not a fan of it.  It's not an awful game, it's just trying to be two types of game, and doesn't really succeed at being either.   It's a fun puzzler to start, but quickly changes into a game filled with frustration, rather than challenge.  A shame, but I just can't recommend this game.

A big part of the game is proper itemization. Making correct item choices and sometimes even predictions is crucial to a team’s success. Naturally, having more farm has its advantages, providing a greater deal of flexibility in itemization, but knowing when to get certain items, and their relative strengths and weaknesses, is still a skill worthy of development.
BKB costs 3975 gold and provides +10 Strength and +24 Attack Damage. Compared to most items in this price range, it is clear that BKB is inferior in terms of stats provided. What it does, however, is provide your hero with several seconds of spell immunity, which, depending on the situation, might either be absolutely game-changing or redundant.
Usually, the first big reason people get a BKB is to counter disables. No matter how high your DPS is, your hero can’t attack while stunned, and BKB is often a necessity. You have to carefully consider the duration and availability of the enemy disables. Moreover, knowing their cast points is also helpful—very few players have enough experience and game sense to anticipate a 0-cast point disable and perfectly time their BKB usage. Obviously, knowing the list of BKB-penetrating abilities is necessary.
Also carefully consider whether you being immune to disables is actually doing anything for your team. As stated previously, BKB is a very weak item when it comes to providing you with DPS—the stats on it are rather low. Having magic immunity is not going to win you fights on its own--you have to actually utilize these precious several seconds to deal maximum amounts of damage. As an early-game purchase, therefore, BKB is only viable on a handful of core heroes, who generally fall into the “glass cannon” category.

Got the Steam version just so I could leave a review on this game.
Do I recommend this game? Yes and no.
If you're looking for an OSU or a DDR clone then you're in the wrong place. Stop leaving negative reviews because it's not the gameplay you expected, that is unfair and childish. If you are looking for games similar to OSU, check out Touch Online.
And no I am not being paid "in-game currency" to publish or write this review. This is all me.
I've been playing Audition Online on and off since the days of Nexon (roughly 2007) and the game has gone through some changes, both good and bad.
For starters: The Steam port is just awful, there is some notable lag spikes in the Steam version versus downloading the game directly from the Redbana website.
This is part of why new users were scared off, the other issue is the lack of noob friendly gameplay and rooms. The community is bad, it's awful, don't let anyone convince you otherwise. I've been banned from rooms for being too good, so I know the pain of getting banned over how you play the game.
The game is also full of non-English speakers, so there is a lot of language boundaries.
Not to mention all of the locked and afk rooms. The game is dying, but not giving it a chance is helping it die faster.
The thing that differs Audition from other rhythm based MMO's is its unique gameplay. It requires a steep learning curve, and that scares a lot of people off. Even back in the days when it was popular, it was scary, but at least noob servers were offered in those days.
Redbana is partly responsible for the game's decline, but so are these negative reviews.
It is corrupt that they tried paying users for good reviews and it is sad that the community is trash, but no one here seems to be trying to fix the issues at hand.
The negative reviews that say all the items in the game cost money are blatantly lying. Yes, some items in the game cost real money, but not all of the items. All MMO's have in-game purchases that are over-priced, get over it.
I'm surprised many people dislike the graphics, if anything they're adorable. The game has a unique look to it. They never tried to be realistic like many other Korean kpop games. There is nothing else like Audition.
The updates are little to none, and not all of the songs are popular, but they lack money. The sheer fact the game is still running is outstanding in on itself. The people behind Redbana have a certain love for it, if they didn't, it wouldn't still exist.
Audition IS a good game. It's fun. Every time I come back I get addicted again. It's challenging and it keeps players on their toes. The game should be reviewed based on its gameplay, and it has fantastic gameplay. There is no denying that. If for a moment you forgot the trash community, the in-game purchases, and lag spikes, you've got a great game.
RECAP:
Pros:
* Character customization
* Challenging gameplay
* Cute graphics
* Many modes
* Lots of songs (This game is very friendly for YouTube gameplay videos, as many of the music is composed by Redbana)
* Items do not affect how well someone plays, a non-paying user is just as good as a paying user
Cons:
* Lack of updates
* Corrupt GMs (game masters)
* Unpopular songs
* In-game purchases (NOT REQUIRED!)
* Takes forever to level up
* Unfriendly to newcomers
* Toxic community
In the end, if you're looking for a challenging rhythm game, Audition Online is for you. If you're looking to make friends or play something similar to OSU, look elsewhere.
