I like a good card game, and I like deck-building games, so I decided to give Star Realms a try and see what it had to offer. As I'm sure many people have said before, Star Realms is very similar to Dominion, but with a few differences. Since I've played both, I can't really review Star Realms without making these comparisons.
The first difference is the win condition. Instead of accumulating a limited amount of victory points, in Star Realms you deplete your opponent's authority (ie. health points) down to zero.
Secondly, instead of having a large selection of cards in limited numbers for purchase, in Star Realms you are limited to five choices per turn in what I'm going to call the "buy zone", one of which constantly replenishes itself (the Explorer), and the other four which deal a new random card to fill an empty spot after each card is purchased.
Lastly, you can, and often do, play all the cards out of your hand in a single turn in Star Realms. There is a convenient "Play All" button for this, though the game will not automatically play certain cards that have optional effects. In Dominion, you are limited in the number of actions and purchases you can make in a turn.
Otherwise the two games play very similarly. You draw five cards to form your hand, cards go to the discard pile once played or bought, and you shuffle your discard pile once your deck is exhausted to form a new deck. The mechanic of "scrapping" a card (called trashing in Dominion, where a card is permanently removed from your deck) to gain effects is also present. Combos are essential for advanced play, and the various "factions" present in Star Realms echo the expansions of Dominion.
Though Star Realms is the same type of card game as Dominion, I found it less enjoyable, as luck is more favored over strategy.
Part of the problem is being able to play all the cards out of your hand during every turn. Because I never encountered a card that had a mandatory effect that also had a downside (ex. forcing you to scrap a card), there are no hard choices to make during a turn as to which cards to play. This has the ultimate effect of overemphasizing the "luck of the draw", as how effective your turn will be depends on your entire hand and how well it synergizes. This also makes the mechanic of forcing the player to discard their hand after a turn ends useless, because I never once encountered a situation where I didn't want to, or couldn't, play all the cards in my hand.
The random composition of cards in the buy zone adds an additional level of luck to the game. When building your deck, synergy is difficult to achieve. You can try and build the best deck you can, but you can't predict when the cards you need are going to appear. Also, there are many lower priced cards with effects far better than more expensive ones, and you never know when those are going to show up to replace what you just bought, leaving your opponent with an easy buy that gives them an immediate advantage. This is not mitigated by the fact that you can see the composition of your opponent's deck at any time, because any counter strategy you might devise is, again, solely dependent on the cards you need randomly showing up in the buy zone, which may never happen.
As for options, the basic game doesn't have many. Campaign play is locked behind a paywall after the first chapter, as are multiplayer and the higher difficulty levels, and the amount of cards is very limited. There are a considerable number of resolution settings, but considering this game could probably run on a potato, they are largely useless. By strange contrast, audio settings are virtually nonexistent. On or off are your only options for music and sounds.
Star Realms does have its upsides. The game plays quickly, the artwork is good (if a little generic), the focus of each faction is easy to learn, and the total amount of money required to fully enjoy the game is low compared to other card games on Steam. Many people find it exciting and more fun to play than Dominion, but I didn't. It got dull too quickly, and the lack of cards in the basic game doesn't help it much, especially considering the base game of Dominion (which contains far more content and doesn't lock multiplayer behind a paywall), is itself now available as a free online game. Dominion's expansions are more expensive than Star Realms', but at the same time, Dominion offers more content with its expansions than just cards.
TLDR; As a cheaper version of Dominion, Star Realms serves adequately, but lack of cards and poor rules make for a game where strategy matters less than luck. Initially intriguing, but didn't have the lasting appeal of its bigger brother.

Before I begin, let me make it abundantly clear that I absolutely love and fully reccomend Euro Truck Simulator 2. This is not a matter of me not enjoying this type of game; I love that game, and honestly, I have really enjoyed my brief time with this one. However, that time will not likely increase.
You will find many reviews about this game that claim that the cost is too high, which is the cause for which I write this review. As there is only one DLC state out, however, it is seemingly difficult to predict how much the full price will be. Many argue, 'they are going to charge us $12 for each of the 47 extra states!' This is flawed logic, supporters of the game have pointed out, as I assure you that you will not be charged the same amount for Texas as you would for Vermont. The base for the amount charged, however, seems to be rather consistant with one factor: the square milage. So if we are to assume that the square milage of each state will corralate with the price charged, we can predict the cost of the game. New Mexico ($12) is 121,697 sqmi, so we can assume that the going rate is 10,141.42 sqmi/$. So, if we use this formula to find the cost of the extra 47 states, then add on to it the base price of the game, what is the predicted total cost of the United States in ATS?
$356.12
Yes, we can assume that, prettied up, the final cost of the full game will be $350. Don't get me wrong, if you are willing to pay that much for this game, I am in no way judging you. Different people have different levels of interest in different things. It does annoy me, however, that SCS are very sneaky about this. It is more obvoius now, but when ATS came out, there was no way of knowing that extra states were to cost extra money without visiting outside sources. On the steam page, there is no mention of this. And it would be OK if the game was branded more obviously (such as the physical box art of the game which has the word 'California' written on it), but as far as I, a consumer paroozing steam, would think, I am buying a game where I can truck anywhere in the US (at least when the states are released).
I'm also not impressed with the content I am buying. $12 for New Mexico is laughable. Why am I paying over half of the base price for a big desert? No offence to anyone in New Mexico, and I'm sure SCS did it very well, but the base game already has deserts in it. Actually, all of Nevada, Arizona, and a large portion of California is desert. Yet I'm going to pay for more desert? Again, I'm sure the SCS portrait of New Mexico is very good, but $12 seems ridiculous. And that's another part of the problem. This game is pretty cheap, as far as modern games go. $20 for a game as expansive as this is generous, and because of that I have no problem paying extra for the states. I have bought all of the expansion DLC for ETS2, and I would gladly give up to $100 or even a bit more for this game. I don't think it is greedy of me, however, to say that $350 is asking a bit too much.
There are also some other issues with the game that help tip it over the edge. The production rate of the states seems pretty slow (and yes, the guys who make ETS2 and ATS are in two different branches, so I don't want to hear it), though I was impressed with the map size increase. There are only two brands of trucks, and four trucks total. This is because of a marketing issue, and I do feel bad that SCS is having a particularly hard time with this. It is, however, a big problem, and making excuses isn't going to change the fact that it is a big stain on the variety. The thought of SCS releasing more trucks in a DLC pack also annoys me.
So, ultimately, I would give a lot of money to this game, but $350 is just too much. I love ETS2 and, to an extent, what this game wants to be, but it is far too expensive. If you like paying massive amounts of money for a moderate amount of content, I would reccomend Train Simulator.

Hey! This game's actually alright. It's not bad, it fits into a niche and it's fresh and interesting in a way that's presented as simple enough to dive into.
It's one of them competitive team hero-based games except it's turn based strategy combat and the commands are treated as simultaneous (they play sequentially for clarity, if you 'die' to a move you will continue with your orders until the move phase including things that heal you to take you out of death range) and are split into four stages: Prep, Dash, Blast, and then regular moving. And it all plays out into this nicely balanced thing with potential for team synergy (moves are very reliant on skill-shot aiming and requiring positioning co-ordination) and mind games (reading a dash attack by pointing your blast attack in the direction you think they'll try to dodge, etc.).
Characters aren't amazing but it's not like Paladins or Paragon where they're trying to make serious fantasy characters just like every other hero game there is to see. Here they slap a cool design and a kit together, we don't worry about the plot details, and it generally doesn't bother us. Characters are expressive and rarely follow any kind of well-worn templates; looking at the cast for the first time was very "Whoa hang on what am I looking at?" which spun around into being refreshing. Not strong, but not drab, boring, or typical either.
Progression's a little weird. Characters have pick-and-choose augments to abilities which are super easy to acquire but they're worth different amounts of points and you have to remove some from others depending on how expensive the mod you want is and it's not something you can see until you're hit by it in combat either. And it's not like I want to play around with it, usually the default mods are good enough and suit what I think I need.
Was easy enough to learn and start playing but I've got a lot of picking up and studying to do if I'm to find out how I can improve, it's not apparent from gameplay alone where you go wrong because taking damage and eventually dying is just par for the course since lining up shots is always putting you in harms way one way or another and you only have so many escape plans. That last one's not a flaw of the game design, having difficulty getting better is just a consequence of it in some way.

An honest review of Atlas Reactor.
__________________________
*As a heads up, I do not have the game installed on through Steam, I have it installed through Glyph. I played the game since it was in its Pre-Alpha stages of development and have continued played since.*
** PLEASE KEEP IN MIND THAT ATLAS REACTOR IS STILL IN EARLY ACCESS/BETA DEVELOPMENT, THERE ARE FEATURES WHICH STILL NEED TO BE ADDED TO THE AND/OR FINE TUNED. ATLAS REACTOR IS NOT A FINSHED PRODUCT YET! **
Atlas Reactor, an easy to pick up and understand group turn-based MOBA with an interesting and deep depth of strategy to the game.
__________________________
Atlas Reactor is an interesting take on the MOBA genre, it plays likes a turn-base strategy game while also having the competiveness of similar MOBAs like League of Legends and DOTA 2.  In Atlas Reactor, you control a single character called a Freelancer with in a team of 3 other Freelancers. Each Freelancer have their own unique abilities and ways of playing. The goal of is to beat your enemy teem through one of these win condition; first team to 5 kills (Kills are points on the scoreboard) wins or the team with the most kills by the end of turn 20 wins. A game in Atlas Reactor will only last for 20 turns unless the score is tied by turn 20, if that happens than the game goes into an overtime/sudden death. The first team to break the tie score wins. While in Overtime/Sudden Death, a game can go on past turn 20 (I have had matches which have lasted till turn 30+ before).
Atlas Reactor plays at a very timely pace for all players, but that doesn’t necessarily mean all players play at the same pace. For some players, the games pacing may be to slow for them or way to fast when they first start playing the game. Matches tend to be played in a similar way that chess is played, you are meant to analyze what your opponent is doing to figure out your best way to outsmart them while your opponent does the same thing to you, the biggest difference is that you only control 1 piece which can perform multiple action in the game and you must cooperate with 3 other players (this can be rather rough to do since not everyone is going to think the same way, but that is the of a competitive MOBA). Because of this, the game will likely be harder for some players to pick up and understand than compared to others who have a “knack” for games like this.
Though Atlas Reactor is turn-base, combat is done simultaneously based on the phase of combat. This means all Prep abilities activate during the prep phase, all Dash abilities activate in the dash phase, all blast abilities activate in the blast phase, and all movement is done at the end of the blast phase.
___________________________
Pros and Cons of Atlas Reactor
+Pros+
+ Unique Freelancers
+ Good Win Conditions
+ Simple to pick up with deep strategy
+ Fairly easy gameplay with a small introductory learning curve.
+ All Freelancers are free forever!
+ The only Payed unlockables are purely cosmetic, no Pay2Win advantages.
+ Able to unlock unique cosmetic content and some purchasable content through crafting in steading of paying for    it
-Cons-
- The game may be more difficult for some players to understand
- The game has glitches are problems within matches and UI (the game is in EA/Beta still)
- Match fluidity varies between slow and fast (matters on how players play the game)
- Some in game information may be hard to pick up on (Ability Telegraphs)
- Match experience in dependent on how players play and how team comps are made (a bad experience while playing Atlas Reactor may be cause of people pick characters that they just want to try without knowing how to play them).
- The games learning curve will very based on a players experience with MOBAs and Turn-Based strategy games.
___________________________
Here is a quick rundown on why this game is a game you are paying for now and not using the F2P model. Atlas Reactor was originally meant to be a Free 2 Play game, its consumer model with originally designed with that in mind and a lot of the games Alpha/Beta players played the game in its F2P model, but there was an issue with it, the game ended up being rather frustrating to play and develop because you needed really grind a lot of hours to unlock a freelancer(s), a lot of the games development was being used to balance and manage a micro transaction method that was surrounded by people purchasing Freelancers. It clashed with a lot of the games fun dynamics because it would stop players from experiencing the game that other who had all the Freelancers unlocked would experience, this also would cause a problem for upcoming features such as Ranked mode. So, in order to fix this problem, the Atlas Reactor development team decided to go from a F2P model to a buy once and play for ever model in order to keep players on even footing and so everyone is capable of having a good experience in the game overall.
This change didn’t settle well with me at first, I wasn’t full against it, but I knew that it would have quite a backlash when it came down to people getting interested in the game, a lot of players will immediately disregard the game and not give it a chance because you would need to either play during a free weekend or pay for it. And for now that can be quite a bit of an issue since the game is still being developed and is rather bare bones still, it lacks content… but it will be added more Freelancers and maps will come out as the game gets more developed. So, the game may simply not be interesting enough for people want warrant spending 20 bucks on it… but in the future it will get there.

I only just discovered this game from a friend and it turns out it released around the same time as the classic Duke Nukem 3D.  Let me just say, Shadow Warrior Classic plays identically to Duke Nukem 3D and that was one of my favorite games growing up. The controls, weapons, health pick ups, enemy movements, and yes, even the main character.  You play as Lo Wang and his one-liners throughout the game are reminescent of the Duke we grew up with - slick, funny and a bit racy with a very obvious Asian accent compared to Duke's notorious American bravado.
Shadow Warrior Redux does of course stick to the original except it is with HD visuals.  There are 47 levels in total (including the two expansions) so you're easily going to get your money's worth.  I am on level 18 and at this point have put in about 10 hours into the game, so you can see that there is a lot of content, especially when you look for secrets and such.   I will note that while it is similar to Duke Nukem 3D, the level design is definitely a bit more complex.  Finding secrets takes some patience and a little understanding of puzzles at times. I can see how I would have struggled playing this as a kid but so far right now, I haven't been stuck badly enough that I needed to check a guide.
Regardless, it is a blast and I absolutely love the variety of weapons from shurikens to katanas, dual uzis, shotguns, missile launchers, grenade launchers, etc.  All of these weapons make for a bloody (there is lots of blood) enjoyable and violent experience.
Had I known of this gem before I would have jumped on the opportunity to play it sooner, but I am glad to be playing it now.  If you want a classic fps that takes you back to the 90's, look no further.

Without sounding like a complete fanboy I'll attempt to cover the goods and bads of the game. Starting with the cons (Please read the entire thing before commenting/voting, I'll come back to everything later on in the text):
*The game offers little to no information about how are what you're actually doing. Without guiding hand you'll probably get completely lost, confused and quit without really steping in to it. This is the reason why a lot players just can't get in to it.
*The game is pay-to-win. By definition pay to win just means that you can use real life money to boost your in game progress.
*The game contains a lot of systems that don't really function as they shoud due to neglect from the devs. All of which adds confusion in priorities of new players.
*Bad rep. I know it's a tad bit confusing for me to add this as a con but people that barely know anything about the game usually just think that it's a massive grindfest and not much else.
*No real end game.
Alright now that we astablished the bad things about the game let's negate every single one of them:
*Although the game itself is void of info the comunity is the best one I have ever been a part of. Any question you can think off will be answered in a metter of seconds from at least 5 differant people in region chat. The unknown actually works to its adventage because the more you think you know about it the more you find out how wrong you actually are. It does a great job one-upping itself so if you stick it out and learn the basics you'll love it.
*If the game was any other genre, I'd agree, pay to win is a horrible practice that needs to die. But Warframe also has one of THE BEST micro transaction systems in the gaming indistry (Aside from Valve games). How's this possible? Well it's because of the fact that it's a coop game where PVP doesn't matter much although it does exist. Pay to win is bad only when players start losing because they didn't spend money but every time that I added money to my account to buy something I never fealt I was doing it because I felt like I was at a disadventage before I addad money, quite the oposite actually, spending money just feels like it adds to your experiance. That being said the game does not contain a pay wall for non-cosmetic items meaning anything but a few cosmetic items can be farmed without real life money.
*Due to neglect a lot of secretion has been piled up, the good news is that the devs are actively re-defining the game by reworking old mechanics and re-integrating them in to the game, albiet at a slower pace than players would like... reworks don't really put food on the table as much as shiny new aditions do.
*Over the years the game changed so much it's impossible to compare the old and the new version. If you played it in the past give it another go, if not then just try asking a friend to show you the ropes, it's worth it.
*Although the devs constantly add higher level content and harder missions they can never make content as fast as we can finish it. So the true objective of the game is to get all the things in the game while looking as good as possible.
And finally I'll just name some stuff on why you should play the game in general:
*Insanely smooth movement system and incredible abilities that make you feel powerful constantly.
*A complex, fantastic, modding system that can make even the worst weapons useful in the late game if you put enough energy and resources in to them.
*More costimization options than you can shake a stick at.
*Fantastic story, lore, art and sound design.
*Constantly rewarding, it really gives you a sense of progression.
*More than 3k hours worth of content. I'm 2k hours in and there's still stuff I haven't touched.
*Constant patches and fixes.
*Runs on a potato
*CLEM
*THE BEST COMMUNITY OF EVERY VIDEO GAME EVER.

This game, oh man this game. I haven't had this much fun since I started playing Pillars of Eternity. In my personal opinion, it's absolutely spectacular! Larian is quickly rising up my list of quality developers. But on to the review now.
+ Fleshed out and nuanced characters that are rarely pure evil or pure good.
+ NPCs that are actually interesting to listen to. I never felt like just skipping through what people said in order to get a quest or something.
+ Vibrant areas and alluring setting. This game looks very nice on ultra.
+ Avoids many common fantasy tropes in an effort to make a unique and rather compelling story.
+ The game allows you to use your environment to your advantage. You can set up a field of oil to slow people down, then light them on fire. Or you can make everyone wet and then freeze them solid, or stun them with some lightning.
+ You don't have to play the first game in order to understand and enjoy this one. Although it certainly helps.
+ There's multiplayer! You can experience the story with multiple people, and I recommend it. It's not almost necessary like in Divinity Original Sin 1 however.
+ Very, very easy to get immersed into the setting and story. If you start playing, be prepared to be sucked into Rivellon for a few hours.
There is quite a bit of reading in the game. Although the vast majority of it is interesting and helps to flesh out the setting.
~ A lot of the humour and campiness of the first game isn't present in this one. I personally enjoyed that aspect of Divinity Original Sin 1 but it isn't a dealbreaker for me. This is a much more dark and serious story than the first game.
~ Elves and dwarves. Probably doesn't matter for a lot of people, and certainly isn't a dealbreaker either. They're somewhat different from Tolkein elves and dwarves in terms of culture, but they're the same in a lot of other ways.
- I've seen stutters somewhat often. It's kinda annoying and breaks my immersion a little, to be honest.
- Fights can be completely trivialized even on higher difficulties through the use of environmental effects and aerotheurge skills. Mainly teleport and nether shift, but aerotheurge by far feels like the strongest magic.
- A single level of difference can spell death for your party. It feels like the power gap between levels is very large, and it hinders exploration a little.
- Still quite buggy in some places. Save often.
- Some things in multiplayer outright encourage party infighting, even punishing you for not killing each other in a few places.
- Lucky Charm feels like a useless skill. It triggers very rarely (5% chance whenever you open a container, doesn't get higher) and when it does, it often doesn't give you anything very good. It's just not worth spending points in when you can get Telekinesis, Barter, Thievery, Loremaster, or Persuasion instead.
FINAL SCORE : 9/10
Despite its flaws, I think this one is a game for the ages. I don't often give very high scores like this. It's easily up there with Baldur's Gate and Pillars of Eternity in terms of quality, and i'd absolutely say that this game is worth your time if you're a fan of fantasy games.

I'll start off by saying that having played through the first one, this game is SOOO LONG with more than double the playtime of the original. That being said, I don't regret a single hour of this beautiful sequel.
Although the gameplay hasn't significantly changed much from the original, the magic (orbment) and skills (crafts) system has been expanded upon tremendously. The original three pages of magic has been expanded to five; introducing newer strategies to the abundant amount of character choices. The new skill, chains, finds itself to be useful in some scenarios. These additions made the gameplay always refreshing, seeing that I've played more than 100 hours fighting shiny pom poms.
The team system has significantly improved since the first chapter. This shouldn't be a surprise since the entire game revolves around changing teammates and parties, but first let me explain the difference. (Minor Spoilers) In the original game, two characters (Joshua and Estelle) would always be playable characters while each chapter offers two other characters that make up the rest of your party. Each chapter changed the party and thus your team strategy. The game struck a nice balance of difficulty and adaptation except for the last chapter. The chapter which allowed you to make your own team with all the characters you've met along the way wasn't very balanced. The enemy encounters grew extremely repetitive and boring, and
However, the second chapter struck a good balance while letting the player create a team themselves. Although the first chapter was pretty repetitive since your options were limited, I found difficult monsters and interesting monster attacks that kept the combat intriguing. In general, bosses were more interesting and carried a 'mood' about them. Again (minor spoilers), but the last chapter's boss fights were beyond amazing. By far the bosses and 'road monsters' are the best thing about Trails in the Sky SC's gameplay.
Now a small paragraph about the OST. I read on a forum somewhere that the OST for SC was supposed to better than FC. For the majority of the game, I questioned this opinion since it reused alot of songs from the first game. But all of a sudden near the end of the game, the soundtrack dramatically improved with new songs. The credits song gave me chills. Good job music writers, although I'd appreciate if the same songs weren't used every single time in the first few chapters.
Retrospectively, I should've talked about the graphics/textures of the game in the first paragraph. If you've gotten used to the graphics in Trails in the Sky FC, then this game should be no problem. Although walking through the same landscape as Trails in the Sky FC is a bit boring, some of the new landscapes introduced are beautiful and well worth it.
Story and characters. Amazing. Marvelous. Hella GOOD JOB Nihon Falcom. Pretty much every character gets their back stories introduced and expanded upon. Some scenes are so fantastic that they definitely should've made a scene select option in the menu. The hidden nature of the Society and some of the plot twists make the game so much more interesting and hooks you back in the next day even after you've spent one entire day playing the game. Afterall, story and character development feels like such a lovely reward after defeating bosses with a sliver of health remaining. By far, Estelle's character development was done beautifully well. My only complaint is that you have to switch around characters in your party to obtain extra dialogue which sometimes can't be done without grinding character levels (looking at you, last area last chapter). Otherwise, the story is great if you enjoy anime stories with a touch of the shounen genre.
Honestly if you enjoyed Trails in the Sky FC, then this game is a must buy. As anyone does, I EXTREMELY HIGHLY recommend playing through the first game first. This game assumes you've already played through FC, so there are many spoilers and the difficulty curve is quite steep in the beginning. If you haven't tried either, I'd recommend buying the FC on sale and testing the waters before you delve deep into this trilogy.

The first 2/3s of this game is great.  The story arcs for each character are dramatically different, the options for character builds allow for a wide variety of play styles, and being able to respec characters (after the first act) allows you to shift style within a game.  Since you get a team of 4 and there are 6 core characters, you really need to play through at least twice to get the backstories.  First playthrough, you should definitely play a team of core characters to get the story arcs.
Turn based combat is good.  You do need to think about combat strategy as doing the same tactics over and over will get your head handed to you at some point – when that happens, rethink how you approached the fight, or come back later.  The division between physical and magic damage adds a little complexity and you need to pay attention to enemy resistances.
It does a really good job of using player vs. enemy level as a hint not to go there yet - if an enemy is a level higher than you are, go do something else and come back later.  You can sometimes win one of these fights, but more often get smacked.  This helps guide you through the open world without being too explicit.
The puzzles range from amusing to “I need to google that”.  Some are stupidly hard and were for me, not fun.
They nerfed the whole crafting system from DOS 1.  In DOS 1, crafting gave you the opportunity to improve what you have - in DOS II, it is pretty useless.  Early on, crafting does provide the means to generate more cash, particularly lockpicks from nails.
Once you get to Arx, things go downhill - it feels more forced, the ending fight and ending are a letdown.  It feels like they ran out of time and energy and wanted to get home to that beer.
I did feel my mood shift as the game went on from “can’t we all get along” to “kill them all, and I will sort them out later”.
This is a really good game and I highly recommend it.

Hi there! I absolutely adore KR0, and I want to lend any of you that are on the fence some clarity on things people are saying, some advice, and lastly, my thoughts.
1. Acts Taking A Long Time To Put Out - Yes, this is a thing that's happening, and we all really hate waiting. However, KR0 is detailed, complex, and very thorough, so I'd imagine it would take a very long time to produce something of its caliber. As well, Cardboard Computer supplies fans with material proving they're working hard on their Twitter, so follow them if you want to stay hyped.
2. Pacing Within Episodes - I'm a really impatient person. That's just who I am. So, when I first played through, there were days when KR0 got on my nerves for being so wordy. What did I do? I closed the game, played something else, and then when I felt more patient and peaceful, I opened it back up and really enjoyed a complete, immersive experience.
3. Things I Like - The music is pretty darn great. Three thumbs up out of two. Writing, of course, is poetic and enchanting. Atmosphere blends emotional response with underlying calmness. Characters are lovable as all heck. (Extra: Their names are all quite memorable, which makes things really nice and easy.) Art direction and emotion-based scenery choices are all really tasteful for the kind of story the game is telling.
4. Things I Dislike - I have a natural distaste for point-and-click games. My index finger gets tired, the sound of the clicking gets on my nerves, and it just results in me not being able to play. However, the controller integration is complete, purposeful, and well done, which made *all* the difference.
All in all, if you need an atmosphere to hang out in, or if you need escape, enchantment, enlightening, Equus Oils, or
, then I'd suggest giving this game a look. Get ready to be swept away.

This is Guitar Hero with an actual guitar, or bass, if you so choose!
I was definitely skeptical about this, as it seemed like a great idea, but I wasn't sure if Rocksmith could deliver exactly what it said it could in a quality program worth the high price. To my surprise, it did end up being worth every penny.
The Rocksmith Real-tone cable (which must be purchased seperately) actually works amazingly well, and when you're not playing in career mode or just playing random songs, you can just go into "Amp mode" and jam out, which contains an insane amount of custimization for sounds and tones etc. and more can be unlocked and purchased.
I really thought this was going to be a hard game, but it starts you off slow and depending on how well you do, difficulty is altered, allowing you to play more notes to a song until by the end, if you're doing well enough, you are playing the entire thing.
The game walks you through every step, from the very beginning, and even though some parts here are slow for experienced players looking to jump right into the game, it's definitely going to be very useful for beginners. When you get to more difficult songs that require chords, tremolos, hammer-ons, you name it, there are tutorials and mini games based on playing those notes that will appear, teaching you how to perform them while having fun at the same time. Even when you do lose, you just want to keep going because every time you get a little better, and after mastering any of these, you truly feel like you have become a better player.
There is an in-game guitar tuner which works better then any tuner I have ever even used in real life. Before every song, you hit each string, and it lets you know if you're in tune. If you're not, the tuner pops up, and tells you how to adjust. Although this may sound annoying, it usually only takes 3 seconds if nothing has to be tuned, and ends up being extremely useful, and practical, regarding tune-age upkeep.
What you are learning here are REAL songs, that you can practice in the game, and then go play later.
In only 24 hours I have learned over a dozen songs, and although I can't play them all flawlessly or in their entirety, some of them I've gotten pretty damn close, and eventually with practice, you can nail any song. You literally start to impress yourself with what you have learned in such a short time. I really didn't think it would ever even be possible to learn popular songs without teachers or tablature, it takes up too much time and is frustrating, so I have mostly only ever played by ear or wrote my own material in the few years that I've been playing, but this game solves those issues and proves me wrong.
I even reccomend this to people who are still pretty new to guitar. It's fun, and actually makes you WANT to learn, because you see yourself progressively getting better. It's faster and much more simple then using tabs, the only thing is you only have so many songs to choose from.
Sincerely impressed by the quality of this game/program/purchase.  They took a great idea, put it together, achieved, and then delivered if not the best possible outcome, pretty damn close to it.

8/10
I would give this game a solid B+. The concept is very cute for a platformer and I enjoyed playing through it immensely. The controls were tight and fluid, which I was not expecting coming for an indie-platformer, but it did control quite well. The momentum of the character was solid and consistent, you could accurately judge and calculate the jump distance. The game is very easy, but given the child-friendly and looking appearance, that could have been an intentional design choice. Rather than fail the level or be sent out from your attempt should you be hit by an enemy or fall from the screen, you are simply sent back to the start of the level. You do keep all the berries and water drops you collected, however, which does make the blow of being sent back not sting as much. The game is fairly short, I completed 100% of the achievements in just over an hour and a half, and the stages themselves only take 5-10 minutes to clear, which gives the game a brisk pace. You will naturally unlock all the upgrades through normal play and quickly, though there isn't much difference between the upgraded leaves themselves, it's still worth noting you will not be forced to grind out levels (unless you are going for all achievements the 3000 berry one will take maybe 20-30 minutes of replay). The music is very chipper and enjoyable and sets a great mood for the friendly atmosphere, though perhaps it is a tad loud in comparison to the sound-effect volume level as it feels quite drown out.
What keeps this game from getting a 9 or 10 in my book is just a few small issues. The camera could have done with a little work, and the ability to move it even say 45 degrees left and right to help you see around a few corners would have been helpful with some of the more tricky jumps. The game is also very short. Currently this game is listed for $3.49 dollars, and it was worth a playthrough to me at that price, but some more thrifty gamers may find the price to be a bit high considering the game can be beaten in an hour-hour and a half. The biggest issue I had however was the lack of options, specifically the lack of volume control. You can change graphical settings and controls easily enough, but even with the games upbeat soundtrack, I think it would have been nice to be able to turn it down or mute it when I was replaying a level.  With a few more options and control mechanics the game would be a perfect little indy platformer, but it just has a few key issues I hope the developers take note of for future releases.
I whole-heartedly recommend Woodle Tree Adventures for a fun little platforming game for everyone of all ages!

Yes, luck of the draw can screw you over, but skilled players will win more often than not. Knowing which cards work well with others is key, and that comes with familiarity. Continued play is certainly rewarded. I won't go into detail explaining the four factions and what works best with others for two reasons:
1) Others have already done so better than I can (check strategy articles on BoardGameGeek)
2) Discovering these things on your own is part of the fun (at least for me)

Play count over a hundred games on mobile. I was dubious after a few plays: was this really any better than Ascension? It certainly wasn't as complex as Dominion or as thematic as Thunderstone. I wouldn't have belived Star Realms would become my favourite deckbuilding game.
Dominion is just as engrossing and if I had a chance to play it more I might prefer it. But here's the thing: Dominion has to work hard to be good. It has to have lots of cards with interesting mechanics and make the players track their turns carefully. Star Realms is just casually awesome. It is fundamentally more exciting in concept. There is anticipation in seeing what ships the trade row delivers (especially once you know what they all are), tough and dangerous decisions to be made in choosing what ships to take and how to built your deck, and tension in the direct competition of blows as you race to be the fastest to beat down your opponent — and pretty much nothing else to get in the way of those elements. If Dominion had cards as simple as Star Realms it'd be crap. If Star Realms had cards as interesting as Dominion it would blow every other deckbuilding game out of the water.

I am a former Magic the Gathering player and a long time player of both board and card games.  I've played several thousand games against the AI and feel like I have a fairly informed opinion of the game.  I have not bothered with the campaigns and will not address them.
The base game is fantastic.  The balance is finely tuned and it is a marvel of card game design.  After you have played several hundred games, you become increasingly aware of just how tightly and carefully designed this game really is and I appreciate it for it's rapt craftsmanship.
The Gambit Set is designed to add some variety to the starting positions of either player.  You are granted two resource cards which can change your starting position by varying degrees depending on your luck and the line of cards available for purchase.  It doese weaken the balance of the game slightly, but the varied starting positions do add interest.
Bases and Battleships adds new bases and ships.  The ships added invariably have different ways of interacting with bases.  It adds more interest, but I feel like this set combined with the Gambit Set can result in some very unbalanced games.  Weaknesses in the AI sometimes become more apparent and the games have more of a random feel.
The Events DLC can be fun for a few games, but ultimately it is just a heap of random garbage that doesn't really add much to the game beyond opportunities for some occassional unlikely come-backs.
Base Game: 5 stars
Gambit Set: 4 stars
Bases & Battleships: 4 stars
Events DLC: 2 stars
All in all, Star Realms is outstanding, quick card game that you can pick up and play in a spare 10 minutes.

Early Access Watcher Reviews Atlas Reactor
Update Version: Initial EA release
Disclosure: This game copy was played during the free weekend promotional event
If one thing can be certain in any industry it is how people are destined to either copy or create adaptations of successful products. This is certainly true in the gaming sphere where a successful new genre IP will eventually be mimicked to ad nauseam. Some happen over night (FNAF clones) while others, in the case of the MOBA genre, have taken years to mimic the addictive Warcraft III custom map Defense of the Ancients (which also had clones to ad nauseam.) This time around, we have a MOBA wrapped in a couple layers of turn based sheets with Atlas Reactor. Is this attempt to deviate from the standard three lane, mob fest the shot in the arm the genre needed or simply a failed experiment? Regardless of what it is, I will commend it for trying something different.
When I first saw this game, I was quite pleased with the aesthetic. The humor they tried to attach to it does not hold up, but the simple designs stand out thanks to the bright color schemes. Characters are diverse from your standard humans to robots and some bizarre aliens. Particle effects and lighting are not as up to par, but the character animations look fluid from movement to ultimate attacks. It does not have a lot of moving parts, but it is easy on the eyes.
This game took a giant risk utilizing turn based elements and it will be a deal breaker for a lot of players. You have four phases that all characters act out even if killed: prep for traps, dash for emergency movement, battle for attacks and then movement. Each character plays out there actions even if they are killed and can even be healed as long as the health recovered is more than the damage received. This is where the majority of the challenge settles; anticipating where a enemy will move, where they will attack and who they decide to gang up on. A simple dash phase can be the difference between a well executed team effort or a narrow escape to disrupt a perfect kill. The problem is with the waiting that is involved after selecting the round action. You need to watch every move until everyone has gone, which can make anyone impatient. If someone is killed, they must wait a full turn (the turn after they are killed) before they can respawn on the map in a random location. The first team to kill five or have the most kills at 20 rounds (or most in overtime) will be deemed the winner. If you play strategically though, you will find it can be a ripe challenge to get even three kills by the 20 round mark.
Micro-transactions are forgivable for a free to play game that is fully released, but if I paid $20 to access the game and then discovered lot of it is in the store, I would be rather disappointed. This is not so much B2P as it is B2A (buy to access). The content on offer is rather slim too with just a handful of maps and around 20 characters, which thankfully have skills you can swap out (after unlocked) to change up the gameplay style a little. As it stands now though, there is not enough on offer to qualify the price tag.
This game is an online title, so the game is only worth it if you can play it. There have been several times I have played only to have my entire team drop out at once with half the enemy team doing the same. Online queues felt rather long, even with the free weekend. I decided to talk with some players outside of the game client to see if this was normal before it came to Early Access and was told that was the case. It just arrived on Early Access recently, but a game with this small a community can make finding matches a pain.
The options menu left much to be desired with only the broad option to set low, medium or high quality and decide if you want full screen or windowed. Volume options, profanity filter and chat options exist, but there really is nothing to incorporate Antialiasing or V-Sync. It could explain why the graphics appear slightly bland on appearance. Frame rate drops occurred from time to time as well, mostly during dash phases when multiple characters were sprinting at the same time. Loading screen freezes also happened to activate while loading into the game using the client, which required a forced shut down of the program. It could certainly be worse, I will give the developers that.
It is always a positive step for developers to try new things, but it doesn't mean the attempt will be received well. The game has an interesting and challenging approach to a genre over saturated to death with routine and meta builds that eliminate the fun required for a game to be great. That said, a game also needs to be worth the price of admission and at this point the game just isn't worth the $20 entry fee. You are also forced to use a third party service that was more trouble using than removing thanks to my anti-virus (not using Avast) labeling it as a threat. It has a great idea to work off of, but it is ultimately a non-recommendation due to technical issues and cost. I will eventually try this game again in the future, so hopefully then it will be ironed out and have a larger community.
Pros
- Visually pleasant to look at
- Challenging tactical gameplay
- Tutorial, Solo and Co-op with bots (plenty of options to learn instead of throwing in blind to the wolves)
- Varies skills and abilities to unlock to allow characters different play styles
Cons
- Micro-Transactions (You paid at least $20 dollars)
- Connectivity issues, frame rate drops, partial loading screen freezing
- Extremely slow combat, a lot of downtime waiting for everything to play out
- Very thin amount of content
- Options and Settings offer little adjustment
- Online community is small, queue times are long as a results

I learned about this game after being a long-time player and fan of another one of Trion's games RIFT. I have spent lots of time, energy and money on RIFT over the years and thought I would give Atlas Reactor a try and I wasn't disappointed.
For me this game is like a multiplayer game of chess, only way more action-packed and fun. After going through the initial tutorial with Lockwood, I found myself spending the rest of my gameplay time learning the different playstyles of all the Freelancers. Some of my friends stuck to one Freelancer and tried to master it before moving on to learning a second character, so that's also an approach one can take.
If you are into VR there's a cool VR Character Viewer you can get too to check out the unique skins and styles of all the Freelancers and whatnot. It's interesting to see where they will end up taking that technology, and cool to see companies starting to incorporate VR as well. I imagine it could be really fun to play a match and be in the first person view of the Freelancer you are using while you are doing your moves and taunting your enemies and whatnot.
Another nice thing about Atlas Reactor is that it offers hardcore players the option to really master all the Freelancers, build teams with other players, and work on strategies to defeat your foes, but if you are ultra casual you can just do one or two matches and be done within 20-30 minutes.
On the Atlas Reactor community forums they even have a section where players can offer up Freelancer Kit Concepts for consideration for future Freelancers that may be added to the game.
Either way there is something for everyone with Atlas Reactor, in my opinion.

The UI is solid, the character and art design is familiar but has it's own uniqueness, and the microtransations aren't invasive (despite Trion's reputation).
Now onto the long review.  I figured I'd TL;DR first since people hate reading a ton of stuff.  I an ex-Quake pro, Street Fighter FGC member, and have been competitive in any game I liked that I could (Legend in Hearthstone, diamond in Starcraft II, plat in LoL).  This game fits right in there with the legends of competitive gaming, easy to learn, tough to master.
Anyone familiar with Xcom's mechanics will feel right at home here.  All turn's are simultaneous, moves are resolved as such, games are quick (15-20 mins), matchmaking is fair and as fast as you'd expect from any game (higher ELO you get, longer it takes).
Microtransations:  What makes or breaks any game.  At the 20 dollar pricepoint, this game gives you access to all current and future characters.  This decision was made as I undertstand, to make sure people always had access to the games main content.  In-game currency is used to unlock the majority of the other vanity content, and it's easy to acquire and it feels like you're always making progress in the system.
The game's lore is tied in well to the "Seasons" content and it feels like you have a good grasp of what's happening in the  world of Atlas, although this aspect of the game doesn't interest me much.
There are part's of the game I have gripes with; most of which are non-gamebreaking bugs
that the developers have been vocal about getting squashed.  Also, the community support from Trion and it's developers have been absolutely top-notch. (In what game can you just PM a developer and get an instant response?).
All and all, I highly recommend giving the game a try, whether it's through a refer a frend code or otherwise.  Just ask a streamer for a code I'm sure they have plenty to hand out.

Let me get it out of the way that this is a very straightforward adventure game, to the point that I would call it an interactive story, rather than an adventure game.  It is still phenomenal and should not be missed.
The Great Recession, from which Boomers and Millenials still bear scars, sets the stage for Kentucky Route Zero.  Conway is a lone truck driver with nothing to his name but his aging dog, working one last delivery for an antique shop.  The delivery goes to an address he cannot find, which requires finding the enigmatic highway, Kentucky Route Zero, which is the only highway that goes *under* the state.  On the way he meets Shannon, a woman whose family has been ruined by the local coal mine closing down.  Together they find the highway.  And well, things get strange.
Basic polygonal artwork is used to an incredible effect, combining fog, lighting and basic visual effects to create a dark, gloomy depiction of the deep south.  Music is miniumal and atmospheric, until bluegrass singers add to the mood at perfect moments.  There are no voices other than the singing, and dialog is entirely text based, telling a story combining fantastical Americana with crushing tales of the American Nightmare historical and modern.  A majority of the adult characters are crushed by debt and financial troubles, a recurring theme.
The story is five chapters, only three are available and the fourth is now being teased.  The team is only an indie studio of two, and this deserves support.  It is not long, and each chapter will leave you wanting more.  Buy this, turn the lights low, enjoy the journey and think about your life while you do it.

Shadow Warrior (1997) is a 2.5D Build Engine FPS by 3D Realms, the same guys who made Duke Nukem 3D, which was also a 2.5D Build Engine FPS. Because of this, Shadow Warrior and Duke Nukem 3D have a lot in common. Like DN3D, Shadow Warrior has some pretty good old-school shooting, varied yet annoyingly mazy level design with a good sense of place, a nice range of weapons that's kinda unbalanced, lots of personality and little touches, pop-culture references, and weird attitudes towards women. 3D Realms clearly had a comfort zone in the mid-to-late 90s.
There are, however, some marked differences from Duke Nukem. The protagonist of Shadow Warrior is Lo Wang, a ridiculous Asian caricature. I say Asian because he's Chinese, but also a ninja, which is a Japanese profession. Now, I'm not saying that Chinese people can't be ninjas, but the main reason for that being the case here seems to be so that 3D Realms can hit every broad Asian stereotype possible. Lo Wang speaks broken Engrish, has a name that sounds like genitalia, brings up his nationality every 5 seconds, finds lots of fortune cookies, kills gassy sumo wrestlers, and keeps running into naked anime girls who are scattered around for no identifiable reason (at least Duke Nukem 3D had some flimsy pretense relating to mass kidnapping). However, despite all of this, he manages to be a fun character as well. He makes lots of puns (most of which revolve around his name, and a decent amount of which are actually funny), has some good one-liners
and seems to be incredibly enthusiastic about everything, from finding a grenade launcher to slicing a guy in half to watching rabbits ♥♥♥♥. Also, he uses the heads and hearts of certain enemies as weapons, which is fun. He grows on you after a while, and though the racism is incorrigible, it doesn't feel as bad as it would otherwise.
The Build Engine has also been improved, mainly by the addition of sector-over-sector at last. However, I'm not sure why they bothered, because Quake had introduced full 3D the year before, and the entire industry was quickly shifting over to that. Still, it allows for some level design that wouldn't have been possible otherwise, so that's nice, I guess.
The gameplay has been improved from Duke Nukem 3D in a couple of ways. There are visible meters for air (when underwater) and boss health now, which is useful. Melee has also been made a more viable option, as Lo Wang's katana can insta-kill a few enemies and do serious damage to others. It rewards charging into the fray and hacking away like a maniac, which is fun every now and then. However, like Duke Nukem, Lo Wang dies pretty quickly, so melee rampages aren't always the best option. Additionally, primitive vehicles have been added, although they're annoying to steer and are only really used to open up a couple of pathways with their ability to shoot arbitrarily harder than you can.
Lo Wang's inventory items aren't as useful as Duke Nukem's, and I barely ever used them, with the obvious exception of the Medical Kit.
Some enemies are just terrible. There's a suicide bomber enemy that you can't bait into exploding prematurely, which would be annoying enough by itself. However, these enemies also have a good chance of spawning a creature when they die that floats around erratically, occasionally becomes invisible, and fires damaging projectiles, which is a ♥♥♥♥♥ to take care of. You can prevent the spawn by hacking at the suicide bomber's corpse with your sword, but it's still very irritating. Also, there are some bees that are like the Snarks from Half-Life, but are worse because they can fly, they don't die after a short period of time, and you can't have them for yourself. There's also a boss at the end of the shareware portion of the game that gets away, leading to a future encounter where you kill him, but after that he shows up again several times. What's the point of setting him up like that then?
You can't rebind any of the controls, which is annoying and additionally leaves four different buttons for activating the Medical Kit, three of which could have been used to make other controls more convenient.
The game seems a little harder overall than Duke Nukem 3D, which I guess makes sense considering that it's sort of a spiritual successor.
The levels are quite long.
It's annoying how your aim is shifted whenever you move onto a sloped surface, causing you to miss a lot.
Overall, Shadow Warrior is pretty good as 90s FPS go. It's fun, it has variety, its protagonist's enthusiasm is infectious, it improves on Duke Nukem 3D in several ways, and it's clearly doing its own thing, which is always admirable. It has its share of annoying parts, but they don't get in the way of the good stuff most of the time. I recommend it.
EDIT: I played the classic version, not the one with the slightly upgraded visuals, and it's a bit unstable. Expect occasional crashes.

I love the hell out of this game. It's what Rock Band and Guitar Hero should have been in the first place; Playing to music with real instruments!
The game has many great features, such as the game automatically adjusting difficulty on the fly, so that you're never forced to play things below your skill level (or above), technique challenges that are pretty easy to pick up, but challenging to master, and games that hide techniques and skills underneath the guise of minigames, so that learning is actually enjoyable and not tedious.
This game is good for either aspiring guitar players who are looking for a not-boring place to start, right up to serious guitar players that want to hone their skills or play a game that involves doing what they enjoy.
There is also a very wide array of songs to choose from, both supplied with the game, and dlc, as well as both guitar and bass modes, as well as local coop (if you have more than one cable).
I do not, however, recommend buying the game online, unless you are 100% sure you are able to buy the required hardware cable from somewhere, or have it readily available, as you cannot use any old guitar cable.
Also, obviously, you need your own electric guitar. You do not need pedals or an amplifier however, so that's a plus.
tl;dr game is fantastic and underrated, and is worth picking up from your local game store, especially if you either want to learn guitar/bass or enjoy games like guitar hero.

A visually charming indie pipe-puzzle game that knows how to grind my gears in the least fun ways possible. Clearly an inspired take on a well worn style of puzzler, A Virus Named TOM starts off with a lovely art deco bang that quickly loses steam as you progress. The whole set up--Dr. X, The City of Tomorrow, etc-- oozes charm, and there are plenty of variables and gimmicks introduced to keep things interesting.
The main issue with TOM lies at the very roots of design; instead of challenging you with complex and fascinating puzzles, TOM forces you to combat its own controls and obstacles while solving the base pipe puzzles, which, while initially engaging in the hecticness of the whole thing, suffers from an overload of obstacles while failing to make up for it with interesting overall design.
Is the gameplay loop bad in any way? Not exactly. While I lost interest almost immediately, I can't deny that there is a certain draw to find the way through the chaotic mess of some of the harder levels. It's fleshed out in certain areas, yes, but I could never move past the sheer mediocrity of it all. There was heart here, and yet my interest waned the more complex it got. It's just not a fun time, at least not for me.
With all of the flaws to be had, I think there is a lot of talent to be had here. As this is a game from 2012, I can only imagine how far the Misfits have come. I don't doubt that their newer stuff has vastly improved, and look forward to playing them in the future. Nevertheless, VNT wasn't something I enjoyed past the aesthetics. Fun in concept, but in execution? Not so much. From the way Tom controlled to the constant feeling of 'this could be so much more,' A Virus Named TOM fails to impress. Give this one a pass, or at least wait until it's in a bundle or something.

The game is about a little tree-stump saving his town from thirst by collecting fairy's tears from another worlds.
Woodle Tree Adventures, is a 3D Platforming Adventure game, where your objective it's to go around the worlds and collect all three fairy's tears.
You only have one attack, with you can improve in the future while you collect "apples" on the worlds.
There's infinite lifes, but if you hit a invisible checkpoint, and if die twice, you will start from the beginning and have to walk all way back.
The game is not long, around 70 minutes to finish the story, and around 2 hours to complete it 100%.
In this game, there are many, little and meaningless bugs (and errors that can be easily fixed), but some of them can mean a lot between win and lost.
The menu has no options, and the default key is on Enter, and Esc is to exit the game, making a lot of players exiting the game except of pausing it.
There is no "tutorial". This game supports Local Multiplayer (Not tested by me), Steam Achievements and two controllers.
The developer is active and it's "open" about fixing glitches and bugs.
The Visuals look like from
, exactly what the developer intended.
The game was meant for kids and adults with nostalgia from Nintendo 64, making a level per world, platforming, 3D, adventure videogame.
The menu looks like it was made in a few minutes, doesn't show the potential that the games shows.
There is only 6 songs (one for each world) without talking about the menu, and intro music.
Those 6 songs, some look sad and others look calm, giving a calm ambient to the game.
The song "CallForAction" seems misplaced, having a very intense and "action" song on a tranquille videogame.
The Sound Effects are pretty nice, they also show the tranquille ambient, as for example the "death" of the enemies are pretty calm and SFW (Safe For Work) for kids and adults.
This game has errors and bugs that could be fixed, but only some of them make the game harder, while the others give a sense of fun.
The game does give the nostalgia for games like
, it's smooth, calm and tranquille. It contains no imagery that can affect kids and it's pretty safe.
Although, I doubt that "kids" will have fun with this game, even though this game was meant for them and for adults with a feel of nostalgia, they are nowadays changing more into First Person Shooters (FPS) for example, and less into "friendly 3D Platforming Adventure" games.
But with no doubt, the game is playable by anyone and does it's job right of doing what it was meant to be - "(...) an hybrid between an art game and a platformer and is meant to be played by adults and children and to bring happiness to all souls".

Star Realms is a pretty simple multiplatform card game (I've only played the 'full' base version without DLC expansions, which may add more mechanics). Good enough graphics/music, story for the campaign is more like abbreviated descriptions of a story.
There are three resources: Authority (player life; win by reducing opponent to 0), Combat (damage; cards you play can give Combat until the end of turn that you spend to reduce enemy life), and Trade (money; cards you play can give Trade until the end of turn that you spend to buy cards in the shared pool to improve your deck). Each player starts with a basic deck of mostly 1-Trade cards and you begin games by spending that Trade to buy cards from the central shared area. When you run out of cards in your deck, your discard/used card pile gets shuffled and becomes your new deck. Eventually your deck will be full of cards you bought and you can rack up nice Combat/Trade amounts if you draw the right combination of cards.
There are various mechanics to play around with. There are faction cards that do extra things if you play another faction card, there are ways make your deck flow smoother (draw cards, cards to remove unwanted cards), you can Scrap (remove from the game) some cards to activate their ability.
It's a card game so luck exists in what you draw, what cards are available to buy from the shared pool, and what cards your enemy can buy/draw. So one turn you can have a great multicard combo and the next a dud where your cards don't complement each other.
I would've liked the option to automatically end turns (giving the normal warnings when non-scrap abilities are left unused) to take away an unnecessary click. Also, I would've liked an option to automatically assign damage when there is only one target.
My experience with the Steam version has been disappointing, but not really from the game itself.
They had a standalone PC version for download on their website but they removed it with the Steam release.
I had an activation code from humble to unlock the standard full version (without DLC) and there is no way on the Steam version to enter the code (and there is nowhere on their website to log in to your account to edit preferences/add codes). I had to contact support to get a website address to enter it.
I eventually registered for a Star Realms account with a legitimate e-mail address (which is required for multiplayer/non-Steam DLC access) but I used a "e-mail+label" format to automatically label and sort e-mails coming in. After playing around in the campaign to get the hang of the game, I went to try online multiplayer. However, despite allowing registration, they blocked my access to multiplayer because my "Email appears to be invalid." And since you are only allowed one account per Steam account (they're linked), I don't really feel like going through support again to gain access to multiplayer.
Make sure to avoid the pitfalls I did and you can probably enjoy the game. I found it fun enough for short sessions (feels ideal for mobile/portable and the UI feels designed for it anyway).

This is an actual serious review of the game. While the 420 blaze it jokes are funny, I do believe most people would like a serious review of this game.
I first bought Oblivion around launch date, I have spent over 7/8 years now playing Oblivion. It certainly hasn't aged all too well, but the modding community is what has kept this game alive and going strong.
1) Breathtaking soundtrack.
2) Interesting story.
3) Good voice acting
4) M'aiq the Liar, Yes, he's that good.
5) Tons of replayabilty thanks to the side quests.
6) Two actual expansions, not just dlc, but
7) Compelling main quest and side guilds.
8) Sheogorath.
1) Magic is useless low levels and broken at high levels.
2) Combat gets very boring after you get to high levels where its just slashing a bandit 40 times.
3) Stealth characters may feel unappriciated.
4) Creatures level up with you, this takes away from the challenge.
5) Prone to crashes due to Memory leaks. (Can be fixed with a 4gb booster)
6) Outdated graphics by today's standards.
7) Without mods, game may feel stale.
Overall I give this game a 9/10, despite its shortcomings it's still held up very well and I prefer it to Skyrim.

It's a simultaneous turn-based multiplayer arena game, and it isn't easy.
I think that's kind of it - the learning curve is pretty steep, and there's no way around it. Knowing when to dash, guessing when enemies are going to do the same, what abilities fire when, and juggling all of that in 30 or so seconds... It isn't easy.
But is it fun?
Hells to the yes. There's so much deep strategy there, and when everyone's acting in concert it's a beautiful thing. It feels a lot like a MOBA in that sense - each character can do a short list of things, and it's everyone's job to make sure the team is greater than the sum of its parts.
It's in Early Access for a reason, tho - they do need to work on some polish, and need ways to communicate ideas clearly without typing (because seriously, that time limit? It makes you think FAST), but the game itself reeeeeeeally scratches that frantic strategy itch.
Go buy it. Go play it.

With a riveting animated opening, gorgeously patterned levels, and addictively fun gameplay, it is no wonder Sonic Mania is a runaway commercial success that puts new pep in the step of the blue blur's supersonic speed. It is like a blast from the past because all of the old things of the original games are there, but they have been augmented or tweaked far beyond what you remember them that makes you go "wow" again and again... and again. The best part about the game is its approachability: you can play casually as a beginner and never get too worked up or feel overly frustrated, or you can spend virtually hours traversing the vast networks of paths with beautiful scenery and hidden easter eggs in just a single act. This is the signature retro Sonic coolness and style you get when you have a team comprised primarily of diehard Sonic fans building the mechanics, levels, and music of your game and who totally get the Super Sonic formula. Be way past cool and buy Sonic Mania today!

I have played this game since its open Alpha period; I reinstalled on Steam so that I could share my review with the community. I love Atlas Reactor and highly recommend it to anyone that likes tactics and strategy games!  Each turn in every ~20 minute game contains a variety of complex choices which result in an unending variety of results. You can take this decision matrix to the next level by grouping up with your friends and creating a team composition to pull of big combos and counter your opponents.
I also enjoy the mods for your abilities which are simply unlocked by playing a Freelancer - the differences that they apply adds more depth to gameplay and longevity to characters.  The devs have made a smart decision by applying a buy to play model for this game since it allows them to focus on game balance and future content instead of a microtransactional economy,
There will be plenty of content to boost their bottom line via alternate animations for abilities, taunts and cosmetic skins.  In my opinion this game has unlimited potential and has uncovered a new space for competive gaming.  If you do try it out make sure to stop by the Atlas Reactor Discord server to chat with people and party up with voice comms.  Hope to see you online ;)

This is one of the few games in years that I've actually stayed up for a full 72 hour weekend binge. If you enjoy turn-based games like X-COM, and team based games similar to MOBAs this is definitely the game for you. With 20 seconds per turn to input abilities and movement, it really feels much more urgent than a normal turn based game where you have all the time you need to plan out your strategy. And don't let my in-game time fool you, I've been playing since the Alpha Sneak Peek, and they only just got added to Steam.
The fact that it's buy to play should not deter you. It's a one-time fee to unlock every character in the game forever, similar to Smite, but you can unlock all of the additional content in the game itself. You never have to pay another cent unless you want to get the skins, taunts, and loot crates faster.
You'll also see the devs in the game, and often. I don't think I've ever encountered devs in other games that just enjoy playing their own game with whoever they get matched with. They even run impromptu "Dev Killer" events that give out special titles to those who win or lose (though you have to be willing to wear the losing one first).
This is just a super fun game, and once you find a group of people that you enjoy playing with, it only gets better. Definitely take advantage of the free weekends and if you feel like you need 3 more days, hit me up on Steam for my Refer-a-friend code.

No background music, one touch from anything kills you, and your arena is a tiny island floating in the void that you can fall off of. I might have lasted 30 seconds at first by running away from things (includes first 13 seconds of relative calm), but kept at it and eventually lasted a whole minute.
It was around then that I saw a top leaderboard replay (click the eye) and found out how to play properly. The leaderboard-with-replays-available aspect makes it a competitive game, and sometimes I'll just click on a lower ranked random player to see if I can steal any tricks.
Some thought has gone into the graphics and sound design. Aesthetically it looks Quake-ish, and not surprisingly one can do rocket jumps and bunny hop to get around. The graphics really drive home the whole "you're in hell, death is imminent" theme nicely. On my 5.1 surround I can hear spawners (???) appearing behind me, and those horned skulls charging from my blind spot....getting ever closer. Surround-sound rigs will get a better experience, for sure.
In a nutshell: Devil Daggers is a purist FPS experience with a focus on arena survival. By itself it would be a good game, but having leaderboards with replays makes it competitive and fun. Lasting longer than ever before is genuinely rewarding, because it's hard to do until you note certain patterns with experience (lots of dying).
Fun to pick up and play a few rounds inside ten minutes and get your fix. Just buy it if you're anywhere near the fence.
**Also, that reviewer who said that "being in the zone creates a state of mind not unlike meditation" (roughly paraphrased) was spot on. This game is all about that feeling. Though being ripped out of said zone makes me curse like a sailor.

text: A poorly optimized, poor simulator, with broken physics. You can build a symmetrical bridge, and when there are no cars on it, the stress is magically not distributed the same way on both sides as you would expect with a symmetric structure. This leads to frustrating collapses in later levels where materials are purposefully limited to make the game harder. Materials don't behave as you would expect them to. The game does not really support multiplayer as much as Guitar Hero. You can play gigs with your friends of course, switching the guitar every song, provided they have some guitar skills of their own. The game has some mini (arcade) games that do not require much skill and I guess those can provide for some multiplayer.
The best thing about it, is that it makes you want to keep on playing and practicing and this is a vital aspect of trying to learn to play any instrument really, so its really more recommendable to novice guitarists, who want to learn to play, but so far really can't seem to put the time and effort in.
The game comes with a cable for plugging your guitar into your PC, so its better to get a physical copy from a story with a cable included than just a digital download, because you can't play this game without that cable (and a guitar to plug in to it).
