Woodle, woodle, now that's a funny word. It refers to your little tree stump character that you'll be hopping and scrambling all over creation with, and it's an appropriately adorable name for an adorable little fellow. I could say the same for the rest of the game, that it has a simple, even precious charm to it. Unfortunately that's about all I can say about it without digging into all the parts that are lacking, so before I do that, let's just enjoy that title a little more. Woodle.
Woodle Tree Adventures opens with a great mustachio'd tree raising you whole from the earth and commanding you to bring water to the land. This is accomplished by traveling to six different worlds, finding the three giant fairy teardrops floating around, and taking them to the three giant Dixie cups at the end of the level. Along the way you can collect piles of berries that unlock new items for you, as well as a gaggle of precious and mostly passive monsters to maybe get in your way.
The colorful screenshots might hearken to mind Mario 64 or any of his other 3D outings, and that's not too far from the mark. Each of the six levels is a mass of blocks and platforms floating in a vast blue sky, and you have full range of moment to scamper about them, hoovering up berries and droplets. Your woodle dude has none of the fancy moves that Mario has trained up over the years, just run, jump, and bat things with his leaf. That's plenty to get through the different worlds of forests and beaches and ice and bees, because there are no puzzle elements or secrets to speak of.
This is where the game starts to show how thin it is, because each level is exactly what it says on the tin. 100 berries and 3 droplets, and you only need the droplets to win. The berries are added up at your house between levels and unlock new leaves to swing, but all the three fancy leaves do are let you shoot an air gust different distances. There's also a bandanna that's just for show and a seventh world you need 600 berries to access, but that doesn't mean you need to find every berry. No, every time you replay a level you can collect all the berries again, so if you were so inclined you could grind out all the unlocks on the very first level (do not do this). And once you beat the sixth world, you get a THANKS FOR PLAYING screen and that's it.
There's not going to be much reason to run around in the game beyond finishing it because the basic elements are just as threadbare. The platforming is stiff in its physics and sticky in how you get stuck on edges and walls. Animations are incredibly basic, rendering combat nothing more than waving a leaf and watching enemies slowly fall over with a sad bloop. There's literally no UI so forget about keeping track of the berries you found, and no camera controls so enjoy 3D platforming from a fixed angle. The camera thing is particularly damning because there are triggers around the levels that flip it to side or overhead angles but don't flip it back when you leave the area, so if you take an unlucky fall you might be doing a 3D jumping section from a profile view.
I had high hopes for Woodle Tree Adventures based on how cute and platformy it looked, but it plays more like a proof of concept than a finished game. There's not even a pause menu for cryin' out loud, just a splash screen with the controls and a button prompt to quit the game. It's a title that's very clearly the work of one developer, and while it's a great accomplishment in that respect it's still lacking the quality of a retail product. I'd love to see a sequel with more polished movement, more professional graphics (and sound, some of the piano tracks kill me), and just more to do. There is actually a sequel, but from the looks of it none of those improvements have been made. So sorry, little friend woodle... your name is a winner but your game really isn't.

I started like many music-gamers with the guitar hero series - nice, but not satisfactory in any way. One year ago I bought my first guitar - a Fender from America - and made my first steps alone until now. So I had a little presentiment of doing it, but no lessons at all.
The start of Rocksmith is hard, challenging but always fair. The negative point is, if you don't have any E-guitar at this time, it is getting expensive. On the other side, the software-aplifier makes a very good impression; so there's no need for an exra amplifier (if you have the right speakers with a phat sound connected).

Do you want to be punished for existing? Do you like being constrained by rules that do not apply to your enemies? Do you like being afraid to talk to NPCs in case they instakill your entire party at a whim? Then boy, is Divinity 2 the game for you.
In this game, if you're not running one of three cookie-cutter builds, and/or you're not playing on the easiest difficulty, you can forget about enjoyable gameplay. Everything costs extortionate amounts of money, in a world that is 100% finite, and traders will buy items from you at one tenth their actual value. Being one level below your enemies means instant defeat, and being one level above means a complete steamrolling - even if you do somehow manage to overlevel, because there are so few quests  - all of which involve combat, most of which completely unfair - that if you miss one or two at the beginning of the game, you are crippled for the rest of your campaign.
Bosses will simply ignore the mechanics of combat, using as many action points per turn and summoning as many allies as they feel like, and using spells that are leagues beyond what are available to a player at that level. This game's understanding of "balance" extends as far as having your rogue - assuming you decided to make one (if not, ♥♥♥♥ you, game over) - pickpocket every living soul from Fort Joy to Arx in order to buy enough equipment to keep you in the same league as enemies of your level, because if your armor is one level below yours, you might as well be wearing soggy tissue paper. Naturally, this punishes you for having a party of more than two people. There are NPCs in this game that, when spoken to, will give you a variety of persuasion options - all of which are guaranteed to fail, even with maxed persuasion stats (I have tested this thorughly) - and when they do fail, the NPC will turn hostile and one-shot your entire party before you are even able to take an action.
The cold, divisive meta of the game is that self-healing is a waste of time, armor restoration is a waste of time, and interesting builds are a waste of time. Spec everything into physical damage or run a 4-summoner party and faceroll the game if you don't want to lose. If you want to be creative with your party build, you're quite welcome to, so long as you don't plan on getting into any combat - which the game physically requires you to do in order to gain experience.
Divinity Original Sin 2 is a beautiful, intricate game - infected with the most moronic encounter design and balancing I have ever seen in a video game, period.

I personally think this game would do much better if there was a ranking system added, where you are matched with players on similar skill level as you.
A drop in clothing prices would probably encourage more purchases as well. If I can buy 5 parts from another game for only $20, why do I have to pay $18+ for 3 parts on this game?
But for now, it's just depressing...
I recently came back, and in all the rooms, I was either better than everyone else or the absolute worst. Both feel horrible. :/

Can't remeber if i've written a review for this already, but if not this will be an updated review.
To start off- yes. I am an old veteran of this game. Do not let the hours clocked on steam fool you. I've played this game since middle school, and stopped playing midway through highschool. I'm now in college.
Yes, this game used to be very popular, fun an interactive. I remember when channels 1-2 would be packed full, and players would have to spill over into channel 3 on weekends. Those were the days.
But this is not the case anymore. This game is absolutely, completely 100% DEAD.
To basically simplfy the rest (and what you really need to know):
PROS
-EXCELLENT MUSIC SELECTION. Whether your a K-pop or J-pop weeb, triple G thug, or EDM acid junkie they have tracks to suit just about everybody. Zeds dead, Diplo, Beyonce, Jay-z, Big Bang, Tropkillaz......etc. even the weekend if you wanna catch some feels about your ex's.
- CHALLENGING GAMEPLAY* (Will expand on in CONS)
-LARGE MULTITUDE OF DIFFERENT MODES so you do not get bored.
-DO NOT HAVE TO SPEND MONEY on in game items to look decent. Spending money is completely optional.
-LEVEL DOES NOT MATTER. It is only a placeholder for the game to display to other players how long you may have been playing and what kind of skill level you may have (as your level up mission becomes increasingly diffcult with level).
-STILL RECIEVES UPDATES TO CONTENT
CONS:
-DEAD COMMUNITY. *IMPORTANT*
Literally the only people still populating this game are old veterans like myself, alot of which have been playing 5+ years.
Assume any noob character is a smurf because 99.9% of the time they are. This creates NUMEROUS problems because when this game was still getting new players (which it isn't anymore), they would quit almost immediately because they would join the game and join a room to play with what seems like other new players only to be horrified when the game starts that all of the noob characters they were playing with were actually smurf alts of people anywhere from lvl 30-70.
Also, If you were to open up this game right now- the only channel that has any kind of population is channel 1 (which is packed full most of the time so GL spamming the enter button to get into the channel). Otherwise your forced onto channel 2, which is very empty.
Here's the kicker though, Even if you were to get into channel 1- the most/only populated channel in the game......half of the channel will be full of AFK'ERS and LOCKED ROOMS. Meaning half the people there aren't really there, and alot of the ones that are there are playing in rooms that have a password required in order for you to enter. Alot of the locked rooms are filled with Veterans of the game who sometimes get together and play for old times sake. Sometimes they leave the rooms open, but you better hope they dont instantly kick you when you try to enter. And even if they let you stay, who wants to play with level 45's on 8 key, 6 chance? (Some of the hardest modes in the game). I digress.
-CHALLENGING GAMEPLAY. So why is this a pro and con?
Depends on if you like a challenge or not, and are okay with investing the time to be good at something. This is not a game you can just "start playing". You are definitely going to struggle, and even after you get the hang of it- you have a million other modes and kinks in the game you will have to learn and conquer. You do not have to master every mode, but the basic mode's for the game are C4* and CC4* (which is C4 but about 2x as hard). CC4 is the basic go-to mode for most players in this game. Most of the rooms will be CC4. You will need to also learn CHANCE* if you want to end up in anything besides last place in every match you play which even with the time I have invested in this game, still sometimes have a hard time with. (*More on these if you DL and go through the game tutorial).
-OUTDATED GRAPHICS. Considering this is a game from 2007, I was really hesitant to list it as a con. I mean the graphics match for the years it was initially released for. Asking them to bring Unreal Engine graphics to this game is pretty unrealistic at this point. The entire game would have to be shut down, updated and reconfigured, then re-released in it's new state. Considering paying money into this game is 100% optional, and the community would probably not stick around to see it's re-release, the game wouldn't survive. And If you even clicked on this game in the first place, let's be honest- your not here for graphics. Although i do agree they could at minimal update the textures/ character models.
-BUGS AND EXPLOITATION. I don't know how many hacks and cheats still exist, but when I was playing this game it was full of many holes. Players could download programs that would cheat the game by giving them an 100% perfect rate (which can more than quarduple your score) and also allowed them to cheat modes that gave out game cash. Bannable offense if reported and found, but who cares if they ban several of your level 1-7 noob ult accounts when you can make more?
Also, this game is buggy. Not to the point it's completely unplayable- it's mostly playable. But don't be suprised if suddenly you lag like sh*t on your 100% working internet connection because the game get's ahead of itself then try's to repace everything- only to mess itself up further.  Sometimes the game will also randomly disconnect you, and once it boots you if you relog you cannot resume the match you were just in. You will be locked out of that game until it finishes without you, you will also not earn any XP or prize money for that match either no matter how far along it was. There are specific maps that don't seem to be configured very well where these things will occur very frequently, and certian mode/song combinations will also trigger the bugs. It's very easy to learn what they are and how to work around them (like avoiding the christmas map).
-UPDATED CONTENT. This is also listed as a con, because even though there a new modes being added, and new songs being added- the base game itself isnt being adressed. You can throw brand new rims on a 1991 chevy, but at its core it's still an old rusty chevy.
FINAL VERDICT:
Game in '07 to '10 - 7.5/10
Game now and probably into the end of time: 1/10.

Star Realms is a self-contained deck-building game.  This is great news for me, as I like card games but the business models of some other deck-builders that can involve hundreds of dollars of investment generally puts me off playing this genre.
The first thing I feel that needs to be addressed is the F2P status on Steam.  Some people seem upset that the game is displayed as "Free to Play" but in fact this gives you access to no more than a demo: you'll get the do the tutorial, play the first campaign and challenge the AI on easy mode.  If you want access to the other AI modes, the full campaign and most importantly the online play you'll need to buy the "Full Game" DLC.  Which costs £4 in my country, what's that?  $6?
So why has the developer decided to approach the game this way?  Well, the motivation is actually a good one.  Buying the game on any platform (mobile or steam) gives you access across all platforms.  So you won't have to rebuy the game on mobile if you enjoy it on Steam.  This is a refreshing attitude in an era where a lot of developers/publishers are cash-grabbing at every opportunity.  A lot of the negative reviews for Star Realms are due to the fact the game states F2P and really it isn't, but once you understand that you are getting the game across all platforms for one price I don't see any reason to complain!
So the game...  You have three stats that effect your strategy: damage, health and trade.  As the game progresses the key to success is balancing these stats as well as of course managing your deck.  Both players start with identical hands and deck management is achieved by buying new cards (ships and bases) through the trade you obtain and scrapping weaker cards via the special abilities on some ships or bases.
The ships and bases all belong to one of four factions (there is one exception).  Many of the cards have an additional action or boost to its stats if it is in play at the same time as a card from the same faction.  So collecting cards from the same faction will improve the overall power of your deck.
A little bit of luck certainly helps whilst playing too.  Getting access to the right cards at the right times can make a big difference.  Understanding the game and being able to adapt your strategy is more important though.  So while a bit of luck can make a big difference, in the long run victory will come down to how good your strategy is.
The graphics are nice and clear and represent the game well.  It looks identical on smart phone and also plays identical.  One slight issue I had on my Z3 Compact phone that due to the display being fairly small it was tough to see the detail on some of the cards.  I can imagine learning on a display that size would be really difficult.  Of course this is no problem in the Steam version!
I love the sound track!!  It may be slightly generic space music playing on a loop but it has a kind of epic feel to it.  Suits the game perfectly.
The online community is great too.  I've found I had to wait no longer than 30 seconds to find a match and most of the time I get matched instantly.  Obviously the benefit of cross-platform and a benefit of the aforementioned business model discussed earlier.  It would’ve been nice to have an in-game chat function, I guess this is one disadvantage to playing cross-platform to people on their smartphones without access to a keyboard.
Playing versus the AI's is really fun.  I'm not one for playing against bots, but I find the AI challenging and the biggest advantage is not having to wait for a human player to make their turn.  Although turns are generally quite fast in Star Realms, the length of time taken per turn generally increases as the game progresses.  This is due to more complex cards being introduced to the decks via trade purchases and players using the special abilities of their ships and bases.
I was a little underwhelmed by the campaign mission I attempted.  The boss fight has special rules that removed most the fun from the game.  The core game is the 1v1 and that is where the game is at in my opinion, playing vs AI or a human opponent.
Best thing to do if you are on the fence about whether to purchase is download the free version, play the quick tutorial and then practise against the Easy AI for a bit.  You'll soon know whether to invest a further £4 for the full game.
There is additional DLC available that introduces more ships/bases and also events.  I'm having so much fun in the base game that after 17 hours of game I really don't want to upset the perfect balance the base game provides!  Not that I honestly expect it to!  If you do play against someone online that has paid for the DLC you will also have access to the exact same cards.  So there is no P2W here.  Good stuff!!
Massive thumbs up to Star Realms!!  Strongly recommended.

I have over 7,000 hours of Dota2 played. I invested a fair amount of time in Heroes of Newerth before that and Heroes of the Storm since. And while this game is probably not an ARTS/MOBA, it has a lot of the elements that drew me to the genre.
Despite being turn based the game never feels slow. All players share the same 20 seconds to decide what they want to do for that turn, which keeps the pacing sharp and rewards quick decision making. It is long enough to remove the 'twitch reflexes' aspect from other games, which is a bonus for me as I'm approaching gamer's old age.
The controls are simple and the mechanics are intuitive. As long as you understand that each phase (Prep, Dash, Blast, Move) is simultaneous within itself it's pretty easy to grasp why a dead freelancer is still able to get off that monster full-team ultimate.
But like the simplicity of chess, it's just a framework to outplay your opponents. The game is only as easy as the enemy team makes it. That 6-hp Lockwood is definitely going to dash and stay alive, right? So your entire team covers places he can jump to and secure the kill. But he just stands there and shoots you all for massive damage. Mind games and bluffing are front and center in Atlas Reactor and to me that's the core of a competitive game.
-Crisp pacing within a turn based context
-Simple controls and intuitive mechanics
-Complex gameplay that heavily features mind games
-Very friendly community (for now, best to assume this will diminish as the game grows)
-Reflexes are irrelevant, but quick decision making is key
-As far from p2w as you can possibly get
-Unoptimized in beta (

Devil Daggers is a game where you, the player, is sent to battle against hell itself. Brandishing magical daggers, you need to survive for as long the beasts of hell will allow. Paired with beautiful and morbid stylistic direction and art, this hearkens back to the likes of Quake, Diablo and DOOM, with it's gritty, enigmatic, demonic, occult, and somewhat Lovecraftian style.
This is a decently "competitive", fast paced game that has tenfold more strategy and metagame than would would expect on the surface, especially for the small retail price tag of £3.99/$4.99 (which you can probably get for less regardless.). The game will test you, as you will test yourself, finding new strategies against the onslaught of demons with the very little and cryptic information that you are given. Learning nuance and piecing together the mannerisms of the demons. Learning sound cues with constant awareness as all of the otherworldly, demonic wails and cries mesh together (seriously, the sound design is stupidly well done, holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ to create a brilliant cacophony you try to make sense of, marking your inevitable defeat.
Best of all? You will try, and try again until you rule out every single variable that you know to get just a dozen seconds more, until something new throws you off and makes your journey through hell even harder.
A must buy if you're into Quake, and if you crave an oldschool, hardcore 90s PC game vibe.
A must buy if you want a game where you need to process dozens of different things in a handful of seconds.
A must buy if you're looking for a game that will test your prowess.

Atlas Reactor is an amazing blend of sci-fi stratergy with a 4v4 team based deathmatch. you select a "freelancer" to play (firepower, support, and frontline) and you work with your team in a turn based way, in a turn there are 2 'phases' you have 'decision phase' and 'resolution phase' in decision phase there are 3 types of moves that ALWAYS happen in this order
PREP PHASE:
this will be heals, shields, and traps, this to buff or debuff
DASH PHASE:
as the name says, you use these abilities to dash out of the way of damage ablilites, but you can dash into a trap to kill yourself, you have been warned ;)
BLAST PHASE:
these ablities will damage your enemy, and will always happen last.
then there will be movement phase, where you move to your selected location. i want to stress this point THERE IS NO RNG AT ALL, i cant stress that enough, in the resolution phase where this all plays out, you may see an enemy shoot 1st, but as far as the server is concerned everything happens at the SAME time, so you can kill the enemy shooting you and die in the same turn
yes there is microtransactions, but purely cosmetic items only, nothing that will help you in game.

At first I could not understand what this game is about, and did not know what to expect. I played this on my laptop for an hour or so but I just found the game strange. I returned to the game again after a month or so and something finally clicked.
This is not a game in the traditional sense, but more of a psychedelic interactive novella. The gameplay, if you can call it that, consists of travelling around a bizarre world and encountering strange characters and events as well as choosing dialogue options (sometimes for multiple characters at once!).
To best be able to appreciate this game I think that you need
* to play with a controller
* to play on a big screen or TV. While they graphics may seem primitive there is a lot of detail in the surroundings, especially from Act 2 onwards.
* decent sound. The sound design in this game is great, but on laptop speakers it is terrible :P
If you like games in the style of "Dear Esther" and "The Vanishing of Ethan Carter" but want a more dialogue-driven alternative, this might be something for you. If you want a traditional point 'n click adventure with puzzles, this will probably not be your cup of tea.
Beware though that the release rate of the 5 acts in the game has slowed down by a lot (act 3 was released 2 years ago).

Actually, the game may really be made of painted bits of cardboard cut into interesting shapes. I do not know, but what I do know is that this game is quite decent.
You start off the story with an elderly fellow named Conway, who is delivering a package in his truck to someone located on Dogwood Drive. To get there, he is told, he must find a way to [wobbly, smoky lettering]The Zero[/wobbly, smoky lettering] in order to get there. What follows is what happens in his pursuit of this location.
I feel I ought to address the issue of the acts, as they stand currently this fine January afternoon in 2016. There are at this time three of five promised acts, and the development of the remaining two acts has been pushed back to an indefinite time. Act IV is purportedly imminent, but the exact timing is still undefined.
It is some folks' opinion that you should wait until the game is completely and totally finished before you bother with the first three acts, as the developers are totally attempting to scam us all by falsely advertising a five-act game while only delivering three.
It is my opinion that if those are your thoughts in this debate, you ought not be playing this game, as I am reasonably certain it simpy is not your sort of game. Having played through the first three acts, I do not feel particularly stiffed in not having the last two yet. I have backed projects on Kickstarter, for goodness sakes, and if that has taught me anything it is that a rushed project will yield nothing but misery. Jelly physics at their worst.
If you fail a level, don't think you've done something wrong, quite often retrying the tests you'll pass fine.
Your steel cables have a habit of detaching themselves for no apparent reason, and suspension cables are almost always useless to you due to having the same bend mechanism as the curved line in ms paint.
To top that off, completely symmetrical drawbridge builds, have a habit of closing lopsided and making your bridge commit suicide - these ones you really need to retest a few times, they'll usually work after a few tries.
Getting worse, the crossframes. The auto build crossframe feature is buggy at best, and has a nasty habit of building them right in the path of oncoming vehicles - at later levels you'll find yourself turning this on and off a few times lest the first bus destroy your creation due to no fault of your own.
Then there's the sporadic forgot the stress colour system, which loves to get stuck on red with random parts - once again changing each time retested with equal things.
Move a connecting point, no parts adjust, just screws you up
Select mode has no toggle feature, so you have to click it, then make your selection and god help you if you miss, you'll have to click select mode again!
Finally, the overall lack of DECENT camera control. use your arrows and it pans, turn on cursor focus and it drifts slowly when trying to place things, try cursor movement off after alt tabbing a single time and it doesn't actually regain mouse focus - you're stuck switching cursor focus on and off again to make larger levels even playable.
Overall, bug riddled.
Don't get me wrong, it was a bit of fun playing, I even enjoyed the vehicle view as it was fun to crash repeatedly.
Just could have been implemented so much better.
As it stands it's near equal to other bridge builder games coded in flash.
It just looks a little prettier.
I'd recommend playing the flash game cargo bridge first. If you can't get enough of that then this may be up your alley.
Otherwise, be prepared to be annoyed by a clunky interface, random physics glitches every time you test, and the everlasting questioning of why, seeing your brand new bridge rammed by a bus due to those crossframes.

I had to think about whether I gave this title a thumbs up or down - I figured the overall package deserved it, but it's not plain sailing.
Essentially a really amp'd-up version of pipemania, this is an interesting indie title that is the gaming equivalent of tightrope walking while dodging waterbombs.
What I liked:
The general style. The music. The characters. The art. It takes place in a zany Jetsons-style futuristic city (think Fallout before the bombs hit). This game didn't actually need any of these but the dev chose to put them in all the same, and the game is better for it. It feels like a quality title.
What I disliked:
I generally don't mind difficult games, but this crossed the line into frustration one too many times. Later levels are patently ridiculous, with the player being expected to multi-task to a degree where there need to be simultaneously dropping Glitches (essentially land mines) to catch two bugs at once while trying to work out the orientation of hidden pipes WHILE trying to re-orientate the known pipes. You don't feel any satisfaction once you've done it because often you win by sheer luck.
It's a decent title. It's well-made. But there's a line between challenging and annoying and this game unfortunately has no idea where it is for the most of the time. By all means, get it in a sale and have a blast on your laptop when you're bored :)

Nearly four years ago before I began writing reviews, I played A Virus Named T.O.M., and shortly after a hiatus I came back to air my grievances in what I thought was a comprehensive review. When I read that review today, the words do not appear the thoughts that I possess now while I agree with some points made by my old self; however, I also see aspects I misunderstood about the game that I find so obvious now.
As someone who studied a little about cognitive development, it’s no surprise to me as brains aren’t fully developed until the mid-twenties. Egocentric tendencies aside, the difference in quality of my criticisms is what strikes me as the most valuable reason to rewrite this review. Having four years of gaming experience as well as practice expressing my thoughts are also reasons why I felt the need to revise my old review, but even if I may not personally recommend this game the feeling of better understanding its shortcomings and appeal is something I’ll always cherish about AVNTOM.
The problems illustrated by my previous self, while true in a sense that the game’s overall challenge is inconsistent, fails to understand how each level varies how much each skill is being tested. Up to World/Invention 5, the game incrementally adds new modifiers like the previously mentioned hidden mechanic as well as indestructible drones, loophole pathways, etc. as well as how much importance is put on one type of problem versus another level. This type of design is reminiscent of the gimmicks of the Super Mario Galaxy games by the constant usage and discard mechanics to make each level distinct.
For example, Level 2-5 will test your ability to focus on solving a simple tube puzzle while also utilizing the stun-ability to sneak around the drones that cannot be avoided otherwise. Level 2-7 also uses this challenge but adds a special drone that must be destroyed in a spot to give the grid power, and Level 2-8 adds the infamous invisible mechanic that still uses a simple grid puzzle. Thinking about most of the game this way, I found that instead of constantly bypassing levels with the skip-tokens I would often find the solution with only the higher-reflex challenges to be an utter drag.
It is only within the last two worlds is the prevalence of high-reflex challenges become an utter nuisance to a puzzle game like AVNTOM. However, an easy solution to this problem that my younger self did not stumble on was adding difficulty modes. If you could affect the speed of enemies for these split-second decision levels as well as make a practice mode and/or give T.O.M. the ability to see the unpowered grids that are invisible from the corners, then at least the methodical approach is not compromised by the sudden emphasis on speed.
To this day this issue still baffles me not because the controls do not work when it should but that a game that emphasizes so much moment-to-moment decision making relies on anchoring the player in a box-like grid is still one of the worst ideas, period.
In levels where speed is emphasized but the puzzles are simplified, this issue, while annoying, is at least salvageable; it’s the later levels that will constantly have you crash into enemies while trying to solve the puzzle (Level 4-10) is where the flaws behind its design begin to show themselves. Especially for levels where you are given limited health, the amount of time you get to stare at the screen and perform the correct maneuver can be so limited on mistakes that you will get tired of trying to solve the puzzle by the inability to focus on the problem.
Part of the problem is probably due to the inclusion of four-player coop which requires something simple for four players to quickly interact with the puzzles and to indicate to the other players what each one is doing on screen. Unlike the difficulty spike, I don’t think there is a simple solution to fix the control issue without compromising on the types of puzzles focused on in AVNTOM.
This statement is as true today as when I first typed out my disappointment. While I think there is a happy medium for players of all skill-levels to enjoy without ruining the fun of the game, I don’t think having a game that challenges both to such extremes leads to satisfying solutions. As much as I love DUSKERS and eagerly await what else is in store from Misfit Games, I sincerely hope someday Dr. X will come back to reboot T.O.M. for another technological anarchy of destruction in some other utopia.

(Review of the free version)
First off, the free version of this game is a demo, not the full game. You are only able to do the tutorials, the first campaign, and play against 'easy' AI. I finished all the 'free' content (including all campaign challenges) in about 4 hours. That's not to say it's a bad game at all. In fact, I would recommend the free version to anyone who is a fan of card games and at $5 I think the paid version is a good value too :)
The game: Star Realms is a drafting game similar to Dominion, where you start with a limited set of cards and build your deck by buying new ones from a common pool. As the game goes on, you get more powerful cards that allow you to pummel your opponent until they die. There are four different 'races' each of which have their own gimmick. Red cards allow you to remove the bad cards from your deck, making it more efficient. Yellow cards cause your opponent to discard, Blue cards are the only way to gain 'authority' (life points), and Green cards...well, they're just really good at beating face.
Pros:
*Easy to learn
*Fast-paced gameplay
*Free? (if that counts as a pro)
Cons:
*The interface is pretty clearly designed with touch screens in mind. It's not too frustrating for a desktop user but things can be a bit clunky. Just adding a function for RMB would make control a lot smoother.
*The basic set of cards are a bit repetitive. There's just not much variation between the playstyles of the different races. Plus the fact that the only way to win is by attacking your opponent means there's pretty much just one strategy.
*The sound effects and music are uninspired and the art is pretty same-y. But now I'm just nitpicking.
Overall, I'd recommend this. It's F2P so there's really no harm in giving it a shot.

Very nice continuation of the First Chapter; do NOT play this game until you've finished The Legend of Heroes: Trails in the Sky. You will be hopelessly lost without prior knowledge of characters and locations from the first game, and wiki summaries are simply not enough to bridge the gap.
The Legend of Heroes: Trails in the Sky Second Chapter (or Eiyuu Densetsu: Sora no Kiseki SC in weebspeak) is quite simply one of the best games I've ever been sucked into. It's not perfect, but it comes close in pretty much every area.
The gameplay is as refreshing as ever; the battles are still on a tactical grid, where you and your enemies take turns to attack each other (and depending on how fast you are, you can potentially take multiple turns before your opponent even moves your way). However, there were several features added to the Trails in the Sky battle system.
The overworld has a few minigames to help melt the time away, such as a casino and fishing. Fishing's especially something to note, since there's an achievement tied to it, if that's your thing.
Additionally, XSEED's even taken some PSP-exclusive content and backported it to the PC version. One of those features won't be seen until the end of the game, but it's worth the wait.
However, the overall story lacks a bit, especially when compared to FC's gradual but well-tempered buildup. Excluding the Prologue, every chapter from Chapter 1 up to and including Chapter 5 is rather formulaic in nature; strange happenings in a province lead to Estelle and friends investigating them, only to find out that an Ouroboros Enforcer is behind it all.
The game picks up pace during Chapters 6 and 7, but leaves you at a pretty bad drop during Chapter 8 (which I can honestly say was my least favorite chapter in all the Trails games I've played, gameplay-wise). The Final Chapter more than makes up for the tedium of Chapter 8, however, and wraps up Estelle and Joshua's story very cleanly.
Speaking of which, the characters and dialogue in SC are top notch; while the plot may be  predictable at times, the characters more than make up for the lacking moments.
Party members receive actual character development, and characters you may have despised in FC have a chance at redemption; Agate comes to mind easily.
Additionally, new characters enter the fray, and they're just as good as the established characters; Kevin Graham, for one, is absolutely phenomenal in all the right ways.
Again, the dialogue flows naturally, and outside of one very, very small encounter in Zeiss, I couldn't help but eagerly read every line of dialogue that popped up. Even NPCs are relatively lively, which you might not expect from JRPGs; I've seen others where town NPCs get a single flavor line at best.
Lastly, the quality of the game is just perfect; I haven't encountered any technical issues at all, despite the somewhat troubled localization process.

Here's to Trails in the Sky the 3rd, Trails of Cold Steel II, and hopefully Zero/Ao no Kiseki!

I bought this game in 2014 when it first came out. I still play it quite regularly.
This is a really god example of good minimalist game design. Though new mechanics are being added as (modular) expansions, the game stays very tightly loyal to its core mechanics. I don't feel like there is a lot of feature bloat here.
The base game, at $5, is a great experience. Each faction has a specific theme that's easy to learn over a few games, but takes a while to really master when combined together. Not all cards are equal, which is part of the learning curve. Less valuable cards are key to the design working, though, and there are ways to use almost any card (aside from the loathesome Viper) in your strategy. I played this base game for 2 years before realizing there were expansions because I had a copy of the game that didn't include any mention of them.
I've since picked up 2 of these expansions and I've noticed that they've done a couple things:
1) The new cards make both players more powerful overall, which means more stategic decisions and less universally undesireable cards.
2) Gambits speed up the first couple of rounds, which helps the game's overall flow.
3) The AI isn't able to keep up as well as you add expansions. This is both good and bad. It means that the game probably isn't so easy to calculate with simple algorythms as before, which means that human players will get more out of it. It also means that the vs. AI mode doesn't provide the challenge it used to, pushing players eventually onto online play.
Should you spend $5 on this game? If you enjoy card games, it's a no brainer. You'll easilly get your money's worth.
Should you invest in the expansions? You'll have to decide for yourself. They're more expensive than the base game when added together, so just balance how much you value your dollars to your time in game. It's certainly a better deal than any free-to-play or AAA game, so you shouldn't really worry too much over it.
Personally, I wished more games were modeled like this. I'm happy to support it.

•	You can retry battles, when you lose (Fights also get easier after each retry so you are
never stuck).
•	Decent turn based strategy, with a variety of customizable skills
Cons
•	There is a ton of dialog, which can slow the pace of the game.
•	There is no way of skipping or speeding-up battle animations.
•	It’s easy to miss some quests. I missed some for the first guild before I got the hang of it.
•	Agate (Though you will like him towards the end of SC)
Conclusion
Trails in the Sky has its problems, however they don’t ruin the experience. It is everything a decent JRPG should be. Many of these flaws can be overlooked depending on preference.
Unlike the games mentioned above, Trails in the sky has an awesome story, that keeps getting better the deeper you get into the game.
This is the biggest fun, on the couch, with friends.

"A Virus Named TOM" is a small puzzle game where you control a little virus named TOM as he goes about spinning circuits and hacking into everything MegaCorp makes. Gameplay is very pipe-mania style where you have to spin pieces around to connect every last one. Varieties of drones add danger and falling energy keeps the pressure on, but the core gameplay is little more than connecting pieces before your power runs out. (Thankfully pipe connection is one of my favorite kinds of puzzle games.)
The art style is cute and charming, even if the story isn't terribly robust beyond a few cutscenes and sternly-worded letters from MegaCorp. This game doesn't have tons of content, but what it has is done well. The soundtrack deserves a mention as well for its pleasing synthesized tunes.
The largest complaint I have about this game is the difficulty curve. The puzzles certainly do get trickier and the drones harder to dodge, sometimes making this game more about twitch reflexes than solving puzzles, but some later levels in particular are positively brutal. If you're looking for a laidback puzzle to pick at, you're not going to get too much of that here.
If you're looking for a charming little puzzle game to wile away some hours (and occasionally frustrate you), this game is a great choice. With puzzles ranging from simple to downright cruel, a lovable cast, and a simply great art style, A Virus Named TOM is worth looking at. But if spending $10 for 6 hours of a robot spinning circuits and madly dodging drones isn't your speed, you can safely give this game a pass. I quite enjoyed this, but can see how others would not.

Star Realms is a deck building card game which was originally a table top game that was published in 2014 by White Wizard Games. The PC version of the game was released onto PC on March 8th 2016.
I am a huge trading card game fan, on a daily basis I play at least three hours of Hearthstone, and have played Pokémon and MTG in the past too. Star Realms is a game which instantly took my fancy from the screenshots. Once you get your head around how to play the game, which sadly the tutorial doesn’t do a fantastic job of explaining things, it is a really simple yet addictive card game.  I love the deck building side of the game since you can pick and choose exactly how you want to build your deck depending on the type of opponent you are facing.
You start each turn with at least 4 or 5 cards in your hand; you can play all of your cards if you choose, this in turn gives you damage points, and resources to choose another card to add to your deck. Games start off quite slowly but soon ramp up to some pretty high numbers being thrown around.  It sounds really simple when it is explained properly, but somehow the tutorial manages to over complicate it to the point where it is almost as easy enough to teaching yourself how to play by just jumping into the game.
The game’s art style is in a pretty generic sci-fi theme. You can quite clearly see the game was designed for a tablet, as the UI is pretty poor for a PC game. The clunky designs of menus are a little off putting. The UI in the game itself is OK, you can see all of the required information fairly easily, but again it is very “tablet-fied”. The audio is pretty sub-standard too, sounds like some stock sci-fi music playing in the background with some fairly generic sound effects too. Although these aren’t all massive pointers for a card game, I would still like to have seen an average attempt at these elements.
Star Realms is being advertised on Steam as a free to play title, but really, it’s simply a demo for the full game. The single player campaign mode is gated after the first chapter, which is only five levels itself and you cannot play multiplayer without buying into the full game. Alas I did actually make the purchase of £3, 99 to get access to the full game, because I was having a really good time playing and wanted to play more. Sadly after purchasing I was greeted with an error message of “401 Unauthorized” and no way to exit out of that screen other than ALT F4ing. A few people on the forums seem to be having the same problem too which isn’t too promising, so I have requested a refund until the developers can come back to me/solve the issue.
IF the game can be fixed to let me continue playing, Star Realms is a game I can definitely see myself putting another 5-6 hours into, or at least completing the campaign mode.  There is a small online community with roughly 100 people being active at any one time, but I would personally only see this as a single player experience at the moment.
Other than the technical issue I have had with the full version of the game, everything else seems to be running fine, and even has support for 4k resolutions too! For me the issue is with the game claiming to be free to play when in fact it is just a demo, which doesn’t sit right for me. There is gated content behind the paywall, which doesn’t seem to be working correctly sadly. I hope this can be fixed in order for me to play the rest of the game. Without the technical faults, Star Realms is a neat little card game, which any trading card game fan will enjoy. A game can last between 5-10 minutes, so has a very casual feel to it. At the moment I am purely going to just recommend this title and nothing more. I really want to be able to highly recommend this game, because I have had such a blast with it so far…. I will definitely be re-purchasing the full game if the developers can fix the issues and I will for sure re-visit my review in due course.
EDIT - I am changing this review to a "Not Recommended". The only way you can get access to the full game AFTER purchasing the game through Steam is to create an account on their website and sync to your Steam account. If you are releasing a game on Steam, it should work completely through your Steam account, not jumping through hoops of the developer's own account system as well

Time compels me to re-write my review, with more hindsight. I can no longer recommend this game. The more I think about it, the more frustrated it makes me. It's the biggest let-down I have experienced in gaming, because the first game was SO awesome, such an amazing JRPG that anyone even remotely into the genre should play. This game, despite being a direct sequel, despite working off of the same system, is not. I will give 2 basic reasons.
1) The game is frustrating. They wanted to continue this game off of the old one, they didn't want to invent an all new system or start you off at level 1 from scratch. Okay. But their attempt to "extend" everything, the leveling, the magic, your equipment, resulted in imbalance. It's too easy now to have an entire party dropping nukes on the battlefield. So their solution to this problem was frustration; simply make it hard to obtain money, magic "orbments", equipment, and constantly force-change your party with new characters who have different elemental restrictions, forcing different play styles (and sometimes, everything that was on the character you lost goes with them, if you didn't know to unequip them ahead of time). This game really requires multiple saves, in case they stick you with someone you have few options for and can hardly use. Fights themselves are now against bullet sponges who spam status effects, have random immunities, and heal themselves. Sometimes it's fun, but more often it just feels annoying, especially if, again, you "messed up" by not already having alot of a certain element so you could exploit weaknesses, even though you had no way of knowing that's what you needed. And good luck getting more, it takes HOURS.
2) While I still like the characters, the banter, the moral dilemmas, the actual story is TERRIBLE. It's like The Empire Strikes Back, but if you had to watch Luke Skywalker getting completely owned by Vader over and over at the end of every act. Your enemy is, I don't know, Cobra, or Hydra, but not incompetent. Global reach, endless mooks, the most advanced technology, infinite money, full-scale mass production capabilities, unparalleled scientific and historical knowledge, all led by demi-gods, every one of which is able to backhand you into a coma without a thought. Why? I have no idea. Why does the second-in-command of this group have mind-control powers? I don't know. No one even asks. It's just accepted as perfectly fine to introduce a character with comic book powers with no origin story, no known limitations, he just can. It's laughable. There's no tension here; you CAN'T win. Just, lose, lose, lose. Every act is the same; something happens, you track down one of these humans of mythical power, you barely survive a fight and then they leave you alive out of pity. You stop nothing, you accomplish nothing, they could have simply removed most of the boss fights because they are a waste of time.
A JRPG is really a combination of a few factors, mostly story and combat, and both fail. While I like many secondary aspects, like the world and characters (although alot of that we already know and is not as engaging the second time around), the important parts are just bad. The game is frustrating, it screws you over, it makes even scrub fights longer and more expensive than they have any need to be, and there is never any pay off for any of it, you're always losing. the equipment system, which was fun and mostly balanced before, is now horribly skewed in one direction and it really feels like tying a weight to your leg when the game gives you one of the other characters who can't exploit that imbalance. Finally, I didn't finish the game; the main story right before you reach the point of no return requires you to deliberately gimp yourself. I did so, only afterwards realizing that this was also the last chance to do about 50 sidequests, which I physically could not do now that I had weakened myself. I had no way of knowing this, and now I had no way of doing any of this optional content. I rage-quit. Maybe the last 3 hours of the story are awesome, but I really, really doubt it. Only fans of the previous game should even consider this entry, and even then, it's really, really a let down.

Being a Audi player ever since Nexon had this and it was popular back then. In fact, my older sister loved the game back then. I didn't noticed that Redbana even got the game until like a few years later and this was actually when I moved from American Audition Online to AuditionSEA which in my opinion was better and how I got into the well known Korean Pop that now spans throughout YouTube.
But let's talk about Audition Online. The one that's now owned by Redbana and I'm sorry to say that this one didn't hit my interest at all...

to include songs from X-BEAT (Audition Online for Japan) and KPOP to bring in more people to play the game. But only a few.

For standard players, there's the usual 4 Key and 8 Key mode that all Audition Online players knows. 4 key with the arrow keys, 8 keys with the number pad.
And from my experience, it's almost impossible to get a single perfect in the game. I'm not joking either. Even songs that are practically impossible to even hold a series of Greats and Cools because 190 bpm.
But if you aren't really satisfied with the normal mode, there's always a buttload of modes to go through. Including the famous battle parties where you literally take on an AI and it scraps a lot of points. Requiring players to work together to beat the AI. Your reward? A load of in-game currency.
There's even Club Dance 2 and Couple Dance for those who like to get their romance on and yes, you can have a couple and get married in this game. A couple garden as well.
Then there's the story mode, which is by far... Not my favorite in my opinion.... The story mode does require you to complete these objectives in order to progress. You know, as of this year and probably next year, we would have cinematic cutscenes and all that. This game stuck to it's roots and provides a text load. Probably not really making you feel so important in the story. However, by completing these missions, you can earn more in-game money or EXP and if you complete a series of mission in a episode. You get a badge for it. I guess you can say it's your alternative way to farm EXP while you solo.
And I have to talk about this... EXP.
You only earn EXP if you either play with other players or complete missions in story mode. This means that if you're hosting a private room for your own self and thinking that you can earn exp that way, you probably have the wrong thoughts. When you're competing against other players, the ranking you're on determines how much EXP you get. Someone in 1st place can get more EXP than someone in last place. Do I think it's fair? Eh... I guess?
Now let's dig deep into leveling.
In this game, when you touch level 5, in order to earn the next level, you have to complete a song with a specific amount of perfects and score to clear the license mode and earn the next level. As you progress through the levels, the bpm will increase. Along with the requirements. And yes, perfect chains is a requirement as well. So if you can't chain perfects well, you're pretty much stuck on whatever lvl you're on until you can master chaining.
Of course, it's not a game without hacks. Yep, there's already perfect hacks being sent out as it goes. It's no surprise that it's even on Nexon's Audition Online. Many hackers would use it for Story Mode or Battle Parties or just use it in normal mode and crush everyone in the room. Badly.
The shop is no doubt a place where you can really deck out your character with some cute outfits. That's true. However, you do have to consider that most clothes, accessories, and all that requires you to pay money. And they only last for like 7 days. Unless you wanna cash in some more money to get the clothes or whatever permanently.
Now... Let's talk about the downfall of this game.
As I'm aware, I heard it came on Steam and released into Steam. Only to be heard that it's forcing players to do a good review on it in order to get a 40 dollar in game cash. Not only that, GMs are corrupted and there's too much drama in the game. Updates are rare in this game. And the game life is just slowly dying. Some of the songs you all hear and love on the radio isn't in the game anymore. Some songs don't even peek an interest. It's clearly proof that this version of Audition Online is slowly dying and Redbana is just milking the game even more to prevent it's death. Even the tourney isn't even going well as there's bound to be hackers wanting to take the top.
So in my opinion, this game is pretty much dead. With all the shenanigans the game goes through, from bribed reviews to corrupted GMs who bans you for no reason. It's literally no doubt that the game is fun yeah. But it's gonna need a lot more work to really get this game to where it was. With the community slowing dying, I don't think this game is gonna last much longer than what it was intended to be. Graphics are no doubt outdated. I can't recommend this game because of what Redbana is doing to make more money.

I'll never understad when people review a game, and then say nothing about the actual game itself.
Atlas Reactor is a team-based, simultaneous turn-based tactical battle arena. The current competitive mode is a 4v4 death-match style arena, with the winner being first to five kills or most kills after 20 turns.
The concept itself is new and refreshing, and it provides a new and unique alternative to the many moba-like games that are emerging. It is infinitely more cerebral than existing mobas, and the depth of the strategy is far better than any existing MOBA game.
The game recently switching from a F2P model to a B2P model, which is clear from some of the current designs. However, this is an early access game that only very recently exited alpha stages. The game and model are evolving rapidly, and the developers make a point to interact with the community on a daily basis, going so far as supporting the "official" reddit discord server. A large portion of the changes to the game have come directly from the suggestions of the community. It's rare to see this level of community engagement, even in an early access game. The only company I can think of in recent history that has committed to this level of interaction with the community is Gazillion, with Marvel Heroes.
As far as the game itself, I have thoroughly enjoyed it. The matches are quick, prediction the enemies' actions is incredibly rewarding, and a single mistake can be catastrophic. Every action  you take and every choice you make plays a critical roll in your success or failure.

Atlas Reactor is a 4v4 arena deathmatch with a goal to kill 5 enemies before they do the same to you. (So yes, there is respawning.) Each character has a unique basic attack, 3 other moves typically with a multi-turn cooldown, 1 ultimate the fills up from using your moves, and then 3 non-character-specific one time use moves. Each turn you will use 1 ability and 1 move (or 2 moves). The other players will be making their moves simultaneously and everyone has 20 seconds each turnt o do so. Games are typically under 10 minutes.
OK, so how well does this work? Pretty well. There are some UI improvements to be made, but all in all the pacing is excellent. Skillful play is rewarded. Like MOBAs, knowledge of the game and characters is extremely important. You can also somewhat customize the skills of your character which can help solidfy your strategy in a premade group. The characters are fairly unique and people will certainly get attached to particular 'freelancers'. There are only 18 characters right now so the roster needs to grow before launch. But the gameplay is more than solid. It's refreshing, it's unique, and it's well done.
The biggest concern is the size of the playerbase. Right now queue times are fine, but $30 will be a steep price to pay when this game launches. I think this is worth $30 since the characters are all included (like Overwatch). However, it looks too much like a F2P game from the outside. And it's a unique concept which can sometimes find trouble taking hold. I think this game would do much better with a $20 price tag (like Rocket League). But I digress. The game is currently free for the weekend and while queue times are fine now, it's not exactly overflowing with players.
So do I recommend this game? Yes. You should play it. It's a fun game that blends XCOM and MOBAs into a unique package with a couple twists. Is it worth $30? Well, that's always going to be subjective. But for me, the answer is yes as long as the population is there.

To get to a serious issue:
A lot of people criticize the game for its slow dlc releases. I didn't notice that what I bought was a "season pass" and not a full game until well after I'd finished playing as much as I could. I honestly loved the game. Its narrative was touching. The music still sticks with me. The game was like a work of art. So I personally did not mind that the game was unfinished. However, the enterence fee is a bit hefty. So: If this is going to be one of the few games in your library, do not buy it. It is a bit of a one-hit-wonder. It doesn't have a lot of replay value, at least not to me. The beauty (or downfall, in some cases) of this game is in the way it tells the narrative. You cannot backtrack on your dialogue choices, and some choices are relatively similar. This gives the whole adventure this feel of permanence. If I were to replay the game, I feel like it would almost water down my first experience. It's almost like a book or movie. I have to wait a while to replay it, otherwise it won't be great.
But with the lack of replay value, the long wait for scenes, etc, is this game any good? Yes. The craftmenship of this game is amazing. It has a lot of moments that captured me. There's this one scene I remember getting particularly entranced in, this moment in a bar where the visuals and audio worked together to recreate the feeling of music. There is a lot of love that goes into this game. It is unlike any other that I have played before. It's strange, but awesome. I guess captivating is the best word to describe this game as a whole. It is definitely a labor of love; you can really tell that the developers put their all into making this game. It's worth playing at least once. Try to shoot for a sale price if you're concerned about the longetivity of the game. This is a game that lasts longer in memory than in playtime.

Now, at the time I'm writing this review, the game is rather far away from completion, with a release rate of barely 1 per year, which has rightly earned them some criticism, because there is most definitely cause and reason to asking for the product you paid for. The format in which I am going to review this product will be with the individual episode, and then, when the final episode is released, a sum-up/TL;DR will be at the bottom.
Episode 1
The first episode sets an incredible standard for the rest of the series to follow, as it sets the stage of an incredibly visceral and surreal saga with awe-inspiring beauty, in even the most subtle of ways. It introduces the player to set characters, as well as the main system of the game, basically being able to write your own character's story and character development, leading to a huge amount of dialogue. Out of the three currently released, this one is most likely my favourite, as it's when the game is still slightly odd (Constantly burning trees, ghosts, .etc) without stepping into the territory of batshit insane.
Episode 2
The second episode allows for the backstory of the already presented characters to come to light, as well as what exactly The Zero is, its relevance to the surrounding characters, and its use. One of the greatest experiences in a game I've ever had the immense pleasure of enjoying was exploring the Zero, all of its nooks, crannies and locations.
Episode 3
The third episode introduces colourful and enjoyable characters into the game, as well as some of the most atmospheric computer segments in a game ever. This was most likely my least favourite of the episodes so far, but I still enjoyed it far more than other adventure games that came out this year (Life is Strange).
(TL;DR before Episode 4: Would I reccommend this game in it's current state? Only if it was to somebody that greatly enjoyed a story intense and immersion based experience.)
But in order to enjoy this game it's true atmospheric glory, I would suggest playing the game with someone in the room, in order to converse the significance of events in the game and characters. After grabbing that person, turn your lights off, close your blinds and explore The Zero.

A decent enough follow-up to the first game, with the exception that it's a re-play of the first game in many ways.
Being an extremely long play-through (which may come at the delight of some) Trails SC often feels like a boring rehash of the first game, using much of the same music, scenery and orbmental tactics with relatively few innovations.
That said, there are many emotionally-involved moments, and ending scenes are epic, touching and rewarding, with a number of challenging battles that require re-thinking equipment and orbments to overcome.
In the final scenes, however, I felt too little attention was paid to the 2 main characters: Their epilogue was ultimately rushed with little care to the emotional attachments of players after everything they've through been with them. To be clear, the final scenes were highly disappointing.
But for the die-hard JRPG fan who (like me) craves recapturing a piece of SNES-style nostalgia, Trails in the Sky SC still proves to be a charming adventure with alluring characters and a twisting plot that leaves you wanting more.
If there is a Third Chapter, I hope it makes it's way to the PC with far more urgency from Xseed, because despite the relatively cosmetic downfalls, it's a fantastic character set and storyline that I can't help wanting to play more of!

I own the physical copy of Star Realms, and have played the non-Steam digital version (same as this one). It really is an engaging and accessible deck-building game with clever strategies and a beautiful science-fiction theme.
The premise is simple:
You and your opponent start off with the same basic hand, and take turns whittling down the other's Authority (health) from 50 to 0. You compete to purchase cards from the Trade Row (5 cards in the middle) to assemble a stronger fleet (deck) and then crush your opponent with it. Your hand will become unique as the game plays, hence the "deck-building" aspect.
There are some really interesting card combinations and great strategies which allow experimentation with the game's 4 factions. Each offer unique cumulative bonuses if you have more than one of the same faction ship in play.
For free you can skirmish with an easy AI as much as you want. The core gameplay is deep enough if you just want to play against an opponent. The expansions aren't really necessary, just more of the same cards types or new ships. You could easily have fun as it is.
If you want a beefier experience however, you can buy the full version with online multiplayer and a single-player campaign.
-Campaign is essentially tweaked challenges for you to play. They alter the normal rules however so your enjoyment is based on whether you like fixed odds.
-Online multiplayer is quick, fast and efficient due to the availability of players cross-platform so it's never troublesome to find a opponent through matchmaking. The game uses an account system so that you can link your purchase across your Android/iOS or PC versions.
So go ahead and try before you buy.
Or buy the actual physical copy at a game store for two players for $12. it's self-contained and a great icebreaker at parties.

This is by far the best JRPG I've played in recent years. Trails in the Sky FC was pretty much the appetizer of the trilogy, but here is the real meat of the story. The game starts right after that heartbreaking cliffhanger from the first game, so obviously it's absolutely required you play FC before SC, otherwise nothing will make sense to you.
I think Trails in the Sky SC's biggest strength is definitely the writing. It's a surprisingly well thoughtout world, richly developed and lovable cast of characters, and memorable story that will reward you with a satisfying JRPG experience. I would even go as far as saying it's better than any of the Final Fantasy or Tales of franchise I played. Although the characters are pretty much your standard anime or Japanese game character archetypes, each one is fleshed out and executed well. The interactions between characters are gold, especially anything involving Estelle and Oliver since they add comedic value. While I can't say much about SC's storyline due to avoiding spoilers, if you thought FC's story was great, well you're in for one hell of a ride. FC took me around 20 hours to beat, SC took me 60 hours. Just let that sink in. Yes, the story has a few extra layers added but it's not overly complicated as long as you pay attention.
The gameplay is the same as FC but with some improvements to the turn based battle system. I really liked the addition of chained special attacks which let's you use multiple characters attack at once. More artes have been added and crafts upgraded for stronger effects. Other than that, just expect FC's gameplay.
I would describe the visual to be modernized retro style graphics you see in playstation rpg games, except a lot sharper. You can tell the production values just by looking at it and the presentation. Let's not forget the wonderful soundtrack. It adds a perfect level of immersiveness invoking a spectrum of emotions on certain scenes of events.
Lastly, I really have to give props to XSEED for their amazing efforts in localizing SC. They released the game not out of business/profit priority, but labor of love. And double props to them for announcing the final game of the trilogy that's currently in the works. While SC can be seen as the finale story, there are some loose ends that will be resolved in the 3rd chapter (I hope). So once the 3rd chapter is up for pre-order, I'll immediately snatch that up paying full price showing my support just like how I did with FC and SC. Thank you XSEED for letting me experience such a magnificent game.
Normally, I don't replay JRPGs as much, but this is worth going through the 2nd time. Overall, Trails in the Sky SC gets my highest recommendation for any RPG players out there.

Fans of the original Trails in the Sky have long awaited this almost ill-fated sequel, not only is the painfully long wait over, but it is exactly what we all wanted to see and more. Trails SC continues the story of the first game and far exceeds expectations in terms of story.
The gameplay is essentially identical to the first game with the addition of Chain Crafts, which allow multiple characters to attack in the same turn at the expense of some of their CP, and a new Orbment system which balances the magic system a bit and allows for more and better magic. The new Orbment system requires slots to be upgraded after unlocked in order to use more powerful Quartz, some of this better Quartz is either improvements of older ones, combination of two effects or brand new ones. The Orbment menu is now thankfully color-coded to know which line you're putting Quartz in and aids to better visualize the Sephith sums of each line. Other than that the game also adds a fishing minigame and some gambling minigames at the casino in Ruan for your leisure. The Bracer Guild quests are back and the game still follows the same chapter structure but allows you to edit your party as long as the plot dictates that they can be in your party. The battles have improved slightly with shorter attack animations, improved Crafts, new S-Crafts and encounters that force you to devise new strategies.
Graphically the game is exactly the same as its predecessor. HD assets and almost every PSP exclusive feature are available from the beginning. In the sound department we have new songs in combination with older ones that add up to a really expansive soundtrack. The new music exclusive to SC is fantastic and probably far better than its predecessor, with more rocking tunes and even the relaxing new ones have a better feel more suited to the current plotline and a final boss theme that might as well be one of the best in the series.
Unfortunately, updating a 2006 game to new standards has also included a slew of bugs. While there are workarounds for every bug I’ve managed to get stuck in some places and in the worst case I accidentally did a sequence break and skipped a major boss fight altogether. The translation also feels spotty at times but with the huge amount of text there is I’m willing to let it pass. Treasure chest jokes are unfortunately missing for the most part.
Just like its predecessor, the plot takes the spotlight in this game and I’d even say outright steals the entire show. Right from the beginning stakes are higher as the story continues right after where FC left off, we join Estelle as she looks for Joshua and tries to become a stronger and better Bracer while getting an insight on the mysterious group “Ouroboros”. Even though the pace remains rather slow, in every chapter our heroes face bigger threats compared to those of the first game and a lot of conflicts that were subtly hinted in the first game unfold. Even the sidequests are a step-up since they no longer involve such menial tasks since now the world is in danger and quite a few involve subplots essential to the world-building of the game. Trails SC is a lengthier affair than the first game, clocking at around 40-60 hours in an average play, with a New Game+ available and various difficulty modes if you ever want to replay it.
There isn’t a lot to say about Trails SC that hasn’t been said in reviews of the previous game other than “it’s bigger and better”. If you enjoyed the first game then SC is a must play, if you didn’t then you probably are missing out on a truly exceptional traditional RPG, one that took a long time to arrive and is worth every second and penny invested into it.

Sonic Mania is a game created by fans of the series that were employed by SEGA to produce this new 2D Sonic game.
With plenty of throwbacks to classic games, fresh new levels, bosses, themes, special stages and much more, Sonic Mania gives fans the 2D classic style game the community has asked for.
As you can probably tell by my play time, I really really enjoy this game... Like a lot.
This game does everything that was good in the classic titles and makes it even better. The adventure takes Sonic through levels from the past games and 4 entirely new zones, all of them providing a fun and enjoyable experience.
The past zones have had major updates and feel like entirely new levels on their own, with the act 2 of the classic zones usually having a major overhaul and have unique and interesting new mechanics to accompany them, there are a few exceptions where the Act 1 has the overhaul though such as Stardust Speedway Zone having a nice mix of slower paced gameplay from Sonic 3's Marble Garden with the fast paced action of the original.
The level design on all the zones have made huge improvements over the classic games as well, making the older levels feel better to play through. The new zones have also got some insanely fun level ideas and overall design, there are several new mechanics introduced and each act ends with a really great boss fight.
That's another thing I should mention, which is that the bosses are insanely good, each provide a fair challenge while keeping the pace of the game fast and enjoyable. I have to say a few bosses aren't quite as good as others but some are just so creative and fun.
Special Stages in this game are also brand new and mesh together ideas from previous games but in a 3D space, with tight controls, fun levels and great visuals. The special stage serves the purpose of collecting the Chaos Emeralds, which again make a return from the previous titles. The special stages along with the Chaos Emeralds within them, can be found by seeking out a giant gold ring, hidden within the Zones you play through, with each act having around 3 to find.
The addition of Super Sonic is also a nice touch, this being available once all the Chaos Emeralds have been attained.
The music, pixel art and overall theme of this game is bright, colourful and polished. The soundtrack is one of this games key strengths I feel. Composer Tee Lopes has done such an incredible job with the music of everything in this game, not a single track feels out of place or unfinished/unpolished. The pixel art done by a few talented artists is also sublime and brings the whole game together, giving a fresh new look to Sonic and the whole experience.
Everything in this amazing title hits the right notes, but for sure it's not the perfect game by any means, it has its flaws like any game, but for what this game offers I don't see them worth fretting over. All I can say is some level design needed smoothing out, some transitions between levels could've been worked on (or actually implemented), the story could've been a lot better and of course more new zones would've been appreciated. Also I feel it's worth mentioning the fan service in this game could put some people off, and there is A LOT of it, maybe too much.
Overall though, the positives majorly outweigh the negatives, obviously the whole DRM situation has been covered a million times already so I won't go in to that, but I feel with Sonic Mania, you can look past it.
Easily I would say this game is a solid experience that should be enjoyed by Sonic fans and many other people who may just want to experience a fun, fast paced, action platformer.
If you want a number score then I'd give it a 8.5/10

Though not as impressive as its younger and older siblings Skyrim and Morrowind, Oblivion still builds upon the world of Tamriel in a manner that fills in the gap between the two other games and manages to be a beautiful and interesting game at times, despite its shortcomings.
The main gripes I have are the setting, which feels a bit bland and generic, and the storylines, which are a bit shallow and one-dimensional, both of which can be solved to a certain extent with mods and I would definitely recommend the DLC to anyone buying this game, as it adds some more exotic locales such as The Shivering Isles.  Despite these shortcomings, it still manages to work decently as a part of the Elder Scrolls franchise and adds to it additional backstory and lore that would not have existed otherwise.  I give it a 7/10.
I would recommend it to anyone who has played other Elder Scrolls titles, otherwise, you should probably look at Skyrim instead for getting into The Elder Scrolls, as that game has a more in-depth story and a much more unique setting and can give you a taste of several different cultures that exist within Tamriel, rather than the faux European culture that exists within Cyrodiil, where Oblivion takes place.
