So, I finished the game. What can I say to those, who came to read the reviews, thinking about buying this game?
I think I'll use default pros/cons list of things doesn't mentioned on the game page:
+  Content/price ratio. It will probably took you about 80~100 hours just to complete campaign. Can be more, can be less.
+  Great feeling of adventure, even the main quest line feels more like an exploration rather than just following the markers on the map (hello to Skyrim main quest).
+  Neat battle mechanics. And again, it's not a straight line of pushing the buttons to deal damage (hello to Dragon Age combat). You can explore the possibilities of different spells effects, you must check resistances of your enemies, you should care about positioning your heroes and seeking good spell combos (at least on high difficulty settings).
+ Good storyline (highly subjective opinion). Some nice twists (one final twist actually can be predicted long before it's happening by watching closely on a particular NPC characteristics, which is nice), characters with different stories (both past and ongoing).
- Despite the story being good (highly subjective opinion), I didn't find characters catchy or very interesting. I would rate them as "okay, I guess". None of them, I don’t know, touched my heart and made me worry about him/her. I guess it's because they rarely showing their personalities through some sort of a tete-a-tete dialogues with your hero and very limited interaction between party members.
-  Bugs. Few in singleplayer (mostly side quests that can't be finished properly and incorrect dialogue sequences, nothing critical, but still it is an unpleasant experience) and a lot in co-op mode (you can find lists of current issues on reddit if you really want, it's constantly changes because old bugs being fixed and new being discovered). Developers fixing them and rolling patches very often, but I think the game without a publisher demanding the product here and now should be polished better on its release.
- When I selected "tactician" difficulty, because default level was too easy and then I find that the “tactician” is easy too, I couldn't go higher because "tactician" doesn't allow changing the game difficulty. WTH?
- Patches are breaking localization. I played the game in Russian, but after some patches some spells began to use English names and some entries in the quest log changed the language.
-  And lastly, I want to mention the dark side of highly variable combat. Huge possibilities mean huge exploits and when battle was too hard for me, rather than winning because I learned something from my mistakes and improved tactics I usually won because I've found a way to cheat the game.  Major "cheat source" is stealth mode and NPCs reaction to it. In most cases, if all party members are Solid Snaking, they will just stay in one place obediently skipping their turns and waiting when you decide to show yourself. Only if combat can be finished without killing all enemies (I think this is how it works) they can start walking and searching for you
.
In the end despite all cons I've found this game really fun to play and rate it 8/10 spooky scary skeletons with buckets on their heads, totally recommend.

Wishing I was an eighties kid. I often go back and play classic fps titles such as The Classic Doom, Shadow Warrior Classic, Blood and Duke Nukem 3D. These games don't give me nostalgia but they make me depressed about how the fps genre has taken a turn for the worst.
This Shadow Warrior Classic Redux gives me the chance to be able experience game mechanics that were common 'back in the day'. From the fixed health system, keycard hunting, beautifully made sprites, actually challenging in a fair way (if you die it's your fault), SECRETS (I love having to discover a secret randomly as I just happen to stumble upon it) and the many effective and fun weapons at your disposal (You can carry them all at the same time! Bring this back to the modern day shooters please! XD).
So far this game has been enjoyable for the most part, The level design can sometimes be overwhelming to a newcomer to these types of games (as I was when I was first playing Doom. I'd recommend this game to anyone who'd want to experience games as they were way back when. If you don't like this game I guess there's too much wang for you to handle.

Edit 1: Gave another shot at this game to see if any option problems were fixed, nope. Also glyph seems to have problems updating the game.
Tldr: With unacceptable business practices and already shadey price structure. This game seems to be another Trion cash grab. Except unlike the other ones, this isn't even good.
This review is not going to mention gameplay, whilst I have thoughts on it, I could not stomach enough hours to have a complete viewpoint.
Atlas Reactor is another game made by the infamous Trion, if you are unaware of this company stop and read to reviews for Trove (another game they made). This company seems to not care about the consumers, and only sell to people who haven't heard of Trion’s terrible practices.
However the main beef with this game lies in the technical and graphical aspects of the game. This game has absolutely terrible performance, which is odd, because Trove was an incredibly solid game tech wise. With an Evga FTW 750Ti I was unable to hit passable frame rates, being one of two games to have that be the case. Also loading screens were at times longer than Fallout 4 (Not a game to be compared to when loading times are involved). Even weirder, I frequently encountered various small and big gripes on the technical side of things, something Trove and Rift did not have. The first weird quirk I dealt with was the game opening two instances, a weird but forgivable issue. The next was the fact the game launched in laptop resolution windowed, non maximized and uncentered, more than ok if this issue didn't happen every time i launched the game. The third was crashes with no explanation, just a windows game encountered an error message. In fairness, Trove did have this last one, but only on OpenGL (and was even fixed).
However the most egregious problem on the technical side is the options menu. Never before have I seen such an abysmal set of options. The first issue with it is the fact there’s only 2 audio sliders, sound and voice oddly absent even when they should be in the game. Also you have to drag from the slider point, no click to go to where you want. The graphics are just low, medium, high, full screen mode, and resolution. For a game with this level of complexity, this is unacceptable, more so when this company should know better (Trove had a pretty solid set of options). Even more of a problem, there are no tooltips, thus I am unable to tell what the options even do.
However let us say the technical problems are fixed (which I doubt), this still leaves another problem as well; graphics and art style. This game follows the cell shaded style of games like Borderlands 2 and some cartoon elements like TF2, however the style ends up looking sloppy and unpolished. The art almost looks like someone picked it solely because it can excuse the poor graphics (which it can’t), and is what's considered the new trend in the market. Which brings me to my next point, this game just looks like it's trying to hop on every trend and see what sticks. Sci fi cartoon cell shaded colorful hero based skin-fest game with abilities, sounds like a mouthful but sums up this new trend, and this game ticks all the boxes, It feels like it's trying to fit with this trend, because that's what people want now.
This still leaves graphics, this game looks like it would fit right in graphics fidelity wise with Borderlands 2, a game that came out in 2012. The graphics are dated, with old looking menus and antique animation. However the real problem (and the one that made me stop playing) is the heavy handed use of blue. It’s everywhere, the menus, the grid, highlights for attacks, the allies info, it’s all blue. If this game allowed me to change colors (hint hint) I wouldn't care, just a quick menu change. However we are stuck with this, and it makes the game harder than it should. Players may not be able to tell what's part of the map, where the grid is, or where attacks go when it all starts heating up. It starts to get pretty crazy and with not enough tooltips or color changes, it makes it crazy when it doesn't need to. This isn't going to be a problem with people who have played the game enough (and isn't as much of a problem to people who play games like this). The thing is, this is a problem that shouldn't exist, someone, somewhere should have stopped and thought “Maybe it shouldn't ALL be blue”. This also makes the game more confusing to watch, especially if you lose track of the easy to blend in cursor.
All in all, gameplay aside, I just couldn't get into the game. With a heaping of problems one after the other my patience wore out, if you are a casual video game player, avoid. If you are willing to slog through the problems to maybe understand the potentially good game, be my guest. However I think I shouldn't have to do so, and as such, won't.
PS: Some have said Glyph (the launcher for this game) is spyware, I have no clue if this is true, but thought people should be aware that's a thing.

TL;DR: Only if you like labyrinth fps games. It aged badly, much worse compared to Duke3D or Doom. Check first the Shadow Warrior Classic, if you like it, the Redux is definitively worth your money, possibly even for full price (and it's a steal on sale!). If you don't like the mechanics, then skip it.
Long version:
I did play with the original Shadow Warrior when it was fresh out on the market, I did even created some levels in it, because I liked the game that much (so, I have much-much more time with the game compared to what is displayed). It wasn't in general better than Duke3d at the time, but the enemy and weapon variety with the crazy Wang fun made the whole very enjoyable, even compared to Quake.
I would also add that I bought Doom3 BFG edition to play with Doom1 and Doom2, and they are actually still as good as they were when they were released.
Coming back to the Redux 20 years later was a letdown. The problem is the weapon mechanics and the level design. To begin with the level design, it is the worst kind of labyrinths, on the level of the first Wolf3d. Doom and Doom2 has some fetch the keycard quests, but crawling around in ventilator shafts just kills the mood for a fast paced fps. The immersion is broken all the time, because you need to look around and find the key to the door somewhere. Now, I have very little played time, but if you are spending more time trying to find a door in an old-school fps compared to shooting things, then that is an issue. Oh and there are some trolling moments, with scripted things hitting you which aren't really avoidable if you don't know that they are coming.
The weapons are hitscans. Hitscan can work ok and less ok depending on the weapon design. In this case, there are too many enemies with hitscan weapons and getting hit cannot be avoided. Also, you will use hitscan weapons, because they will work better. Yes, for example Doom uses hitscan weapons too, but because of how the enemies are using their weapons, you have a chance to aviod them.
If you want something from the same age, get Doom1/Doom2/Quake1, they are still fast paced, immersive and have much better game mechanics. Shadow Warrior Redux is an excellent port if you still like the old game as it is, but make sure to check the (free) Shadow Warrior Classic before, as it aged badly. If you did like it 20 years ago and want to have the same fun, Shadow Warrior (remake) is the way to go, it is an extremely well paced, fun game which has all the charm the first Shadow Warrior had once upon a time.

One day it would be so great to go up to Hideo Kojima, the creator of the Metal Gear games and say to him about A Virus Named TOM, ''Sir, you have created a game that is both original and good. Sadly the parts that are good are not original and the parts that are original are not good.''
Harsh? I don’t think so. A Virus Named TOM is a massively overrated game. Although it breaks new ground in it fantastic graphic and superb sound, its gameplay is often badly flawed and plotwise is almost laughable in its political naivety and Z-grade writing. But before we get started here is the obligatory information stuff that all reviews must contain by law in case you have never heard of this game before.
A Virus Named TOM is a game that probably needs no introduction, but here is one anyway. It was released in 1999 by Konami on the Playstation and updated into three dimensions the adventures of Solid Snake a covert operative from the group Fox Hound. Previous adventures on the NES and MSX were fairly basic but innovative stealth action games were going in with all guns blazing was not the sensible option. The PlayStation incarnation saw Solid Snake being sent to a base in Alaska where former members of Fox Hound have taken control of a huge robot called Metal Gear Rex and its Snakes job to defeat them and return control of Rex. Unusually for such a console style game, it was also released for the PC a year later to a fairly muted reception.
You are supported by various helpful people via a radio in your ear called your Codec. This allows you to ask advice, gain info and save your game. Controls wise you action is viewed from a top down third person viewpoint that can be switched to first person (static) view for looking around in detail. Support items such as infrared goggles, cardboard boxes etc are kept on one side of the screen and weapons such as the Socom and Nikita on the other. One can be assigned to each and as you progress through the game you collect a fearsome arsenal. Each type of weapon is effective against certain Bosses, for example Sniper Wolf needs to be taken out with a sniper rifle, the Nikita Launcher needs to be used versus Liquid Snake and his helicopter. Your main tactic is to sneak about, sneaking everywhere is the key. You rarely need weapons unless you are in a boss battle. The elegant controls give you a wide range of crawling, sliding, ducking options.
The graphics and sound are beautiful on the lowly PlayStation, despite the colour palette being heavy on the greens and greys it was still a stunning achievement from the little grey box. Breath clouds in the cold. However the voice acting is still far superior to most of what has gone before or since. The plot forms a huge part of the game with long discussions and cut scenes cropping up at regular intervals. With its strong anti-war message the game is often preachy and unsubtle in it's ''fighting's bad mmkay'' proletising and considering the overall content of the game one of the rankest pieces of hypocrisy ever to be committed to any medium.
So what’s wrong then? Well lots. For a start, the much vaunted stealth aspects of the game are not as original as many would have you believe. the first NES games may have included stealth elements for the first time in gaming but the way they have been implemented in AVNT are much more reminiscent of N64 game Goldeneye and the superb ninja stealth game Tenchu. But whereas in those games enemies could spot you from a great distance and if a surveillance camera spied you, it was pretty much mission over, in AVNT its just plain dumb. For example if you are spotted by a camera or guard you only have to avoid them for about ten seconds before they get bored and go back to patrolling. EH??? And for some reason these genetically modified genome soldiers can only see ten feet in front of them. Stay out of range using your handy radar and you can run right in front of them and not be seen. Ridiculous.
In the same vein, the super bad bosses who are so much tougher than you, all seem to have very low IQs. They happily pause and show you a weak spot for you to hit, and as you spend four hours wearing their health down, they will refuse to change tactics, which is nice. Its also in a blatant attempt to make the game seem bigger, much backtracking to unlock doors early on in the game using key cards obtained later on. There are also some terrible attempts to introduce postmodernism into videogames. That means a cultural text that acknowledges it is a work of fiction by addressing the reader/viewer/player. In this case, its demanding you remove the controller in a boss fight, having Psycho Mantis read your memory card and Snake referring to the vibration of the controller to sooth his poor, sore arm. This struck me at the time as a rather odd thing to do, when so much of the game is supposedly geared to sucking you into its story. to suddenly bring you up short by yelling ''hey this is a game yah know!'' seems to be very strange and schizophrenic.
Where A Virus Named TOM tries to break new ground is via its storyline. It tries to present itself as quite radical in its condemnation of war, fighting and the effects on the human spirit. Yes, that’s very nice, but the constant whining of Solid Snake about how bad his lot is and how Meryl shouldn't want to be a solider is not great, just grating. Especially when you have a bajillion items to commit all kinds of murder in your possession and can strangle and break guards necks with your bare hands. Also by the end the plot seems have careered off at various bizarre tangents. What started out as an interesting tale about political intrigue and genetic experimentation has turned into some kind of idiotic farce. Every other person turns out to be a traitor, and the great threat turns out to be a big robot that can fire missiles off its shoulders or something equally stupid.
Perhaps its worst fault is its moronic vision of global politics. The world we live in is not ever likely to be threatened by super enhanced terrorists using a giant robot to launch nukes. To even try and present it seriously (with footage from global conflicts and Hiroshima amongst others) is an affront. As we have always been shown, if terrorist want to hurt us they attack out basic freedoms by targeting our transport, leisure and centre's of commerce. What irritates the hell out of me about AVNT and the like is the stultifying effect it has on the minds of players who sink into a kind of apathy about world affairs, always assuming there is a quick and violent solution to the deep, protracted, long-term problems of this sick world we live in.
A Virus Named TOM is a lovely game to look at and makes nice noises. But if you really listen to it and probe what its trying to say you’ll find its nothing more than primary school politics, with a moral message delivered with all the subtlety of a brick in the face. Its stealth-based gameplay is badly flawed and has been done better elsewhere, both before and since. Snake is possibly one of the most tediously self-centred “heroes” ever to appear in a videogame and to cap it all, the villain, Liquid Snake has an English accent(!). Oh Hideo, stick to the Mech games you obviously really want to be making, this Snake needs a mongoose to put it (and us) out of its misery.

Stalker is a series that defies logic, is both a stupidly broken game that is stupidly addictive.
Ask any fan of the series and they'll tell you the same thing, it'll break and you'll die to some random act of nature just because the engine felt like it, but you just can't help forgiving it and wading back into the Zone for yet more punishment.
The difficulty of the games is refreshing, similar to the Arma games you have a physical ingame body and if the AI shoots you in the head, luck or otherwise, you die. It makes firefights intense, what makes them even more intense is the randomness of them. a 1 way fight between you and a squad of bandits can turn into a turn war between 3 or 4 factions and some mutants thrown in for good measure.
It's tense, atmostpheric, and takes place ine once of the most interesting game worlds iv'e ever explored, even though the main story is a little "out there".
I highly recommend the entire series but if i had to suggest just one, Stalker:CoP wins as it is the most refined and least buggy of the lot.

I remember that I bought this game early on and then could not play it for years because it had some kind of a bug with my hardware that made the game just turn black at random. Despite this, my excitement never waned.
Fast-forward to now when I have a new PC and this bug is gone, and I can say that this is an incredibly shallow game. Every 3-5 levels a new gimmick is thrown into the mix, but they don't really make it better so much as just turn a set of levels into something beyond the basic Pipe Dream gameplay. The biggest issue is that, unless there's some late-game revelation I never got to, the board remains roughly the same size and you're just trying to connect everything, sometimes before it all locks up and screws you on a few stages. Scoring is just based on speed, turning a puzzle into an action game if you want rewards: figure out the solution, then do it 30 seconds faster without dying.

Though not as impressive as its younger and older siblings Skyrim and Morrowind, Oblivion still builds upon the world of Tamriel in a manner that fills in the gap between the two other games and manages to be a beautiful and interesting game at times, despite its shortcomings.
The main gripes I have are the setting, which feels a bit bland and generic, and the storylines, which are a bit shallow and one-dimensional, both of which can be solved to a certain extent with mods and I would definitely recommend the DLC to anyone buying this game, as it adds some more exotic locales such as The Shivering Isles.  Despite these shortcomings, it still manages to work decently as a part of the Elder Scrolls franchise and adds to it additional backstory and lore that would not have existed otherwise.  I give it a 7/10.
I would recommend it to anyone who has played other Elder Scrolls titles, otherwise, you should probably look at Skyrim instead for getting into The Elder Scrolls, as that game has a more in-depth story and a much more unique setting and can give you a taste of several different cultures that exist within Tamriel, rather than the faux European culture that exists within Cyrodiil, where Oblivion takes place.

I decided to play this game after it had been in my library for almost a year from a Humble Bundle I had purchased. I thought it would at least keep my attention for a while as it was classified as a puzzle game, but to my dismay it wasn't really a puzzle game overall.
The game is mostly a twitch/reaction game with some puzzle elements. The game takes its roots in the genre Pipe Mania made popular. You have to move circuit pieces around so that you have a complete circuit/flow of the virus and the level is complete. You may ask "But isn't that a puzzle game?" and to that question I would say it is a puzzle game.The last half of the game it introduces too many elements for it to remain a puzzle game. The later elements all rely on the player moving quickly and trying to think on their toes and often that leads to death. A good puzzle game gives the player time to do the puzzles and doesn't require ADHD levels of movement while still trying to solve a puzzle.
Many design choices made in the game are inherently flawed. After you complete a level it takes you back to the main board to select a level wherein you will often find that you have to move around a couple times to get to the next level. I would have liked to see the game progress you to the next level after a level is completed. My next issue is with the music. There felt like there were 3 tracks of music that were randomly selected at the start of a level. I would have liked to have seen a couple tracks for each world and I would have liked it if the music didn't change every single time I had to restart a level. The sound effects are some of the most nerve-wracking I have heard in a while that I ended up just disabling sound to play the game.
Overall the game is an "Okay" experience but I know for sure that I will not play it anymore. It's not worth $10 and has the same amount of content I would expect from a $3 mobile app. I'd have to say to all my friends to give this game a pass as there are plenty of other games you can get that are better for the same price point.

Sonic Mania is a game created by fans of the series that were employed by SEGA to produce this new 2D Sonic game.
With plenty of throwbacks to classic games, fresh new levels, bosses, themes, special stages and much more, Sonic Mania gives fans the 2D classic style game the community has asked for.
As you can probably tell by my play time, I really really enjoy this game... Like a lot.
This game does everything that was good in the classic titles and makes it even better. The adventure takes Sonic through levels from the past games and 4 entirely new zones, all of them providing a fun and enjoyable experience.
The past zones have had major updates and feel like entirely new levels on their own, with the act 2 of the classic zones usually having a major overhaul and have unique and interesting new mechanics to accompany them, there are a few exceptions where the Act 1 has the overhaul though such as Stardust Speedway Zone having a nice mix of slower paced gameplay from Sonic 3's Marble Garden with the fast paced action of the original.
The level design on all the zones have made huge improvements over the classic games as well, making the older levels feel better to play through. The new zones have also got some insanely fun level ideas and overall design, there are several new mechanics introduced and each act ends with a really great boss fight.
That's another thing I should mention, which is that the bosses are insanely good, each provide a fair challenge while keeping the pace of the game fast and enjoyable. I have to say a few bosses aren't quite as good as others but some are just so creative and fun.
Special Stages in this game are also brand new and mesh together ideas from previous games but in a 3D space, with tight controls, fun levels and great visuals. The special stage serves the purpose of collecting the Chaos Emeralds, which again make a return from the previous titles. The special stages along with the Chaos Emeralds within them, can be found by seeking out a giant gold ring, hidden within the Zones you play through, with each act having around 3 to find.
The addition of Super Sonic is also a nice touch, this being available once all the Chaos Emeralds have been attained.
The music, pixel art and overall theme of this game is bright, colourful and polished. The soundtrack is one of this games key strengths I feel. Composer Tee Lopes has done such an incredible job with the music of everything in this game, not a single track feels out of place or unfinished/unpolished. The pixel art done by a few talented artists is also sublime and brings the whole game together, giving a fresh new look to Sonic and the whole experience.
Everything in this amazing title hits the right notes, but for sure it's not the perfect game by any means, it has its flaws like any game, but for what this game offers I don't see them worth fretting over. All I can say is some level design needed smoothing out, some transitions between levels could've been worked on (or actually implemented), the story could've been a lot better and of course more new zones would've been appreciated. Also I feel it's worth mentioning the fan service in this game could put some people off, and there is A LOT of it, maybe too much.
Overall though, the positives majorly outweigh the negatives, obviously the whole DRM situation has been covered a million times already so I won't go in to that, but I feel with Sonic Mania, you can look past it.
Easily I would say this game is a solid experience that should be enjoyed by Sonic fans and many other people who may just want to experience a fun, fast paced, action platformer.
If you want a number score then I'd give it a 8.5/10

It’s every child’s dream, to be a superhero (or a princess), and everyone knows the most awesome superhero was Batman (he’s not a princess).
Unless the child is a bit odd, then they wanted to be a Supervillian; just like the Joker (also not a princess, no matter what he says)!
That dream never leaves you, maybe it gets a bit tarnished by the real world, but it’s still there at the back of your mind; the urge to fight crime while dressed like a maniac!
Gotham city Impostors is what happens when grown men and women give in to that urge; (no not the one about dressing as a princess) dressing as Heroes with costumes inspired by Batman and Villains with costumes inspired by the Joker and go to war in the streets, amusement parks and industrial building of Gotham city!
Using weapons and gadgets inspired by both the ones Batman uses and the Joker’s sense of humour; it all ends up just as twisted as it sounds: jack in the box bombs, home made gliders and even home-made rocket launchers shooting out bottle rockets!
There’s quite a few costume pieces that can be unlocked in the game (or if you really are crazy: Bought with Microsoft points), allowing you to dress your character up like crazed hobo versions of Batman and the Joker!
You can even wear nothing but a mask, cape, underwear and rollerskates!
A very fun game, with the ability to find a play style that should suit anyone!

Woodle, woodle, now that's a funny word. It refers to your little tree stump character that you'll be hopping and scrambling all over creation with, and it's an appropriately adorable name for an adorable little fellow. I could say the same for the rest of the game, that it has a simple, even precious charm to it. Unfortunately that's about all I can say about it without digging into all the parts that are lacking, so before I do that, let's just enjoy that title a little more. Woodle.
Woodle Tree Adventures opens with a great mustachio'd tree raising you whole from the earth and commanding you to bring water to the land. This is accomplished by traveling to six different worlds, finding the three giant fairy teardrops floating around, and taking them to the three giant Dixie cups at the end of the level. Along the way you can collect piles of berries that unlock new items for you, as well as a gaggle of precious and mostly passive monsters to maybe get in your way.
The colorful screenshots might hearken to mind Mario 64 or any of his other 3D outings, and that's not too far from the mark. Each of the six levels is a mass of blocks and platforms floating in a vast blue sky, and you have full range of moment to scamper about them, hoovering up berries and droplets. Your woodle dude has none of the fancy moves that Mario has trained up over the years, just run, jump, and bat things with his leaf. That's plenty to get through the different worlds of forests and beaches and ice and bees, because there are no puzzle elements or secrets to speak of.
This is where the game starts to show how thin it is, because each level is exactly what it says on the tin. 100 berries and 3 droplets, and you only need the droplets to win. The berries are added up at your house between levels and unlock new leaves to swing, but all the three fancy leaves do are let you shoot an air gust different distances. There's also a bandanna that's just for show and a seventh world you need 600 berries to access, but that doesn't mean you need to find every berry. No, every time you replay a level you can collect all the berries again, so if you were so inclined you could grind out all the unlocks on the very first level (do not do this). And once you beat the sixth world, you get a THANKS FOR PLAYING screen and that's it.
There's not going to be much reason to run around in the game beyond finishing it because the basic elements are just as threadbare. The platforming is stiff in its physics and sticky in how you get stuck on edges and walls. Animations are incredibly basic, rendering combat nothing more than waving a leaf and watching enemies slowly fall over with a sad bloop. There's literally no UI so forget about keeping track of the berries you found, and no camera controls so enjoy 3D platforming from a fixed angle. The camera thing is particularly damning because there are triggers around the levels that flip it to side or overhead angles but don't flip it back when you leave the area, so if you take an unlucky fall you might be doing a 3D jumping section from a profile view.
I had high hopes for Woodle Tree Adventures based on how cute and platformy it looked, but it plays more like a proof of concept than a finished game. There's not even a pause menu for cryin' out loud, just a splash screen with the controls and a button prompt to quit the game. It's a title that's very clearly the work of one developer, and while it's a great accomplishment in that respect it's still lacking the quality of a retail product. I'd love to see a sequel with more polished movement, more professional graphics (and sound, some of the piano tracks kill me), and just more to do. There is actually a sequel, but from the looks of it none of those improvements have been made. So sorry, little friend woodle... your name is a winner but your game really isn't.

Shadow Warrior is an FPS running on a more advanced version of the BUILD engine, the same engine powering Duke Nukem 3D, released in 1997 by 3D Realms to continue their tradition of a technically inferior yet much more entertaining and interactive engine that gives games like Duke3D their personality and charm. Compared to Quake and then Quake II which had made the leap to actual 3D, but were more concerned on technical prowess while keeping the gameplay safe (staying in the realm of Doom) than to do novel things like flushing toilets and paying strippers. Whereas Duke3D paid homage to action films of the 80's and 90's SW was an Oriental spin on mostly the same kind, making references to John Woo and Jackie Chan, as well as traditional Asian culture as SW takes place in Tokyo while Duke3D was in Los Angeles.
The story is fairly straightforward, you play as Lo Wang, a master ninja assassin for over 20 years, a shadow warrior, and Lo Wang was the best of the shadow warriors. All the major companies in Japan had a shadow warrior: a negotiator, a protector. In layman's terms someone who isn't afraid to get their hands dirty. Lo Wang worked for Zilla Enterprises, a corporation that had its hand in every industry, from children's clothing to military power. Too much power in fact. Power is known to corrupt, and Zilla's company was corrupt to the core. It got out of hand furthermore once Lo Wang discovered that Master Zilla was aligning himself with creatures from the dark side, with the ambition to unleash ancient and evil power to overthrow the other companies and rule Japan. Being a man of honor Lo Wang quit, and thus Zilla tasked his demonic army with their first objective: to kill a man. A shadow warrior. Lo Wang.
The gameplay is similar to Duke3D, as you traverse several varied environments with two major themes, from modern institutions like cities and factories to ancient lands with villages and temples. There are twenty levels in all, with eleven levels representing each theme, counting two secret levels. They're for the most part well designed and highly interactive, have detailed architecture and a good atmosphere. Secret areas are everywhere so paying heed to your surroundings like in Duke3D in unique and imaginative ways can net all sorts of rewards or easter eggs. The updated BUILD engine also adds further interactive elements, some of which were not seen until later FPS games, like using turrets and driving vehicles, climbing ladders and the multiple firing modes of different weapons. There's true room-over-room as well as water you can see through as well as shoot through from both sides.
Like Duke3D, Lo Wang has a large arsenal of weapons suited to different situations, including a deadly Samurai sword and the ability to toss shurikens in the ninja fighting style, to more 'conventional' means with a four-barreled riot shotgun that can shoot one barrel at a time or rapidly via all four, an UZI that can be dual-wielded, a large missile launcher with three types of ammo and a powerful mortar-style grenade launcher, to more exotic stuff like sticky bombs that stick to surfaces or enemies, high-tech railguns and even using some of your enemy's body parts as weapons like the head of a Guardian to unleash a variety of magical napalm attacks or the heart of a Ripper to summon a doppelganger of Lo Wang to assist him in fighting. Most weapons have a secondary function like in Blood or an alternative weapon altogether (switch between the katana or your bare fists). The explosives are largely the most satisfying to employ as ammo isn't uncommon and it's often easier to just blow everything up instead. Being a BUILD game you have an inventory system for different items to store for later use, with ninja-themed novelties like caltrops and flash bombs, to more effective gadgets like the smoke bomb that makes you temporarily undetectable and night vision goggles for those pitch black areas. Duke3D's atomic health also makes an appearance in the form of fortune cookies, which not only reward you up to 200 hit points but also come with an often crude message to boot.
The enemy cast is themed around the game, with evil Ninjas of varying toughness that come in different colors via their pants, this color coding signifies their style of attack and are the most common enemy in the game, essentially SW's version of Duke3D's Assault Trooper or Pig Cop. They can do most of the player's actions like climbing ladders and crouching behind cover, sometimes even committing suicide from being fatally wounded (the manual refers to this as 'from a lack of honor'). There are suicidal Coolies who are literally walking explosive barrels who sometimes have a chance to get revenge from beyond the grave in the form of a Coolie Ghost, phasing in and out of existence and throwing damaging gobs of bloody goo at you. Female Assassins who fire crossbows and lob sticky bombs in your direction, and a small host of various demons with the ape-like Ripper who comes in a couple different forms and the 10ft Guardian with a katana for close range and shooting volleys of fireballs at long range. They're not exactly the most interesting enemies to fight but they all hit incredibly hard, with even the common Ninja being able to wittle you down to low health very quickly. Typical of the era there's a couple of bosses that show up normally the first time and then later on in mini form as regular enemies with the mighty Serpent God and a demonic Sumo who dabbles in toilet humor.
Visually the game is on par with Duke3D and the-like, therefore it's competent and shows a good level of detail. Sound design is rather loud and bassy, usually satisfying but sometimes annoying in conjunction with the Ripper in pain and a riot gun on automatic, but more or less on par with an Octabrain in pain and a ripper cannon in Duke3D. Voice talent of Lo Wang by John Galt is OK but isn't as enjoyable as Jon St. John's impression of Duke Nukem or the excellent portrayal of Blood's Caleb by Stephen Weyte, and is often far too stereotypically racist to be genuinely funny, more immature than anything else and Lo Wang as a character is simply obnoxious to listen to after a few levels. The soundtrack is in CD audio only unlike Duke3D which was midi and Blood which used both formats and is pretty decent, typical Oriental instrumentation which lend to a nice atmosphere in some levels from time to time.
Criticisms include unfortunately quite a bit. George Broussard in 1996 had stated 'we want Shadow Warrior to surpass Duke Nukem 3D in features and gameplay and that's a TALL order.' A tall order indeed, as Duke3D was 3D Realms' lightning in a bottle and frankly their only good game as a company as I don't think they were able to capture the magic a second time with SW. Combat is incredibly lopsided, it's easily the hardest BUILD game but for the wrong reasons. Balancing is♥♥♥♥♥♥poor with the most common enemy being the most dangerous in the game (especially the dreaded Shadow Ninja, always save your game before confronting one and use the smoke bomb if you have it). Most enemies don't work together as well as they do in Duke3D with a lot of them being either massive pushovers or plain cheap with the high amount of damage they deal. Weapons like the riot gun and UZI also aren't as satisfying or as powerful as they should be and the sticky bomb is wimpy in comparison to Duke3D's pipebomb and Blood's TNT. Then there's things like insta-kill traps you won't see coming and annoying puzzles that can stop the action dead in its tracks on more than one occasion. The gameplay overall is just chaotic. Chaotic in a bad way, so save the game and save it often.
At the end of the day though I can still recommend SW but just passably so. It's OK if nothing special, and definitely worth a go if you like BUILD engine games and oldschool FPS in general. Just know what you're getting yourself into.

It looks to use concepts from other successful games such as league of legends (Champion system with 3 normal abilities and an ultimate) with a tile system like Final Fantasy Tactics (tiles on the ground but with different gameplay elements.) Each of these tiles can have various powerups as well (Extra Damage, HP regen, or Increased travel distance) The game lasts a set amount of turns, OR until one team has killed the enemy 5 times. So let's break it down into the four types of abilities the game offers.

Just briefly here, it's not really a phase. It applies to everyone. This is solely a movement phase. You choose on the map where you want to move, all other abilities are greyed out for this turn.

This is where things get interesting. Every character is offered numerous abilities with various powerups/mods you can apply to them. There are FOUR different phases/types of abilities the game employs in a specific order:

The prep phases occurs before any other action takes place. For example, some characters place mines on the ground or launch a nuke into the sky that will show where it is going to land. These prep phases occur before anything else happens and usually will activate at the start of the next turn with a few exceptions, but anybody can see them take place.

I like to call it the dash phase. This is where you make dem crazy jukes. You're in somebodies line of sight, barely any hp left? Well you can use your dash ability (lets you move BEFORE the attack phase. Read below) and you can dodge the attack causing them to waste their turn, sometimes dash abilities can even cause damage to really let you gain the upperhand. You can also use this strategically to block predictable incoming enemy attacks for your allies.

Where♥♥♥♥♥♥goes down. Literally. Everyone uses your attack here, but it's always planned out before hand. So if you choose to use an attack on somebody, but they've qued in a dash already it's going to miss. That's how the game works. BUT... If you predict where their dash is going to go... You can REALLY screw them over. This is where the complexity of the game comes in, and seeing how dashs also have huge cooldowns, counting turns is also a great idea.

Finally the movement phase, at the end of the turn you can move your character. Remember in prep phase that tactical nuke we sent out? Well if you place it correctly, you can screw them over by having them walk into it at the end of this turn.
In a nutshell the game goes Prep>Dash>Attack>Movement ALWAYS in that order.
Feel like I've been rambling for awhile, so I'll sum up the game in a tl;dr with some pros and cons
-Multiplayer so you can play with friends
-User friendly and easy learning curve, but for higher tiers of play expect to start counting cooldowns, planning attacks out carefully, and knowing what other characters do
-Interesting selection of characters - Theres a champion for everyone whether it's a tanky champ, support, or dps.
-Very good voice overs
-Not pay to win. You get a free champaion rotation, and every champion is purchasable via a "Ingame currency" you get after every match similar to league.
-Bot matches for people that don't like PvP
-Good art - fun looking maps
-Online - some games you will have an ally disconnect
-Some characters might feel OP. I don't consider this really a con since once you learn, it's actually quite balanced.
-Not very many maps, but already confirmed via their live stream more will be released
-Smallish champion pool, but more are coming
Final Thoughts:
This game is hella fun. It's really addictive and I've enjoyed it a lot. I can't think of anything thats horribly wrong with the game besides the obvious facts of playing a game online. Give it a shot and you won't regret it at all!
Final Rating: 9.5/10

I consider myself pretty knowledgable in knowing what major games or classic games are out there - I may not know much about them, but generally when somebody mentions a substatial game, I can generally say I've heard of that. I actually don't think I've heard of Shadow Warrior until I saw of the Classic Redux and reboot. I was more familiar with Duke Nukem due to it's impact on gaming, and honestly, I probably only knew of it because of the PSX/N64 releases - as I only barely dabbled in PC gaming around that time. So seeing SWCR was a refreshing surprise that I had no nostalgia for, but was "nostalgically familiar" with due to being built of the foundation of Duke Nukem 3D - same developers, same engine, same crude humor, same gameplay. You won't enjoy this if you're easily offended.
I can't offer much insight to anybody that was a fan of the classic game. A friend told me this was largely a slightly modified re-release of a fan patch/edition of the game. I know nothing of that, but what I can tell you is that the game crashes relatively frequiently. This is usually either due to alt-tabbing or sometimes upon loading a level or sometimes when dying or loading a save. Seems silly that a somewhat ugly, 19 year old game can't run well on modern hardware, but it happens. Also, the screen flickers if you don't make a mouse or keyboard input after a few seconds. I don't think the game always has done this, and may be due to a recent update, but it annoying and looks silly when you leave you are AFK for a moment. Also, Multiplayer is missing and this is a major complaint on the discussion forums. I'm not honestly interested in it, but it's abscense is a bit silly.
The game can get kinda difficult and I only played on the 2nd difficulty, Cheap enemy placement, unfair traps and events, high damage from self-friendly-fire when much of your arsenal can hurt you. SAVE OFTEN - this game is about trial and error.  You'll get a wide variety of weapons to deal with enemies though, and many of them have alternate fire modes. Much like Doom and Duke Nukem, all levels have multiple secrets for new weapons or more ammo, and I was able to find them a bit easier than I could in those games.
The stability issues makes this a bit of a tough recommendation, though I can't deny that I enjoyed my experience and I got my money's worth from it. If you never played this or Duke Nukem 3D, you can play the actual classic game for completely free on Steam.

Initial review - Nov 2015; two years after I bought it:
If you haven't bought it; don't buy it. As it is unlikely to ever be completed.
The price point of an Early Access game should also reflect the risk that the game will not be completed; as you have effectively waived basic consumer protection laws despite Steam's updated emphasis that Early Access is not intended for crowdfunding prototypes. The developers have most likely found their indie game to be unprofitable and have discontinued development.
In any case, there are games that better reflect the strengths instead of the weaknesses of the Early Access model. If you haven't been entirely put off the model like I have thanks to games like Kentucky Route Zero.
Update - May 2017:
So, now we are 4+ years on from its initial release. They haven't abandoned it, which is good; but the entire premise of "early" access has been deconstructed by these clowns. Thing is, I could maybe, just maybe, accept 20% of something in Early Access on launch, then 80% of something by the fourth year in if it was best game I've ever played and if it was an casual-sandbox game whose gradual increase in content didn't impede its ability to be enjoyed (see Slime Rancher for an example of Early Access done right)  - but not for a mostly linear narrative story-based game.
Just because game experiences are subjective doesn't mean you can lie (directly or by omission) about what a game will have or when it will have it. Eventually digital distributors will be hauled over the coals for looking the other way and pocketing money selling games that simply don't meet basic consumer expectations. Could you imagine a shop selling a DVD case that may or may not have a DVD in it?

Gameplay
In Woodle Tree Adventures, it includes 6 levels that are needed to complete the game. In these levels, you collect magic water drops and berries till either there are none left, or you reach the end, and fight enemies with a leaf. 3 magic water drops, which is explained to help feed the land at the beginning, are hidden in each level and are needed to progress and unlock the other levels. Berries, however, are more to unlock an optional level, a headband and three different leaf colors, The leaf colors only having an additional ability to have a whirlwind projectile to get enemies from far away with a different swirl. There are also achievements that goes with collecting berries, but you can go through the whole game not knowing there are collectables. The game tells you it's to aid you on your journey, which I thought was a way to get more lives before I saw how many there were, and the fact that they are located in the back of the starting yard. It wasn't till I was at the last level before I decided to walk behind the house and saw these unlockables. Though it doesn't save what you got if you exited and launched the game again.
The platforming absolutely needs to get used to before you can progress or avoid being killed by it. The perspective somewhat causes this, but the controls can somewhat be delayed. In some cases, a current that launches you up does not work even though you hit the area it activates this. Nor does it keep you in the air at some points, since it is so easy to hit it and move away immediently, while some go downwards where you automatically die if you go that low (this could of been solved if it didn't show the hitbox for it lower than you can go). The speed of your character also seems way too slow than it should. Sprinting helps, but the default speed is not desirable. The speed in the water is not desirable either, being slower than the default even if you are only one inch deep.
The camera positioning and spawning points is one of the big problems. You can only zoom in and zoom out, while it changes only if the area dictates it, So if you die, you are ultimately stuck with the last camera angle till you go to the area that changed it. This makes for awkward platforming, and in some cases frusturating, as you can not change the positioning. While the spawning points are far and few between to the point that I thought there were none. The spawning point is often the beginning, but others are not unlocked unless you already past that particular area. It would make sense if it is when you first arrived, but not after. This causes a lot of frusturation, especially if you die by an enemy you thought was far enough (or right after you killed it) or fell off.
A small thing is that the enemies don't seem much like enemies at first. One of them does since it charges towards you, but not the others. The enemies are noted to be defeated by falling over and disappearing, accompanied by a light colored smoke. Some just stands there and others walks or runs. These seem just regular people that inhabit these places, so why do these be pegged as enemies while caterpillers and ladybugs can't hurt you? It would be better if these were inhabited by creatures obviously harming the area. The snow is also handled poorly, only being a block of white placed on the land, you and the enemies clipping through it (it doesn't seem like you should since it doesn't leave a trail). One of the things I would of liked to see is the tree stump and the leaf changing based on the season of the level, to give more of a sense of immersion. Instead of the leaf color only being changed if you select the unlockable.
Replayability
It only has replayability in doing the unlockable level and collecting enough berries to unlock the two achievements. It could have more in the muliplayer aspect, but I couldn't get it to work (both the keyboard and the controller controlled the main character, non controlled the beaver). If you like playing the same levels over and over, I suppose this has a lot of replayability value.
But It Was Developed By One Person
Personally, I didn't know it was developed by one person till I saw another review mentioning it as a Pro. But this shouldn't exactly mean a game automatically deserves to be recommended. I have played other games developed by one person that was better for the lack of words. You are being advertised for the game, not how many developers worked on a game.
Overall
+ Good for 5 year olds and younger
+ Art style bright and cute
+/- Soundtrack (generic, doesn't stand out. I couldn't necessarily remember it after a few minutes of playing)
- Camera Angle
- Perspective/Platforming
- Spawning Points
- The speed you can go (especially in water)
-The dialogue boxes, in the beginning and the end, go way too slow as well (you can't skip it if you already read it all)
- Enemies don't seem they should be enemies
- It seems way too slow than it should be
- Couldn't get multiplayer to work
- Can sometimes crash when you Shift+Tab, causing you to restart your computer (since it locks your mouse to the game)
Woodle Tree Adventures may be fun to kids 5 years or younger. But otherwise, there's problems that does not let this game shine. If you just want to play a game to waste a couple hours, it's on sale (or happen to get it from a giveaway), and don't want/have another game to play it takes that role. In normal circumstances, I wouldn't get this unless you don't mind the issues it has.

Multiplayer turn based strategy is generally slow, plodding, and tedious. Half the time yelling at your friend to click "turn done!" while they ponder out the best move. In this game you only have one character to take care of and a small set of actions but you have to figure it out what to do in 20 seconds.
Big team fights and coordination happen all the time, but because they run in 20 second steps, they don't feel rushed or chaotic. Position and tactics are everything instead of reaction time or APM.
With the buy to play model, it has the advantages of Dota 2 over League of Legends in that you don't have to risk spending $10 per freelancer for someone you might never be able to play. One time $30 (or less if it's on sale) and you get to mess around with the full roster and find those characters you like best, not the ones that just happen to be available.
It may not be your game, but check it out on a free weekend. After the tutorial and a couple matches you'll know if it's for you.

Ah, the party game. Since 2006, you've been milked over and over again on several casual devices, and now you've lost all your credibility. What happened to the good old days when Mario Party was more about testing your luck on fun boards and decently-controlling minigames, instead of attaching weird gimmicks to itself, taking away all the fun parts and worsening minigame controls at the same time? Well, 100% Orange Juice is, admittedly, not quite what I had in mind, but it's pretty darn close.
The game is mostly luck-based, although there is some skill involved. Each player takes turns on a board (some of which are unlockable) and depending on the space they land on, they either collect or lose stars, fight an enemy, warp to another area of the board, or draw a card. There are also specially-marked areas with numbered poles which, when you land on them, require a quota of a certain amount of stars or enemy kills. Meeting the quota allows you to level up. When you level up five times, you win. But you also have to compete with players who are not only out for your blood, but also have the same bad luck that you do. Can you make it?
Stars are the game's currency, both during play and out of it. When you finish a game, you receive an amount of stars afterwards that you can spend on booster packs, extra characters, extra stages, pallete swaps for characters, etc. During play, stars are required to meet the first quota, after which you can choose to meet the quota by collecting more stars or fighting enemies instead. Collecting stars is faster, but also riskier, since getting killed and landing on drop spaces cause you to lose stars. Killing enemies is slower and harder, but safer, as your kill tally isn't deducted at any point.
Cards also play a big part in the game. Cards have specific effects that can either benefit you or hurt other players (and you, if you're not too careful). Battles are standard turn-based fare, and are similar to Dokapon Kingdom's battles. Each combatant has a chance to attack once and defend once. Die roll determines the outcome of the battle. If neither combatant is defeated after both turns have been executed, the battle ends with no victor. When a player downs another player, the winning player steals half the loser's stars. Fallen combatants are revived if they roll a high enough number.
So that pretty much explains the rules of the game. How you enjoy it may vary, but for me, it's quite fun, especially when playing with friends. Campaign mode, however, can be a huge chore because of the luck-based nature of the gameplay. (The unfair difficulty spike in certain segments doesn't help things, either.) Maybe it's just me, but I don't like dedicating as much time to a single-player mode in a party game as I would in a 50-hour JRPG.
Now, the presentation is another story. This game looks like it could fit on the Sega Dreamcast with it's vibrant, colorful 2D anime aesthetic. The generous amount of Japanese voice acting in the game is also quite good and fits the whole anime theme well. Despite my complaints against Campaign mode, I enjoyed the characters' banter. Only part of it is voiced, which is quite a shame, but I still liked the snarky, lampshading dialogue in some parts. The music is good, with quite a few standout songs here and there. Sound effects are nothing to complain about.
So, do I recommend this game? Absolutely. The only thing that drags it down for me is the difficulty of Campaign Mode, but who plays party games for the single-player stuff? I'd recommend playing this in short bursts, and most definitely with friends. Just make sure to go into every game with great patience, or the RNG gods may leave you red with anger.

Bridge Project is one of those games that doesn’t really know where to put itself, it's obviously a simulation game, but a bizarre mix of casual and complex themes makes it a difficult game to review.
You see, with Bridge Project you create bridges using a set amount of materials given to you, however the pros and cons of these materials is never truly explained. It's as though the game assumes you are already mid-way through a bridge engineering degree. With little to no tutorial level aside from a few help pages which inform you only of how to navigate menus and not build bridges, you are left alone to build a bridge out of your wood, iron and suspension cables. This inevitable leads to you building a bridge which looks more than safe, only to have it unexpectedly explode into a thousand pieces.
As the game never explains why your previous bridge failed, you are left alone to try again. Eventually one of your attempts may hold up just long enough to support a bus, and you can progress.
The control system is surprisingly hard to get used to considering its simplicity, a very limited menu system means building the bridge is made even harder, and the lack of motivation or reason behind the game means it becomes a chore to move on to the next level.
Most simulators fit into one category, they are either fun to play or they teach you something, however Bridge Project is desperately trying to fit both categories, and missing both because of it. I had very little fun playing it as it felt like luck was the main factor in a bridges success or not, and i learnt nothing about bridges or how they work. This works fine as a flash or mobile game, but to justify its current PC price tag this game needs to be finished.

This is a nice game, with some replayability, which quickly gets you addicted. The game, however, is extremely flawed. Some flaws are easy to ignore, others are not.
The interface is quite cumbersome. Having played the "Bridge It" demo a few days ago, I found this game's interface much worse than Bridge It's.
The worst part however, is the dynamics and physics. It is all wrong. I have a background in mechanical engineering, so this game has quite an appeal for me. This also makes me look at it with a more critic point of view, and my expectations are quite high in this kind of game.
My negative evaluation of this game comes exactly from the engineering parts of it. It is inexcusable for this game of game to not employ the proper structural calculations. Finite element analysis has come a long way, and it would be a great approach on a game like this.
So, my opinion is: if you want a game like this, go for "Bridge It": it has nicer graphics, a better and more intuitive interface, is faster and more precise calculations.

Do you like deck building games? If yes then get this.
Do you like quick games with some swingy luck but ultimately based on choices you made? Yes? Get it.
Do you hate Space? Think of it as something else. But what the heck is wrong with space? This game has ships and bases blowing up stuff but it is really just trying to get more victory points quickest.
Try it for free, if you don't like it then don't bother paying for DLC or the online play.
Otherwise this has provided many horus of fun in many quick battles on the tablet and for the physical version.
The Campaign is just a way of trying out new deck combinations verses a certain challenge. The AI is a bit rough if you let it get out of hand and will buy cards in that help it the most if it can afford them. The goals for each stage in the two difficulty settings almost feels like random luck but is tied into the way you build your deck during the game. If you are looking to complete it with all stars than I wish you luck and be careful with your spending.
The Music and Sounds are repetitive and are something you will likely turn off after a while or at least turn down.
There is no real story. Save for the bit of text between campains which is just an excuse to tie in the opponent or boss level you are fighting.
The Ui is ok, it tracks all the stat in the game like life totals, money, and battle points. And will tell you when your many online opponents have completed their move so you can take your turn.
The async play is where the game does very well, however with any updates or a lack of play you might lose track of games.
The Mouse is the prime way to interact with everything and it a bit better than touch controls since you can right click to look at a card text.
But in the end this is a very quick little deckbuilding game which is ok to play online and well worth looking into if you are a fan of the physical game.
You still may be beat out just because of how the random nature of the "store" row is dealt and which cards you draw each turn. And this can be said for both the AI and people you play online. Don't get too thinky about this one. But do consider the economy of your deck and what it can offer to best you opponent before they beat you.

Star Realms is a fast and strategic deck builder. Your objective is to buy cards from a common pool (and building your deck with them) to attack your opponent until he is defeated. Physical and mobile versions of this game exist elsewhere and have been well received by critics; as of this review, it is the 65th best game on all of boardgamegeek rankings.
For the record, I have played many hours across the physical, mobile, and non-steam PC version of the game.
As far as I can tell this steam release is the same PC version that was available before from the developer and which seems to be a port from the mobile version. Although this is usually something to be weary about, the port is very good because the app also was good. Something important to note here is that the purchases are linked to your account, so whatever you buy here is available on mobile and so on.
I have only played the full version, so I can't offer information on the free one offered here. The game is very enjoyable and offers a good variety of cards, so the gameplay remains fresh and deep for a long time. This version offers AI opponents, a campaign, online play, pass and play and a tutorial. There are sufficient settings for this kind of game, like fast animations, screen resolution, rudimentary graphics options.
One reviewer before me points out that card fonts are too small, however every card can be viewed in detail by right-clicking it (this is covered in the tutorial, of course), and the details are easy to remember since every faction has a very specific theme. Although subjective, this is a point to consider, even if it doesn't bother me at all.
From me, this game gets high marks as it brings a lot of enjoyable strategic elements to a fast and well implemented version.

This looks like a puzzle game in the "twist and route" category, and for the first few levels, it is. However, by about halfway through the second schematic, it has morphed into some sort of strange hybrid between "Pac-Man" and a memorization test, wherein your primary goal is to avoid getting hit by the bad guys while dropping bombs in their path, and trying to memorize the entire layout of the level in the split-second that it is shown to you when you succeed at dropping something in the right place and then hiding long enough for them to run into it.
I am aware of the "skip tokens", but there is absolutely no reason to believe that things are going to go anywhere but downhill past this, given the progression so far.
Oh, and for those who figure they can sit and think through their movements before trying to brave the play field? Heck, even Gauntlet doesn't do that to you anymore, on a home game.

I think the physical game is quite well designed and worth a purchase if you like deck builders. As someone who has racked up a lot of time in the iOS version (played on both phone and tablet), it really irks me that the EXACT SAME problems still exist in this PC version, and have existed without fix for years.
The main problem is that the cards are mostly unreadable at any resolution. Even with my nice big monitor I thought I would FINALLY be able to read those cards without having to zoom in but nope the text is still super tiny. They are really married to the idea that the cards have to look EXACTLY the same as the physical version with no thought to usability.
The other problems are that the campaign is mostly luck-based (prepare to restart a campaign mission thirty plus times to try for the "perfect start" and even then you probably only have a 10% chance of winning against some missions), and that the online multiplayer is at most functional, but with no extra features you might have come to expect from other, better produced games.
Edit: Replying to comments:
I'm fully aware that you can zoom in cards. I even said: "without having to zoom in...".
The fact that you have to zoom in on cards that, on average, contain between 1 and 4 words is RIDICULOUS.
This is the only card game I have ever played where such small amounts of text are illegible at the default card view. Sure, games like Yugioh or Cardfight Vanguard, which have almost a PAGE of card text on them, can be hard to view in their pc/mobile games, but Star Realms cards have almost NO TEXT and are still UNREADABLE!
The cards in the games are just scans of the actual physical cards and no one bothered to make them any more legible for the digital version of the game. And it has been this way since the digital version came out.
Just look at the screenshots of the game on the Steam Store Page. Do those look like well done cards that are readable?

I hoped I would like this game, because I'm a big fan of the pipe-connecting puzzle games, and it has co-op, which makes everything better. It also features a fun story/theme and decent writing.
Unfortunately, many of the mechanics the game throws at you are just plain Not Fun to play with. Starting just a few levels in, the game adds invisible pipes. You can't actually plan things out now - you just have to rotate each piece, one by one, until you've got them all connected with the water source. Then you can see you were rotating them all wrong and have to start over. And did I mention there's a timer? And enemies that take away your time? Be prepared to restart the level a lot. Does this sound like a fun puzzle game to you?
There's challenging, which is fine, and there's obnoxious. The developers of AVN TOM don't seem to appreciate the difference. Not being able to see your pieces in a puzzle game isn't difficult, it's just frustrating and tedious. In the end, I would recommend this game for modern gamers that can still enjoy DOOM style "find the key, unlock the door" type of gameplay. The humor, art direction, and general badassery make it a very memorable experience.
Story time: In case you didn't know, Steam offers a DOSBox version of this game for free (The original 1997 version). I installed and played the first level of the original, but had to stop because of how poorly the graphics and menu/saving systems have aged over the years. I then discovered this remake and picked it up on a sale. This remake fixed every issue I had with the original DOS version, which is great because now I get to enjoy and old '97 classic in 2016.
Visually, the remake brings the old look of the original game up to modern HD standards. Think Half-Life or Quake style 3D environments with DOOM style 2D sprites.  The run and gun action is pretty solid and the humor is pretty great (even if it's extremely racist). The story takes a back seat, but that's not really why anyone would play this game.
Also with this remake, you get access to the Twin Dragon and Wanton Destruction expansions (though you cannot access them in the base game's menu system which makes no sense to me). Overall, there's probably about 15-20 hours of gameplay in all of Classic Redux.
The biggest issue with the game overall is the confusing and cryptic level design. While this is a DOOM clone, the levels aren't nearly as spacious or sprawling as DOOM or DOOM II. The design is very, very dense with lots of backtracking and random puzzles. I had to use a guide in about every other level just to get through. While the design is annoying, I still enjoyed the game overall. I completed the base game and Twin Dragon but was turned off by the level design and had no interest in starting up Wanton Destruction (Twin Dragon has really confusing level progression to the point of extreme frustration).

I cannot recommend this game, for a variety of reasons. This game used to be rather good. It is now a mess, after a series of patches came which broke the game a little more with each one.
Here's a list of the game's issues:
-Above all else, lack of interest/communication from the devs. All the other problems stem from this, as the devs are in charge of  upkeep. Chivalry's devs have been largely silent, and obvious flaws with the game are not fixed for months, if ever.
-Poor server quality. While good 3rd-party servers can be found, the official Chivalry servers are trash. (Multiplay Game Servers, I'm looking at you!) Inexplicable ping spikes, servers booting 3/4 of the players randomly, stutters, freezes, crashes, desyncs, you name it.
-Large amount of bugs. A lot of these are blatant and have been in existence for many months. They are too many to list, suffice to say they have been reported enough on the forums/ steam.
-Ridiculous exploits of game mechanics. Behind-the-back instant hits with the heaviest weapon in the game (the maul), which can one-hit kill any class. Basically, you can make any weapon as fast as a dagger if you know how. Balanced? No sir, not even a little.
-Poor map quality. A lot of the maps, especially the newer , user-made maps, are not up to par in terms of quality. Many are imbalanced to heavily favor attacker or defender. Many have bugs that effectively break the map. For example, gate doors remaining up after being battered all the way down, preventing players from accessing the next area, despite the attackers having 'won'.
-Team stacking. Often one team will often have many more skilled players. The autobalance is a joke, because it throws just any player onto the other team to balance the numbers. It should pick an appropriately ranked player to level the teams, but it doesn't. Also: PLAYER TEAM DISTRIBUTION SHOULD BE RANDOMIZED, TO AVOID STACKING. All the good players often flock to one team, leaving the other team without a hope.
-Flaws in the game engine/design. Here are a few: Attacks phasing through enemies and doing no damage. Blocks not working when they clearly should. Attacks being blocked when they shouldn't be. Shields turning illusory and letting attacks through. Mouse inputs ignored sometimes (you click and nothing happens). Spawn points up high enough that the whole team takes damage jumping down. Ambiguous custom armor colors in team-based games.
-No autokicker. Not for high ping, or teamkilling, or hacking even. What online game has ever had an autokicker, right?
-Few, if any admins. I've never seen one on an official server.
So there you have it. I'm sure there's more stuff I didn't mention. A fun game with a good concept ruined by out-of-touch devs, numerous bugs and various other issues. If you're really into the idea of a 1st-person, skill-based medieval melee' combat game, then give Chivalry a shot, you might just fall in love. Otherwise, steer clear.

I'd seen stuff about this game over and over and decided on a free evening to download it and play it.  I sat down alone in my apartment, plugged in some headphones, and started.  That was the beginning of one of the more beautiful adventures I've been on.
This game isn't like most games.  It's gameplay entails nothing more than clicking and moving your character(s).  You are a truck driver making his last delivery, with nothing but your dog by your side, and the sounds of the road to accompany you.  The people you meet are each unique, some are nice, some are mysterious, but each has their own personality.  The few hours I spent in this game had me confused, mystified, and uneasy at points.  But I felt a sensation of calm throughout.  Only 3 of the 5 acts are out so far, so I can't speak for how the story has or will change me.  But even if the story ends up disappointing in the end, the real reason to get this game is for the journey.  To drive around Kentucky on a late afternoon and watch the sunset fall, to listen to the cars driving by the highway, to stop in a diner and talk to the waitress, to listen to the sounds of bluegrass bands play soothing and thoughtful music.  And most of all, to explore and experience this myterious world.  This game is a work of art, through and through.
I'd highly recommend this game.  It's not a life changing experience, it's not the best game you'll ever play.  Hell, maybe you'll only play it once and never touch it again.  But sit yourself down with headphones for an evening, with a hot cup of tea or coffee, and just experience the calming adventure of Kentucky Route Zero.  There are few people who will be able to tell me it wasn't money well spent just for a beautiful experience.

An interesting mash up born when you cross Pipe Mania and Qix. The game plays a lot like Pipe Mania with the player controlling Tom, who moves around the gridded game area and spins the 'pipe' pieces by moving around them and holding a button, all while avoiding enemies. Tom has 'health' (time bar) that slowly drops over time and is reduced further when hit by an enemy.
This game has potential, given its inclusion of a bare but amusing story that gives context to the player's actions, as the game slowly introduces new concepts, powerups and enemy types. It also rewards the player with a few 'skip tokens' every new world, so if you are really stuck on a level you can still continue playing.
Unfortunately, I just feel that the game lacks polish and refinement as the difficulty spikes and curve seem to be pretty uneven, and the very fast and 'instakill' enemies just seem to throw the balance out of whack. There is a nice mix between standard puzzle and enemy levels, however the game as a whole did not hold my interest very well with the fairly plain looking levels, fairly shallow game mechanics and unfair 'twitchy' game movements required in later levels just to survive, all while trying to think how to solve the actual puzzle.
Overall, an enjoyable but flawed puzzle game that hardcore difficult puzzle fans will love but most people will find just too unremarkable and difficult to be enjoyable. 6/10.
Finally, kudos to the people in the audio department for a memorable and enjoyable soundtrack! One of the best parts of the game for sure.
