STALKER: Call of Pripyat builds upon all the positive aspects of its predecessor; Shadow of Chernobyl, and improves the mechanics and speed of game play. All the STALKER games are classics in their own right, but Call of Pripyat is arguably the best. Truly a triumph in atmospheric horror, there is rarely a moment when your palms and fingertips wont be sweating against your mouse and keyboard. Intense and suspenseful, the zone lives and breathes with an excellent AI (for its time) that will throw you into various organic and unpredictable situations. The Zone is open and free to roam, while it isnt massive, and there are fewer areas than SoC, it never feels small. STALKER games deliver a unique and atmospheric enviroment that either feels terribly wide open and exposed or trapped and clastrophobic, and in a good way. Monsters and mutants in CoP are abundant, anomalies are more complex and harder to navigate. The biggest shift from SoC is the artifact hunting, which is much more engaging in CoP, you now use a artifact geiger-counter like device which only reveals the artifacts once you are right on top of them, often in the middle of a maze like anomaly. Artifact hunting is more dangerous and more rewarding. You can also now repair and modify gear and weapons using mechanic NPCs, and you must hunt the zone for very rare and well hidden plans for major weapon upgrades. The story is alright, CoP feels a little less story driven than SoC, but there are more faction options, in Pripyat you can cooperate with bandits instead of just wasting them. It is not necessary to play the STALKER series in order, as CoP's plot stands fairly on its own with only circumstantial references to the events in SoC. However CoP is an improved game, and you will most appreciate it if you play SoC first, and experience the original STALKER, in all its buggy bare bones glory. You must kill Strelok at least once.
PROS:
+ Artifact hunting mechanics
+Weapon and gear repair
+Weapon and gear upgrades
+More weapon attatchments
+Good faction missions and conflicts
+Duty faction getting lost in parallel dimensions
+Can be a bandit
+Cheeki Breeki
+Vodka
+Areas are based on real life locations in Chernobyl and Pripyat
+NPCs are more prone to betrayal and have more tactical AI
+Radio chatter is more useful
+Fewer bugs than SoC
+Improved graphics
CONS:
- Less Cheeki Breeki than SoC
- Can get very OP once you have late game gear
- Zombie Stalkers are better at shooting than you are
- Duty exists
- No wishgranter
- Still a lousy selection of food
- Lacking different brands of vodka
- fewer hilarious bugs than SoC

Build a deck. Then DO something with it.
In Star Realms, you will build your fleet from a common deck as the game goes on. Much like with other deck builders, you start with a little purchasing power. Unlike other deck building games, you also start with a pair of Viper attack fighters. That's right; no dead or useless cards.
As you build your deck - really a fleet and supporting space stations - you will use your might to go on the offensive against your opponent. Each turn you will play cards with currency, or buying power, and attack power. The former will be used to buy better ships and stationsl the latter, you will use to actually attack your opponent and their stations.
Star Realms is fast and fun. The game plays smoothly. Its easy to learn. And while it will never have the depth of a Magic or even some other deck building games, what it does have are quick turns, fast, varied game play that is easy to pick up and just enough depth and variation to add some important decisions along the way.
Highly recommended for fans of deck building games.

This is one of my favorite card games.
I own 2 physical copies as well as all the expansions. It's a strategic deckbuilder game where being familiar with the cards is an advantage. Games are fast, and if both players know what they're doing, are very close.
I had this game on Android and would play it all the time against the AI and real opponents.
First few games should go like this:
1st game, figuring out the mechanics, lose to AI.
2nd game, try out some strategies, maybe spamming one faction, lose to AI.
3rd game, realize how good scrapping and deck optimization is, lose to AI, maybe win a few games.
4th game, lose to AI because it spammed bases, try out the strategy.
5th game and on, at this point you're probably familiar with most of the good cards, have a few games with huge draw cards combos and fleet hq and completely overkill the opponent.
It really boils down to internalizing the relative value of cards and possible events.
EDIT: People are being bitter about this game being marked as F2P. It's more like free to try. It says it on the page the full version costs $5. The free part is basically a demo against AI so that you can learn the game before you get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked online or in the campaign.
EDIT2 in response to comment:
Online activity is as expected of a small community. It's a bit like an online chess game where there is some time between turns and you're playing multiple games against multiple opponents.
UI is fast, controls are straight forward. It's useable on a small phone screen and on a big screen. Art and graphics complements the setting, you can admire the artwork by zooming in on the cards. Sound effects and music is there, but I tend to turn it off.
There's no story but there is progression in the form of single player missions that get progressively harder or introduce new scenarios.
The game is well balanced. All strategies can be countered with skill and planning. Things like scrapping, heal focus, draw focus, base rushing, etc.
The card drafting aspect is one thing that some players might not enjoy due to the sheer number of cards. The way the AI seems to work is that the harder AI can assign a value to a card better than the easy AI. It takes several plays for a human player to know what cards are valuable. The difference is that a human player knows what cards are valuable for the current situation, but the AI does not.
I like this game because it offers more variety and theme than a game of Dominion. It's not really fair to try to compare Star Realms to other video games because it is a digitized card game. And the digital form is much faster and more fluid than the actual card game.

Check out the several old Final Fantasy games first, or the recently Steam re-release of Disgaea( I want that at some point)
That being said both games have a slow first 1/3,  the 2nd 1/3 builds up, and both the first and second game's last 1/3 had me on the edge of my seat.  The first game involves a sister and (adapted...) brother, Estelle and Josha, traveling around the kingdom and doing odd jobs in the various regions, but as you progress it becomes clear a sinster conspiricy is afoot that threatens the kingdom of Librel( this becomes why the final 1/3 had me on the edge of my seat).  The second game picks up after the first and it becomes clearer why the Society mentioned in the game description did what they did in the first game. I can understand the slow first 1/3 to an extent since we get to invest in the characters and meet people around the kingdom giving us a sense of investment when the games' climaxes occur.
In general making something longer doesn't make it better, and I feel like there just isn't enough art assets to cover both the 1st and 2nd game and keep it fresh throughout.  Even though the designers clearly tried to rearange the buildings in various towns and such I can't shake the nagging feeling that despite it LOOKING different, the envirnments just don't FEEL different.  Could just be me though.  Ah yeah,  dungeons don't give you an overhead map so it makes navigating them frustraiting if they are in a forest or underground cave due to their irregular layout so do not rotate the camera while in those dungeons.  It helps keep your bearings.
Combat I feel misses a few marks. Granted at the same time of playing through Trails in the Sky SC I am also playing XCOM 2 so that may be coloring my expectaitions of a turn based combat system. It is a standard square based grid you move around. You can attack, special attack or do orbal arts( ie magic).  The game makes a big deal about building your magic circuit up with various kinds of gems in order to get the best stat upgrades and by experimenting withlinking the correct gems together to unlock new magic spell.  Unfortunitly the game also makes them somewhat expensive, so I feel like the game isn't giving me the room to experiment.  I found the characters special attacks and basic attacks more effective most of the time since magic requires a turn to charge up.  Granted I was playing the 2nd game on easy so that made the combat a bit dull, mainly becasue normal diffculty on the first game had a difficulty curve that was flat for the first 1/2 then spiked during boss fights, which was just frustraiting.  So in the end I felt combat could have used a once over in the development of the game, and a more consistently rising difficulty curve so I don't instictly pick easy.  One last thing, prioritize upgrading Estelle and Joshua since the other characters come in and out of use depending on the needs of the plot.
Which leads me to the plot, while engaging, does interfere with the game progression on occasion. Why should I spend resources to upgrade these other characters if they won't be around to help in a fight?  Also the frequent traveling to and around the various hub towns is begging for some kind of fast travel option to warp back to the nearest town to complete a quest. This could probably have cut a lot of unecesary faffing about, and ultimatly removed less interesting game time with minimal cost to the overall experience.
Last but not least the soundtrack of the first game is decent, and the second game is excellent.  Every track works well in the situations they are played and as I'm updating this review I am listening to the 2nd game's OST
So in the end the 2 Trails in the Sky games are worth your time if you want a somewhat classic JRPG with a solid story  and characters.  The gameplay, while flawed,  never gets near ragequit territory.

Played hours of this both in physical form and in the pre-Steam release, both on PC and on Android.
Star Realms is a quick strategic deck builder. Both players always start with the same base cards and then buy other cards from any of the factions from the trade row, the goal is then to use your cards to eliminate all of your opponent's health.
The game is quickly learned and sessions can either be done very quick, or over the course of a longer period by playing with 48 hour turns. There are online leaderboards where your progression is stored and as you go up in rank you earn more avatars -- everything else in the game remains the same so you are only held back by your skill.
The free game already comes with singleplayer campaign that functions like a tutorial, but the full game adds online multiplayer, as well as additional campaign levels and increases the AI battles to three difficulty settings.
On top of that there are currently three expansions that change the game in various ways. By signing up for a Star Realms username you keep access to any expansions (including the full game) on all platforms if you buy them here, likewise if you already have any of the expansions you can easily restore them to the Steam version and keep playing.
If you like strategic card games, Star Realms is a really great entry. Give it a try and maybe we'll meet in multiplayer :)

My Take: Think Pipe Mania and Tron Lightcycle. Redirect the virus' infection by rotating the circuits while dodging the anti-virus countermeasure drone spiders. Elements such as locked circuits and red game over blocks get thrown in later. Eventually, you get to a point where it's solely based on timing your moves around the spiders. Tedious.
Graphics: The character and level design are simple, but worked for what they are. The little cutscenes follow an art style reminiscent of what you would see on Cartoon Network in the mid 90's, just not as good. Also the resolution is locked at 1280x720 so if you switch the settings to 1980x720, you get a horrible border all the way around the screen.
Sound: So little going on here that the only thing worth mentioning is the respawn noise is annoying.
Music: Surprisingly solid with a track or two I'd actually listen to outside the game.
Controls: Simple enough bindings, you've got directional controls, glitch drop, and circuit rotation. The game recommends the controller, but you can honestly make do with the keyboard. I couldn't tell any difference in the gameplay between the two.
Did I Finish It: No.
Will I Finish It: Eventually, but I'm so irritated with the later levels, I'm taking an indefinite break.
Should You Buy It: Only if the concept interests you, snag it in a bundle or if you see it for 80% or less.

This game is a fantastic example of how to make a great MMORPG with very few flaws.
If "being too Asian" is going to disuade you then you are simply limiting yourself to a much smaller pool of games. That being said, a great selection of the available music is, as best as I can describe it, "Asian music." Basically everything sounds like the genre K-Pop which I discovered and inspected for a matter of moments before I could conclude it was not the genre for me. I say "basically everything," but there are also a good amount of other great songs by popular artists such as The Weeknd and Childish Gambino. There are others you may recognize as well, but I am not quite musically cultured and mainly prefer rap and hip-hop. In addition to songs from various recognizable artists, the game also has a plethora of original tracks (albeit quite Asian).
Music being too Asian is an understandable reason to avoid playing, but if you can get past that, you have a regular Asian game with the intended audience being the youth. Children's Asian game sounds bad off bat, but the childish part is simply the fact that you aren't going out to slaughter bad guys in dark dungeons to gain loot. One of the greatest parts about this game is that there is no "loot," but simply cosmetic items that you buy with in-game or real-life currency.
I am not very far into the game, but the pay-to-win elements are quite miniscule. There are some weird things that you have to pay for yourself, but I am not convinced that you are unable to obtain them without spending money on the game as I have received many "cash items" through chance boxes and other events that trigger rewards. Odd things you have to purchase (but may be able to obtain via alternative means) include an upgraded messenger, a wedding ticket, and an item that hides your level. They're kind of weird, and I hope you can receive these via alternative means, but I don't know if they're completely necessary for f2p players. For instance, I have no clue what the upgraded messenger does for you. What you should note is that you can pay for 3x cards for beats (in-game currency) and experience. This may help you either obtain more cosmetic items or level up faster respectively, but what one should note is that in order to level up (after the first few levels) you must pass a "license test" which is based off of your skill in the game. You will not obtain levels without having the skill to surpass the level you are on and that is one feature of this game that I think is quite beautiful.
The entire game is skill-based. There are some "Asian-y" or childish nuances, but past that is a great rhythm game with an incredibly high skill ceiling. Jumping into this game, you could be a master from experience with past games, or you could be completely terrible and not even able to pass the level 7 license test because you can't string together 2 perfects to save your life. The thrill of going for a license test is awesome and always excites me.
What I think many people may miss when it comes to conceiving an opinion on this game, is that it's just a damn fun social game. You can become a couple and get married to someone you meet online, or your real life significant other. You can dress up in weird outfits with your friends and try your hardest to dance in-sync. And best of all, you can just compete with your friends and prove who the best dancer is. The incredibly high skill-ceiling allows you to always be improving which is made easier and less repetitive by an incredibly long track list with songs varying from 80 to 190 beats per minute.
Of course, at the end of the day, you're just pressing buttons to make your character dance some pretty silly (kind of overly-feminine at times) dance moves, wearing some super Asian outfit to super Asian music, but damn do I love it and wish more people would play it. This is seriously a great game and I hope that any fan of rhythm games try this out because at its core, this game is a fantastic rhythm game that even veterans of other games will have trouble mastering.

This was the game that started it for me and converted me overnight into an Elder Scrolls fanatic. Huge scale, especially for it's time, and you're simply thrown right into it the moment you finish the tutorial. The entirety of this gorgeous, meticulously-crafted world is open to you, with surprises and distractions at every turn. Walk in a straight line for not too far, and you'll find a door to a dungeon with a story, or a person with a request, or a concealed chest with a few goodies in it.
The stories the game tells are all great and well-written, not least of all the main quest; but I can almost guarantee the progression of the main quest will be only a mere fraction of the time you spend in this world. You will write your own stories in this game - Join the Thieves' Guild, become a cult assassin, travel the world as a mage apprentice, earn honor and glory in the Fighter's Guild, or hell, do all of that at once! If open-world and character-progression are your things, TES Oblivion is a quintessential game to have in your library.

As someone else said - this is the best game I have ever given a negative review to. 146 hours on record as of this writing.
1. Some of the fights are virtually impossible on any difficulty except the easiest. The scarecrow fight is a great example of a fight I lost dozens of times on anything but the easiest difficulty.. I respecc'd every character several times and spent 20,000 gold on spellbooks and gear and still could not win this fight on any difficulty but the easiest (explorer). Some of the voidwoken fights you end up with two dead in your party by the end of the first round (usually the casters and bow users) because they get two-shotted. The enemy cooldown on spells is short - some can fear/curse/blind/terrify every other round....far more often than you can cure using peace of mind or other spells.
2. Crafting is nearly useless. 90% of what you craft is crap. the food benefit is minimal. The crafted weapons and armor are only good for the first hour of the game and then you will never need again. Potions are ok, but the action point cost to use them means you miss out on a round of damage for the small gain they bring. (breakeven at best).
3. No resurrection spell. <edit> I was informed this spell is available late in the game. Not helpful and this means I have to pickpocket every vendor with a ressurect scroll in their inventory to have neough to get through the fights.
4. Pickpocket is badly overpowered. Simply engage the target in conversation with one character and then switch to another character to do the pickpocketing. Once you have everything, move the person with the goods a screen away. Then change back and get out of the conversation and run away. By the time the npc goes their their "I've been robbed" drama all your characters are too far away for them to be searched.
5. Most non-human enemies can teleport/fly. This means they are all over the place and nearly impossible to kill using melee. Best party is 3 mages who all can summon multiple minions/totems and a ranger. (all must have restoration and teleport spells). The concept of a "tank" does not apply very much to this game since the enemies are all over the place and move around every round.
6. Wands and staffs are useless. They dont do enough damage to warrent using them when you can use another spell for those same two action points. Give your casters any two items that increase their spell damage (sheild, wand, sword, dagger, etc).
7. Highlighting - Why some things are highlighted and not others makes no sense. a flower across the map shows up but not the barrel/box/bones right next to you. The valuable painting on the wall does not highlight but the useless cooking pot does?
8. Stacking - I have 8 items in my inventory all called "garlic" and sometimes they stack and sometimes they dont. Same with pumpkins and other things.
In general, I find the game frustrating with moments of enjoyment.

I was first drawn to the game by a screen shot of the unique art style. Its unique blend of pixel/3d brings wave of nostalgia for a gamer like myself, fed intravenously on the first person shooters of the nineties. Also, I love challenging rpgs of any shape or size. This game seemed to be hitting all of the right notes and critic and user reviews seemed to positively reflect this. As soon as I saw it on Humble Bundle, I snatched it up and installed it. Quite a feat considering the towering shadow my steam back catalog casts on me with shameful disapproval every time I turn on my desktop.
This game was nothing like I thought it would be. It is not an rpg. It does not have a story. There is no customization. I love it. It is brutal. It is terrifying. It is beautiful. The game is so hard you have to quickly mop up your tears of how unfair it all is and decide to try and overcome odds that would make Han Solo go pale. Once you crest that initial sense of crestfallen despair, every small second, literally, is a gaming rush like none I can recall in recent memory. You are Gandalf. You will fall. But you will take the demons with you.
In pure mechanics Devil Daggers breaks down into a first person shooter where you have one weapon, a magical dagger spell, and your own raw skill. You are then faced against a horde of enemies so massive, countless, and terrifying, in a Lovecraftianly dark fantasy sense, that you know there is no hope for survival. There will be no happy ending. So with a mindset of Spartan martyrdom you begin to relish in the ecstasy of each and every additional millisecond you hold back the gates of hell. This game makes my heart pound, my mind churn faster than humanly possible, and leaves me hopelessly addicted to come back for more.
Devil Daggers isn't for everyone. It is a game that will visually chime with the retro shooter crowd, vibe with the masochistic challenge seeker, brutally scar the dreams of the horror aficionado, and give unadulterated ecstasy to the fps player who thrives on skill alone. One of my favorite games this year, and I'm really more of the Xcom or Skyrim guy. Happy Devilween.﻿

It's an actual, honest-to-god skill-based hardcore game. Little to no unfair randomness, success is entirely up to the player, genuinely difficult instead of marketing difficult *cough* Dark Souls *cough* Darkest Dungeon *coughcough*.
To sum up the gameplay, the game is an arena/wave based shooter where the only objective is to survive for as long as possible. You can only take one hit and only have one life, your one weapon can fire either a continuous stream of projectiles (think the Nailgun from Quake) or a powerful shotgun blast and can be upgraded by collecting gems. While the arena is completely flat and enemies spawn in the same order every playthrough and only their spawn positions are randomized, the game is chaotic enough that no two runs are quite the same. Despite the arena being flat, the enemies' swarming AI, extreme numbers, mechanics and size come together to shape the boundaries of the arena. The game has one difficulty setting but there are risk/reward mechanics in place to make the game optionally more difficult without instating a difficulty setting.
Pros:
Uncompromising design that demands excellent aim, ability to quickly pick up game mechanics and analyze situations, skillful movement and situational awareness from the player. Dark artstyle driven by an engine that faithfully simulates older 3D graphics. The excellent audio and visual design come together to create a palpable atmosphere of malice towards the player, which fits thematically because the game absolutely will hurt you. Over and over. All aspects of the game complement eachother perfectly to create a cohesive theme. The gameplay design is a finely-tuned and inventive mix of both pre-existing and original mechanics that demonstrates an excellent talent for game design from Sorath and it is a game that is absolutely worth discussing and analyzing.
Cons:
Might give you a heart/anxiety attack. No biggie!
It's not for everyone. There are no options for casual play, and there probably won't ever be options for casual play as introducing them in a way that doesn't cheapen the core game would likely be a difficult task.
Might not satisfy you if you want levels, exploration and a huge arsenal of weapons but, then again,

It's really a shame that I wont recommend this game because it had such promise and I was looking forward to playing it before the first episode was even released.

You're always going to have to wait for the complete package in an episodic game, but after 2 years without news it seems like we wont ever be getting the rest of it. I fully recognize that this game is made by a really small development team and that these things take time, but whatever the reasons for the lack of updates, it doesn't change that the game has not not been added to in years. Charging $25 for 3/5 of a game without being up front about the fact that there's no schedule for the other episodes verges on deceptive at this point and no one should waste their time and money unless the full game is released.
If the game is ever completely I might consider going back and playing through the whole thing again, and will update my review accordingly, but for now it's barely more than half of a game that we probably wont ever see the end of, so there's no reason to play it.

STALKER: Call of Pripyat builds upon all the positive aspects of its predecessor; Shadow of Chernobyl, and improves the mechanics and speed of game play. All the STALKER games are classics in their own right, but Call of Pripyat is arguably the best. Truly a triumph in atmospheric horror, there is rarely a moment when your palms and fingertips wont be sweating against your mouse and keyboard. Intense and suspenseful, the zone lives and breathes with an excellent AI (for its time) that will throw you into various organic and unpredictable situations. The Zone is open and free to roam, while it isnt massive, and there are fewer areas than SoC, it never feels small. STALKER games deliver a unique and atmospheric enviroment that either feels terribly wide open and exposed or trapped and clastrophobic, and in a good way. Monsters and mutants in CoP are abundant, anomalies are more complex and harder to navigate. The biggest shift from SoC is the artifact hunting, which is much more engaging in CoP, you now use a artifact geiger-counter like device which only reveals the artifacts once you are right on top of them, often in the middle of a maze like anomaly. Artifact hunting is more dangerous and more rewarding. You can also now repair and modify gear and weapons using mechanic NPCs, and you must hunt the zone for very rare and well hidden plans for major weapon upgrades. The story is alright, CoP feels a little less story driven than SoC, but there are more faction options, in Pripyat you can cooperate with bandits instead of just wasting them. It is not necessary to play the STALKER series in order, as CoP's plot stands fairly on its own with only circumstantial references to the events in SoC. However CoP is an improved game, and you will most appreciate it if you play SoC first, and experience the original STALKER, in all its buggy bare bones glory. You must kill Strelok at least once.
PROS:
+ Artifact hunting mechanics
+Weapon and gear repair
+Weapon and gear upgrades
+More weapon attatchments
+Good faction missions and conflicts
+Duty faction getting lost in parallel dimensions
+Can be a bandit
+Cheeki Breeki
+Vodka
+Areas are based on real life locations in Chernobyl and Pripyat
+NPCs are more prone to betrayal and have more tactical AI
+Radio chatter is more useful
+Fewer bugs than SoC
+Improved graphics
CONS:
- Less Cheeki Breeki than SoC
- Can get very OP once you have late game gear
- Zombie Stalkers are better at shooting than you are
- Duty exists
- No wishgranter
- Still a lousy selection of food
- Lacking different brands of vodka
- fewer hilarious bugs than SoC

For a long time the STALKER series has been the definitive atmospheric, open world, post apocalyptic FPS. The reason for this is because the experience is both memorable during playtime and afterwards and offers a semblance of reality. Exploration and horror, survival and combat cozy up to one another seemlessly. Whether it be with the sun shining down or deepest dark of nighttime, the atmosphere antiquates strangeness in an open world not too unlike our own and is delivered profoundly from it's fictitious and non-fictitious history. Due to the lack of tutorials at the moment, Conan Exiles can have a somewhat painful learning curve.  It's not a difficult one, and it's not as complex as it seems, but strangers to this genre may have some trouble.  Once you understand the mechanics, it has a simple to use interface and the features of the game are easily comprehensible.
The combat is as simplistic and straight forward as it gets.  Arm your character and hit a button.  This system is evolving, however, and may become more interactive in the future.  Personally, I either use a bow, or sword and board to feel a little more involved in the action.
I play single player in admin mode, so I can't speak of the social elements of the game.  However, there are servers dedicated to various aspects of the game, from straight PVP to RP, and they usually have active administrators to help regulate behavior.
There is no campaign at the time of this review, but the developers are working on one involving the titular character.  For now there's just lore to collect in the form of journals and notes, and the seldom conversation with one of the very few friendly NPCs in the game.
On that note, almost every NPC you come across is hostile.  The few who are not either share lore, teach emotes, or both.  Fortunately, most enemies have a use to you - especially at earlier levels.
Thralls are one of two things I enjoy most about the current game, and they're constantly improving them in updates.  Rare ones will teach you unique recipes, and are also harder to get, but all will boost your production.  Fighter thralls are kind of mediocre, but archers can be invaulable if used correctly.  Though as I said, they are being improved little by little with some neat prospects for the future.
Building is the other great thing I enjoy about the game.  It's a little clunky every now and then, and sometimes a challenge depending on what you wanna do, but I feel it's a rewarding experience for the effort you put into it.  From small fishing villages to architectural wonders, there is a lot of freedom and flexibility to be found.
All in all it's a fun game.  With 143 hours into it, I still haven't explored the whole map.  It's a massive world with a fair amount to see and do, but eventually that starts to wear thin.  I've reached a point where I've started to long for more updates from the developers - something that has been fairly consistent since I began the game.  In its current state I'd give it a 6 out of 10.  I'm confident my score will increase when the developers release their most talked about features.

Bridge-building games are a weakness of mine. The challenges are well-defined yet open-ended - the game doesn't care if you support your road with a rectangular truss, with an arch, or with two big towers and lots of cables stretching downwards as long as the result is solid enough to do the job, but no bridge, however beautiful, can succeed if it is not solid.
Unfortunately, the physics engine of Bridge Project is not solid.
Let me tell you what I would like to do in this - and every other - bridge-building game. I would like to make a bridge that can do the job and keep doing it forever without a problem. A bridge that 'passes' the tests with popped bolts and cracked pavement is a bridge that doesn't pass the tests in my book, and once I got into the later levels in Bridge Project, making a bridge not fail became an exercise in sheer madness. This was especially evident in my first drawbridge level, when the pistons themselves would torque the roadway into destruction ... but only on the right-hand side of my completely symmetrical design. Bridge Project does not seem to be able to make steady, predictable models of bridge behavior.
This problem would not be so thoroughly frustrating if the interface were better, but it is not. There is an Undo but no Redo (and the Undo only remembers five or so steps), keyboard shortcuts exist for some things but not others (and none of them are explained), many of my favorite bridge gimmicks (e.g. making trusses with a triangular cross-section, meeting above the center of the bridge) are impossible for no apparent reason, the only kind of save file is the quicksave button ... given the trial-and-error aspect of bridge building games, the way Bridge Project makes it a pain to iterate and retry is painful.
The experience is not all terrible - the scenery is pretty, even if the bridges are not, and it is nice to require that bridge designs not block the passage of vehicles - but the frustrating, random, stupid aspects make this a decidedly inferior game. Get it on the cheap or don't bother.

This review is somewhat limited as I have yet to fully complete the story, nor tried the dnd mode, yet I have a good idea of everything the game has to offer.
I think Larian have done a fantastic job in creating a grounded, well-rounded, and enthralling RPG. The narrative is imagnitive and captivating. Characters and npcs are unique and interesting, with good voice acting they really feel like individuals who each have their own personalilty, some could respond well to charm, others might threaten to kill you. Combat is challenging, fluid, and forces you to stay alert, using your head to figure out the best action to take. The visuals are gorgeous for the type of game it is and help to preserve the verisimiltude of the world.
One thing I would note is that the game is designed to be challenging by nature and is sometimes very slow and frustating, so if you lack patience and prefer only action, it might not be the game for you. For those of us who grew up playing Final Fantasy or other turn-based games, it is a very refreshing reminder of how fun these games can be if done right, especially with the unique twists this title adds. I would fully recommend the game, to the stage I am even using it for a college project where my task is to create an informative video, similar to ones seen by Mark Brown.

This game, is beautiful. Easily the best five dollars I have spent. The graphics are nostalgic heavily based on the original quake. Polygon jitter, heavy pixellation filter. A ton of other rendering techniques to produce a game that looks beautiful. I would love the option to toy around with these settings, as after playing for so long the games visual nostalgia wears off. The game has a soundtrack that can be played through the steam music player. It doesn't play in-game but some parts of it do. The soundtrack really sets an uplifting yet corrupted dark atmosphere.
I personally enjoy playing darksynth music while I play, it makes me feel like a complete badass. Mowing down hundreds of skeletons with my demon arm.
This game is a perfect ♥♥♥♥♥♥ of nostalgia, and superb sound design, and feeling like a complete badass whenever you beat your high score slowly climbing to the top. Until your reflexes are godlike, wiping the floor with demons, and strafe jumping around perfectly dodging enemies left and right, while managing trying not to fall of the map.
Do I recommend this game? ♥♥♥♥. Yes.
Seriously though the games system of progression is so simple, yet bold and rewarding. Slowly figuring out enemies movement patterns, and using them to your advantage in order to reach the highest scores.
Listen to some Perturbator on spotify while playing this, otherwise its hard to get into. Seriously darksynth, or synthwave in general will keep you going. Eventually your musle memory will kick in and be doing all the work for you, if you continue playing it will become instinct, and you will just be desicrating everything in sight. Before realizing, holy♥♥♥♥♥♥I just did that.
Also back on the sound design, every enemy has a distinct and different sound so you know what enemy is behind you before you even turn around --- as well a nice touch is the fact that enemies don't randomly spawn, they all have set time periods to spawn. So its not completely random, you have to progressively memorize different enemies spawning in different time periods. This comes in handly with the timer at the top of your screen.
Also one of the best things I love about this game is the fact that your hitbox is so small you could fit through things thought impossible. It makes you feel badass running between the tiniest crevace between two enemies.
This is easily one of the most impressive games, that actually manage to make a 'hardcore 90's shooter right'. Rather than just luring people in with neon-esque colors, and an awesome soundtrack. It actually delivers on the promise, both with the gameplay and visual design.

It's an evil, cruel world out there, and "Woodle Tree Adventures" opened my eyes to the reality of it all. You are born into a life of crime. From the day you are born, you are running around collecting debts owed to the family, being fruit, of course. If they can't pay up, then their tears will suffice. Sometimes you have to use force, because sometimes they fight back. Your only weapon is a leaf, but I swear I have yet to see a leaf capable of so much pain and destruction in all my years as this one, and I've seen a lot of leaves, my house has windows. All it takes is one fell swoop and any retaliator or rebel is vanquished. Sometimes innocent lives are lost as well, caught in the crossfire, however some live to complain and tell the tale and must be taken care of later. Their deaths are most tragic and graphic; they fall backwards as a sign of submission, then right after they give a little "squee" they burst into white flakes, completely vanishing from existance. Families will forever be torn apart, populations drastically affected by the murders, but you remain unphased. This is what you were meant to do, and you do it with a smile. I value the time I've spent playing "Woodle Tree Adventures", as it has shown me a side of this world that I would have never seen outside of my bubble. It not only immerses us in the hard life of crime, but has an underlying message of love for one's family and how far people or small tree creatures will go to do what is best for the family.

Ever wanted to play as a tree stump before? Woddle Tree Adventures may seem promising to you. However, there are a few things you need to get past if ypu want to play this.
In Woodle Tree Adventures, it includes 6 levels that are needed to complete the game. In these levels, you collect magic water drops and berries till either there are none left, or you reach the end, and fight enemies with a leaf. 3 magic water drops, which is explained to help feed the land at the beginning, are hidden in each level and are needed to progress and unlock the other levels. Berries, however, are more to unlock an optional level, a headband and three different leaf colors, The leaf colors only having an additional ability to have a whirlwind projectile to get enemies from far away with a different swirl. There are also achievements that goes with collecting berries, but you can go through the whole game not knowing there are collectables. The game tells you it's to aid you on your journey, which I thought was a way to get more lives before I saw how many there were, and the fact that they are located in the back of the starting yard. It wasn't till I was at the last level before I decided to walk behind the house and saw these unlockables. Though it doesn't save what you got if you exited and launched the game again.
The platforming absolutely needs to get used to before you can progress or avoid being killed by it. The perspective somewhat causes this, but the controls can somewhat be delayed. In some cases, a current that launches you up does not work even though you hit the area it activates this. Nor does it keep you in the air at some points, since it is so easy to hit it and move away immediently, while some go downwards where you automatically die if you go that low (this could of been solved if it didn't show the hitbox for it lower than you can go). The speed of your character also seems way too slow than it should. Sprinting helps, but the default speed is not desirable. The speed in the water is not desirable either, being slower than the default even if you are only one inch deep.
The camera positioning and spawning points is one of the big problems. You can only zoom in and zoom out, while it changes only if the area dictates it, So if you die, you are ultimately stuck with the last camera angle till you go to the area that changed it. This makes for awkward platforming, and in some cases frusturating, as you can not change the positioning. While the spawning points are far and few between to the point that I thought there were none. The spawning point is often the beginning, but others are not unlocked unless you already past that particular area. It would make sense if it is when you first arrived, but not after. This causes a lot of frusturation, especially if you die by an enemy you thought was far enough (or right after you killed it) or fell off.
A small thing is that the enemies don't seem much like enemies at first. One of them does since it charges towards you, but not the others. The enemies are noted to be defeated by falling over and disappearing, accompanied by a light colored smoke. Some just stands there and others walks or runs. These seem just regular people that inhabit these places, so why do these be pegged as enemies while caterpillers and ladybugs can't hurt you? It would be better if these were inhabited by creatures obviously harming the area. The snow is also handled poorly, only being a block of white placed on the land, you and the enemies clipping through it (it doesn't seem like you should since it doesn't leave a trail). One of the things I would of liked to see is the tree stump and the leaf changing based on the season of the level, to give more of a sense of immersion. Instead of the leaf color only being changed if you select the unlockable.
It only has replayability in doing the unlockable level and collecting enough berries to unlock the two achievements. It could have more in the muliplayer aspect, but I couldn't get it to work (both the keyboard and the controller controlled the main character, non controlled the beaver). If you like playing the same levels over and over, I suppose this has a lot of replayability value.

Got it from Humble Bundle and enjoyed a few hours of it. It's graphically polished however the physics (the main gamplay element for a bridge building game) are flawed.
Symmetrical bridges will have massive stress on one side and no stress on the other even with no load. The tension physics for cables are flawed to the point where they will randomly decide to increase in length and then cause your bridge to fail.
The high scores and steam workshop integration has yet to work which is a shame because it is required for an achievement.
The level design is good with a small amount of variety, pistons add a nice speedbump to the game but when coupled with the poor physics they can cause perfectly good bridges to collapse for no reason.
Considering I got it for almost nothing off Humble Bundle it's not too bad but I can't say it's worth anything near the store price.

Nobody likes having their ideas stolen. For Dr. X, it's more than just a clever invention, but his entire livelihood being taken away by a mega corporation, framing and imprisoning him in the process just to make it abundantly clear what a bunch of greedy♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥they are. Unfortunately, they forgot about a little virus named Tom, who's about to turn their billion dollar company into a pile of rubble, one computer at a time.
A Virus Named Tom is something like a pimped out Pipe Mania. Guiding Tom through computer mainframes, you need to redirect the flow of the hack by twisting panels until the infection has spread across the entire board. Simple in theory, but in execution it becomes quite an elaborate challenge once anti-hack bugs, hidden and unmovable tiles, and the intricate maze designs start to pile on more and more things to keep track of. One of the most impressive things about AVNT is how it balances these elements into a gradual but brisk increase in difficulty. Rarely did I feel overwhelmed by any of the mechanics, instead rather impressed with myself that I was able to solve what initially appear to be incredibly involved puzzles. It's constantly rewarding and satisfying to progress, even with the surprisingly long single player story (which doesn't take into account the entire separate coop campaign which I've yet to even dip into).
As a puzzle game, A Virus Named Tom resides pleasantly in the realm of the best pick up and play arcade classics. It's challenging and enjoyable whether in short bursts or drawn out sessions as you try to attain a gold medal on every level, and never once managed to outstay its welcome for me however long I spent with it. It also features a fantastic electronic soundtrack, and some rather charming and humorous cutscenes which somehow manage to make mass hysteria and deconstruction feel lighthearted and amusing. Really, if a game can't sell itself to you with a dog that doesn't poop, I don't even know what more there is to say.

Last fridayI woke up with a headache, decided not to go to school and check out the games i have installed that night. Call of Pripyat was the first game on the list due to my love for post apocalyptic role playing games and slav cultures in general. I played the game nearly for 4 hours straight and absolutely loved it. I had a Russian accent when i got off the computer but i guess thats just a minor side effect.
It feels more rogue-like compared to Shadow of Chernobyl. It feels like my own story instead of the "Marked One's" story. Yes it is easy and yes it doesnt have many quests but every NPC feels like an actual real person with feelings, motives and fears. Trapper, wants you to vengance his fallen friend Fox by killing the chimera that killed Fox, an insane guy living in a scrapped ship named Noah (who also belives big mutant waves will destroy everthing in the Zone) teaches you how to teleport using an anomaly. Some random stalker asks your help to find another stalker who happens to change his name, sit in a train station and just tell fake stories about how he fought with a chimera alone. I fought with a chimera alone too. It took 8 lives to kill the ♥♥♥♥ing thing. The actual story was this scumbag betrayed his squad, stole their gear and artifacts and ran off with the loot.
It's moments and stories like these that makes the creepy and hopeless wasteland of Stalker an alive and a real place. It's stuff like these that makes you actually feel like you are in an artificial reality. A reality filled with bandits that yell Cheeki Breeki all the time, mutants that will sneak up on you and attack you no matter what. A reality with a creepyly charming atmosphere and this artificial reality lures me into itself whenever i think about it.
The biggest negative of the game is the lack of the feel of progression. You start the game with a decent armor that will probably last and serve you well until the 3rd and the last chapter of the game, an akm, some ammo and a pistol. You can use the equipment you have at the start in end-game and kill pretty much anything. There is ammo everywhere, and money is so easy to make it feels like you have infinite credits. Other than that this game is my favorite post apocalyptic role playing game to date. Don't expect the depth of Fallout New Vegas or gunplay of Call of Duty. Nothing can make you "feel" S.T.A.L.K.E.R better than playing it. Just get it and see it for yourself. Plus the community is still alive and making insanely detailed mods for every S.T.A.L.K.E.R game out there. So even if you get bored of the vanilla game or its too easy for you dedicated online stalkers got you covered.

Not a bad game. Easily the best Sonic game since Sonic & Knuckles was released over 20 years ago. The blue sphere game from Sonic 3 makes a return, it now rewards you with silver medals that unlock rewards in a set progression....however once you have collected all 32 medals you no longer have any reason to play these bonus stages any more (unless you really want to of course, they just have no further reward).
Stages are mostly well laid out, however I found far too many times that I was just holding "down" on my controller and waiting to see when Sonic would stop moving. It was an interesting experience to NOT be playing a game despite the main character moving around so much.
5 out of the 13 stages are new, with the other 8 stages being edited versions of their former selves with several throwbacks to Sonic 1, 2, 3, K and CD including level layouts, hazards and badniks. Of the 5 new stages only 4 are full stages, and those stages are each unique in their own special way with even more throwbacks to the original 5 Mega Drive Sonics.
Special stages! They take the best part of the Sonic CD special stages and actually make them good. I can't say more without providing spoilers really.
& Knuckles. 'nuff said.
Bosses: Gone are the days of "Boss is here, jump at it's center of mass". The majority of bosses in Mania have gimmicks intended to increase their difficulty such as one boss you fight in an elevator, when the elevator moves up your gravity is increased and vice versa.
Overall I'd say this game has too much happening all the time. Either you're magically flying around a stage on a set path just holding "down" to maintain ball-form or you're maneuvering through a needlessly complicated maze that requires incredible precision. Many times you are introduced to new game mechanics that last for only one zone before they are forgotten about forever, further reinforcing the feeling of too much happening.
Tl;dr - It's not bad, but it's not Sonic 3 & Knuckles. It's seriously overdesigned and strays from the simplicity of the original Mega Drive/Genesis series. It's still fun, but don't expect too much.

A month ago I wasn't expecting to be playing this game, even less so to write a review about it. Where to begin? If you haven't bought and played Trails in the Sky (the first game) what are you doing in this page? Go and do so! Remember, you need to play the prequel to this first before playing this! This is a amazing direct continuation of the prior game, together they make a pair.
Others have already hit on what makes this game so great. If you're looking for a short version, I'm going to  write mine below:
* Everything about the prequel is about twice as good here. Liked the first? You'll love the second. There's twice as much content here (literally, my play time is just about double) and I still missed quite a bit (~10 hours worth). The price tag is worth it -- between the two games you get about ~140 hours of game. This is fully scripted, text rich, game-play. How many games will give you an epic game of this length for $50 USD total? Even at full price, buy this. It's a no brainer.
* The character development is absolutely outstanding and should not be underplayed. Since this is a LONG game, it's not unreasonable to say you become attached to the cast of characters and many of them are on their way back in this game. Of course, there a few noteworthy additions.
* The amount of depth that goes into what you have done in Liberl and how it makes subtle changes is a joy. Sure, we have games like Skyrim where micro-changes in the world state causes all sorts of different behavior. However, Trails takes this one step further and gives each character unique reactions to situations and the ability to further expression their personality during events. For example, during key battle events each character may have their own commentary they provide based on their history or what had happened tens of hours ago.
* This point is debatable -- the battle system is dated but I think it is still a joy to play, just not on normal for RPG veterans. Hard-mode is too top heavy, that is more difficult towards the beginning. For most players, I would suggest hard mode but you have to have patience to get past the first ten or so hours... and that is disappointing. Luckily, this is a sequel so you'd be consider buying this if you fell in love with the first.
That being said, play Hard or Nightmare, Normal is too simple. However, that ALSO being said, this game can absolutely stand on its own without the battle system... so play on Normal if you just want the cinematic feel, I guess!

So I just finished this amazing game and wanted to give my 2 cents both for the players that are thinking about getting it and for the developers in search of feedback. So here it is:
Gameplay: this is likely the best aspect of the game. No other CRPG has the many and unique features of DOS2, likely thanks to this game using its own engine. Unlike in other isometric RPGs, the game is fully in 3D and so it is possible to interact, move, grab and attack a large number of elements of the environment, allowing a lot of creativity when solving the problems that are presented to us. One of the most famous aspects of the game is the interaction between elements. Thus, the pool of blood left by an enemy being stabbed can be frozen with an ice spell creating slippery surfaces. Water can be electrified which will paralyze enemies and oil or poisonous clouds can explode if set on fire. The enemies are ruthless and intelligent, blessing the fire that you have placed around them and transforming it into a healing blue fire, or cursing the harmless pool of water at your feet to transform it into a lake of worms and disease. The duration of the game easily reaches 100 hours and the progression, although limited to resolving the 4 acts of the game 1 after another, is extremely non-linear within each act, allowing you to solve the situation at your own pace and your own way, which gives a lot of replay value. Also interesting how the game lets you kill every NPC out there and still find a smart way of reworking the main quest and at the same time create consequences for what you have done. DOS2 is all about freedom of choices, both gameplay-wise and narrative-wise, and their consequences. Added to this, a multiplayer mode that really lets up to four players to share a world and leave their mark on it.
Setting: the graphics are already over the top for isometric RPGs, but they could improve in how detailed are the models of, at least, the main characters. The world is instanced in 4 big maps, which are very open, beautiful and overall really well crafted, filled with detail and secrets that make exploration a rewarding and a very entertaining process. There is also just the correct balance between battles and puzzles, so both elements keep being interesting until the end without becoming a tedious experience. The cities feel alive and the NPCs wandering both the cities and the roads always have interesting (or at least funny) things to tell us and/or sell us, sometimes even presenting us an exciting side quest. The NPCs will react to us committing a crime such as stealing from their pockets or from the nearby table, confronting us in different ways or actively looking for the culprit if we are sneaking. Regarding the sound aspect, every dialogue in the game is dubbed (even the ever present narrator voice) which is remarkable, and the music gets the job done and even gets to shine here and there. As good as the setting is, things could still be added to make it even better, such as a day-night cycle and a weather system.
Narrative: the narrative aspect is likely the weakest part of the game, as it happened in the first game too. About its good points, I could say the story is delivered in perfect dosage, giving you pieces of the plot little by little, always avoiding being overly verbose, and shifting depending on your methods of approaching a problem, which includes which character you use for that. Also the game is filled with really entertaining side quests, and the personal quests of your party members are no exception, keeping interesting and relevant until the end by adding new objectives with each arc. Another interesting option is how the character creator lets you play as one of the party members giving us interesting replay options. Despite all this, the plot is however, not at the level of complexity of popular CRPGs, nor are the party members that, even with their very good side quests, just lack enough dialogue to avoid flatness. Same goes for the antagonists, that lack the relevance you would expect from them and never get to the point they should be, being physically absent for most of the game and sometimes even bordering the comical and the cliché in their scarce appearances.
In summary, DOS2 is one of the surprises of the year, and both its gameplay and its world should be the role models for the CRPGs to come. Regarding the narrative, there is still a lot of room for improvement.
If I had to quantify its quality, I would give it a solid 9.

"This bridge falls apart rather quickly"
Steam is starting to build up a collection of bridge building games for users interested in them, with Bridge It, Bridge Constructor and Bridge Project to pick from. It  took me a while to get this title, but I ended up getting this for a dollar from the Humble Bundle site during a Weekly sale. I'm beginning to feel I paid too much for the game.
Story
No story to this, you are just some random idiot building bridges that can't support the weight of a feather. Why do they keep giving me this job?
Presentation
The game looks nice for a bridge building title, but seems it isn't optimized as well as other titles, with me having to reduce graphics settings rather than leaving everything maxed. It does at least have different cars crossing the bridge, rather than several identical vehicles.
The game has a few basic tunes to listen to as you put together the monstrosity you call a bridge, along with different sound effects for the various vehicles, placing pieces and even a victory fanfare for completing a level.
Controls
Not quite as good as the other games mentioned at the start of the review. Placing pieces works, but the pointer is inaccurate. You might have it aimed at a certain point, but the piece will be aiming at a different section of the layout grid. This really needs some work. Removing pieces is also an annoyance. You need to right click a piece to bring up a menu to remove pieces. Which would be fine, if it responded as it should. The inaccurate aim seems to affect this as well, meaning you may need to repeat the action several times.
Gameplay
Alright, outside of the problems that the controls will cause, jut how fun is this game? Well, its alright. You lay down some pieces, send the vehicles across, watch it fail, then repeat until it works. You might notice I didn't mention a need to edit the bridge. Well, this game has some wonky physics. Just because the bridge didn't work the first time doesn't mean it won't the second time. Don't worry too much about building a perfect bridge, that failure still has a chance. Also, if you have an impressive failure, take screen shots now. I missed out my own chance because of the physics.
This game is starting to look pretty poor, but don't worry, it isn't all bad news. One thing it has over the other titles is what you can throw at your bridge. Think you have built a real sturdy beast of a bridge? Send out the tanks! That will crush it in moments. There is cars, buses, trains, tanks, earthquakes, high speed winds and the occasional boat if you are doing the right level.
Lifespan
This game has 4 different level sets, those being Rural, Cities, Canyons and Varied. Each set has 12 levels to figure out. Its not too bad, the later levels will have you working hard to find a solution that doesn't collapse. It also has a limited level construction tool so you can make your own levels to share on Steam. Lastly, there are a small number of achievements, related to game progress for the most part, with only one being a weird challenge. Constructor has much more interesting achievements if you care about these.
After spending some time on this game, I'm going to have to say this is the worst of the three bridge building games. While it has the most vehicle options and even custom levels, the flaws of the game prevent it from being as good as Bridge It, or even the much cheaper Bridge Constructor. Save your cash and wait for one of the other two to hit a sale or bundle.

Devil Daggers is an amazingly fun game to play, and if you're someone who's into games about seeing how far you can get, this is
game for you.
The game on its own is fun, but what I see as the reason that people keep coming back to it is the leaderboards and just how well they're implemented. Not only does it give you a sense of progression, seeing yourself move up thousands of spots at a time, but also of competition. You compete not only against your friends, but the entire world.
The best part about the leaderboard system (in my opinion), aside from making you feel great, is how replays are implemented. You can go to the leaderboard and click the eye button to download the replay of someone else's game. You get to learn new techniques and strateegies by watching other people play the game, from inside the game. Woah.
If you aren't the kind of person who wants to play games purely to get better at playing them, this isn't your game. If you are that kind of person -
Five bucks isn't that much and you'll get hours of entertainment.
That's more than buying a cup of coffee would give you.

Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is a gem within the Elder Scroll series.
What was good about Morrowind was brought over to this 4th installment of the series, and of course, what was bad. Was either taken out, or refined and polish for a much smoother experience.
This game is huge, then what the game let's on. From quests just about almost everywhere you go. With impress lore and backstory. Not to mention the various challenges in these dark and creepy dungeons. Another great thing about Oblivion is it's class system. Unlike in Skyrim where you play as you want. Here you play based on a set of class. And therefore the game experience for you could either be hard or easy, Depending upon what class you play as.
To add on the 500+ in Oblivion you got a stable (still active) modding community plus DLC quests like Knights of Nine and Shivering Isles. Which that place adds even MORE hours into Oblivion.
To add on this amazing experience is these beautiful towns and cities filled with the sam- der i mean different variety of characters each one having their own set schedule, personal opinon, and even the way they see you (through fame or infamy status) the world is very active around you within this game.
There are at least two negatives about this game, that i can point out.
1. NPC's are literally forgettable, this being the reason why Skyrim's NPCs are vastly superior than Oblivion's NPCs, and more flexiable than Morrowind's NPCs. The Oblivion character models are literally the same, except with a few minor face tweaks with the hair, nose, eye color and so on. Plus with the same voice acting it doesn't really help who is who in the world.
2. Combat is sluggish, Yes. Even though it's a class based system. It will take a while, a long while before finding the right tune for your character to even remotely survive in the combat. Really it's just: block, lung, block, fire a spell, block. Rinse and repeat. Sometimes you are on the defensive the entire time or not even bothering going through that dungeon and just drinking buffer poitions outside the dungeon. Can you say it's because of the player level..perhaps. But even then the combat is still sub-par.
If you love a cross between Morrowind and Skyrim. I highly recommend getting this game. This is the one to have in your RPG collection.

So this is an interesting one...
Kentucky Route Zero is a very abstract, chilling, beautiful, well written, brilliant, emotional, confusing, mesmerizing journey. I wouldn't try to describe the story for two reasons:
1. Story is affected by your choices
2. It is open to interpretation
I have seen this game described as lynch-esque. A statement I will have to agree with. I wouldn't be surprised to find out "Lost Highway" has been an inspiration to this game. This is actually more than just a game... It is an experience. Definitely, not for everyone. But if you are looking for one of the most absolutely stunning and breathtaking experinces you can get, get it right away. If you are looking for "action" or some mindblowing mechanics, you would probably want to stay away. But if you care for the story, and decide to dive into it, I can promise you, that playing this on my bed at 3 am, in a dark room, is just an experience I can hardly even begin to describe. Some scenes in particular are just beyond breathtaking... they are an experience on their own. Art wise and direction wise, the way the developers chose to emphasize certain things and dialogs, the way the story unfolds in different ways, to me, is not short of brilliant.
It plays out in a unique way, which, to me, reminded me of fever dreams I had. When your forehead is boiling at 38 degrees, and you stay at home, sleeping, in a doozy state, as your mind drifts apart, floating in abstract, unclear settings...
It is majestic, nostalgic, chilling, mesmerizing, breathtaking, and probably worth your time.
The only thing that keeps it from being featured on my Steam profile is the fact that it's not fully released yet, as 2 more chapters are slowly making their way into the game. But I can with a full heart say that at its current state, it is worth it - or at the very least feels worth it, for me.

Devil Daggers is a game that has a
going for it despite being incredibly simply. It captures the best elements of the arcade and brings it into the PC market. You get one life, an unlimited number of chances, and infinite possibility. The game lasts as long as you do. The only elements present are you, a dagger, a floor, unending darkness, and a plethora of monsters whose only job is to make your life as short as possible.
The game mechanics are dirt simple. You begin on a large circular platform with a dagger, and from the moment you grasp it, demons begin spawning trying to kill you. You can run, jump, strafe, get a real bunny hop going if you're so inclined, and shoot in two ways - either a endlessly fluid stream of daggers shooting out from your person, or a harsh, brutal shotgun burst that disintegrates anything unfortunate enough to be immediately in front of you. This is really being overly simplistic: there are more mechanics to the game than that, ones that you will realize while playing that lie in enemy behavior... and there are power crystals to be collected that will power up your weapon which belie a dastardly game design decision: the only way to power up your weapon is to stop shooting, because shooting causes crystals to move further away from you. Of course, this is Devil Daggers, and the moment you stop shooting you might regret it big time.
You don't need to kill your enemies - all you have to do is survive. There are no unlockables, no goalposts, no carrots dangling over your head except for the glory of the leaderboard. Your attempts will be dismal. I can last 3 minutes on a good day; the world record is a bit over 14 minutes. It doesn't take long to learn what Devil Daggers has to offer, but it can take forever to see what you are capable of.
That's the crux of the game - easy to learn, difficult to master. And it's the hallmark of a good one. Anyone can pick up Devil Daggers and understand it in seconds. Make no mistake - the game is hard, brutally so, but that's the point. You
die, it's only a matter of how long you can prolong the inevitable. Killing enemies only serves to stave them off until more arrive; and sometimes you will want to kill enemies in certain orders to better strategize how you can move amongst them. If you're good enough, you'll meet your end in a flurry of red, brown and grey monstrosities when you're no longer able to squeeze through the gaps in the hell that engulfs you.
The game's presentation is slick as hell (no pun intended). Its graphics are pixelated and obscured... a sea of red and and brown and grey and orange that seeps out of the screen like fire from the darkness of your screen. It's a simplified look that matches the gameplay. Monster designs are great: they range from simple skulls to horrific swirling tentacled monstrosities, each of which look like something ripped out of H.P. Lovecraft's work and all of whom want you dead.
Sound design is on point here. The music isn't overly complex, but varies between a low-key thumping to hellish industrial music that sounds like it was ripped from the original Quake. The feel, in fact, shares a lot with the original Quake's feel; a very simple 3D game done very well... and speaking of 3D, the surround sound here is fantastic, and you'll want to listen to it no matter how nightmarish it gets, because the different enemies surrounding you give off sounds that will betray their position and give you important information about what is swirling about you when you don't have the time to look.
In the end, Devil Daggers is incredibly simple;
. If that type of game isn't for you, though, you're not going to find much to enjoy here. Simply watch the trailers for the game: if it appeals to you, then know that it's worth every penny. If you don't see the appeal, playing it is unlikely to change your opinion. Devil Daggers only gives you what you're willing to put into it.

One day, you might find yourself browsing the Steam store. On this day, you may stumble apon a weird game called 100% Orange Juice. When presented with this title, the first thought through your mind will probably be : "Wat."
Do not be alarmed, this is a normal reaction. It was my reaction, and the reaction of many others who would soon take the journey through Orange Juice together. A game that you buy as a joke, because it looks silly. A game that you continue playing after one match, because it looks interesting. A game that absorbs you, takes control of your gaming habits, and gives you the most fun boardgame experience of your life.
This is the story of 100% Orange Juice. A game about chibi-anime videogame characters that murder each other in cold blood to get stars and be the first to reach level 6. A game so heavily reliant on RNG that you will go from praising the lord RNGeezus to cursing all that is holy within a matter of seconds.
The game is repetitive, without a doubt. Each match has the same objective - collect stars or beat enemies, and land on a home space to level up. First person to do this five times wins the match. So what makes it so replayable, so enjoyable, so...citrus-y? The online mode, somehow. Playing with friends and strangers alike over the internet, with weird characters and a constantly changing goal in mind (thanks to the disgustingly RNG-reliant system for EVERYTHING) really makes this game one that you can play over and over without ever really getting tired of the concept. The game doesn't have many, if any bugs. The developers clearly care and add new content at a lively pace. The community is friendly, and the experience unique.
A great experience that most videogame-enthusiasts should give a shot - especially for the low price of $6.

Should you buy and play Conan Exiles?
Short answer is YES but brace yourself for bugs are plenty.
Pros:
- beautiful graphics
- interesting lore-rich universe with huge potential
- in-depth, constantly evolving crafting and gathering system
- very flexible and fun base building system, best I've seen so far
- tons of placeable items for decorating your home and RP
- massive map with two completely different biomes for you exlpore. And more is coming!
- PvP has a lot of potential
- trebuchets!
- very active developmment and devs are listening to the community
- interesing features coming in on monthly basis
- very cool survival system (heat/cold/food/stamina/poison/disease/corruption)
Cons:
- bugs are common in almost every area of the game
- AI is still in its infancy
- PvE content is currently mostly passive (meaning you have to go and look for adventure/foes/danger if you're playing on PvE server). For me this is a problem as it renders base building on PvE servers obsolete. Hopefully this is going to change.
- combat is simplistic, but it's being worked on.
- fighter and archer thralls are useless right now, so you have very little passive defences for your base.
- game is quite grindy
Generally pros outweigh the cons and I'd recommend this game to any fan of survival genre or Conan universe. Once PvE content is expanded and a bit more active (like animals and NPC threating your home) and bugs are fixed this will be a perfect game for both solo and team play.

18 days ago we were told the game was being delayed for "optimisation". Today we discover that SEGA (the publisher, not the developer) delayed Mania for the implementaion of DRM which prevents offline play (remember that Sonic Mania has no online features besides the time attack leaderboards) and only serves to delay pirates, rather than prevent piracy altogether. Once the DRM is removed I'll be able to recommend you buy this.
-EDIT- The offline play issue has been patched as of 2017/08/30. The DRM remains though.
-EDIT 2- Denuvo DRM is now being cracked faster and faster, proving that it has absolutely no use whatsoever and is a waste of money for the developers....and yet it remains in Sonic Mania.
-EDIT 3- The game has been out for over three months now and....nothing. No more patches/updates. No communication with SEGA. Just "Thanks for the money". At least it doesn't have loot boxes. It's not a bad game, but don't buy it. If you really have to play it then don't let SEGA get your money.
==========
Actual review
==========
Not a bad game. Easily the best Sonic game since Sonic & Knuckles was released over 20 years ago. The blue sphere game from Sonic 3 makes a return, it now rewards you with silver medals that unlock rewards in a set progression....however once you have collected all 32 medals you no longer have any reason to play these bonus stages any more (unless you really want to of course, they just have no further reward).
Stages are mostly well laid out, however I found far too many times that I was just holding "down" on my controller and waiting to see when Sonic would stop moving. It was an interesting experience to NOT be playing a game despite the main character moving around so much.
5 out of the 13 stages are new, with the other 8 stages being edited versions of their former selves with several throwbacks to Sonic 1, 2, 3, K and CD including level layouts, hazards and badniks. Of the 5 new stages only 4 are full stages, and those stages are each unique in their own special way with even more throwbacks to the original 5 Mega Drive Sonics.
Special stages! They take the best part of the Sonic CD special stages and actually make them good. I can't say more without providing spoilers really.
& Knuckles. 'nuff said.
Bosses: Gone are the days of "Boss is here, jump at it's center of mass". The majority of bosses in Mania have gimmicks intended to increase their difficulty such as one boss you fight in an elevator, when the elevator moves up your gravity is increased and vice versa.
Overall I'd say this game has too much happening all the time. Either you're magically flying around a stage on a set path just holding "down" to maintain ball-form or you're maneuvering through a needlessly complicated maze that requires incredible precision. Many times you are introduced to new game mechanics that last for only one zone before they are forgotten about forever, further reinforcing the feeling of too much happening.
Tl;dr - It's not bad, but it's not Sonic 3 & Knuckles. It's seriously overdesigned and strays from the simplicity of the original Mega Drive/Genesis series. It's still fun, but don't expect too much.

Just finished the game. Hands down one of the best JRPG's there are on the market. Heck. Trails in the Sky is one of the best JRPG's ever made.
I am a "veteran" JRPG player, been playing since elementary school. I have played a quite big number of famous titles (Final Fantasy etc.) and also other less famous titles (Wild Arms etc.). Only a few of them had me hooked up, making me have all sorts of emotions while playing. This game being one of them.
The story of Trails is one of the most deep and emotion twisting story of all the JRPG's i played. From the start it seems like a simple "cliché" story about a girl trying to climb to be the best [insert job here]. But, the lore of the game and everything happening around the protagonist(s) are overwhelming. I personally think you can write a whole novels series based on this one game alone.
The plot of Trails is one of the best in its genre. The battle system is unique and fun. The soundtracks are somewhat nostalgic, I don't know why. The NPC's have their own relations to each and every other character in the game. Yes, EVERY NPC.
Even after beating the game, I am still curious about the rest of the plot around the game, hoping XSEED will quickly release the translated Trails in the Sky TC.
If you are an avid player of JRPG's, I definitely recommend Trails in the Sky FC and SC. It won't disappoint.
