This game can be co-op up to four players and there is PVP arena mode as well as GM mode. But I never tried it. So it will be an overall review in single player perspective.
is awesome, it's about god and stuff, the writing is exceptional as well as voiceover, which is mostly a narrator style (think Bastion). Dialog choice is a 3rd person rather than a sentence. The plot twist is good, the lore is great and not out of places (most fantasy game that contains gods and magic mostly not explained well.) and are all connected with every character in the game. There's some noticeable rush in writing in the last act, though.
is OK, not much pixel-hunting but last act is not that great and might confusing.
system is well-designed, there's not much hand-holding and marker much and you can literally kill everyone and not break the game. However, quest item can be sold or dropped, be careful about it.
There are
in this game, Human, Lizard, Elf, Dwarf, all with their Skeleton version (8 in total) and can be customized, their lore is interested and not that cliche, the design is very exotic for Lizard. However, Elves do have some weird armor and facial but have interesting lore.
is just good in tactical stuff, this game used the Round-Robin style where you move one character for each turn, who have the highest initiative(speed). Because of this, a lot of thinking will be required whenever you want to burst someone down or set up some potential combo with environment effects using magic. (Oil/Poison + Fire = Burning Ground, Water + Electricity = Electrical Water or perhaps turning Burning into Steam then electrified it? or blessed fire for healing instead?) There's friendly-fire on magic, so be careful not to kill your melee characters.
This game used Armor system (think Barrier from shooting game like Mass Effect) where most negative effect only worked when particular armor is depleted. Which IMHO, work better than RNG system in the first game.
AI is also meanie, so don't go in blindly or grouped up too much. They're quite smart.
There's quite balance issue in the late game, though, where you literally OP, especially with the usage of Source Abilities.
Although
isn't composed by Kirill Pokrovsky (RIP) but Borislav Slavov (Crysis Series) is doing a great job also! the theme is very memorizable,
is just too good, the combat music is nice (which also based on instrumental selected on character creation),
is story climax combat. There's one vocal song too.
, however, not that useful and a couple of recipes are useful. You might pick up a lot of junk thinking it as crafting mats, only to be used with one common scroll recipe.
, means there will be QoL mod, overhaul or a campaign for you to play. This disables achievement but there's a mod for it.
TL/DR: Looking for a good single/co-op cRPG with exceptional story and lore that is well-connected with awesome races (Lizard <3), a tactical turn-based combat that required a lot of strategies, perhaps just a game OST for your collection, or doing some RP with Game Master mode? then go ahead, full price!
Now, that's the potential GOTY award for 2017. My The “Suspension of Disbelief” Award.

I've played a lot of adventure games and they are undoubtedly my favorite genre.  I don't have nearly as much time to play games as I used to so a purchase and commitment like this is somewhat a big deal to me and as such I researched this fairly heavily before jumping in.  I have to say, I regret it.   People talk about the great writing, but I think it's more non-sensical, abstract dialogue rather than something meaningful.  It's sort of like back in college when you'd sit around with your friends on a Friday night in a chemical-induced haze and say things like "But doesn't *everything* matter?  I mean *matters*!" and you'd all think that you guys were speaking brilliantly about life.  People will talk about the story and what not, but even that is so muddled.  At the start, it seems like it's going to be a ghost story but Act III almost devolves into some sort of corporate dystopian theme and it's not a good direction.  Even the music scene that people rave about is nothing special.  I was expecting a big setup but it's really just a meaningless musical number in the middle of the game.  There have been some great games with great writing, great story, great dialog, and even great music.  This game attempts to be all that but in the end is just pretentious at best and a waste of time at worst.  That said, I see value in this type of "game" -- that is, the game that's more of an interactive novel rather than the traditional puzzle-solving quest.  However, there's a way around that -- just buy a better adventure game and play it using the walkthrough.  It is guaranteed to be a better experience.

One day, you might find yourself browsing the Steam store. On this day, you may stumble apon a weird game called 100% Orange Juice. When presented with this title, the first thought through your mind will probably be : "Wat."
Do not be alarmed, this is a normal reaction. It was my reaction, and the reaction of many others who would soon take the journey through Orange Juice together. A game that you buy as a joke, because it looks silly. A game that you continue playing after one match, because it looks interesting. A game that absorbs you, takes control of your gaming habits, and gives you the most fun boardgame experience of your life.
This is the story of 100% Orange Juice. A game about chibi-anime videogame characters that murder each other in cold blood to get stars and be the first to reach level 6. A game so heavily reliant on RNG that you will go from praising the lord RNGeezus to cursing all that is holy within a matter of seconds.
The game is repetitive, without a doubt. Each match has the same objective - collect stars or beat enemies, and land on a home space to level up. First person to do this five times wins the match. So what makes it so replayable, so enjoyable, so...citrus-y? The online mode, somehow. Playing with friends and strangers alike over the internet, with weird characters and a constantly changing goal in mind (thanks to the disgustingly RNG-reliant system for EVERYTHING) really makes this game one that you can play over and over without ever really getting tired of the concept. The game doesn't have many, if any bugs. The developers clearly care and add new content at a lively pace. The community is friendly, and the experience unique.
A great experience that most videogame-enthusiasts should give a shot - especially for the low price of $6.

I have not played this game for a very long time, however I noticed one thing over the course of all of this time... I kept remembering this game from time to time. As somebody who is not a fan of jump scares and the "horror"-genre, in general, I was surprised by just how much I enjoyed this game.
I was all about the open world. This world is very atmospheric and it really felt like you were just trying to survive, even if in reality it did not take much to become a bad♥♥♥♥♥who could go in with guns blazing most of the time. There were still plenty of surprises and challenges, some of which took a while to figure-out because there were more than one way to approach the situation, however the FEELING of "OMG, I have to stop the bleeding, find food, sell of this stuff to make money, and get ammo for my gun!" was always present. Never have I played a game where I was actually afraid of walking out at night and actually tried to get back to a safe area before darkness... kind of how you would do in real life, right? The atmosphere, especially with the lighting effects, and the creepy anomalies, made me explore every nook and cranny. Sure, you could probably run through the main story in a solid 10-15 hours... but why? I had a blast just exploring, at times doing repetitive artifact farming just because it was FUN figuring-out the spots where you could make a profit and simply LIVING in this world.
If you like open world exploration (divided into several very large maps/area) and appreciate a focus on atmosphere, you will probably be able to look past the occasional cheap horror jump-scare and enjoy the game for what it is: an exploration masterpiece that ends waaaay too soon even after 54 hours. You will remember this one, unlike the many other games you may have also played along the way to get to this one.

Zeus Vs Monster is a game that could be used for schools, that's why I have it in my library. Besides, practicing maths skills and discovering the Greek mythology is a nice mix. I've also seen that a French version was available, which is a serious lacking feature for many educational products. Besides, the game exists also on Android, iOS and Mac, which covers many devices.
You're Zeus or Athena depending on your choice of Hero and your goal is to beat enemes coming to you by answering correctly to the proposed calculs. Every five levels, a mythological creature is also appearing, with some details about it and is the ending boss.
What's good is that the French version is only necessary at these moments. However, the translation may be correct but isn't still perfect as many faults are present.
You can adjust the difficulty, not in the settings though. Indeed, for the developers, the difficulty equals the speed of the enemies. Besides, changing this parameter during a playthrough will launch a new save file, without erasing your progression in other difficulties.
If you want harder calculs, before each play, you can choose the operations you want to show, the range of numbers (0-10 for the addition for example, multiply/divide by 1,2,5,10, etc..). That's where the game is very interesting, as not a lot of them propose a precise configuration. Also, you can follow how many answers were right or wrong in each of these parameters.
My big negative point is probably the fact that the help isn't clear. I mean, I've seen that you can use ASD or the arrows or the mouse. But in my head, I didn't associate these (apart the mouse) for answering the questions, it was for me to move my character. In reality, A/left arrow is for choosing the left answer, S/down arrow is for the middle one and D/right arrow is for the right one. I would have preferred a title saying that it was the commands to answer so that my brain didn't switch automatically in my usual habits in gaming.
Graphically, the game is correct. The soundtrack is also enjoyable.
Zeus Vs Monsters is a nice game about maths, thanks to the difficulty management that is precise and to the little entertainement to learn about mythological creatures, even if I can be a little disappointed in the translation. I can see the game to be used as a drill or as a reward.

TL;DR: If you played the first game and liked it, this game is worth your time and money. Buy it when you have the finances for it. If you didn't like the first game for certain elements, you most likely won't like this one either since it retains basically all of them on top of all the new stuff.
[Story - good]: It picks up mere hours after the first game's ending. The heavy dialogue is still there, be prepared for a lot of reading. The atmosphere changes however. Instead of being about a fledgling bracer learning the ropes and introducing elements of the world, it shifts to a more mythical and politically charged setting with a lot more at stake. There is also no huge cliffhangar ending like the first game. You will be mostly satisfied with how it ends but it still manages to leave some loose ends open for The Third.
[Characters - excellent]: Without trying to spoil much, I can say that if you didn't like Estelle's treatment in the first game, it's like night and day in the second. She does nothing but improve as a character. As for other characters that didn't get much development or explanations, that all changes too. Aside from a couple of new characters introduced to tie SC together into the Third, everyone gets some sort of character progression.
[Graphics - depends]: I already mentioned that I love these graphics in the first game's review. SC also reuses a lot of the same areas from the first game but manages to make them feel different from when you visited them the first time through. It deserves to be noted that there's some very awesome in-game graphics cutscenes AND some epic feeling animated cinematics in SC.
[Music - excellent]: Like the graphics, SC reuses some of the music of the first game. However there's still a lot more variety than what the first game had which I think was a good move on Falcom's part. Overall it feels a lot more epic to fit with the change of atmosphere of the story.
[Combat - good]: There was a lack of variety with the first game's combat ultimately. SC does manage to add more though. Chain Crafts for combo attacks, new Quartz allows for more spell options, a slew of new equipment and accessories allows for more freedom with how you set your group up. You can also choose your party setup more frequently with more options on who can accompany you and with the rebalancing of character's Crafts, you should have a tougher time deciding who you want to take with you.
[Length - good]: As it has been mentioned so many times already, let me reiterate, the first game can take 40-50 hours to beat the first time through... SC is at least 80 hours or more depending on how thourough you are, so at least twice as long as the first. No matter how much I like the story, I feel it's important to mention that the pacing can really slow down, to the point that you may feel like stopping. It is worth trudging through the slow points though because when it picks up, it really picks up!
[Replayability - average]: I haven't actually been able to play a new game+ yet but I'm willing to bet that some people may not want to play through a second time or more due to the pacing and length. However, the upside of playing the Trails games multiple times is that you may miss things (item, story or character-wise) the first time through because you're focused on reaching the end. One of the greatest stregths Falcom games have is the details they add to characters or the environment that makes them feel more worth exploring, this doesn't matter to everyone who plays RPGs but to some, it makes a difference.
[Bugs - average]: I haven't kept up as much with SC on what's broken or fixed because I haven't had as much time to dedicate to it. But I'm confident XSEED is still hard at work trying to smash the problems littering SC. At the very least there was one potentially game-breaking bug late in the game but has an in-game workaround to avoid it entirely... plus the game has only been out for a few months and the team dedicated to Trails is rather small, patience is a virtue.
My big negative from the first game still exists in SC, not being able to skip animations during combat. At least with more spell variations now, I can cast more than just White Gehenna spam though. :)

Pretty good RPG with a classic feeling to it. A lot of content and a lot of replayability. I would recommend it and I'll just highlight 3 aspects of the game that were memorable about it in the good, the bad and the ugly (okay, the neutral).
The good: I hate any tactician turn-based game. Often they're overcomplicated. But this one? This one was ... definitely complex but somehow I came around to like it. Everything made sense and learning how things works by setting EVERYTHING ON FIRE was a fun experience. Gameplay is just fun, making a builds and testing them out was great, there's a lot of possibilities to go around. Lots of things to find, lots of ways to resolve an issue, lots of surprises. If gameplay is what you're after then you won't be disappointed.
The bad: BUGS. Oh my god the bugs. Not many - true, but one extended turns in a certain boss fight to make it last forever for enemy to finish his turn. Another one made me lose about 15 hours of progress, because I couldn't access "home-base" waypoint and had to load older save. And yet another - by a chance we found out a bug that can make you immortal duplicating an Idol that ressurects you for no cost at all so you could gear up your whole team with immortality idols and pass the game in easy mode. What the hell. Larian fix your game, bugs in key moments are not acceptable, especially after the game came out of early access.
The neutral: Story and lore. Honestly only story for your companions was any good and made you care. Overall the game is about ego trip to become divine and often we were in a pretty good spot to not care about anyone else than our own quest to power. Factions and key characters even when they started as good, sooner or later they ended up not so rightous to a point I didn't mind killing most of them. Never felt there was any greater incentive to be "the good guy" or choosing "the lesser evil" in this game. The whole world felt not worth fighting for. Maybe that is the point? It's not bad, it definitely had some depth to it, but still felt "meh".

First off, this is a wonderful game, and a sequel to another wonderful game, Trails in the Sky: FC.  It's somewhat odd to be saying that, considering a month ago I didn't own SC, and had had Trails in the SKY: FC sitting on my hard drive for a year.  I started playing FC in late 2014, but the story is a bit of a slow burn.  10 or so hours in and not much had happened, and so I ended up shelving it for awhile.  In December of last year, I decided I needed to start playing it again and finish it.  It's interesting what happens sometimes when you take a break from a game you're not into at the time - after only a few hours back into FC, the character and plot needles had moved enough to keep me going, and before long I had become well and truly sucked in.
I played FC religiously at that point, fully-invested in the detailed characters, the growth they displayed throughout the game, and the ever-growing story.  That game, as you may have heard, has a real doozy of a cliffhanger, one with a lot of emotional punch.  So, there was only one thing for it - immediately purchase Trails in the Sky: SC and plunge headlong back into the world of Liberl.  Was it worth it?  Damn straight it was.
The character and world-building elements of SC are every bit as great as in FC, to which game it is a direct sequel.  I loved the characters, loved the story and loved that you could tell a lot of care was put into this game.  One of the things that's especially nice is that there's a true sense of humor on display at points, as well.  The anime-style character portraits do a wonderful and often-humorous job of conveying the characters' emotions, and, as in FC, there are treasure chests that, if you interact with them post-looting will give you a sarcastic message about doing so.
So emotion and humor and character and all of those nice RPG elements are present.  What about the gameplay?  I tend to be a fan of JRPGs that show you the monsters onscreen instead of having random battles (not that I don't love a number of those, as well), and if you're careful or have the right equipment you can always decide if you want to stop and fight or are in too much of a hurry to be bothered with it at the time.  You shouldn't need to grind in either FC or SC - the game rewards experience based on comparing your level with the enemy defeated, so underleveled characters play catch up fairly quickly.
The areas are generally well-laid out, although there are a few dungeons late game you might find yourself getting lost in if you aren't paying attention.  Design is good, and there is attention to detail everywhere.  The graphics are somewhat dated but plenty serviceable and there are options for things like anti-aliasing, anisotropic filtering and HD fonts and features that make the game more presentable on a modern system.  You'll notice that its technology is older, but unless you're really invested in that aspect, you won't care.
"Regular" battles can be somewhat tedious, though if you set yourself up right you can usually eliminate normal opponents pretty quickly.  The orbment system is interesting and versatile, and for those who played FC there are a number of further upgrades and changes that enhance battle and the number of arts(spells) you have available.  My understanding is that originally FC and SC were one game that had to be split into parts, and you can definitely see that here, as SC builds and expands upon what was already laid out in FC in a very natural way.
Most of the music is good, some of it great (although I miss the battle music from FC).  I still hate the music that plays in the city of Bose.  I think if Bose had catchier music I would not have put down FC for so long, and it returns in SC.  Oh well, you can't have everything.
There are a couple of gripes - in the back third of the game, you do some retreading over prior ground and have a section where it's "go here, fight X enemy" followed immediately by "go here now, and fight Y enemy" that is kind of a grind, but there's still more than enough story to carry you through. Anyone who likes RPGs will enjoy this game, so it has to be a thumbs up. Yet, there's a few aspects to be aware of that may ruin it for some players.
First, this game is not completely polished. There are bugs, ranging from lockups to party members getting stuck. The UI is often clunky or difficult to work with, including the inventory management, which is improved since DOS1 but still feels far more cumbersome than it ought to -- especially in a game that seems to expect you to hold onto one or two of everything just in case it's needed for a quest later.
Second, the game is hard to enjoy without quest walkthroughs. Yes, you can just go at it blind, explore, and figure stuff out, but you will miss a lot of things through no fault of your own simply because you found/did something before you talked to the right guy, or whatever. It's not even about maximizing rewards: many quests simply can't be finished unless they are gone about in precisely the right way.
Third, half the fun of this sort of game is experimenting with different party compositions to figure out what works best or is the most fun. Yet the game gives you very little control over this initially, other than with your main character. You meet the other "origin characters" relatively early on and you get an initial chance to change their premade classes, but that's about it. It's not until the game's second act -- many, many hours in -- that you get the ability to just create the exact party you want with fully custom characters.
But the biggest for me is the combat. It's often extremely difficult, and seems to invite you to find ways to break or exploit the game mechanics. For example, you will run into occasional fights where, even if you are over-levelled, enemies will literally destroy your party before you even get a turn. You quickly learn that while the baddie is doing his pre-battle speech, having your other characters teleport people, monsters, and objects around to optimal positions turns an unwinnable fight into a cakewalk. It makes no sense that you can do this -- you're exploiting the weird fact that participants in a conversation are essentially paused -- but it's sometimes the only way to proceed. It's strategy of a sort, I suppose, but it feels cheap and unrewarding.
All that said, the developer is releasing frequent patches, and there's more than enough awesome stuff in the game to make up for these annoyances.

Kentucky Route Zero is a ghost story. Not the kind to spook you, but the kind to make you stop and think about life.
First off, the bad. It takes a hell of a long time between episodes, which many people have complained about and is a valid issue. Gameplay wise, it's a fairly standard modern adventure game. you explore, solve an occasional puzzle, and talk.
Other than that, this is a beautifully designed, beautifully written game that evokes everything from early 40's americana, to the 80's computer revolution, from Lynch-esque surreality to Springsteen-esque yearning. The artstyle is minimalist yet vast, with each scene having a distinctive palette and tone. The writing is top-notch throughout, mature and emotional where a lesser game may have been corny. The music and sound is stellar, combining traditional bluegrass and folk with dark ambient soundscapes.
There are choices in the game, yes, but they are not the kind of BIG, GAME-CHANGING choices that you'd see in a TellTale style game. The choices you make define who these characters are, what their past is, what they want to be. There's a beautiful scene in the third act where
. Scenes like this are what make the game for me.
If you're a fan of adventure games, of litterature, of ghost stories, I highly recommend this game. If the lack of a release schedule bothers you, or if you play adventure games more for the puzzles than the story, you might find this lacking.

My friend got a four pack of this game when it was on sale for, i quote; "Less than an actual pack of orange juice", and gave one to me and the others to our other friends.  When we played it, we were expecting nothing more than a sub par anime themed mario party knockoff.
But what we got was so much more
Developer Orange_Juice has truly created something unique with this party game. On the surface it seems to be a somewhat normal board game, but it gets intricate really quick.
Everything that happens is determined by either a roll of a die, the use of a card, or both. Players compete to level up based on number of stars (basically stars are to 100%OJ as Coins are to mario party) or number of wins. Yes, wins. Theres combat in this game, and like i said before, its rules are governed by cards and die. Every card has a unique effect, and every character (aside from 6 of them) has a unique hyper card only they can use. Throw all of this together and you get an addicting RNG fest that will make you hate your friends almost as much as Mario Party did! Almost.
tl;dr its basically Orange_Juice's other games + Mario Party + Yu-gi-oh + a lil bit of DnD RPG mechanics, and its addictive as all hell

There is almost no strategy; sure, you can pick characters who differ slightly in combat attributes, and you can contribute your choice of cards to the main deck. I have not played this game for a very long time, however I noticed one thing over the course of all of this time... I kept remembering this game from time to time. As somebody who is not a fan of jump scares and the "horror"-genre, in general, I was surprised by just how much I enjoyed this game.
I was all about the open world. This world is very atmospheric and it really felt like you were just trying to survive, even if in reality it did not take much to become a bad♥♥♥♥♥who could go in with guns blazing most of the time. There were still plenty of surprises and challenges, some of which took a while to figure-out because there were more than one way to approach the situation, however the FEELING of "OMG, I have to stop the bleeding, find food, sell of this stuff to make money, and get ammo for my gun!" was always present. Never have I played a game where I was actually afraid of walking out at night and actually tried to get back to a safe area before darkness... kind of how you would do in real life, right? The atmosphere, especially with the lighting effects, and the creepy anomalies, made me explore every nook and cranny. Sure, you could probably run through the main story in a solid 10-15 hours... but why? I had a blast just exploring, at times doing repetitive artifact farming just because it was FUN figuring-out the spots where you could make a profit and simply LIVING in this world.
If you like open world exploration (divided into several very large maps/area) and appreciate a focus on atmosphere, you will probably be able to look past the occasional cheap horror jump-scare and enjoy the game for what it is: an exploration masterpiece that ends waaaay too soon even after 54 hours. You will remember this one, unlike the many other games you may have also played along the way to get to this one.

Now, take this review with a grain of salt because, yes, this game is unfinished and there have been absolutely no signs from the developers as to when the next acts will come out (currently there are only 3 acts out of a presumable 5 available).
This is an incredibly unique game unlike any other narrative-driven game out there. The plot and basis of this game is incredibly refreshing in its originality, not only introducing its lore but completely submersing the player in it. At times it can feel hard to follow because all you want to ask is "What the hell is all this?", which you may. But at the same time you can just say "Well alright then" and dive deeper.
The game gives you control over not just one character, but the entire cast of the game, manipulating the dialogue and developing the characters as you see fit. Each character has their own personality and background that could be interpreted in many different ways, and the game allows you to interpret them however you like and expand upon it through the dialogue choices you make.
This is very much an exploratory game; a large world with nooks and crannies giving more insight as to where you are. Don't expect the game to point you towards hidden trivia, take the time and find it yourself. And if you get stuck not knowing what to do, eh you'll figure it out. It's a slow-paced game, treat it as such.
Alright now down to brass tacks. Is this game worth buying? Yes. When will the rest of the game be released? Hell if I know, go harass the developers if that's your style. Buying episodic games before they're finished is an investment, and I believe that the current 3 acts released is a good sweet spot of available content to allow you to get your money's worth and pray that you get some return.

Wacky fun. That's really the best way to describe it. A 2D digital board game made solely for the anime-girl enthusiast, you and three other players collect cards, gold, and experience from traveling around a flat map and killing monsters and each other. Unfortuantely, the game isn't really self explanatory and it helps to play with friends when figuring out how things work. Each player has a set of cards that they put into the game deck, which are then shuffled and dealt out to players randomly. These cards can either hurt a player by dealing damage, heal damage, lay traps, give coins, etc... The players take turns moving around the board and landing on spaces, which give coins, cards, or spawn monsters where the player must fight with dice rolls. You can also fight other players to make them lose their next turn, or lose gold and slowing down their progression in levels. The objective is to level up to level 5 first, by either killing enough people/monsters to get experience or by collecting coins from spaces and other players. There's definitely a difficulty curve, but the online multiplayer is surprisingly very stable.
The art might turn people off at first, but at the end of the day this makes for a very fun game to play online with your friends.

Two things
1. Don't listen to these negative reviews claiming the game is a "scam".
2. Don't look for anything on this game's story, if you think you're going to buy it, buy it without an idea of the story you're about to witness.
It's true, Kentucky Route Zero has been in the making for over a couple years now. But how can you blame a 2 person devolopment team? Especially when they offer so much with each episode. Not to mention the INTERMISSION episodes they release for free on their website
.
It's been over a year since the last episode, and they have a srict rule of not having release dates for each new episode. An admirable stance as release dates can be a source of stress for indie developers, and often cause skimping out on certain aspects of the game.
So they work at their own pace, working to make the story they aim to, with no restrictions. And they've done an excellent job so far.
I refuse to say anything about the story, as I walked into this game with no prior knowledge beyond it's good reception. I've found it incredibly amazing and all the more engaging because of this.
I will say this game is very close to the peak of the "Weird Americana" story genre. It's a game filled with ghosts (in more ways than one), tall tales, shady backgrounds, and many old things.
It's a story of missed connections, faded relationships, longing, and regrets. The developers say it will be a tragedy, and I believe it.
A major complaint is the illusion of choice in the game. Being text based, it offers you many different conversational options. The main character's backgrounds, feelings, and dialogue are all filled in by you through these options. But episode to episode they don't make much difference.
But is that a real complaint? The developers have the story they want to tell, I don't blame them for not making these options integral to the games plot.
But furthermore, why must these options have tangible effects in the game world? Each of the characters aren't total blank slates, but they do leave much room for your own filling in. I've found myself creating these character's intangible personalities, and basing my decisions off what i've created.
And it's not like in life there are either options A, B, or C that all lead to different outcomes. Some decisions dont matter in the larger sense. Some don't make a difference.
In short I love this game and if you're into narrative video games, grab this ASAP.
A last warning though, I can't agree with the price either. I happened to get it on sale for 10 dollars, and I suggest you wait for a sale too. I don't see any problems with offering the individual episodes for the people not totally committed to the story, or skeptical of it's entertainment. BUT, I do see that it's a good excuse to say "hey, if you buy it all, why not play through them?".

I might be bias when I say I love Audition, that is only because I have been playing it since it was under Nexon. And while I can say that it was indeed better under Nexon as far as songs, I honestly say that it's not that bad as it is today, owned under Redbana. So I will try to give an honest review:
First off, They may have gotten rid of some songs, but they keep the old school Audition songs that you know and love. I love the songs they have right now, but I can't deny that I miss the old ones (Magic City, Sunshine, Large by Helix). Their currrent songs by Audition are still there, and they are catchy, and everytime they bring a new song in it is pretty catchy. Plus with recent updates you don't have to go scrolling through the long list of songs anymore unless it is to find the ones you absolutely love to add to your "music list". Which is a whole separate tab of songs that you ABSOLUTELY love so you can just easily search and pick them from there, then just dance! I haven't tried out the BGM List feature yet.
I have never seen anything about sex talk or immaturity of players. Clearly must be hanging out with the wrong crowd. A lot of the people that I have met are nice, and I actually see a lot of foreign players where I can't even understand what they are saying.
Clothes? Yea, it sucks that the only cash items they have are available for max up to 7 days, but if you play the right modes, you can look super cute! I was getting frustrated for that same reason when I saw that cute items cost 500k+ beats and I only had a mere 100k that I saved from the past year. Then my friends (who I met on Audition) introduced me to Beat Rush Battle Party, which is a PHENOMENAL way to earn beats, and now my character is cute and I have no reason to buy cash, and best of all it is permanent. I earned the necessary amount needed in a short time! So once you get used to the game, start doing Beat Rush, Beat Rush Battle Party, or Beat Up and your character will look great!
If you are complaining about the cash items having an expiration date, all you have to do is not buy them, and save up beats to get clothes that are just as cute! Beats aren't hard to earn. And if you must spend cash, it will be to reset the NPC's in Beat Rush Battle Party, which is very much worth it.
Speaking of clothes, this doesn't affect me, but for those of you coming in, you are lucky I have got to tell you. They changed their default clothes! So you don't look like a 10 year old girl, or a homeless dude who got picked up off the street! They are more "hip" and "modern" so to speak. Girls have a cheer leader-type outfit option, and a sweatshirt and sweat pants. Which my personal favorite is the cheer shirt, sweat pants, white sneaks combo. It's perfection for a starter outfit!
A lot of people on Audition by now are pretty pro, and it sucks when you come in last for almost every dance, but hey, I still have fun, and it takes practice. If you don't like the way they are running their room, find a new one, or make your own! If you don't want to practice in front of everyone and make an embarassment of yourself, feel free to observe, and practice anyway. They have arrows their so you can practice as if you were dancing yourself.
Audition has some great qualities, and I'm not exactly sure why it has gotten so many bad reviews. So I wanted to do this game justice by writing a review.

My friend got a four pack of this game when it was on sale for, i quote; "Less than an actual pack of orange juice", and gave one to me and the others to our other friends.  When we played it, we were expecting nothing more than a sub par anime themed mario party knockoff.
But what we got was so much more
Developer Orange_Juice has truly created something unique with this party game. On the surface it seems to be a somewhat normal board game, but it gets intricate really quick.
Everything that happens is determined by either a roll of a die, the use of a card, or both. Players compete to level up based on number of stars (basically stars are to 100%OJ as Coins are to mario party) or number of wins. Yes, wins. Theres combat in this game, and like i said before, its rules are governed by cards and die. Every card has a unique effect, and every character (aside from 6 of them) has a unique hyper card only they can use. Throw all of this together and you get an addicting RNG fest that will make you hate your friends almost as much as Mario Party did! Almost.
tl;dr its basically Orange_Juice's other games + Mario Party + Yu-gi-oh + a lil bit of DnD RPG mechanics, and its addictive as all hell

If you're a board game fanatic like me, DO NOT BUY this game.  There is almost no strategy; sure, you can pick characters who differ slightly in combat attributes, and you can contribute your choice of cards to the main deck.   Unfortunately, the gameplay relies almost 100% on dice-based luck, and only some very lucky card draws can overcome bad dice rolls; the extra +1 to attack or whatever you might get from picking a certain character doesn't augment your combat rolls enough to matter in the long run, and ANYONE can end up winning any match.
It is also very likely (and has happened to me many times so far) that in any particular match you will be repeatedly dying and accomplishing nothing, while the opponents who are running circles around you and are close to winning the match keep missing the "check" spaces by pure accident, thus extending almost indefinitely a game that you have no chance of winning.  These matches take too long to be as luck-based as they are.
I was expecting this to be sort of a cross between Monopoly and Magic: The Gathering.  What I got was, essentially, Craps.

American Truck Simulator offers the unique American environment, landscape and trucks, while the game itself shares many similarities with Euro Truck Simulator 2. That means excellent gameplay, good physics and more than decent graphics for an overall relaxing and unwinding game. Modding is just as easy in ETS2 as it is in ATS and there are several mods that you can download for the game to enhance your experience.
The big plus with this game though is the quality of the map and environment. The developers at SCS showed the community that they do put effort in mapping with the Scandinavia DLC for ETS2 back in 2015, and then there was ATS. The states are really nicely done and I hear that they are very realistic too (though I can't personally confirm that myself). You really do feel like an American trucker to some extent with this game, as you drive into the sunset with your American truck crusing on the desert. I would have thought that with all these new assets and improved map quality that performance wouldn't be as good as it was with ETS2 but I was proven wrong. As far as I can see, it is a win-win situation.
My only gripe with this game would be the time taken to release new content for this game. It has been over a year since Arizona was released that we saw New Mexico in game. Given that many still prefer playing ETS2, I'm not sure if SCS' current development strategy and resource allocation will see many new fans for ATS. I don't mind the price as long as it is reasonable, but I do think that I would have spent many more hours on ATS if the content kept on coming because unlike ETS2, ATS really needs it to expand its fanbase.
Overall though, I would recommend the game, especially at the 6,79€ that Steam is currently asking for during the Autumn Sale of 2017. It is a game worthy of its price.

Pros:
The story line is good.
The battle is good.
Cons:
The camera is aweful. Navigating the map is a stressful mess.
When your party member finds a hidden treasure, he says he spotted something, but the map is so hard see that you can't tell where that shining mound is.
The NPC will tell you of a location of a cave, but even if you are standing right in front of it you can't see the entrance.
Exploring the world is supposed to be full of surprises and a sense of adventure.
Instead it just feels like a series of rotating the camera in order to understand your surroundings.
The UI is aweful too.
You can learn a few dozen skills in the game, but you can only see one bar of skills and need to toggle the bars all the time to use the skills.
The only way to manage skill bars is by adding one skill or deleting one skill.
There is no sorting for skills so you have to manually sort the skill bars.
And when you have your skills sorted and you want to insert a fire skill that you just learnt, you have to delete a skill in that slot, meaning you have to reorganize every skill after the skil bar.
Maybe sorting is too hard to implement, but why can't we just insert a skill?
Inventory management sucks too.
There are mildly valuable things on the streets, but as you keep picking them up your inventory becomes a mess that you don't want to look at.
The content of the game, the story and the battle system are good.
But the interface is so horrible that it is impossible to enjoy them.
I would love to play the game if the camera is a normal third person view,
and the UI gets polished enough or the game rule changes such that you don't need a polished UI (limit the number of skills you can memorize to 8, don't litter the world with trashes so your inventory doesn't clog up.
At this moment it feels like they made a world that they wanted to make without caring about how the player experiences it. They might think the game is strategic and fun when you have 4 members full of 50 skills and items, but in reality having to manage all these things is too much hustle.

Wacky fun. That's really the best way to describe it. A 2D digital board game made solely for the anime-girl enthusiast, you and three other players collect cards, gold, and experience from traveling around a flat map and killing monsters and each other. Unfortuantely, the game isn't really self explanatory and it helps to play with friends when figuring out how things work. Each player has a set of cards that they put into the game deck, which are then shuffled and dealt out to players randomly. These cards can either hurt a player by dealing damage, heal damage, lay traps, give coins, etc... The players take turns moving around the board and landing on spaces, which give coins, cards, or spawn monsters where the player must fight with dice rolls. You can also fight other players to make them lose their next turn, or lose gold and slowing down their progression in levels. The objective is to level up to level 5 first, by either killing enough people/monsters to get experience or by collecting coins from spaces and other players. There's definitely a difficulty curve, but the online multiplayer is surprisingly very stable.
The art might turn people off at first, but at the end of the day this makes for a very fun game to play online with your friends.

In 10 years, this game will truly be considered a classic -- If that's not the case already.
There's a lot of juggle in this game, but once mastered, it's so rewarding. There's nothing better than starting a save as a Count and working your way up to be King, all while keeping your Vassals in check, maintaining a healthy bloodline, improving your settlements, silencing threats to the throne, defending against raiders (or going on raids yourself), seducing the wife of a nearby ruler (I think you need the Way of Life DLC for this), looking for the White Stag (still hasn't happened for me), join a Crusade for Jerusalum (or not), setting laws for your kingdom, using marriage ties to form powerful alliances, assigning tasks to your "loyal" Council... The list goes on and on.
I bought the Charlemagne, Ruler Design, Way of Life, The Old Gods, and the Customization Pack DLCs and they're all great additions to the game. It's a bit annoying that you need certain DLCs to play a ruler with a different religion, but I can understand that the developers need a way to generate money to be able to create new content. It's great that Paradox is still releasing content for a game that came out in early 2012; I believe they just released The Reapers Due this week.
Besides having to pay for most of the DLC content, the only other issues I have with the game is that most mods break the ability to gain achievements and the game is a bit daunting when you first play. If those are the two downsides to the game, then it really shows how good it is.
Turn-based strategies aren't everyone's cup of tea, but if it is, CKII is the game for you!

I played on a keyboard, my brother has been playing the co-op with me and he’s been using a controller, the game controls are very straightforward.

The achievements are rather dynamic and more complicated then I want to get into. The puzzles get really difficult and complex making getting all the achievements in this game a bit tricky, and the specialized achievements are a headache.
The price for A Virus Named TOM is $9.99, I’d recommend getting the game on a steal sale, or a humble bundle. I’d place the value on this game closer to $5.00. It is just a puzzle game, so naturally; most people won’t want to spend very much time playing it.

Ok, first of all, although I am a gamer for over 25 years, this is my first time playing a MOBA, and this is my first review ever.
Now, let's cut to the chase. I didn't have a clue about Awesomenauts, until a friend of mine recommended it. At first I was a bit skeptic, but a steam sale did the trick and I bought it. To be honest something about the 2D platform style helped a bit my decision.
I started playing the game, played a few practice sessions and then decided to go to the "real world". And then you start to die like a fly!!! You get to win a few matches with the help of a good team, but at the beginning, you get to be nothing but a burden to your team mates. The match making isn't always good and you find yourself with experienced opponents that can make the game not fun at all! And this is a crucial moment. I kinda got bored and tired, so I stopped playing for a couple of weeks until I decided to give the game another chance. And now, after about 70 hours (at the time of writing the review) I can say this! The game is amazing! I am totally hooked.
Sure there can be times when lag problem ruin a session, some characters seem to be overpowered against another, but in the end, the game is really fun to play! Ronimo tries to balance characters with patches now and then (not always with a good result, but I believe in good intentions). All that it needs, is to be patient and haves some time for exeperimentation. Game after game, you can find a couple, or more characters that are in your gameplay style.
The game comes with a ton of DLCs to buy (skins, announcers, the Starstorm expansion) but the good thing is that none of this affect the core gameplay, so no "Pay To Win" here, thank God!
If I had something to recommend to Ronimo, that would be something like a "noob league" or so, that can help inexperienced players learn the basics while playing against humans, and not bots!

Great follow up to the first game. Playing the first one is a must since this is a direct sequel. Pretty much continues everything good from the first game with a few improvements.
The music is definitely a step up from the previous game, while there are also now even more orbment combinations for those people who love tinkering with their arts/stats setups for each of their characters.
Story is still great, however the predictable structure of the first couple chapters got very boring once you realised what was happening each time. There are a tiny amount of annoying cliches in there as well, and some backstories to a few characters could have been done better. There is also a feel of backtracking a lot of the time since it's set in exactly the same place as the first game, but that can't really be avoided.
Despite it's cons, I still highly recommend this game since to me the characters/story, music and combat system are what make it so fantastic.
TL;DR
Pros:
- Awesome characters
- Even better music this time around
- More arts/orbment options
- Last chapters have awesome buildup
- Improved turn related changes in combat (i.e. showing specific effects of AT Delays etc.)
Cons:
- First 4 chapters have very formulaic structure that gets annoying
- Not too much of a pain for me, but there are definitely a few points where backtracking might annoy a lot of people
- Some character backstories/motives are pretty silly
Overall Verdict: Great game, highly recommend.

Trails in the Sky SC is a strong follow up to the first Legend of Heroes: Trails in the Sky.  The story picks up just hours after the cliff-hanger conclusion of the first game, creating a seamless adventure that sometimes feels as much like a wonderful novel as a video game.  The plot is well placed, if a bit meandering at the start.  What really pulls the whole game together is the interactions of the charming and varied cast, as well as the phenomenal localization.  The dialouge never feels stilted or clunky, which is important because this game is verbose. The earlier book comparison is accurate: expect to do a lot of reading.
From a gameplay standpoint, the combat is incredibly similar to the first which is both a strong reason to play this game as well as a bit of a knock against it. There was very little innovation in the implementation of battles. Fortunately, the base was already very solid and it is hard to find fault with the system.
All in all, I would strongly reccomend this game to anyone in search of an emotional, character-driven, intrigue-filled adventure; however, lacking an understanding of the story from the first game will really inhibt one's ability to follow what is happening in the early portions of this game. It might almost be wiser to consider the two together one long game rather than a prequal and a sequal.
TLDR; An absolute MUST play, provided you've payed the first one.

I thought that Trails in the Sky SC was an amazing game and experience that really built on the first chapter`s adventurous feel and elevated it immensely. It was obviously a lot darker than the first game with its introduction of new villains working from the shadows and narrowing down most characters` individual pasts and stories. The game felt so intense with each new chapter and was really exciting at times but always introduces time for a little laughter. Even the NPCs were quite lively and had their own tales which intersected between chapters and made them more lively. The overall length was very satisfying and did make ends meet with most characters but still left a few lingering questions and mysteries that are yet to be known.
I`ll admit that some parts of it were definitely very predictable like being saved at the last minute in most scenarios. The game does over-use that trope and breaks the mood but it is nice to see other characters jumping in the spotlight. I personally felt that the choice to freely pick any party member was nice but it also does limit what we get out of having all characters shine. In the first game you had a select party for each chapter and could really get a feel for what makes them unique and also how you can really adapt to their abilities in battle. So in the SC its more like you can choose to experiment with different members while also trying to be aware of what abilites may be effective or not with others. The dialogue scenes can be lengthy but they are also touching at times which complements that along with its lovely soundtrack.
Ultimately this has been one of the best JRPGs I`ve played in a while and I would definitely recommend it to others since it is rather unknown but is an amazing game nonetheless.

So, I finished the game. What can I say to those, who came to read the reviews, thinking about buying this game?
I think I'll use default pros/cons list of things doesn't mentioned on the game page:
+  Content/price ratio. It will probably took you about 80~100 hours just to complete campaign. Can be more, can be less.
+  Great feeling of adventure, even the main quest line feels more like an exploration rather than just following the markers on the map (hello to Skyrim main quest).
+  Neat battle mechanics. And again, it's not a straight line of pushing the buttons to deal damage (hello to Dragon Age combat). You can explore the possibilities of different spells effects, you must check resistances of your enemies, you should care about positioning your heroes and seeking good spell combos (at least on high difficulty settings).
+ Good storyline (highly subjective opinion). Some nice twists (one final twist actually can be predicted long before it's happening by watching closely on a particular NPC characteristics, which is nice), characters with different stories (both past and ongoing).
- Despite the story being good (highly subjective opinion), I didn't find characters catchy or very interesting. I would rate them as "okay, I guess". None of them, I don’t know, touched my heart and made me worry about him/her. I guess it's because they rarely showing their personalities through some sort of a tete-a-tete dialogues with your hero and very limited interaction between party members.
-  Bugs. Few in singleplayer (mostly side quests that can't be finished properly and incorrect dialogue sequences, nothing critical, but still it is an unpleasant experience) and a lot in co-op mode (you can find lists of current issues on reddit if you really want, it's constantly changes because old bugs being fixed and new being discovered). Developers fixing them and rolling patches very often, but I think the game without a publisher demanding the product here and now should be polished better on its release.
- When I selected "tactician" difficulty, because default level was too easy and then I find that the “tactician” is easy too, I couldn't go higher because "tactician" doesn't allow changing the game difficulty. WTH?
- Patches are breaking localization. I played the game in Russian, but after some patches some spells began to use English names and some entries in the quest log changed the language.
-  And lastly, I want to mention the dark side of highly variable combat. Huge possibilities mean huge exploits and when battle was too hard for me, rather than winning because I learned something from my mistakes and improved tactics I usually won because I've found a way to cheat the game.  Major "cheat source" is stealth mode and NPCs reaction to it. In most cases, if all party members are Solid Snaking, they will just stay in one place obediently skipping their turns and waiting when you decide to show yourself. Only if combat can be finished without killing all enemies (I think this is how it works) they can start walking and searching for you
.
In the end despite all cons I've found this game really fun to play and rate it 8/10 spooky scary skeletons with buckets on their heads, totally recommend.

DISCLAIMER: It's been awhile since I played this game and I am finally getting around to reviewing it. I put off reviewing it for so long because it's such an odd game and I didn't know what to say about it. Anyway, the point is that I am going off of my faulty memory.
I liked this game but it's not for everyone. It's really hard to pin down. It plays like the graphical adventure games of olden days--King's Quest, Police Quest, Space Quest, etc. except you don't really collect items in an inventory, neither do you really solve any puzzles. It almost feels like a surreal text adventure populated with quirky characters but with some impressionistic graphics and haunting music to go along with it. It's like a game that Sierra On-Line would have made back in the day, if David Lynch and William Faulkner had worked there.
The game feels more like a tone poem. It's eerie at times, but not scary. It can be hauntingly beautiful at times, leaving you feeling melancholy. Sometimes it can be weirdly comical. As I said before, you don't really solve any major puzzles and you only occasionally feel like you are pursuing any sort of goal or are part of any story that is advancing toward any kind of resolution. You sort of go along for the ride and you do have decisions to make, but those are mostly just selecting dialog. The gameplay, what little there is, feels like mostly just adding some subtle nuance to the way the characters interact with each other.
Looking back over what I wrote, it can seem like I am being negative about the game, but I can say that it was a very unique experience and I thought that the presentation, however odd, was enjoyable. If you want to try something really different, I suggest you give this game a shot when it goes on sale.

You're gonna want to play this game (and the other stalker games too) on the highest difficulty because the lower the difficulty, the lower the chance of a bullet hit counting as an actual hit. Whereas shooting an enemy in the head on the highest difficulty will always kill the enemy (assuming your gun does enough damage).
Not a great difficulty system, but knowing about it is gonna save you a lot of frustration.

Furthermore, the atmosphere is also really interesting. Its really hellish and creepy. The graphics are also very minimalistic and therefore work really well for this game. All of the monsters look great and the sound design is great too of how each monster has a distinctive noise and they all buzz around you as you around. The weapon, which you can alternate between rapid fire and shotgun blasts on the fly, is really fun to use. Definitely worth giving this game a go!

Basically there isn't much in the way of making your own fighting style even though everything that isn't another player attacks you. The AI is bad. No other way to put it really. This game is a scam.
There.  I said it.  I tried to come up with a nicer way of saying it, but I just can't sugar-coat the truth.  This game is a complete and total rip-off, and here's why...
They're charging full price for a game that isn't just unfinished, but shows no signs of ever being finished.  Simply put, the game is trying to follow the pattern of timely episodic releases popularized by Telltale Games.  There's just two problems with that:
1) You can't buy individual episodes.  The only purchasing option on Steam is a full Season Pass.  You can't buy the first episode for $5 and then decide if you like it enough to buy the rest.  Nope, it's all or nothing.
2) Releases have been anything but timely.  The first two episodes came out in January and May 2013.  The third was released in May of 2014.  There is no announced release date for the fourth.
Think about that for a second.  They are charging full price for a game that has been only 60% done for over a year.  Early Access games wish they could get away with this.
What's worse is that game critics have been tripping over themselves trying to heap praise on unfinished product, and it's not hard to see why.  The visual are striking, the music perfectly captures the feeling of rural Kentucky, and the story certainly has me on edge for the next two episodes...
What's been delivered is certainly worth an 8/10.  Unfortunately, since two fifths of the game is missing, that gets dinged down to a 4.8/10.  Until the developers get their♥♥♥♥♥♥together, I suggest you turn your attention elsewhere.

To briefly summarize my recommendation:
Sonic Mania is a game recommended by me with two thumbs up.
Pros:
- Classic style and Modern mechanics collide into an amazing blast from the past
- The difficulty of the game and its mechanics were a moderate difficulty to learn and fun to succeed in
- Bosses were reimagined and referenced great memories of SEGA's past
- Levels had many ways to progress and offered a rewarding feeling to rerun
- Sonic, Tails, and Knuckles all had personality to them with the great sprite animation.
- Special Stages provided an entertaining and challenging break from side scrolling action
- The title screen and introduction to the game after waiting a while itself shows just how much passion there is within the Sonic Community.
Cons:
- The need for at least one more original stage between the remix of memorable locations in the Sonic 2D Universe is something I really wanted more of. Although, nothing a DLC in the future can't fix!
- I would prefer more assignable controls for those using an Xbox controller (or PC based controller) especially given the fact that I feel as if third-party programs risk the validity of the game license in terms of avoiding triggering any anti-tamper.
- I'm only going to graze this but the PC launch did not have the best reception and end results and I hope Denuvo and the results of its implementation from day one provided a learning experience. And, I hope it does not cause any problems with the future release of games.
POTENTIAL SPOILERS BELOW - Be warned!
To give the game a more thorough review...
As an obviously avid Sonic Fan I am glad to see a breath of fresh air brought back to what made Sonic good as a high speed, high stakes, and highly anticipated game to say the least. To begin, I must first praise the amazing work of sprite animations and overall graphical quality of the game. That being that animations were smooth, the rotation to stabilize Sonic after running up a ramped wall really shows just one of those extra touches. The original made levels (Studiopolis, Press Garden, Mirage Saloon, Titanic Monarch, and even Egg Reverie) really caught my eye in how they brought new sights, mechanics, and just an overall fresh environment in between the memorable places every Sonic Fan can remember which each have a new quirk while keeping a consistent theme and match to the original. The most memorable Boss Fights were the Chemical Plant Act 2 and Hydrocity Act 2 bosses which engaged to me a very humorous and surprising spin to the overall experience Sonic Mania has given to me. I almost would not mind even seeing Labyrinth Zone added to the mix…Almost. Jokes aside, the game itself provides a followable story that has its parts that raise more questions than answers while others while making references to mechanics of the level, like Stardust Speedway to name one, as you transition into the next, unless you get transported again by the Phantom Ruby.  The speed I feel in the game is just right as Sonic makes a slow advance across to the right of the screen as he runs while Tails is a manageable while still at times able to really fly at times through a level and do the same himself. There is also to mention a big amount of potential for future expansion of the game as resources and other hidden easter-eggs are found showing currently dropped assets, personally I would like to see a strong moding community towards things like Online Multiplayer, but more importantly I hope to see a future in Mania beyond the base game (maybe even a sequel). The last thing I found great was the use of Chaos Emeralds being standardized for Tails instead of venturing further for Super Emeralds. I mention this only because it might mean that he’s all grown up enough to be at Sonic’s side and not just to abuse his invulnerability. Not, that I am a sucker for Tails… Don’t look at me like that!
To wrap it up, this game is everything I expected it to be and much more than I could ever ask in a Sonic Game. Seeing how things make it seem to play into another…more modern and well three-dimensional release that is approaching in November. Christian Whitehead, Headcannon, and PagodaWest Games have captured the true passion and drive of Sonic Fans and expressed it into a wonderful piece of modern and classic art of which has captured my heart as a long-time fan of Sonic the Hedgehog. It is great to see Sonic once again standing tall as the one true icon of SEGA and as a classic hero that I admire (along with his companions for sure Tails and Knuckles as well).
And, with that I Thank You,
~Invert

Kentucky Route Zero is a game. Kentucky Route Zero is also an experience. It is possible to perform in-depth analysis of the many notable references within the game and experience, but I will not do it here. Kentucky Route Zero is divided into five acts, out of which only three have been published at the time of writing. This three-fifths situation does not stop me from preparing this quick review. Kentucky Route Zero is worth it.
Many games have the character of a novel or a short story. Kentucky Route Zero is more like poetry, and as poetry it has a story to tell between the lines. The narrative starts when Conway, a truck driver, stops by a darkened gas station (Equus Oils) somewhere in Kentucky to get directions. He needs to make a delivery to an address which he cannot find, and is informed by the old man at the gas station that he needs to take the somewhat mysterious Route Zero to be able to make the delivery. Hence Conway starts his journey through the Kentucky night in search for the Zero.
Along the journey, Conway meets several characters with interesting and rich background stories. Examples of these are the cousins Shannon and Weaver Márquez that have lost contact with each other over the years, the young boy Ezra whose parents have disappeared and now lives with his unusual brother Julian, and the motorcycling musicians Johnny and Junebug. During the night, Conway also uncovers more and more details about a complicated story from many years ago involving the three then college students Joseph, Lula and Donald:
.
One of the main themes in Kentucky Route Zero is that of being too late, or to some extent not in phase with the present. It takes its form in the use of old electronic equipment, stepping into abandoned industrial sites, handling bureaucracy and lost love, and visiting museums. It is also reflected in the general gameplay, which is mostly the point-and-click style of old adventure games. The strongest example of this theme is shown in the Lower Depths bar in the most powerful scene in Act III of the game. That scene may actually be the most powerful one I have ever experienced in a computer game. The magic of that scene must be experienced in the game; it cannot possibly be described by me in words.
The atmospere in the game fits the story perfectly, both with its, somewhat angular, visual appearance and its almost perfect music score. The changes in the mood and the tone are often subtle but efficient. The writing is excellent, and the way that the character controlled by the player changes over time opens up for good variations in the way the story plays out. However, the last aspect of course also opens up for some confusion along the line.
Is the game perfect? No, but I think it is very good.
Is the experience perfect? No, but I really like it.
I am looking forward to the final two acts of the drama.

This is a board game. Don't go in expecting anything else. Consquently, the game is mostly centered around luck (with a small amount of skill involved) and the single-player is, at its best, an overly long tutorial on why you should hate Poppo. Before you purchase, make sure you understand all of this.
With that disclaimer out of the way, I would like to say that this is one of the best-designed games released in the last couple years.  If you can find a few friends to play with, or look into the (reasonably active!) community, you'll find quite a bit to love in this game. The mechanics are everything that they need to be, the soundtrack is top-notch where it matters (unless you main Marc or Poppo), and if you're trying to experience everything the game has to offer, you'll actually be here for quite a while.
The gameplay, while leaving you constantly at the mercy of the RNG, is just as likely to screw over anyone else. In single-player, that can get tiresome, but once you've started playing multiplayer, that's all part of the fun. Life is short and so are individual games. You might lose one round to a crappy defend role, and you might win the next because of a lucky six. With the overall speed at which a game can be completed, it's all part of the fun. You're rewarded almost equally regardless of whether you win or lose, so don't get too caught up with all of that - just relax and let the dice craft wonderful webs of agony while you and your friends suffer in succession. All in all, it's one of the few multiplayer games I can consistently say that I have
playing. And since this is a game, that's the important thing, isn't it?
That might not sell the game to you. It should, but it might not. And if it doesn't, then I'd like you to take a look at the update history for a moment. For this obscure $7 board game with a cast that's virtually unknown in the west, Fruitbat Factory has done the most stellar job of supporting a game post-release that I've ever seen. Not only have they added characters and maps to a small-name game released in
, but they actively look at user feedback and have introduced countless new features by popular demand, such as in-game chat and online avatars. In an era where publishers are eager to throw crap out the door at the first opportunity, I'm simply astounded at the work they've put into perfecting this little boardgame - for over a year and counting, now.
I have to wonder how Orange Juice feels. Perhaps they're amused at how their shooting-game characters are possibly best-known in the west as characters from a board game? Maybe so. They should be very pleased with themselves, though - they, along with the publisher that they've partnered with, have become one of the most brilliant examples of what the game industry could be in an ideal world. Rather than looking for new ways to milk their audience, they've been constantly at work improving this game from a simple tribute project to what is probably my favorite game that I played last year, and it's only getting
from here as they find more and more ways to add to the game.

Now, in Conan Exiles, I can build my own town, populate it and dictate what everyone is wearing, even what colors they display. Lots of dungeons to explore, lots of loot to be found. Killing boss mobs and learning new recipes is just awesome! With over 1,400 hours of game play over the course of a year I still find this game re-playable. I first tried out the game on a demo and fell in love with the concept of playing a dynasty over the twenty years in that demo. I later bought the game during a steam sale along with as many of the DLC I could afford at the time, and bought the rest of the DLC on another steam sale. I have experienced many things in this game and hope that my helpful review will get any who read this a clear picture of what this game is.
When you first start the game you will get the option to chose any ruler on a list of bookmarked dates or just select anywhere on the make that is selectable. (If you got the ruler customization DLC then you could make your own ruler after selecting a realm.) The earliest start date is 1066 without The Old Gods and Charlemagne DLC, but with them your start dates are move back to 769 as the earliest.
Some would say that this game cost too much if you buy all the DLC. To that I would say yeah they are right. Don't buy all the DLC in one day. Buy it over a period of months or do what I previously mentioned at the top. Note that some of the DLC may cause performance issues for those who have a not so great computer setup.
The game also come with an extensive tutorial game mode to help those who are newcomers. I highly recommend those who buy this game to take the tutorial mode that is offered in the start screen. Once you have mastered it though the game dose become a lot easier the more you play.
For those who will want to play multiplayer, you may need to learn of the other players attitude that they have adopted. You see if they do not know you or you have not gone to the CK2 forum to scheduled a game session, then you will be kicked by the host more than half of the time. They do this because the CK2 multiplayer has some syncing issues. If you lose your sync you would have to disconnect and reload the game from the desktop. Most people just don't want to quit and reload their games for a random who joins, but they would do it for a stranger they planed an evening or entire day with... strange right?
Now for the main reason you should get this game. Mods! Yes the mods on this game can be real awesome like the guys who made an entire conversion of the Game of thrones world  to down right funny where every line of text is Hordor. The mods are extensive and plus the major ones have their own little community forums on the paradox website.
In all this games replay ability with or without DLC should be your reason to get this game. Its multiplayer is something to be desired, but once you get a game rolling it is just as fun if not harder than playing by yourself. So by the time when another great steam sale comes, I hope to see you in game.

In 10 years, this game will truly be considered a classic -- If that's not the case already.
There's a lot of juggle in this game, but once mastered, it's so rewarding. There's nothing better than starting a save as a Count and working your way up to be King, all while keeping your Vassals in check, maintaining a healthy bloodline, improving your settlements, silencing threats to the throne, defending against raiders (or going on raids yourself), seducing the wife of a nearby ruler (I think you need the Way of Life DLC for this), looking for the White Stag (still hasn't happened for me), join a Crusade for Jerusalum (or not), setting laws for your kingdom, using marriage ties to form powerful alliances, assigning tasks to your "loyal" Council... The list goes on and on.
I bought the Charlemagne, Ruler Design, Way of Life, The Old Gods, and the Customization Pack DLCs and they're all great additions to the game. It's a bit annoying that you need certain DLCs to play a ruler with a different religion, but I can understand that the developers need a way to generate money to be able to create new content. It's great that Paradox is still releasing content for a game that came out in early 2012; I believe they just released The Reapers Due this week.
Besides having to pay for most of the DLC content, the only other issues I have with the game is that most mods break the ability to gain achievements and the game is a bit daunting when you first play. If those are the two downsides to the game, then it really shows how good it is.
Turn-based strategies aren't everyone's cup of tea, but if it is, CKII is the game for you!
