I was on a JRPG kick, and it was on sale. And from those humble beginnings, my journey with the greatest RPG in a decade began.
The Legend of Heroes: Trails in the Sky feels more like a novel than a video game. This is somewhat true in a literal sense: there's a lot of text! But where it really shows up is in the intentional design decision to have the story be the central focus. And what a story it is. It starts out small. You play as a teenager cutting her teeth at her newfound vocation, with the stakes to match: a lost cat, a maintenance kit for a lighthouse, unreturned library books. Nothing life-changing. Certainly nothing world-changing. But these seemingly trivial tasks allow the world and the characters to establish themselves and breathe, allowing them to become more than nameless faces. A dizzying amount of random townsfolk NPCs have their own storylines going on, and the game lets you watch these threads unfold. The main plot is slowly building in the background, but the game unapologetically focuses on letting the player slowly absorb the country of Liberl for the first thirty hours or so and watching the slow growth of Estelle. And it's the better for it, because when the plot gets into gear, all that time spent with her starts to really pay off. The game mechanics are decent, but they're obviously secondary: like a novel, the real meat of the game is the characterization and worldbuilding.
That's what happened in the prequel. Which you have to play before this one, because this one is where that characterization and worldbuilding established in the first one starts to pay incredible dividends.
In SC, the stakes are increased from the very start, but again, the game lets the central plot take the back seat for a while and focuses on worldbuilding and character development. You go back through the same towns as the first game, with the same NPCs and even the same dungeon layouts. And it's like visiting an old friend. You see how the NPCs handle the ongoing crises, how they've adapted, how they've soldiered on, how they've gone about the business of living their lives. It gives a richness and depth to the setting that is matched by few other games, and almost no other JRPGs. I can't stress this enough: the focus on world-building isn't a seasoning trying to add depth to the main course, it's part of the main course itself. I could spend the entire game running errands and talking to NPCs (and listening to the fantastic soundtrack!), and it'd be worth it. That's how good this element is.
Of course, like in the first game, the main plot is always slowly building up in the background. And like in the first game, it starts to take center stage around 30 hours in. And like in the first game, the hours upon hours spent with following Estelle and her growth add a depth to the narrative that causes it to shine. Trails in the Sky is a story about Liberl, but it's primarily a story about Estelle, and the game does a beautiful job of linking the world-changing events happening to the personal growth of Estelle and her companions. It's a complete masterclass in writing, and if the country of Liberl is the soul of the game, then the journey of Estelle is unquestionably the heart. There are some improvements to the battle system, but again, this game isn't about the battle system. It's the story of a country and the story of a girl, masterfully weaved together into a single must-play experience.
There's been much written elsewhere about the long, hard, probably cursed journey this game took to Western shores, so I won't repeat the story here. But I would be remiss to not offer my gratitude to Falcom, to Carpe Fulgar, and to Xseed. Blood and tears were given to bring me this game, and my thanks and money seem woefully inadequate a recompense. But it's all I can offer for now, so it will have to do. So thank you to everyone involved in the development and localization of this game, for your fantastic job at giving me one of the best gaming experiences I've ever had.

I'm a fan of the Conan novels, I was a fan of Age of Conan, and I've been hoping for a game like Conan: Exiles to come for quite awhile. A game that looks realistic, with weapons that are to scale, and colors that don't look like a rainbow exploded. This is not an MMO with different classes or roles of characters, endless quest chains that drive you mad, and dungeons you will not see unless you have 20+ friends to join you. Here, a couple of friends will do.
Surviving the wilds in this game is only a challenge at the early levels. After that, surviving vs other players is the challenge. Combat is simple, similar to Skyrim at this pre-release stage, but the "combat system" has yet to be implemented... it is coming soon, as is the much anticipated Sorcery aspect.
While anyone will enjoy playing this game, leveling, equipping, and building your house/ castle/ base or whatever you want, the game is incredible for roleplayers in particular. It's possible to create entire cities where you can be whoever you want; A merchant, a farmer, a bounty-hunter, a guide, a king or queen, a thief, a warrior, a cannibal, a knight, an archer, a hunter, a slave-dealer; almost anything you can imagine. Or you can be ALL those things with the same character. You are not limited in abilities as you would be in an MMO.
This game looks beautiful, the environment is very immersive, and Funcom is staying true to the Conan universe, not selling-out or giving in to the players who want to make it a different game than Funcom does.

Though I wasn't originally a fan of this game when it first opened early access back at the beginning of 2017, I'm happy to say they've since developed the game a LOT, and the game as it stands today is a completely different beast--and has completely won me over.  Back then I thought this game would be another ARK or Rust and languish in buggy hell forever, but I was wrong, and it's now my favorite game.
Though release is coming up in a few months, it's still in early access as of this writing, so the usual caveats for all early access games apply here.  That said... I love it these days, and while I can't wait to see what else they manage to include before release, I'm now comfortable reccomending the game as it stands, even before taking into account the additional content still being added every week.
This game has the best and most satisfying base-building of any survival game I've played, and the most interesting world.  Exploring is fantastic, building is fantastic, fighting is... good. More fun than any other survival game I've played, but not quite as good as some solo RPGs.
The biggest downside to the game right now is that it is still early access, which means some bugs get introduced with patches--though, for anyone who played the bug-tacular initial release, it's worth noting it's orders of magnitude better than it was in that regard, and they're usually hotfixed quickly.  The devs have been phenomenal, open and engaged with the community about any issues as well as the game development as a whole.  The unscripted weekly livestreams are refreshingly honest and really show the passion the team has for this project.  As early access games go, this has grown into one of the very finest examples of early access done right, but it IS still early access, so if that bothers you, you should wait for the final release.  Otherwise, I look forward to seeing you out in the world!

Conan Exiles is a crafting/building game with PVP and RP capacity set within a new section of Robert E Howard's Hyboria. The Exiled Lands are not in any related stories, but it fits so well. I am pretty sure the Nameless City could be the ruins of Acheron, but it doesn't quite fit with the intro of Conan freeing an Exile from crufixion and providing her with a weapon. One thing fans of Howard's Conan stories will particularly enjoy are the look and feel. The brutality, sexy nudity, hardened strength of the characters and immersive world are all a heady mix, especially when combat begins and the gore ensues. And yes, just remove your bracelet or jump from a very high cliff to see some impressive gore. Never gets old.
The ecosystem is unrefined, but it is Early Access days yet. I look forward to a mounts system and hopefully even warmounts. Once the fungeons are all open and more critters walk the world it will be like Nerdvana (at least, for me). Death isn't the end in this story and if you grow bored, you can remake your character aka destroy your cursed bracelet that keeps you bound to the Exiled Lands even through death. The way the story is hinted at through clues in the ruins, but is not fully exposited is well-played on Funcom's part. I love the combat system, but it could do with more complexity and finessing. I am sure Funcom have something glorious in the works for us. This is one ambitious game! I enjoyed Ark and Skyrim and Conan: Exiles is like both of them. There are so. Many. Mods. I even saw a mod for level 1 trillion. Even though it is only Early Access days there are always players online on the dedicated individual server I play on, even very early in the morning before work. I find that it is easy to pick up whatever I left off doing. I have also had some fun destroying other players' fortresses and looting their possessions. It's a hard world, is Hyboria. I have even seen people ragequit over it. If you play on a PvP server, keep in mind you will lose stuff you spend hours building and crafting so understand that nothing is precious and it is all easily remade. The bottom line is to have fun. It's destruct-o-clock! The Exiled Lands are kind of like what Australia was as a prison colony. All Exiles are criminals and you are given 3 crimes at character creation that you have been crucified for. Mine were skullduggery, bugger and punching a camel. It just doesn't get any better than this!

This game has a lot of positive aspects which have been mentioned everywhere by now. So despite unquestionably recommending this game I'll be only focusing on the negative parts. Although I won't talk about bugs, just game design.
Example Enemy = HP 200 + Phys Armor 300 + Mag Armor 300
With a hybrid team you would need to remove 800 Total HP to kill this enemy.
With a physical or magical only team it’s just a total of 500 HP.
So a team consisting out of 2 fighters and 2 wizards is WAY weaker than a 4 wizard or 4 fighter team.
Easy fix: Just one Armor type which is reduced by phy and magical dmg.
The balance issues obviously apply mainly to the Tactician Difficulty. If you don't mean to play this game on the hardest difficulty setting this probably won't bother you.
Warfare is by far the best combat ability in the game. It multiplies your overall physical damage by 5% for every point you spend on it. As a nice bonus you also get the best Crowd Control skills on top of it.
You know something is broken if even rangers and rogues have to max Warfare to get the most dps instead of their main Combat Abilities.
And since the Lone Wolf trait doubles your Warfare points, the damage output gets ridiculous.
Pro tip: If you want that Tactician / Honor Mode achievement, just play two Warfare Lone Wolfs and its an easy walk throughout the game.
When you reach high levels, the scaling on gear is immensely higher, to the point where (roughly speaking) a weapon two levels higher than your own, without modifications, can be close to twice as powerful.
That epic level 18 Sword you just found is great, right? Well it sucks once you hit level 19.
And the game naturally scales enemy health at a similar rate, and expects your equipment to be up to par.
So the strategy narrows down to out leveling your enemies instead of outsmarting them, like it should've been.
Everything feels wrong about the last Act, especially compared to Fort Joy.
The first act is obviously the strongest part of the game:
It's not surprising why most of the ~20 hours reviews dish out 10/10 ratings. It is really that good in the beginning.
Once you reach the last Act you realize that either the passion or/and the time ran out to finish the game properly.
Arx is a huge city map which feels completely empty, filled with generic Citizen and Soldier npcs. Everything is grey and ugly. Some areas, Characters and specific Items are not tied to any Quests so it feels very rushed.
Once you reach the middle of the city you can go in any direction. But most of the enemies end up being level 20 so it doesn't hint you where you might want to go first.
I felt really over leveled with my level 19 party when I arrived in Arx, since the act before was literally a stomp. But due to the Item and enemy scaling those level 20 guys would just destroy my party.
To make things worse you will get ambushed by enemies which are lvl 20. You can make them run twice but the third time there is no going back. This fight is really frustrating if your party is below 20 and not properly geared up. This just punishes exploration in an area which is already not that interesting to explore.
There are way too few interesting encounters in Arx. And some are just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t level of hard so you have to cheese them (mirrors fight).
Most items you find or get rewarded in Arx are level 18 and completely useless for your party.
This is the part of the game at which point you want to spend all your remaining Gold on the best gear. But you can't even do that since Arx offers the worst vendors in the game.
You keep running around looking for interactions just to be disappointed. You didn't skill persuasion? Might as well not talk to any relevant NPC.
Every direction is a dead end after you complete a quest. You have no idea whether a quest connects to your main quest or not. So you run around blindly just to complete a quest and stare at a dead end. Go back to city square and run in the other direction, complete this quest and another dead end. Again and again until you did everything or you stumbled upon the right quest to progress the main story.
As if the game flow wasn't bad enough, you have literally an inception level of secret vaults. A hidden vault within a hidden vault within a hidden vault within a hidden vault? Are you kidding me?
And after a confusing pipes puzzle with a horrible interface you expect finally some action don't you? Wrong! More lever puzzles!
Even the performance gets worse. While the game runs perfectly on high settings throughout act 1-3, the FPS counter crashes down in some areas of Arx.
I’m not going to spoil anything relevant to the story. I will talk about the mechanics of the final battle and the way the end is presented to you. Skip this if you feel it might spoil something.
.. is very poorly designed. It has 2 Phases and you just have to nuke one enemy to progress to phase 2 and nuke one enemy again to finish the game. Really? This is just stupid trial and error.
If you chose to submit to your enemies before the fight, it skips phase 1 and you get to fight with a lot of strong "allies" who should've been your enemies instead. This feels like Hey you don't want to try to win the last battle so here get a free win. After all that build up you get this lame battle? Really?
You choose one of three options to get a different ending. It doesn't matter what you did before, whether you killed everyone or played a saint. This is literally the same as the Mass Effect 3 ending. But where is the outrage? I guess the reviewers didn't even finish the game to bring this up. Can't really blame them though.
Don't get me wrong, this game really deserves the praise it gets, but seeing all those 10/10 posts seems a little wrong. It's still a beautiful game with a lot of strengths which overweigh the negative aspects. But we shouldn't forget the shortcomings of a game we like. Let's hope that Larian fixes this in the future and gives us the enhanced edition this game really deserves.

Shadow Warrior is Duke Nukem 3D's younger brother in the sense that both are born from the Build engine. Shadow Warrior achieved far less fame and notoriety, which is a shame because it's at least as good. The graphics and general presentation here have not aged well, but then again I would say the same thing about DN3D. At least thanks to Devolver we can play in more modern resolutions. On the flipside, Lo Wang's oneliners are timeless and the rest of the audio is great as well. But the most memorable thing is probably the level design.
The upside of the level design is that it is great. This was a time before cutscenes and story-based shooters. There is only a bit of narrative here, and all of it is told without words, by the levels. By the environments and how one meshes into the next, a sort of journey emerges. I especially love the detailed interiors that had a lot of work put into them; the atmosphere they convey is superb and many of the houses shown are fully livable and fleshed out, from bathroom to garage. Oh, and fully functioning mirrors, something that eludes most contemporary developers... Across the base campaign and two expansions there is a total of 43 (47 if you count secrets) levels and they are delightfully varied. If you lament the single-player components of modern shooters as too short, this might be a treat.
The downside of the level design is that you'll spend a significant amount of time being stuck. Retracing your steps time and again, looking for that one key or switch that you missed and which is now completely blocking your progress. What's more, back then being stuck was considered content ("you're playing the game aren't you?!"); it was a time before the descent into casualization had begun. If you expect waypoints, onscreen indicators and corridor-shaped levels from your shooters, consider this your stark warning. There are also technical issues that I simply can not defend. Rare (but kinda regular) crashes. Occasional (but severe) graphical glitches. Issues with quicksave/load. Devolver's modernization is playable but could've used some more work. All in all this is a gem but not everyone will have the patience or perspective to appreciate it, and if you don't, I won't blame you.

Yes, but at the same time a big, resounding "no".
Play until you get to level 16 (there are servers dedicated to new players), because unless you're inclined to spend maybe a hundred+ hours on this game getting... "gud" ugh.. it's questionable whether you'll have much fun afterwards.
And here's why:
Much as the combat system is pretty straight forward (swinging your sword + dudes in sword's arc = hurt and bloody dudes) your weapons follow specific routes depending on what kind of weapon and what kind of attack you're making, but these arcs are subject to manipulations by the the player's movement - which is a cool mechanic.
However, some players have found ways to "utilise" this, by contorting their movements to get the most out of a swing - por ejemplo: crouching with their back to you and bending over backwards to effectively overhand-strike you, crotch to head. If that sounds silly to you, it looks even worse... Combining several of these movements into freakish combi, you stand little chance to parry. You will meet many of these players, and you will die in seconds.
This effectively splits up all players into two groups: those that can do this, and those that subscribe to a more dodge/block/parry/riposte-style of classical swordplay: ACTUAL SWORDPLAY.
(Myself included, if that failed to appear evident)
The balancing issues... it's probably what you'd expect. It's like there's zero regulation as to who goes on which team.
It isn't unusual to see one team made up of level 35+ players and the other team having maybe one dude that's over 40, in addition to being outnumbered.
Server lag. It's a thing.
The toxic community!
Rampant taunting, bullying, sexism, and a teaspoon of racism. There 'are' good people playing this game.. usually the ones staying the f*ck away from chat.
Due in part to the game's age, there is a degree of veterancy among the majority of players.
Rough (and biased...) numbers incoming:
90% of the players I meet are lvl 20+
60% of those are above 30
and 20% of those are 40 to max.
These contortionist sadists are those whom you'll face once you exit the confines of the 0-15 servers...
And if I sound salty... it's cus I am.
To sum up...
Pros:
- Intricate combat system
- Chop off your opponents' various limbs
- Multiple match modes (incl. but not limited to: deathmatch, free-for-all, duel, team objective etc.)
- Multiple classes (ranged dude, reach weapons bloke, nimble attack guy, heavy armor bro)
- Customization (somewhat limited without paying)
- Flexible computing requirements (admirably fleshed-out options menu)
- Easy to learn, hard to master
Cons:
- ...VERY hard to master.
- Balancing issues
- Server lag
- The most toxic community I have ever experienced (granted, I've never been on tumblr)
- Surplus of veteran players
Don't get me wrong, I've had tonnes of fun times with this game but that has usually been with friends.
If you do go ahead a try this, by now, very dated game - here's a few tips on Chivalry etiquette:
- NO FEINTING! (despite being an actual combat mechanic, it is heavily frowned upon)
- In duels, it is customary to bow before coming to blows.
- Read the room.
- Some players (usually in free-for-all's) seem content to simply sit in a corner and observe/write in chat... while they are certainly fair-game, expect to face the entire group if you decide to attack.
- In group fights, use overhands or thrusts,  more precise and easier to control; team-kills are a b*tch
And lastly:
- a scrawny archer with a knife can be just as deadly as a plate-clad knight with a battleaxe;
NEVER underestimate your opponent in Chivalry.
(At least not until you become a greatsword-wielding sadistic contortionist yourself.)
If you played D&D for hours on end in college, this game is for you.

-On my brand new Alienware desktop, the game looks pretty dang good. There are a few issues I can mention, but it would only be me nipicking. I'm not a huge stickler for graphics anway.

Cons:

In everyday use and in kinematics, the speed of an object is the magnitude of its velocity (the rate of change of its position); it is thus a scalar quantity.[1] The average speed of an object in an interval of time is the distance travelled by the object divided by the duration of the interval;[2] the instantaneous speed is the limit of the average speed as the duration of the time interval approaches zero.
Speed has the dimensions of distance divided by time. The SI unit of speed is the metre per second, but the most common unit of speed in everyday usage is the kilometre per hour or, in the US and the UK, miles per hour. For air and marine travel the knot is commonly used.
The fastest possible speed at which energy or information can travel, according to special relativity, is the speed of light in a vacuum c = 299792458 metres per second (approximately 1079000000 km/h or 671000000 mph). Matter cannot quite reach the speed of light, as this would require an infinite amount of energy. In relativity physics, the concept of rapidity replaces the classical idea of speed.

Trails in the Sky SC not only equals the original game in terms of storyline, characters, music, battle system, humor, and many other aspects, but improves upon these elements as well. For those of you who have already played the first chapter and enjoyed the experience, you're in for a treat. Get the second chapter--no discussion. If you're a big fan of story-heavy JRPGS with the classic Japanese battle system playstyle but haven't played the first or the second chapter and want to enjoy one of the best if not THE best JRPG series of the decade, then look no further.
The story is deep, rich, and full of surprising plot twists that will take you on an emotional rollercoaster. The characters are unique and interesting, each with their own quirks and way of speaking. EVERY single individual in this game has a personality to them. Even the seemingly unimportant NPCs like farmers, shop keepers, inn managers, etc. Also, a lot of times the music of some games may seem underwhelming when placed in context of a great story. But this is not the case with Trails in the Sky. Falcom did a great job in composing and implementing masterful pieces of music into the game. Each scene, boss bottle, environment,  and conversation have different feelings. And of course, the battle system is what the player is responsible for in the game. Although the thought of another turn-based JRPG may turn you off, don't be fooled. It's not your typical JRPG. Crafts, arts, random buff generator on the side, teamwork, and strategic placement of your squad is essential to ensuring your success in the battles. Overall, the game is extremely well-done in terms of XSEED bringing Trails in the Sky to the international stage. Little to no bugs, English translations that are not only grammatically correct but have life to them. It's truly a masterpiece.
The worst part of my experience playing this game was getting to the end and realizing that it will take another several years before the next game is localized for the English-speaking market. Hopefully this game does well on the international market so it encourages XSEED to think about localizing the 3rd game!!

I'll recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of JRPGs made in the old style, names like Chrono Trigger or Final Fantasy 6. To be perfectly clear, the graphics are nothing to write home about and the combat system is functional and does it's job, while providing a fair degree of customization regarding how you build your characters via the quartz system and its associated buffs/debuffs.
It is the story where the game really shines. There are a lot of NPCs in this game. A mindboggling amount. And most of them have their little stories to follow and something useful to say. The main cast is excellent, with Estelle being an interesting change from the usual 'woe is me' burdened protagonist we've often seen. There isn't much I can say apart from recommending you to at least try it, or the first game. If the characters grow on you, it'll be a game very much worth the 80+ hours you might spend on it.

This is by far my favorite game of all time.  The base game itself is incredible, allowing the player to conduct massive scale battles while at the same time allowing them to zoom in on the detailed action.  The mods make it ten times as fun.  Only in Men of War could you have the German army fight the Empire from Star Wars.  If setting up AI battles isn't for you, there is a great multiplayer with an active player base to participate in.  The best part of Men of War has to be the way the battles are conducted.  No two battles are the same, even if it is the same map and same armies, the AI reacts differently and realistically every time.  Even if a battle is unbalanced, the outgunned team could barely manage a victory.  I personally have seen countless cases where one brave soldier has held off scores of enemies.  Overall, I highly recommend Men of War: Assault Squad 2.  If you are interested in the World Wars, or Real Time Strategy in general, this is the game for you.

The game that you all thought was dead is now back from the dead!
This re-release of the game seems to have removed the copyrighted characters that were found in the last version though this version still has the Mario theme on the piano when placing objects in the "Edit" mode which I assume falls under fair use as it isn't a direct rip of the original sounds but an interpretation of them. There also might be some ripped sound files from Super Mario 64 just with a higher pitch when doing run jumping so this game might be taken down again for copyrighted content.
The game still has the same issues the last version had which I will list below:
-You cannot delete your world from the database once it is uploaded
-You cannot delete your comments once they have been posted
-You cannot delete your replays once they are posted nor can you delete others on your levels
-Some words are still in Chinese
-The game seems to get slightly blurry when making it fullscreen
-Several objects in the game are blurry, mainly the player and NPC's when scaled up
-There seems to be a little mouse input lag, the in-game cursor isn't as precise as it should feel
-The movement of the player character seems slippery and not as precise as you would expect
Suggestions to make the game better:
-Fix everything above
-Fix the horrible hitboxes for the enemy characters
-Continually add new blocks, enemies, and more
-The ability to create underwater levels to mix things up
-The chat blurb system from Mario Maker (Chat bubbles within the levels, including drawings)
-Work on your presentation (Create a Steam Store Page that's actually informative and interesting to read)
-Achievements
-Multiplayer functionality
-Modability
Overall this isn't a bad game but it has its flaws. I'm really hoping the developer behind this actually puts time into improving this game as time moves on, it would be extremely nice to get a decent Mario Maker-like game on the Steam store so part of me is hoping that this isn't a cash grab.
Edit: BoxMaker includes copyrighted sounds from Super Mario 64, the Long Jump from Super Mario 64 is present in BoxMaker but with the speed and pitch shifted up to mask it. The jump in BoxMaker can be accomplished by double tapping left or right and jumping three times in succession. I directly recorded the sound, converted to a .wav file, and altered it in Audacity to try and get it back to the way it originally sounds to make sure it was the actual ripped sound.

Devil daggers is a competitive First Person Shooter where you fight endless enemies whilst fighting on a small arena.  What I mean by competitive is that you are put on leader boards and obviously if you’re on a leader board you’re tempted to get higher.
In the options menu there are a few options; those being the input options with the obvious look sensitivity, keyboard options and you can invert y axis. However you can also adjust what hand you want to shoot with so instead of default which is the right hand you can have it on the left hand. This is an option called flash hand but I’m not sure what that is. You also have the audio option which doesn’t have much but there is a HRTF option which is interesting; what HRTF stands for is head-related transfer function which basically is a response that characterizes how an ear receives a sound from a point of source. And finally you have the video options which has the obvious full screen, FOV and v-sync, nothing too special
You also have a leader boards menu where you can obviously look at other peoples score. Finally in the menu you have the obvious play and exit buttons.
The game play in this game is reminiscent of the touhou project games which are bullet hell type games akin to this one but this isn’t “bullet” hell, this would be considered an enemy hell type game which is a game type where instead of too many bullets there are too many enemies flooding to your location and a genre I just made up also this game isn’t a top down shooter.
The enemies in this game are mainly comprised of bone but there are squid enemies which have tentacles. The enemies in the game consist of skulls, skulls with horns, squid type enemies, spider like enemies, centipede demon, a fortress skull thing which I have yet to face and apparently there is a crab boss but I have not got up to that point. There are two types of enemies which can spawn the skull enemies you first see. Those enemies are the squid which is the very first enemy you see which can spawn skulls and one skull with horns the other enemy is a spider which spawns eggs which will hatch if not taken care of. Also on a side note there are different tiers to the skulls and squid and of course each tier will become stronger and have more health.
There are upgrades in this game which enable you to do more damage but the final upgrade allows for homing bullets. There are also 2 secrets in this game.
Overall this game is a great hell game, it’s similar to dark souls in the difficulty sense but I can defiantly say this is much harder because it is endless. So in conclusion it’s a great game with great pixel graphics which is why I give this a 7/10.

David Lynch's "Twin Peaks" meets the Lucas Arts classic "Full Throttle" meets Beckett's "Waiting for Godot" meets an ingenous DIY play texture with a rich and carefully plotted story. This game MUST be played with headphones, in the dark, with utter concentration. "Kentucky Route Zero" is not taxing in the twitchy way you might experience a FPS, it's an engrossing and whole body experience; by the time you're done with the story's third act, you'll be exhaling cold, damp cave air. A wonderful game that — for enjoyment — requires attention to details and an open mind. What sets this one apart, is that KR-0 will not provide you with obvious feedback. There's no health bar, for example. The 2D map (a central interface in the first part of the story) is somewhat unreliable and appears, at times, to be working against you. And, well, things get sort of meta-exploratory from there. Open mind, I said.
Oh, and Junebug, Junebug, Junebug.

I love Chiv. It's a great game. But it's only good for so long.
See, the thing is, there's an enforced ranking system. The only servers on which rank actually matters on are the 0-15 servers, everything else is 'any'. Once you get past level 15, you're not allowed on the low-rank server (which are the most populous servers, coincidentally) and are forced to play on the 'any' servers.
I mean no disrespect to Torn Banner, but the only people who regularly play Chiv to the point of gitting gud are exploiters. Not hackers, exploiters. The engine that handles the swordplay is highly abusable. Crouching and staring at the sky allows you to instantly throw an overhand swing. The same goes for crouching and staring at the ground. There are many more that're worth listing, but this review is already dragging on.
It's a hell of a lot of fun while it lasts. Fair fights feel like you're actually there, actually in the boots of your character, actually swinging your actual sword.
After ranking up, it feels like a game of 'who can break the engine faster'. I don't like that game.

Above all, the story is at times mystery and morbid and heartwarming, and it works.

Sometimes when you're flying through space you end up meeting a robot. Sometimes that robot is wearing a dress and rides a motorcycle with another robot. Sometimes that robot plays the keytar and likes to sing in dive bars. Sometimes that robot knows the entire history and future of the world in which you live. Sometimes that robot is Lieutenant Commander Data. These scientificially observed facts are called Scalzi's laws of robotics. A robot can only be one of those four things. Kentucky Route Zero is a game that explores what it might mean for the laws of robotics to be slightly relaxed (not unlike how Star Trek slightly relaxes the intergalactic speed limit), allowing a robot to be multiple types of robot at the same time. That's right, in Kentucky Route Zero, Lieutenant Commander Data puts on a dress, picks up a keytar and plans your destiny from his dive bar. This is a wonderful game that really makes you think about the universe and doesn't contain any disturbing skeletons.

I just finished the game, and I really wanted to write a review on it. After playing SC, I can see why FC and SC are split into two parts, and that both are worth getting. I've been following XSEED on their development on translating SC and they weren't kidding about the script size. It's huge and plays a huge factor on why this game is so good.
SC (Second Chapter) is significantly darker than FC (First Chapter) in many respects, but still maintained a light tone throughout. I mean, it goes deeper into the overarching group Ouroboros and explains a lot of the things which FC doesn't.
Comparing with other JRPGs, the most unique thing about Legend of Heroes is the parallel storylines that takes place throughout the entire series. Most of the NPCs have their own storyline that runs in parallel with the main story, and sometimes they overlap and change the scripting around based on the actions our heroes take throughout the game. So, while the game can technically be rushed, the full magnitude of the world of Liberal can be appreciated simply by talking to each NPC after completing each milestone. It's a tedius process but it's very very worth it. It brings so much life to the game, it's actually really impressive with the amount of detail they went into the scripting. I can go on and on with examples, lets just say pretty much nearly every NPC with a name has a story one way or another! I would get this game just because of that! And after starting a new game+, not only does all of the main characters have this nostalgic feeling to them, even the NPCs have a nostalgic feeling... something I do not normally get from other games.
While SC was significantly darker than FC, both FC and SC stayed very true to oldschool JRPGs. The style, the character development and the unravelling of the main antagonists and twists. The progression and the fact that there's already a diverging storyline early on in the game makes the game have replay value. I honestly did not expect the game to be this thorough, something that I find to be lacking in more modern rpgs. Most playable characters have so many ties to the world and from it there is a great deal of character development throughout the series. Every character was unique and enjoyable. The plot turns in the story was also very good, the cutscenes are great and there were a lot of funny moments. Olivier is my favourite character in the series =P.
There are also side quirks in the game, like gambling, fishing, and cooking which all ties with how the scripting is handled in the world at various times. They also help you in same way as well so there is incentive to work on them. There are also bracer points to maximize, which gives you reward items and scripting changes as well. There are some puzzles in the game, however they are not an integral part of the game.
The music is fantastic. The battle system is great, with some battles being very difficult, especially near the end! The customization with the orbments gives some unique tactics throughout the game. Every character also has their own unique S crafts and weapons, which brings additional flavour to how each battle is played out. One major difference between SC and FC are that there are interchangeable characters throughout most of the story, meaning that you can pick, from a group of characters, 4 to take with you to progress the story. This changes the scripting based on what characters you choose, and adds to the replay value to the game.
While the graphics is a bit lacking compared with modernized RPGs, I must say it adds to the nostalgic touch to the game. However some might enjoy this because it allows room for the imagination to fill in the gaps. The cutscenes/fight scenes are still very good.  And honestly, albeit the lack of graphics, how Falcom made use of it still captivated me throughout.
What can I say, I banked a good 110 hours on this game and that's just online. Looking at some other recommendations some of them banked 200 hours even! As far as the bang for the buck for an RPG is concerned, this game is pretty much worth it, as currently I am paying ~30 cents per hour for the game, and I suspect this number to decrease after this review is published. Most other JRPGs I would expect aronud 50-70 hour play time.
Buy this game, not only because it's good, but also if you also want to support more JPRGs that focuses more on the storyline/character development itself! Also, SC practically one-upped FC in so many ways as well, so if you liked FC then be prepared for a treat!

The downside to this game is that the engine has always felt a little clunky. It simply lacks the "smoothness" you get in some other similar war RTS games. But on the flip side you can do much more with the units in the MOW series. Your troops can pick up inventory off enemy troops -- so they aren't just pre-built - if you want a flamethrower guy or to stea; an enemy tank you just make do with what's on the field. Overall a fun game but it has its flaws which for me are mostly in the engine itself.

The Trails in the Sky duology are the best RPGs of all time.
If you want to get lost in a the purest jRPG experience, then this is the game for you.  No, I am not talking about lame anime trope nonsense like tsunderes, schoolgirls, or any of that garbage. I am talking about: well-writen characters that provide fun dialogue, an insanely deep storyline that keeps you entertained all the way through, and a plot that ties between both games smoothly while wrapping up nicely.
I wish I can tell you how great the stories and characters are without spoiling any of it but it's just something you have to play for yourself. Otherwise, you wouldn't be able to enjoy it to the fullest.
It's a masterfully crafted video game and we are blessed to have the best localization possible thanks to XSEED.
Battle-wise, it's easily one of the greatest turn-based combat systems out there because of how fun your strategic options are. Position is important for optimal plays, buffing allies actually makes a difference rather than being a minor nusiance and the same goes for debuffing. And lastly, its customization option makes anyone and everyone a fun and viable character. Everyone has a place in the party, in terms of both the story and party composition. Unfortunately, the battle speed IS a bit on the slow side but that shouldn't turn you off completely.
In terms of content, this is by no means a grinding game. I spent 87 hours on this game and this was all for the story, doing sidequests, and exploring every nook and cranny for all of the possible secrets in the game. All of those hours spent was pure fun and not because I was grinding my characters up, getting lost in a dungeon, or retrying difficult boss fights over and over again. But that's just me being crazy in love with this game, anyone else can beat it in probably even half the time if you really wanted to.
Like I said, this is one of the best jRPGs of all time. It shares a lot of good traits as Xenoblade Chronicles so if you've played that, then you'd love the Trails duo. Please give this game a try or recommend it to a friend so we can support XSEED, Falcom, and more masterpieces like these coming over to us!

Ok....maybe I should actually write a serious review for a game for once...maybe...

The Legend of Heroes: Trails in the Sky Second Chapter is a turn based strategy JRPG set in Liberl Kingdom, a smaller country in Zemuria (the continent that the Trails franchise is set in). SC is the second game of the series set in Liberl, so play the First Chapter first. You play as Estelle (yes, a female protagonist, and most definitely best one I have ever seen) just like in FC.
This game paints one of the most developed fantasy worlds ever. Unique geopolitcs, history, resource production areas, pop culture, underground groups, etc all bundled into one game.
The character interaction is stellar. I love watching the characters go through their struggles together, and learn from their interactions with one another. The NPCs all have their own story. They don't seem like just NPCs, but people that actually have a life and don't rely on the player characters so much to do everything. They travel around and react to different situations in the game. The villians have their own reasons to be the villian and not just "because lel"
In other words, people actually act like people instead of random anime tropes.
The gameplay is pretty good. The battle screen uses a grid based system, where positioning matters. Staying close together increases your chances of taking AOE damage, but makes healing and buffing easier. The orbment system allows you to customize what your characters do... especially people like Estelle who have balanced orbment slot setup. Art casters (magic casters) became more balanced vs taking physical attackers than in FC, which were generally less powerful than art casters. Sidequests don't seem repetitive (except a very certain thief), and can range from monster hunting to helping a guy impress a girl by keeping sober while drinking lots of alcohol... (don't ask.) The most important part of the sidequests is not the content, but that the sidequests

I have only played an hour of this game and I have to say I am enjoying it a lot. Devil Daggers is as the description says : a 90's themed, bare bones FPS arena shooter (Quite Literally an arena shooter). The way I see this game is as an endless runner. Survive for as long as possible in a simple arena. As you progress in time, so does the difficulty of enemies. As I am experienced in Arena Shooters, it did not take me long to understand how the game works as well as its mechanics. So is it worth buying this game if there is so little content. Yes it is. Why ? Because the developers of this game have put effort into making the game so fluid and responsive. The enemy variety is also a big plus.
Do not be fooled by the games simplicity however. Without all the fancy things being an issue, this game is brutally unforgiving. It forces you to be extremely twitchy, always on the move, always listening for sound of wails behind you and around you. One mistake could cost you your life and your run. But with every try, you gain more knowledge and more skill and because of its endless runner style, you will always be stuck in that phase of 'oh just one more go and I can beat my score'. Arena shooter veterans and fans, I highly recommend this game to you. You will enjoy the living hell out of it. I still recommend it to everyone, but then again not everyone is good at arena FPS. With such a low price like this, there is no reason to pass this game up.

Devil Daggers is a nightmare that I keep coming back to. It’s demanding and frightening – an intensely difficult first-person arena shooter set in some forgotten circle of hell, where survival happens only a handful of seconds at a time and death is constantly looming over your shoulder. But it’s also exhilarating, a frantic high-score chaser that buries hours of rewarding playtime deep within its punishing core for only the most determined players to claw out.
Devil Daggers grounds itself in the look and feel of old-school PC shooters of the ‘90s like DOOM and Quake, then strips the experience down into its purest elements and drops you in without explanation. There are no weapons to pick up, no armor, and besides collectible crystals that power up your dagger shots in tiers, there are no items whatsoever. There are no stats to increase and no levels to beat, either. It’s just you, the daggers that inexplicably fire from your outstretched fingers, and an endless legion of hellspawn battling it out in a dark arena for as long as your skill can carry you, which probably won’t be that long.
Trying, failing, and trying again is a particularly brutal process in that abyss, where there’s always some new monstrosity threatening to cut your latest attempt short. Hordes of floating skulls and disembodied demon heads spew out of tentacled behemoths, mindlessly giving chase while increasingly grotesque beasts spawn from all sides until the mobs become too overwhelming to fend off any longer.
With the amount of intensity packed into a single second of gameplay, even a one-minute run can feel like an eternity. The relentless thrill of blasting baddies and the smooth transition between the game over screen and a fresh start (tapping R instantly resets it at any time) make it easy to get sucked in, losing entire hours to the black hole of “just one more try.”

As simple as Devil Daggers’ run-and-gun routine may seem, there’s enough technical detail to make exploring and exploiting its various systems one chaotic hell of a good time. Unlike other twitchy, reflex-based games from recent memory, this one doesn’t spawn your opponents randomly. It might be hard to believe at first, but there’s a consistent order to the waves of enemies that appear. As I played more and more, I grew accustomed to the exact conditions and exact timing of moves that I needed to pull off before the next sequence began.
If I didn’t have all four skull spawners from the first wave destroyed by the time the first spider shows up, I’d inevitably find myself over-encumbered by the next wave of upgraded spawners. If I didn’t take the spider out immediately after the first centipede spawns, I’d lose all the centipede’s crystals to the spider’s gem-converting powers and have dozens of critter-spewing egg sacs to deal with. Every single error compounds on each other, making things exponentially difficult going forward and adding intense levels of urgency to your every move. Memorizing and maintaining a mental checklist of pixel-perfect motions isn’t necessary to have a good time shooting down demons, but it does make every run feel like a puzzle that I grow closer to understanding each time I return to it.
There are certain games that the speedrunning community has spent ages chipping away at, learning how to exploit weak spots in their code and defy their boundaries, but also working within their restraints to pull off seemingly impossible gaming feats. Devil Daggers feels like a tribute to that spirit, a throwback to a time when games were simple and uncluttered (but not shallow) and completely unapologetic about their intense difficulty.
The faithfulness with which it adapts these principles makes Devil Daggers more than just a retro-for-no-reason gimmick that slaps on the unfiltered textures of old games as a cheap nostalgia trip. It earns its low-detail art direction because it also has the appropriate playstyle to boot.

Despite the apparent simplicity of the controls and your abilities, there are plenty of ways to stay a step ahead of your enemies. Fluid movement physics allow ample opportunity for mastering new techniques in speed and agility: bunnyhopping to gain a slight boost in speed became a near-constant necessity as I wove my way around deadly spawners, leading swarms of skulls around the arena until I could take them all out with a good clean side shot.
The Devil Daggers equivalent of rocket jumping (firing a shotgun-like blast of daggers into the floor mid-leap) let me soar over my pursuers, adding some Z-axis movement to the featureless circular arena. Staying on the move is vital, so it’s a huge plus to have smooth controls that make pulling off these quick and cool moves feel great. Your failures will never result from your character not moving or jumping how you told it to. And naturally, you can rebind keys, invert the y-axis, switch to left-handed mode, and adjust your look sensitivity in the options menu for added comfort.
There are only two ways to use your dagger shots to destroy enemies, but the lack of variety becomes more of an interesting gameplay restraint than something unfairly limiting. Holding down left-click shoots a steady, machine gun-like stream of daggers great for precision aiming, while tapping left-click fires off a shotgun-like blast for dealing with close-range threats. Both firing modes become more powerful after collecting 10 crystals, and then again after collecting 75 crystals, but they don’t change beyond that. Finding the right ways to make such a standard weapon work in the increasingly chaotic realm of Devil Daggers is part of the fun.
This is especially true in the way this means of attack interacts with the way different enemies move through the arena, and the way the locations of their weak spots affect how you move through it as well. While your typical floating skull can be taken out with one shot, the horned ones take a few direct hits – or one slower shotgun blast – to kill. Other threats, like spawners and spiders, have to be shot in their weak spots (clearly marked by those coveted red crystals), creating tricky situational challenges.
Devil Daggers also puts its incredible sound design to practical use. In lieu of a soundtrack, every enemy’s unique, continuous noise – from the cackling of the skulls to the insectoid click of giant spider legs – combines over time into a rising chorus of Hell. The more crowded the arena gets, the louder and more intense it becomes. This chilling cacophony doubles as a warning system for your impending doom, a signal to step up your efforts to cull the herd or change your priorities to deal with a new threat. Distinct and deliberate sound design makes it possible to know which enemies are where without even having to look – a clean way to work around the restraints that come with an arena shooter that’s first-person, rather than top-down. Spatial awareness and mob management are required for survival, and Devil Daggers’ combination of fluid movement and utilitarian sound design acknowledges both beautifully.

Devil Daggers’ stripped-down and distilled essence of first-person shooter intensity will take up a lot of my time in the weeks to come. Every second longer that I survive in its hellish arena is a new record for myself to break, over and over again. It’s a brutal, but brilliant shooter that finds strength in its minimalism, stretching a few seconds of action here and there into endless hours of dreadful fun.

This is just a collection of jigsaw puzzles, nothing more, presented in a very bad way.
The creatures you see on the screenshots, walks around automatically, you cannot control her. She walks a few steps, a jigsaw puzzle starts, solve it and she walks a few more steps, then next puzzle. Over and over again.
You have to start with very easy puzzles, that gradually (slowly) increase in "difficulty", aka more pieces per puzzle. In other words, if you want to begin with a large amount of pieces, it's not possilbe. At least to the point where I stopped playing, there is nothing else to it but more pieces. Maybe rotations later, I don't know.
The pictures you assemble, are ugly landscapes, made even uglier by the terrible resolution. Since they're so ugly, and since there are piece outlines in every puzzle, you will often use the outlines instead of studying the image to find out where a piece goes. And btw, the no-rotation + piece outlines makes this a VERY easy game. Since that's forced, it's a very bad thing.
A good puzzle game needs features like choosing image and amount of pieces, ability to turn both pieces outlines and rotation on and off, and using custom images. This game has NO OPTIONS at all.
Even though it's cheap as dirt, I would have requested a refund if I could, but it doesn't seem I can for this product, though. Both because I don't support this kind of lazyness from a dev, but also to completely delete it from my library.
This is NOT a game I recommend, even if it was completely free.

If I had to describe Divinity: Original Sin 2 in a word, that would be it.
Without a doubt, it’s the best modern cRPG game up to date. And as an oldschool gamer, I can understand when someone is saying that nothing can stand in one line with games like Planescape: Torment or Baldur’s Gate. Well, it couldn’t. Until now. Times changing, and so gaming industry is changing.
It has to be said, even if we are sentimental.
The world of Divinity: Original Sin 2 is full of content and what’s the best,
There are no boring NPC’s with exactly the same dialogue lines. In this game everyone is unique and has something to say. Also, we are talking here about huge cRPG game that is
(!) and it’s not Oblivion-like voice acting with 5 actors. The main narrator, who is with us most of the time, and all the other voice actors, did an outstanding job here. Every character sounds special.
If you have played first Original Sin you know what to expect from fights. They can be approached in many different ways. Even in tough fights, one properly used scroll or skill can change everything. Of course in both ways, because we can easily lose.
Comparing to other cRPG games it’s one of the best parts of Divinity.
It took me roughly
to finish the game once, so it can be said that Divinity: Original Sin 2 is one of the biggest cRPG games.
Every character has its own personality and its own origin story. By playing with different characters we have new quests and we can approach many situations in totally different way – origin characters have their own interactions across whole game. The main story is interesting and I have never lost my interest. I don’t want to spoil anything, but it’s just really good piece of writing. Side quests are keeping high level as well. Same as in first Original Sin, we also receive minimal amount of help in all the quests.
I have completed this game few days ago and to be honest, I can’t wait to play it again. I am thinking about new characters and about making different decisions in several points of the game. It’s something amazing. There are many huge games, like The Witcher 3 or Fallout 4 that can give you +/- 100 hours of actual playtime, but those are mostly single experience games. You are not playing them again.
In Civilization series we are saying about “one more turn” syndrome. Here we have “one more hour”, “one more evening” and “one more day syndrome”!
The game is quite fresh, so there are still bugs. I haven’t experienced any gamebreaking bug though, but there are many small things that for sure will be fixed in the future. What’s more, the final act and final battle are both the weakest parts of the game. You can feel that devs were in hurry here, but on the other side, whole game is so good, that
It simply can’t.
Divinity: Original Sin 2 is, in my humble opinion, the best game of year 2017. Let’s just hope we will see more cRPG’s like this in the future (Obsidian, we are looking at you).

A haunting, beautiful episodic game (3 of 5 episodes which are available at present, kickstarted). The game starts off with a a lost deliveryman's request for directions to the highway; where it goes from there is anyone's guess. Conversations are branching though inexorable, and I found myself constructing a narrative for each character that evolved organically over time (e.g. role playing in an adventure game).
The story and characters are perhaps this game's strongest suite, and the art style is both minimalist and highly expressive. On a personal note, it is simply unlike anything else I have played, and tends to evoke a powerful sensation of longing and cheerful melancholy that I've simply not expressed in any other media.
Gameplay is limited (point and click), so if this is a major criteria for your enjoyment of a game Kentucky Route Zero may not be for you. However, If you enjoy a strong narrative, highly stylized art, and are looking for something a bit different,  I strongly recommend this game.

Shadow Warrior Classic Redux is the complete old-skool first-person shooter.  Forget the story.  Forget the graphics.  These were the sorts of games where it was all about the gameplay.  Theres lots of short fast-paced levels to explore.  Discover obvious and not so obvious secrets.  Massive amounts of relentless combat to enjoy. Including a large arsenal of weapons with which to gib an assortment of enemies with.  Periodically tough bosses stand in your way to be defeated.
Its clunky graphics may be outdated and the game speed a little too fast unless you're too young not to have played this the first time around but, the un-PC nature of the voiceover is hilarious and will make you laugh-out-loud.  Those of you who dont enjoy single-player need to push aside their PvP addiction and just try it.  If you feel the need for some old-skool Lo-Wan style kickassery then you cant do worse than start with this.  Sure there is a modern day version but this game still reeks of fun.
Retro FPS at its finest.  Holy cow!!!
Retro FPS.
Fictonal martial-arts themed universe where corporations run the world.  With weapons.... lots of weapons.
You are Lo-wan a shadow warrior.  A one man army of unparalleled skill and destruction.  At least thats what the store page says.  You goal is to clear the levels and finally defeat the evil Lord Zilla.
Old-skool style single-player FPS.  Contains all three episodes of around fifty levels.
OLD-SKOOL
+ Old skool layouts that are lean and mean.  Very few areas that serve none or little purpose.
+ Levels are themed differently to provide variety.
+/- Find keys to open locked areas.  Allowing you to access parts of levels when they are opened up.
- Design factors/elements are few and therefore some left or parts thereof will eventually feel the same.
GOOD
+ Fast-paced gameplay from a by-gone age.
+ Large inventory for ten weapons and a half-dozen special items.
+ Lots of gear and ammo to pick up means you can go all rambo or choose your shots.
+ Marvellous amounts of gibbing your enemies.
+ A few levels have vehicles & gun emplacements to mix-up how you deal with your foes.
+/- Secrets can be fun for the first few levels but can get boring.  If you like me cant see a secret for toffee there is a function that displays how many secrets you have still to find for that level.
- There are a very few locations that need finger-twisting difficulty to jump to the next transistion point.  Very difficult with keyboard if you arent adept.
- Its old-skool strafing
GOOD
+ Around fifteen different types of enemy provide decent variety.
+ The best ones are the Sumos that fart deadly gases when dead.
+ The worst are the explosive carrying kamikazes who come back to life as ghosts when they die.
- None of them are deadly and can be overcome with ease.

+/- A.I. is as old-skool as the game.  Basic brute-force design means the enemys only concern is to patrol is designated area and shoot when it "sees" you.
+ Aiming however is top notch and thus unless you have very fast reflexes you will take some damage in almost every encounter.  Meaning there is a challenge in playing the game.

+ Original PC controls have been brought along and kept at the required level for us PC users.
+ Customizable interface allowing max equipment/inventory info can be displayed.  Or minimal if you prefer to see
OLD-SKOOL
- Bad if you're into modern day graphics.  Even if they are completely remastered.
+ Great if you love blocky old-skool graphics. Played at 1920x1080 fullscreen with 400+ fps at all times. Not many games you can say that about. :)
VERY GOOD
+/- Good old-skool midi sounds, but its the voice-over dialagoue thats thats the star.
+ Lo pan's non-PC regulated one-liners are a throwback to the 80s and will make you smile even after hearing them for the 100th time!
FAIRLY EASY
+/- It has several difficulty levels.  My play through was on 2nd toughest which provided a decent challenge for the most part and a few areas that taxed my skills.  Who wants wang!?
GOOD
+ A mixture of level completions, perform x tasks Straightforward if 25% are not so fast to collect.
OKAY
- Mostly has limited appeal.
+ Fans of nostalgia or old skool FPS.
OKAY
+ Theres a good 15h+ to complete all levels.  More if you dont get the achievements or find all the secrets for each level.
+ If you enjoy replaying levels, they are quite short and use a formula that you will pick-up once youve played a few levels.
NONE
+/- Its single-player only so no community interaction.
+ A few die-hards still post in the forum if you need help with running the game.
GREAT
+ Given its age, will work a dream on any modern system.  Even my Core i3 was getting 400 fps!
- May be too fast for some older players! :P
- Crashes from time to time.
+ Will prompt for a report to be sent to the devs and restarts the game automatically.
GOOD
+ All "expansions" from the old-skool original are included.
+ For such an old game the devs who made this compatible with modern system deserve a nod.
+/- Doubt there are any plans for patching but I guess support is not quite abandoned by the developers.
MINIMAL
- Gamespeed was to fast for my tired reflexes.  Only due to the aging game engine and my "modern" spec PC.  If you cant compenstate you, can try one of those CPU-slowing utilities.
- Only stability issue was if I pressed Quickload key twice to fast.  Instant CTD.  Annoying but not gamebreaking.
OKAY
- Not sure if even the most retro-loving gamer would get this at full price.
- There are better FPSs out there, even if most are politically correct.
+ Worth it on sale.  Especially if you are a fan of the franchise.

Gear Up is a very promising f2p shooter aiming to claim the best elements of some other contenders of this genre.
Its sort of like Robocraft and TF2 had a baby.
The games biggest strength is the customization and the many purchaseable parts you can gear up your tank with. Progressing is easy, parts can be unlocked at a very decent rate which is pretty nice since games of this kind tend to make you grind for hours for getting those so desired pieces of equipment. The game offers very fun ways to blast your opponents into pieces, want a wall climbing double barrelled heavy sniper tank, a lightning fast rocketspewing hovercraft, a slimeballsteering machinegunned killing machine? All is up to your taste in Gear Up!
The game does however have some flaws which you should be aware of. Currently the greatest problem of the game is that it has very few players which potentionally limits your options when you want to decide what gamemode you'd like to play also, though parts are pretty easy to unlock non-premium users have a hefty limit on how many parts they can own at the same time and have only one tank slot(you can rebuild your robot in game if you'd like so basically all the premium feature does is to save you some time) which is pretty embarrasing at times. Leveling up does grant you additional inventory space for parts so after you are into the game for a lil' while it becomes less and less of an annoyance. The game has a lot of room to improve on this level and the developers seem really nice so Im certain that the game is going to progress a great lot in this section.
Performance wise it is clear that we are playing a new title. Optimization updates are released frequently to help lower end PC players also enjoy this wonderful game.I have had some occasional crashes though but nothing too great of a negative impact. Even if i DCd i just relaunched the game and hopped right back in the match i've been playing(saying a quick farewell to my score.Won anyway) The Graphics are cartoony but solid and on higher settings the game is surprisingly good looking.
Judgement:
Gear Up! is a great lot of fun, especially if you have some friends to play with. Its easy to learn and has lots of room for customization and experimenting with weapons. Altough thegame has a lot more contentwholes to fill.Weapon balance is something to be worked on and im hoping that the game will let lose of its current premium features and comes up with something that is not based upon "if you pay you can have your cutdown legs back". Currently it has the basic gamemodes(TDM,DM,capture and hold...etc) but clearly if a game like this wants to grow big they need that little extra to really set themselves apert from the lot. Gear Up has that potential and i highly reccommend you trying it.

Recommended for fans of Duke Nukem 3D and its Build engine. If you were a fan of Blood, this game lacks of weapon precision plus enemy movement smoothness. Better than DN but worst than Blood, which made a far better use of Ken Silverman's Build.
The character is indeed the american-asian version of Duke. With a mouth full of cliches, being himself one. It's a fast paced game as were all shooters for the era. The level design is good and not repetitive, but unfortunatelly the enemy movement is not smooth and the precision isn't any better either, so until you have a good control of the keys you'll be shooting to the walls even if the enemies are 3 meters away and moving perpendicular to your sight. Explosive kamikazes round the corner can be exasperating too, forcing you to reload after being killed by a type of enemy that, well, shouldn't exist.
Apart of these two bad things all other are positive: Agile game with beautiful levels, challenge everywhere, humour, a good tactical experience (but only from afar) with well settled enemies that will hide when possible, conventional and exotic weapons, tons of secrets and huge final bosses. The two expansions kept the same freshness and fit very well, giving the whole product integrity. The experience won't be ruined by unbalanced changes. After ending the main pack if you liked Shadow Warrior so far, you won't leave Wanton Destruction or Twin Dragon unfinished.
If you liked DN, you have to try this one. If you enjoyed Blood the flaws on Shadow Warrior will be evident, but will be still enjoyable. It could be better with slight changes, but overall is a decent game which was even better in the time. The openGL does its job by adding the real mouselook, so you don't need to rely on autoaim.

Don't get me wrong. I dont like Free2Play games, or pay2win for that matter. I'm not really into these random indie games either, but a friend was playing it and I asked how it went. I was told try it. So I did.
Minimal download of 700MB. The graphics are simplistic and detailed, yet cartoonish like TF2. My 660ti powers through it at ultra settings on a 1900x1200 display. I would imagine it'd run acceptabbly well on some low-ended machines.
Game play? Have you ever played Unreal Tournament (2003/2004/UT3) or TF2? You'll catch on quickly.
Three modes: Hold the point, Team DM, and DM/FFA. All are self explanitory once you start playing.
Physics IS used in this game. Dont expect some top-heavy tank build to not roll over. It will!
Who wouldnt want a spider tank? This alone is incredibly amazing for the vomit inducing disorientation using it makes. Hanging up-side-down while popping off a few tanks is quite impressive.
I was surprised when I was rewarded for playing a match with XP and Credits/Crowns despite loosing the match. You're not forced to be a try-hard. Even the casual can get in and have some fun.
Now some Cons:
-No single player or Tutorials. It's all trial by fire.
-UI needs a bit more work when building your tank.
-Need explinations of each part and how they fit together.
-Crashes fatally after a few rounds with a runtime problem. I hope they fix this.
-8 maps. They get old fast.
-Premium purchase gives you 100% unlocks. Meh...
-Flame weapons are brutal
-Maps are too small and too much water!
Final thoughts:
It's a really well ballenced game. I was amazed how I was able to hop in within the first thirty seconds of the game and start blowing things up with the starter tank. Even besting the more veteran players with well placed shots and kill stealing (Oops, did I just say that?).
You can purchase the "Premium" package. While I do NOT recommend this as it gives you no sense of achivement, it does however, not in any way give you "God Mode". No pay to win here maggots! I recommend you just earn the creds to buy the parts and buy the Basic package.

So this game is INCREDIBLY fun. First off: It's a sidescrolling MOBA. On the surface, Awesomnauts isn't very SRS BIDNESS. It has a rather nice roster of characters, and each has items you can buy from the store for it with currency you get from killing things. There is no effective "Levelling". Each level that it says, is actually how much gold you've earned. 100 is 1 lvl. Your characters' two skills are purchased in the shop, and once purchased, you can then purchase up to three upgrades out of six possible for each ability, and then three to upgrade basic attacks (passives are often lumped in) and then three upgrades for positive character buffs, like making CC effect you less, increasing your movement capabilities, Some can heal by collecting money, that kind of thing. After each game you gain exp to level, and each level grants you more and more possible upgrades to purchase in a game. Other than this system, there is no way to gain extra statistics to use in matches, and all purchasables are cosmetic. Due to simplified systems of the game, there is a rather large amount of skill and co-operation involved with actually getting somewhere. Both teams can pick the same characters, but your teammates cannot pick the same character as you within a match. I think that's about all? But I really enjoyed it, and you should definately give it a go, especially if you find it onsale. I rate a solid: 8.5/10

I love me some history and alternative history, and especially Norse history and mythology. I was skeptical about this game, but to me, it's a gem.
The lore and details in the game are very enjoyable, and the RPG aspect is fulfilling. It can be brutal at times, but Viking life isn't a pony camp. You break a leg, you're in for a rough ride. That's why any battle feels intense and not another mob slaughter. You can get permanently injured, which I like a lot
The timer is brilliant as well. There's a storyline here which tries to immerse you. Without a timer, you're just playing another RPG. There's plenty of open world RPG's out there, this isn't it. This is more of a historical tactical RPG.
One negative point on the combat though: there should be a bit more defensive options. Early medieval battle was brutal, yes, but sometimes it feels that every attack will hit, so positioning your men is crucial. But you can't position them defensively enough in my experience. That, or I'm just not good enough yet :p
Either way: brilliant game. If you let yourself get lost in early Viking age life, this is a great ride. Yes, there is room for improvement, but I dare you to find another game that's as historically correct ànd fun to play as this one (when it comes to the Viking age).
Recommended!

Where to begin?
Men of War: Assault Squad 2, I’ll just call it MOWAS2, is the Arma of strategy games. Seems a little far-fetched at first, but there are some amazing parallels in between the two series. Decent single player campaign that gives you a good idea of what you are doing, multiplayer that’s relatively active, editor that can pretty much be your game if you learn how to use it, and a workshop page that is incredibly active.
I love the game, as you can see by my 600+ hours, but the fact is that it isn’t for everyone.
The average multiplayer gamer won’t stick around forever for a good bit of reasons. The first being that the game modes are lacking to a certain degree. The game modes of multiplayer, just as any other game, get tiring after a while. Most multiplayer games end up in the same regard with the process of first contact->offensive->counter-offensive->repeat several times-> someone comes out as the winner. The game still has some balance issues regarding multiplayer, and the average gamer probably will be indifferent to the multiplayer overall. If you love WWII stuff to a certain degree, you will probably find multiplayer to be pretty fun, with the gameplay being more accurate rather than balanced.
Single player gamers can enjoy the campaign, but only so much. There are 5 sides, each with at least 8 missions, all with the premise centering around a modified multiplayer game mode, particularly the famous assault zones. The battles are spectacular at first, but the more you play the more you realize each mission is just reissued to another setting under another name. It gets boring after a while, but that is what the editor is for!
If you have a good amount of spare time, take it and figure out how to use the editor. About 80 percent of the time im playing this game, it’s on the editor simply because of how limitless it is. With the scale of the game being so large, you can recreate the actual entire battle of Bastogne if you wanted to. And with the mods that the workshop can bring, it just makes the game all that much better.
The actual gameplay is pretty f****** amazing. Again, people who are particularly invested in WWII games will appreciate this game more than the average strategy player. Then again, this is an epic strategy in scale, so the average strategy player will appreciate the MAJORITY User Interface.
The A.I. and micromanaging within the game is a slightly different story.
Each little infantryman has his own little inventory, name, kill count, and even a counter for how much combat he has seen (veterancy). But, managing this feature when it comes to a battle with 1000 men on the field is tough. This can come in to play particularly when repairing field equipment and vehicles. If you have a downed tank in the middle of a battlefield that can be repaired, it is a NIGHTMARE to repair said tank. You have to take a man, go up to the tank, look in its inventory, grab the repair kit, and then you can start repairing it. It sounds like a little issue, but the venerability that the infantryman owns when repairing that tank is very high, and the height of it comes when he tries to grab the repair kit. There are only a few little issues like this in the game. The A.I. can be bad at times, but doesn’t that just apply to most strategy games in general?
I have almost nothing bad to say about the graphics, pretty amazing in general. You will need a big computer to play this game at a normal pace. For how amazingly big the game is, the graphics surprisingly go beyond what you would expect in an Epic-RTS.
For those who love WWII games, strategy, and creating missions in editors (ex. Age of Empires) I encourage you to click that add to cart button.
For those who like strategy RTS games like Age of Empires and Command and Conquer, this is a little more complicated than the average RTS, but it can be fun once you get used to it.
For those who have never played any game in any category I mentioned, I really don’t know why you’re even reading my review, lol.
