Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is a multiplayer-focused hack and slash developed by Torn Banner Studios as their first commercial title. The game is set in a fictional world resembling the Middle Ages and offers similar gameplay combat to the developer's previously released Half-Life 2 mod, Age of Chivalry. On September 20, 2012, a trailer was released which set the release date to October 16, 2012. The developers had confirmed that the game would be PC exclusive initially, but in October 2014, they confirmed that the game would be coming to PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 in December 2014. A standalone expansion pack called Chivalry: Deadliest Warrior was announced on August 23, 2013 as a tie-in for the television series Deadliest Warrior.It was released on November 14, 2013.

I'll split this into pro and contra and try to explain my negative aspects. The pro will be shorter because they don't need explanation.
The game is not for everyone. Many however will still like it. So if you are considering a buy, read the below points and ask yourself if they are important for you.
I am a completionist. I tend to explore every nook and cranny and I like to manage equipment and skills in RPG's. I'm an old school RPG lover, always comparing classical RPG's to giants like Icewind Dale or Neverwinter Nights 2.
Pro
- Much heart was put into this project. There is love for detail which can be especially well seen in the area design and side quests.
- The music is, like in it's predecessor awesome.
- The diversity of spells and skills is impressive
- there are many secrets, hidden areas and treasure to be found everywhere
- The first act feels like the last game, it has a clear goal, you get a big area with sub areas to explore
- There are difficulty settings to adjust for different playstyles
- Modability is there and it's easy to mod or add already existing ones
- It's relatively bug free
- For an isometric RPG the graphics are really nice

Contra
- The UI: It's ok in the beginning, but later in the game you have to fight a war against cluttering of hundreds of small items with no availability of a search function. Item and craft UI feel half heartedly done and clumsy.
You don't even get nameable bags to put stuff in to sort it manually.
- Romances come late but then way too sudden. There is almost no personal idle banter and when they happen, it's like being forced into a relationship with someone you know nothing about, even while traveling with them the whole time. There is no additional remarks/chats/mentions/opportunities after you take a romance. You feel like being "together" with a robot. Also companions don't see/care what you do and with whom. You can romance all options and then, late pick one. Still no idle banter. No personal conversations at all.
- Bugs are few but the ones that are in can break your game or kill all your fun. (possible spoiler example below)
- After the first Act, the pace of the game slows down to a crawl. Instead of being able to chose areas to explore like in the grand RPG's of old: Baldur's Gate and Neverwinter Nights, you get one freakingly huge area and are thrown in without much word of what to do and where to go. This paradigm stays until the end of the game. You don't get much info in your journal of what to do and where to go. You get the huge areas and can go explore all of it. The problem: you are expected to explore the places in the order Larian thought. But get no info on what order that is - apart from too hard (or too easy) enemies.
You can't simply take one single area and explore it as everything is connected and around every corner is another sidequest. Why do you do them you may end up asking yourself. The answer: to get the levels necessary to do your main quest. That's not roleplaying. That's powerleveling.
- Equipping new stuff is a horror: when the old item provided skill points that you used to learn and activate abilities, then on equipping something else you immediately deactivate all abilities your new gear doesn't allow you to wear anymore - without any warning. You then have to look through all the learned skills by yourself and find the ones that were deactivated. Becomes super annoying late game as there are easily a few hundred skills available.
- A few hundred skills is simply too much. It may be a nice idea to have freedom of using what fits the playstyle but with 30ish skills for every school (warfare, scoundrel, hunter and all 8(?) magic schools) and on top of that dozends of secret spell-combinations it's just overwhelmingly too much.
- The main quest feels awkward to play. For most of the game I was uncertain if the story aims to force the player into some kind of Battle Royale with their friends. I quit the game at the last dungeon because I lost any interest in finishing it so I don't know if it indeed does. The feeling however, kinda ruined the atmosphere pretty good. And the companions did nothing you would expect in an RPG in such a situation. No long discussions about friendship/love/the right to live. They just say "yeah, yeah later".
- The world Larian paints in this game is so ugly and imoral, that in the late game I was even considering of ending it for good. Whereever you look, you see discusting atrocities being done upon innocent people and beings. And not just from "the bad guys". Beggars torture their dogs, innocent and virtuous seeming (and presented, and behaving) girls who are first saved by you, turn into the next Hitler of their race and want to kill all intelligent life that is not of their race and ready their people for war. People (including your companions and yourself) seem to just shrug off the fact that they talk to mass murderers (your party). It's a cruel, dark, heartless and worthless world. Whatever ending one pursues, it's made clear by Larian that the world may change. But not the nature of it's inhabitants.
Surely a completely different from what we saw in the brilliant Original Sin 1.
- Riddles are really just time wasting unintuitive walls to make you google the solutions. They are not fun, not interesting and the bigger ones are annoying to handle. I just quit one after trying to solve it for 45 minutes. No hint. No reaction to what you do. No response to if you got something right or not. It just sucks and destroys all fun still left.
All in all I can't recommend this game to anyone who thinks my negative points would be important for them too. Else, enjoy. If all negative points are unimportant to you, this will be a great experience for you.

It's hard to find a game that really scratches the itch in want of a multiplayer shooter in the customizable mech/robot niche genre. Too often do games rub you the wrong way, ruined by pay-to-win features (MWO + many others), too much customization allowing ugly player builds and unfixed bugs (Robocraft), or glaring balance issues and console exclusivity (Armored Core). Then there are other games, like Hawken, that hold a ton of promise, but the developers give up and change hands.
Gear Up is an endearing indie game that does its best to maintain balance and fun, and avoids pay-to-win. While Gear Up is a bit casual, and still in development, I have to say it is the closest game I have found to really enjoy and come close to scratching that itch of finding a solid mech shooter.

Woodle Tree Adventures is a fun, cute little game and easily better than many of the child-level PC games I played back in 2006. However, this is not 2006, and the little bugs and hitches that were common back then make today's games flawed and annoying.
By far, the most annoying thing about this game is the respawn system. Checkpoints are few and far between, and when a small design flaw causes a death or two, you are sent back almost halfway across the map, which makes deaths stressful and irritating. This is an easy fix for the game and I hope to see an update that adds more support for this.
Besides this, the game is
+ cute
+ playable
+ easy on the eyes
+ great for kids
As a side note, there are a few things I would like to see added.
- Camera angles are a bit buggy in places but nothing that affects the gameplay too much
- Adding secrets/easter eggs would make this game amazing
- The tree guy from the first cutscene should have voice acting
If all of these features were added, this game would be well worth the $2.99. In the meantime, get a free key online from the dev.

Alright, let's get this out of the way. I love this game. The levels are very well designed (except you specific section of Press Garden Act 2), I've played through the entirety of this game, and I can't express how much I love this game's level design and overall look. However, there is one thing about this game that I don't think many people address, the bosses. I hate them. Well, not all of them, just most them.
Green Hill - Act 1 and 2 - Actually pretty decent. Not too difficult, but hey, it's the first zone.
Chemical Plant - Act 1 - Damage boosting almost feels required.
Chemical Plant - Act 2 - As much as I like Puyo Puyo, I would have liked a proper fight. Hell, Eggman isn't even much of a challenge.
Studiopolis - Act 1 - A simple fight that I had hard time with as Knuckles. Knuckles' gimped jump really makes this boss difficult.
Studiopolis - Act 2 - Too much waiting.
Flying Battery - Act 1 - More waiting, especially as Knuckles. Kind of boring to be honest.
Flying Battery - Act 2 - Easily the worst boss in the entire game. I dread playing this zone purely because of this boss.
Press Garden - Act 1 - Damage boosting doesn't feel required, it IS required. Seriously, this boss is just annoying.
Press Garden - Act 2 - One too many projectiles, but I actually think this one is fine.
Stardust Speedway - Act 1 - Once again, another boring boss.
Stardust Speedway - Act 2 - I like the concept of this boss, but it goes on for way too long, just like this review.
Hydrocity Zone - Act 1 - Creative, but it doesn't have more than the gimmick going for it.
Hydrocity Zone - Act 2 - No.
Mirage Saloon - Act 1 - Whoever thought this boss was a good idea should rethink their life choices.
Mirage Saloon - Act 2 - I love the return of the "Fighters" characters, but it felt underwhelming. :(
Oil Ocean - Act 1 - Oh boy I love instant death traps. /s
Oil Ocean - Act 2 - I never really found this boss too difficult. Sure the falling platforms are stupid, but other than that I never had much of an issue with this boss.
Lava Reef - Act 1 - I actually like bosses that properly use the enviroment. I actually kind of like this one.
Lava Reef - Act 2 - The arena is really glitchy for this boss. Other than that, I feel like it needs to be adjusted a bit more as the hitbox is way too small.
Metallic Madness - Act 1 - Whoa ok, Sonic 1's final boss on steroids. Pretty stressful. For it's placement in the game I feel like it was about time for an actually difficult boss, especially this late in the game.
Metallic Madness - Act 2 - Very gimmicky and can take a while to complete. Once again, cool concept, but could have been executed better.
Titanic Monarch - Act 1 - A remixed version the eye boss thing from Sonic 3. Goes on for a little too long though.
Titanic Monarch - Act 2 - A proper final boss. Fairly difficult.
Egg Reverie - Underwhelming. Pretty sad considering it's the Super Sonic boss.
I do like this game, but the bosses are, for the most part, bad. Also this game really likes crushing the player. Like, a lot.

The basics of the game involve a single jump followed by a spinning double jump ability that can damage enemies. You also have your ranged attack that can be upgraded to a special weapon through chests littered about the levels, just be warned that ammo is limited for these special weapons. One enemy per level will drop a key, and picking this up allows you to choose from one of three upgrades at the end of each stage. The variety and utility of these pickups is impressive, and really adds a lot of replay value. Speaking of replay value, all the enemies drop gems that can be gathered and used to purchase upgraded new suits for your hero. These new suits are permanent and really offer some fun incentive for continued play and gem collection. At the end of each "world" is a boss to be fought before moving on, and while I've only faced one, the encounter was fun and challenging. The only negative I can levy against the title is that I would like to be able to drop back down through platforms, but this may have been included intentionally to make you "think before you leap." Awesome game and an even better price makes this one a winner in my book. Great job Dev!

It's strange how sometimes playing a game relates so deeply with your current situation that it feels as though it was made specifically for you at that moment. You get a pit in your stomach and when you stop playing you see the world in a whole new light. Perspective changes and you just feel as though a weight has been lifted off of you when you turn your attention away from the screen after that last pivotal plot point.
Personally I am going through an extended transition from previous Military experience, then school, and now a professional career with a family, life can be pretty confusing. That confusion has nothing on Kentucky Route Zero by developer Cardboard Computer. There are words that can describe the game: surreal, strange, odd, uncanny, bizarre. You can describe the things that happen in the story by sequence, but completing the ideas as to how or why these things happen is impossible.
The game itself isn't so much a game as a series of events that captures you and allows you to shape the adventure and it's contents as a concept of your own design. The events are all going to happen regardless of whether or not you make certain choices, the only thing that may change are dialogue options and responses. You even begin to have conversations with yourself through multiple characters gradually. This is interesting because now both sides of the conversation have different possibilities, and somehow the conversations seem less mechanical even if they are with yourself.
Going back to describing the game, there are words to describe it, but each of those words seem to have connotations that don't fully encompass the ideas portrayed. The feeling is fuller, than those words can describe. It's very odd, and I don't want to give any of it away as a spoiler.
Things that are strange and unbelievable happen and the characters seem to take it with a grain of salt. Things like traveling on an inter-dimensional highway with arbitrary markers made of everyday items, replacing a leg with a metal skeleton prosthesis (and not reacting), taking a shot with a skeleton with a tape recorder, flying on a giant eagle that moves houses daily. These are all taken by the characters as something completely acceptable if a bit odd. No explanation of why these things are happening, just that they do.

There is no time or place to explore why these things happen, so taking them with stride is forced on the player as well as the characters. You can only move forward and there are no places to take breaks to look for answers. So you derive the answers from events as they move along, and accept what doesn't make sense, and just move along. Eventually events in the story that didn't make sense are after the fact, and become a part of the plot. So even surreal happenings can become important regardless of how illogical or insane they seem at first.
The entire interface is a point and click adventure, but there are only so many things you can point and click on and they are all labeled for convenience and to keep the story moving at a reasonable pace. This doesn't detract from the experience, as the game itself is surreal enough to keep you entertained. If anything it keeps things interesting as you always want to move forward to see what strange happenings are next.
The strange is the spectacle. And the glass through which you look is your own mind. The experience is engrossing.
You'll like this game if: You enjoy M.C. Escher and Picasso, and want to play a game designed by them. Strictly for those though that enjoy being told a story, and not necessarily molding it.

A more detailed review, you ask? Here you go. The game is exactly what you would expect, you drive a truck, in America, delivering cargo. You can gain more driver experience as you make more deliveries, allowing skills points to be spent, and new deliveries to be unlocked, leading to more experience, etc. The journeys can be long, or short, you have full choice over how long you want to spend.
The controls are responsive, and although the best experience comes from having the best control scheme, the game is still perfectly playable with a mouse and keyboard.
Visually, it can be stunning, but still looks great for the most part, however something likes seasons would be nice. The same old summer vibe can be tiring and break the immersion, especially if you're like me and facing snow outside at the moment.
The audio is agian player preference, you can play your own music, listen to actual radios, or choose to just hear you and your truck together.
Feature wise is where the game is lacking. There's a large amount of potential that hasn't been incorporated yet, and ☆odminstar 📱✔☆ sums up a lot of what I think.
And lastly, as far as I'm aware not all 50 states are available, and you will only get 5 free, the rest are going to cost 12 dollars. If you do not wish to pay the cost, don't, it's still a great game. However there is much effort put into adding new states, so I believe it's perfectly reasonable to put a price on them. End of review, have a swell day.

Great game and gameplay, terrible endings.
From the first steps, you are diving into perfectly tailored adventure, as historically accurate as possible, with great quests and events.
You are shaping the politics of the 9th century Britain and Danmark, getting kings to the throne or killing bishops and plundering churches. The ancient world of old Sagas lies before you! You are doing your best to tread carefully between bloody violence and clever business deals (almost as the real Vikings of the past did). You forge the alliances, kings consider you as their friend!
... aaand suddenly the game ends.  And although you had 80/100 in Power and 70/100 in Prosperity, the Picts want your help to invade the Britain and the Orkney Islands still wait for your attention to became your British base - the game tells you "you lost", Not just lost, you FAILED. The developers spent a good deal of their time to make sure you got the message. Your mother tells you this, Alting is one huge fail and then there is a movie of the "death and destruction" in your fjord.
FFS guys, if the dependencies on the Power/Prosperity scoring are influencing the ending in such drastic way - tell it! Explain it to the player! Not just "here is your story blah-bla-bla, you lost by the way".
Summary.
Do not try to play this game in the way Egil Skallagrimson or Gunnlaugr Serpent-Tongue would do. Just select Power-line or Prosperity line and stick with it. It will limit your options but will allow you to get the better ending.
And do not try to explore or travel, the timeline is ridiculously short.

A short, but neat little game. And by short I mean "less than an hour" short. There are 7 chapters and each one toys with a different idea. The first one is basically a tutorial, the second is a sequence of small puzzle levels, the third is a "boss fight", the fourth is a flying level, the fifth is another boss type thing, the sixth is a forced loss I think? and the seventh is a three-part sequence. The meat of the gameplay is probably in the second chapter and the seventh chapter, all the other ones are fairly short and those two are the only two where the concept feels fully fleshed out, though the other chapters do well to not overstay their welcome.
The central theme of basketball-related gameplay is pretty interesting and makes for some neat game design ideas. The aesthetic is simple but pleasant to look at, the soundtrack's pretty alright, and the story is cute. Only gripe is that replaying the last chapter three times is a bit tedious, but ehh. Other than that it's a neat little game that I'm glad I played, even if I'm unlikely to return to it. I don't feel an experience this short is worth $5 but if you can get it for under $2 I say go for it.

At the time of writing this it's simply riddled with bugs and a clunky UI that feels like it's from 2007 not 2017.
The way you set your respawn location is through sleeping bags placed on the ground. You can only use sleeping bags that you or your clan have placed, which is reasonable. However if you click on a sleeping bag in the wild, of which there are many, some hidden underneath bushes or areas you mine, it deletes your spawn location. You can't spawn on the sleeping bag you misclicked, and often I haven't even realized I clicked on a bag as I'm running around pressing E to pick items up off the ground. The same button you press to pick items up also deletes your respawn information. It's a pretty huge oversight and nearly every time I've died I've had to start fresh at the beginning even though I crafted beds properly.
I also died of heat stroke during the night recently. There's a system in the game where hiding in shade will lower the amount of heat you take. So at night you would imagine that, well, you're always in shade. Not the case. I suppose it actually gets hotter at night in the Conan universe. It's the only explanation that makes sense. In the day you're dealing with direct sunlight, so for the night to compete with direct sunlight the overall temperature would need to be significantly warmer.
So you craft an bow and some arrows, the bow crafts and is placed automatically onto your hotbar. Great. So you go to use it, says no ammo... But you've crafted ammo... Alright so you need to load the ammo, press R? Nope. Drag and drop the arrows onto the bow? Nope. You need to unequip the Bow which was automatically equipped for you when you crafted it, then and only then can you drag the arrows onto it  to load them. Then you move the bow back to your hotbar. Again, honestly, is this 2007?
Stat points don't honestly seem to do anything for you. Vitality and Endurance are the only two I see as actually improving your gameplay. Accuracy allegedly improves your ranged damage yet you kill enemies with the exact same number of arrows with 0 accuracy as you do with 10 accuracy. The survival skill doesn't seem to make heat stroke easier to avoid. Maybe it's just hunger/thirst but I haven't had any issues with either of those yet anyways but I run into heat stroke often enough, it basically just makes you move slowly through certain areas and it heavily penalizes you when you're trying to retrieve your corpse because if you don't have any armor on you get heat stroke ridiculously fast. Also apart from the very basic armor which is practically useless, the Light armor isn't exactly easy to craft. You need a specific crafting table and about fifteen minutes worth of grinding resources. So if you die and like I explained above your respawn location was reset, you can basically kiss finding your corpse goodbye. The corpses despawn fairly quickly in this game.
I've also experienced glitches where my Bow just stopped working. I had arrows, it was fully repaired, but it just wouldn't fire. It would go through the motions of firing but no arrow would actually be shot. I tried crafting a new bow. I tried relogging. I tried closing the game and restarting my computer altogether. It just wouldn't fire for me. Eventually I ended up dying and after that I was able to fire the bow again. Maybe I should have thought to kill myself earlier, I don't know. Also experienced glitches where I was stuck with no stamina, normally it respawns after a second or two of resting.
Overall this is yet another incredibly negative EA experience for me and I'm kicking myself for giving another developer the chance at releasing an unfinished game. I still have a bitter taste in my mouth with DayZ. Steam really needs to require these developers to have more options for refunding during EA. More and more companies are taking advantage of EA and simply never finishing their games. Raking in tons of cash for what is more or less just a demo of a game.

Second Chapter follows the story directly where Trails in the Sky First Chapter ended. The game goes on a much grander scale in both story and battles, and does it well. You're expected to have have played First Chapter in many places and are rewarded for remembering small details.
Like the first game SC has a bit of a slow start as it builds the world and backstory but really picks up and gets crazy later on.
There's some small changes to the combat system with 'chain crafts', new spells and crafts but it's still very much the same. It's sort of like a grid-based strategy RPG battle system but simplified. However there is a lot of customizability to your characters and party and many ways to approach each battle. For environments the dungeon design is good and varied, especially later on.
Unlike a lot of JRPGs there is almost no reason to grind enemies for experience. The experience gained from battles scales massively with your level so if you bring an underleveled character to a boss it might actually gain enough XP to go above the others.
A big part of what made FC great for me was that the characters had a lot of personality and the dialogue was well written. In SC a lot of characters remain effectively the same and there aren't a ton of new ones you learn to know. But especially Estelle and Joshua have a lot of character growth as you might expect. At the same time you certainly get a lot of backstory on everyone as the story progresses.
The music throughout the game is superb. Especially in the final areas of the game I was really awed by this. In my opinion it's a big part of what makes the game so good, as it's effectively switched around to set the mood.
In general the game builds on all of the things I liked about the first chapter. As for a few (mostly minor) dislikes:
I expected Second Chapter to be darker toned than the first. The 'secret society' tends to follow anime tropes and hide behind mystery rather than truly seem evil or do horrible things (with some exceptions). This is a matter of taste of course. I sort of preferred the political plotting of the first game and how the society appeared very sinister there. Speaking of anime tropes, the 'saved at the last second' thing is used so many times in SC that it gets pretty silly.
I think the game could've had a little less of the same kind of content as First Chapter. Things like fetch quests walking around Liberl to progress the story. A playthrough of SC can easily take 70 hours. I wouldn't have minded it being some hours shorter and having less of the same from FC.
In a way because of recycling many areas SC obsoletes FC content wise, which isn't necessarily a good thing. They're two halves of the same story, and the first half should still be fun to revisit after playing SC.
The battle system is fun, but like First Chapter normal difficulty doesn't have many challenging encounters if you use all the tools at your disposal. While it's easy to make your own challenges by setting limitations you can't be expected to know which ones work well on your first playthrough.
This is personal preference but being able to mindlessly beat certain bosses by repeating the same strategy draws me out of the story, so better difficulty options could make it more fun.
Hard and Nightmare difficulty don't appear balanced without a New Game+ save file. Most people seem to agree that the final prologue boss is impossible to beat without getting a lucky pattern when starting a new save. Difficulties apart from normal were unlocked after beating the game once in the PSP version so it's not intentional but still unfortunate.
Just like in First Chapter all animations in battles are still unskippable and watching them makes up a lot of time in a playthrough. I didn't mind the slow pace caused by this because the game is so good overall. But I'm sure it could get annoying, especially on repeat playthroughs.
In short, if you enjoyed the first chapter this is a must buy. It's a bigger game that expands on the world and directly continues the same story bringing it to a satisfying end. The game is well paced without much filler and has an impressive endgame. The combat system is fun and tactical but on normal difficulty will not be particularly challenging for veterans of the first game. A great soundtrack brings the story and combat together nicely.
For people new to the series I would still recommend starting with First Chapter, since SC assumes you remember what happens there without recapping it.

When I first saw this game, I thought it would be some little game strung together for the sake of it being there.
What I found instead was quite interesting.
100% Orange Juice is a computer board game that roughly works like a cross between monopoly and munchkin, although it has MANY things which make it unique, at least from anything I've ever played before. Throughout an entire game session, dice-battles and star-collecting (stars are the currency of the game) occur on every turn, but the game is only won once five goals (or "normas", as the game calls it) are achieved, which is determined by the number of stars or the number of enemies beaten. What's very nice about the norma system is that you can chose between either of the two goals, although it should be warned that a norma can only be advanced once the player returns to a home square.
With lots of things that affect the progress of the game, it's not a kind that you sit down and relax to as you play it: one wrong move or half-baked thought can be detrimental. However, I wouldn't reccomend this to anyone who wants to have a solid strategy-focused game either, because at times, outcome can be as random and undefined as a game of poker. But for the patient, this is quite a cup of tea, and a great one, in fact. It's fun to experiment with the different elements of the game, seeing which might bring about a more likely (though still uncertain) victory.
Oh yeah, and there's apparently a plot to this game. Haven't wasted my time enough to know all about it, but the other aspects alone should provide more than enough to satisfy.
Much like a cup of actual orange juice, 100% Orange Juice is a sour kick if you're not ready, but tastes very good once you let the sweetness make its way in, even making the tartness feel like it truly has a purpose.

Shadow Warrior Classic Redux is a 2013 remaster or update of an original Shadow Warrior game that came out in 1997, used Build engine and was made by 3D Realms. Or "Lo Wang is Shadow Warrior" if we are to belive what cover of a box said. It's an old-school FPS game and can be descriped as eastern bro of Duke Nukem 3D.
Classic Redux also includes original DOS version, as well as all two released expansion packs, which are freeware anyway. There is no multiplayer from original. Original had competetive (DM) and cooperative modes, though it uses service which isn't there anymore, so you can't use original. Or at least as far as I am aware.
As for technical side, there are occasional crashes. They can happen randomly, but mostly when I rushed with katana and would get blown up. Anyway, save often!
A more serious issue with this release got to be circular ground mines in Twin Dragon expansion. In original they would lay on ground, emitting a beeping sound like sticky bombs. When you come close to them, they will first rise into ground and then explode hard after few seconds, so you have to get into range to activate it and then run away. Sadly, mines are glitched in Classic Redux, they are actually sank into ground, so you can't see them, but painful explosion still happens over ground. If you hear bomb beeping nearby - save and get ready to do some blind work.
The setting is awesome, while plot is non-existant. You are Lo Wang, an asian pervy old fart, who is Shadow Warrior by the way. Which makes you think that he is a stealth master, but in reality he likes nuclear weapons. He worked for Master Zilla as a bodyguard, until Lo finds out that Zilla's corporations goes as low as using demons to do dirty work, and his code of honor does not approve that. Zilla doesn't want some Wang this way either.
So you go around in either villages, temples or even cities and wreck mutants and monsters up. While meeting anime girls randomly. Hm, just like tentacled womans in Duke Nukem 3D, but most of them think that Lo Wang should just go away. They should have released a collab FPS title so we could get tentacled anime babes.
The game is a lot like Duke Nukem, though it doesn't have as much of city levels. But they are still gimmicky and overdetailed. Like, you can play Panchinko machines. Kinda. Or punch training equpment to regenerate your health without limit like a Shadow Casual. One liners are still funny, though "ancient Chinese secret" pops up too much. There are more cool stuff in it too, like more useful items that include "grenades", though only Gas one is for throwing. Some weapons have few modes which you can change with alt-fire. You can even use occasional vehicle, even though they are rare and kinda suck and have horrible collision.
Actually, when I played this last time seriously times ago, I didn't like it so much. It wasn't fun, it seemed like game had too much punishing hitscan. Now I beat this game and had no issue for some reason, it was enjoyable a lot. Strange. Maybe that's because before that I played on Hard (3th skill), while now I played on Normal (2nd skill), maybe the gap between these two is huge. Then again, hard hitscan enemies are always awful idea. Or maybe the mouselook and WASD of Classic Redux made it easier than doing it on keyboard-only of original DOS. Or maybe I just learned that some 90s FPS aren't as awesome as Doom and you have to often retreat and use indirect ways to fight, instead of circle-strafing into every encounter. And if you ever meet Shadow ninja, then you are supposed to immeditly retreat, unless you want to get one-hit-killed.
I mean, you got a Grenade Launcher in this game. In other FPS it's like Rocket Launcher but worse, with arcing grenades. You usually can hit things around corner only if you measure accurately and usually you are just a fool when you can just shoot into face. Not in Shadow Warrior! This bloody thing here has a freaking nuclear radius of explosions. What it means is that it's actually useful to clean rooms around corners, while you don't want to use it to fight face-to-face, as it's weaker than rocket and easily hits you too. Actually, it might be way too good, ammo could be less common.
I really suggest you to check out Steam Guide of Quick Tips by Joseph Hicks, it really is a good one.
And yea, there are also some strange balance and choices, like railgun doesn't have much use and it annoyes me that it shoots misaligned compared to crosshair. Katana is a fun melee weapon that at least instakills most common ninjas. You still look like a fool when swinging it over tougher enemies. Hmmmm, this game would have been better if it had cheesy colorful human ninjas from American stuff instead of mutant-ninjas.
As for Classic Redux, well, this update comes with some cool stuff, mostly modern controls, widescreen support, renderer and Steam Integration so you can just use Steam Workshop! If you don't like it, DOSBox-supported original is also included.
It has a bunch of interesting stuff done in it. Main theme was remixed, though I prefer original. Weapon graphics were tweaked a bit so it doesn't look weird on widescreen, like katana was made longer by looping parts of it. It sure looks better!
You can even change if you want shurikens or darts graphics for the second weapon you have. That's because the British version of original game was censored and had darts instead. I would say that darts make more sense in this case as the weapon feels very weak. Well, aside from part where they ricochet off walls. Don't tell me about "it's not bad weapon as you can recover them off walls", the game has problems with vertically when it comes to "use" action, so it's weird and hard to get them all back.
Sadly, some cheats don't work. Mostly level select one. Aw.
As you expect, like all full versions of a game, it comes with two episodes: Shareware episode "Enter The Wang" made of 4 levels and Full-Game-only "Code of Honor" made of around 18 levels. Shareware episodes uses full version's CD Music instead of MIDI, but the only thing you miss is that one track sounded like nothing in registered version. Heh, you can notice how those Shareware levels were much better than Registered ones. Some probably were dissapoint after purchasing game. First half of Code of Honor isn't particulary hot.
It also comes with both expansion pack. Both were released for free due to being kinda considered abandoned by that time. Or just too late for party. They were being developed by other companies and publisher didn't feel like investing more, or something.
Twin Dragon was released in 1997. It kinda had half good levels like Lo Wang's house and fish village, and half of generic levels, like those sewer mazes. Some guess that it wasn't complete release, as there is no new soundtrack like promised. Also, final boss, who is reskin, spamming "there can be only one".
Wanton Destruction was found in 2005. It's really all good stuff, it even reskinned most enemies into humans. Recommended, mhm.
They say that they found materials of Deadly Kiss, the third expansion out of three, that was considered being lost. Maybe we will get it some day.
And heck, at least this game has awesome boss fight music, unlike Duke Nukem 3D who is a sissy. And Lo Want no sissy! Most of arcade or old gamers know that this is the most important element of any game.
In the end, outside of some glitches which aren't ruining whole game, it's a pretty good redux of a decent game. Pretty fun. At least on Normal, since it abuses hitscan a bit too much at times for 90s shooter. Even though it didn't bring multiplayer, but these are single-player focused games after all, multiplayer was just for fooling around. Big levels full of secrets ahead!

I haven't progressed past level 7 on the starting zone so far, so this review might change later on.  What I can say is that I love the freedom this game offers you so far as just wandering around, interacting with NPC's and the environment, and that most questlines are optional.  There is a main questline you must finish along the way, but mostly at your pace.  This feels like fairly bug-free turn based combat, decent character customization, and the group play option is way more flexible than I expected.  It's nice that my biggest gripe about the game is that the tooltips are lacking in helping you quickly understand what skills and abilities do for you.  I'd also like to see a confirmation dialogue when selecting attribute points and skill choices, but again, it is nice that those are my biggest gripes about the game.  It really is a fun game, and I've started over a few times to see how I like the different classes.  I love that there are no rules for multi-classing!  If you are a fan of turn based combat, old school RPG feel, and freedom to kill and/or explore, this is the game for you.

There's something just slightly off about Kentucky Route Zero.
Not the sort of "off" that turns you away and makes you consider whether it ought to be locked up with its unnerving peers, but the kind that leaves you puzzled and transfixed upon the play of sorts being performed before you. The unusual atmosphere and odd interactions with characters is at once unsettling and hypnotic, its logic clashing with reality yet somehow seeming entirely natural in this bizarre segment of road you've found yourself lost on.
The plot trickles out through nebulous exchanges with persons that may or may not even exist, giving you answers as they simultaneously create an abundance of new questions you haven't time to ask. This ambiguity could very easily be the downfall of the game, but there's a self awareness to the narrative's construction that holds it together as it continues to distort its world into a mysterious cloud of disconnected yet overlapping plot lines.
I'm being intentionally unclear with my descriptions because Kentucky Route Zero relies so heavily upon the player's unknowing of what exactly it is. Were I to have come in already versed on its events, I have little doubt that the magic that kept me engrossed as I tried to fit the misshapen pieces together would have been lost, and what I would have been left with would be an artistically inspired but far less stimulating experience.
After only playing the first act of five, I haven't a great deal more to say about Kentucky Route Zero besides how immensely it made me
to explore more about it and learn its secrets which it has only just touched upon. It's hard for me to pinpoint exactly what makes it so interesting to me, but more than anything it is likely the endless possibility of what could be in store after what was essentially a prologue of sorts.
Perhaps I'll have better answers when I've been through the remaining acts, but regardless of what they contain, Kentucky Route Zero has already established itself as wholly compelling. It feels like the road I'm heading down could take me anywhere, and I want to see everything along it.
After completing the second of Kentucky Route Zero's planned five acts, the first is now clear as existing as a sort of necessary introduction to what is to come. It displayed hints of an almost hypnagogic second world hidden beneath our own, setting the story in motion without drifting too far from reality as it slowly allowed its mystery to reveal itself.
Act II is when the Zero is finally allowed to take the spotlight, where former pretenses are rejected as the developers firmly take our hand to guide us through the play being performed in front of us. Kentucky Route Zero's vision of what it is and what it will be is so strong, so confident, that it need not hamper itself with explaining its events as its method of storytelling so entirely encompasses its plot that it would almost be detrimental to the experience should any clear answers be given, or perhaps exist at all.
As its dreamlike world comes more into focus I still have no idea where it plans to take me, and oddly I'm entirely accepting, even excited by that lack of knowledge. Kentucky Route Zero is keeping me in the dark, but its steady reassurance that it knows the way through is enough to keep me moving onward. Wherever this might end up, act II showcased nothing that leads me to believe it has any chance of losing focus, only becoming more captivating as each new piece of its overarching narrative is introduced and I'm taken further inside boundless imagination.

I heard about Woodle Tree through the likes of Indie Game Battle (as I also have a character playable in that game), so much to my craving for 3D platformers, I got curious about this title and gave it a shot. Basically, there were things I liked about it and things I didn't, but I THINK there is just enough for me to say the good outweighs the bad. Nevertheless, I always feel the need to explain everything in detail. After all, this game's getting a sequel soon, and it's best there's improvements to be made for it.
One thing that stuck out for me was the visual style. I kinda have a soft spot for it. It has a homemade feel to it, with a hint of Nintendo 64. The levels also drive home a sense that feels much like Super Mario 3D Land. As this adorable little tree log, you simply have to get to the end of each level, while collecting three floating water drops along the way for each. It's simple, but cozy. For the most part, anyway. I do wish the soundtrack was more upbeat and catchy, but the platforming is fairly enjoyable, and your attack has decent range, making for enemy kills to be reasonably tangible.
Not as reasonable is when Woodle Tree gets hit. For some reaosn, the checkpoint system seems to only work when Woodle Tree falls off a ledge; when you get hit by an enemy, you instantly have to start AT THE BEGINNING OF THE LEVEL. Granted, you have infinite lives and still have track of the water drops collected, but why can't I always start off at a portion of the level regardless of how I died? The control is also not the most intuitive it could have been. For some reason, you can't run and jump when moving up or down, nor can you do diagonal jumps. The control issues definitely need fixing up. To a lesser extent, there's the camera. I'm not as bothered by its clunkiness as everyone else was, but it can still be glaring for a game like this.
Lastly, the game is over quickly and abruptly. I beat it in almost an hour's worth of game time, and while I'm the kind of guy that doesn't mind a short game (especially when the price is as low as it is), I was expecting at least an hour or two more than there was. And it wasn't like there was a boss battle or anything to close the game with; it just...threw an ending screen and that was it.
So yeah, this is definitely a flawed game. I wouldn't even really call it a great game, but I still at least recommend it if you can spare a few bucks for a small dose of indie 3D platforming.............Just as long as you can deal with the control and checkpoint issues.

I really enjoyed BasketBelle. One word I would use to describe it is charming. It's a short game, roughly 1 hour, give or take if you try for the final achievement, but it's very well made. This review is a short overview - there's not too much to cover given the game's length, but the execution and charm more than make up for it. Definitely worth playing if you already own it, or if you get on sale - the full price would be fine for people that don't mind game length so much.
The story follows a young lad trying to find/ rescue his sister after she is kidnapped. The story has lots of warm moments, and I was pleasantly surprised how in such a short span of time, such vivid feelings were conveyed. You'll see what happens when you play the game, there's not much to elaborate without giving away everything, but the story was sweet and warm.
The gameplay uses several mechanics of basketball, and the controls are fairly simple - run right and left, slide, and jump-shot. The simple controls are the basis of some puzzles in the game, and overall I found that it made sense that there weren't complicated controls. The levels all have some different settings and layout, and you'll get the general feeling once you play. Again I was impressed with how the devs progressed the levels and story, and they fit together nicely, in such a short span of time.
Overall, I really recommend this game - it's short but the story is charming, the gameplay engaging. This is an example of an indie game made with love and care, and it conveys the feeling to the player well.

Gosh, this game is such a blast!
The controls feel just as tight & responsive as they were in the classic games, and there's a few new moves in here, such as the drop dash, as well as beign able to have tails lift you to higher areas.
The music is also fantastic! The old tracks are updated & remixed, but still have the same vibe of the original versions. The new tracks are incredible and fit right in with the rest of the Sonic music from that era. All of the tracks tend to evoke the Japanese Sonic CD soundtrack, while not being entirely derivitive and adding in it's own unique flair.
The graphics are also incredible, being updated to that the animations run at a super smooth 60fps. it gives the whole thing this buttery smooth look that even exceeds the classic games. This is like blast processing on steroids, folks! :P
The one thing I would hold against the game is that a bonus stage appears at every checkpoint you pass (as long as you have over 25-30 rings). Now, Sonic 3 also did this, but in that case, the stages were short & sweet, and you got back into the action fairly quick. The stages this time around are the "Get Blue Spheres" stages from Sonic 3, which can last much longer than just a few second. This causes a break in the action which is somewhat disappointing, but can also be ignored easily enough. I'm hoping they will patch in an option to keep tese stages from appearing at all, though. Or perhaps an option to have them appear at the end of a stage, similar to how it worked in Sonic 2.
In any case, this game brings back everything you ever loved about the classic Sonic games, and revamps it with smoother animation, hot new tracks, remixed classic levels, new original levels, a new bonus stage, and plenty of extras. I've wanted a Sonic game liek this to come out for ages, and I went in with exceedingly high expectations, and it met all of them, and then some! Bonus stage complaints aside, this game is an absolute joy to play and is well worth the price of admission. I definitely reccomend it to anybody who is a fan of retro video games, and highly reccomend it to Sonic fans, of course.

One of the biggest complaints I have about BasketBelle is that it starts horribly as a game: the tutorial sets the right mood, but the next stage is just a boring and tedious puzzle platformer. This is why most people never experience the later exciting high-speed chases and streetball puzzles. They should though, as they are rather fun!

Wahhey, Trails is back! And isn't that the truth - Trails is BACK. The atmosphere hasn't changed much from the first game, and honestly, that's a great thing to see. The characters are very lighthearted & happy go lucky, despite their being a lot of bad stuff going on. It's a refreshing break from other RPGs, where cracking so much as a smile is a rarity. Trails' approach to storytelling, combined with the quality of writing and attention to detail, put it above most JRPG franchises out there.
The Bracer quests are also back, and while the ol' familiar "X Monster needs to be eliminated" request, there's also plenty of new & unique sidequests to go on. It's pretty amazing how varied the dozens upon dozens of quests are, but if you see one you don't like, you needn't worry about missing out on the rewards because the game is generous enough to give you what's required to get by well with just picking the ones you fancy (personally, I try to do them all).
A lot of music from the original game has popped back up without so much as an alternate mix, which is somewhat disappointing, honestly. I do like the soundtrack to the original game, and while I do like the new additions made in SC, I feel the original pieces could've done with a bit of oomph to help them stand out, y'know?
One thing I will say though is that you definitely want to play FC before jumping into SC. Not only will EVERYTHING make a lot more sense, but you can effortlessly carry over some of your choices & interactions from the first game into SC, which will make the experience both more personal & enjoyable.
Just like FC before it, I recommend Trails in the Sky SC 110%. SC is probably the stronger entry, but the entire series deserves playing through from start to... Well, SC and beyond.
Thanks to XSEED for bringing this over!

Now when I first picked up Awesomenauts, I found myself intimidated by it's associated definition of "MOBA" or "Multiplayer Online Battle Arena." From what I had heard about the harshness of MOBA gaming, like such titles as League of Legends or Dota 2, I was more than terrified of the idea of playing a MOBA, at least against other players. But from the moment I stepped into the world of Awesomenauts, I found myself right at home.
Awesomenauts is indeed a MOBA, as it has a roster of unique characters, titularly called "Awesomenauts" or simply "Nauts" and that you have a set of abilities at your disposal, which you must use to destroy the enemy turrets and destroy the objective they are protecting.
However, it has a unique take on its gameplay in that it places you in a 2D Sidescrolling Arena instead of the common 3D Overhead Map perspective. This allows for the player to remain focused on their character and the enemies, rather than have to micromanage a large map. Some may argue that this removes a bit of the challenge from a MOBA, but for newcomers to the genre, it will be a nice way to ease into things.
All in all, Awesomenauts is a well made game that controls easily, has plenty of wit and character crammed into it, and will keep you wanting to play it, and it's recently released expansion Awesomenauts: Starstorm, for hours. Overall, I give Awesomenauts an 8.5/10.

The Good:

All in all, if you're willing to ignore a lot troubles, it's a fun game. Disclaimer: I really do love this series. So I may be a bit biased. This is an updated review of my previous one.
Another thing I want to highlight is just how much work went into the localization of this game. I recommend you read this article
to appreciate why publishers like xseed really deserve your support.
TLDR: If something like Final Fantasy XIII is like a slab of factory manufactured galaxy chocolate, then Trails in the Sky SC is like a homemade chocolate cookie. Only a awesome, homely and delicious cookie. Maybe not the best cookie ever made, but good enough that you made another 10 and ate them all in the weekend whilst the galaxy bar is still in your chocolate stash.
Main Review:
If you loved first chapter, then you will probably love this game. Playing FC is recommended, especially if your a completionist however I played FC years ago on a psp and so I went into this without a max BP cleared FC save and the bonuses you miss are really non-consequential (you miss a item drop increase quartz, a heal/haze combine quartz and a rare accessory) and you miss the continuation of certain miniquests).
Pros:
The new combined attacks and the upgraded quartz system really make both preparing for battles and playing battles more interesting. I always felt that FC felt skimp on the number of artes and abilities. SC doesn't have this problem, as with plenty of new characters and the upgraded quartz slots give you a huge amount of customization.
I have always loved the music from this series. It is nostalgic but has a touch of sutble change, as it is a new OST compared to FC. Obviously you will recognise versions of silver will etc... but there are also some fantastic new themes as well. Go check out the Super Arranges of many of the theme tunes on youtube, they are superb.
This game is absolutely charming. I've played 4 final fantasies, 2 tales of, radiant historia and more (you get the gist), but the game that sticks close to my heart is this series. Why? The script is just overflowing with personality. All the characters in the game mature and develop, even if it takes its bloody time. Even though I hate cliches, somehow I never get annoyed or bored of the cliches or the characters that occur in this game. It has some great and memorable scenes, and doesn't pull plot devices out of its ♥♥♥.
You can only have a party of 4, yet every single character has unique dialogue for every single event. It is quite an achievement. Additionally you can really feel the world the developers were trying to create. As events occur, the NPCs in the game react LIKE REAL PEOPLE. Earthquake? All the towns people are concerned about it. Mayor elections? All the NPCs are talking about it, telling you who they support. There are even NPCs advertising the candidates. After almost every single major plot progression you can walk through the whole town and find that the scripts for NPCs has changed in practically all the towns to reflect the change in events. All the NPCs remember your aultristic acts and respond in kind. It is apparent that this game was made with love and a crazy amount of attention to detail.
Mixed (i.e. can be a pro or a con depending on what you are like):
This game is a completionist nightmare (or haven). Tons of optional sidequests with pretty narrow completion time limits. Tons of choices that if you chose wrong you will not get the full BP. Lots of treasure and secret rewards. Personally I loved it.
Might be too much story. Its like reading a visual novel, which is a plus to some and a negative to others. To put it into perspective the lord of the rings trilogy has 455,125 words. This one game has 716,401 words. That's over 3 million characters. This is a long game.
Additional difficulties and new game+ add an element of replay value, but once you complete it you probably aren't going to play it again (unless you have another 80 hours to spare...)
Cons:
It is a dated game, which is evident by its graphics. Personally I think the graphics are charming though.
Battle system can get a bit dry sometimes. This is a problem with all rpgs though, not just specific to SC.
Game needs a scene skip function, particularly for the early game.
The start of the game when you REALLY want to know what happened to Joshua etc is really slow... it actually takes a huge amount of time to get the plot properly rolling and you will go through a huge amount of sideplot.
A decent amount of backtracking occurs in this game as the events take place in the same areas as FC. So if you have played FC then you might find that annoying.
Tips: talk to everyone, sometimes more than once, unequip your side characters before main events (often you are forced to used other characters and then realize all of you good equipment was equiped on a character that has disappeared. For example, before the chapter 3 boss fight because I forgot to unequip all my characters, I went through 3 boss battles with suboptimal gear and quartz. It really made a difference, and I was forced to use a ton of items.
Overall review: if you are a hot headed gamer who just likes to blow things up... this might not be the game for you. If you are patient, do not need instant gratification, appreciate character development, a good plot and needing to think for your fights then this game is one of the most rewarding games you will ever play. For me it is a 9/10.
The game has a great foundation and is slowly growing into something great! If you like PvP and survival check it out. If not avoid this game.

A Virus Named TOM is a fast paced action/puzzle game with core gameplay similar to Pipeflow based puzzles. Initially, the puzzles are timed, so you must think relatively quickly to solve them, and you receive points based upon speed. Most of the puzzles require small thought during this part of the game. Later, the difficulty ratchets up to keyboard destroying frustration, as enemies infiltrate the puzzle board and move across it as fast or faster than you can control poor TOM. Then, the game introduces enemies that home in and seek you out, all the while your time runs out. With limited counterplay options, it becomes a race against your inevitable demise to solve a puzzle in your head by looking at the board while avoiding the AI, and then a question of dexterity to actually pull off the necessary movements without dying. A Virus Name TOM is a well designed hardcore puzzle/action game that became so frustrating to play that I uninstalled it. I would only recommend it to people who already hate themselves.

Okay, I'll star tthis review with this: if you thought Mario Party was rage-inducing, you've never had victory stolen from you by Marie Poppo hyper just as you're about to get to your home base.
*ahem* now that I have that formality out of the way, on to the review.  This game is brilliant.  It combines dice rolling and battles in a neat little package that delivers hours of fun for you and friends or random strangers playing this game.
pros
- Marie Poppo
- nice cast of characters to choose from
- worth the money for DLC content and great pricing (it also goes on sale from time to time)
- Poppopopopopopopopo!
- currency system to buy in-game cards and other character custom colors, bosses and regular NPC enemies as playable characters (so release the inner chicken in you and fight the others!)
- unique character attributes and specials
- Did I mention Marie Poppo?
- story mode available to get used to the game and unlock other characters
- map variety
- build a deck of 10 cards to throw into the mix of other player's cards
- cards from the mixed pack DLC can be used by people who don't own the DLC as long as the cards are put in by a person who owns the DLC
- Seriously, Marie Poppo!
cons
- not all characters are given to you out the box
- the only way to earn levels is to play online games
- maps also must be purchased and unlocked based on level
- character colors also need to be purchased or earned while playing the game (not entirely bad though)
- you MUST buy card packs to get new cards
- some of the items can get expensive
- playing AGAINST Marie Poppo
- DLC for new characters and a new card pack set (however, the price per DLC is pretty inexpensive, so this is a minor con)
Gameplay is pretty straight forward and easy to understand.
The graphics are colorful, especially for a board game, and do their job.
The music is extrodinary, as every character has a set theme song associated with themselves.  Each player who completes a norma (objective) gets their music played for everyone to hear.
As I said before, the replay value is pretty high, as you can play against people online and every game is different with the differnt customizable decks you can make and use.  I will say this: the single-player storymode might seem a little unfair with the AI and RNG, but nonetheless, it's beatable.  Sometimes, the RNG can be extremely evil (rolling nothing but 1s or using a certain card that has an effect that ends on a KO and rolling nothing but low numbers (or in the case of one of my games I've played online, 3s).
In conclusion, those of you who love a good multiplayer game without being too serious should definitely check this one out.  It's fun for just about everyone, and the hilarity of screwing over your opponents with just the right card is most satisfying.

When I first saw this game, I thought it would be some little game strung together for the sake of it being there.
What I found instead was quite interesting.
100% Orange Juice is a computer board game that roughly works like a cross between monopoly and munchkin, although it has MANY things which make it unique, at least from anything I've ever played before. Throughout an entire game session, dice-battles and star-collecting (stars are the currency of the game) occur on every turn, but the game is only won once five goals (or "normas", as the game calls it) are achieved, which is determined by the number of stars or the number of enemies beaten. What's very nice about the norma system is that you can chose between either of the two goals, although it should be warned that a norma can only be advanced once the player returns to a home square.
With lots of things that affect the progress of the game, it's not a kind that you sit down and relax to as you play it: one wrong move or half-baked thought can be detrimental. However, I wouldn't reccomend this to anyone who wants to have a solid strategy-focused game either, because at times, outcome can be as random and undefined as a game of poker. But for the patient, this is quite a cup of tea, and a great one, in fact. It's fun to experiment with the different elements of the game, seeing which might bring about a more likely (though still uncertain) victory.
Oh yeah, and there's apparently a plot to this game. Haven't wasted my time enough to know all about it, but the other aspects alone should provide more than enough to satisfy.
Much like a cup of actual orange juice, 100% Orange Juice is a sour kick if you're not ready, but tastes very good once you let the sweetness make its way in, even making the tartness feel like it truly has a purpose.

Let me preface this by typing out why I really thought this would be a game that I enjoy and would be able to recommend:
I played and loved pretty much all of the classic point & click adventures in their golden era. From the Sierra adventures to Maniac Mansion, Monkey Island, all the Lucasarts games really, Simon the Sorcerer, Baphomets Curse, you name it.
In more recent times I really enjoyed the Telltale games and also the more philosophical approach of The Stanley Parable for example.
If you are in a similar position and thinking about getting this, it is actually not enough to tell if you will like this game or not. I cannot recommend this to you with a straight face.
First off, the graphical fidelity is really limited, as you might have seen already, but I wouldn't really count that as a negative point. The art style is very distinct and on point, and amplifys the creepy and uneasy mood throughout the whole game. They also manage to get some stunning panoramas and effects out of this minimalistic style, it definitely works for this title.
As for the gameplay, there really is not much to speak of. It mainly consists of walking, driving and dialogue. The conversations aren't voiced so get ready for reading. A lot. Also a lot of really basic small talk that has no connection to any part of the story whatsoever. There are also frequent, short (mostly optional) detours from the main path that happen entirely in text form, no visuals.
As far as I've seen there is no form of puzzles or decisions in the game that have any impact on how it unfolds. I disagreed with people that said this is the same in Telltales games. Although the end result is pretty much always the same, there is at least an illusion of choice and advancement, using a thing with another thing to make something happen. Getting the player busy. There is none of that in KRZ, if anything it is very close to a graphic novel where things play out for you, not through you. (This is also evident in the way it is broken up. Acts and Scenes.)
It does a few really neat things, like seamlessly switching the character you control without you actually realizing it.
Well then, the story. This is where I seriously got lost. I can't really tell all that much without spoilering anything, but I can tell you that it is basically all over the place. There is a goal or finish that you know about, but it gets replaced with another goal in the first few minutes of the game, and this new one never gets questioned, just accepted as necessary.
Come to think of it, everything in this game just gets accepted, nothing is questioned. As a result, nothing gets explained or "solved" either. It's like a very elaborate acid trip. A ride you hop in that trails you along, getting crazier and more confusing by the minute. And you really have no choice but letting it happen and not thinking too much about it, moving on.
You would think that the game would make fun of itself through it ridiculous developments, but it doesn't. Apart from literally one or two very brief instances (one "running gag" and a kid), the tone of this game is dead serious.
The soundtrack is used very sparingly, but to great effect, and it's phenomenal. If anything, I really recommend getting that.

When I saw that "LA soul" was a game with 4408 achievements, I had to laugh - I mean, it's patently ridiculous.
Yes, you guessed it, this is another one of those achievement-crazy games that have been appearing on Steam as of late.
Oh well, I thought; I can get past that bit of stupidity and enjoy a new car driving game, even if it is an el cheapo one (some of the cheap driving games can be quite fun).
Boy, was I wrong!
This isn't a car driving game at all, which I had wrongly assumed it to be (I should've watched the video on the store page).
"LA soul" looks to be a rip-off of a part of one of the "Grand Theft Auto" games, where you have to hit your arrow keys to make your low-rider car move about, in line with a succession of arrows which move across the bottom of your screen.
That's all it is. One stationary car, moving about (up, down, left and right) to a sequence of arrows. No driving about whatsoever.
Boring. Really boring.
By all means play it long enough to get the achievements (if you leave it running as the primary programme on your computer for about three hours, you will get all of them).
However, don't expect to get much in the way of enjoyment from it.

BasketBelle is an experimental Basketball-platformer-puzzle arcade game.
While the game itself is very simple each section offers it's own unique challenge and mechanics, wither it's playing in a one-on-one basketball game with a person or monster, using your basketball to solve platforming puzzles or flying through the sky avoiding obstacles. Each section is short and sweet and could have been developed into their own much larger/longer games but here they last just long enough to give you a taste before the next course of this delightful meze.
Visually the game looks amazing like a pastel drawing full of blues purples and yellows. The sound design also deserves a mention with an excellent soundtrack that just matches the games mood and feel. The game also has a interesting narrative, while simply told through cut-scenes and gameplay it culminates in a beautiful and charming little story.
On the downside the controls feel a little loose and floaty, which isn't a massive problem as it doesn't require a great deal of accuracy and precision, but can be a little frustrating in certain areas. The game is also rather short being able to be finished in under an hour. Three of the four achievements are unlocked while playing through the story, the fourth involves replaying the last segment a couple of times to get the slight ending variations. There are no hidden secrets or items, no extra levels to unlock just the main experience.
Thankfully that main experience is very enjoyable for the time that it lasts. At time of writing the game sells for about £4 (£3.99GBP) and is certainly worth the asking price, not too much for such a short game with relatively little replay value other than the fact you could quickly share the game with friends. If this doesn't sound like something you'd like I'd still recommend checking it out when it's on sale.
Quick Summary
+ Varied Gameplay
+ Lovely Visuals and Soundtrack
+ Simple but enjoyable gameplay
- Short
- Floaty controls
- No replayability

Gosh, this game is such a blast!
The controls feel just as tight & responsive as they were in the classic games, and there's a few new moves in here, such as the drop dash, as well as beign able to have tails lift you to higher areas.
The music is also fantastic! The old tracks are updated & remixed, but still have the same vibe of the original versions. In any case, this game brings back everything you ever loved about the classic Sonic games, and revamps it with smoother animation, hot new tracks, remixed classic levels, new original levels, a new bonus stage, and plenty of extras. I've wanted a Sonic game liek this to come out for ages, and I went in with exceedingly high expectations, and it met all of them, and then some! A relatively quick story from my current game playing as the Isle of Man:
This is a simple story of two brothers. Elud is the elder, a not particularly bright but very pious man. Serigi is the younger, a brilliant diplomat and generally likable guy. Family traditions include infighting, cursing the Welsh, attempting to conquer Ireland, actually conquering the Faroe Islands and watching as Norwegians take the Faroe Islands back.
This is a story of the women in their lives. Patyiker is Elud's wife, she's well connected to the kingdoms ruling the Balkan states and ambitious beyond the bounds of her actual talents. Hildemund is Serigi's wife, she's a charming young Frankish woman who one should not tick off lest one find a dagger in one's back.
This isn't really a story of their Uncle Gwrgant because his name is really annoying. Gwrgant never had any sons and his choice for an heir is either Elud or Serigi. Serigi was his chancellor and his ability to fabricate claims out of thin air resulted in a number of conquests for Gwrgant's forces. Gwrgant naturally chose Serigi to succeed him. In the meantime both Patyiker and Hildemund begun plotting the deaths of the brother they aren't married to. Gwrgant looks the other way regarding all this scheming. (I figured Patyiker isn't great at it and if Hildemund succeeded, well Gwrgant never really liked Elud anyway)
Serigi succeeds Gwrgant as Petty King of the Isle of Man and ruler of Ormond, Thormond, and Connacht(some of that conquering of Ireland has been working out), he reforms the Isle of Man into a Merchant Republic(the Petty Most Serene Republic of the Isle of Man). Pictland(aka Scotland) almost immediately declares war. Serigi struggles to defend it, taking out a massive loan from Jewish moneylenders to afford a band of Swiss Mercenaries. Combined Swiss-Manx forces defeat the Picts in battle and lay seige to a few Pictish castles before the coffers run dry and Manx forces retreat to the defensible Isle of Man. Manx forces defeat the Picts in battle again and Serigi takes the opportunity to spend some quiet time at the castle. He goes to a rather nice party attended by Elud and Patyiker. It is the last party he ever attends.
I forgot to tell Patyiker to stop trying to kill Serigi after I became Serigi. Oops. So I'm Elud now.
Elud makes peace with the lovable Picts, but his marraige with Patyiker is on the rocks. He was a devout Catholic and a friend to Serigi, he's not cool with Serigi's murder. A few years later he has the chance to seduce a woman at court. It's Hildemund. Serigi's widow. They have a child out of wedlock, an adorable daughter, under a year later a depressed Patyiker dies. Elud wastes no time in marrying Hildemund, already the mother of his youngest daughter. The two of them live happily ever after, she supports him in his old age and through his struggles with cancer while occasionally taking their frustrations out on the Irish nobility. Happiest ruling couple the Isle of Man has seen in a hundred and fifty years.
Typical Crusader Kings love story. Boy meets girl. Girl marries boy's brother. Boy meets and marries other girl. Other girl kills the brother. Boy inherits Isle of Man from brother. Boy meets girl again. Other girl dies. Boy marries girl. Boy and girl live happily ever after and conquer a little bit of Ireland.
Just a relatively quick example of why CK2 is awesome.
