A very well made RPG with an entertaining variety of handcrafted battles.
Pros:
- The turn based battles are fun and allow for a ton of viable strategies. You can specialize your character for tanking, rushing enemies in melee, or picking them off with bows. You can equip axes to pull away the shields of enemy tanks (badly needed on Insane difficulty, where you run into enemies with 100% block chance), or swords to bypass enemy damage resistance (which can also reach 100%). You can build a poison-focused squad that applies DoT effects on all enemies and just defends until everybody is dead, or a group where every party member can taunt, or heal, or buff, or, or, or... The game's classless skill system really works beautifully here, and is much better balanced that I originally expected. There are many bigger and more successful developers who should take a cue from Logic Artists here.
- The historical setting is perfectly sufficient to have some strange, surprising, and interesting RPG adventures. At a time when 90% of all new RPGs seem to be fantasy games, it feels good to play a game that tries to be grounded in the real world, and confronts the player with "real" people.
- The pacing is generally strong. The game's predecessor Expeditions: Conquistador often felt padded and bloated, with long stretches of running around gathering camping supplies and dealing with trivial random encounters. Expeditions: Viking feels much more tightly designed, with fewer, but more interesting battles replacing much of the busywork (there are still a lot of optional battles available at "Occupied Campsites"; I suggest that you skip all of those).
Cons:
- Weak AI and lack of challenge even on the hardest difficulty. I played the game after the latest patch, with every difficulty slider turned up to maximum. I also added a few self-imposed challenges on top of that: no knock-outs in battle, ever, and no injuries to party members or allied units, ever. I also played through 95% of the game in non-lethal mode, which prevents your party from landing critical hits, and had a main character with maxed out social skills and attributes. Despite this rather immense set of challenges, I still had a surprisingly easy time with most of the battles. The most noticeable problem is definitely the dumb AI, which occasionally wastes its actions on utterly pointless things, like using Cure (cures status effects) on a character who has no negative status effects and full health. I've also never seen an enemy archer do a move-shoot-move sequence, which is something that player characters can (and should) do.
- As a related issue: despite the good overall skill balance, the game just gives you too damn many skill points to play with. By the mid-game, I could accomodate all the available skill sets in my party, and by the endgame, I could double or triple up on many of these skills. And while the balance is generally good, there are a few abilities that should probably be nerfed - like the Bow skill "Cripple", which totally disables a character for one round (the tooltip is misleading) and does not allow a saving throw to resist it. Still, I don't want to criticize too much: despite all of these problems the combat always felt good and enjoyable.
- The camping system feels more like busywork than a genuinely interesting gameplay mechanic. I interviewed the developers two times before E:Vs release, and they were clearly very proud of the resource management and resting mechanics in their games. Personally, I find the resting to be extremely repetitive, totally unchallenging, and not even necessary. I fought many of the battles in the game with a party that was fatigued and starving, simply because I'd rather have a slightly longer and tougher battle than to bother trekking over to a camp site, sit through a loading screen, go through 12 hird members and make sure that they were all doing appropriate tasks, hit rest, watch them perform their tasks, and then go through another loading screen to the campaign map. The resting system just takes too much time and too many clicks for me to enjoy it.
- The dialogues are occasionally pretty awful, Some of these 8th century Vikings and Picts talk just like regular 21st century people who got snatched off the street and transformed into video game characters. But I understand that trying to adopt a different register and exotic mannerisms would have been a lot of work for the writers, and I doubt that it would have helped the game to sell any better.
- There should have been more skill and stat checks. E:V is mostly a combat-focused game, but the other, auxilliary gameplay systems are important to provide a sense of variety and diversion. For example, the game has an entertaining, but very short sequence where you go on a treasure hunt in a cave, squeezing through rocks, diving through water filled tunnels, etc., with your success depending on your party composition and stats. It would have been great to see a few more of these "adventure" segments. The social skills are also a little disappointing; I only found one single situation that required maximum Diplomacy skill, and that was to win an encounter that was the easiest battle on the whole map.
- Weirdly long loading times. This seems to be a common pattern among Unity games.
These are a lot of Cons, but they are not game-ruining problems; they are simply areas where the developers might offer some improvements in their next title. If you're looking for an entertaining turn-based combat RPG, Expeditions: Viking would be an excellent choice.

One of the best shooters I've played.
Devil Daggers is the perfect example of minimalism in game design. Limited graphics. Empty arena. Enemies move in predictable manners. Only one weapon. No health, no ammo, and only one power-up. No music!
It's a niche, I admit. If you're expecting anything more than an arcade-style score attack, you'll be rather miffed. For those after a real, intense, incredibly immersive challenge, this is it.
+ Incredibly smooth controls, all rebindable.
+ Reviewer has experienced no technical issues on a mid-range NVIDIA (920M). Smooth framerate.
+ Amazing sound. (Headphones are a MUST, or a surround-sound speaker system.)
+ Intuitive movement. Straferunning and rocket-jumping has been simulated in engine.
+ Replays and leaderboard built into engine. All scores on leaderboard have a replay attached!
- Only one level and one mode. Flat arena, timed survival.
- Graphically busy in late-game or when many enemies spawn.
- No character progression, story, upgrades, cosmetics. Only one Steam achievement.
I'd love to see an update (or hell, a DLC) that adds an alternative arena. Maybe another dozen enemies in a secondary game mode? What's here is great, but if setting high scores has never been your thing then you're going to get tired fast.

I personally think Oblivion is better than Skyrim, though Skyrim is less buggy and better in some ways. Obviously the graphics aren't as good as in Skyrim though they can be improved with mods if you don't like them. There are a few things that make Oblivion better than Skyrim in my opinion:
More spell types and the ability to create your own spells
More weapon/armour types
Weapon/armour degradation (must be repaired with hammers)
Better guild storylines (the Dark Brotherhood guild especially is amazing, pure art)
Bigger and more interesting cities (Imperial City is HUGE, so much stuff to steal as a thief)
Another big deal for me is proper class distinction. Oblivion is traditional to the fantasy RPG genre in that it has set classes (or you can make your own if you wish) such as warrior, mage, thief and many other hybrid classes such as spellsword (mixture of destructive magic and swords) and battlemage (mixture of heavy armour and supporting magic) and so on and so on. This is a big deal for me because in fantasy role-playing games your class is who/what you are. It defines your character. In Oblivion, if you take warrior (with primary attributes of strength and vitality) then you're a warrior, pure and simple. You can use magic and increase your magic attributes if you like, but you'll never be as good with it as a proper mage class, it will merely be a minor supporting aspect. Plus wearing armour in Oblivion makes magic spells less powerful; the heavier the armour the less powerful spells become. In Skyrim, the ability to be every class all at once made me feel like I didn't have a specific class/role. One moment I could be an awesome warrior with a big axe, the next moment I could take my armour off and be an awesome mage, and in the next slip on some light armour and use a bow and sneak and be an awesome thief/assassin. I feel more at home in the traditional RPG custom of specific classes. It feels natural to me because it's what those games have always been based around. Like in real life, everybody has a specific role, making each person feel unique in some way. In real life you have carpenters, salesmen, lawyers and so on and so on and in traditional RPG's you have warriors, mages, thieves, assassins, alchemists - everybody has a unique role.
There are some things I don't like about Oblivion though. The ruthless level-scaling means that when you are level 1, every other person/creature in the game is also level 1. When you are level 99, everybody else is level 99. You never feel truly in danger and you never feel truly heroic because everybody else is always just as strong as you are. Fortunately this is fixed perfectly in an amazing mod called Oscuro's Oblivion Overhaul - I highly recommend this mod. I would never play Oblivion without it. It removes level-scaling entirely and makes the world an extremely dangerous and harsh place for newbies, but as you gain levels you become higher level and more powerful. So at level 1, you may run in to a level 3 mage bandit who kicks your butt. But when you get to level 10 he is still level 3 and you can show him who's the boss.

But even without the included Shivering Isles and Knights of the Nine expansions there would have been plenty to do apart from saving Tamriel. Basically, you can pick the sort of thing you want to focus on and let everything else fall by the wayside, for now or forever.
The soundtrack is *amazing* and wonderfully complements the game's colourful, wide-open, lore-rich, populated world.
It also runs great in Wine, if configured correctly.

100% orange juice is a casual card/board game. That has a cute anime chibi theme to it, from the characters you play, to the cards you use.
Gameplay: 8
The game play here is pretty solid. You start off with a character, then you build a deck of cards that is used in the main game. Once everyone has made there decks the game will start. Once in the main game everyone's decks are placed into one pile in the middle of the current board. Which will be used to draw cards from. So that mean you can draw other players cards while they can draw your own. You'll find your self playing on different boards that can have a different setup each time you play. Each board has there own "board event" from doubling up on Star, cards, or losing stars, to being randomly teleported to a different square and much more. 
You have 6 different square types. Home, Card draw, star bonus, star lost, monsters, and teleports. most of these are self explanatory. Home is where your character starts the game off at. Home also is used to accept and complete missions also While it can heal you or anyone else for one hp if landed on it.  However one of the benefits about your own home is no matter what you roll if you end up going to it or passing it they game will allow you to stop at your own home and if you do so, you won't be able to use the rest of your movement. Monster squares are two fold. Monster Squares are events where you end up fighting a basic monster to gain more stars. But be careful they will fight back and knock you out resulting in you losing half your own stars. After so many turns every monster square will turn into a monster boss square which spawns harder monsters to take down but gives a greater star bonus when defeated. After a boss has been defeated all monster squares goes back to normal monster squares.
You start a new game off with one card that is drawn from the deck in the middle. You are able to get more by landing on the green squares. Some card require you to pay and/or have the right level to use it. While many different card types to be used like Traps, Hypers, battle, events, and boost. Each can effect the game differently while adding more strategy to your game plan.
Characters have there own character cards that shows there stats to attack, Defend, Evade and HP while some have card Ability’s. Every character has there own hyper card that is unique to them, However it is possible for other players to take this card from you and use it.
The goal of the game is two fold. Either win by having 200 or more stars, or winning fights between monsters and other players. At the start of the game each player starts off at level one. To be able to level up you must complete missions either by collection enough stars or winning enough fights. The high level you can become is level five.
Combat in this game is determine by a dice roll on a d6( a six sided die). When entering combat with a player or a monster your allowed to choose one card from your hand that can altar the fight, Keep in mind that only certain cards can be played during combat. The attacking player will always go first. While in combat your base stats will effect your rolls. When someone attacks the defending player or monster they have a chance of rolling either a Defend or an Evade roll. Each one plays out differently. While choosing a defend roll you Subtract your roll to the damage that is being inflicted on your character to a minimum of one damage. While Evading you MUST roll at least one number higher than the current attack number to avoid taking all damage, If you roll equal or less than the attack you will take the full on coming damage to your character. Both sides will be given a chance to attack and defend. However there can only be one attack and one defend roll for each side. There are cards that can effect this however. When fighting a fellow player, if you successfully knock them out you will gain half of there stars into your own pool. After a player is knocked out, every turn that comes they will need to roll to be brought back up, if they fail to get back up the rest of there turn is skipped.
Now the bad part about the game play is the RNG (Random number generator) factor. However do not let this discourage. There will be times you feel like the game is cheating you while other time you feel like things are playing out in your favor. If you get easily upset or take game seriously then this game is NOT for you. This game is a fun casual game that almost anyone can pick up and play. And If you don't mind the RNG factor then you might find this game to your liking.
When finishing your current game, every star you have collected will be added to your game profile to be used in the store. The store is where you buy booster packs, More characters, Color pallets for characters, and boards. However the bad part about the store is that you must level up your profile to unlock more stuff from with in the store. To do this you have to play online with either friends or random players. It's not much of a big deal really but it still would of been nice to have a leveling up system in single player for the people who are just wanting a fun quick game and not have to play with others. However this is still a minor thing.
Graphics: 7
The graphics in the game are very colourful with an anime style look and feel to them. All the characters are chibi form. The game has very playful and inviting graphics that is simple but yet nice to look at.
The only real problem i can see with the graphics is when you are playing on a board the background has the same repeating design over and over. It's nothing major. Some people may find it distracting or annoying.
Music: 8
The soundtrack is great mix of easy listening music, to upbeat techno, to anime style music. One thing that can be a problem is while playing the music can repeat it's self over and over again.
Story: 3
The story is all over the place. There is no real “story” being told here. Every character you can play as has a some what of mini-story to it. The story’s are mostly a random reason to play the game with other NPC's you end up meeting. Some of the reason can be cute and funny.
Online: -
I normally don't review online play for games. However with how the game is setup it forces you play online to unlock more stuff as I stated above. Over all it doesn't bother me that I have to play online. However I believe a game shouldn't force you into playing online to unlock everything. There are much worse examples out there that does this than this game does.
Final though. I give this game a 8 out of 10.

What is BasketBelle?
Well, BasketBelle is a simple piece of art where you control your main character with the four arrows and X to use the mechanics of basketball in an easy 2D platform adventure game.
There is not much to say about this game, it is very short but each chapter feels unique. It takes about an hour to play through the game for the first time, and then much less since you know how to do everything. You have to replay the two final chapters at least two times to get all achievements, which is a bit annoying but not too bad if you know what to do. All in all, it takes around 90-120 minutes to get all achievements.
Would I recommend BasketBelle? As a game, no. The gameplay is nice and a bit varied, but it is too short, Once you went through the game, you saw it all, there is no replay value.
As a piece of art, yes. Definitely play through it once, enjoy the (crazy but not too good) story, the art style and how the unusual visuals, the gameplay and the music fit together!
Recommended: Play through it if you have it. If you don't have it, wait for a good sale or skip this title entirely.

The Legend of Heroes: Trails in the Sky FC and SC combined create the best RPG experience of all time. Before playing FC my favorite RPG series was Fire Emblem. I love the Fire Emblem series for the huge amount of character interaction, the great gameplay, great music, great stories, extremely charming graphics/animations/art styles, and amazing replay value. In my opinon those features are what make RPGs the best video game genre.
Trails in the sky FC alone bests Fire Emblem in most of those aspects and is equal in art style and gameplay. Obviously two very different games but speaking in over all RPG experience. Add the Second Chapter (which picks up mere hours after FC's story making it basically the same game) and there is no longer any room for comparison. There is just too much (good meaty) content in Trails in the sky for any other RPG to compare. There are 13 games in the Fire emblem series and I believe there is more content in just these 2 games.
If you plan on trying out FC just prepare to sit back and read for hours on end. These games are mostly reading, they are RPGs after all. Don't go in expecting action packed gameplay or amazing AAA graphics. You are going to read, explore, talk to 100s of unique NPCs who all have something to say, read, do sidequests that have their own little storylines, read, and sometimes play through some satisfying turnbased combat (which in my opinon is on par with the fire emblem games)
Also Hard mode in SC is very challenging and really forces you to utilize the items/skills at your disposal immediately after the tutorial. If you are looking for a challenge then SC delivers. You can also choose Hard for FC as well although I haven't tried FC on hard.

Hi, I'm the token negative review, and I'm here to give you reasons why you SHOULDN'T get Trails SC.
Disclaimer: I'm a Trails fanboy and Trails FC is probably my favourite JRPG of all time; it might even be my favourite game, period...until I finish SC, anyways...
First things first: this game should be treated as an EXPANSION.  Yes, you can technically buy it on its own, but the game picks up right where Trails FC left off and you're gunna be pretty damn lost if you jump into this right away.
This game is VERY TEXT HEAVY.  VERY.  Try to find the picture of the scripts for the Trails in the Sky trilogy sometime; Trails SC is longer than the Lord of the Rings Trilogy (so says Kotaku) in terms of raw text.  This means lots of cutscenes, lots of sidequests with lengthy chats, and NPCs with walls of text unto themselves.  Technically this is a selling point, but for some it's a killer.
2006.  The original release date for this game was in flipping 2006.  At a time when Japan barely cared about PC gaming.  If you can't stand old games, or indies that style themselves after old games, you're gunna have a bad time.  Also, Anime asethetic, but the promo art should've made that clear already.
The interface is kinda clunky.  It's either arrow keys + ZXCV + Enter, or you can do it entirely with your mouse; you can also use a gamepad, but that produces the same result as arrows + ZXCV (I've played the PSP version on a Vita).  You should probably remember to use ESC for any KBM control set, too.
The problem with arrows + hotkeys is that, even with the PSP version, navigating the menus you inevitably have to handle requires a ton of keystrokes for simple things, especially equipment and consumable usage (so many flipping consumables).  In larger fights this can sometimes mean cycling through every unit to pick the right target.  If you're a programmer, leme put it this way: your single-action algorithm is O(n^2).
The problem with using mouse controls is that a lot of things like to move around.  Your cursor frequently warps when you open menus, and the combat camera repeatedly zooms in and out, constantly altering your cursor position and making it hard to play with speed and precision.  The cursor warping can be convenient for some things, like quickly moving through the Save/Load menus, but at other times it'll arbitrarily close menus because you didn't move your mouse at a perfect horizontal.
Combat is actually a pretty significant debate among Trails fans, with most opinions ranging from "rather bad" to "pretty decent."  I haven't personally found anyone who thinks the combat is "actually good/great," and if they exist they're fairly few in number.  All I'm going to say here is this: turn-based, initiative system, tile movement, plain flat boxes for combat arenas.
TL:DR
Old game with clunky controls and walls of text.  If you're looking for the reasons why you SHOULD buy this game, there are a billion other reviews for that.  I'm just here to provide the counterpoints.
EDIT:
Yes, this is a heavily unbalanced review.  Thing is, going through the "most useful" reviews, they're ALL heavily unbalanced in FAVOUR of the game, with no consideration given to people who aren't in the target audience for Trails.
Trails is not a perfect game.  Don't try to pretend it is.  I'll suck this game's shlong any day of the week if you want me to, but people need to be informed about the things that they won't enjoy, and the current "front page" as it were completely fails at that.

Imagine the hacking minigame from Bioshock, except that you rotate existing tiles instead of placing existing ones. Also imagine that you control Frogger, who hand-rotates these tiles while listening to techno and dodging traffic on a highway.
If you dismiss indie games as being EITHER fast, tough-as-nails platformers OR artsy atmospheric environments, I highly encourage you to give this game a shot - this is a fine example of original gameplay that requires split-second precision and risk/reward decision making. I had beaten (not gold-medalled) the single-player campaign in about 4 hours, but don't take that as a knock against the game - I preferred to play in 10-minute intervals to give my nerves a chance to recover from the frantic pace, and I haven't played much of the other modes yet.
The soundtrack by Ian Hicks is extremely well done - 7 tracks that nicely complement the setting and gameplay that are well worth purchasing and adding to your mp3 player. The 8th, which is used in the trailer, feels out of place and I've removed it from my playlist. Recommended.
Speed and precision required: Yes
Straightforward 100%: No
Soundtrack format: DLC, mp3

Shadow Warrior, not surpringly, plays a lot like Duke Nukem 3D.  Only with some real improvements.  The weapons in this game are more varried, and include some staples of later games that originated here (Sticky Bombs, Railgun).  The katana makes a wonderful melee weapon in this.  Other weapons range from shurikens to a missle launcher with a little bit of extra oomph.
The engine was also enhanced.  Free-moving vehicles (though other games, such as Necrodrome, had those before this, and the vehicles in this are literally build as part of the stage, just the floor elevated), water you could see - and shoot - into, level on level 3D.
As for the story, it's pretty basic 90's FPS fare.  Threadbare but enough to get you through the game.  Level designs are fun and in some places quite nice to look at (for the time).  The expansion packs are both mostly more of the same.  The updated engine allows this game to run better on modern machines, including wide screen support etc.
There are problems.  No multi-player is featured in this.  And we are still missing the unreleased expansion, Deadly Kiss, despite supposedly having the assets available to them.  But for the most part, it's a fun retro FPS.

I haven't progressed past level 7 on the starting zone so far, so this review might change later on.  What I can say is that I love the freedom this game offers you so far as just wandering around, interacting with NPC's and the environment, and that most questlines are optional.  There is a main questline you must finish along the way, but mostly at your pace.  This feels like fairly bug-free turn based combat, decent character customization, and the group play option is way more flexible than I expected.  It's nice that my biggest gripe about the game is that the tooltips are lacking in helping you quickly understand what skills and abilities do for you.  I'd also like to see a confirmation dialogue when selecting attribute points and skill choices, but again, it is nice that those are my biggest gripes about the game.  It really is a fun game, and I've started over a few times to see how I like the different classes.  I love that there are no rules for multi-classing!  If you are a fan of turn based combat, old school RPG feel, and freedom to kill and/or explore, this is the game for you.

A deliciously comfortable RPG experience, basically. Less dreary and washed-out visually than Skyrim (if that's something you care about) although the latter does look better in general. Despite Oblivion's notoriously absurd NPC conversations Skyrim's towns in particular feel more inhabited; nobody in Oblivion really seems to have a job, for example.
Not too fond of the way the entire game world's population seems to be levelling up along with you. It's all easy going at first, but eventually you'll have random fort-squatting bandits with peculiarly super-precious equipment. Would much prefer having areas that're difficult from the get-go, leaving them temptingly accessible but barely survivable for new players. (As always, there're mods for that.)
The main chunk of the main quest gets a bit dull, too -- the excursions into Oblivion to close one gate after another play out roughly the same, just with varying levels of where-do-I-go-now.
But even without the included Shivering Isles and Knights of the Nine expansions there would have been plenty to do apart from saving Tamriel. Basically, you can pick the sort of thing you want to focus on and let everything else fall by the wayside, for now or forever.
The soundtrack is *amazing* and wonderfully complements the game's colourful, wide-open, lore-rich, populated world.
It also runs great in Wine, if configured correctly.

100% orange juice is a casual card/board game. That has a cute anime chibi theme to it, from the characters you play, to the cards you use.
Gameplay: 8
The game play here is pretty solid. You start off with a character, then you build a deck of cards that is used in the main game. Once everyone has made there decks the game will start. Once in the main game everyone's decks are placed into one pile in the middle of the current board. Which will be used to draw cards from. So that mean you can draw other players cards while they can draw your own. You'll find your self playing on different boards that can have a different setup each time you play. Each board has there own "board event" from doubling up on Star, cards, or losing stars, to being randomly teleported to a different square and much more. 
You have 6 different square types. Home, Card draw, star bonus, star lost, monsters, and teleports. most of these are self explanatory. Home is where your character starts the game off at. Home also is used to accept and complete missions also While it can heal you or anyone else for one hp if landed on it.  However one of the benefits about your own home is no matter what you roll if you end up going to it or passing it they game will allow you to stop at your own home and if you do so, you won't be able to use the rest of your movement. Monster squares are two fold. Monster Squares are events where you end up fighting a basic monster to gain more stars. But be careful they will fight back and knock you out resulting in you losing half your own stars. After so many turns every monster square will turn into a monster boss square which spawns harder monsters to take down but gives a greater star bonus when defeated. After a boss has been defeated all monster squares goes back to normal monster squares.
You start a new game off with one card that is drawn from the deck in the middle. You are able to get more by landing on the green squares. Some card require you to pay and/or have the right level to use it. While many different card types to be used like Traps, Hypers, battle, events, and boost. Each can effect the game differently while adding more strategy to your game plan.
Characters have there own character cards that shows there stats to attack, Defend, Evade and HP while some have card Ability’s. Every character has there own hyper card that is unique to them, However it is possible for other players to take this card from you and use it.
The goal of the game is two fold. Either win by having 200 or more stars, or winning fights between monsters and other players. At the start of the game each player starts off at level one. To be able to level up you must complete missions either by collection enough stars or winning enough fights. The high level you can become is level five.
Combat in this game is determine by a dice roll on a d6( a six sided die). When entering combat with a player or a monster your allowed to choose one card from your hand that can altar the fight, Keep in mind that only certain cards can be played during combat. The attacking player will always go first. While in combat your base stats will effect your rolls. When someone attacks the defending player or monster they have a chance of rolling either a Defend or an Evade roll. Each one plays out differently. While choosing a defend roll you Subtract your roll to the damage that is being inflicted on your character to a minimum of one damage. While Evading you MUST roll at least one number higher than the current attack number to avoid taking all damage, If you roll equal or less than the attack you will take the full on coming damage to your character. Both sides will be given a chance to attack and defend. However there can only be one attack and one defend roll for each side. There are cards that can effect this however. When fighting a fellow player, if you successfully knock them out you will gain half of there stars into your own pool. After a player is knocked out, every turn that comes they will need to roll to be brought back up, if they fail to get back up the rest of there turn is skipped.
Now the bad part about the game play is the RNG (Random number generator) factor. However do not let this discourage. There will be times you feel like the game is cheating you while other time you feel like things are playing out in your favor. If you get easily upset or take game seriously then this game is NOT for you. This game is a fun casual game that almost anyone can pick up and play. And If you don't mind the RNG factor then you might find this game to your liking.
When finishing your current game, every star you have collected will be added to your game profile to be used in the store. The store is where you buy booster packs, More characters, Color pallets for characters, and boards. However the bad part about the store is that you must level up your profile to unlock more stuff from with in the store. To do this you have to play online with either friends or random players. It's not much of a big deal really but it still would of been nice to have a leveling up system in single player for the people who are just wanting a fun quick game and not have to play with others. However this is still a minor thing.
Graphics: 7
The graphics in the game are very colourful with an anime style look and feel to them. All the characters are chibi form. The game has very playful and inviting graphics that is simple but yet nice to look at.
The only real problem i can see with the graphics is when you are playing on a board the background has the same repeating design over and over. It's nothing major. Some people may find it distracting or annoying.
Music: 8
The soundtrack is great mix of easy listening music, to upbeat techno, to anime style music. One thing that can be a problem is while playing the music can repeat it's self over and over again.
Story: 3
The story is all over the place. There is no real “story” being told here. Every character you can play as has a some what of mini-story to it. The story’s are mostly a random reason to play the game with other NPC's you end up meeting. Some of the reason can be cute and funny.
Online: -
I normally don't review online play for games. However with how the game is setup it forces you play online to unlock more stuff as I stated above. Over all it doesn't bother me that I have to play online. However I believe a game shouldn't force you into playing online to unlock everything. There are much worse examples out there that does this than this game does.
Final though. I give this game a 8 out of 10.

This game is poetry in motion.  I remember begging all of my friends to vote for this game on greenlight.  I had never played it before on Desura or otherwise until it came out on Steam.  I was hoping for an extremely unique experience and i was not disappointed.
Basketbelle is a game of its own.  If it were to be categorized it would be....well it would be it's own genre.  One could say "music based", or "platformer", "puzzle",  or even "sports".   It has the basics of all of those, but in reality it is none of those in a complete sense.  Music plays throughout the game, and to the beat of your dribbles, but the game is not totally dependent on that.  There are platforming elements in the game, but those become more based on solving puzzles than the platforming itself.
You shoot baskets to complete levels and beat enemies, but those baskets are just as much about the puzzles and platforming as they are about the shots themselves.   The music also plays its role in how you play.
The graphics in this game are what you may call "minimalistic" but in the many many years ive been gaming i've never seen an art style/graphics quite like this.  The look it has is truly unique.
The game itself is a complete circle of multiple elements from multiple genres put together to create a totally unique game.  It is very short (I beat it in less than an hour) but if you like fresh, well made games this is well worth the price of admission for 5 bucks.

Woodle Tree is not a game that was without potential. The developers seem to have tried to create something good, but there are sadly some major issues holding it back
Woodle Tree Adventure is not entirely unpleasing to look at. While the models are simple, and the colouring is relatively flat, everything is stylized in a way that gives it some consistency.
Sadly the often flat colours makes it needlessly hard to judge your exact position in relation to other objects, which makes platforming annoying. This could have been fixed by giving the ground textures some more definition, which would have made it easier to judge distances.
The sound design is lackluster. Your weapon, a leaf, makes an unimpressive sound. While it's understandable that a leaf does not make a "clang" noise, giving your attacks a stronger sound effect would have helped give the game some more life. Right now the game just feels empty due to its lackluster sound.
Woodle Tree Adventure tries to be a simple 3D platformer, and the controls themselves work well enough. You jump, you attack and you move around, and it feels natural. Sadly the camera angels work against you. Moving up, down, left or right in relation to the camera is easy enough, but sadly the camera angles are often so that narrow platforms are at a very slight (and hard to see) angle, which means that if you just hold up, down, left or right you'll fall off. So you constantly need to nudge yourself in the right direction, which is just tedious, and due to the flat colouring, it's hard to actually tell if a platform is at an angle, and how big it is, when the angle is slight. This is really the biggest problem with the game, and it kills it.
Woodle tree would be an inoffensive little 3D platformer, had the sound effects & camera angles been better. It would not have been a masterpiece, but as it stands, it's a bad game. And that's a shame, because it feels like the developer really wanted to create something good.

Basketbelle is a great non-traditional platformer.  It has a beautiful art-style, a touching and engaging narrative and a wonderful soundtrack.  The basketball themed platforming gameplay is enjoyable, but I also don't think that the gameplay is what really drives this game, rather the narrative and ambience.  The game itself is around 30 minutes long, and I easily got all the achievement in the game within an hour.
I can't recommend this game to everyone, as I know not everyone shares my values when it comes to games.  While the game has 3 endings, after seeing all of them, I don't think there is much replay value.  And while the game is very inexpensive (and in my opinion, well worth full price), others may not find the amount of gameplay justifiable for the price.  In my opinion, though, there are a few games (like Gone Home and Thomas was Alone) that allow you to look back and value the experience as a whole long after you have completed the game, and Basketbelle is another addition to that list.  So, if you are the type of person that resented Gone Home for the game-time/money ratio, than you may not be that into this game (although 5 bucks is hard to beat).
My other (somewhat) warning is that I think reading the genre as platformer may be somewhat misleading to peoples' expectations.  This game is definitely unique, and plays differently than any other platformer.  It is not a difficult game by any stretch of the imagination, and I think that with many games (like Super Meat Boy) the gameplay comes first, where as with Basketbelle, the gameplay is very much secondary, and is a vehicle for the experience.  The gameplay is good, but definitely secondary.
Anyways, that is enough trying to appeal to people that are unlike me in a review, if you are at all an 'indie game nerd', this game is a no-brainer.  I loved the concept, the aesthetic, the story, and how all of these were carried out.  I also think that the price is worth it for the EP alone, this game has a great soundtrack.  There were also some neat little touches, like, when your character idled, the sound of him dribbling the ball formed a clave against the soundtrack.  I decided to play this game after really enjoying Soundodger+ (also by Studio Bean) and its sound track, and was not disappointed at all.  If you want to try something new and fresh, this is definitely a game to check out.

Very good game with excellent graphics. Comparable to old school RPGs, with one major exception--- The game is faster than those old school RPGs. What i mean is that the movement is fast (during the normal out-of combat exploration) and you can change your combat speed (And i absolutely recommend everyone to do this once you start getting into the motion of the game as it makes it so much more fluid and fun). This is a *great* game for those who want to try and get into old schoold RPGs but could never get over the fact that they were very slow.
The game is surprisingly easy if you build your characters well. The story is easy to follow and the voice acting is great. One thing to note is that the game isnt fully voice acted; only some dialog is voice acted and the small talk between your companions are voice acted; other than that you will be greeted with texts to read through and i do recommend reading through them.
One annoying aspect of the game is trying to juggle all your companions' morale as pretty much every choice you make would affect their morale; and this in turn affects their resistances. Another thing that i find tedious (not terribly annoying) is the wound system. The wound system is great as you are penalised for getting you or your companions down during combat. However it isnt terribly unbearable as, again, once you get comfortable with the game and you've built your character well, you hardly go down; so no wounds to worry about.
tl;dr : Very good game. Highly recommend if you're trying to get into the world of old school rpg's as the game is rather fast paced. Interesting story and setting. Beautiful graphics.

Hi, I'm the token negative review, and I'm here to give you reasons why you SHOULDN'T get Trails SC.
Disclaimer: I'm a Trails fanboy and Trails FC is probably my favourite JRPG of all time; it might even be my favourite game, period...until I finish SC, anyways...
First things first: this game should be treated as an EXPANSION.  Yes, you can technically buy it on its own, but the game picks up right where Trails FC left off and you're gunna be pretty damn lost if you jump into this right away.
This game is VERY TEXT HEAVY.  VERY.  Try to find the picture of the scripts for the Trails in the Sky trilogy sometime; Trails SC is longer than the Lord of the Rings Trilogy (so says Kotaku) in terms of raw text.  This means lots of cutscenes, lots of sidequests with lengthy chats, and NPCs with walls of text unto themselves.  Technically this is a selling point, but for some it's a killer.
2006.  The original release date for this game was in flipping 2006.  At a time when Japan barely cared about PC gaming.  If you can't stand old games, or indies that style themselves after old games, you're gunna have a bad time.  Also, Anime asethetic, but the promo art should've made that clear already.
The interface is kinda clunky.  It's either arrow keys + ZXCV + Enter, or you can do it entirely with your mouse; you can also use a gamepad, but that produces the same result as arrows + ZXCV (I've played the PSP version on a Vita).  You should probably remember to use ESC for any KBM control set, too.
The problem with arrows + hotkeys is that, even with the PSP version, navigating the menus you inevitably have to handle requires a ton of keystrokes for simple things, especially equipment and consumable usage (so many flipping consumables).  In larger fights this can sometimes mean cycling through every unit to pick the right target.  If you're a programmer, leme put it this way: your single-action algorithm is O(n^2).
The problem with using mouse controls is that a lot of things like to move around.  Your cursor frequently warps when you open menus, and the combat camera repeatedly zooms in and out, constantly altering your cursor position and making it hard to play with speed and precision.  The cursor warping can be convenient for some things, like quickly moving through the Save/Load menus, but at other times it'll arbitrarily close menus because you didn't move your mouse at a perfect horizontal.
Combat is actually a pretty significant debate among Trails fans, with most opinions ranging from "rather bad" to "pretty decent."  I haven't personally found anyone who thinks the combat is "actually good/great," and if they exist they're fairly few in number.  All I'm going to say here is this: turn-based, initiative system, tile movement, plain flat boxes for combat arenas.
TL:DR
Old game with clunky controls and walls of text.  If you're looking for the reasons why you SHOULD buy this game, there are a billion other reviews for that.  I'm just here to provide the counterpoints.
EDIT:
Yes, this is a heavily unbalanced review.  Thing is, going through the "most useful" reviews, they're ALL heavily unbalanced in FAVOUR of the game, with no consideration given to people who aren't in the target audience for Trails.
Trails is not a perfect game.  Don't try to pretend it is.  I'll suck this game's shlong any day of the week if you want me to, but people need to be informed about the things that they won't enjoy, and the current "front page" as it were completely fails at that.

The long awaited sequel to Legend of Heroes: Trails in the Sky FC, SC succeeds in upping the ante in almost all forms over its predecessor. More party members, new battle actions, spells and S-Crafts (limit breaks), new quests that utilize new item systems, and of course a continuation from the jaw dropping finale of the first game. Containing new content brought over from the PSP version, as well as HD portraits and assets from the Japanese Playstation 3 version, this is arguably the most definitive version of the game next to the PS3 version which never made it out of Japan (PS3 portaits look ugly anyway, but they do get full voice acting whereas this version only has battle voices).
For those just learning about this series, Trails in the Sky is a Japanese Role Playing game series with a heavy focus on Story, characters and exploration. For this reason, it is HIGHLY advised that FC (short for First Chapter) is played before this one. Sc does not feature a catch up feature that reminds you of the events of the first game, so new players will be fairly lost, in addition to having key parts of the final act of FC spoiled for them.
If you are looking for a JRPG series with a lot of heart, a LOT of dailogue, great characters and great story, Trails in the Sky is where its at. Also, the battle systems are turn based for those who either like/can't stand that sort of thing.

The game is pretty amateur, but that's part of it's charm.
Most gamers these days are spoiled by AAA games that have perfected formulas and are made with millions of dollars and hundreds of talented people. I started gaming with the Atari 2600 and I can tell you what a real bad game is.
Woodle Tree Adventures is not a bad game, it merely is an ambitious game made by one person and it hits more highs than lows... at least for the prize. It's cheap.
First the bad: The camera is the worst part of this game. The levels are floating in the sky and you can easily fall and have to start all over again (you keep everything you've collected which is nice though). The animations are slow and the enemies are more annoying than challenging.
The good: Good graphics. Game ran at 60 frames per second for me. Nice enough music. The levels were challenging but never felt unfair despite the bad camera. There are a lot of cute touches like ladybugs and other creatures.
This game is great just to see what a single person can do. Making games is hard, but making a 3D platformer is very very difficult. You might not care, but I do and playing a flawed albeit perfectly enjoyable game made by just one person makes it so much more interesting. Also it's cheap.

This game still has a lot of rough edges, but overall has some very promising systems and brings in Zelda-style dungeons into the mix of the Survival Sandbox genre.   The atmosphere and environments are excellent, the thrall system lends itself to an interesting dynamic where you can eventually build up your own personal kingdom, and all-in-all it feels quite different from the other Survival Sandboxes out there once you get into the meat of the game.
Private servers with friends are unfortunately a hassle right now to set up, but they are doable.  Co-op mode is not advised at all due to the horrid leashing that they use, likely due to this game being out on consoles too.
The skill system is a detriment in the sense that you're forced to specialize or else ignore learning all optional crafts.  They spread it out way too much IMO as some skills will give you multiple new things to craft while others only give you one weapon/armor piece/etc... which doesn't make sense beyond forcibly extending the grind and forcing specializations.
There's still a lot of glitchyness and the game feels like it still has a lot of work to do, but at the very least this game is worth it when it's on sale for ~$20.

Conan exiles the latest Conan the Barbarian IP  offering by Funcom  is a survival game, that is actually somewhat different from the dozens of gun and zombies survival games that flood steam early access on any given Tuesday., the combat system while clunky shows promise already,  despite the planned combat revamp replacing it in entirety with a supposedly even better system, which can only improve the gameplay.
The building system is one of my favourites in a survival game, simple snap-together parts allow you to build anything from a small hut to a massive fortress limited only by your ability to defend it.
Upcoming patches will bring a horde mode which very much like 7 Days to Die brings a reoccurring PvE threat against players bases.
So if I like it so much, why did I uninstall?
the simple answer is bugs and glitches, the game is in early access alpha so they are to be expected, but that still doesn't remove the annoyance of losing 2 weeks work due to a bug which causes gameplay to become impossible, some major recent issues I will outline below.
Cooking like a Lobster!
The tempature system in conan exiles gives a nice surival element, the threat of being baked, or frozen giving an extra challenge when setting off for the least hospitable of places, the system even has varying stages of extremes form mild stamina or hunger debuffs, to health reducing heatstroke and hypothermia, drinking water, swimming being in doors or standing by fires can chill you down or heat you up, when working correctly, a recent bug saw many players unable to wander from their door as even  walking naked owuld see you rapidly overheating, I tested swimming during this bug and boiled alive in the lake.
I believe I can Fly!
The fall damage system is needed to avoid epic mountaintop dive into other players bases, I get that, but to lose 50% health when simply jumping up and down? there are several glitched areas in the game where you can risk dying from a simple 2-foot drop, a sprained ankle sure if you land funny, but death?
Cheaters never..never mind.
cheating right now in Conan exiles is rampant, out of control and spoiling the fun of thousands of players, and that's after massive boosts to the anti-cheat systems, it was worse before, much worse, but it's still bad, while each update does address issues, it will be a fair few before cheating is under control.
DIY Improvement.
Steam Workshop is thankfully part of Conan exiles, which open up a world of much-needed content and fixes, the Age of Calamitous makes the game so much better and closer to what it should have been, to begin with, with vendor,s currency, new building parts, factions and ai changes it should all be core.
Worth a buy?
After all this I must say yes, at sale prices personally I suggest a sale price purchase and wait till the full release to avoid being burned out rebuilding the same base/character over and over due to bugs, but if you buy and play or buy and wait, I hope this review helps you see the good and bad points with this title.

You have probably already played a similar game to this if you grew up in the 1990s or early 2000s. There's Duke Nukem, Power Slave, Doom, Blood and finally Shadow Warrior.
The mechanics between each game are pretty similar: a somewhat interesting protagonist armed to the teeth is confronted by hordes of things determined to slaughter him as he searches large, sprawling levels for keys to progress only hindered now and then by the occasional boss. That sentence could have described any of those games.
I have played all these games to certain degrees but Shadow Warrior is on the better side. It's heavily Asian themed, chock-full of stereotypes and tropes of older Asian/ninja action films. The protagonist, Lo Wang, is honestly more enjoyable to play as than even Duke Nukem so there's that.
This game is a redux which means it's suited for modern computers. In that regard it does its job with only a few new changes here and there (better OST, smoother graphics) but it's still the same game basically.
I would recommend this to fans of the early 1990s shooters. If you like them you will like this. If you're new to them it is a hit or miss.

This game has a somewhat shakey beginning, gratuitous amounts of farming, and a steep difficulty curve, But if you stick with it you'll have a very memorable experience. As you progress you'll eventually even feel EMOTION. When was the last time a Free-to-Play game gave you that?
With plenty of customization, you can find a playstyle that is truly unique to you. Somehow DE has managed to not only make every Warframe feel different and singular, but weapons and companions too. None of the weapons feel like "this is the same sword but with different stats".
On top of that, every graphical aspect in the game is so damn beautiful. The Tenno themselves look sleek and stylish, of course, but then you get a look at the enemies and their lairs. Let's look at the first enemeis you meet. The Grineer are initially repulsive (mainly thanks to your hideous meeting with Vor, who gives not the best of first impressions), but upon closer inspection you start to notice all the beautiful little details in their ship designs, their surroundings, their treatment of nature, in them themselves. It gorgeously paints a fully-realized tragic culture of industrial exploitation and overzealous cloning, barely surviving in a system that has left them behind.
...Of course, all Grineer are horrible people though and need to be exterminated.
All in all, Warframe is the best F2P game on the market right now. You have no reason not to try it out. Give it a shot and you might just fall in love.

As has been pointed out in comments for this review, the developers - Christian Whitehead, Headcannon and PagodaWest - are probably not responsible for the game's plaguing issue. From the little I've played and everything I've heard from the console releases, they have done some stellar work which is tragically undermined by some abrasive DRM they seemingly had no say about.
---
Immediately upon release the game has been found to contain a restrictive anti-consumer measure known as Denuvo. Worse, the End User License Agreement that is required to install the game does NOT mention this. The closest it comes to it is the following section:
16. TECHNICAL PROTECTION MEASURES
The technical protection measures of the Product may require you to download certain data to your device in order to authenticate the Product. If you disable or otherwise tamper with the technical protection measures, the Product may not operate properly and you are in material breach of this Agreement.
This seems innocent enough, but consider that the predecessor of Denuvo - SecuROM, made by the same group - once managed to permanently break both a new DVD drive and a reasonably new SSD drive of one of my past machines.
I am beyond disgusted that this was installed without any warning.
Fortunately I pre-ordered the game after the PC version was delayed, avoiding the Sonic 1 "gift" that was tied to Mania and broke the refund process. This meant I could wait two weeks to give Sega a chance to remove Denuvo, and refunded the game when they did not.
This game should be avoided at all costs until a Denuvo-free installation is offered and independent analysis confirms that it is completely removed. Sega should unreservedly apologise for any distress and all damage this astonishing mistake may cause their most enthusiastic paying customers.
Sega have responded to suggest the lack of DRM warning on the store page or EULA was an innocent mistake, which has been strongly questioned. At best it was careless, at worst it was purposefully duplicitous by leaving out a notice that would have prevented many users pre-ordering. Some have even suggested that the two week delay and the Sonic 1 compensation were measures to block refund attempts, but that seems a little too hard to believe for me. Predictably they offered no apologies.
One other thing worth mentioning; though it is not responsible for the always-online requirement, Denuvo DOES regularly "phone home" an authentication server to allow the game to be played. If that server disappears, the PC version of the game will expire for everyone. Users are rightly complaining that this game is presently not a purchase but a rental of unknown duration.
Just under 7 days after release, Denuvo has been defeated. Walking. Watching the sun slowly rise, it could've been a scene from a thousand years ago- with no cars, no lights, no noise but the animals and wind through the trees.
Human interference seemed so minute, I barely noticed the subtle gunfire in the background, the cracked and blistered road I walked across.
Then suddenly-
CRACK.
Something small and fast whizzes past my head like a bee.
No time to check.
I hold shift and book it.
There's a van nearby. Maybe two metres, maybe four.
I make a line straight for it.
CRACK.
I hear the bullet thump into the road. A plume of dust floats past the van i'm hiding behind.
I pull my gun out from it's holster.
It's a 357 magnum revolver. Condition is terrible, and rust visibly coats the gun like fungus on a tree.
Three shots. Better make them count.
Pull the hammer back, ready to fire.
I hold it steady, creeping my way to the edge of the van.
I peak out the side. Slowly. Carefully. Don't make it obvious.
Binoculars out.
In front of me is a hill. Tall and green, with a thick layer of grass and foliage covering the top like mould.
Something flashes in my eyes. Movement. I track it like a sniper.
The grass is moving, alive like some unknown mutated creature of the zone.
I look closer.
Whoever it is, his outift blends in well with the greenery. He evidently hasn't noticed me yet, and he's moving down the hill no doubt for a better view.
On his back is a long gun. Maybe a rifle, maybe a shotgun. It's metallic sheen stands out like a sore thumb amongst the natural hues surrounding it.
I check my gun again. Yeah. Definitely just three shots.
I wait.
He reaches the edge of the hill. Cautious. Careful.
Starts running.
Not close enough yet.
As soon as he goes past the van, that's when I'll start moving.
From over his shoulder he reveals his gun to be a shotgun. The long barrelled 'over-under' type.
It'd be deadly if I give him the chance to use it.
His aproach is swift, not wanting to be caught out in the open road, completely disregarding the van I could be hiding behind.
Now.
I slowly creep to the back of the van.
Small, miniscule steps mark my way as I go, gun aimed with an intense trigger finger.
It finally centres over his head.
I stand up.
Calmly walk out into the road. Gun still trained on his head.
I wait until he notices something. The subtle echo of footsteps, or just good situational awareness, he eventually hazards a look behind him.
"ANNU CHEEKI BREEKI IVV DAMKE," I scream in real life, as I hit mouse1.
The gun jerks back as a plume of smoke appears at the front end of the barrel, and my vision goes hazy at the edges for a moment.
Then it happens again. Then again. What? What the hell is happening? The same sounds, the same bullet sound, over and over again until -
"X-ray engine has stopped working. Windows is trying to find a solution to the problem,"

Legit, they throw unique concepts into every level without ever really utilizing them, they're broken mechanics at that point and only serve to make the levels worse.
Many times if you press ANY buttons during sections that genuinely don't look like you aren't supposed to push anything (this includes moving the direction Sonic is being thrusted) you'll die, and what you're supposed to do is AS SOON, as a specific section comes up and you touch it, let go of the controller, or else you're gonna fly off the map and die.

I've never been a big fan of sports. Despite being extremely competitive and athletic there's just something about traditional sports that bores me to tears. That said, there's always been something almost ethereal to me about shooting hoops with a basketball, transcending my typical dislike of sports into something simply delightful. BasketBelle sort of taps into that sort of feeling, beginning as a basic basketball game but quickly veering into strange and imaginative directions with only an ever bouncing sphere to keep us grounded.
There's a very heartfelt elegance to BasketBelle, as if the adventure we're going on is as unknown and limitless to the developer as it is to us. Though it takes but thirty minutes to play through, every moment of the experience is so creative and sweetly framed that it conveys a far more meaningful and touching narrative than its brief length would have you expect. The relationship between the nameless protagonist and his little sister, Belle, is beautiful in its playful innocence, not needing to be complex or troubled to turn these faceless purple people into characters I could relate to and which made me smile.
Sure, BasketBelle's gameplay is fairly limited, its controls anything but smooth, and its length incredibly brief, but none of that really mattered to me. The imagination and love flowing through the constantly evolving journey was all I needed to allow me to sink into its gorgeous backgrounds as I dribbled with alien monsters, learned to fly, and bonded with my sister all in time for bed. I would have gladly spent much longer in such a delightful world, but what's here is an almost perfect expression of a developer's odd idea that turned into something rather lovely. Good show, Bean!

An hour into the game, it's pretty damn obvious why it took forever for SC to be released in English.
It was worth the wait.
All right, all joking aside, a more serious review:
I haven't actually finished the game but -- 20 hours into it, I'm just BARELY starting chapter two. And if there's nine chapters, I'm pretty sure the amount of playtime for SC is going to be double or even triple that of FC (I averaged about 45 hours in FC; 90 in two playthroughs). There's TONS of content in the game and, if you are playing the game with an imported save from FC, it's worth it to talk to all the NPCs. They actually remember you! And stuff you did! There's even a SC achievement for talking to a specific NPC multiple times!
Even aside from the frankly remarkable amount of effort that went into integrating the two games (enough I was grateful I replayed FC a few weeks before SC's launch), the story itself is compelling, the character interactions are great, and I spent pretty much every cut scene going "why am I not fraps'ing this????" Even more, there's enough variation to make replay worth it as there's a choice early on if you want to travel with Schera or Agate as your primary companion (basically filling the space Joshua did in FC); I understand the main jist of the quests, main, side, and hidden, aren't changed but the interactions and dialogue do have some differences depending on your choice (for the record, the Agate path which I'm playing is great and every single interaction between Agate and Olivier is basically magic).
As far as game play, there's a lot less bugs than I would expect from a freshly launched game; especially since I remember some of the gamebreaking bugs of FC's launch. Basically the only thing that actually effects gameplay is the lack of chest phases (which I read on the forums that will be fixed in a later patch?). There's about five or six different chest phrases that seem to be on rotation, rather than individual phases of the first game. Something that's a minor disappointment but ultimately I'd rather have the game than the return of Chairman Meow.

BasketBelle is a short "art game" based on basketball with approximately 30 minutes worth of playtime. While the exact game genre varies depending on your current objective, it usually varies between a puzzle game with mild platforming elements and an action game in which you have to dodge obstacles.
Generally I'm not the biggest fan of art games, but the scenes of the main character with his family were well-done and clicked with me, and the plot steadily getting more and more over-the-top was pretty great, too. The music is also amazingly synchronized to the gameplay action, as apparently the game design started out as an experiment in, well, synchronizing music with gameplay action.
I wholeheartedly recommend BasketBelle if you're in the mood for a short and well-crafted interactive experience - the only real downside is that it doesn't have all that much replay value and is only about 30 minutes long, but on the other hand, that's exactly how long it should be.

A game from the simpler times where just having a gimmicky concept, controversial content and a bunch of cultural references cobbled together with somewhat bearable gameplay was enough to make it a well beloved hit for decades to go.
You play as a chap named Lo Wang, and you need to defeat an evil corporation you used to work for that is bent on taking over the world with zombies, mutants, and sexualized females.
The game tries to look as a cheap Oriental B-movie and succeeds at that greatly. Old and clearly used without permission posters from the 90s cartoons and ads, random Japanese text all over the place, cliché locations, and of course the protagonist spitting out one ham-fisted quote after another as you progress through the game, all that gives certain charm to it, but at the same time makes it as much of a knock-off as the things it tries to parody.
The levels are fairly diverse, with areas ranging from a train station, to a shrine complex in a bamboo forest, to everyone's most beloved generic factory buildings. While the early levels are OK in terms of navigation, the further you go, the more their layout defeats common sense and makes you roam around the map for minutes trying to figure out what nook and cranny with That Very Important Switch, Key or Vent that you have missed.
Something also needs to be said about the portrayal of female characters in the game. All of them are shown as feeble, scantily dressed (if not plain naked) and highly sexualized cartoon "babes". While it could be considered a cute throwback to the stream of cheap anime flooding the Western market at the time and all its cliches if it was done in moderation, 3D Realms goes all the distance, putting them in nearly every level, bathing naked, farting on toilets, tied up and left for a slow death, or even getting disemboweled.
Content aside, the "Redux" version has serious stability issues, at least on Linux, where the game would keep consistently crashing at some spots, making you have to replay the same "buggy" segment over, over, and over again.
All in all, I cannot recommend the game to an average player for it having a bunch of unjustifiedly offensive/disturbing elements in it, obsolete and fun-defying gameplay, and severe stability problems.
If you are interested in it as a piece of video game history, however, you should by all means play it (even if just a couple of levels), but do choose
instead of Redux. That version is absolutely free, with the only difference being that it does not come with an updated engine by default （which is extremely prone to crashes as mentioned earlier anyway, and can still be obtained from
and installed manually）.

Devil Daggers is an extremely deep, challenging, arcade-style score-driven fps. I say that like I'm putting it into a well-known category of game but as far as I know it is the only game that would fit in this category.
The game takes place in a single, circular arena. Monsters spawn according to a fixed and increasingly aggressive schedule, and you try to survive as long as possible. One hit kills you. You can fire a steady stream of daggers by holding the mouse button down, or fire a shotgun-like burst by clicking. These weapons can be upgraded by collecting gems dropped from fallen enemies, and (pro tip), releasing the fire button momentarily will draw in all pickups toward you. It's a feeling shmup fans will find very familiar.
Devil Daggers is executed well on every front. The controls are crisp and responsive. You can strafe jump and bunny hop, and the timing for them is more forgiving than in quake. The weapons are powerful and have good feedback, making them very satisfying to use, especially in their upgraded versions. The graphics are a faithful homage to the original quake big pixel software rendering mode, but still easily readable. The sound design is phenomenal. Each enemy makes its own distinctive chatter, and thanks to the excellent 3D positional audio, this essentially becomes your "radar". You will not score your best times while listening to music.
I've seen people criticize the game for not having much content, and in a way it's a fair point. Some games have a lot of varied and detailed backdrops, environments, and cutscenes for you to look at while you keep performing the same simple gameplay tasks throughout the game. Devil Daggers doesn't have any of that. The only content here is the very very tight game mechanics, a dozen or so enemies, and a series of very carefully designed encounters. It's enough to keep you busy for a long, long time. However, if you don't actually enjoy the gameplay, there's nothing to distract you from this fact.
Personally, I've put 35 hours into the game so far and I don't intend to stop playing it before I've joined the 20 or so players who have lasted longer than 500 seconds and earned the game's only achievement. I'll be proud of myself if it only takes 35 more.
If you like old-school fps, or chasing high scores, or to be challenged, Devil Daggers is a no-brainer. If you aren't enthusiastic for at least one of those things, it probably won't grab you.

Let’s have a moment to appreciate the developer’s honesty and humor on the story-telling. Bloop Reloaded Is a Puzzle and Physics game that includes: a lovely art style and very encouraging animations. The gameplay involves you doing various tasks, such as: Moving fluids to their designated potion bottle - creating a path for the fluids to slide into their bottles - at harder levels, it will include obstacles too.
The controls are minimal and easy to understand. Players are informed of what to do in most, if not all levels and given clues to their objectives. There should be no question or confusion for the most part.
Art and graphics is one of the highlights to this game for me. The splattered effects and animations gives a funky feel to the theme, along with the fluorescent colour schemes. The gradients and mixtures you would get from mixing two colours is one that I find entertaining to witness when playing. There is also the messy aspect too. When you place the blobs onto the opening of the bottle: don’t be surprised to see some of the fluid oozing down on the sides and having to pick them up again. That, with other unintended leaking and spills.
The game play is also accompanied by light-hearted music, which alternates time to time as you progress through the levels. You can expect to hear a lot of splash while you move or drop fluids and they hit a surface. The game does fulfill the audio aspect for the atmosphere of the game.
To wrap things up - You can say that I have a ‘chemistry’ with puzzle games. Hence, why this game caught my interest with the theme design. It’s simple and stunning. I recommend playing Bloop Reloaded.

It's hard to call this a game, really - it's more of an interactive film.  But what a film!  The surreal and ever-mutable "script" reminds one of Charlie Kaufman and Neil Gaiman works without being an obvious ripoff.  And the vector animation is brilliant, hearkening back to the old sega genesis classic Flashback, but far beyond it in execution.  The scenes show unprecedented depth and the ambient soundtrack and fx are outstanding.  It's the little things, like watching an office floor full of bears head-track your every movement, the fluid shifting of perspectives from character to character, or the subtle shimmer of every appearance of the word Zero on the screen that make this title just so damn interesting.
If you're looking for straightforward action/strategy/puzzles/etc, this title is probably not for you.  On the surface, it's perhaps easy to overlook the the unspoken details of this experience - it's very light on exposition.  But if you enjoy reading, indie films, and video games as I do, there's a really rewarding experience waiting for you.  Let your brain be engaged in the story, and trust me, you'll love it.

Have you ever driven down a completely dark stretch of highway in the middle of the night?  The entire world seems to shrink to exactly the size of your headlights illuminating the road.  The nighttime is almost another country, one where it seems anything can happen.
Kentucky Route Zero takes this idea and runs with it.  It evokes a sense of magical realism that permeates the game, and coupled with a fantastic, slightly-pixellated-but-not-really art style that reminds me of Sword & Sworcery, launching the game is an immersive experience, one that doesn't let up until the act is over.
You play as Conway, a deliveryman working for an antique company trying to find an address.  As you might imagine, getting there isn't easy, and according to several of the characters around it requires travel on the Zero, a conceptual highway.  The destination doesn't really matter in KRZ, though; as ever, it's the journey that's truly breathtaking.
Between story beats you can (and I wholeheartedly recommend) just drive around the little bit of Kentucky and explore all of the different sights, abandoned buildings with weird little encounters in them.  These are where the game truly shines, the little vignettes that occur largely through text as you explore different areas.  I wouldn't want to spoil any of them, but let me just say that they're not to be missed.  Every time I finished one I felt this kind of Zen serenity, like I had just read a koan.  Finishing an act is even more overwhelming, usually with something utterly fantastic happening, and I just had to sit for a good five to ten minutes sorting through it in my head.
I recommend Kentucky Route Zero, but only if you like a slow-paced, introspective, slightly weird experience,

This game is recommended for anyone that likes FPS games but only want to shoot arrows. It is recommended for fans of Game of Thrones or mideval themes. It is for anyone who like hack and slash, and for anyone who likes trash talking in middle-english.

As has been pointed out in comments for this review, the developers - Christian Whitehead, Headcannon and PagodaWest - are probably not responsible for the game's plaguing issue. From the little I've played and everything I've heard from the console releases, they have done some stellar work which is tragically undermined by some abrasive DRM they seemingly had no say about.
---
Immediately upon release the game has been found to contain a restrictive anti-consumer measure known as Denuvo. Worse, the End User License Agreement that is required to install the game does NOT mention this. The closest it comes to it is the following section:
16. TECHNICAL PROTECTION MEASURES
The technical protection measures of the Product may require you to download certain data to your device in order to authenticate the Product. If you disable or otherwise tamper with the technical protection measures, the Product may not operate properly and you are in material breach of this Agreement.
This seems innocent enough, but consider that the predecessor of Denuvo - SecuROM, made by the same group - once managed to permanently break both a new DVD drive and a reasonably new SSD drive of one of my past machines.
I am beyond disgusted that this was installed without any warning.
Fortunately I pre-ordered the game after the PC version was delayed, avoiding the Sonic 1 "gift" that was tied to Mania and broke the refund process. This meant I could wait two weeks to give Sega a chance to remove Denuvo, and refunded the game when they did not.
This game should be avoided at all costs until a Denuvo-free installation is offered and independent analysis confirms that it is completely removed. Sega should unreservedly apologise for any distress and all damage this astonishing mistake may cause their most enthusiastic paying customers.
Sega have responded to suggest the lack of DRM warning on the store page or EULA was an innocent mistake, which has been strongly questioned. At best it was careless, at worst it was purposefully duplicitous by leaving out a notice that would have prevented many users pre-ordering. Some have even suggested that the two week delay and the Sonic 1 compensation were measures to block refund attempts, but that seems a little too hard to believe for me. Predictably they offered no apologies.
One other thing worth mentioning; though it is not responsible for the always-online requirement, Denuvo DOES regularly "phone home" an authentication server to allow the game to be played. If that server disappears, the PC version of the game will expire for everyone. Users are rightly complaining that this game is presently not a purchase but a rental of unknown duration.
Just under 7 days after release, Denuvo has been defeated. This means it confers no benefit to Sega anymore, and its continued use accomplishes absolutely nothing but to punish legitimate customers by occasionally preventing them from being able to use their valid purchase and eventually permanently taking it away from them.
Steam Spy figures for the game after release week show that the game's total sales FELL for consecutive days once most offended customers were able to process their refunds. Though they have since recovered the total sales by day 9 were still below those of day 3 which is incredible for such a positively-rated game.
With the critical launch window over my estimation based on extrapolated sales figures is that using Denuvo has COST this game 15% to 20% of the sales it would have made, which is surely more damaging than first-day piracy would have been.
