It is amazing what SCS has managed to push their game engine to do, when comparing to it's counterpart ETS2. Basically they appear to the same game engines, yet driving these big rigs feels so different. The big-nosed US style trucks handle differently on the road and they are a bit more challenging to squeeze into those tight delivery locations, compared to how the cab-overs handle in ETS2. SCS has yet again managed to create stunning environments to drive in, while staying faithful to the real areas. Driving into Las Vegas the very first time was like you see in the movies.
One of the major differences between ETS2 and ATS is that ATS offers a great deal more challenge to dropping off trailers at the delivery locations. Some locations are so narrow and tight that it becomes time consuming trying to squeeze that dolly coupled trailer into that tiny spot just over there. Those used to drive the cab-overs in ETS2 will be surprised by how much longer theres amazing big-nosed US trucks actually are when trying to maneouver into these small tight spots. I can only highly recomend giving ATS a shot - I see ATS becoming a trucking sim legend just like ETS2 has.

Absolutely amazing game with a superb atmosphere and interesting locations, people, and storylines.
Pros:
-Great atmosphere and doesn't overdo the horror element, but the intended parts *are* truly scary.
-Unique locations, while some locations are underused, there is a wide variety of different things to look at and experience.
-Interesting backstory that captures a lot of mystery. While the main plot is good itself, a lot of the best moments come from the side quests.
-Enemies are well done. There is a decent range of different mutants with different focuses.
-Alive world. Unlike something like skyrim where 99% of the encounters are scripted, the game's entire world has different squads and mutants shifting about. Since practically no NPCs are unkillable, this can lead to some people you have invested a bit of time into being killed while on patrol.
-Better ending(s) than Mass Effect 3. While this game doesn't have a lot of traditional RPG elements, the branching endings make a lot of the questlines more meaningful.
Cons:
-The world isn't that big. Okay, this is probably a more extreme version of what I experienced with skyrim. After the 500th hour or whatever, you know the landscape to an extent to where the game world can't offer anything new. But yeah, the way the world is split up into three areas really limits the spaces you can visit without a guide. The earlier games handled this much better with smaller maps, but a seemingly larger space in total. Now, of course, this game does pretty much everything else better.
-Bugs. It really doesn't seem that bad, but they do occur and I pretty much unconciously ignore them since I'm used to that type of thing. I would still consider it less buggy than Skyrim. I haven't ever had any quests break entirely, but I have had to reload my last save a few times.
-AI. On any mission where you have to follow/lead around any AI, its failures become readily apparent. Due to some of the unreasonably strict casualty limitations to get some of the better ending slides, this can either require some save-scumming or just dealing with the worse ending. But seriously, the AI is extremely sucky against mutants and grenades. They feel like CoD level NPCs where they aren't even trying to fight properly against the enemy.
-Graphics. I really don't give half a crap about graphics, but it is definately worth mentioning. Anyway, the "Complete" mod would be worthwhile for a second playthrough (or a first if you are particularily pedantic). It nice-inates the graphics while staying mostly true to the game. For better graphics you can try the Misery mod, but of course that changes a ton of stuff. While I have done 1-2 playthroughs with it installed, it adds instability to an already somewhat instable game.
Anyway, its a great game that I would totally recommend!
(Note: I got this game for free, but simply with my computer a few years back and not for any promotional thing or whatever by the devs. With hindsight, I would buy it at double price in a second)

If you're a fan of old school RPGs in the same vein as Baldurs Gate or Neverwinter Nights and tired of the graphics-first, on-rails technical demos that are passed as 'modern' RPGs then you should give Expeditions: Vikings a playthrough or three. The setting is based in the realities of 700-900ad with the only fantasy elements being those based on Norse mythology. No wizened wizards here except old, One-Eye and his ravens; no dragons to slay until Jörmungandr comes to poison the skies and devour the world. Simply put, be ready to focus on tactics to put your hardened steel to use instead of slinging Thor's mighty mjolnir. The story has many parallels to the shows Vikings and The Last Kingdom and in fact the difficulty settings use some of these more recognized names as their monikers. Similarly, many of the decisions you make in game aren't locked into good or bad (like many of todays RPGs), but rather shades of grey. You're a viking, sure you always have the option to rampage across Britannia but with some of the more subtlier options you're never going to come out feeling clean even if you get exactly what you wanted. As I pointed out at the start, this isn't a triple AAA title like The Witcher. It has some rough spots visually but for the most part the game does compete with the like of Tyranny or Pillars of Eternity and it also has a beautiful sound tracks to match.
As someone that played and enjoyed Expeditions: Conquistador, this is a dramatic improvement in play experience (especially the camping mechanic and involving player made hirdsmen in events / dialogue). My only request would be to increase the amount of interactions / dialogue with your companions/world as the vignettes currently ingame are what really sell the setting and keep things grounded in reality and engrossed in the story once you really get the grand adventure going where it's easy to fall into a detached, meta-gamey feeling.
Overally I would give the game an 8/10 and feel like this studio has the potential to be the next (classical/pre-EA)BioWare.
Edit - Nominated for Choices Matter Steam Award

Wow. So a pretty choppy RPG.
I've played about 23 hours as writing this review and well into what I can imagine is the second act of this game (Northumbria).
I can see where they were trying to go but just didn't fully get there. A couple of notes:
1. This game tries to be "realistic" in it's interpretation of health, stamina, hunger and battle. For that I actually applaud it, it really gives you a sense of mortality to your play through. However, this game tries to have it's cake an eat it too by removing the realism in other areas to make the game more difficult. Case in point, Arrows flying through large boulders from across the map to hit my team. After defeating  an enemy with armor, shield, sword, knives, etc. some how their corpse is completely devoid of useful items to steal (a cardinal sin of the RPG world these days.)
2. I love the aspect of rebuilding your settlement, they even took the time to visualize the changes when you return to your little kingdom. However, you can only perform one action at a time. And in most cases you just won't be able to get a perfect settlement completed before the end game.
3. The currency is just weird. And you can't just buy equipment. Somehow all the blacksmiths have nothing to sell until you give them "salvage" to turn it into weapons, armor etc.. Crafting is much the same and so far I've had no instruction as to the value of certain resources, nor how I should use it. I'm new to "Expedition", but regardless, having some idea as what is going on would be good, especially if you want to make an entirely new currency system from scratch. In the end, this system appears to just be change for change sake, I can't really see a benefit worth noting in it and as such is just annoying.
4. Too much story, not enough open world campaigning. It seems, again, there are two minds at work here. I'm the kind of player that actually likes to create a kingdom from the ground up and choose how I want to survive and prosper. And the Viking setting is great for that. However, you're stuck in a linear story track trying to manage your kingdom rebuild on a clock until the end game and then it just ends. I had the same disappointing experience with Fable 3. I was looking forward to managing a kingdom in that world, but it was all lipstick in service of a straight line narrative. Over all story is good, but I feel like it should be either one or the other. At the moment, I feel like I'm reading a good viking book, but every once in a while I just need to remember to feed the dog (my settlement). Why?
5. How in the world do you heal people?! I figured it out eventually, but man, I had to restart the game more then 4 times before getting the right start on my character builds to best manage that part of it. Again....just annoying.
The design is good, character and voice acting is great, dialogue is well thought out and story is great. Just too much "annoying" here. If you haven't tried the Expedition series before and are thinking of jumping on, I don't think you'll regret it. But know the learning curve is massively steep (in my opinion) and so far, there doesn't seem to be any beneficial pay off to my investment in time overcoming it.
----------
After finishing the game:
At 90-some hrs....
Well a lot of what I said earlier is still on my mind. I still think the story is great. after checking out the options in act 2, there is a refreshing amount of replayability in terms of how you want your character to be remembered. King of GB or just a good trade partner, etc., but I still standby my comment on accessibility.
Steep learning curve, for sure. I'm not an expert at all, but right before I played this, I played Divinity 2, so maybe more pallette cleansing was in order. But even if that was true, expect to restart this game maybe 5 times before you feel satisfied by your choices at the beginning.
Nothing against the developers, having seen how they participate in users questions or comments (of which there is a lot), I believe they care very much.
All in all, I'm changing my "recommend" because fair is fair. I was beyond frustrated but I couldn't stop and had to see this to the end.

I played the 2013 version first then came back to this game. It was very much worth it. It lived up to it's reputation (although it didn't really have any). I'd say the 2013 version is better because Lo Wang has a better character. + there's Hoji. This is still a great game though.
It's suprising that this game doesn't have the same amount of hype Duke 3D has though. Even though this game is Duke 3D's little brother, it's miles better than that game. Although that may be because I didn't like Duke 3D. If you ask me, that's one of the most overrated games ever made. It has nothing going for it except the character itself. Duke's level of profanity is something else (although this Shadow Warrior also has a lot of kinky jokes).
The fun thing about this game is that it gives you lots of powerful weapons, which you get to use very frequently. E.g. you get to use the rocket launcher particularly lot. It's not just something you save for bossfights. But even the simpler weapons, like the shurikens and the sword remain highly useful until the very end of the game and it's a lot of fun to use themThe one I used the least is probably the sticky bombs, because those are a bit of a hassle (enemies might get close to you by the time they explode). Then there's fun stuff, like shooting fireballs from a severed demon head, Ripper heart which creates op clones of yourself AND AN ACTUAL F*CKING NUKE!
I also played through the Twin Dragon expansion. It was worth it. That expansion had lots of interesting maps, although the final battle was a bit... anti-climatic (remember Doom 2's original final boss level? yeah kinda like that).
There are even anime references in it (Slayers, Sailor Moon). Then there' stuff from warious movies and games (like Mortal Kombat and Lara Croft)
Oh and the invisible ninjas are the best enemies ever invented. Not too tanky, but stacked with damage. They have insanely powerful fireball spells, which usually insta-kill. Sounds OP, but this creates great high-tension clutch play moments and the game gives you similarly op tools to kill them. When you encounter this ninja, I just get this adrenaline rush that a lot of games fail to give me these days. This is how monster design is done! "If everything is op, nothing is op!"
Buy this instead of Duke 3D. Much more worth it.

Hello, Bonsoir, Buenas Tardes, ect.  Today, I will be reviewing the still-popular Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion.
First of all, I'd like to say how well the Elder Scrolls series have progressed, take Skyrim for example.  It's been active for 4 Years, and there are thousands, and thousands of mods, those still coming.  I'd also like to say I did play Skyrim before Oblivion, and I'm not really sure why there's so much hate between the two games.  I rather fell in love (figure of speech) with Oblivion, and I almost play Oblivion more than Skyrim.
Now there's many great things about Oblivion, Skyrim, Online, Morrowind, Daggerfall and Arena, but of course there will be bad things.  Okay, this is starting to sound like a review for all of them, and a discussion rather, moving on!
The Graphics:
The graphics are actually pretty well done considering how long ago this was made.  I was very surprised by how well done it was.  Now, I'm sure this will be a very considered factor in many gamers, how well it looks.  But, unlike most Skyrim Fanboys, I actually kept an open mind and remembered this game was made in 2006.  Take a look at my profile picture, which is a shot of my character in Oblivion.
The Voice Actors:
Yes, yes, yes this is a minor factor, but yes, I will include it anyway.  The voice actors in the game are very limited, so you will find perhaps a couple dozen of characters that sound exactly the same (but the Emperor is special, he's Cpt. Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation!) But, given that there are a plentiful amount of characters in both Oblivion and Skyrim, you are bound to find some characters with the same voice actor.
The Story:
It may not be the best story in history, but it is really good, except for the later ones.  You're basically the new Emperor's delivery boy in those.  You may also find similarity with Oblivion's and Online's, as Tamriel is in danger in both (again), a Daedric Prince is trying to bring the realms together, and in both there are...gates...everywhere.
The Combat System:
This was an amazing improvement than the previous Elder Scrolls game's.  It's not based on the roll of dice, there's actually some stratedgy to it, such as if you're actually hitting it, how much power you're hitting, if you're decently skilled at it, ect.  This is starting to sound like a rage to Morrowind, moving on(!).
Other content:
You could easily spend 20 hours in Oblivion, and STILL not have everything done.  Especially with the Shivering Isles DLC, which probably adds another ~8 hours.  There's the Dark Brotherhood questline, Thieves, Fighter's, and Mage's guild, Arena Questline, only could take about an hour or so.
Well, I'm outta time, so have a bonne jour.

Bloop Reloaded is a very colorful puzzle game in which you will use the physics to solve several levels. This game has very nice art as you can see from the preview screenshots. The concept of potion-making, the art and the music combine to yield an atmosphere that is also quite joyful. It will make you want to play some more, even when you are struggling on a surprisingly not-so-easy level.
Regarding the learning curve, I think it would ideally need a bit of tinkering, and that's actually the only negative point I've seen in the game so far. This is also probably one of these things that are too difficult to fix on an already-released game, but I hope the developers will take their customers' opinions into account for their next game.
The progression between some levels was a bit weird, although you can just avoid playing these and play the next ones if you're stuck. But let's be honest, 1. I prefer playing the levels in the order they were supposed to be played and 2. it's not so much that the puzzles are difficult, it's more that sometimes it can get a bit tricky to do exactly what you plan, especially when the fluids manage to flow to places they weren't supposed to be able to go to. I've been building more barricades than a revolutionary while playing Bloop. The physics of the game can be quite unforgiving... In particular, there was one level I spent what felt like almost half an hour on (the first level where you're supposed to mix the star-potion with the blue shiny potion) because the potions kept leaking to the bottom of the level in quite fascinating ways. After these somewhat-30 min, I thought I was reaching more complex levels, but it still ended up being followed by a few 30-second levels. This is a bit weird in term of learning/difficulty curve (but I still had fun trying to figure out what was happening with these crazy potions flowing everywhere except where they were supposed to).
Anyway, except for these one or two levels that seem a bit out of place but still manage to teach you valuable information for the rest of the game and increase your barricade-building skill level by 25, this game is a really nice one that I would recommend to anyone who likes physics-based puzzle games. The developer probably tried hard to give a real identity to their game... and they succeeded. Bloop Reloaded really is a nice game, with both great gameplay and amazing aesthetics.

Are you looking for a fast paced arcade FPS that is hard as balls with an average life span of 100 seconds? Welcome to Devil Daggers!
Devil Daggers does exactly like it says, inspired by 1990s FPS and arcade games with the gameplay of Quake/Geometry Wars, sending you to damnation in hell in an abyssal arena to face endless legions of skeleton demons. You have 1 purpose... Live as long as you can. More importantly, getting the 1 achievement in this game, which is "Survive 500 seconds." Sounds easy right? Hahahahahahahahahaha wrong! Be happy if you can make it past 100 seconds!
In DD you only have 1 weapon, the Magic Dagger. As you progress, certain enemies will drop "Gems" which after collecting so many will power up your dagger to shoot more daggers and deal more damage. As you would guess, progressing farther also means the gets even harder, spawning in more enemies at a time, or spawning in a new enemy type. There is 13 different enemies in this game, all have really unique models, and all produce their own unique sound, so you can have an easier time keeping track where certain enemies are. You have no health, you get hit once, you die. Standing still will get you killed in this game.
When you complete your run, you are given your score, which is how long you lasted. My best record after numerous attempts was 195.9962. The cool thing is your best run is saved as a replay, so your friends can view it, or other people can look on the leaderboard and view your run. This idea is cool, as you can watch how other people played and learn off them to get farther. After watching the top players, I've determined that I will never be that skilled in being able to make it to the final boss, and beating the 500 seconds achievement. (Also convinced the few top ten that made it over 700 are aimbots based on how they move and aim.)
For a game that was coded from the ground up in a custom engine, this game runs smooth and is rock solid! Runs at a silky smooth 300FPS and does not lag or glitch ever. There is an FOV slider (which I guess wasn't in the game originally) that goes from 75-120. The game boots up fast and loads almost instantly. There is also a soundtrack which was added in later, and it's metal as f**k!
This is a fun little game that just makes me go back and "play one more round" till my adrenaline gets way too high, and have to stop and take a break. I would play more, but I just don't think my heart can handle it. Some people would argue that there isn't much "Content" in this game, but this is for those hardcore old school FPS fans that love that extra challenge. For the $5 it's a great buy and great to support the Dev. I would LOVE to see the Dev make a full game similar to QUAKE, as they clearly have the know how.
Pros:

Sonic Mania was a game that I was looking forward to, but not to the extent some other fans were. I grew up with games like Sonic Adventure and Sonic Advance when I was growing up, and I was a massive fan of those games during that point in my life. My interest in the series dwindeled a little bit after discovering very lackluster entires in the series such as Sonic '06 and Sonic and the Secret Rings (both terrible titles). Regardless, a 2D Sonic platformer that harkons back to Sonics' glory days during the 90s was certainly something I was looking forward to.
The PC version of this game was delayed by 2 weeks, supposedly to implement Denuvo. When the game launched on PC, the game would not function without being connected to the interent. Besides that, it has also been an alleged cause of damage to computer hardware with SSD's most notably being bricked by the software due to writing unnecessary amounts of data to the drive. Sega has recently patched the game to work offline, but I still have empathy for people who still refuse to purchase the game given the other problems with Denuvo and the mere notion that a 2D Sonic platformer has DRM.
Despite the obvious issues with this and my gripes with DRM as a whole, I still believe that Sonic Mania is an incredible experience on all levels.
The graphics of the game resemble that of a 16-bit Genesis/Mega Drive title from the 90s. However, it has been blessed with a wider color palette, inspired level themes (for the new ones at least) smoother animations, and stunning effects that can only be done with modern technology. It's a visual marvel despite taking inspiration from a style that was done over 2 decades ago.
The gameplay of Sonic Mania is pretty much identical to the gameplay of the old Genesis classics; high speed platforming. You have the option to play as Sonic, Tails, and Knuckles (<- see what I did there?). All characters come with their own unique abilities: Sonic can run faster than the other 2 and also has access to a new "drop dash" ability, a mechanic that allows Sonic to fire off at a fast speed after he lands from a jump. Tails is able to fly and can jump a little bit higher, making him what I would consider the "easy" mode of the game. Knuckles is able to glide, punch and even goes through entirely different level layouts at some points, making his playthrough almost an entirely fresh experience, on top of an already fresh experience. Sonic Mania had me a little bit concerend at first. I was worried that the game would rely too much on old level layouts that we saw in previous game, and more or less just make the entire game seem more like a remaster rather a sequel to Sonic 3 & Knuckles. Thankfully, Sonic Mania doesn't do that. It instead takes levels seen in the 90s games and "remixes" them to create an entirely new experience for the player. In Chemical Plant for example we not only see the classics gimicks from the original stage in Sonic the Hedgehog 2, but we also see elements of Wacky Workbench from Sonic CD. This remixing is constant througout the entire game, with the exception of the completely new zones that Sonic Mania has to offer, and in my opinion they're the best part of the game. All of the new zones are visualy jawdropping to look at, and they use their own unique gimicks to play around with the basic gameplay of Sonic and create a fun and memorable experience that you will without a doubt want to play again once you have finished the game. It is a game that manages to do so much with surprisingly so little. It's an element I feel many game developers could and need to learn from, since we have so many games in the modern era that have many different mechanics, but sadley are not fun to play.
Sonic Mania is a game I felt was going to be good even if it was just a glorified remaster. But I'm happy to say that Sonic Mania is far more than that, as it is a lovely new experience for fans and a solid platformer alltogether. There are a few minor sections with some more dull level design compared to the rest of the game, but that really isn't saying much. Also I feel that they should have added  some more original levels since they were the best part, but they only take 1/3 of the entire game. Despite these minor problems Sonic Mania is a platformer that I would consider very good to the average gamer and a true masterpiece for Sonic fans.
FINAL VERDICT: 9/10
Closing statement: A few dull moments that were generally negligable, and could have used more original levels. Incredible gameplay that recreates that classic Sonic gameplay perfectly, remixed levels create an interesting and fun new experience for fans, and beautiful pixel art/animation.

Absolutely amazing game with a superb atmosphere and interesting locations, people, and storylines.
Pros:
-Great atmosphere and doesn't overdo the horror element, but the intended parts *are* truly scary.
-Unique locations, while some locations are underused, there is a wide variety of different things to look at and experience.
-Interesting backstory that captures a lot of mystery. While the main plot is good itself, a lot of the best moments come from the side quests.
-Enemies are well done. There is a decent range of different mutants with different focuses.
-Alive world. Unlike something like skyrim where 99% of the encounters are scripted, the game's entire world has different squads and mutants shifting about. Since practically no NPCs are unkillable, this can lead to some people you have invested a bit of time into being killed while on patrol.
-Better ending(s) than Mass Effect 3. While this game doesn't have a lot of traditional RPG elements, the branching endings make a lot of the questlines more meaningful.
Cons:
-The world isn't that big. Okay, this is probably a more extreme version of what I experienced with skyrim. After the 500th hour or whatever, you know the landscape to an extent to where the game world can't offer anything new. But yeah, the way the world is split up into three areas really limits the spaces you can visit without a guide. The earlier games handled this much better with smaller maps, but a seemingly larger space in total. Now, of course, this game does pretty much everything else better.
-Bugs. It really doesn't seem that bad, but they do occur and I pretty much unconciously ignore them since I'm used to that type of thing. I would still consider it less buggy than Skyrim. I haven't ever had any quests break entirely, but I have had to reload my last save a few times.
-AI. On any mission where you have to follow/lead around any AI, its failures become readily apparent. Due to some of the unreasonably strict casualty limitations to get some of the better ending slides, this can either require some save-scumming or just dealing with the worse ending. But seriously, the AI is extremely sucky against mutants and grenades. They feel like CoD level NPCs where they aren't even trying to fight properly against the enemy.
-Graphics. I really don't give half a crap about graphics, but it is definately worth mentioning. Anyway, the "Complete" mod would be worthwhile for a second playthrough (or a first if you are particularily pedantic). It nice-inates the graphics while staying mostly true to the game. For better graphics you can try the Misery mod, but of course that changes a ton of stuff. While I have done 1-2 playthroughs with it installed, it adds instability to an already somewhat instable game.
Anyway, its a great game that I would totally recommend!
(Note: I got this game for free, but simply with my computer a few years back and not for any promotional thing or whatever by the devs. With hindsight, I would buy it at double price in a second)

The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is a massive open world game developed by Bethesda and released March 20, 2006. It would take too long to list all the various quests, armor, weapons, enchantments, and magic spells you can learn/create, simply trust me when I say this game is an adventure waiting to happen.
This is probably one of my personal favorite parts of Elder Scrolls of Oblivion, once you get out of the starting area you can make your own story, or follow the main story, or go search for your own quest. If you wanted, you could become a villain, you could also become a hero. The choices are completely up to you.
The whole Elder Scrolls series is very rich is lore and diversity of environment, you can read in-game books and learn useful facts about the monsters you fight. Not everyone will do this, but I ended up learning what all Trolls are weak against, and I've been using it in all Elder Scrolls games since.
I won't say much more about the story, because most of the fun is in finding the quests and stories yourself, and of course forging your own tale.... however there is one additional thing to note, in the Game of the Year Edition you get the Shivering Isles Expansion, and there you meet my favorite character in the whole series.
You can control the camera to play in third person, or first person. (personally I always thought third person looked silly... the knee's bend funny, and when you jump your legs stay straight. seems like an indication of "play in first person").
You could be a necromancer and summon skeleton hoards, you could be a thief and sneak into combat, you could be a warrior and smash your enemies faces in, you can be a mage and even create your own skills, you can be a ranger and pew pew, a monk, an acrobat or any hybrid combination of what I've said and much much more.
There are no Steam Achievements in this game, you can certainly find plenty of challenges online to test your skill in the game, or simply increase the difficulty of the game.
The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion Game of the Year Edition is priced at $19.99, as always, I suggest you wait for a sale, but if you already know you like this style of game you won't lose money out of it, since the game is getting "old"
you should probably look for a good deal out of the game, it goes on sale often.
This was the first Open world game I ever played, I absolutely loved it, and I still remember the fun I had playing the game. The stories/quests are very memorable and the game play was dynamic and very fluid. I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys open world or RPG's.

This game is a total awesomeness. Lots of easter eggs, lots of one-liners, lots of guns and enemies ... Shoot like it´s 90´s. Yea, I know, the graphics. But it is not that bad, and if you consider yourself as a true gamer, you need to play this polished classic. Very well playable on gamepad.

The visuals are very nice, with vivid colors and surreal landscapes, though it can be hard telling what counts as a foreground object and what's merely a background detail.
Unfortunately, everything else about this game ranks between "mediocre" to "inept". The music is the same unimaginative minimalist orchestral stuff you hear in every other puzzle game these days. The gameplay itself is cluttered and confused, with clashing mechanics (the "click and drag your water to the target" mechanic is just astoundingly awful, and the "click these random blobs to refill your click-and-drag meter is jarringly out of place and seems to serve no real purpose), and the level design comes across as thoughtless and random, like playing random community-generated maps in other games.
If the devs had stuck to what works (building platforms on surreal landscapes to guide water to the target) and focused on designing levels that were thoughtful and shaped along a natural difficulty curve, this would be a fun little casual time-waster. But this game is a good example of "more is less", and the asking price of $9.99 drags it down from "mediocre" to "hahahahahaha absolutely not".

There are a lot of people that rave about this game, and to be fair there are a lot of positives to it. The combat is very satisfying, the writing is good and the storyline is alright. I like the character creation and customisation through the game, and the ability to customise the Origins characters is a really good addition.
However, none of that is enough to make up for the hours you will spend pixel hunting, reading through online walkthroughs and sifting through inventory screens with no search function and the most awkward 'sort by' system imaginable. There is a skill you learn to be able to see ghosts, but it is hardly ever hinted when you need to use it (even to finish quests), and at one point you even need to use it to see levers which is literally never mentioned and never happens again in the entire game. The questlog is equally illogical, and essentially tells you what you have already done without giving you any idea where to go next, and the waypoints on the map seem like they were put in the game by someone who has not read the plot. Sometimes, you are encouraged to explore with amazing loot as rewards, but other times without any notification at all you can go too far and come back to a town to find half the people dead and quests uncompleteable. In fact, I only found out those people should have been alive because I read it on an internet walkthrough after the fact.
A lot of people praise this game as a throwback to the golden age of RPGs in the 90s and early 2000s, and I get that. But for me, some aspects of gaming have moved on - I dont want to walk around in circles looking for an item that no longer exists because I chose the wrong option in dialogue 3 weeks ago and the quest didnt update. What specifically irks me is that before I bought the game I researched it, and in an interview one of the devs claimed they had made it all but impossible to miss quests by going the wrong way or doing the wrong thing - and in my opinion that is just bull****.
There are people that will mistake this frustration for the game being difficult - it isn't. Once you get a hang of the game mechaincs and level up enough to get decent skills there are very few fights that pose any kind of threat even on the hardest difficulty. What it is is time-consuming, frustrating and illogical unless you want to follow the one-dimensional path the game devs set out for you into a trap that is obvious from the middle of act two, if not earlier.
In my opinion you should just watch a playthrough on Youtube instead of buying it, and if after that you still are interested at least wait until it is on sale - because you are going to need that money to buy a new screen after you smash a hole in your old one.

Pros:

* WASD + mouse controls of pure bliss. The mouse feels exactly right with no hint of acceleration or smoothing. In one word - precise.
* Sound effects and (short) soundtrack that many horror titles can learn from.
* Enemies don't spawn in the same location, but there are patterns you can follow.
* Extremely satisfying when you get in the "zone".
Neutral:
* Hitbox is a little weird. Sometimes I'm in a situation where I think I should've died, but the enemy somehow didn't touch me. Other times I think I should've been fine, but instead die.
* The skulls follow a certain pattern, which they change in the worst possible moment. This is very frustrating.
* >tfw can't get to 500 seconds ;_;
Cons:
None.

Fallen Earth is a wasted opportunity of something that could of been bigger and better than what it has become.
In the past 2 years+ Gamers First has virtual abandoned the game. They use to have Gms in game, communicating and being involved with the game community. Not any more. Now they have 2 GMs that rarely come online and when they do, are silent and distant. It is like they log in but don't look at their screen after inputting their passwords. There is no longer any events held by the company, support is non existant, they haven't rotated sale items in their online marketplace in over a year. There is no updates, no new content and forget bug fixes.
The population has declined to 20-85 online at any one time. They are mostly the die hards that refuse to leave or stay because of memories long past. On days when the lag makes it impossible to play, you are lucky to see 10-15 people online.
Now lets discuss the lag. It happens regulary. At least twice a week for 1-2 days each time the lag makes it impossible to play. You can not complete missions, talk in chats, loot, craft and even fast travel can take you 5-10minutes from the moment you click to travel. Think about that. Waiting 5-10 minutes to finally travel to a location after selecting it on the terminal. Forgot trying to get your mail, you can't. Buying from merchants is also very time consuming if you can do it at all. So all that is left to do is wander around aimlessly and hope you bump into someone to chat in local. Usually that is the only chat channel not lagging.
PVP is dead. What little  PVP there is, is just the same people. Mostly banned players that have come back with their hacks and aimbots. So you see the same 6-8 people PVPing. Such a sad thing to watch.
Due to the dupers and rerolls the economy is wrecked. There is no way a new player could afford the outragous prices people charge for items. A low level pistol now costs 2-4 yellows (2,000,000-4,000,000 chips which is exorbitant). Same pistol only 6 months ago was only 4-5 red chips (40,000-50,000). As new players are limited to 10 red (100,000 unless they purchase something from the online marketplace with real money, this common and easily obtained pistol is out of their reach until they can get to the area to get it. but by that time, they require a higher level pistol so don't need it.
No one should spend money on Fallen Earth. It is a waste as there is no support and you cannot play it all the time. Those silly few that do think they are supporting the game with their marketplace purchases think they are keeping the game alive but the twice weekly restarts are not signs of support. It is just a sign that G1 only care enough to restart it to stop the flood of support tickets to rectify the lag (though this is only a temporary fix). Easy for them to placate the dwindling population with a restart than actually look after them properly.
Sadly I wouldn't recommend this game to anyone and hope that soon, for the sake of those that love the game, they finally pull the plug and never switch it back on again.

Okay, so Gear Up is a tank building game. It's pretty self explanatory; build yourself a tank, shoot the bad guys, earn cash for a better tank, repeat. A concept seemingly hard to screw up, however Doctor Entertainment appears to have done just that.
Pros:
Decent graphics.
User-friendly interface.
Super tight controls.
Cons:
No matchmaking system.
Limited backpack space for free players makes it difficult to actually build anything.
VERY repetitive.
Tank customization could be better.
Although the limited backpack space annoys me to no end (the fact that they offer you ONE extra backpack slot for joining their steam group making it twice as insulting), let's touch upon the lack of matchmaking for a second.
In a game like this, where buying parts with ingame currency determines how well your tank will fare, having the only way to actually get in game be through a lobby system is a big no. Let's look at a common scenario: You're starting up a game. At your starting level (with the default tank) it is VERY easy get matched into games with veterans, most of whom will have much better armor, guns and tires than you will. Bam, straight into a respawn timer. This is exactly what happened during my first gameplay (and likely what will happen during any new player's as well). An experienced player's tank can take multiple shots from a default tank before it dies, all while frollicking around the map literally one-shotting anything that moves with rockets and flamethrowers.
Did you catch that one part? "Literally one-shotting". Because that's actually a thing that can happen.
That's no way to introduce new players to your game.
Gear Up could honestly be something great, but as of right now, the lack of matchmaking coupled with the limited amount of backpack space for free players makes it merely a pay-to-win Robocraft clone. I'm sure I speak for a lot of the community when I say I am thoroughly dissapointed in this game. I don't care how good the graphics look or how solid the controls are, if you can't play with a matchmaking system, all the Free-to-Play tags in the world won't make Gear Up worth my time.

Sonic Mania was a game that I was looking forward to, but not to the extent some other fans were. I grew up with games like Sonic Adventure and Sonic Advance when I was growing up, and I was a massive fan of those games during that point in my life. My interest in the series dwindeled a little bit after discovering very lackluster entires in the series such as Sonic '06 and Sonic and the Secret Rings (both terrible titles). Regardless, a 2D Sonic platformer that harkons back to Sonics' glory days during the 90s was certainly something I was looking forward to.
The PC version of this game was delayed by 2 weeks, supposedly to implement Denuvo. When the game launched on PC, the game would not function without being connected to the interent. Besides that, it has also been an alleged cause of damage to computer hardware with SSD's most notably being bricked by the software due to writing unnecessary amounts of data to the drive. Sega has recently patched the game to work offline, but I still have empathy for people who still refuse to purchase the game given the other problems with Denuvo and the mere notion that a 2D Sonic platformer has DRM.
Despite the obvious issues with this and my gripes with DRM as a whole, I still believe that Sonic Mania is an incredible experience on all levels.
The graphics of the game resemble that of a 16-bit Genesis/Mega Drive title from the 90s. However, it has been blessed with a wider color palette, inspired level themes (for the new ones at least) smoother animations, and stunning effects that can only be done with modern technology. It's a visual marvel despite taking inspiration from a style that was done over 2 decades ago.
The gameplay of Sonic Mania is pretty much identical to the gameplay of the old Genesis classics; high speed platforming. You have the option to play as Sonic, Tails, and Knuckles (<- see what I did there?). All characters come with their own unique abilities: Sonic can run faster than the other 2 and also has access to a new "drop dash" ability, a mechanic that allows Sonic to fire off at a fast speed after he lands from a jump. Tails is able to fly and can jump a little bit higher, making him what I would consider the "easy" mode of the game. Knuckles is able to glide, punch and even goes through entirely different level layouts at some points, making his playthrough almost an entirely fresh experience, on top of an already fresh experience. Sonic Mania had me a little bit concerend at first. I was worried that the game would rely too much on old level layouts that we saw in previous game, and more or less just make the entire game seem more like a remaster rather a sequel to Sonic 3 & Knuckles. Thankfully, Sonic Mania doesn't do that. It instead takes levels seen in the 90s games and "remixes" them to create an entirely new experience for the player. In Chemical Plant for example we not only see the classics gimicks from the original stage in Sonic the Hedgehog 2, but we also see elements of Wacky Workbench from Sonic CD. This remixing is constant througout the entire game, with the exception of the completely new zones that Sonic Mania has to offer, and in my opinion they're the best part of the game. All of the new zones are visualy jawdropping to look at, and they use their own unique gimicks to play around with the basic gameplay of Sonic and create a fun and memorable experience that you will without a doubt want to play again once you have finished the game. It is a game that manages to do so much with surprisingly so little. It's an element I feel many game developers could and need to learn from, since we have so many games in the modern era that have many different mechanics, but sadley are not fun to play.
Sonic Mania is a game I felt was going to be good even if it was just a glorified remaster. But I'm happy to say that Sonic Mania is far more than that, as it is a lovely new experience for fans and a solid platformer alltogether. There are a few minor sections with some more dull level design compared to the rest of the game, but that really isn't saying much. Also I feel that they should have added  some more original levels since they were the best part, but they only take 1/3 of the entire game. Despite these minor problems Sonic Mania is a platformer that I would consider very good to the average gamer and a true masterpiece for Sonic fans.
FINAL VERDICT: 9/10
Closing statement: A few dull moments that were generally negligable, and could have used more original levels. Incredible gameplay that recreates that classic Sonic gameplay perfectly, remixed levels create an interesting and fun new experience for fans, and beautiful pixel art/animation.

After haveing now finished the game once in a "not 100%-run" but, lets call it a "seen-all-quests"-run, I can recommend this game with a resoundeing;



----------------------------------------------------
It's a fun little RPG with turnbased combat. The skills are all rather straight-forward and easy to understand. They are rather grounded in reality and despite the "moral"-skills haveing the global effect of magic, everything happening can be explained with "religious-frenzy", albait flimsily.
All in all the game is historically representative with a little twist here and there reflecting the more "uneducated" more "mystically-inclined" view of people who might live in that time.


The plot itself is interesting enough, allthough a little reminicent of the show "Vikings", which shoud be a given seeing how both are based on the real exploits of the Danish Vikings.
It never really makes you gasp or fools you into twists and turns, but it forms a nice circle plotwise, where the game starts with blood being spilled and ends with it -

There isn't really much in terms of roleplay-potential, in my opinion, as, much like your Charname, you're forced into a role and have little wiggleroom to fullfill what is asked of you.
The mainfocus of the game is definitly the combat.
-------------------------------------------------------------


It's a turnbased 2-actions system. Some skills need both actions, some can be used after movement. There are directed, global and aoe skills. The staples of games like this are all represented. CC-skills, DoTs, Buffs and the likes. It's in all honesty, for being the mainfocus, rather boring. I played on the medium-difficulty, so I can't speak for the higher difficultys, but after a while I spend most fights useing the same strategy.
Sure, you could roleplay different builds, but I feel like it would only spell out doom as most fights are even after the patches, usually full to the brim with enemy archers.
There isn't enough units for shieldwalls or quick berserkerlike rushes so that a slow methodical approach is allways the optimal way. This means you mostly have a few sword and board units who tank arrows, while your archers pick off the enemy archers, so you can finally move into remaining meele-enemys.
There's plenty of consumeables, but I never used them.
All in all, the games mainpart is hurt by the games decision to stay more grounded than fantastic. There is a reason why archers were such an effective unit in warfare. Were they as effective as the ingame-archers? Probably not, but then again, you'd be frustrated to see your archers miss their shots all the time.
The Economy of the game is rather simple and easy to exploit. I never used valuables except in a few questbased uses and had my partys key-units equipped with "endgame"-gear by the start of the mid-time of the campaign. Allthough the biggest spike in power was the "best dmg"-bows, which made combat quicker, since your archers could down weak targets reliably, every turn. And a certain pretty much overpowered lootitem.
So in conclusion, there isn't really much to keep the combat interesting despite simply stacking the odds agaisnt the player by enemy-numbers or stats/dmg, which, in my humble opinion, is the mark of a weak core in the combat-engine.
There is cover, but honestly, it only made the game more tedious. Different terrain-effects are not implemented, while heightdifferences exist but are at best sporadically used and not really transparant in their use.
-----------------------------------------------
Why would I still recommend it? Mostly because I think you can have fun with the game in a lower difficulty and without the obsessive need to powergame your decissions, like doing every quest possible in the way too big timelimit.
It's a fun game with a average story. It's nothing that will make you look back in a few months, still reflecting on some characters or decissions you made in it. It's nothing you will talk about with your buddys or workplace-aquaintances.
It's the equivallent of a movie you watch because you like the theme/sourcematerial but go in knowing full well that you'll forget it in T minus 30 seconds, to steal a Youtubers rateings.
A spacefiller.
___________________________________
On a sidenote: While the devs did try to improve and DID improve a lot of the frankly buggy releaseversion, the game still likes to crash. Refuses to start sometimes. Has huge loadingtimes, even installed on a SSD and has the occasional gamebreakeing-bugs that force you to reload a save from earlier.
FREQUENT USE OF THE QUICKSAVE IS ADVICED!

This game is similar to classics like Lemmings. You guide an oject to an objective. The main difference between this game and Lemmings is that while Lemmings deals mostly with a programming aspect to guide the objects to the objective, Bloop Reloaded uses physics to guide liquids. You must create platforms to guide the liquids to the bottle, avoiding hazards and sometimes mixing to liquids to get an end product. Aside from the pre-level setup of platforms, the player can use the right mouse button to pick up and move quantities of the liquid.
This game suffers a few design flaws that make it less fun to play. Being able to pick up the liquids and move them around defeats the need to solve a puzzle. If Lemmings allowed such a function, the game would not have been as successful. The fact that this ability can be active for a certain amount of time and then be recharged hurts the gameplay. Having the skill slowly recharge would make the skill more interesting than having to switch tasks to find the skill recharge items. It plays like two distantly related minigames that are expected to be perceived as a whole game. I really like puzzle games for their need to plan out how to complete a level, but the right mouse button skill negates the need to really plan for anything.

Who want some Wang? As a young lad I played the shareware version of the original Shadow Warrior many, many times. The opening four levels that comprise what is now known as "Enter the Wang" represent to me a high point in classic shooters. Shadow Warrior was the logical evolution of the kind of gameplay pioneered by Duke Nukem 3D. It was no longer enough simply to have big guns, explosions and ludicrous gibs, no, you must also have interactive environments and a smartass protagonist offering witty, post-kill one liners! And so did 3D Realms deliver. Together with Duke and Monolith's horror-flavored FPS, Blood, Shadow Warrior forms the holy trinity of Build Engine FPSs. Shadow Warrior is in most respects a superior game to Duke, with more potent weapons, smarter level design and improved world details- many objects that were 2D sprites in Duke are now 3D models, albeit blocky. You are Lo Wang,  raunchy, east-asian pastiche, professional mercenary, and wise-cracking old master, on a quest to exact revenge on the evil Orochi Zilla and his army of gun-toting demons. At your disposal is an arsenal of ballistic, explosive, and outright magical weaponry, and you will need it all to survive the game's punishing difficulty. Shadow Warrior, like most FPSs of the era, is not an easy game, but it is an entertaining one. This rerelease also includes both the game's expansions, Wanton Destruction and Twin Dragon. If you enjoy this game, I recommend moving on directly to Flying Wild Hog's excellent remake.

This "Redux" version of Shadow Warrior is identical to the "Megaton" edition of Duke Nukem 3D: The idea here is to have one compilation for the game that contains everything from the original, classic FPS.
1) We have Shadow Warrior here with enhanced graphics. This includes higher resolution options, vsync, smoother lighting and overall better textures. There is a new main menu and slightly changed music. This game still kicks♥♥♥♥♥
2) The classic Shadow Warrior is also available. This has the good old main menu (it now looks quite dated) and the original graphics. I'm not sure why this is here since the enhanced version has the same core elements, the same atmosphere anyway.
3) Wanton Destruction and Twin Dragon expansion packs that contain new stories, new levels. I like how Wanton was released in 2005 - almost 8 years after the release of the original game. It proves it truly became a classic and it was properly looked at and authorised by 3D Realms.
But then what is Shadow Warrior? It is a game with a funny protagonist similar to Duke Nukem's. The player now assumes the control of Lo Wang who fights Zilla Enterprises with his Katana and dozens of one-liners. Some of the weapons are quite creative: you can use a heart as a weapon (needs to be ripped from one particular enemy) and by pressing the heart a clone of Wang appears and fights alongside you. There is also the head of a certain enemy that can be used to launch fire at the opponents.
The idea is the same here: shoot first, ask questions later! We collect key cards, kill enemies, look for secret areas (grab the fortune cookies always for the funny messages!), fight some pretty tough bosses and kill even more enemies! Classic '90s but a bit more challenging perhaps than Duke Nukem. Some of the weapons barely have ammunition or their spread / accuracy is just awful (shurikens, shotgun). I'm sure this was intentional. Just as picking a dark shadow as an enemy who can quickly launch fireballs at you. That is some tough son of a b*tch!
This is a highly recommended compilation especially if you are familiar with the game and / or already purchased Duke's Megaton Edition. Beware: The Classic version can be bought separately but since the Redux edition includes it there is no need to grab that one.

I did not expect to like this game so much, a board game with CCG-style deck building and a little dice-based PVP. Best when played against human opponents bantering in in-game chat. Not so great with the game's AI opponents which make many mistakes.
Everyone's decks get shuffled together into a pile all players draw from, so deckbuilding involves including cards that will benefit your character more than they will help other players. (This also means that if you don't get the DLCs increasing the pool of cards you may build your deck from, you'll still be able to play with the DLC cards your opponents bring to the table.)
The game mechanics allow big late-game reversals of fortune, so a skilled or lucky opponent can often find a opportunity to come back from behind. Often ends in a race to the finish with other players ganging up on whoever's closest to victory so that they don't win first.
Game developer Orange Juice pays attention to its players and actively tweaks things in updates to improve game balance. They also continually add new characters to the game via cheap DLCs, which seems to be their model for funding their continued development. While the DLCs aren't necessary to enjoy the game, achievement hunters may be annoyed that every time they add a new character DLC, they add new achievements that can only be obtained using the DLC characters.
If you like CCGs and board games, give the demo a try.

A cute Point and Click adventure that I would totally recommend. It was short (6-7 hours until completed), but longer than I expected from the first look.
While the characters seem simply illustrated, the world and background is in fact quite detailed and charming, while still making it simple enough to find all the objects you can interact with.
The game draws up its very own world with quirky characters and unique creatures. I was really drawn in by all the details and listened to almost all dialogs to get to know about them. The world and the story kept me immersed, captivated and engaged enough to play through in only a few sessions. The game has great humour in the dialogs and interaction, which makes it just so much more fun and worth exploring all the possible conversations. I had myself chuckling at the screen on so many occasions.
Also, the voice acting is great and well paced. While in other games I find myself skipping a lot of the dialog, I listened to most of it here, as it wasn't too slow or long and brings the characters to life in such a great way. If you wanted though, you could skip every dialog and cutscene.
The difficulty level isn't exactly easy, but the interactions and combinations mostly make sense (unlike other point & click adventures) and there's no need to randomly combine things. If you do get stuck, there's quite a good hint system that helps you out by giving you information in little pieces, trying not to spoil anything.
I found the story interesting with a few surprises, not very obvious. That being said, I would have loved a more thorough ending.
Also, in conversations you can talk about a single topic several times. I clicked on all of them, because I wanted to explore all the conversation and not miss anything, but often they keep blabbering about the same topic without really giving more content.
I also liked that you don't have too many scenes at once were you go looking for possible things to do, but I was annoyed at the loading screen between them, which made me really impatient. One scene in particular, where you have to go back and forth a lot had me waiting so often that it kinda took away from the fun.
Also, the achievements aren't very hard to get. If you read the descriptions, you could get almost all of them in a single playthrough. That might spoil some of the story though, so I wouldn't advise it.

The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is a massive open world game developed by Bethesda and released March 20, 2006. It would take too long to list all the various quests, armor, weapons, enchantments, and magic spells you can learn/create, simply trust me when I say this game is an adventure waiting to happen.
This is probably one of my personal favorite parts of Elder Scrolls of Oblivion, once you get out of the starting area you can make your own story, or follow the main story, or go search for your own quest. If you wanted, you could become a villain, you could also become a hero. The choices are completely up to you.
The whole Elder Scrolls series is very rich is lore and diversity of environment, you can read in-game books and learn useful facts about the monsters you fight. Not everyone will do this, but I ended up learning what all Trolls are weak against, and I've been using it in all Elder Scrolls games since.
I won't say much more about the story, because most of the fun is in finding the quests and stories yourself, and of course forging your own tale.... however there is one additional thing to note, in the Game of the Year Edition you get the Shivering Isles Expansion, and there you meet my favorite character in the whole series.
You can control the camera to play in third person, or first person. (personally I always thought third person looked silly... the knee's bend funny, and when you jump your legs stay straight. seems like an indication of "play in first person").
You could be a necromancer and summon skeleton hoards, you could be a thief and sneak into combat, you could be a warrior and smash your enemies faces in, you can be a mage and even create your own skills, you can be a ranger and pew pew, a monk, an acrobat or any hybrid combination of what I've said and much much more.
There are no Steam Achievements in this game, you can certainly find plenty of challenges online to test your skill in the game, or simply increase the difficulty of the game.
The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion Game of the Year Edition is priced at $19.99, as always, I suggest you wait for a sale, but if you already know you like this style of game you won't lose money out of it, since the game is getting "old"
you should probably look for a good deal out of the game, it goes on sale often.

What a beautiful, amazing, fantastic adventure and point and click game. I adored it from the very start until the breath-taking – and somehow - a bit sorrowful ending. No worries – no spoilers. It is a good story.
The story is eminent in all details. Just eminent.
It folds out again and again and all of the characters come to life. You really do believe in them as the story unfolds.
All characters matters. Good or evil.  Because it is a game of good and evil – could it have been anything else?
The graphics are well composed; all of a sudden you notice details that you did not pay attention to earlier. The details may not have anything to do with the story, but it doesn’t matter.
But this is how you can tell that the developers really cared. That the game really mattered to them in all those tiny details. And then it matters to you as well.
Be in for a game with some nut-cracking puzzles – some of them may not make any sense at first, but we will figure it out sooner or later.
And maybe we will not…
If it is a problem, the game has an amazing hint system: You can ask for a hint – but only a little piece of hint little by little. It is unfolding to the length of your need. Nothing more...
I have played a lot of games in the same genre on Steam and on other platforms, but this is truly the best way of helping the players if they are stuck.
As you can tell, I really enjoyed “The Inner World”.
Nah: I was carried away to another world, and I wished I could stay there forever. It was one of my best game experiences ever.
I will give it a 10/10, and I am going to play again and maybe again. I might have missed some obscure details… In fact: I know I have…
If you like point and click, well-thought-of voiceovers (sorry I didn’t mention those – they are terrific), lots of surprises, astonishing characters and a good length of a game, you should just buy it. It is AMAZING!

Men of War: Assault Squad 2 was a game recomended by a friend that took me pleasantly by surprise, despite me not being a RTS-crazy gamer. Going for a Company of Heroes-like economy, it saves you the hassle of base building and quickly brings players straight into the conflict. The game is pretty friendly to new and veteran RTS players alike due to it's simple Skrimish modes as well as the ability to play Co-op against enemy AI which I've spent hundreds of hours on.
On a tactical level, I quickly realized that many real-world concepts work here too; infantry works best in squad-level engagements, with MG teams covering an assault group, lone tanks or vehicles easily falling to sneaky anti-tank troops or even normal grunts with AT grenades, and the superiority of combined arms assaults. The immersion and environment sounds are simply amazing.
Replayablity is defintely a plus due to Steam Workshop compatablity. Community content allows players to set up their own missions, port entire campaigns from previous games and custom scenarios from other time periods such as modern warfare, hypothetical cold-War conflicts, other IPS (e.g. Star Wars, Warhammer, etc.) and I s#!t-you-not, the
black powder conflicts.
P.S. If on sale, it's best to buy the entire bundle with all DLC to save A LOT of money.

This game is a lot of fun and reminds me a lot of those oil and water dripper games that I used to really enjoy as a kid.  The presentation is nice and the fluid physics seem to be pretty spot on.  They react how you expect them to react and do so reliably each time which is important for physics based gameplay like this.  It seems like it would be a simple concept that would be difficult to find challenge in, but the levels do up the ante as you progress.  Very early in I was presented with a few that really had me scratching my head a bit.  But they weren't so difficult that I left the experience frustrated.
Most importantly, the dev is very responsive to the community and you can tell they are very passionate about the game.  I had a small scoring issue which I posted about and got a reply within hours.  The bug was not only fixed within the week but followed up on in the comment thread by the dev to let me know.  It's a pleasure to support devs who are so active with their community and willing to fix things even when they can't replicate the bugs we're seeing.  It's a refreshing change from so many of these unfinished or bug-ridden games that release then wallow for months without updates.  Well worth a purchase if even just to support those qualities that we should be looking for in game devs.  It doesn't hurt that it's pretty fun to boot.

As of Episode 3, Kentucky Route Zero is one of the very best games of all the time. I know that sounds like utter hyperbole, especially when people call tripe like Bioshock Infinite the Citizen Kane of games unironically, but its not, KRZ is amazing to an almost baffling degree for a video game. KRZ is an adventure game focused on exploration and character development, the main crux of the gameplay is exploring the Kentucky backroads and the enigmatic Route Zero and having a hand in shaping the cast's personalites and pasts along their journey.
A melacholic sense of loss and slow decline just permeates throughout the game.The graphics are minimalistic but beautiful and really adds to this lonely and mysterious atmosphere. The level design  and how its all framed is also great and it can get quite unique, showing the game world in different and interesting ways. The game's fantastic soundtrack also really adds to the atmosphere and  it is used to great effect making for some really memorable scenes. KRZ's writing puts every other video game to shame and it has a creativity and skill that most games lack. The characters are also quite likable and you want to see their journey through. Overall KRZ just sucks you right in and really feels like you're on an adventure into the unknown.
Episodes have been slow going but its been totally worth it. Wait if you want to, but if you buy it now you will not be disappointed. KRZ is just a great example of what video games can do with storytelling and really needs more love.

Woodle Tree Adventures is a game about a walking log that must collect fairy tears in several different themed worlds and one optional level that gets unlocked when you collect 600 berries, which are the equivalent of coins. It's a 3D platformer that really reminded me of Super Mario 3D Land. I wanted to like this game, but unfortunately after playing it I can't honestly say it's any good.
+
+
+
-
- Sometimes it was too zoomed out, sometimes it was right up in the character's face. I often fell down holes I couldn't see or got lost because the camera angle kept changing. It doesn't help that your berry sack just gets bigger and bigger, obscuring your view as you struggle to get onto the platforms.
-
- Your regular walking speed is very, very slow and your running speed is way too fast. It only gets worse when you're in the water and you slow to a snail's pace, even when running. When you jump, you always go forward whether you want to or not. The whole thing felt like an ice level; I was sliding around all the time and accidentally fell out of the world many times because of it.
-
- Noticed lots of clipping issues, from my character being half inside his own berry bag to enemies walking through each other. It's hard to tell when you're going to hit an enemy, especially with the default green leaf, because the hitboxes are messed up. Even when standing right next to an enemy and hitting it with the leaf, it didn't die.
-
- In some levels, it's okay, but in others it's absolutely grating. In one world, it's just a bunch of piano keys being played seemingly at random on loop. In others, it's simply not there at all and you can hardly hear it.
-
- In some parts, it's very easy to die not necessarily because the level is hard but because of unfair controls and the camera angle. When you do, you're ether sent all the way back to the start or sent to a checkpoint far from where you died. The checkpoints seem really inconsistent, too, because sometimes when I died I was sent to one and then I died later on and went back to the start. It's hard for the wrong reasons. Enemy AI is extremely basic (either standing still or moving along a very basic path) and the levels themselves aren't too difficult. It's just that the controls coupled with the camera make everything far harder to do that need be.
This doesn't feel like a finished game at all and would need lots of work to be worth the money. I got it free from a giveaway, but I definitely would not consider buying it if I hadn't. Don't get this unless you want free achievements and trading cards.

The Inner World is a very charming point-n-click adventure game of the Lucasarts variety, where there are no actual failure conditions, and the game can never get into a no-win state.  The Linux port, which is the one I played, is unfortunately pretty awful, but in the end I'd recommend it even on that platform (though see below for specific complaints about the port, and be prepared to hit that Refund button if the workarounds aren't good enough for you).
Back to positives, the puzzles are often quite inventive and unique, while also generally not being overly difficult.  There's some great pervasive humor throughout, a fairly touching (if predictable) story of personal discovery throughout, good background music, and great voice acting!  It's a very nicely self-contained story, and it's a world I'm excited to get back to in the forthcoming sequel.  My only real complaint storywise is that the main villian turns out to have one of those nonsensical "let's just destroy everything for no adequate reason" type motivations, but whatever.  The game is, IMO, well worth your time.
The Linux port, though!  Man.  It's rough.  I actually gave up on trying to play the game a few years ago because I couldn't for the life of me get any of the cutscenes to play, though recently (and on a different distro) I gave it another go and was able to get through the game.  I'm gonna enumerate the issues on the Linux version, so you can judge for yourself whether you're willing to fight through 'em:
Even now that cutscenes in general worked for me, there were many cutscenes which
play.  Some of which included vital clues that you'd need to solve puzzles, too, so it wasn't just story you'd be missing out on.  I did figure out solutions for all but two of the game's cutscenes (and the two were pretty minor ones), though, so check out this post for workarounds for those:
This problem is, honestly, extremely galling because it gives the impression that the devs/publishers literally never played through the game to completion on Linux, despite offering a Linux version for sale.  It was pretty basic stuff.
You'll note that my playtime just says "0.6 hours."  I promise you it's much more than that; I've solved the game.  It just doesn't generally talk to steam at all.  Interestingly, I think the only time it DOES record your time properly is when playing cutscenes, since I always get the Steam popup in the corner when one starts.  (The cutscenes, on Linux anyway, always play in a completely new window, which is why that's possible.)
Adjusting the volume sliders is a bizarre and unintuitive combination of frantically clicking around, hitting arrow keys, and occasionally seeing the sliders move around with seemingly little relation to what you're actually doing.
Early in the game, for instance, you can climb up on a balcony overlooking the temple.  You have several interaction options up there, but only one of them actually accepts mouse clicks properly.  Later in the game, I noticed that inventory interactions would often choose "Use" when I clicked "Look."  I encountered one place which would reliably seem to cause all game-related input to be ignored for a few tens of seconds before magically starting up again.  In general this didn't pop up too often, though, at least.
This, at least, has an easy workaround by hitting Tab, but still.  Lame.
This can be regained by hitting <Tab> and then the wrench icon, to bring up the options menu, and then returning to the game.  Sound will resume once you do that.  (It'll also come back on its own after you move to a new room or two.)
I didn't take the time to pin this one down exactly, but there were many points in the game where a dialog line just wouldn't be spoken.  Not a huge deal since it was still onscreen, but still.
Not a huge deal, obviously.
There's a weird bug where you can jump ahead to the third section of the game, when you'd just started it.  (Minor spoilers follow) [spoilers]The first time I hit the button on the paper airplane machine in the Root Forest, it showed cutscenes for all three directions and gave me the final result of the last cutscene (which was not the position the machine was in originally).  Also the guard keeping you from the Laboratory and Throne Room, in the Basylian factory hops about 100 pixels to the left after each interaction, sometimes reverting back to his original spot but more often ending up completely off the screen.[/spoilers]
Anyway, as you can see, it's
a good port by any means.  The main problem which makes the game borderline-unplayable is the cutscene issue, which thankfully can be worked around by the methods I describe.  It's a measure of how much I enjoyed the game otherwise that I'm willing to recommend it on Linux
all the lack of polish on here.  I'm excited for the sequel but I'm also going to be waiting to hear how the port is before putting my money on it.

I was looking for an in depth RPG to play and I was slightly hesitant about Vikings at first. Yet I loved the story very much. Don't expect a huge game: this is an excellent limited experience with sufficient depth, story and warmth to keep you interested throughout.
This game is more tactical in some ways than other similar isometric games, since you have no magic available. You have only limited options to put in skill points towards your survival. I found myself mulling over many options while I played, since points put towards survival in the wild are points that cannot be spend in combat. Time spent tending injuries cannot be spent towards creating food, or scouting for resources. In combat you are constantly kept thinking about the ideal tactical options and wrong moves are punished harshly. Most impressively for me, I actually lost a couple of battles, or missed objectives, but only once did this end the game.
The game in the end is limited, as said before. These limitations are clearly made so by design and they never impeded my ability to play the game to its full potential. They instead immersed me in the story and required me to stay actively engaged in how to play. A few times, I did find the lack of options grating, but no more than one would find a lack of options grating in real life... so it actually added to the realism.
Expeditions: Viking is an excellent game that does what it set out to do. It is neither expansive nor expensive, so do not be afraid to pick this game up for the time you have with it. I found it worth every cent.
