The first thing I want to say is that this was a very enjoyable game and I’m surprised to see that more people didn’t pick this game up when it came out in April. That doesn’t mean this game isn’t without its flaws. But I think this game is worth getting into if you’re into turn based strategy games akin to games like XCOM or Divinity. So if you’re looking for a decent strategy game at a decent price I would say this one is well worth your money. Buy this game is what I’m trying to say. It’s a good addition in your steam library and I’m glad to have played it.
So I can’t really say enough about this game. The combat is fresh and challenging. The story is well crafted and intriguing. I have spent a lot of my time playing this game the last couple weeks adding up to almost 50 hours. Honestly this game had me hooked with the word Vikings as I’m a sucker for historically based games. You have a free reign to choose your own path whether you want to be a raider, a diplomat or a trader. The outcome of the game is based on the play style you choose. I can’t honestly articulate why I had so much fun with this game other than its challenge and many diverse options in dialogue and combat. The challenge adds depth in combat causing you to figure out solutions to problems. Sometimes the best option is to literally rush into your opponents to keep archers from picking off your men. It’s a breath of fresh air to not have a game that holds your hand every step of the way and let you live with your mistakes. But altogether this game has fun combat, well-crafted dialogue between characters and diverse options for what type of campaign you want to do allowing you to craft your own story.
So I want to air out some of the flaws I think the game had these are few and far between though because the game functions perfectly for what it’s intended to do.  First off the game seems lopsided to favor the enemy no matter what setting you have the difficulty on and this can make some of the battle you’re involved in utterly frustrating. I’ve also noted that in some cases the enemy can literally shot you through walls not certain if it’s just a minor bug but it’s frustrating all the same. I also had a problem with the ending. While the game can run you through almost 50 hours of gameplay the ending feels rushed and kind of falls flat. Hopefully they release DLC to add an endgame mode that continues the lifespan of the game. I’m not sure it just ends so abruptly that it doesn’t feel satisfying more or less just kind of empty. They could also update the animations a bit to add variety to your actions outside of combat. I also found that sometimes the game would drop you in a battle with full option to attack the enemy but in most cases you combat will start at a handicap not allowing you to perform actions only to move your first turn. There isn’t a way to predict when this will happen when starting combat. And there are few dialogue options that allow you to gain the upper hand in combat through deceptive means which I would appreciate. But those are just some minor irks I have with the game as a whole and in no way makes me rethink my review as positive.

You've played action games. You, one badass guy with a bunch of guns (or his fists and feet) against who knows how many enemies. Well what if he was a she? And you decided if they had to use a gun or their fists? And you decided where to kick♥♥♥♥♥first? Oh, and it took more than 4 hours to finish?
This is the action RPG. Or at least Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion. My experiences with Role-Playing Games have been small, memories only including the likes of X-Men Legends and some samurai from the N64. I haven’t had a problem with them; it’s just the battle systems I can never stand. That’s why I prefer the action RPG to the regular one. And I love this game.
There’s no need to explain what this is or about. If you don’t know by now, you obviously have no interest in it. So I’ll just get to my thoughts. Honestly, I put this on my Gamefly Q because when I heard you had to create someone, I knew that a female had to be in realm of possibility (don’t ask). Anyway, I like the experience I’ve had so far.
The customization is crazy. You create a person from scratch, and you choose which abilities your character is "born" with, like whether they hack and slash or they defeat enemies with magic. As you go on, you improve these abilities, which allows you to fight the tougher enemies later on.
For a game as complex and vast as this, I find it a bonus that every single person speaks lines and even say a varied amount of things (there is some repetition, but that’s expected, and it’s not enough to worry about). I like the battle system, as it’s actually fighting, in either first or third person perspective, even though it’s secretly rock paper scissors based on your abilities compared to your opponents’, like RPGs usually are.
The overall world looks just amazing, and you’ll realize why you have an Xbox 360 once you see this. I should note this is from a person using a SDTV, so I guess it’s even better in high def. The people look realistic (even the non-human looking races) the textures on vegetation just plain creeps me out it’s so detailed.
That’s pretty much it. There’s no way you could not like this game. Seriously. This comes from a person who plays usually plays racing and sports games.

Awesomenauts is a variation on the MOBA style, except it is played in an objective 2D mode. This is seen in every screenshot of the game on the Steam store.  The teams (for now) are all 3v3, which makes it much easier to keep track of who is good, and learn other characters while you learn the one you are playing.
There are a few maps, I'd say around 6 in the base game with a few more added in the expansion.
The thing that sets awesomenauts apart from other MOBAs is there are no items.  Each hero has two base spells.  Now, that sounds not very complicated, but each spell has 6-8 "powerups" that you can choose THREE from at the beginning of the game.  Each of these powerups have 3 level ups that go throughout each match.
This MOBA is much easier to get into than the other games in it's genre, and still has the same addiction factor. I've played 4-6 of the 'nauts and I have somewhere around 20 hours in the game. I play it to master a certain hero and then move to the next once I have a good grasp on the hero, so that is in no way indicitive of my experience in the game.
I've found a few characters to be frustrating to play with/against, but it's usually because early-level vs late-game strengths.  Each game is pretty short (20-30 mins) so it is fast paced.  I've found it incredible how far you can be behind and still come back if you play smart.

Eh. Crusader Kings 2 is embletic of Paradox's greatest virtues and flaws. On the one hand you have a truly immersive game worth hundreds if not thousands of hours of gameplay, but at the same time any attachement to the game itself erodes as they go for breadth instead of depth. In an year in the lifespan of one of their games, you can be sure that as much as six months will be unplayable for one reason or another due to the cycle of DLC - > Bugs -> Patch -> Bugs -> Patch - DLC that leave the base game a complete mess for new players and forces you to take on the whole of the DLC to get an actual cohesive experience. Expeditions: Viking is a fantastic RPG game that is well worth your time. If you liked the old Infinity Engine games, you will like this one (even though it is turn-based, not real-time).
What initially struck me about this game, besides the beautiful art style and fitting soundtrack, was the interaction between several systems in the game. You see, the conversation choices matter more than just directing the storyline (which, compared to some RPGs, there are some interesting ways the story can go based on your choices!). Each of your party members has 4 attributes that they like in their leader (Such as Aggression, Peaceful, Conceited, Honorable, Cunning, etc). If your conversation choices match what a party member likes, they will gain morale. Choose the opposite option and they will lose morale.
What does morale do? Well, it will increase or decrease the character's physical and mental defenses. A high physical defense might prevent a character from being knocked down in combat and a high mental defense may allow a character to resist being taunted. Also, if you want to romance the romancable characters, they better have a high morale!
For another example, look at the lethal vs. non-lethal options in combat. When fighting, you have the option of being lethal or non-lethal. In non-lethal combat, none of the enemies will die (they just fall to the ground and writhe in pain), and you cannot critically hit anyone for extra damage. In lethal combat, sometimes the enemies will die and you can critically hit for massive damage. However, by keeping certain enemies alive, it may assist you in completing a quest or even later in the story.
However, this game is not perfect. There are still a few bugs (which, to the credit of those who made the game, they are actively fixing), so be sure to have a couple different save games handy.
Also, you get to be a Viking, so why aren't you getting this? YOU ARE A VIKING. YOU GET A SHIP! A VIKING SHIP!

I've played thorugh most of the game and I'm quite dissapointed so far.
The UI is awfull. You can decide if you want to kill enemies during combat or just leave them unconscious. All you have to do is uncheck the skull while in combat. The problem is that you have to click it every time you start an encounter.  I've set myself a goal at the beggining to not kill people unless it's necessary. Half way through game I've given up, because it's very easy to forget to turn off lethal blows and I've already messed up few fights.
It's very easy to miss click. I've played through many turn based RPGs and never ended up miss clicking so much.
Of course there is a quck load/save option, but the load times are long. Even moving the game onto SSD from HDD didn't help a lot. You can't quick load/save while in combat so it can be quite frustrating during long fights.
Poor voice acting. There's are few voice lines which you can hear at the beggining of few dialogues or when a character deals a critical blow or gets injured. I find those very annoying and would rather have no voice acting.
Pointless time limit. You can turn it off but it will disable achievements. Game tells you how much time you have left, but it's hard to judge how much of the time you can spend exploring. I had to play throught the first area twice to be able to explore all of the campsites.
Pickable items highlighting. It's annoying you have to hold the button to have it on. I mean, why wouldn't you want to have it on all the time. Some of the pickables are so small and are very easy to miss and can be worth quite a lot. I think this should be a toggle on/off.
Engaging in combat can be quite a struggle. If there's a fight at the end of dialog, your characters will be placed on the closest hex to the position where they were standing before dialog, so sometimes your archer might be put on the front, right next to few enemies and your shieldwearer trapped between other characters.
Those are the things that were bothering me a lot. Now, moving onto things I liked:
Very detailed difficulty settings can provide a fair challange for anyone.
Character progression is quite satifying and rewarding. Each skill upgraded can change a lot. There's no skill reset option, so you have to choose wisely.
Weapon, armor and usable items crafting is very simple and clear.
Camping system is great, although the interface is a mess.
So far the storywise the game is all right, you can optionaly take part in more detailed conversation if you're into it. Gameplaywise, for me it was a disappointment.

Shadow Warrior is one of the best FPS games ever made.
This rerelease of the 3D Realms 1997 classic is the definitive version - it doesn't require DOS Box (which is half-functioning at best), has full resolution and graphical options while keeping completely hands off the original game. If you're going to play a version of Shadow Warrior, this is your best bet.
Like most 2.5D shooters of the era, Shadow Warrior eschews story, character arcs (Though Lo Wang is a charismatic lead), and just about every other modern sensibility in favour of hectic, insanely fast and satisfying gameplay. In a way that's typical for 2.5D shooters, Lo Wang strafes around the levels at a million miles per hour pouring out a machinegun tequila, at a rate that makes returning to modern shooters an absolute chore. They feel like the world's slowest malfunctioning elevator in comparison.
Where Shadow Warrior stands out isn't just excelling at the gameplay, it's the support material. The level design is some of 3DRealm's best, combining truckloads of recognizable assets with traditional labyrinthine layouts to ensure that you're never bored, never funneled through some patronizingly limited corridor environments, but never lost either. Each room is a landmark, every area instantly recognizable.
Accompanying the fantastic level design is the gorgeous, satisfying weapons on offer - from your own fists to the best flamethrower in a videogame to date. Most weapons have alt fires of varying usefulness; it wavers from halving your own firepower for no reason, to firing a nuclear warhead that will  annihilate everything, yourself included.
It's from concentrating all its firepower on these aspects to absurd degrees that makes Shadow Warrior so good. No fluff, no mess, just a pure satisfying game.
It's not perfect. There's low enemy variety, with most just being slightly different coloured versions of each other. There's two well done bosses, but after the initial encounter they spam those bosses to miniboss levels. The final boss isn't even worth mentioning and neither is the ending.
The Achievements introduced are pathetically token - instead of incentivizing you for pushing the game to its limits, it just rewards you for normal play.
Not least, but last, the expansions are absolute trash. They just reuse assets from the base game constantly, introduced no new items or enemies (recoloured reskins aside) feel like lazy cash-ins through and through, with Twin Dragons in particular filled with advertisements to some long dead modding clan. They're more bang for your buck, but it's a pathetic bang not worth bothering with, that sours the experience as a whole.
But these are minor quibbles on the glorious ride Shadow Warrior takes you on. If you're in the mood for some of the 90s best, this is one of the best examples - and as Lo Wang says, it's all in the reflexes.

Chivalry is definitely an interesting game. I started playing back in September 2013 and in 680-odd hours and 46 in-game levels spread between then and now I've built up a pretty solid impression of the game. I'd have to start by saying I am quite heavily biased; Chivalry was the first game I ever sunk a worthy amount of time into and it is dear to me, however there are a number of factors that weigh heavily against it in my mind so I'll start by clarifying that this is very much a subjective review and based entirely on my opinion. I am a gamer, not a game developer, so there is no expectation for you to agree with me!
First off, the game requires a certain mindset to be enjoyable. Folks like me who hold themselves to a very high standard and don't like dying over and over are going to have a struggle with CMW because for the first hundred hours or so that's exactly what you'll do. This apparent century of frustration is broken here and there by amusing glitches, people getting walloped in the spleen by a faraway ballista and that one archer telling you 'the battle's this way, gorgeous' every couple of seconds but by and large the vast majority of players will have a rough introduction to the game. It really requires you to be able to maintain your calm and find the humour in the game and is best suited to players of games like Dark Souls (where dying stupidly and repetitively is routine). Special 'low rank' servers (for players under level 15) soften the blow for complete newbies by pitting them against other similarly vacant-minded players in clumsy pantomimes of a real Chivalry match, but the learning curve is stiffer than an Irishman in a Guinness factory as soon as you outlevel them.
I have to add that the above is especially true nowadays as the skill ceiling has absolutely exploded amongst players. Most public TO servers are regularly staffed by at least one level 50+ player (with a few 40+ cronies for support, the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s) identified fondly by their gold, black and (if you're really unlucky) pink helmets. The general consensus is that Torn Banner released a broken game and later out of laziness incorporated the bugs as 'tactics' (with regards to dragging etc.) and this, whether true or not, unfortunately has a huge impact on the game for the average player. The main idea behind CMW is, of course, melee warfare and the melee system at first comes across as much simpler and more fluid than games like War of the Roses. Empirically it is; specific keybinds perform specific attacks, parries and feints on key down and there is little more to it. The human physics of a game however are another aspect and players with enough time and experience (or tutoring) are able to run rings around newer players utilising a variety of moves that appear physically (and geometically) impossible and immediately shatter any immersion for the casual player.
If you are a player that enjoys diving into a game and developing an incredibly high skill level, you will immensely enjoy Chivalry. There is almost no limit to how a cunning player might bend the mechanics to achieve victory and the beautiful gore and sound effects make kills INCREDIBLY satisfying no matter what the situation. There are competitive clans scattered across and a load of helpful players that nurture tight and good-natured communities based around the game. There are of course bad apples, but in my nigh-700 hours I have never experienced a CMW server chat that was any worse than, for example, Battlefield 4's in-game chat. There will always be bellends and Chivalry is no exception.
With new, more polished games like Mordhau on the horizon CMW's community seems to be migrating ever so slowly on to greener pastures. Chivalry was many people's introduction to the genre of melee-based FPS combat, and its incessant urge to take the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of itself makes it a laugh with friends whether your team is winning or not, but I cannot help that feel that the game is entering its twilight.
Final verdict: if you're the type of player that is a glutton for punishment and enjoys a challenge, you may well enjoy what could be the last few months of a vibrant and... interesting community. If you like to win your games, buy something else.

Kentucky Route Zero is a masterfully crafted point-and-click, narrative adventure with the conceit that indirect storytelling is an effective form of character building. For the most part, it succeeds. Dripping with rich dialogue and gorgeous atmosphere, Kentucky Route Zero peers into the life and past of Conway, a down-on-his-luck deliveryman, as well as a cast of other strange folks driving the less traveled ‘Route Zero’. Conversation options are creative, often giving control instead to whomever Conway is talking to.  After most scenes, you return to a roadmap where you can drive around freely. There is no marker on where to go outside of directions gleaned from dialogue. KRZ does not contain any ‘action’ outside of narrative choices and the driving sections. Where KRZ shines is its unforgettable imagery and its strangely relatable cast.
If you are not a fan of ‘art games’ or tons of unspoken dialogue in your games (which is the crowd KRZ is catering to), you probably won’t enjoy this one. For everyone else, KRZ really is a must-buy… if you can find it on sale. The price has not fallen much since it's release.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Call of Pripyat is the final installment in the series. It's a sequel to Shadow of Chernobyl that doesn't follow it's main protagonist, but rather Major Degtyrev, a special agent of the most hated faction in the zone - Ukrainian Army. He is sent undercover to the zone for a rather simple task - find several mysteriously crashed army choppers, find causes of the crash, and look for survivors. Along the way, Major finds a lot of things to do with different factions - which is likely where CoP excels among other two games. The side missions aren't simple fetch/kill quests, but they rather have stories and arcs that lets the player learn a bit about everything in the zone - from human conflicts, to hunting mutants, to doing highly classified science work, to finding mysterious dark corners of the Zone.
While the premise of the main story is nothing to be too excited for, the player will do a lot of different type of quests that feel much more rewarding than they ever did, as well as traverse locations of epic proportions - there are only three areas in Call of Pripyat, compared to other two games. But these three areas are way bigger and way more dynamic and contentful than any other location from the previous games. There is also a long underground sequence that can serve as fourth location, but the players only traverses it once - however it provides one great sight of atmosphere.
I am having a hard time choosing whether i like Shadow of Chernobyl more due to it's superior plot/arc, but there was just too much effort invested into Call of Pripyat to improve the game in each aspect of gameplay. I really enjoyed playing Call of Pripyat, and i think any S.T.A.L.K.E.R. fan would.

The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion Game of the Year Deluxe Edition
Be prepared for a detailed review of this game. If you're considering purchasing this, have a read and see what you think before doing so!
+ Pleasant graphics for a game almost a decade old (2006).
+ A huge assortment of quest to complete, such as the Thieves' Guild, Dark Brotherhood, Fighter's Guild, Mage's Guild and Daedric God storylines. Lots of miscellaneous quests too.
+ Massive map to explore, lots of locations including caves, bandit camps, forts and ancient ayleid ruins. Snowy regions and lush forest, open grasslands and swamps, very varied terrain.
+ Wide array of weaponry, many, many skills to level up, use magic, archery or melee combat to strike down foes. Mix your own potions with alchemy, become a master of acrobatics or conjure powerful beasts to do your bidding.
+ Hundreds of hours of gameplay to engage in. Fun for the first 100-120. Anything in excess of level 40 starts to see boredom set in. I recommend taking regular breaks to avoid the repetition, in which case it won't be so noticeable.
+ Large mod community.
- Extremely flawed and stupid monster levelling, giving you no sense accomplishment when you progress to higher levels. Many creatures will be levelled to you, meaning that, at higher levels, you'll be required to spam click attacks for ages to get kills (ogres, goblin warlords, gloom wraiths). Keep in mind this is using the best weapons available, with the highest skill level. Much to your disdain, you'll spend hours clearing out caves or forts filled with insanely high hitpoint enemies. Not fun, not a challenge, just a complete and utter waste of time.
- Caves, dungeons and other places have a lot of loot potential and you'll have fun in the beginning collecting fragments of armour, potions and gold to pay for adventuring supplies and purchasing houses. However, after awhile there's literally nothing to spend your cash on. All of the equipment I've sold has resulted in stockpiling over 300,000 coins, with nothing practical to spend it on. Every elder scrolls (even the latest instalment to the series, Skyrim) has had this issue.
- Dumb AI that gets stuck when you jump onto rocks and cast magic or shoot arrows. It doesn't understand how to reach you. The AI scripting for conversations is also ridiculous. There are only a limited number of discussions citizens can have between each other and these all feel very, very unnatural. It's as if the designers didn't bother to implement realistic dialogue.
- Many textures for forts or caves are re-used and do not look unique. This gets dull later, rather than sooner, but it's still a great downfall of the title. The layouts of many locations are similar. They might have different pathways, include an underwater cave or a bridge, but for all intents and purposes, most locations have a familiar feel to them. There's little excitement in that regard.
- Modding requires excessive use of complicated tools that are not only time consuming but annoying. Not to mention the countless glitches that conflict with gameplay.
- Character levelling comes to a sudden halt around levels 40+, it becomes so infrequent that you feel like you're achieving nothing at all, apart from going on errands for a number of characters you don't care much about.
The Shivering Isles Expansion:
+ New textures compared to the base game, an entirely new environment, new colours, new armour and weapons, new characters, new monsters and new quests. Consequently, this expansion does have a feeling of freshness to it.
+Around 30 hours of additional content, which is not unreasonable for an expansion.
- Despite the fact that there are various changes and new features, the dreadful monster levelling system remains, which never fails to detract greatly from the experience (unless you go to the Shivering Isles at a lower level, at which point it becomes bearable).
- Rather horrible voice acting for Sheogorath, too try-hard in its approach, quite off-putting and didn't seem like a genuine portrayal of the characteristics the developers wanted to exhibit, which was a God of Madness.
Knights of the Nine Expansion:
+ A new and intriguing storyline (for the most part) based around the Nine Divines, where you must complete a series of tests to retrieve the ancient armour of Crusader Pelinal Whitestrake, in an effort to defeat the infamous Umaril, a Daedra who poses a threat to Cyrodiil.
+ Some extra locations to explore which have been added to the map during the expansion, but nothing really new other than aesthetics (the Crusader armour and weapons).
+ There's a real feeling of reviving the old Knights of the Nine Order, as people will approach you to swear their allegiance. You'll fight side by side at the end against Umaril's minions in a big battle, which is cool.
- Many of the places you'll visit are filled with the standard enemies you'll encounter in the base game, there is little difference in the design of these locations to other ayleid ruins or forts in the base game as well.
DLC Add-Ons:
+ A number of new houses for those interested. There's a Wizard's Tower, a Castle and an underground Cave that can become new homes, some of them include enchanting and spellmaking areas for convenience.
+ A few additional activities to partake in, like collecting dwarven artifacts stolen by bandits, to repair an Orrery at the Arcane University. You can also investigate the caverns beneath anvil to find the resting place of a pirate ship and the mystery behind it. In the East of Cyrodiil you can travel to Sundercliff Watch, a fortress that holds the powerful Daedric item, Mehrune's Razor.
- Some bugs which interfere with how the house DLC works, causing problems with them being unable to be purchased or relevant questlines not progressing.
Overall Score: 7.5/10

Have not written a review in quite awhile, but i feel this game certainly deserves one! TLDR at the bottom.
Expeditions Vikings is a cRPG set in the 8th Century. You begin as the son or daughter of a Thegn (Thane - Lord) who was lost on a raid to Britain some time before. Your stead is in a poor state and the way things look at the beginning, your clan will not be around for much longer... unless you act.
Its hard to write a review without spoilers so i will try to keep it free of them. You have a great deal of freedom to decide how to save your clan, be it raiding, trading, diplomacy or a combination of all three. How you deal with others will have consequences for good or ill later down the road. You can and infact must if you wish to be prosperous, strong or both expand and upgrade your holding.
You will also need to gather together a strong Viking Hird (personal warband) to accomplish your goals. These men and women have their own personalities and varying loyalty to you depending on your actions. Not unlike the previous game Expedition Conquistador by all accounts, which i have not played but anyone who has will understand how it works.
The combat is turn based and tactical. You have a cover mechanic, attacks of opportunity, morale, consumables, ailments and buffs and the weather and time of day can have an effect too.
I thoroughly enjoyed this game and i cannot say i have played a game as good since i finished the Witcher 3 (on GOG). Its one of those games you wish did not ever end.
Pros
For the type of game the graphics and hand crafted locations are simply gorgeous and immersive. A real feel for the time period and history.
Music score is excellent and the old celtic ballads really add to experience.
Combat is a lot of fun and an cRPG fan will enjoy it in my opinion.
Plenty of locations, content to explore to plunder or otherwise.
Memorable characters throughout the game.
Do it your way, mix it up or focus on a set goal to get you on the road to power, prosperity or both. With consequences.
An interesting camping mechanic to keep your Hird at its peak.
Superstition and witchcraft realistic for the time period.
+/-
Some mythical references and experiences which while i think add to the lore some might not agree.
Archery is deadly in the right hands. I like it but if you do not plan or are plain unlucky it will hurt. Needless to say this works both ways.
Cons
For me whenever i quit the game, steam would freeze and eventually close. Could be because i run more than one game at a time.
One consumable in particular is not very realistic and hugely overpowered but cannot be crafted till mid-late game.
Without spoiling anything, lets just say certain fortifications cause more problems for you and your Hird than help. Yet later on the enemy use them fine.
Overall personal rating for enjoyment: 9.5/10. Loved it!

takes place between 1066 and 1453, and there are literally hundreds of characters throughout that span that you can play as. is complex, and the tutorials explain perhaps a third of the stuff you’ll really want to know. This game is now my most favorite game, I played DOS twice, one playthrough by myself (150 hours) and one with my friend (60 hours). I can say that I really enjoyed the first game and was really looking forward to DOS 2. I'm almost 200 hours into it and I am not even done with the campaign. But being nearly done I think I can give a proper review.
Combat: So most people criticize the game for being turn-based rather than a real-time with pause function. But it feels right in place as the combat still feels so engaging. The combat is tougher since a lot of skills that you have, the enemies have as well. This makes the combat harder but also more rewarding once you get past it. The game is hard yet fair. There are fights that seem impossible but the game provides us with the tools to win or hides the tools within the world. A lot of the skills feel strong and useful. But towards the end game, I find that magic damage started to be more obsolete as it is much faster and easier to physical as that it the most reliable way to damage. Though that might be because my team consisted of 3 physical dealers and one wizard.
Story: This is by far my favorite part of the game. The story is rather simple yet done in a way that makes it compelling. And as someone who played the other Divinity games, there are a lot of surprising plot twists that I was surprised by. But where the game shines the most is the origin stories. You can either create your own character or choose one of 6 pre-made origin characters that have their own backgrounds. And and these stories are very well-written with equally well made characters. It is so interesting to see how much the game changes because of who you are. If you didn't pick an origin character, you can still recruit them but after a certain point, they will become unavaible. It is a rather intersting thing of being a side character to the origin character's stories though. And each origin chracter will have a personal quest which will result in some drastic endings. But some advice, do not play as Lohse. Not because she is bad, she is a great character with a one of my favorite stories. But Lohse is best when played as a companion and her personal ending yields the best reward a video game has ever given.
UI: I will be blunt about it, it's bad. Inventory management is a nightmare. Sadly it is also required in powering up your weapons in the end game. You will spend a long time in your inventory looking through it to find a single item. Crafting can be done through a seperate menu but most of the time you will be combing random stuff together and that is horrible. In the end game, you will have so much clutter mostly involving books and paper with no swift and reliable way to dispose of them.
Other Notes: The game has quite alot of bugs as well. The first area will be rather polished because it was in early access for a long time. But the game is large and some parts are even broken at times. But I would like to say that I have not faced a bug bad enough to take away from my enjoyment. The game is best played (in my opinion) with a roll with it attitude. Just accept mistakes that happen. It is really fun to see all my mistakes bite me in the♥♥♥♥♥later down the line. And before I forget, the soundtrack. It is a masterpiece. DOS 2 has a different composer from the past Divinity games (RIP Kirill) but the new composer has truly put his heart and soul into it and it is an absolute joy to listen to.
Just buy the game. Larian deserves all of the praise and hopefully they will make a console version so we all can share in the masterpiece that is Divinity Original Sin.

After almost 1,000 hours of playing CONAN EXILES... I can honestly say this game is worth owning at any price!
... provided you are into base-building, exploring an open world, crafting and more crafting, killing tons of stuff, resource gathering, enslaving thralls (NPCs), base design and customization, and you enjoy an immersive experience.
Now for the Pros and the Cons:
*  Amazing graphics and resolution
*  An enourmously huge map - from tropics, to desert, to frozen tundra... its seriously big!
*  Constantly improving physics engine
*  Unlimited and uncapped potential in base-design, base-size, and base-complexity  (seriously mind-blowing)
*  Gorgeous landscape and enviornment - so must diversity and depth in this open world enviornment
*  Variety, variety, variety - in items, weapons, armor, base materials, craftable goods, animals & NPCs, etc.
*  Exploration encouraged - many of the best items, armor, weapons, emotes, crafting skills, etc., come from exploring
*  Crafting and Skill Tree - very expansive and diverse, allowing for customization to the milllionth degree
*  Major expansions and additions planned to add additional content (new areas, dungeons, items, skills, etc.)
*  Regular updates and improvements - while still in its infancy, CONAN EXILES already show more potential then any other "open world" game in existence today, and still has descent stability for its grand scope
*  Server inconsistency - depending on what server you choose, you may have a wonderful experience where the server is very stable, and you a very friendly community, where everyone helps one another... Or you may have a bad experience where the server is a toxic community of angry kids, trolling one another (and this is why I recommend PVE or PVP, as PVE servers tend to be less toxic then the PVP servers)... but even then, without server admins, trolls may abound (its the internet after all)
*  Lots of bugs & glitches - obviously because its a true "open world" game still in its infancy, it has plenty of bugs & glitches to annoy and frustrate  (but not game-breaking).
major bugs & glitches of note:
-  Server lag and server instability, often as a result of disabled item decay timers and/or disabeled base base decay timers, this can cause issues with you from everything to be mobbed by NPCs and dying, to causing your inventory items to temporarily disappear, or get moved around, or sometimes even go missing... as well as causing chrashes and other issues.
-  Tempature system can cause you to take damage sometimes, even if you're not exposed to extreme heat or cold
- Weather system allows the rain and wind inside your base (but Funcom promises to remedy this soon)
-  Anchor point (your bed) may not always work 100% of the time, resulting in finding yourself at the starting point, far from your base
-  Snap-to positions for certain base pieces may sometimes have issues in snapping together the way you want, and you have to finesse them into doing what you want (use your repair hammer to verify foundation stability isn't the issue)
-  No build limit (can be seen as a pro or a con), the upside being you can build a gigantic castle or village, and the downside is that a troll can build a 200-story tall wall around your base, or wall-off a public resource, or block a high-traffic area so other players can't get by {they are protecting more and more public resources and landmarks, and they may add build limits in the future}

Im gonna skip the amazing graphics, sound, atmosphere and gameplay, and tell you the most important thing: this game has the best AI in any game to date. The developer was inspired by FEAR in terms of AI in battles: the enemies flank you, sneak up on you, take cover, give commands.
But this is not just an FPS, it is also an RPG, and HOLY CRAP! if this aint the best RPG out there, then please let me know! Thus, the AI extends outside of combat. Monsters travel in packs and engage in fights with other monsters and humans for survival's sake. If the fight seems to be in their favor, they will engage, otherwise they will fall back and move along. Squads of stalkers patrol the Zone: sometimes to defend their base, sometimes to recapture a point. Sometimes it's just one greedy stalker trying to retrieve an artifact from an anomaly so that he can sell it later.
And that's another thing about this game: artifacts and their anomaly counterparts. You see, this is the Zone. Radiation has chnaged many things, not just animals and humans. You will find these mini puzzles with an expensive artifact as a reward. Sometimes it's a timed electricity trap. Sometimes it's a gravitational anomaly that holds the ground and water up in the air in an unnatural fashion.
Marketing is killing the gaming industry nowadays. Sales people push developers to improve on graphics and numbers: more DLC, more weapons, more maps, more more more. And it seems like everyone has forgotten the other ingredients that make a game good. Such as AI.
If you haven't played this game yet, buy it now! I have spent most of my time playing STALKER: Clear Sky (cheaper), which puts more emphasis on factional warfare. But as far as I can tell, this one is just as good, if not better.

In this point-and-click adventure game, you play as Robert, an adorably naive boy in the land of Asposia, an entire society built on the inside of the world rather than on its surface (hence the name of the game). Asposia runs on wind, but only wind fountain out of the original three in Asposia is still functioning, so the lights are going out and the residents will soon suffocate. Also, there are attacks from the wind gods, who petrify anyone deemed "immoral." Robert gets unwillingly pulled along for the ride. It's a great story with some interesting puzzles.
Pros:
+ Great story and worldbuilding. Very unique.
+ Good humor. Robert is adorable and sheltered, leading to some hilarious situations like him not understanding sexual innuendo or is naive enough to believe a holy man when he claims that he's "meditating" while at a slot machine. There are lots of other fun characters, like helpless researchers and blockheaded guards.
+ Decent music. Not super memorable, but good at setting a mood and not intrusive or annoying.
Neutral:
~ Generally fun puzzles, but there were a few that were annoying because they involve combining a bunch of non-related items to solve a puzzle, and it's not obvious what you're making until it's finished. Having the "A-ha!" moment AFTER you've built a thing is definitely the wrong order.
Con:
- Game is a bit buggy. I had a game-breaking bug in the last chapter, but fortunately, there are save game files available in the Steam community for all the chapters. Also, you have to have Adobe Air up to date or the game will freeze after every cut scene.
Overall: 8/10. It's a fun game, and definitely worth a play if you like adventure games.

As a technical note, I've played this game until its final culminating 10 minutes, because the game just doesn't manage to keep itself running when I reach a certain point in the final evacuation, about halfway through the mission. After seeing videos about the final minutes, I haven't missed too much.
So, S.T.A.L.K.E.R.. Perhaps my favorite game series of all time. In many ways a review of this final installment of the series is a commentary on them all. Excluding obvious technical remarks about poor optimization, poor stability at times and glitches ranging from hilarious to potentially game-breaking, I have mostly praise to deliver.
Stalker-games all center around on adventuring - and at times, merely surviving - in what possibly is the most wonderful theme that has ever blessed mankind, which at the same time is one of the most horrific disasters striking that said mankind. Stalker-games' relation to the accident at Chernobyl is tangential at best (the same could be said about its relation to the Roadside Picnic novel and Stalker movie), it still captures enough of the real to make for compelling fantasy. Reality does not stop at the theme itself, but the fact that much of the speech and non-spoken text is also preserved in its original form of Russian (even though it should probably be Ukrainian, but what do we stupid self-centered westerners know?) makes the game feel so much more genuine than your run-of-the-mill modern shooter, where the most foreign element you encounter is heavily accented English.
Even though Stalkers do not aim to be ARMA-like simulators, they nonetheless take certain pride in their genre. Iron sights are viable, even mandatory, and different weapons and alternative ammunition are plenty, if somewhat dumbed-down in this third installment, compared to the first game. Armor and weapons can be upgraded with numerous convincing-sounding doodads which, while not always presenting itself too clearly what their actual benefit to the player is, serves as an addictive middle-term goal. With some differences I would say all Stalker-games can be discussed as a one entity. Even though balance changes between each game, and the first game being possibly mechanically most poor, if you like one Stalker-game, you probably at least tolerate them all.
To say something about Call of Pripyat itself, while being immensely recommendable to all shooter game fans, it still falls short compared to what I see as the Ultimate Stalker, Shadow of Chernobyl. While it does quite well exploring its own side of the universe, it still manages to deliver the story as more simple, much less mystical and intriguing as the first two games did. It feels too much like an epilogue, which it irreversably is. Possibly this is partially planned. Without going into too much (spoiler-)detail, to the player the Zone no longer bears any mysticism. You have already learned its secrets, already know what makes it tick. You no longer even play a lone wanderer intent on deciphering its secrets, you are a government man on a mission that only accidentally happens to uncover more of the truth. And even in this it manages to do so in almost sorrowful frontier fiction -fashion: now that mystery is solved, control can be established and the myth has to make room for reality. What was already a world of the past ceases to exist altogether. In a considerably concrete way the game punts you out to the post-Stalker world. The Old can be revisited, but never again experienced in the same way. Or that is how I, with a touch of melodrama, understand it.
S.T.A.L.K.E.R.-games offer a quite unique and compelling setting in an enjoyable, if unpolished way. Their genuine delivery feels exceptionally loving treatment of an IP, at least comparing to many modern shooters, or games in general. If one requires alleviation to Stalker-withdrawal, Metro-series is a worthy runner-up, if not a perfect match. 5/5 x 3.

"The Inner World" is a point & click adventure from Germany that is suitable for and recommended to beginners and lovers of adventure games.
Its story takes place in Asposia, a world that mostly lives from wind and light but suffers under its dictator Conroy. His adopted son - or should I better say "slave" - is the protagonist and by accident he stumbles out of the palace he has lived all his life and begins an adventure which will make him discover the outside world, love and some (ugly) truths.
This point & click adventure is easy to control and to understand. The way you select your items and go through dialogues (all displayed with symbols) is similar to "Sam & Max: Hit the Road" (thus also playable for illiterates by the way).
So your main task is to progress in the story by talking to characters, finding items and combining them with other things. You can't die in the game or get yourself into dead ends.
The difficulty level is fine, the puzzles aren't child friendly-easy but also not too hard. However, as in classics like several LucasArts adventures or "Simon the Sorcerer" you definitely need to think laterally a lot in order to progress. So it's still challenging here and there. If you're still stuck, there is an in-game help but I personally don't know if it's good (I never used it).
What makes the game for me is this universe and its culture you're introduced to, the story and its main character. It's a game full of charme and a good dose of humour. However, the further you get the darker the story feels which is also pretty cool. Even though you can't die in the game you experience more and more traces of darkness, dictatorship, superstition and threats in this world. That's when the humour comes handy and brings extra charme to the game. And as for the characters, especially Robert is great here thanks to his naive but optimistic nature, his design and his English voice actor Mike McAlpine.
Speaking of, let's quickly talk about the graphics and sound.
The animations are or are like digital Flash animation. It's not glamourous graphics but the cartoon style is original and likeable, you can connect to those Asposians and the other creatures very well (at least I can). Original is also the character design. The backgrounds look more detailed and not only that, they look beautiful. Also despite of the cartoonish style it's never in too bright colours, the colours are actually quite subtle.
The soundtrack is very nice. So nice though that I purchased the soundtrack DLC after finishing the game. It's beautiful and serves a lot of the game's atmosphere. When it comes to voices you can choose between the German and the English language. Even though the game's from Germany and so am I, I personally prefer the English version. I just like chosen voices there better, especially Robert's voice (as mentioned before).
Are there things I don't like in "The Inner World"? Just a few minor things that never seriously destroy the game.
There are little flaws in the animation (people who have created vector graphics in general or flash animation may know what I mean). Also I wished that the world of Asposia had at least more background characters. Most of the time it looks like you save a world that's barely populated at all (and yes, I know, why a certain amount of people are gone but still...).
What about extras? Well, there's a "Play Flute-Nose" option in the main menu which allows you to play Robert's nose as a flute à la "Guitar Hero" (react to the music by pressing certain buttons in the right moments). I haven't played this often because it's not that great for me but if you enjoy this kind of music game or a bonus mini game in general, you might like this.
There are also Steam achievements and trading cards.
So: Do I recommend "The Inner World"? Yes, definitely, if you enjoy adventure games.
Personally I enjoyed it very much. I don't consider this one of the greatest adventures ever but it's still very good and since I know that there's a sequel game coming in summer 2017, I'm so looking forward to it and can't wait to play it.

Very deep game with interesting gameplay systems, marred by a lack of polish and a really bad UI.
- After four years of development there's still no way to assign a title to someone from that region's details view, you have to do it the other way around and select the character first! Makes assigning vassals to conquered land sooo tedious. And that's just one example. One wonders why they don't let you export/import that stuff so you can edit it in LibreOffice Calc or Excel, it would actually feel better. <troll> Just provide a CKII skin DLC for those programs </troll>.
- The much-touted roleplaying elements are nothing more than a bunch of dialog boxes. And they do love to obstruct your view by spamming dialog boxes. You know some games like Civ 5 have a better way of presenting updates to the player, right guys?
- The combat isn't particularly interesting.
- Doing anything in this game is typically a lot of work, often for little reward
- The Youtuber/Streamers that seem to have fun with this usually exploit the system to the max, exploits that Paradox then takes out of the game, often without a proper replacement. Don't expect to have fun like them.
No matter what you do, unless you love frustration don't play the William the Bast.erd start where you have a big army and go after England. The game mechanics don't support this scenario well neither from a gameplay or historical point of view, and the devs haven't made any effort to make it better since the game's release. You've been warned. (Curious? The game will usually snatch your victory from you just as you were crushing the last English province. Your King allies with your enemy and cancels your war, no option to rebel despite technically having your own kingdom now. That's the usual outcome of the
... thanks Paradox, know what we'd like instead of more DLCs?)
As an aside, I don't like Paradox's new policy of releasing a bunch of DLCs along with free patches. It means that feature introduced in one DLC can't interact much with others, and that they're unlikely to get revisited later. Please go back to the old "patch-expansion" model we were used to with Hearts of Iron III... people think they can pick and choose and pay less now, but they don't realize what they lost along the way. Newcomers, in particular, who get the base game for the cheap to try things out, will never know if they disliked their experience because they just don't like the game, or because it would have been better with 200$ of DLCs. A bit steep, to try a game the average gamer is statistically likely to dislike? And forget the refund policy, you need more than a hundred hours to make your mind on this one, not two.
Despite my dislike for this game I might come back to it. So many people defend it as amazing that I can't help but wonder if I missed something or I just didn't experience the right scenario. But even if I discover it it will have been at the cost of close to 100 hours of my life, not sure that's worth it.
Heck, if the idea is "make your own fun", I'm pretty sure I've had exponentially more hours of fun and satisfaction with a soccer ball, purchased for a small fraction of this game's cost.

This game did plenty of things right, and plenty of things wrong. The quests and story are done beautifully. The voice acting is fantastic. The graphics were excellent for the time, and they are still decent to this day, but only when maxed out and with mods. There is plenty for you to do in this game, and plenty of locations to explore. With all the content, I can see why people put hundreds of hours into this game.
However, I found myself getting bored very quickly with the combat. For a game that is intended to be played for many, many hours, you would expect the combat to remain exciting and not become stale. That's not the case with Oblivion. Swing your sword, block, swing, dodge, swing, block, fireball. That's all there is to it and it gets tedious very quickly. It's just very simple combat.
The leveling system is broken. You can spam spells on yourself and level up your skills like cake. It's very easy to exploit the system, so the urge to do it will be there. Some skills level up too fast and some don't level up fast enough. I ended up using console commands and maxing out my skills and my level just so I wouldn't have to deal with it. I feel like this game doesn't even need a leveling system at all.
Glitches. This game is very glitchy. You will find glitches all the time. You cannot escape the glitches.
This game is much better with mods. Be sure to download plenty of mods.
Even with all my negative talk, I still had some fun playing this game. Maybe you'll enjoy it even more than I did.

Vikings has provided me one of the most narratively fufilling experiences since Planescape Torment and the golden era of CRPGs. In summary points:
+The engine is well put together and flows well, especially since the early bug patches.
+The visuals are simple, yet striking and effective.
+The combat is visceral and requires well executed strategy and tactics.
+Management of the warband in downtime and deciding what each member does is great.
+Your actions aren't 'good' or 'bad', they only demonstrate your traits (Greedy/Honourable/Altrustic etc), which impact how your followers react to you.
+The narrative for the game is excellent. Full of sweeping plot arcs and smaller personal moments.
+The number of options for how to tackle not just individual siutuations, but the entire campaign are staggering.
+The main character feels as if they belong to you, rather than just a faceless protagonist on a pre-set track.
-The later character development becomes a little stagnant and could use more options
-Inventory organising and separating good from chaff items is a little tedious
-Its very easy to waste time, skill points and resources on ill explained crafting
-Sometimes the narrative locks you into siutations where you are forced to fight ill prepared or with crippled party members with no warning. Save often with multiple files.
On the whole this game is a solidly 'Great' title with only a few technical flaws and perhaps the lack of any multiplayer (not strictly necessary) holding it back from being a perfect example of a modern classic CRPG.

Okay so in my opinion this game is fantastic, but I'm going to get the bad stuff over and done with for the people reading it that are slightly sceptical.
One of the things I've noticed in a lot of the negative reviews of this game is the fact that people don't like the lack of diversity: this is true, there is only one map in this game, which is a relatively small arena with no obstructions and nothing to stop you from falling off. I can see why people would think this game is bad because of that and I would say to people who are after a game with a story and lots to do (as much as I like those games myself) this is probably not for you.This is a game where all you can really do is strive to defeat your last score, and maybe your friend's scores, nothing more beyond that.
That is simply how the game is and I don't believe it's right to criticise it for that, but I also don't want people to buy this thinking otherwise.

Now for some positive stuff. The reason I got this game is because it reminded me of DooM. The ambience of the sound effects and the way things fade into the dark and the demonic theme of it all just makes my soul melt. I genuinely think it's an indie gem. It reminds me of Doom a lot, which is another plus. The movement is fluid and feels natural, and it doesn't overburden you on buttons; in fact it's very minimal with only WASD, Spacebar and right mouse button needed. But that in itself is enough to make the game diverse. The two modes of firing are pretty simple, but all you really need. I adore the shotgun as it gives me more DooM flashbacks.
One of the things that took me a while longer to notice was the surround-sound effect it has with all the sound effects in the game. It makes a lot more sense why it has music, as I've learnt to depend on the sound of spires spawning to locate them and get a head start on destroying skulls. It's very subtle but it's a really nice touch, and way more thought went into that game than I originally imagined.
Now I thought I'd have more to say but I think my brain died. A quick conclusion is: pretty graphics (if you're into darkness and demonic sculls), cool sound effects (if you're into hearing abyssal whispers, eldritch hisses, and demonic roaring), smooth controls (if you're into feeling like you're gliding through hoards of your worst nightmare and love closing gaps like a graceful dagger-toting falcon), cool♥♥♥♥♥models for enemies (if you like skulls and other such like), and great gameplay (if you like dying a whole lot).

Weird doesn't even begin to describe this game.
Employing pretty unorthodox narrative style Kentucky Route Zero tells a story of a delivery truck driver Conway on his way to the mysterious Dogwood Drive.
The game supposed to be point-and-click adventure but in reality clicking is just means to involve you in the story. You won't see an inventory or puzzles, and the dialogue choices don't have consequences as such. The narrative moves at an uneven pace while keeping you interested. One second you might be controlling Conway but the next you're choosing dialogue option for the person he's talking to. The character you're controlling can be changed literally mid-stride, while two of them just running around. One scene can be told from a perspective of your main character and the next from the perspective of a guy he's seeing for the first time. I would say that is quite innovative for a game narrative.
This game is text-heavy with many dialogues and has beautiful eerie atmosphere. This weird atmosphere and shifting narrative reminds me a lot of David Lynch movies. That would certainly be the way to "gamify" his works. The game is divided into acts and scenes (out of five of which only three are currently released) and has a distinct theater play feel to it.
While most of the playing time is running, clicking and dialogues, among the the odd activities you encounter here are a karaoke session, flying on a giant eagle and playing text adventure on an old oscilloscope.
I would recommend playing this game if you're ready to read a lot and would like to experience gloomy atmosphere and surreal Lynch-esque story through rather experimental storytelling. This is a true work of art.

As a technical note, I've played this game until its final culminating 10 minutes, because the game just doesn't manage to keep itself running when I reach a certain point in the final evacuation, about halfway through the mission. After seeing videos about the final minutes, I haven't missed too much.
So, S.T.A.L.K.E.R.. Perhaps my favorite game series of all time. In many ways a review of this final installment of the series is a commentary on them all. Excluding obvious technical remarks about poor optimization, poor stability at times and glitches ranging from hilarious to potentially game-breaking, I have mostly praise to deliver.
Stalker-games all center around on adventuring - and at times, merely surviving - in what possibly is the most wonderful theme that has ever blessed mankind, which at the same time is one of the most horrific disasters striking that said mankind. Stalker-games' relation to the accident at Chernobyl is tangential at best (the same could be said about its relation to the Roadside Picnic novel and Stalker movie), it still captures enough of the real to make for compelling fantasy. Reality does not stop at the theme itself, but the fact that much of the speech and non-spoken text is also preserved in its original form of Russian (even though it should probably be Ukrainian, but what do we stupid self-centered westerners know?) makes the game feel so much more genuine than your run-of-the-mill modern shooter, where the most foreign element you encounter is heavily accented English.
Even though Stalkers do not aim to be ARMA-like simulators, they nonetheless take certain pride in their genre. Iron sights are viable, even mandatory, and different weapons and alternative ammunition are plenty, if somewhat dumbed-down in this third installment, compared to the first game. Armor and weapons can be upgraded with numerous convincing-sounding doodads which, while not always presenting itself too clearly what their actual benefit to the player is, serves as an addictive middle-term goal. With some differences I would say all Stalker-games can be discussed as a one entity. Even though balance changes between each game, and the first game being possibly mechanically most poor, if you like one Stalker-game, you probably at least tolerate them all.
To say something about Call of Pripyat itself, while being immensely recommendable to all shooter game fans, it still falls short compared to what I see as the Ultimate Stalker, Shadow of Chernobyl. While it does quite well exploring its own side of the universe, it still manages to deliver the story as more simple, much less mystical and intriguing as the first two games did. It feels too much like an epilogue, which it irreversably is. Possibly this is partially planned. Without going into too much (spoiler-)detail, to the player the Zone no longer bears any mysticism. You have already learned its secrets, already know what makes it tick. You no longer even play a lone wanderer intent on deciphering its secrets, you are a government man on a mission that only accidentally happens to uncover more of the truth. And even in this it manages to do so in almost sorrowful frontier fiction -fashion: now that mystery is solved, control can be established and the myth has to make room for reality. What was already a world of the past ceases to exist altogether. In a considerably concrete way the game punts you out to the post-Stalker world. The Old can be revisited, but never again experienced in the same way. Or that is how I, with a touch of melodrama, understand it.
S.T.A.L.K.E.R.-games offer a quite unique and compelling setting in an enjoyable, if unpolished way. Their genuine delivery feels exceptionally loving treatment of an IP, at least comparing to many modern shooters, or games in general. If one requires alleviation to Stalker-withdrawal, Metro-series is a worthy runner-up, if not a perfect match. 5/5 x 3.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Call of Pripyat is a mystery to me. There are SO MANY problems with it, and yet I still enjoyed playing it. Is it a great game? NO. But is it a good game? MAYBE.
I have seen other reviews claim CoP is a better, more challening Fallout, but this is simply not true.
VISUALS
Everything in this game is repetitive and ugly. I have seen multiple reviews, even professional ones, claim that the visuals in this game are great, and I absolutely do not see why! I am not talking about graphics, which are so obviously below standard it's not even worth criticism. No, I mean atmosphere and appearance. First, every area of the game has the same open fields, short hills, boring trees, bushes, and grass. There is nothing in the natural scene that is beautiful or scary (I even installed Atmosfear, which is a beautification mod). Every building is square and industrial, filled with empty, useless rooms. This, far and above, is awful to look at. CoP is FILLED with identical buildings!
Second, the oft-cited tense and scary atmosphere is present, albeit rarely. Truly scary or tense moments are governed by the RNG and therefore often missing. One of the "strengths" of this game, similar to Skyrim, is how independent the world is. Monsters and NPCs will spawn semi-randomly and often collide with the player and each other. However, this also means that the chances a creature will appear in empty building #127 that you exploring is actually very rare. Often I navigated a creepy abandoned factory (they're all factories, remember?) at night, with only a flashlight to guide me, all the while expecting some monstrosity to come at me, and NOTHING HAPPENED. I would find my loot, and go back to the safe zone, yet again. Boring. The best creepy moments, were the scripted ones at the end of the game! (which were few)
COMBAT
The second thing this game is known for is the FPS combat. One positive element of the game is that almost any enemy can kill you all by itself. Supposedly, this means you have to be very cautious in any combat situation and fight tactically. In reality, combat is the simplest rinse-and-repeat affair I have seen in many other games. Human enemies are a great example. If you are within firing range they WILL hit you (apparently every fool in the zone is an expert marksman) and kill you in a few shots. So, what is the strategy to defeat them? Easy: 1) hide behind cover, 2) pop out and headshot him, 3) consume a medkit to recover any damage. THAT'S IT. These three steps are pretty much the same for every enemy in the game, except for one that can go invisible (which is actually EASIER to kill). Headshots do very high damage (as they should in any serious FPS), but the moronic AI just stands there and shoots like a British Redcoat, so there is nothing stopping you from dropping enemies like flies. I have put hundreds of hours into TF2, so a headshot on a non-human player is like shooting fish in a barrel for me. I have literally stood in an open field, without cover, and killed four human attackers (NOT zombies) all firing at me without dying. Then, I just popped a couple medkits and waltzed away.
WEAPONS/ARMOR/ITEMS
*SPOILERS: I mention the names of weapon items, so if you want to learn them on your own, skip this section. *SPOILERS*
There are many weapons in this game, however, half of them are nearly identical, many of them are completely useless, and the good weapons are both rare, and hardly used. First, all pistols are useless and can be abandoned in the first ten minutes of the game once you kill a single human enemy and take his rifle. Second, the first three assault rifles that you have access to are nearly identical, and the most common one you come across, the AKM-74/2, is a superior weapon for more than half the game. You can attach a scope and a grenade launcher to it. The next best rifle that is encountered in the second area of the game, TRs 301, is the literal successor to the first one. It too can be upgraded with scope and grenade launcher. This or the SGI-5k, will serve you for the rest of the game. Finally, all you need after this is a shotgun and again, the second shotgun you will likely encounter, the SPSA-14, will serve you for more than half the game. I easily beat the entire game with this assault rifle and shotgun combo. I never needed another weapon. There are several stronger special weapons, but the big problem is, you don't have access to them until you reach the final level, which is something like 80% into the game! So you get these cool new weapons, and no time to use them. BOO.
Another note about weapons/armor. You can upgrade your weapons with technicians in safe areas, however, you have to find tools to give them to get access to the higher tier upgrades. It was an absolutely STUPID choice to put the final-tier tools in the last area of the game! Also, there is absolutely NO HINT where they are located, so you just have to exhaustively search every building in the final area to find them. What does this mean? Well, first, you will encounter every major enemy in the third area and kill it BEFORE you get the tools! Therefore, you will have fully explored the final area of the game BEFORE you can upgrade your weapons to the highest level! What that hell good is that!? What good is the amazing targeting scope on my sniper rifle when I already killed the 12 enemy fighters in the apartment building BEFORE I got it!? This is even worse with the armor. The best armor in the game does not allow you to run while wearing it until you have the final tier upgrade for it. Once again, this armor is completely uselss for 90% of the game.
MAP LEVELS
The final frustrating element of this game is the map itself. So many players completely overlook that this game is really just a walking simulator. There is NO transportation or fast travel in this game. YOU. WALK. EVERYWHERE. Or more accurately, you sprint, walk, sprint, walk, eat a sausage, sprint, walk, sprint, walk, everywhere! You spend SO MUCH time walking! It's enfuriating. This game is not like Fallout/Skyrim where interesting events happen to you while you travel. At best you may happen upon some humans fending off a mutant attack. Honestly, the best strategy here is just to watch, because usually the mutants kill the humans, and you can loot their bodies. Otherwise, there is no reason to waste hours walking. To make matters worse, because your primary source of money in the game are special items called artifacts that are located in the far corners of each map and that respawn at random every few days, you will do A LOT of backtracking.
Furthermore, the map is divided into three levels that you can only travel between by use of a guide. This "guide" is basically fast travel, since you talk to him, pay him money, and then you are instantly transported to the next area. You CANNOT access the other areas of the game on foot. You must PAY a guide to take you EVERY time you want to change levels (which is a lot). The reason for this is so obvious: the developers needed to separate all of the assets in the game so it wouldn't completely overload our computers. Finally, the third level of the game, which is really your primary goal, is both small and extremely short. What should be a climactic final level, is over in a handful of quests.
Honestly, there are so many other things I could complain about, but I still choose to recommend this game because you can pick it up for nearly nothing during a sale. This game barely registers in the positive for me at a 6/10, but if you have a couple extra bucks come the next big sale, you may want to give it a try just to see what all the fuss is about.

takes place between 1066 and 1453, and there are literally hundreds of characters throughout that span that you can play as. Being a king is very different than playing a count, but neither’s journey is less interesting. The stories play out constantly, whether you play a provincial count or a godlike emperor. While your goal is ostensibly to sustain your dynasty as long as possible,
is more about the journey than the goal. Getting there is more than half the fun.
is complex, and the tutorials explain perhaps a third of the stuff you’ll really want to know. After a week of play you still have burning questions about major game systems that just aren’t covered in the tooltips or manual. But the potential is totally there, so long as you can stick with it and conquer the sometimes-overwhelming interface. There are little buttons everywhere, and while the interface is pretty useable once you get used to it, it’s never as easy to find specific characters or visualize their relationships as it probably should be. This in particular makes the game feel impenetrable at first.
Overall
can be a heck of a lot of fun. The more you understand, the more fun you have. Once you start getting past the learning curve you’ll find yourself more and more absorbed by all the complex little dramas that swirl around your nobles.

- Strategic interpersonal relationships
- A complex and deeply rewarding system of diplomacy
- Many DLC's for expanded play

- Steep learning curve

With pretty artwork and graphics, and an interesting story and characters, this game comes highly recommended from my experience. A lot of games bill themselves on "choices matter" type gameplay, when the reality turns out to be a shallow pool of limited approach that feels deceivingly railroaded.
Not so in Expeditions: Viking! You can craft and mould the story and how it twists and turns by the choices you make. How you choose to resolve problems, settle fueds and deal with enemies has an actual impact on the story and the game, and how people react to you from various factions and groups. Telltale Games could learn a lot about what "choices matter" gaming really is from the people who made this game.
There are some bugs still, which can be annoying, but these things are being eliminated as time goes by, and I even got a response from a developer on my forum question about an issue I was having.
If you loved Baldurs Gate or Icewind Dale, and want to see a game like that with more of a "choices matter" spin to it, you have to get this game. You should also get this game if you like RPGs, Vikings, beards or longboats.

Eh. Crusader Kings 2 is embletic of Paradox's greatest virtues and flaws. On the one hand you have a truly immersive game worth hundreds if not thousands of hours of gameplay, but at the same time any attachement to the game itself erodes as they go for breadth instead of depth. In an year in the lifespan of one of their games, you can be sure that as much as six months will be unplayable for one reason or another due to the cycle of DLC - > Bugs -> Patch -> Bugs -> Patch - DLC that leave the base game a complete mess for new players and forces you to take on the whole of the DLC to get an actual cohesive experience. For me it's kind of telling that the most solid previous generation game they had was Victoria 2 which ceased recieving DLC a long time ago but was still a lot of fun and almost never had any bugs at end of focus period.
When you add into that Paradox's tendency to decide how you can or can't play your game (closing off North Korea mode, multiple "fixes" to player-chosen game-styles and not allowed achievements in single-player), then it becomes a very love-hate relationship with a largely well-meanign company slightly too reliant on DLC to keep their franchises going. I'd give CK2 a thumbs up purely for appreciation for the hours of quality gameplay provided but given how burned out it's left me on Paradox as a whole I find myself unable to do that.

Shadow Warrior is another one of those classic games that any FPS fan should own.
This game was made by 3D Realms, the same company that made the highly acclaimed Duke Nukem 3D. Shadow Warrior is sort of a spiritual sequel to Duke Nukem 3D, using the same engine and having similar gameplay, only with an Asian theme. However, Shadow Warrior is a great game in its own right. The combat is fast-paced, there are a variety of weapons and enemies, and many of the levels are fun to explore.
One minor downside is that there are a few frustratingly parts where you have to figure out how to do something in the level with no guidance from the game. Of course, this is how many classic games were, and most of the times it's nice not to have a game holding your hand the whole way through. Although there were a few times when the lack of guidance was frustrating, this was ultimately a very minor blemish on an outstanding game.

Everything you could ask for in an RPG:
* Turn based combat that really is deeply strategic with a perfect learning curve
* A wide variety of characters that feel unique and complex
* Engaging story with many plots, characters, and choices for solid replay value
* Moral choices far more complicated than a stright good/evil scale
* Huge maps filled with battles, quests, puzzles, characters, and secrets
* Difficulty options ranging from "easy enough to enjoy the story fully" all the way to "certifiably insane"
* Signiture character building system that encourages experimentation with truly custom classes
PLUS a sizable supportive community means:
* Tons of mods for your custom gaming pleasure
* Wikis, forums, and spreadsheets to help you however you like
What else can I say?
I'll try to come up with some negatives:
* As is always the case with Larian, there are still bugs and other small issues that can disrupt immersion. These are mostly minor. While Larian is still patching at the time of this review, I know they stopped patching the first game before getting to all the bugs. Didn't bother me that much.
* If you don't like inventory management, you might get a little frustrated. You can pick up an insane quantity of items for selling, consuming, cooking, and crafting purposes.
* The crafting system could be more logical and streamlined. Fortunately there are mods for this.
I also have one personal gripe: because the choices and moral options in this game are so very diverse and non-linear, it can be very disappointing to find places were the choices DO end up being "good" or "evil" when they were presented as being more complex. This is rare, but the spots where it does happen bother me.
OVERALL, this game is absolutely amazing, worth every penny, and, having taken 120 hrs to do my first playthrough, I'm now going to go back and do at least two more to explore different choices and character paths (and mods).

Steam asks me to say "yes" or "no", so I choose "no" in this instance. With that said, if you are interested in what games can do, this is a must play. Absolutely.
Between the art and the soundtrack, Kentucky Route Zero is beautiful. You watch scenes literally construct and deconstruct. The ever present ambient music calms you. Personally, the musical performance at the Lower Depths in Act III justified my purchase (though I did buy it on sale). The unfortunate part is that it isn't a game and there isn't a plot. There aren't even characters. It's simply a world that you explore. There's a foundation for a strong game, but the execution relies on one aspect (atmosphere) and abandons everything else.
I admire its ambitions--the dialogue selections become a personality test for the player through (sometimes seemingly endless) dialogue selection, and the pacing, when done well, is done VERY well--but, for me, it hasn't (as of Act III) been successful. Random things happening to / at / in the vicinity of empty shells of characters drives me away. I found myself skipping dialogue, hoping to push everything along. Conway limps through the entirety of Act II, nearly slowing the game to a hault by discouraging you to explore the world. Even magical realism and surrealism need a tether; and that may occur in the remaining two acts but that's a little too late for me.
