The developers of this game appear to have seen that other games have used platforms, but didn't quite understand why. In a good 3D platformer (like, as mentioned in the game description, Mario 64 and Banjo Kazooie), there is challenge in navigating the environments. You see where you are trying to go, and the trick is figuring out how to get there, usually with tricky leaps, hidden paths, timed puzzles etc.
This game doesn't do any of that.
The only reason there's any challenge at all, in fact, is because every level is suspended over a bottomless pit. As such, every jump is either entirely safe, adding nothing to the experience, or is instant death, dumping you back at the start of the level. (Well, technically it will *sometimes* put you to a checkpoint part way, but there seems to be no particular reason why. It's never very close to where you were anyway, and subsequent falls with inevitable forget the checkpoint was there.) There are two types of pickups; berrys, which are everywhere and just unlock weapon upgrades (and one extra stage), and droplets. The berrys are sometimes hidden, but as they all respawn when you restart a level, it doesn't actually matter if you miss any... this game has no concept of 100% completion. The droplets are always out in the open, and easily accessible, if perhaps off the main route.
Have I mentioned the camera? It's *awful*. You have one control; zoom. This doesn't help when the camera decides it wants to be at a flat, low angle to the player, making it impossible to tell where any of the platforms are in relation to your character. It's no even like, given time, it will rectify itself. Nope, if you can't see, tough look; better try anyway, maybe the camera will be nicer after you respawn. Oh, also; you can zoom out forever, and in doing so things on every level that were clearly not meant to be seen, like random platforms from other level, berries floating out in the middle of nowhere, and (for some reason) *something* submerged near the player's spawn point, on every level.
Combat is entirely redundant. Enemies take one hit to kill, invariably. The ones that move have just one action; run towards you. (OK, technically two; there are bees that slowly drift up and down in place, but come on.) With the first leaf, attacks are melee. Everything is easy to kill, with most deaths I suffered happened when I turned away from the enemy I'd just killed, my sack had touched their dying animation, and that was that. Once you get the first upgrade, you can kill anything from a safe distance while they just stand still, often by accident. The two next upgrades... increase your attack range? Maybe? I don't know. Nothing actually useful. No idea what the bandana is for.
After an hour I completed the game, and had a good few seconds to run around in the big wide opening area that I had work so *very* hard to bring water too before the credits ran. This is mild in comparison to the rest, but let me talk game design here, for the rare beast who's read this far and is considering making their own game. If your game concept is based around the player bringing water back to their home land, you should probably do the following: first, make the land look dry and barren at the beginning, lot filled with lush greenry. Second, allow the player to pop back to that land whenever they like, and see how their work has made a change. (If you want to get all creative-like, have the changing environment allow them to access powerups, easter eggs, additional levels, or something to give them a solid feeling of having an effect. Third, when the player has finally completed their task, let them enjoy the paradise they have created. For a game that never felt like a climax was coming, this was still anti-climactic.
On the plus side, the main character looks kinda cute. 10/10 GOTY 2014.

Put short and sweet, this game is very, very addicting.
A bit of a personal story:
I started playing in 2007 when Audition was still under Nexon and remember playing it for hours upon hours. Come 2009, I quit because of technical issues and thought I would never play the game again. I honestly completely forgot about the game under one day in 2014 I somehow heard a song that I remembered was from Audition. Overcome by an extreme sense of nostalgia, I searched up the game, was surprised to find out that it still existed, and re-downloaded it immediately. I expected to only dabble in the game for a short while to satisfy my nostalgia, but it was too late--I was addicted again, and have been very active ever since.
Now why is this game so addicting? Well, there's a variety of possible reasons, since there's so many things about the game that could make it addicting.
The most common reason would be the community. Many of the active players have been playing this game for years, so they know each other quite well. The game doesn't have many players when you compare it to more popular games, but that makes this game have a close-knit community. Even if you never talk to some people, if you play at least semi-actively you can recognize the IGNs of various other players. Like every game, there's going to be people you like and people you don't like. But the people you get along with can make the game so much more worth playing. You can join a FAM, which is like a guild, and the easiest way to make friends. You can also get a "couple" and get married, and enjoy various features of the Audition marriage, including gaining couple points and taking care of your own couple garden.
Of course, the gameplay itself is Audition's main feature. Audition is a rhythm-based game that features various "modes" you can play. You don't necessary have to play all modes, but the most commonly-played one is the "Normal" mode, which involves pressing a specified sequence of keys and pressing Spacebar or Ctrl at the correct beat. The Normal mode itself consists of various different modes as well. When most people first take a peek at the game they think that it's like DDR on the computer, but in actuality the only modes that are somewhat similar to DDR are Beat Up and Block Beat. I would go into detail of all the various modes, but the best way to learn is to play the game yourself.
Like many other games, you can "level up" on Audition. When you play with other people, you gain EXP. After you gain a certain amount of EXP from playing a number of games, you reach the "license mode." This is only applicable after level 5. In order to level up past level 5, you must pass this license mode in order to reach the next level. The license mode will be a certain Normal mode and a certain song depending on the level you're about to reach. You must pass certain requirements involving the "combo," amounts of "Perfects," and the score.
Some people have a goal to reach a certain level. There's this culture of "EXP spamming" in which people accumulate various EXP multipliers and play a certain mode on the shortest song. This is generally more common among people of higher levels, as much more EXP is required as your character increases in level.
Another popular aspect of the game is the shopping mall. Audition has a wide selection of clothing that is mostly Korean in style since this game originated in South Korea. You can buy "beats" clothes, which has a small, relatively decent selection of clothing that is rarely to never updated. The upside to this is that beats clothes don't require any real money, as beats are Audition's in-game currency. You can also buy "cash" clothing, which offers a wide variety of clothing that usually gets updated at least once a month. Bana Cash can be bought with real money through various mediums such as credit card, GoCash game cards, and now Steam Wallet. Cash clothing can be bought for various time intervals: you can buy them for 7 days, 30 days, 90 days, or indefinitely. The quantity of cash required per outfit doubles with the aforementioned time intervals. Something to note is that not all cash clothing can be bought indefinitely; however, the selection of indefinite clothing is updated once every few months.
There is also something called a "Tournament," which exists for certain different modes at specified times, everyday. Here you can find some of the best players of each mode as they battle it out for the final goal--the medal. Tournaments can get quite competitive, but it is that competition that many players are looking for as they seek to improve themselves in certain modes.
I don't play other rhythm games, so I can't really compare Audition with other rhythm games, but I definitely would recommend Audition to people looking for a rhythm game with a competitive yet welcoming community. If you have any questions about any aspect of the game, feel free to contact me, as I would be more than willing to help.
To all the new players, I welcome you to the community and hope you have a great time!

... Let's get right to the meat of it. Arena shooters aren't for everyone. I don't want to refund this because the gameplay, the atmosphere, the score, the sounds, the art are all deeply tied to my memories and beliefs of what a game should be.
And I desperately want to see an actual game, with levels and maps and more then 1.5 weapons in it, but this game that ain't.
And here's the cardinal sin, the one that makes my bones rattle in utter discontent.
I don't think it's hard. No, I'd argue this is essentially a tech demo; the game ratchets up the foes the longer you survive, but the waves are largely predictable, meaning that as long as you pay attention, you should be able to learn the skills the game requires very quickly.
My time as I posted this review is six minutes of gameplay time, and I already feel it's outstayed its welcome.
Quite a few people would disagree, which is fine, and here's where it gets important.
Do you like arena shooters?
Do you you prefer a small box-arena with guaranteed enemies to a series of levels?
Are you worried about spending seconds getting back to where you were, so you can see new formations or new enemies or hear new bits of background ambience?
Do you care about leaderboards?
If you like the thrill of one-upping your best score, seeing your numbers rise above someone elses' on the leaderboards, and aren't bothered by a lack of variety, go for it!
But if you don't... There's nothing. You'll learn all the skills necessary to be good a few deaths in, there aren't really any new weapons, and as beautiful as it is in every respect, that's not a reason to get the game.
No, I won't refund it; I'd kill to see a proper game with alien skyboxes and gritty kills in this style, hear music that puts the original Quake soundtrack to shame, ramps up the difficulty through level design and item starvation rather then just expecting you to not pay attention. I'd like to see a good, old-fashioned FPS.
... And this isn't.
~ Pros:
- Beautiful, in every sense of the word.
- Smooth, when you can get it to run; though there's only one real weapon, it handles with the satisfaction you find in Doom, Heretic, Quake, etc.
- Sound design is perfect and almost every new enemy has a sound or light cue to react to.
- If you're not good at adapting rapidly, this'll be one hell of a ride.
~ Cons:
- If you don't care about leaderboards and aren't driven by your own desire to surpass your high score, you'll probably get good enough to see all the game has to offer very quickly.
- Difficulty dependent on the surprise of new enemies and lack of familiarity; once you can live past a wave, you'll live past it again unless you stop paying attention.
- The arena size seems less dangerous then it should (underutilized?), at least after you get a sense of how big it is.
- Who would just kill a skeleton that fires smaller skeletons..?

I dont want to give this game a negative review. Its a great game, an awesome game even, however there are a few things horribly wrong with it. First and foremost the game is bugged as ♥♥♥♥. Constant crashes, bugs and other ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t limiting the game severely, even this long after release.
Secondly a fundamential game feature is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. You really need ressources in this game. How do you get ressources? Run around the city and TAKE EVERY SINGLE CRATE as if you were playing Skyrim. No. Just no. Why do this people let you steal all their stuff? Why does pillaging your own town give more ressource than playing the game normally? Why should you choose such an extremely tedious and annoying mechanic as the best way to gain vital ressources? This is absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. There isnt even a quick loot system a la baldurs gate, you have to manually click every ♥♥♥♥ing crate in every ♥♥♥♥ing town because there are ridiculous amounts of ressources in them.
The last point are the quests. There are a few quests which feel super forced. Lots of early fights cant be prevented by dialogue. Sure these guys hated your father but making it absolutely impossible instead of just super hard to convince them that you will tackle things differently? Thats bad design, at least when you do it this often. Also sometimes quest just dont make sense from a logical point of view. The worst example of this forced quest design and one of the worst quests i have ever seen in genereal is the quests which involves killing rats.
Warning: SPOILERS:
The quests starts neatly. You think "Hey this is the obligatory kill rats quest". Than you see the rats are actually children. Now it gets interesting. Its a moral dilemma, take the easy way out and just beat them up or kill them or do something hard to not do something immoral. Except the DEVs do not want you to complete the quest the second way. The only way to complete the quests without fighting the quests if you have banished a few people earlier and their home is now empy. Even if you only banished the men you cant force the women of the banished family to adopt the rats. You also cant persuade anyone else in the town to give them shelter, not even the church. There are charred ruind nearby with an intact cellar which would be big enough for them to live there, but you cant send them there. You can kill a certain guy on a different side quest and now there is a nice big comfortable empty longhouse, but you cant send them there. You cant send them to your village which was just attacked and could need a few helping hands. You cant pay anyone to take them in. You cant give them ressources to build their own home. You cant even tell the quest giver to ♥♥♥♥ off so this quests stops clogging up your quest log. All you can do is either kill or beat up the kids. This is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and lazy design. The DEVS incentivise violence against kids even beyond logical rules just because they were to lazy to come up with alternative ways to tackle this quests. It makes no sense why there is no other way to solve this quest, 5 minutes of brainstorming shoudl be enough to come up with a ton of more solutions. Because the quests starts out so well and is such a refreshing spin on the usual RPG quests this stings even more. Its disappointing.
I will lay down the game for now because i dont see the quests and the bugs and teh mindless looting becoming much better soon. I will return and update this review when there is a patch that fixes this, until than this should warn players that this is a game with great promise but terrible execution at the moment.

I bought Oblivion May 1, 2012, it was my first time to ever buy it and...I found it completely unplayable because of how  ugly and dated it is.   The bright 1950's Technicolor movie look was a turnoff from the start.   The character models were ugly, the character faces were all generic, oval and ugly and the animations were  stiff and artificial.   The way the game drags you face to face to talk to an NPC drove me crazy.  The fact that there are around ten generic NPC voice actors grates on me still...its common to hear what sounds like an NPC taking to himself because both NPCs in the conversation use the same stiff, generic voice.
Having said that...thank the Nine for mods.   I started modding Oblivion February 2014 and I've been playing it quite a bit now.  Without mods I would never have played Oblivion, with mods its playable and somewhat more immersive.  All my mods are aimed at toning down the bright colors to something more natural, replacing the default heads with human looking heads, better textures, ect.   I'm not trying to alter how Oblivion plays just make it look better, less dated and less technicolor.   I'm sure eight years ago it was a wonderful game...but it hasn't aged well at all.
Combat in Oblivion feels sluggish and unresponsive.  For example I'll see an enemy preparing to hit me and try to block but by the time my shield raises often I've been hit 2-3 times and staggered then block after the attacjk is over.   Sword swings have the same unresponsive feel to them often initiating late causing me to hit the enemy after its blocked.    When you click to attack or block you expect those actions to occur not hesitate a few seconds, it really makes Oblivion's combat feels really loose, slow to respond and unsatifying.
Personally I find a lot of the quests are pretty dull fetch quests in towns with a few dungeon delves tossed in so you don't die of boredom fetching someone lost Slippers of Doodad Magic.   I've had more fun just exploring and dungeon diving than doing the actual quests for the stiff cardboard NPCs.   If you're a fan of The Elder Scrolls and never played Oblivion try it, you may like it.   Out of Morrowind, Oblivion and Skyrim I think Oblivion is the weakest of the three modern Elder Scrolls games.
I really want to like Oblivion more than I do but every time I start to get immersed in it the game slaps me in the face with really bad dialog delivered stiffly and reminds me its just a game and a fairly average one at that.   Its a shame because there is a lot of potential in Oblivion that was just out of the grasp of the Bethesda development team because of the limitations of the technology when it was made.   I give Bethesda an A for effort but a C for execution.

Easily one of the most amazing and affecting games ever.  Some people claim it's "not a game" because it doesn't have puzzles like a traditional adventure game, but that sells this game short.  The makers definitely don't care what your pre-concieved notions of a "game" might be, but the interactivity is very high but in ways I've never seen before.  You don't so much choose what's going to happen as you craft the characters past while going on this bizarre, amazing journey with them.  The visuals are stark and striking.  The regular soundtrack is equally stark, but subdued.  Where it stands out are the bluegrass songs that suddenly appear out of the blue, like the band playing in the shadows of the foreground in the first act, or the melancholy lone banjo in the forest of the second act.  The third act, in addition to an excellent bluegrass song includes a stunning and unique interactive song that really blew me away.  GET THIS GAME.

I bought Oblivion May 1, 2012, it was my first time to ever buy it and...I found it completely unplayable because of how  ugly and dated it is.   The bright 1950's Technicolor movie look was a turnoff from the start.   The character models were ugly, the character faces were all generic, oval and ugly and the animations were  stiff and artificial.   The way the game drags you face to face to talk to an NPC drove me crazy.  The fact that there are around ten generic NPC voice actors grates on me still...its common to hear what sounds like an NPC taking to himself because both NPCs in the conversation use the same stiff, generic voice.
Having said that...thank the Nine for mods.   I started modding Oblivion February 2014 and I've been playing it quite a bit now.  Without mods I would never have played Oblivion, with mods its playable and somewhat more immersive.  All my mods are aimed at toning down the bright colors to something more natural, replacing the default heads with human looking heads, better textures, ect.   I'm not trying to alter how Oblivion plays just make it look better, less dated and less technicolor.   I'm sure eight years ago it was a wonderful game...but it hasn't aged well at all.
Combat in Oblivion feels sluggish and unresponsive.  For example I'll see an enemy preparing to hit me and try to block but by the time my shield raises often I've been hit 2-3 times and staggered then block after the attacjk is over.   Sword swings have the same unresponsive feel to them often initiating late causing me to hit the enemy after its blocked.    When you click to attack or block you expect those actions to occur not hesitate a few seconds, it really makes Oblivion's combat feels really loose, slow to respond and unsatifying.
Personally I find a lot of the quests are pretty dull fetch quests in towns with a few dungeon delves tossed in so you don't die of boredom fetching someone lost Slippers of Doodad Magic.   I've had more fun just exploring and dungeon diving than doing the actual quests for the stiff cardboard NPCs.   If you're a fan of The Elder Scrolls and never played Oblivion try it, you may like it.   Out of Morrowind, Oblivion and Skyrim I think Oblivion is the weakest of the three modern Elder Scrolls games.
I really want to like Oblivion more than I do but every time I start to get immersed in it the game slaps me in the face with really bad dialog delivered stiffly and reminds me its just a game and a fairly average one at that.   Its a shame because there is a lot of potential in Oblivion that was just out of the grasp of the Bethesda development team because of the limitations of the technology when it was made.   I give Bethesda an A for effort but a C for execution.

Oh man, what a game, seriously, this has got to be one of the best RPGs I've ever played, and I play a lot of RPGs.
For the TL;DR skip to bottom.
Let’s start off with character creation, it’s in depth and fun, your background story actually changes based on how you create your character which is awesome. The story itself is basically just the plot of the TV show Vikings, which is actually great because that show has a great plot. If you wished Vikings was a video game, then this is the game for you. This game is also really appealing to anyone into Norse culture and mythology, I found myself enamored with some of the events in this game. The combat is excellent, it’s turn based and tactical and fun. The combat has excellent pacing and balancing and never gets boring or feels tedious, which is a big deal for a turn based game. The RPG aspect of the game, the choices, they are wonderful, seriously one of my favorite things about this game. This is your kind of true “your choices make a difference” kind of RPG. My actions and decisions have weight, and additionally, they are varied in morality, essentially I can be a nice guy or a total piece of ****. That’s something sorely lacking in today’s RPGs, the ability to be an ***. Another thing is, I just finished my first playthrough, which took 46 hours to do pretty much everything, and it was really entertaining. Pair that with the game’s ridiculous replayability and you have hundreds of hours of content. Another big thing is that the game has two, maybe three branching main storyline paths, where you can choose between 2 or 3 factions and they have different quest-lines, which is awesome. So that varies your play experience. The music fits the setting and atmosphere so well and is very pleasant to listen to. The artwork for the loading screens is very nice as well. The only reason why this game can’t be considered perfect is due to some minor things like minor bugs, and some of the game design feels wonky at times, like my companions drinking from infected water 8 times over the course of the story when they should’ve learned not to drink from nasty-looking water after the first 2 times. Of course, these minor issues are easily overlooked seeing as how the game has a plethora of amazing qualities. The game, overall is complex but also fairly easy to grasp, and It also really pulls you in and feels very well crafted. I seriously love this game, it reminds me of a top-down Dragon age origins mixed with Xcom’s combat system, both of those games are personal favorites and fantastic games. I have been looking for another hardcore RPG like DAO for a while now and this one is just what I was looking for.
TL;DR
Excellent Music
Excellent Story
Excellent Combat
Well-written characters
Beautiful, immersive atmosphere
Very nice graphics
A few minor issues that prevent it from being a perfect game, but don’t inhibit your experience very much.
Overall: 93/100

A short adventure game with some charm and enough of a hook to keep you interested for a playthrough.  While it is polished enough to be worth your time, it hasn't enough charm or substance in the storytelling to keep you engrossed.
A first stab at the adventure genre by the developers, they've told a story of a little boy who is a member of an underground civilization plagued by a number of problems, first are all these wind gods turning people into stone and the second being the absence of wind.  The world is foreign and interesting enough with its own history, culture, and physics that keep you guessing and interested in what is happening and what led up to the present sequence of events.  The story is, boy gets caught up in problem, meets anarchist girl, ends up in revolution, discovers past, bad stuff happens, uses past to save the world, live happily ever after.  The story is adventure game fodder and is not done exceptional enough to make it seem new or like something I haven't played already.
The dialogue was translated from German and it was done well enough save for some patchy words which made it into the localization, misnamed objects, odd sentences and the like.  As far as that goes, there is a LOT of dialogue.  Your mileage may vary if you consider this a good or bad thing.  It provides a lot of exposition, character development, and world building.  It also starts falling into the land of monotonous walls of text.  If you are having any issues with a dialogue puzzle, you can expect to see the same lines repeated several times.
The art is done to give the game its own style.  It's cartoony, imaginative, and contributes to the development of the story and world.  The only issue I had with it was it had so much drab and brown, but that's for my own tastes.
The puzzles, dialogue and inventory, are done well and help the pacing, which is all I can ask of puzzles in an adventure game.  They are well-made and don't require the use of LOL logic to figure out.  Their difficulty improves gradually over the game and helps immersion and pacing.  If you have problems, the game has an interactive hint book which can help push you in the right direction.  There's nothing really bad I can say about them other than the repetition you may face if you have issues with a dialogue puzzle.
In all, the game is ok and I had no real problems with it.  The only problem is, it exists in a genre swamped with better games and other games no better than this one.  If you are an adventure game fan, you can play this for something new.  Otherwise, look for something else.

At this point only three of five parts have been released.
Not so much a "game" as an interactive story. There aren't defined "puzzles" and gameplay is limited to interacting with certain things in the environment, but it's still a fascinating experience.
In this game, you play Conway - an aging delivery driver for a failing antique store. When out making a delivery, you stop to ask for directions where an unusual man directs you to "the zero". The world is very well built, with the entire design being beautiful - soundtrack, visuals, writing... everything. Characters are compelling, well developed, and just as odd as their surroundings. Everything is pretty abstract but there are stunning moments of beauty. I've sat at a still screen for minutes at a time just soaking in the atmosphere. It helps that there's somewhat of a "less is more" idea at work - the narrative isn't thrust upon you, but builds from your experiences.
But that works to its advantage. A lot of what you get from the game isn't a result of the choices you make, but the choices you make don't railroad you down a certain path. Different bits of story will open based on your choices, but they're more a reflection of how you intend to play the game than how the developer intended you to play the game.
Definitely pick it up. It's a storytelling experience I'm very happy with thus far.

I've finished the 1st Act and I have to say I'm impressed.
About 10 years ago, I went to a university course on "Hyperliterature and new forms of narration". It was very enlightening, we studied some of the new waves of storytelling, watched some David Lynch movies, played some live rpg games (based on Kult, best rpg ever) and so on... best course I ever attended, shame it was so short. I remember writing an essay about videogames, mostly focused on my experiences with graphic adventures and a game I couldn't stop playing by then called Half Life 2.
I just wish I could go back again today, after playing Kentucky Route Zero. It feels like the kind of game I was wishing for in those days.
KR0 is a captivating exercise of storytelling, sucks you in from the beginning and minimizes the interface to focus on the audiovisual experience. Same goes for all the technical aspects of the game. Graphics, music and gameplay are well polished and just let you enjoy the story without getting in the way. They all do their part, and do it very good.
The enviroment is dreamlike, inmersive, deceptively lifeless. So many details  appearing out of the corner of the player's eye, so many left to the player's imagination.
This is not a usual adventure, but more an interactive story. The narration comes mostly from what you see and what you hear, saving you from reading huge walls of text. Actually, the text is just another element, and it doesn't give any important information most of the time. It does add up to the overall experience and it's a pleasure to read.
Something that caught my attention is that you never seem to be in control, just like in a dream. Your mind will struggle to follow a logic path to the story, but the game will break your will and ultimately take you for a ride. Just sit back, get comfy and enjoy it.
I can't wait to go back and continue with the game, just wanted to recommend it to everyone looking for a good, innovative experience in the already bursting indie scene. Games like this make me feel proud to be a gamer and, having passed my 30, look to my friends who jumped off the videogame train because it wasn't mature enough for society standards and think "You don't know what you're missing".
PS. Big points for the references to Gabriel García Márquez, recently passed away colombian writer, creator of the magic realist that influences this game heavily. I bet he would be proud and happy to play this game.

This is fairly traditional point and click game, i.e. you have to collect everything not nailed down and rub it against everything else till the story progresses. This kind of gameplay can get frustrating when you cannot work out the insane combinations of items required to solve the puzzle but this game gets round this by a very nice hints system. Unlike the hints systems in some of the Telltale games which gives you hints that only make sense if you know the solution, this hint system gives you loads of little hints and if you keep clicking it eventually just tells you what to do. This is a really nice system as you just use it till you get the bit of information you need to make all the clues click together into place without having to go away and look up a full walkthrough. Aside from that is has a cool world with likeable characters and a good story which is really what you are looking for in a point and click game.

I think the developer could go back and clean up some of these issues to make the game an even better experience. A really fun game. If you like turn-based combat and role-playing where story choices you make affect the storyline, this game is fairly priced at $30 -- but an even better purchase during a sale.
The game's biggest wins are its fun premise and the choices you make having a big effect on the later story. The use of area maps makes the game a big improvement off Expeditions: Conquistador, making this a much more realized game. (No more burning food while searching the world map aimlessly!) It's an easily accessible game, there's strategy and you can even make weapons and armor, but it's done in a simple, clear way without unnecessary mechanics. Making a trap and planting it is a fun mechanic, but the game would need to create much more tailored battles to make it useful.
The game is fun just based on its 20 or so hours of playing through once. I imagine most won't want to do it again, because it seems like you'd be going through almost all of the same missions again. The difficult settings don't seem to effect the AI being randomly smart or dumb, so I'm not interested enough in a replay to see what other choices might yield. But I almost am, and my being "over" the mechanics of the game is timed exactly with my finishing it. So, I'd have to call that a fun and well-designed game overall.
Conquistador was inventive, but this game is fully realized. If the next game in their series is as much of an improvement, it will be great!

Amazing RPG set in what feels like a pretty accurate historic viking setting, which means no magic or monsters, though there's no shortage of supersticious people talking about both, and (both the norse and christian) religion obviously plays a big role.
The RPG-system is really solid, resulting in some cool fights with loads of costumization, but at the same time leaving enough wiggle-room to also give your characters skills outside of combat.
The story is quite unique, in it not being the traditional "you're the hero, go do hero-stuff!" story, but fully embracing the fact that the vikings where actually kinda ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s to most people not directly related to them/part of their own little town if they could get away with it, which is refreshing. You can still play like a nice and helpful kind of guy, but it always has that underlying sense of "yeah, I might help you now, but in a month or two I might be back to raid and pillage you all" :)
I bought it on sale and feel like I got more than my money's worth, so unless you're short on cash I'd actually say the full 30 Euro price-tag isn't unfair if you're looking for a different spin on the traditional turn-based, story-heavy isometrical RPG. So far I'm 33 hours in, and I'm guessing I'm not even ½-way through the game, so it's actually pretty big.
In short: If you like good ol' fashioned RPGs like Baldur's Gate or Pillars of Eternity, this is definately worth a look!

Expeditions: Conquistador was an excellent turn based tactic game with an interesting historical setting, and like that, Expeditions: Viking doesnt let down and offers a good, mature RPG set in realistic historical world and culture.
The trailers mainly show combat aspect of the game, but actually this is very story orientated game with plenty of talking and planning. Main challenges come from the combat, but combat itself is only half of the focus of the game. Turn based tactical combat works pretty well, and is rewarding in higher difficulties. Once you get used to the system and skills, it isnt really that hard though, but there is certain satisfication you get from getting flawless victories in outnumbered battle, chopping the enemies head down with your heavy viking axes. Due to level up system, you will also be gaining new skills to play with through the game, so you wont have to rely on same skills all the time. Thats in theory though. Some skills are quite over powered while some are less so. After you find the best way to combine your team, you really dont even need the later skills. Nevertheless, even though the battles do get a bit repetitive, I didnt ever find them boring.
The story of the game is actually quite similar to the television series of the same theme, you feel like you are in the same world doing your own things. There is quite a few of different factions you can do missions to gain their alliance, and different paths will alter the ending as well. While the writing is mostly good, I felt that my character was semi-forced into a common errand boy a bit too much. You could skip those errand boy missions I suppose, but that would mean that you will be just missing some content of the game, and as a perfectionist that wasnt an option for me. The further you go, the less you have those small and irrelevant missions though.
One aspect that I found very irritating was that you can upgrade your town, but the game never really explains what is the actual meaning of it. Yet it actually plays a bigger picture in the grand scheme of things, and wrong construct of your town will actually hinder your RPG choices in the end. As the game didnt hint about the importance of this, in the end I was blocked out of the way of things I wanted to do for the whole game. I was so frustreted about this, that I hacked my save file to get things right there. A mechanic like this should be better hinted at least, since eventually its the biggest choice you will make in the game -without you knowing of it.
Technically game is solid. Nice graphics, nice animations. Excellent music that reminds me of the movie Last of the Mohicans. Some scripting small bugs here and there due to the open nature of the game, but nothing game breaking.
Overall I liked the world of Vikings given to me. But if I would have to choose, I still liked the previous Expeditions game more. It felt much more like an actual expedition where you have to search the unknown world yourself and never know what awaits you. In Vikings, you always know where you are going, due to story narrative being much more direct, and world map being rather simplified compared to the previous game. You dont have to search for the locations yourself in the game, all locations are told by NPCs where they are, and you only need to click the world map icon to travel to those. Game is open and you can still choose your path, just that the paths are always pointed to you and you dont have to find anything yourself.
The general feel of Conquistador was more of a strategy game with RPG elements, where Vikings is much more traditional RPG game with tactical elements. But there is not many historical RPGs around, so I still highly recommend the game for anyone who is fan of RPGs, or viking culture.

My only critique of the game (if you want to call it that) would be that it left me wanting more.  While the game is really good, I feel that with a larger development budget and more developed features/detail, this game would go from really good to GREAT easily.  If anything though this should serve as a compliment to the small development team that managed to accomplish a lot with this game with what is likely limited resources .
At full price this game may seem a little expensive for some, but on any sort of sale this game was an absolute must buy for me.  Looking forward to the next installment in this series.

Now out of all those titles, crusader kings 2 overall  probably isnt any better than its counterparts europa 4, hearts of iron 4 and victoria 2..but it does have something that none of the others do..in fact while the aforementioned games are  similar to each other crusader kings 2 stands out..europa 4 attempts to combine various aspects from  all of these titles into one large jack of all trades that everyone can enjoy, victoria 2 embraced the economic side of paradox strategy with some hearts of iron style warfare..hearts of iron 4 while a massive improvment on the third entry in that series is still a war sim far far more than anything else.
Crusader kings was intended to be grand strategy meets rpg, and it pulled that off wonderfully in the process however something uniqe and special in the gaming world was born..something that i have never been able to find a sutiable comparison for when looking at all aspects of a game..there just isnt another game that pulls of making you feel like you are that indivudal king or queen even though you arent because they are often actual historical charaters .so that every year of thier rule feels personalized to you despite the fact that the game isnt tryin gto say YOU are that ruler.
At the same time your ruling for hundreds of years over dozens of rulers so how could each ruler feel individual, and to an extent that applies however..imagine the old idea of re incartaion, throughout the eons you are reborn essentialy the same sould but into different bodies and lives ((or as a tree)) adapt that slightly and you have what playing a ruler in crusader kings 2 feels like.
Now i could elaborate further as i intended to cover the other points i wished to make but this review is getting a bit long so ill wrap it up...there would have been at least four blocks that size.
The point is this game does something you will not find anywhere else, you may find individual aspects in other games or even a combination of a few but overall there simply isnt another comparison, at least not yet.
So very simply put if you like the idea of roleplaying as a king or queen while running a country paradox style than this is the game for you.

A really interesting game! This one might be a little long, sorry guys!
I tend to be very on or off with point and clicks, It doesn't happen very often that i get into a game of this genre, don't get bored half way through, and actually manage to get to the end of it.
The tendency with this genre for me is that if they don't flow well enough, if i get stuck on obscure item combinations (which happens a lot with point and clicks) or if it's just not interesting enough, i'll give up and not bother going back to it. This is one point and click game however that i am happy to say that not only could i actually bare to get through it, but it's actually a really good game. It's been the best point and click game i have played since the Deponia series, which i adored.
In ways, this game reminded me a little of that series. I guess in just style and art. I was actually somewhat convinced whilst playing that it might be by Daedalic Entertainment, but alas it's not!
Admittedly when i first started playing this, i thought it was quite slow (maybe i was just in a particularly impatient mood that day?). The dialog seemed like it was paced too slowly and i was generally dreading the trek ahead to completing this game. Although I'm glad to say i changed my mind very quickly with that one.
The story is very inventive and i found it quite interesting. The game was fun to play through and the ending was definitely not disappointing. I think i can safely say that it's not the plot twist of the century, but it's not entirely predictable either. Either way it was great to see things unfold and i loved the creativity and humor involved.
In terms of characters, I love them. There are some very lovable characters in this game. Including our main star Robert. A well mannered, polite, silly and somewhat naive little Asposian.
The graphics are nice. It's very soft, light and nice on the eyes. A light-hearted, hand-drawn and cartoon-like style. With that said, i did have a few problems with crashing/freezing. Sometimes the loading screen between chapters just wouldn't load. It was usually fine because the game tends to autosave before the "end of chapter" cutscene. So you don't really lose anything, but it's still a minor annoyance having to reboot the game.
I found that if you tended to not move or click anything whilst the cutscene was playing or it was trying to load, it'd usually load fine. If you pressed buttons and clicked your mouse, that's when it tended to have a hard time and freeze.
That being the only negative thing out of the way, back to the positive stuff!
The help system in this is quite good. I usually try not to use hints whenever i can, but being stuck on something for a long while gets a bit frustrating. I was quite impressed with the hint system, I wanted to see how many hints it would give you and how obvious they'd be. It gives you a few little nudges in the right direction before just spelling it out to you. Plus, you still don't get it? It'll spell it out to you even more blatantly. Literally to the point of "Go pick this thing up over there, and use it on this".
Lastly, achievements!
This one is pretty easy to complete 100% and i think my method for doing so was a decent way of doing it.
I basically started a game file (it allows you up to 3), I played through a chapter, then went back to the main menu and started a second game for missed achievements throughout each chapter. Every time i would complete a chapter in my main save, i'd go back to the secondary save to complete it again whilst getting any missed achievements.
The chapters aren't too long and once you know what you are doing going back and getting the missables in a second game file isn't as tedious as it sounds.
There is one lonesome guide for this game that details "missable achievements" you can either read the names/descriptions and try to figure yourself how to get them, or you could just use the guide to know what to do. (In my opinion it's fairly easy to figure out how to get them just from reading the title or description)
Also, there are a few achievements that having two saves actually makes it easier. For example, there is one achievement for not using the guide at all and one for using the guide frequently. So either way really, you'd have to play it twice.
All in all i really loved this game and i'm glad i decided to have a go with it. If you're a fan of the genre i would definitely recommend it to you.

If you enjoyed this game back in the old days, you'll find a lot to enjoy here. However, as someone who played Shadow Warrior's close relatives Doom and Duke Nukem 3D (both as a kid and recently) but is only playing this now, I can't really recommend it. My problem with the game boils down to this - the other two games I mentioned, and others like Heretic, work perfectly well and are fun to play even if you never find a single secret because they flow well and are laid out intuitively. Their hidden areas and items are rewards for going out of your way that you're happy to look for because you're enjoying yourself. In Shadow Warrior finding these hidden areas is often mandatory to proceeding (usually with vital keys hidden this way) and even if you're looking for them anyway, one will still frequently be left standing there thinking "...okay, so what now?" which can really break the flow. This is to say nothing of those parts where you need to mess around with the physics puzzles, which have aged like a fine milk. As part of the "Hardcore, oldskool sprite-based shooters" gang it's still head and shoulders above a Modern Military Shooter, for example, but when compared to many of its peers it stands on much shakier ground. If what I described sounds like heaven to you, then it probably is, but maybe save this one until you're bored of better games like it.

===
Okhlos is a partially procedural, 2.5D roguelike dungeon crawler. Set in the ancient Greece, Okhlos talks about a time when the Gods betrayed their loyal subjects and became evil, using their powers only to fullfill their goals, reducing the population to misery. In these dark times, a few brave Philosophers decide to unite and stand against the Gods, by inciting the population to fight back. And so, many philosophers around Greece started rallying massive mobs of angry people, decided to topple the Gods themselves and earn back their freedom.
In Okhlos, the player will impersonate one of the many Philosophers (be them named or not) which decided to challenge the Gods. As a Philosopher, you will be able to convince people found around the levels to join you and your Mob, in order to fight the Gods' armies. The player will be in control of two different things: the first is thye philosopher himself, which acts as the commander of the mob, and the Mob itself, which can be directed with the mouse and has only two simple commands, attack and defend, unless you have special carriable items that activate on command with 1, 2, 3, etc. keys and prodice various effects such as healing or area damage.
The mob will consist of any kind of person who wants to join the fight: you will be able to recruit common folk, noble citizens, warriors, healers, other philosophers, defenders and even animals and special units along your campaign, each with unique abilities. To do so, a philosopher, be it the Commander or another one, must pass near the said unit and it will be recruited, as long as the Mob is not at its maximum capacity, which can be increased in various ways. Other than common people, you will also be able to sacrifice part of your Mob to certain Shops found between one area and another, to recruit powerful Heroes, each time you are at a shop the selection will be of 3 random heroes, each having a cost and unique abilities, only one Hero can be taken at each shop. Shop may aswell have a selection of regular units to convert in other units, for example you could be able to convert 5 Warriors into 5 Philosophers if you need, or vice-versa.
During your adventure you will face a great variety of foes, each time randomized to a certain degree by the procedural game engine, they are basically of two types, Minions, which are displayed on the minimap by a white skull, and are regular enemies, and Mini-Bosses, displayed with a red skull, which obviously are much stronger than regular enemies and often have special devastating abilities which can seriously endanger your Mob. To defeat such foes, your Mob will need inspiration, which is very important to get your men efficent. On the top of the screen there is in fact a Morale Bar, which can be charged by defeating enemies and breaking props around the map, each level of this Bar will increase your mob's statistics and efficency, making it stronger! The bar will deplete over time so don't waste any and keep up the fight!
Stages in Okhlos are generally pretty short, 10-15 minutes will usually be anough to complete a level, but the random factor and increasing difficulty after each stage will always keep you alert. At the end of each stage there will be a Boss, randomized aswell to keep up variety, which usually will be a God. These Bosses have their own skills and attack patterns, timing in ordering your Mob to Defend and knowing each Boss' capabilities will be fundamental in order to defeat them. Also, a good, balanced mob structure not lacking too much of any statistic will greatly increase your chances to survive.
Before or later you will DIE. If your Philosopher dies and no other Philosophers are present to take its place, it will be game over! But do not worry, as after each playthrough you will proceed a bit further towards unlocking many unlockable Starter Heroes, with you since the beginning, and Named Philosophers with unique skills each, all of these are unlockable with specific challenges, all lsited in  specific menu found at the Agora, your base. There also will be Cryptos, secret words well-hidden in the game, that will unlock special game modes and bonuses, so keep an eye out. As a roguelike, Okhlos' key element is replayability, and in this the deveopers did a great job to keep the experience fast-paced, varied and never boring.
===
Do not be fooled by appearence, because under the pixelated simil-2D guise of Okhlos there is very good technical work.
Speaking of Performance, Okhlos runs well and has been optimized decently. Even with massive amounts of enemies and buildings breaking into smithereens left and right, there will be no problems such as stuttering or FPS drops even on not very recent systems, so it is safe to say Okhlos is a game even old machines could run pretty well.
Speaking of Visuals, Okhlos' graphics style is very peculiar, drawing 2D characters in a 3D environment set in a 2.5D view. All props in the game such as barns, buildings, pots, fountains and whatnot are physical, destructible objects that will beautifully fly away into pieces when your angry Mob destroys them. Same goes for characters to some degree. Behind its appearence, Okhlos mounts a modern graphics engine with all the recent phyisics and effects we all like.
Speaking of AI, enemies have pre-determined attack patterns, will  run away when they are in disvantage and will help each other if they have the possibility to do so. A sufficent, standard AI which is fine for a game like this.
As far as the Sound goes, it fits well with the setitng and pace of this game. The music remind of ancient ones, but "remixed" with some electronic, giving it a fast pace which will emphasize the fast-pacedness of the game itself. Effects are alright nothing extraordinary but are varied and decent.
There are no major issues or bugs to report.
===
Okhlos is a very original roguelike dungeon crwaler, with a lot of style and uncommon mechanics. It will give lots of fun to anyone who likes the genre, and also to novices to it. Each playthrough will be fast and diverse, and overall the mix of elements runs very well. If you are for deep and complex game systems, then this might not be your kind of games, but if you like fast paced madness and violence, then be my guest.

For its time this was a pretty great use of the BUILD engine and there is a lot of fun to be had here. The level design and settings are creative, and theres plenty of enemy types and weapons to keep you entertained. My only complaint after 15 or so years is still the same... this game is brutally difficult, even on normal setting. As with many sprite based games using the build engine... the hit detection is pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥. My advice is to turn off the crosshair and turn on auto-aim for a less frustrating experience. The enemies you face have pinpoint accuracy from any distance... while you can unload two full uzi clips at an enemy 10 feet away and hit absolutely nothing. The riot gun functions similarly and its spread makes it utterly ineffective without autoaim. The game wasn't quite ready for full 3d aiming yet and like many of the great sprite based FPS of the times it really shows. Beyond that it's worth a pick up for nostalgic fans and fans of old school FPS.
On a side note... I just noticed that the person playing in the trailer on the steam store page is using GOD mode and running all over blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up... just note that that is NOT how you play this game lol. I maybe should have looked to see whether there was an option to turn off the music within the game. I recommend that any potential buyer, who intends to play multi-player, wait until this game is released. I am a fan of Early Access titles, having spent years playing ARK in Early Access. I'm fine playing a game that has issues, as long as the development team schedules them to be resolved, fixes the critical issues quickly, and communicates with the Steam community (where we all buy the game).
Unfortunately, Funcom has been dropping the ball repeatedly over the last couple of months. They have allowed game-breaking bugs to go unaddressed for over a month. The most severe of this is the duplication bug (which you can still exploit as of the time I write this). So any server you play on is an environment where players will have had nearly two months of time to duplicate to their hearts content. That's not the only issue, just the most important one in my mind.
If you intend to play this in single-player, then you can probably pull the trigger and buy it. The only person exploiting the game will be you, and the Admin Panel makes it much easier to do than exploiting bugs. However, there is still a considerable amount of content lacking from the game. Unless you just want to build and build and build, using the game assets, there won't be much else to do (ie explore the map, kill the animals and humanoids (few species, but they spawn in abundance), and kill animals and humanoids in the few small dungeons that have been implemented, enslave NPCs to guard you against no one (since it's singleplayer) or craft things for slightly less materials than you can do on your own. There are worse ways to spend money, but you can probably find something better in the Steam store.
One last thing: There is an imminent patch coming, followed by a wipe on the servers. And we don't know which servers are getting what kind of wipe (everything gone vs you keep your levels). So, definitely wait until the next patch is applied before playing multi-player.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R: Call of Pripyat is a fine example of what every open world survival horror game should be.
Like its predecessors, Clear Sky and Shadow of Chernobyl, Call of Pripyat is set in a very warped exclusion zone.  Compared to the previous entries in GSC's fabulous series, it is the most stable by far, most graphically appealing, and perhaps the scariest.  The AI is superb.  Beyond superb.  I remember reading somewhere that in Shadow of Chernobyl, they had to tone the AI down to make the game playable.  In its original state, an npc could have easily beaten the game itself without player influence.  It was that good.  And it still is amazing.  GSC managed to take probably the best AI model I've seen and place it in the scariest, darkest, and outlandish things imaginable(and unimaginable for that matter).  When placed into monsters that make villains like Chris Walker and SPC-106 seem like drinking buddies, it puts you into ITS ballpark.  In S.T.A.L.K.E.R., you don't get to smirk at stupid decisions by bandits or monsters.  In fact, I've been outsmarted by the AI.  And that doesn't happen often.  The AI isn't supposed to outsmart the player in video games.  YOU'RE supposed to outsmart IT.  GSC essentially threw that to the wind.  I'll give an example.  In one of the quests, you have to hunt down a creature called a Bloodsucker.  Which is already a name to run away from really fast.  So I packed up my AK, a few bottles of Vodka, a few first aid kits, some bandages, and headed out.  Aside from distant gunshots and screams that you just can't mistake for anything besides a human being torn apart, it was a pleasant enough day.  I reach the hunting spot.  Now, Bloodsuckers can turn invisible.  The standard way to deal with them is to get them to chase you in a straight line, then flip around and unload assault rifle fire in their faces.  The bloodsucker however decided to run away from ME.  So I chased after it and it led me on a wild goose chase around the map until we reached the swamps again.  Guess what had happened while we were gone.  Its friends had formed an ambush, while the first creature tired me out and lured me back to give them all an easy kill.  And that was the AI's doing.  No scripting, no cutscene, no quicktime event.  It did that all on its own.  And that's only one of the nightmares you will encounter in this game.  Most horror games scare you by giving you no defenses or weapons.  You're only choice is to hide or run.  In this, you have plenty of weapons.  And I still get scared out of my wits while I play this.  Because in GSC's rendering of Chernobyl, all the weapons in the world aren't going to give you an advantage.  Overall it has a solid storyline, believable characters, and fun sidequests.  So in short, it's probably one of the best games I've ever played.  And if you ever start to get bored of the bounty of content in Call of Pripyat, the amount of player made mods will take care of that.  To make a long story short, this game is worth EVERY. SINGLE. PENNY.  Of course, if you don't like games where you're not a god, where the world isn't at your mercy, don't buy this.  Because in S.T.A.L.K.E.R, you aren't god.  You're mortal just like everyone else.

Probably the most stressful element is gavelkind succession rules, which seem to require more time to master than I've put in so far (about 150 hrs). This basically means that if you have more than one kiddie then the goodies you've built up during a reign, or a whole succession of reigns, get divided up into separate states. And you don't get the choice which one to play in the new generation.  So you can begin to see why some folk knight this game Sir Infanticide.  It can be gut wrenching.
One of my more successful runs came close to unifying all the English duchies into the much sought-after kingdom, but then that awful warning sign bobbed up that there was no successor of my line, so the game will end when my current archduchess character dies. Entirely my fault since I've been artlessly given away in youth into regular patrilinear wedlock. There was a niece of my house and some distant relly with no lands.  But when the warning came i already had four or five kids counted as some poxy frankish house.  What can you do?  Its just destiny. Meanwhile I'm transferring almost all my lands and titles to the older relly.  Preferable to give them to the niece and marry her off matrilinear, but the game won't allow her to receive titles so young.  Male bias for sure.  However having reduced the reigning family to one daughter, it turns out you can't imprison a daughter. WFT in spades after arresting and slaughtering two sons, plus a continental husband tied to some very powerful thrones there.  Lots of threats, lots of revolts, all evaded or put down by a massive standing army i don't dare disband.  Well eventually my evil duchess persona dies and the game ends well shy of my just deserts.  If this doesn't demonstrate fem bias i wouldnt know what would.
Nevertheless I'd recommend this game. You just need to spend some time, and tears, getting to grips with the rules.  There's a lot.

There's no autobalance like some other combat games, so if your team mates leave, you're on your own for the rest of the match, even if it's 5 on 1.  Hope you enjoy dying.
Furthermore, when you first start playing, you're at a massive disadvantage in firepower, mobility, and armor unless you pony up the cash.  You've got the most basic of all options, and compared to anyone else, you're the fine china in their bull shop.  Again, hope you enjoy dying.
Then there's the fact that the controls aren't really what they say they are.  The strafe controls don't work, and hitting the slightest hill tosses you into the air and sends your treads spinnning, so when you land, good luck finding forward again.  Your turrent can turn 360 degrees, which is nice, but forward isn't always the direction your turret is facing, so it's nice to be able to circle an opponent and lay down fire on him constantly, but at the same time, the disruptive effects of the terrain make navigation annoying.
Feels incomplete, unbalanced, though it is a nice "free" game for people who don't mind being on the losing side all the time, unless you pay up.

By any modern standards, "Shadow Warrior" sucks on all accounts. Period. From a nostalgic standpoint? Yeah, I can see its appeal. However...
... maybe I'm in the minority, but I don't like it even as a trip down memory lane. Maybe because I have no memories of this kind of arcadey FPS. I began my FPS career with "Medal of Honor" on PS1, in 1999. That was 2 years after this game's release. The difference is vast, mainly in approach.
Old video presentation (aka graphics) aside, "Shadow Warrior" features:
- a character that moves faster than the Flash; you tap a directional key and you're flying all over the map
- confusing level design, a simple A to B mess
- loads of dumb enemies that just sort of rush at you
All these characteristics are basically shared by all of the so-called FPS classics, the arcade shooters. It seems these just aren't my cup of tea. If you're like me, I guess chances are you won't be liking it, too.

After playing Kentucky Route Zero (up to Act 3) I could say the game is a lot of things, but it is not a game like any other I have played before. It is unique, compelling, meditative, immersive, and gorgeous. Its summer evening pace and sleepy backroad soundtrack belie an experience that is incredibly thoughtful and stirring without becoming overly sentimental.
Although KRZ's gameplay is like that of a text adventure game (in fact, it pays quite a handsome tribute to that genre), the choices made by the player are more expressive than narrative. I'm not usually one to enjoy games that feature more storytelling than action. But KRZ's evocative visuals and expansive dialog (sometimes terse, sometimes laconic, and always poetic) feel far from constricting. In fact, its decision to skip the moralizing and deliberately obtuse puzzles that are staple features of the adventure game genre are part of what distinguishes it.
I played this game over a couple of quiet nights, cocooned in the darkness, and felt myself transported to the still Kentucky evening where encounters with the unusual and the supernatural felt as immediate as the quiet, ever-present purr of Conway's delivery truck. Give this game a shot when you have time to sit down and drink it in. Unlike games that largely consist of perfunctory hops between goalposts, Kentucky Route Zero offers an experience in every small moment of gameplay. There is as much to savor en route, during drives down the rural Interstate or the mysterious namesake Route Zero, as there is in each new pit stop. I found myself making excuses (which the game provides in abundance) to drive down side roads and muse aloud to my hound dog companion.

I've played Fallen Earth for quite some time now (700+ h) and I got mixed feelings about it. I'd actually like to recommend it but I simply can't and here's why:
The pros (yes, there are pros :p):
-If you live in the U.S. (or somewhere else close to the server - yes, there's only one server) you might get a decent connection.
-Since it's f2p you get a whole lot of game for your money.
-Story isn't too scabby and I found myself enjoying it.
-If you're playing on a low-end computer it will most likely still run.
The cons:
-If you don't live close to the server but somewhere in let's say Europe - like I do - you will get a lot of lags which are so bad on most days, that it's impossible to play the game.
-Graphics aren't very pretty. I'm aware that the game is from 2009 but we got 2017 now and from my current standards it's outright ugly.
-If you're not a premium user there is a cap to how much chips (in-game currency) you can have, you can only put one item in your crafting queue and only craft 8 hours per day (which is ridiculous considering how long crafting for some things takes) and you can't access the global chat.
-The devs stopped caring about the game quite some time ago. There are no updates, no bugfixes, lots of broken achievements and the customer support is a bad joke.
That's it for now. Thank you for reading :3

I have no idea how this has such high reviews.
If you want a half-baked RPG with flimsy mechanics and frustrating combat, this is the game for you.
I was intrigued by the concept and the opening story, but everything after the first hour goes down hill. I spec'd an Archer, but you get so many party members immediately that I don't think your class matters much. Regardless, I found myself getting absolutely crushed in every single battle. They say that the losing is part of the game, and this is introduced by an early-game duel between a character who's pretty much guranteed to defeat you at least once or twice. It's revealed that the duel is a best out of 5, so you go multiple rounds, but the subsequent losses I experienced were not story-related.
No matter what quest I did, I was overwhelmed and outmatched. The opposing side did an incredible amount of damage with no real insight on how to counter the onslaught of death. Every failed quest booted you to the overworld map, which implied that these weren't meant to be difficult encounters, I had just failed them.
There's a lot of mechanics that I have no understanding of how they work. For example, in many RPGs there's an "attack of opportunity," if you are next to an enemy and then walk away, they get to attack you. But these attacks of opportunities also apply when you attack an enemy you are standing directly next to. But it doesn't happen every single time. There's some internal game logic that decides when AoO happen and when they don't. Specifically, they never occur for your team, only the opposing side.
The leveling system is also very poor. Whereas many RPGs give you stats that you can dump points into, this game exclusively has a variety of perks you can upgrade. For example, "+10% damage against the opposite sex" or "+10% backstab damage." These are fine in addition to a real system, but in the few hours I played there was no option to, say, increase damage, or health, or anything like that. This gave me the impression that even if I were to "grind" lower level quests, my heroes would not get significantly more powerful.
I'm sure you can chalk this all up to me being bad at the game, but it was incredibly frustrating. The concept sounds incredible but the game as it is right now is poor at best.

Another simple game that's suppose to "brings you back to the old days" while also implying that it's that dreaded word; "Classic." Absolutely disgusting. But is Devil Daggers able to back itself up on its claim?
You're thrust into combat almost immediately after grabbing your titular devil dagger. Faced with hordes of demonic monstrosities and stuck on a circular arena, you're forced to fight to the death in an excellently designed game. Devil Daggers only has one game mode, which is to survive, and it makes sure you're on your toes at all times. Your weapon feels responsive and powerful, upgrading when you've killed enough enemies and collected gems, and your character moves with agility and responsiveness. Imagine playing a DOOM style game, but with only one weapon and hordes of scumbags to mow down. Absolutely hectic fun that any one will get addicted to in no time.
Devil Daggers looks pretty good for what it is. The models are very well done and nothing is particularly hampering to gameplay. It may get a bit painful to play for extended periods of time though. With no pause button and some pretty flashy lights, you'll quickly grow tired of looking at the screen. Play in moderation, kids.
Absolutely a must buy if you're looking for an excellent time waster. With fun, enticing, and simple gameplay, and a functioning high score board, Devil Daggers manages to go back to our arcade roots and give us a kickass experience. Pick it up, whether at full price or on sale. Definitely worth the investment.

Speedrunners is a fast-paced platformer racing game (finally) that offers a robust experience in competitive and casual gameplay. As you make your way through the "mario" ranks (entry, beginner) to the "monkey" ranks (advanced, expert) and all the way through the "spiderman" ranks (bronze, silver, gold, platinum, diamond) you will notice a vast difference in not only your own skill, but the levels you pick to play. Games in speedrunners can be ultra-competitive matches to social rooms or even rooms with people messing around. There is even a level editor which allows you to make levels as crazy as the levels the developers created; oh wait - these ones suck! Yeah. The list of curated workshop levels to play in ranked is probably going to be your best bet for a good use of skill and a good experience of speed. The community levels require more advanced skills such as "Grapple Spamming" to the "backflip" whereas the official levels are all walking straight and hopping your way above crates. Don't get me wrong - Speedrunners is an excellent game - and if you are questioning your own decision of whether or not to purchase the game, I reccommend, no, I URGE you to buy this. But no game, not even Super Mario Galaxy 2, is perfect.
That's right, this game still has it's drawbacks. The progression system is more of a measure of how many ranked matches you have played, as it is possible for someone who obtains the skill of a silver league player to have a badge above their icon that says "Advanced League." This can often spoil matches because it can cause a Bronze or Expert player to lose vast amounts of ranking points, although it's all in the underranking of the player you are against. Another problem is ELO (not ELO, the band) seasons. Many people can improve a lot within one month, and that can cause a big stirr in the regular time, as the range from advanced to bronze can mean the skill of advanced to bronze.... what I mean by that is essentially ranks get mixed up - and an advanced player could be as skillful as a bronze player and have to play hours and hours of rank to get to the rank they deserve. Another problem is that item spammers always get their way. That's right - starting at Expert League or Bronze League, items are considered evil, and whoever keeps killing a perfectly good player due to a cheap item (powerup) their day will be ruined. And the sad part is... no matter what rank you are in... they will always haunt you, because the more cruel item spammers climb their way to the top out of the ranking board. Regardless of the tacky ranking, Speedrunners is still a fun, potentially competitive, potentially funny, fast-paced platformer game that we have all been waiting for ever since the concept of platformers was introduced.
