I know that Steam says (at the time of writing this review) that I only have about 21.5 hours on record, but I assure you that I put hundreds of hours into this game on my Xbox 360 before I got my PC. This game is undoubtedly one of my favorite and most likely one of the greatest games to ever be released. I can almost guarantee that you will like this game if you are an Open-World RPG fan. Let's open this game up and take a look inside one of the best isntallments in the Elder Scrolls Series.
Gameplay:
The most important element in a video game is the gameplay, and the Elder Scrolls IV has that down to a science. Sure, this game does a bit more hand-holding compared to its predecessors, which is completely undeniable. This game also has a simplified dialogue system and, in my opinion, terrible voice acting, but do not let these cons detract from the great game this is.
Oblivion, being one of the only titles in the series to not be named after its main setting, offers amazing exploration and rewards it nicely, especially for you dungeon-crawlers. With the vast and open world of Cyrodiil at your fingertips, you can explore and discover some of the most beautiful and historical ruins, forts, hamlets, cities, castles, rivers, lakes, caves, mines, and many other dungeonesque sites. you won't just find enemies at these sites, though. Like I said before, exploration is rewarded.
As for a replay-value: you will never play this game the same way twice. Sure, with the lack of "radiant" quests that are present in Skyrim (Oblivion's 'sequel') you basically know what's going to happen in any given quest you've already done, but you don't have to approach these quests the same way you did before. Perhaps in one playthrough you are a battlemage that wields a Dwarven axe whilst sending a barrage of lightning bolts towards your enemies, but in another playthrough you are an assassin that wields an Elven bow whilst sending a barrage of poisoned arrows towards your foes. With the class system in this game, you won't ever have to be the same character twice. I have had several different characters in this game, and each time I have played I experienced everything differently than before.
Combat:
The combat in Oblivion makes so much more sense than it did in Morrowind (Oblivion's 'prequel') in which you would swing your weapon into an enemies face and it wouldn't even phase them, but here in Oblivion, every hit is rewarded with a blade covered in blood and a scream from the other end of your sword. While the game doesn't do a very good job of challenging the player in combat as long as they follow the course provided for them, but there are places in this in which you will be absolutely brutalized if you go in unprepared. This is where exploring and being prepared come into play.
Bows and arrows, swords, daggers, magic staves, maces, axes, or your own bloody fists are all at your disposal when it comes to combat in this game. Each comes with its own positive and its own negative, but the more experienced you become with your weapon of choice, the more rewarding your trudge through the cons will be. Choosing a weapon choice and becoming proficient with it is always a great choice, but, of course, you are not forced to do this. If you want to use swords and axes at the beginning and then halfway through decide that you want to use bows and arrows, go for it! You won't be held to the weapons you use in the beginning, it will just make the journey a bit more difficult on your way to mastering your new weapon type.
Finally for combat, there is the Arena. This is perhaps one of the most popular features in ES4, and rightfully so. At any point, you can enter the Arena, join the team and fight for glory and money in a gladiator style throwdown. This is a great way to not only get yourself into the swing of things when it comes to combat, but it can also help you level up pretty quickly near the beginning of the game; be careful though, because the further you get in the Arena, the more challenging the enemies become!
Graphics:
I won't lie to you, the graphics in this game aren't the best, though at the time of its release (I remember very well) these graphics were some of the best I had ever seen! Without the proper mods, this game makes everyone look like they have  a potato-face and makes blood look like a powdery substance rather than a liquid. Fret not, though, like I said, mods are a beautiful thing when it comes to this game. I downloaded a buttload of mods and now my Oblivion looks almost as good as Skyrim. Don't worry, graphics have no effect on the gameplay anyways, unless graphics are very important to you.
Immersion:
As is the tradition when it comes to Elder Scrolls titles, immersion is a key feature in Oblivion. From the small details like being able to pick a random magical gem off its stand in a random tomb or being able to go for a stroll and pick flowers and mushrooms, to being able to commit murder on any unsuspecting NPC for no good reason and then going to prison because of your vile actions. Your actions have consequences, and almost everything you do will have an effect on how the world treats and sees you.
Have a beer, read a book, eat dinner, spend the night in a hotel, buy a horse, ride that horse to another town and repeat the process. Any small action you can think of, you can most likely do it (no f@pping guys...)
Performance:
Considering this game came out almost 11 years ago, I'm pretty sure everyone on here will be able to run this game on at least the lowest settings and still hit 60 fps, but who knows.
-Ratings-
Gameplay: 9/10
Combat: 8/10
Graphics: 10/10 (At the time of its release)
Immersion: 9/10
Performance: 10/10
=Conclusion=
Definitely give this game a chance. If you're still on the edge of whether or not you want to buy it, watch some gameplay on Youtube, or look for some streams on Twitch, you are guaranteed to find something online somewhere that allows you to get a glimpse of the amazing game that Oblivion truly is.

I own and have played all the Heroes of Might & Magic (HOMM) games from editions 1-6.  In my opinion, I will list them from favorite to least favorite:
HOMM 5
HOMM 4 ties with HOMM 3 (for different reasons)
HOMM 2
HOMM 1
HOMM 6
Since the beginning, the HOMM franchise was split into two genres: one was an action first-person type of game, and the other was the strategic turn-based game.  (Really.  You could buy two different games with the HOMM name on them.)  The action-based ones were hits, but not my style.  The turned-based ones always tickled my fancy, though the artwork was generally cheesy.  Starting with HOMM 5, the HOMM franchise moved to this French company called UbiSoft.  Things have been pretty lame since then, though HOMM 5 was a great introduction for them.  (Except for the hideous DRM that they implemented, which was beyond atrocious at the time, way back in 2006.  We were all mad at bad companies like EA (U.S.A.), UbiSoft (France), Paradox (Sweden), and the fly-by-night German and Russian companies that misled the gaming community with their cheapshots and hit-and-run tactics.)
Anyway, HOMM 5 was sort of like what The Force Awakens is to the Star Wars franchise.  Basically, a new, huge company put a lot of resources into a classic franchise that they acquired; did well at first; and then gradually declined.  (Has that happened for the Star Wars franchise yet?  I don't think so, but time will tell.)  But yeah, HOMM 5 takes the favorite elements of HOMM 3 and HOMM 4 and puts them together in a truly 3-dimensional experience.  The way that the player can upgrade his characters is pretty darn cool; and the HOMM community really put out some great material for us players.  (Better than UbiSoft has, which is a money-grubbing you-know-what.)
The good stuff about HOMM 5 are the graphics, sounds, and strategies.  The bad stuff are the French company that is out simply to milk you (essentially useless expansions), the extreme difficulty in modifying your game (unless you know how to write scripts in a programming language - yeah, that difficult), the lame DRM and game forums, and the atrocities that have followed since.
Have you seen HOMM 6 or HOMM 7?  If you play them, they will make you hate the HOMM franchise.  What has been going on over there at UbiSoft?
My advice is that you just play and modify HOMM 4 to your little heart's content, if you can find that game anywhere.  If you play HOMM 5, you won't be disappointed.  The HOMM 3 remake available on Steam really is not worth your time or any money, as you cannot get the wonderful expansion pack for it anymore.  HOMM 1 & 2 are easily forgotten hits, unless you can remember seeing or playing them back in the 90s like I still can.  Avoid HOMM 6 & 7 like the plague.  Avoid any other games from UbiSoft like two plagues - wait for them to fail and have their titles sold to better developers.
If you have the patience, then good things will happen.  Believe it.  The HOMM franchise is in the wrong hands right now.  Boycott these thieves until they go away.  Then get HOMM ten years from now when it is good again.
Oh, and I should mention that HOMM 5: Tribes of the East gives you everything you need to play a complete version of HOMM 5.  You do not need the base game or the dwarves expansion pack.  All of that is available in Tribes of the East, a stand-alone product.  (Yeah, UbiSoft are crooks like that.)

In terms of length this expansion totally lives up to the main game of HOMM 5, which I remember playing for the better part of 2007. On the micro scale Tribes Of The East is as good as a Heroes 5 game can get with all the cool turn-based strategy and the different fractions and abilities. That's all good. Unfortunately what they've done is, that they've extended it way past it's capabilities. It doesn't have the steam to build a 100+ hour game yet that's exactly what you get. I still feel trauma whenever I think back on the size of those maps. I think it took me some 8-9 hours to complete the larger ones. By the time I had an army large enough to take on the particular map's final boss, I had long reached the max level available and the whole world had become this empty, trodden space with nothing left to explore. At times this came to be when I was still a good couple months behind from facing the final boss. In that sense the game's doing a very good job at wasting your time. Much too often it lost the momentum from where on it just became grinding to get the level done and much too often I found myself asking 'why am I doing this?'.
BUT, to end with a lighter tone - on the micro level you've got a solid 'Heroes' game and maybe you have a hundred hours to waste, maybe you're in prison or something, then it will definitely help you pass those hours.

A hilarious and adorable adventure game that I will remember fondly as one of my favorite point and click advetnures in some time. Phenomenal voice acting, cute characters, charming dialogue, good puzzles, and just an overall fun experience watching the characters try to save their people.
We begin with Robert, an orphaned boy who is being raised by a man named Conroy. Conroy is the ruler of this little world of Asposia, and right away, as you can in all animated tales, we realize that Conroy isn't the nicest of fellows. In fact, he seems like a downright meanie. :P One day while Robert is playing his flute nose (yes, I said flute nose) for Conroy in his favorite 1 note tune, a pigeon that Robert has been playing with as one of his only friends comes in and steals Conroy's necklace and flies off. Robert, being the ever dutiful 'son' goes after it and finds himself down in the city of Asposia with all the peasants for the first time outside the walls of Conroy's castle. His adventure is ready to begin...
Robert soon meets residents of Asposia and quickly starts to realize that Conroy may not be the great hero that he was raised to believe he was. Most importantly he meets Laura. A wanted thief, general troublemaker, obvious anti-establishment hero, and the girl of Robert's dreams. Robert is incredibly naive, but falls in love with Laura at first site. She is more worldy and they play off one another fantastically as she teases him and he shows his innocence again and again as a kind and generous boy. Their conversations are great, and Robert is pretty funny no matter how innocent he is.
I didn't find any issues with the game UI, or the puzzle mechanics. They are the standard hover over the bottom of the screen to pop up the item menu, with options to drag them to world objects, combine them, etc. Some of the puzzles are a bit strange and take some trial and error of jsut screwing aroudn finding what items interact with things, but overalll they aren't too illogical most of the time. The game has a few loading screens between areas that on my medium level PC took about 3 seconds to load wasn't a problem for me.
I had no bugs in the game that I can recall. Certainly nothing that made me stop, although the save system is not one that is the type to be friendly for Achievement hunters. The game can be saved manually, or using auto-saves, BUT you don't have a choice about where you save other than picking a slot for your current game. So you have one save and if it auto-saves and you miss an Achievement you will have to start the game over. So...if 100% Achievements is your goal then you better take a look at some Achievements guides BEFORE starting. There are a few that are full game achievements and a couple of them contradict. One side is really easy and can be gotten with a quick restart early on, but the other requires the full game to be played a certain way so you want to make sure you understand these early on before finding out halfway through you will have to play all the way through again.
Game is probalby anywhere from 6-10 hours long. My playtime is longer because I left the game on for 12 hours one day. :)

This is the first multi-player tower defense game I've ever played, having picked it up in a Humble Bundle somewhere. The game characters are quite varied, I've enjoyed them all, and I'm glad to see expansion in this area. I do, however, find myself often wishing for more arenas. The ones there are great, but more are desperately needed.
Other players seem much tougher to beat now versus when I first started playing Awesomenauts back in August, probably because I took a few months off. I also see a lot more players teaming up now than when I first started playing (either via local co-op or flashing the same clan tags). This teamwork is usually the key to winning, and it is immensely difficult or impossible to beat a well-organized team. That said, this game has surprised me more than once with down-to-the-last-tower-comeback-from-behind wins against overconfident teams.
I've had many good experiences with other players, but lately it's been not as good. I think the Starstorm expansion soured some of the community both by bringing in inexperienced-and-frustrated noobs and by giving people a scapegoat with an expanded for-pay character.
And yet, I still haven't met anyone in person who has heard of Awesomenauts. It just seems like a small community of players. Maybe that's because there's no "search mode" for joining in-progress matches.
Finally, never rage quit. Be a good sport and finish well. Don't trash your teammates. This is a game folks. I really, really, wish there was a reputation system or other mechanism for avoiding some of the immature members of the community.

This is proably one of the best and most fun games I've ever played. In terms of real time tactis and strategy it is quite superb. Phenomenal WWII amosphere, music, and details make the battlefield come alive.
The gameplay is actually complex, if a bit on the micromanging side. However, after really getting to know the game, you learn how to use various soldiers, squads, vehicles and equipment and it enhances your sense of control on the battlefield.

The only major things that are essential to figuring out early is ammunition and perhaps direct control. Setting up soldiers in defensive lines is only as effective as what they're defending against and how mucht time they have to react. Certain "dug in" enemies and heavy armor are best dealt with personally. However, there are many possibilities to achieving victory and the game delivers a fluid, organic experience. Infantry need to be careful around snipers or heavy machine guns. Armor needs to watch out for AT. You can use environmental concealment and cover and use enemy equipment and vehicles guns as well.
I keep coming back to this one. It is challenging and immersive.

The game launched with a rocky start, with plethora of bugs that plagued it. 3 months later, however, the developers managed to get most if not all of the game breaking bugs out.
the game itself is really great. it's a great turn based RPG akin to its previous entry Expeditions: conquistadors. you fight in a hex-grid battlefield with several people. with great, engaging gameplay and well written, personal story it is worth to dip your time into.
the gameplay itself consist of combat and exploration. while abandoning the old conquistador's exploration format, i welcome the new, more classic rpg like exploration. instead of big overworld map, there are locations with its own map you can visit. you cannot camp anywhere anymore, instead you take over campsites from unwary travellers. despite the format change, the survival/management elements still exist and arguably are more complex if you count the excellent camping system that allows you to heal and rest your party.
with this format change, however, it feel less like an epic exploration that conquistador's grand expedition feeling. the random encounters are noticeably less numerous and less varied. that said, the trade between grand exploration and a location map that you can explore, NPC's to interact, secrets you can discover are a fair trade that make Expedition: Vikings isn't a re-skinned version of conquistadors.
the story itself is simple. your clan is in danger, other clans turn their backs on you, so you have to sail across the sea to gain allies and resources. in the vast island of brittania, you will encounter intrigue, plots, politics and everything that entails. ally yourself with certain faction to seal your alliance, or trample them all beneath your mighty vikings boots and pillage their wealth.
in its simplicity, there is beauty though. you don't set out on a grand adventure to defeat evil, you're forced to set sail to save your family. the story is supported with excellent writing and great moments, and reinforced with choices and consequences that entails. the quests and choices are done pretty well in this game, and more often you will make alot of uncomfortable actions in the world of gray morals.
with 2 major factions in play and plethora of quests that can be solved in a different way, Expeditions: Vikings is a highly replayable game. you might want to try to at least finish the game twice to try out the story of each majaor factions.
the characters are well balanced, with their own stories and personalities. unlike the characters in conquistadors, they're more developed, feel like a person instead a pawn. the trade though, is the lack of variety of characters that you can bring. in conquistadors, your first and second playtroughs can consist of totally different characters, and backstory. in vikings, the exchange for freedom are rewarded with the more detailed characters and their story arcs, although your first and second playtrough will consist of more or less the same people with the same player character backstory. you're always the firstborn of gunnolf, your parents, village, your childhood friends are all predetermined and there are not alot of wiggle room ro create your own character backstory. is the exchange worth it? other types of players might say not, but i think it is a great direction to bring the game into.
it is still a shame that the game launched with such a bad condition, but after the hard work by developer constant patching, listening to community feedback, i think it is a good time to finally set sail  gain into the lands of Expedition: Vikings. there will still be updates, fixes, tweaks to come and the long promised ironman mode, etc.

Here's something you don't find every day. A tactical RPG and not a rifle, pistol, fireball or magic missile in sight. Instead you grab an axe and immerse yourself in the world of the Danes as you control your little group ("hird") of Vikings roaming around Denmark and later Britain. Raider, trader or diplomat, the choice is yours.
Let's run some numbers
8/10 - Great! It's classic Unity engine, not awe-inspiring but gets the job done. The maps are nice and detailed and you see your merry little band change apperance as they become better equipped.
9/10  - Excellent! From grunts and boisterous battle taunts to minor voice acting for important characters and a sweeping music score that really puts you in the mood.
10/10 - Awesome! This is where the game truly shines and you can tell the developers know their subject. Family, Honor, Power struggles, Romance. All the ingredients of a good tale told by a skald during a long cold winter. The writing is on point and the characters feels like people.
8/10 - Great! Perhaps on the easier side if you're a grizzled tactical genius. But I highly enjoyed the mix of combos and different status effect you could employ.
6/10 -  Not bad! There are a couple of different paths through the game and lots of minor dialogue choices that branch into different outcomes. Playing a hulking berserker, a sneaky archer or a silver tounged diplomat will yield vastly different experiences.
7/10 - Good! As of the version at the time of this review (1.0.5) I only ran into a few occational graphical hiccups (characters getting stuck in the ground, or corpses falling through the world and denying me of loot!). Nothing totally gamebreaking.
If you like games like the Shadowrun series, Wasteland 2, Planescape: Torment and Baldur's Gate I think I can safely say you would enjoy Expedition: Vikings as well.

Speedrunners is a fast-paced platformer racing game (finally) that offers a robust experience in competitive and casual gameplay. As you make your way through the "mario" ranks (entry, beginner) to the "monkey" ranks (advanced, expert) and all the way through the "spiderman" ranks (bronze, silver, gold, platinum, diamond) you will notice a vast difference in not only your own skill, but the levels you pick to play. Games in speedrunners can be ultra-competitive matches to social rooms or even rooms with people messing around. There is even a level editor which allows you to make levels as crazy as the levels the developers created; oh wait - these ones suck! Yeah. The list of curated workshop levels to play in ranked is probably going to be your best bet for a good use of skill and a good experience of speed. The community levels require more advanced skills such as "Grapple Spamming" to the "backflip" whereas the official levels are all walking straight and hopping your way above crates. Don't get me wrong - Speedrunners is an excellent game - and if you are questioning your own decision of whether or not to purchase the game, I reccommend, no, I URGE you to buy this. But no game, not even Super Mario Galaxy 2, is perfect.
That's right, this game still has it's drawbacks. The progression system is more of a measure of how many ranked matches you have played, as it is possible for someone who obtains the skill of a silver league player to have a badge above their icon that says "Advanced League." This can often spoil matches because it can cause a Bronze or Expert player to lose vast amounts of ranking points, although it's all in the underranking of the player you are against. Another problem is ELO (not ELO, the band) seasons. Many people can improve a lot within one month, and that can cause a big stirr in the regular time, as the range from advanced to bronze can mean the skill of advanced to bronze.... what I mean by that is essentially ranks get mixed up - and an advanced player could be as skillful as a bronze player and have to play hours and hours of rank to get to the rank they deserve. Another problem is that item spammers always get their way. That's right - starting at Expert League or Bronze League, items are considered evil, and whoever keeps killing a perfectly good player due to a cheap item (powerup) their day will be ruined. And the sad part is... no matter what rank you are in... they will always haunt you, because the more cruel item spammers climb their way to the top out of the ranking board. Regardless of the tacky ranking, Speedrunners is still a fun, potentially competitive, potentially funny, fast-paced platformer game that we have all been waiting for ever since the concept of platformers was introduced.

--- THIS GAME IS IN EARLY ACCESS, AND AS SUCH LEAVES THIS REVIEW OPEN FOR REVISION ---
This won't be a full-on review just yet, simply my opinion on the current state of this project.
I bought this game earlier this year. It ran poorly, suffered from buggy netcode, and left much to be desired in terms of combat. While it is by no means a complete game in its current state, many improvements have been made that have led me to update to a positive review.
In general, the flow of gameplay is similar to Rust or Ark. You start naked, gather materials, build a shelter, survive. However, Conan excels in offering interesting foes and difficult encounters even in PvE. While a high-level player can easily take down many of the mobs, as a fresh spawn it is nice to enter the world and be able to fight NPC camps of barbarians or wandering creatures who become enraged at your disturbance. It offers a nice dynamic of PvE within a PvP setting to make the solo grind and exploration enjoyable.
The combat itself is pretty basic, but does offer some intricacies such as dodge rolling which adds to the moves at a character's disposal. As you level up, fights will definitely become easier, but depending on how you treat them they can be interesting.
The rest is fairly self-explanatory as it follows the familiar gathering and crafting formula of other games in the genre which will be explored and detailed once I feel the need to write a full review. Just know that Conan Exiles offers more on top of that, such as enslaving NPC's to work for you, speeding up the crafting process, or unleashing gods via constructed temples and artifacts at higher levels. Some of these mechanics lead to a stark imbalance, but a solid server will offer an enjoyable and entertaining power struggle between these high-level god-tier players and the rest of the population.
One of the most important improvements is optimization. I could barely run this game prior to getting back into it now, and with the same hardware as before I am able to achieve ~60fps on medium settings which was unreachable before. Lowering some settings allows an ease into the 70-100fps range while still retaining some decent graphical fidelity.
It is disappointing how quickly this game dropped off in terms of player count, but I'm sure as more improvements are made and talked about the player count will ramp up as fans of other games in the genre may find this one to be a better fit for them. If improvements are exponential from here up to whenever a full release occurs, the final product should be an enjoyable survival sandbox with added layers of depth not found in the likes of Rust or other games.
Here's to hoping that developent continues at a steady pace, and the remaining playerbase instills confidence as to encourage a timely release so this commendable project doesn't fall unto the Early Access graveyard.

Say what you will about the repetitive oblivion gates and the potato face character models, this game is a triumph in open-world gaming.  Radiant AI makes the game feel much more alive than previous Elder Scrolls installments.  The Dark Brotherhood faction remains the single most intruiging questline I have ever played in a game.  You will hear npcs telling rumors of events that you yourself participated in, making you feel that your actions have had some impact in the world.    The Shivering Isles expansion that comes with this game is probably the best DLC I have ever played.  It is arguably a tighter experience than the base game.  Morrowind fans will likely experience a bit of nostalgia from the alien landscapes featured.  This game's only real problem is that everything that it tries to do doesn't always work as intended.  This is most obvious with how npcs interact both with you, and with each other.  You can have a perfectly pleasant conversation with an npc, only for him to tell you to shut up and leave him alone when you say your goodbyes.  While this is oftentimes comical, it is also immersion breaking, which is a bit hit for a game whose biggest draw is making you feel like an inhabitant in a living world.  Also, dungeons can feel a little repetitive, as designs are often reused.  It's hard to have every dungeon feel unique when there are so many of them in the game, but I would still expect a bit more variety than what we got.  I wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys rpgs or open world games.  The amount of solid content you're getting for 20 dollars or less is incredible, and should not be passed up.

If you're looking for a game that you can waste a large amount of your life on and not even be upset about it, this is it. Early game is fairly confusing to most and I do remember those days... after a while though this just grows on you and grows on you until you're throwing money at DE for reasons you couldn't even imagine doing so with other developers.
Literally everything in the game is farmable, you don't need to spend a dime on the game because they give you everything you "need' through Alerts and events. If you are impatient however few bucks here and there gets you everything you need as well. I can quote another review I saw somewhere a long time ago, "It feels almost criminal" with how much you can get in this game without paying a dime.
If you however do not like loot driven games, such as Torchlight, Diablo, etc then this game may not tickle your fancy too much. On the other hand if you don't like those games and love third person shooters you may still need to give this a shot.
Now I will say that "end-game" content in this game isn't very deep. There are two raids, with Nightmare (harder) versions of said raids. Sorties are considered end game, and these are basically three specific missions that change daily with certain modifiers attached to each mission to increase difficulty. Other than those you basically have longer "endless" missions you can do that, as time passes, scales enemy levels to increase difficulty.
Most other reviews praise the game's community and I have to say they are correct, you probably won't find a nicer community in a loot driven game, or even a third person shooter game.
The game is not without faults, but it's part of the growing pains. This game is one of my all time favourites, I love the personal scale of it and the stories that are created. I expected a high-class strategy game and got that, but also to my delight a game that revolves around story-telling, not in a verbal way of course but you get to play through and influence important decisions all through the life of generations. This is what is most memorable to me in the end, and I´d like to share one such story.
It is a story of a ill-fated marriage, playing as the king of Sweden one of my vassals and a distant relative, the duke of Norrland, got children late in life but was blessed with twins that both turned out to be good leader material. The brother was kind and a natural leader of men, the sister was charismatic and intelligent though a little too good at lying for her own good and far more interested in women than men. As their father died and the brother inherited I felt content that I could look forward to a long life as king with my loyal young vassal supporting me from the north. To further influence him I helped him secure a marriage with a good norwegian girl in my court, thinking that she was also kind and seemed generally nice and they would be happy together. I settled back feeling like I had made a good move, but a couple of weeks later I got a message from my spymaster warning me that he had caught wind of  a plot against the duke. I investigated and found out that it was his twin sister that was plotting, that the dukes norwegian bride had become the sisters lover and joined in the plot, and everything seemed utterly messed up. I had little time to think about what to do about it for the duke was brutally murdered in his sleeps shortly thereafter. This made me pretty upset, and while the murderous wife escaped to her relatives I ordered the arrest of the newly crowned duchess of Norrland. I felt that seducing you brothers wife and getting her to murder him in his sleep is just too foul a thing to accept, and I felt obliged to execute her for her crimes. Justice had been done, bitter as it was, but then I noticed that the rest of my vassals were furious with me. Turns out it was a really unpopular thing to do, they thought me a tyrant for imprisoning and executing a duchess who also happened to be a relative without what they considered proven justification. This chain of events turned my long reign from a peaceful stable time to one of turmoil and constant rebellions from vassals, getting thousand of people killed in useless battles with malcontents.
Things didnt turn out well, but along the way I hade choices that could have influenced events. I could have been quicker to threaten/bribe the sister to perhaps prevent the murder, I could have accepted the murder after the fact and pretended I didn´t know the dark truth, or I could have settled for just imprisoning the duchess and not executing her, and so on. This is part of the greatness of this game, the way your choices really makes a difference.
I would also like to write about Berserker-Bjorn, the faroese chiefs only son who was named in order to invoke favour from the gods, and who later in life did indeed become a berserker and warrior of such epic ferocity that he personally killed upwards of a dozen french noble characters on the battlefield, and continued leading the charge at the age of 65 despite being maimed in battle in his thirties, and still killing young men in single combat with ease. His tale is too long for now though so I leave you with that.

Played through twice. Once to complete and once again to get the achievements I'd missed. Second playthrough took about an hour and a half with me skipping all dialogue and cutscenes, the rest of the time was spent going through puzzles and watching loading screens. Actually that made me notice a lot of the puzzles had a lot of wandering back and forth between locations but that's a minor criticism. Otherwise the short playtime is to be expected when you already know the solutions to all the puzzles, so it shows there is a decent amount of content there. I'd estimate 6 to 10 hours depending on how quick you are on the uptake.
First playthrough I completed with know guides or help from the hint system. I did scratch my head occasionally but it's not an exceptionally hard point and click adventure. The majority of the puzzles make logical sense and most the time you know what you want to do and the challenge is more in finding the right items to do it. If you are stuck it usually means you need to go back and talk to someone now you know more or you just missed and item in another area. Holding down the left mouse button shows all the hot spots for objects you can interact with on the screen so thankfully pixel hunting is not a barrier like the old days of P&C. If you do get stuck there's an in game help system that tells you what your goals are and can get successively more detailed hints on what to do next from, so you still wont need a guide to help you complete it.
The art style is styalised as you can see from the screenshots above. Appeal comes down to personal opinion. The quality of the art assets is adequate for what they are trying to convey. I didn't find myself not knowing what something was when I looked at it.
Sound wise the voice acting is decent enough, soundFX are adequate to indicate what they are and the music sets the mood without been noteworthy enough to get in the way of your attention. In otherwords it all serves it's purpose.
The story is well written and very original. There's a decent amount of lore to give depth to this unique universe and it is delivered with good pacing to keep the mysteries unfolding all the way to the end. Characters are well designed, you like and contempt them as appropriate and as such feel satisfied when they get what they deserve (good or bad). Dialogue is amusing whenever it's not supposed moving. I would say it's laugh out loud funny but I went through most the game with a bemused smile.
The emotional drama isn't exactly gripping, in spite of it's content it doesn't feel super dark and gripping or a tear jerker like some other games in the genre (try some deadalic titles like chains of satinav of whispered world for that). It's interesting, it walks a tight right where you do feel sympathy for the characters without been devastated by the tragedy constantly befalling them. In other worlds it's pretty light hearted if still a little grim at times.
Loading times aside (they are short but still noticeable enough to annoy you when you realise you have to backtrack because you forgot something) my biggest criticism would have to be stability. Very occasionally the cut scene animations didn't play correctly when completing a puzzle (no impact on gameplay you just miss out on the visual) and the game would periodically crash, I'd say you can expect it to do so 3-5 times between the begging of the game and completion. Thankfully the game autosaves after literally everything you do so you never lose any progress. Another example of how it's not super polish but enough work was put in to make sure things are good enough to preform to resonable expectations.
In summary this is a solid addition to the genre and at the end of the day the game left me hoping for a sequel to be released in the future, which in my book is as solid a recommendation as any.

I'm going to start by saying this game is not for everyone, but for those it is for, it is great.
Kentucky Route Zero is a story-heavy point 'n' click game with minimum gameplay and maximum aesthetics. Rather than focus on puzzles, it focuses on exploration (of both environment and story), immersion and atmosphere, and uses these mechanics to create a brilliant game (I considered putting the word "game" in quotation marks, but no matter how you look at it it is still a game, that you play (and enjoy)).
It has an interesting take on the typical 'choice' system. Generally the choices you make in a game shape your future, but the choices you make in Kentucky Route Zero shape and explain your past, this works seamlessly while still involving the player.
I have seen a lot of complaints about the episodic release, but for some reason I wouldn't have it any other way with this game. The excitement I get from waiting for the next episode, any news filling me with joy, is all part of the experience. I almost feel like the game was designed for the player to have relatively long breaks between episodes, and the episodic release does allow them the opportunity to release neat little interludes (Which in and of themselves are pretty darn great (And free!)).
I also feel the need to throw in something about the soundtrack, but I got nothing other than: It's great. Good job, Ben Babbitt and the Bed Quilt Ramblers.

Okhlos: Omega is a rather unique strategy game that unfortunately gets boring extremely fast.
The core idea is cool enough. You control a disorganized mob that's out on a rampage to take down the Greek gods. Unfortunately the actual gameplay is extremely simple and not particularly engaging. The game also suffers from rather poor controls.
Also, a few design choices make the experience much less enjoyable than it would be otherwise. First of all, the size of your mob is strictly limited which makes the game much more tedious. Also, for some baffling reason the game has permadeath, which seems such a pointless way to prolong the game.
I only played Okhlos for a few levels but didn't find the experience fun at all. Not recommended.
The good:
- Nice concept
- Decent and often witty writing
The bad:
- Underwhelming and shallow gameplay
- Sluggish controls
- Some dubious design choices
- Soundtrack is decent but doesn't fit the theme of the game at all
I abosultely love this game, but I warn you that the game isn't as beautiful as the screenshots lead you to believe.

I am blown away by the level of atmosphere and story that the heightened RPG elements have brought to this turn based strategy game. The art work is beautiful as is the music, the combat is tactical and satisfying with diverse character skillsets to customise that can change the way you play and the scale of the game borders on epic. Dialogue is well written and there are very few quests that don't contribute something to the atmosphere or overall narrative. In short I have been waiting for a game like this for many years.
Don't be put off if you weren't too impressed with Conquistador (which I didn't think was all that great) as Viking is leaps and bounds better in every way. I am mystified as to why it doesn't have a higher overall user review rating as I have thought about what faults it may have and the only thing I can think of is that there is an excessive ammount of barrel bashing. I guess you COULD just ignore them altogether but then you wouldn't have the best resources for crafting and for upgrading your settlement.
There are just too many positive elements for me to detail here. It's a better RPG than most recent RPGs and it's a better TBS than ALL recent TBS games. If, like me, you have been yearning for an RPG with meaty depth and size where combat is sufficiently complex, or a TBS with satisfying tactical combat and an engaging storyline then you really need to play Vikings. If I had to make a stab at a percentage I'd give it 92%.

Expedition: Vikings is a CRPG which combines the turn-based combat a la XCOM with the choice and consequence of the older Bioware games.  The music and writing are wonderful, and the camp-companion system is innovative--it's a rare RPG where you actually have all your companions, even the ones you're not having tag alongside you, be useful in keeping your arms repaired, your camp guarded, etc etc.  It also happens to be one of the most historicity-laden games I've played this side of a Paradox grand strategy game.  In an industry where bloated, gaudy, uninspired crap like Ryse or the latter members of the Assassin's Creed series treat the historical context like Godzilla treats Tokyo, it's hard to put into words how grateful I am to be playing a historical RPG which seems to have a real passion for preserving a sense of authenticity.
The game shows its budget in places--the interface can be a bit unintuitive at times, there are bugs here and there, and the voice acting is almost non-existent; but due to the writing and various interactions, I feel closer to the people in my party--even the customs ones I created--than the desultory Mass Effect: Andromeda or Dragon Age: Inqusition bands.

Maybe, just maybe, one of the best RTS's in existence.
I came over to MoW from playing the original Company of Heroes, and immediately fell in love. It's still somewhat arcadey. An infantry at point blank can be killed by a single rifle shot, but at the maximum rifle firing range, it might take dozens. But it's more realistic at the same time. Infantry have hitboxes, as do tanks. In fact, tanks don't have HP. You either disable their tracks, turret, gun, engine, or crew members, or you manage to temporarily/permanently disable it (sometimes in a spectacular explosion).
You get to control every single man individually. Even the men in the tanks. They will actively use cover, which doesn't provide a "cover buff", but allows your men to duck behind the wall away from incoming fire. A wood fence will provide some protection, maybe stop a few bullets, but some bullets will pass through at reduced damage. Oh, and EVERY shot is rendered. So if you miss, that shot will fly across the map.
Explosions are realistic. If artillery shells rain down, your men should dive for cover. And after that first barrage, another one is coming? Crawl into the shell craters, unless that artillery gets a direct hit, you should be safe. Likewise, explosions will push objects away, and multiple times I've seen a grenade explode far in the distance afer another grenade blew it away.
Five factions, each with a fair assortment of vehicles, units, and equipment.
And speaking of equipment, everything has an inventory. Your men will run out of ammo, but if formed into a squad, they will share their ammo around. Your tanks can run out of ammo, and fuel. You can loot corpses for more ammo, weapons, bandages, grenades, sandbags, camouflage kits, throwing knives, dynamite, satchel charges, signal smoke grenades, flamethrower backpacks, bazooka rockets, anything at all.
And the range of things you can do is huge. There's a stealth mechanic, each unit type has a stealth stat to help them hide from and see other units. You could crawl a man under the noses of your enemy to cause havoc behind their lines. You knocked out a Sherman with your Panzer IV? Which not take the Sherman's 50 Cal and mount it on your Panzer? Your tank refusing to take a shot because there's a wooden house in the way? Direct control that tank and make it shoot through the house. The enemy have abandoned an AT gun and you want it? Reman it, or even better, drive a vehicle up and tow it back to your line.
The best thing is, these aren't gimmicks. They are genuinely useful features.
I love this game, and I'll close with an example of how all these features work together. There is a unit in the game called the radio operator. They use a flare gun to mark targets, which then gets fired upon by off-map artillery. In one game, one of these was harassing my tank. I sneakily crawled a man up near to where the radio operator was, and waited for him to fire. When he did, I moved my tank away, and then told my man to gun him down. The man died and dropped his flare gun on the ground next to himself. If I could take that, I would get to call in my own off-map artillery. But he has the area covered by other men. So I manually control my man to get him to throw grenades just behind the gun. As each grenade explodes, it blasts the gun closer towards my man, until eventually he picks it up into his inventory, equips it, and fires a barrage back (though unfortunately he only gets one signal flare barrage because the rest of the ammo is on the dead radio operator's body).
All of that happened in the space of about 10 seconds.

Completely mediocre in practically every way, Woodle Tree Adventures looks good in screenshot, but is substantially less impressive in motion.
The game opens up to a quiet scene of a tree with a mustache talking to a new anthropomorphic stump. The dialogue is bland, not voiced, and sticks around for far, far too long and is, as far as I could tell from my random button pushes, unskippable. It sticks around for a few minutes at the most, but isn't actually a deal breaker.
What follows is. Being a 3D platformer, the way the character feels is imperitive to a good experience. This stump guy does not feel good. He walks far too slow, and runs far too slow, which not only clashes with the cartoony vibe the game seems to be going for, but seems to undercut itself as a platformer. The leaf this character uses as a weapon feels about as effective as an actual leaf, and the hitbox for the attack is just about as large as the leaf, ensuring you have to thoroughly snuggle up to the enemies that damage you on touch in order for you to hurt them. I also had a problem with a camera angle or two not giving me a very good idea of where the enemies were in relation to myself.
The stump also has a pretty floaty jump and the sound of him running around doesn't match up to when his feet actually touch the ground.
I also had a bit of input lag, but i'm not sure I can blame this on the game or not. My computer isn't anything special, but it's been enough to play Tomb Raider 2013 and Bioshock Infinite along with the vast majority of the rest of my library. I see no reason it shouldn't be able to run this game appropriately.
All in all, the cute graphics and models can't make up for a game that fundamentally feels bad and has such poor initial presentation. I only played five minutes into the first level before I was thoroughly sick of it. Dying also sends you back to the beginning of the stage (unless I died before a checkpoint), and I wasn't very keen to repeat the half I've done.
Maybe this game gets really good later on, but that doesn't change a first impression.

It's a great RPG with a good story, interesting characters, a fun combat system and co-op. If you liked the first DOS or if you're a fan of cRPGs in general, you'll most likely enjoy this game.
You can create your own "generic" character or you can play as one out of 6 Origin characters with a proper backstory, unique dialogue and personal quests. You can also have up to 3 origin characters as companions.
The main story is you and your companions are on an adventure to obtain Divine power and stop bad guy from coming from the Void and destroying everything. The main story is alright, but nothing special. The stories of origin characters and their quests were much better, I was more interested in them than in the main story. The characters themselves were interesting and well written too, with some great voice acting.
It's nice to have a modern RPG where you can actually
. Any game with a leveling system gets called an RPG nowadays. Divinity: Original Sin 2 is an
roleplaying game. In dialogue you get enough options to respond the way your character would respond, some quests can be tackled in multiple ways, there are no """essential characters""" whom you can't kill. The way your responses in dialogues are written is especially nice, they are something like *Tell her that you accept* / *Refuse her offer* instead of "Yes, I will do it" / "No, I'm not interested". So for roleplaying purposes you can voice the exact words that your character would say, phrasing it the way you want it. It's a small feature but I like it. There are responses unique for certain backgrounds such as Soldier or Scholar or Barbarian. Origin characters have their own unique responses in certain dialogues too. Persuasion checks feel alright, they are not great, but they work well enough.
Some different characters will react differently to you depending on your race. Overall, I can't express why exactly, but the game makes you feel that you are playing as a person of a particular race. If you're a lizard, you'll deffinitely know that you're a lizard and not a human with a lizard character model.
The sidequests are interesting for the most part. Some quests do suffer from bugs though, to the point that you might not be able to complete some of them, but there aren't that many bugged quests in the game, I had only 2 or 3 problems in my 2 playthroughs. You might want to wait untill they are all patched though.
The turn-based combat and characters' combat abilities are pretty good. You have your melee fighters, rogues, rangers. summoners, mages of various elemental schools and any combination of any classes is possible, even if not all are feasible. If you don't like your build you can respec anytime for free after beating the first act of the game, which is nice. The combat is similar to the combat in DOS1 but with some major differences. You still can create different surfaces and clouds to change the battlefield, like setting an area on fire that will damage anyone who walks through it. Or you can create oil surfaces that will slow down the characters, or electrified clouds to stun them, etc. Different elements can interact with each other like puddles of water or blood and lightning, which, if it hits a puddle, will stun enemies standing in it, or oil puddles that explode if hit by fire. There's now highground advantage that will increase all ranged damage if you have the highground. There are plenty of useful abilities and spells for each class, such as heavy damage dealing ones, crowd control, buffs and debuffs, teleports, etc. The combat is engaging and remains interesting for the most part of the game. It did start to get a bit easy and repetitive after 3/4 of the game, but it's a really long game that took me around 80 hours to finish for the first time, so I've had a lot of hours of great fun.
If you liked the combat in DOS1 you might or might not like the changes they made in DOS2. The biggest change is addition of physical and magical armor, which completely changes your priorities in combat. Unlike in DOS1 you debuffs/stuns/damage-over-time abilities now don't have a random chance to apply. Instead you need to destroy the enemy's mag/phys armor first by doing some mag/phys damage and then it's guaranteed that your abilities will apply to the enemy. Given how important crowd control is in this game, you always have to focus on destroying the enemy's armor first and since armor is split into magical and physical, you'll want your mages to be focusing one target and your melee fighters focusing another one. This makes party builds like 3 mages and 1 melee guy less viable, you want either 4/0 or 2/2 split. This makes the combat feel less teamwork'y than in DOS1. Additionally, the enemies' health feels much less important than their armor. Once you knock their armor down they are as good as dead since your crowd control abilities have 100% chance to apply. I personally am ok with armor. For me it didn't make the combat feel worse, it made it feel different from DOS1. Surfaces, on the other hand, were definitely better in DOS1.
Surfaces now feel less useful than in DOS1 and they were the best feature in that game. Since (for most surfaces) their debuffs/damage/stuns don't go through phys/mag armor, they often feel irrelevant. You can set an area on fire but the enemy won't be burning if he's standing in fire untill you knock his magical armor down, and by the time you knock his armor down you'll want to stunlock him anyway so it doesn't matter much if he's burning or not, if he's stunned he is as good as dead anyway. Another difference, which makes surfaces feel less useful, is how often you'll encounter fire and cursed fire surfaces. If you're fighting Void enemies, expect everything to be on cursed fire. There's one fight, the Backpits, where the whole screen will be completely filled with cursed fire which you can't put out. There's just too much of this cursed fire in the game. Another problem is that too many enemies have teleport skills. You can create your surfaces all you want but the enemies will often just teleport straight over them to safety. So the best feature of DOS1's combat, surfaces and their interactions, feels much less interesting in this game unfortunately.
The combat is not perfect. There are some useless skills and (especially) perks, Lone Wolf perk is so poorly balanced that it makes the game on Tacticial  difficulty a cakewalk, item scaling in lategame gets ridiculous, but with that said, I still like the combat. It's fun and can be challenging at times and it doesn't get boring too quickly.
The graphics are great, the sound, music and voice acting are great. The controls and the interface are fine.
Overall, it's a really good fun RPG with tons of content, well worth the price.

Even being a bit dated and lacking a big population, this game is still great and worth a try, it's free anyway!
Pros:
+ character customization, both cosmetics and skill-wise
+ crafting system
+ customizable hotbar system like Neverwinter Nights
+ biggest open world map you'll ever see in a game
+ cool mounts and vehicles
+ hundreds and hundreds of weapons and itens
+ graphics are decent, a bit like Fallout 3 / New Vegas
+ Faction system (help one faction, be hated by the other...and there are 6!)
+ PERMANENT freemium status if you buy anything for the marketplace, or get the Steam bundle.
Cons:
- Combat system is a bit too simple and a bit buggy
- Mutations aren't as appealing as I'd wish to see
- AI is very basic
- Crafting requires real-time, some advanced recipes need hours and hours (but you don't need to be logged on)
- Free-to-play status is very limiting, specially the 10 red chips (100k cash) money cap. It's ok to try the game, and you won't feel an urge to get freemium until level 15 or 20 (or come across a very rare item which sells for a million in the Auction House and you discover you won't be able to get the money because it hits the cap like I did lol)
- Population isn't as big as it was some years ago

Shadow Warrior is a true classic in the FPS genre. Forget your slow♥♥♥♥♥baby shooters, this is a game for manly macho men. Players familiar with the original Duke Nukem 3D and even the old DOOM will no doubt enjoy this fast-paced shooter. For you youngins who grew up on Call of Duty and Battlefield, buckle the ♥♥♥♥ up and get ready for one hell of a crazy ride.
Unlike most modern shooters, the original Shadow Warrior is fast-faced and in your face. From the very moment you start the game, you're bombarded with enemies. Not ready? Too bad. You're dead. If you survive the initial encounter, you'll find yourself in an open-ended albeit still linear succession of rooms. Rather than long, linear corridors, you're given a more open ended back with which to familiarise yourself and explore as you progress through the level.
Combat is fast and fluid, with a wide variety of weapons to obliterate your foes. And if you run out of ammo? Go find some. It's up to you to find more either through exploration. Don't worry too much if you can't find any, though. The sword is extremely fun to use, and kills many enemies in a single hit.
As for the story... there isn't one. If you have a good sense of humour, you'll get a chuckle out of the game's overt and offensive jokes.
In the Classic Redux version, you also get the Wanton Destruction and Twin Dragon expansion packs in addition to some optional updated visuals and a remixed main theme. That's plenty of content for the price, and whether you're an old school hardcore shooter fan or a newcomer looking for a faster, more difficult experience, you should find something to love in Shadow Warrior.

Sonic mania is the throwback sonic game to the old classic days of sonic with Sonic 1, Sonic 2, Sonic 3 & knuckles and Sonic CD. This game is a most pickup for fans of the classic games as it has everything those games had and more.
The story is very very very simple. Eggman gets his hands on a ruby, time gets messed up and sonic and his pals gets throwed to different zones. Sonic stops eggman, The end.
This game is not a entirly new entry, I see it more as a sonic generation classic version more than a new game but that's because they have mixed levels. Lot's of old levels returned where act 1 is just the same level from the original and act 2 represents new idea to the old levels. there are 8 old classic levels with 4 of those being remade and then there is the 4 completly new levels. This is a good thing for the people that want to relive the old stages in hd quality. For me it's a bummer, I loved the new stages but i grew bored of the old returning stages. This is completly my opinion, If you love to replay old zones in HD that's completly up to you.
The bosses are all completly new and creativ with 3 different type of bosses, The classic Eggman, The Five elite robots named Hard-Boiled Heavies and then some random bosses that was presented in sonic 3. For the some bosses was great and some was just questionable. I wont say more to avoid spoilers but This is like the classics where lot's of bosses are presented and you will have a opinion on each of them if you enjoyed them or not. All i can say is that the bosses wanted you to take damage a lot and then just attack with your immunity frames wich for me isn't a good design on some of them and a specific boss was just stupidly broken at times.
The soundtrack is good as always. I don't have much to say in this as my opinion toward the soundtrack is mixed so i just say, Listen to the soundtrack and determ yourself if you like it or not.
My opinion - Sonic mania is a good game if your a fan of the classics or if you just want the classic feeling gameplay, Pick this game up. if you want something new, that's where mania can't stand on it's own 2 feet. Hopefully if they do another one of these games in the future, I hope they go all for new stages and that was the best parts of the game in my opinion.

In short:
-It play great
-It looks great
-It sounds great
-It cost 20 bucks
-It can run on a potato at 16k 240 fps, if it wasn't locked at 60fps...

In not so short:
For 20 bucks it is a great value. The thing is that it's a bit short, there are only 12 zones (+ the final boss zone), each in 2 acts that can be completed in a few minutes.
The graphics are really good, it's designed to look like updated Genesis/Megadrive graphics, with more colors, details and some techniques unavailable on the original hardware like sprite rotation and scaling, all used very well.
Some have complained about the presence of 3d graphics in the game, but the thing is that it's really rare and well used, mostly in the chaos emerald stages, which are full 3d.
And it's also the king of 3d that a sega 32x could produce and the game was designed to look like a game that could have been released on a console between the Genesis/Megadrive and Saturn.
The difficulty curve seems f*cked up, I remeber Flying Battery Zone (zone 4) being much harder than Mirage Saloon Zone (Zone 8) for exemple, it's not consistent at all. Same for the bosses, most of them are really easy but, overall, most of them are really well designed, I can't go into some details because of spoilers but you will have quite some good surprises.
The best part of this game, for me, is it's sound track, there is no misuc in the game that I don't like ! And the sound design is on point, everything in this game sound great.
Also sometimes there is collision errors and the intro video is really compressed, it looks like a YouTube rip, it's quite a waste of this wounderful animation.
My verdict:

The Inner World is a classic point-and-click adventure game about a strange, alien planet, a meek protagonist who ends up on a world-wide conspiracy, and some old-school hardcore problem solving, all wrapped within a cosy atmosphere.
The Inner World is so far the largest game released by German independent developer Studio Fizbin. It is the kind of point ‘n’ click adventure that doesn’t shy away from ludicrous puzzles, but gives you a really unique storytelling experience in return.
It takes place inside a world where natural laws differ greatly from ours. An alien planet which seems quite “human” in some respects, but different enough to leave the door open for creativity, imagination, and overall good writing.
You play a very naïve, shy hero, whose day starts off with a seemingly small accident, but he soon finds himself in a revolution against an oppressing religious dictator for the control of the most precious commodity: air. Don’t expect the usual story development though, because the plot has a few clever tricks along the way.
The cast is quite small, but even the supporting members are enjoyably memorable. The voice actors do a decent job, but nothing spectacular.
As an adventure game, it is moderately difficult. The item usage follows a really weird and twisted logic, but it is not completely impossible. (Plus it has a step-by-step hint system as backup.) Thanks to this, the play time can easily be pushed over 6-7 hours, which is fairly decent for this price category.

This is a tough game to rate. TL;DR: A very fun time killer if you buy it super cheap. I wouldn't pay $13 for it though. Maybe $5 MAX (I got it in a Humble Bundle). If you like permadeath roguelikes that unlocks stuff to make the next playthrough easier, this is pretty fun. I beat it on my second try though. Nowhere near the value of Rogue Legacy.
On the one hand:
It's a really fun roguelike with procedurally generated worlds. The mob feature is pretty cool and there are a lot of other features that make the game replayable. After every sublevel, you can make 1 of 3 selections to trade types of people in your mob for heroes or other mob types i.e. trade 5 citizens for a hero that adds 25% to morale, or 5 slaves for a different hero that does something else, or 5 warriors for something else as an example. The cool thing about this is there are quite a few heroes in the game so you could play for 10+ hours and not see all of them.
Just like most roguelikes it is permadeath, but you get something for it almost everytime you die. For example, after the first game you unlock a special starting area where you can pick your leader with special abilities, and add heroes to your group, also with special abilities. The number of starting heroes goes up (everytime?) you play, and I have unlocked "something" on almost every playthrough.
There is also a "cheat" feature. As you go through the game, you will come across billboards with bright green text. If you see one of them, you can type what is on the billboard into the "crypto" on the main menu and you will start a new game with some type of special feature. Just don't destroy the billboard before you can read what it says. I have only found 1 of those so far though, and it wasn't even in the main game, so they are pretty rare to find, but you can always google them.
The bosses are semi-random. The first 2 or 3 levels have a random boss, with the subsequent bosses being static. There are hidden bosses as well, which is pretty cool. Also, if you beat a hidden boss you get a free hero too.
On the other hand:
It's a really short game. You can beat the game in about 2 hours, but it has replay value especially since the campaign unlocks extra levels when you beat it (not sure how many times this happens). I have beaten it 3 times and each time I played after beating it I ended up playing either an additional world, or the end boss changes as a result of me killing the previous end game boss.
It gets repetitive, but everytime I play I end up unlocking something else, so maybe this is a neutral point, I don't know. There isn't a whole hell of a lot of strategy either. There is some strategy when fighting mobs and bosses, (learning when to block or run away) but it isn't really in depth and I haven't found the game difficult to beat.
All in all, I think it's a really fun game worth a few bucks, but don't expect a game that will hold your attention for any significant length of time.
Edit: I have seen some negative reviews due to bugginess. To that I say, I have noticed the sound is a little screwed up. Sometimes sound effects will go into a constant loop. Also, I have experienced very choppy sound and choppy gameplay at certain points but it isn't enough to give it a negative review IMO.

is an adorable 3D platformer that allows players to step into the shoes of a tiny tree hero. The game itself is very simple and straightforward. Your goal as Woodle is collect Fairy Tears which in the game look like giant tear drops. Apparently your land needs water and these Fairy Tears can help with that. That’s it -
. You also collect berries which will unlock things when you collect enough. The game is also very short, it only has six main levels and one bonus level and has little replay value.
The game is fun and would be great for younger players, however, I found a glaring problem with the game play. This game is 3D as I mentioned, however, the camera doesn’t act like it. You can’t control the camera outside of zooming in and zooming out. You can’t rotate the camera to see where you might be jumping and it causes depth perception issues as well lots of falls. It turned a fun and cute game into a frustrating experience.
because I couldn’t see where I was jumping properly, and then where you respawn is random. Sometimes it’s near the beginning or maybe you’ll get lucky and land close to where you before. There also no checkpoints which would help with that, but if the camera worked properly you wouldn’t need checkpoints because the levels aren’t that difficult. While I think a child would love this game I don’t think it would be fair to give them something this frustrating. On the plus side you have unlimited lives so you can keep dying forever.
. I kept pushing through the game despite the countless deaths because I found it so cute. The art is bright and amazingly comforting, even the enemies are adorable. All the worlds are well-designed and have fitting music to accompany them. Aside from the simple controls, you can jump, run and hit things, the aesthetic aspects of the game were the only good parts unfortunately. I really wanted to like something so cute.
If you can handle the wonky camera you may like this game, I did but it was too frustrating. This would be a perfect game for children or people looking for a casual experience. My only other issue with the game is lack of explanation on what the upgrades do, I really saw no difference between the yellow, orange and white leaf weapons.
so if you can put up with the camera I say get it but I can’t fully recommend this sadly.

(Been playing with 2 friends for now 40 hours and still going strong)
-They choices in this game are far reaching and meaningful, so you can actively meet people you saved earlier or some people might be angry at you for killing someone. You can act like a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥or a savoir, but most questgivers offer choices which go more into moral grey areas. This in itself is a great thing to do in every RPG, at least in my opinion. EVERY CHOICE HAS MEANING. It's like a real world with real people in it. It's a loveletter to everyone who likes Baldurs Gate 2 or even Planescape: Torment. Still the replayability in this game is through the roof. You can play this game 5 times and not see every choice you can make.
-The Story is superior to the Original SIn 1, which in itself isn't all that hard to achieve but this time they actually made more of an effort to engage you in the story. It starts with you not knowing what's going on at all, but after some time it gains traction and becomes pretty engaging, which is partly due to the great voice acting. Everything in this game is voiced, which is itself is an achievement in itself. There are about 84000 voicelines in this game, which is absolutely staggering. This time around you feel a lot more important in the story and more epic overall. Plus the cutscenes have some of the beautiful art you can get in Video games.
The turn based battle system feels honed and intuitive. Every skilltree is viable and adds to your character in a meaningful way. Want to be Necromancer, Summoner? You can be and it's strong tree to actually invest to. Want to be a mage? You can be in so many ways it's hard to actually count the things you can to in this game. Want to be a Ranger or Melee? Me and my friends are actually going all physical and it's working great. There are many ways to win. The magical/physical armor on every enemy makes it possible. If you smashed their armor they are able to be stunlocked, which makes for some interesting combinations.
The Bad: These are some minor issues overall, but stil should be talked about.
-Minor bugs with quests. And the questlog can be pretty convoluted at times, so you have no idea what you can do, or must do to finish some quests. (Which can be a good thing if you're into that stuff)
-Your equipment becomes irrelevant pretty fast in later levels so buying new stuff for every character can become tedious at times (which can be bypassed if you have friends and they actually do that on their own).
The difficulty in later levels is pretty uneven. Early into the game it's pretty hard and you will die if you approach a fight the wrong way. In later levels it's getting to the point where it's pretty much impossible to die if you know what you're doing. Luckily you can change the difficulty, so it becomes more challenging.
In conclusion:
This game is a loveletter to anyone who likes RPGs. The goods heavily outweigh the bads in this game. This game shackled me to my computer for hours on end.
I implore you don't pirate this game, the developers deserve your money, you can see their love for games in every fiber of this game.
This game is a masterpiece and should be treated as such.
Buy this game you if you even slightly like games, you will not regret it.
