GOOD: Great story, great characters. The player's choice and ability to navigate the story and choose different outcomes is there. While the individual quests are all fairly linear and with limited choice, the story itself branches and allows for you to interact with the people of the British Isles however you want: be a friendly diplomat or merchant, a marauding viking, or a manipulative back-stabber who plays factions agaisnt one another.
Gameplay is tight and enjoyable: combat is turn-based and party oriented, with the player controlling bands of about six fighters going against similarly sized opposition. Having a party with varied abilities and knowing how to make those abilities synergize is key to success and feels incredibly rewarding. Similarly, there's a fair variety of combat abilities, and all the weapons your warriors can use have clear and distinct styles of use. The game does a great job making all these turn-based fights feel different: sometimes you're just beating down highwaymen, other times you're trying to overwhelm a camp of guards without letting any escape, other times you're defending and fending off waves of enemies.
Evening managing resources outside of combat feels great. Time and effort are as much a resource as things like food, medicine, and iron are, so camping during overland travel turns into a surprisingly fun puzzle of figuring out how to best spend your party's time, and balancing their need for rest with your need for them to hunt, make medicine, repair equipment, or stand guard.
Art-style manages to be both realistic yet appealing, and the music is just as fitting and just as good. Party members and unique characters get beautifully rendered portraits that are always both a joy to look at and another way for the writers to characterize someone: clever and quippy characters look appropriately snark, grizzled warriors look appropriately tough, smug characters and villains have appropriately punchable faces.
BAD: Glitches are common. Some abilities are just plain useless, with no way to re-spec your characters: though useful skills outnumber the useless ones, it can still feel like you've gimped your character by investing too heavily in abilities that turned out to be useless (looking at you, Unarmed and Throwing). Meanwhile, certain ranks of skills are locked until you invest a certain number of skill points elsewhere. While this is arguably a necessity for balance, otherwise you'd be able to have a fully-leveled sword skill while the enemies are still on level two, it pretty much forces you to make a jack-of-all-trades character. Granted, there's enough abilities that you can still have your characters specialize in stuff without everybody having the same set of skills, building your character feels like throwing points into stuff you don't care about or skills you won't use until you can finally put more points into a skill you DO want to use.
Some other elements of gameplay can also become really tedious. There's little caches of supplies hidden around every level, be it a plant that yields herbs for medicine, or barrels that can be opened for small amounts of money or other building materials. Emphasis on 'small'. Really what this means is that every time you enter a new area, you can either jog across every inch and click every single container you find (which feels like a chore, as well as a great way to get carpal tunnel) to scrape up every last resource, or completely ignore it and deal with potential shortages. Late-game, once you have a big party with well-developed skills, camping pretty much becomes "make sure your preset camping schedule isn't messed up, then click the camp button and watch the night pass while doing nothing yourself".
While combat feels great when it challenges you or goes your way, sometimes, encounters are just set up to kick you in the teeth. Due to the turn-based nature of the game, encounters with lots of traps and/or archers become very punishing very quickly. Positioning is key, and sometimes the game tries its hardest to absolutely botch yours by having your archer start adjacent to three enemies, your spear-person completely exposed to the enemy archers, and your shield-dudes all bottled up at the back of the pack and utterly useless.
Finally, though the music is great, the sound track is limited and individual tracks are short. Expect 2-3 turns of epic battle accompanied by rousing music, then awkward silence, or just a constant loop of that epic music until you're as desensitized to it as you are hearing 'Careless Whisper' in a hotel elevator. Up close, the 3D character models just look... they just look awful. Animations can be a bit gangly too, but the good news is that for 90% of the game you're going to be looking at everything zoomed-out so it's not so big a deal.
FINAL VERDICT: The good definitely outweighs the bad, and Expeditions: Viking is totally worth the price point. Fun throughout, highly replayable, and with plenty to do. Devs say the game takes about 30 hours to beat the game depending on how much you rush through it, and I totally agree. If you really explore everything and do all you can, that playtime can easily hit 40 or more hours on a single playthrough. If you like turn-based RPG's with as much story as gameplay, you'll like this game.

This game falls deeply in the "casual" hashtag, and it's a great throwback to my Kongregate background - I've been playing Flash games for years literally - and it also runs greatly with low graphics and in windowed mode (I love to play these games in windowed mode on my gaming laptop), everything runs smoothly with no lag at all even when the screen is crowded with zombies and characters!
Of course, 4€ is more than crazy for a game like this, so it must be purchased when it's on -90% (I'm pretty sure I bought it with a 90% discount coupon) so that yeah, if you pay less than 50 cents (of dollars, or euros it's the same xD) you're all right in matching what the game offers you.
It's basically a 2D side-scrolling game as we saw tons of times throughout the Internet, but still it isn't a copy of other games both for what concerns the gameplay and the graphics, which are simple but enjoyable overall. Plus I think it was originally conceived in Russian and features some spelling mistakes (like "powerfull" or "carbine rifle" instead of "carabine") but as I said the game focuses only on the 2D zombie killing/stomping/crushing so really they don't make any kind of problem, there isn't a story to read xD
So, you are a hard rock guy (hence the title I think, since there aren't hard rock or music themes in general xD) on a truck (which looks more like a quad motorbike for its dimensions) and while it moves automatically forward, you still can use the AD keys to make it run faster or to slow down. The other keys are used for support weapons: W launches air force (on your head), S is for the grenades and keys from 1 to 4 are for the different weapons you can unlock (you start with a basic rifle and you'll arrive to a mini-gun); the mechanics of course are the same of every other zombie/enemy 2D crusher side-scrolling game - the more enemies you kill, the farthest you go and the more money you earn.
There are four different tracks (you start in the desert) with little differences (even because the game it's quite basic since you can't jump, change routes, go down and such) but that's ok to me.
And there's also another important thing you have to do - you must save (I mean, you don't have to harm them) cats and people marked with sounds and on-screen exlamation marks. I think that this point has to be cleared: in order to save people and not kill them with your rifles or under your wheels, when they (of course, it's a zombie game so they're survivors coming your way xD) come on the screen you simply have not to shoot them or use grenades and such, so that they will hop on your truck and they will be going on your side for the rest of the level.
So, all of this in order to refute other reviews: the game's not glitched, the achievements are all unlockable. It's just that it is required to save survivors in order to get the bosses come out and so, to finish the levels.
It may be true that this developer doesn't answer to players and this isn't of course something good, at all, I had also reviewed negatively other games by him (or them), but this game if you understand the mechanics isn't glitched or bugged at all, it just need triggers to complete the levels. I mean, 30% of the players have obtained the rarest achievement so they can't be bugged, you just don't have to abandon the game after 30 minutes and stick with it :)
All said, it's definitely enjoyable for some hours and if you find this game on sale to me it's worth to play. I love these games on Flash websites and here you can also adjust graphics and window size to fit your style so as far as it runs smoothly and has all what I told you here it's a nice indie game in its genre!

I'm mainly doing this review because after reading the others i see they missed some of the game mechanics. (i'm by no means saying they are good)
You're on a tractor rolling down a highway shooting zombies using 4 weapons (3 unlockable), grenades, and a friendly glider that will shoot from the air. the zombies mindlessly move and jump toward you and sometimes a bigger threat will come along all until you reach 1 of the 4 bosses. if any get past your car and get off the screen you'll lose health.
The thing the other reviewers miss was you need to save 3 people to reach the boss. you can also save cats but you don't need to save them for any one reason. how do you save these then? well there will be a sound and a "!" will come up on the screen when a survivor comes out and the cats will screech when they come out. both will only run on the ground so shoot high though when the survivor gets close they will jump over your tractor and hop in the back after leaving the screen. once you have 3  in the back of the tractor the boss will show up. to not kill the cats you need to use your boosters (space bar by default) to jump over them.
Bosses: it took me a bit to figure this out but you need to shoot the things they throw (even if they go over your head) as well as the boss because once they explode they will take some of your hp. you also can't move (or not supposed to) during boss fights though you can still jump.
i got this in a bundle and had fun with it but i'm not sure i would have payed money for it outside the bundle. if you feel $4 (or whatever it will be when on sale) is a good price for less than an hour or so of fun well go for it.
p.s. if you don't want to look in game for the controls they are (w) air strike - a glider will come in and shoot at an angle down (s) grenade - explodes a few feet from your tractor (a) slow down (d) speed up (spacebar) booster - jump in the air (1,2,3,4) use these to switch weapons you'll need to buy 2, 3, and 4 (left click) hold this to shoot your main weapon (r) reloads your weapon but you can just hold fire and your guy will do it on his own.

Who remembers the arcades?
Again, I start my review with that particular sentence. The
last time was with Blue Estate: The Game, which too gave me
nostalgic memories of the arcade-cabinets that I frequently
visited as a kid.
This time though, the memories center towards the competetive
aspect of those times. Trying my damnest to top my friends
high-scores on particular game and Devil Daggers reminds me of
that a great deal. Moreso than Call of Juarez: Gunslingers
Arcade-mode, which is another game currently waiting for a
review.
But enough of nostalgic babble, let's have a look at the game.
Devil Daggers is a fast-paced 1st person survival game, where
you go against an endless horde of demonic monstrosities. Each
with their own behaviour, form and dissonant sounds.
Mechanically, the game is rather simple. Survive as long as
you can, whilst collecting gems to upgrade you attack in small
increments. Avoiding all damage..
Yes, all damage. You die in one hit, which I could argue
shifts the category towards bullethells.. But, let's not get
into that.
Avoiding all damage and surviving as long as possible, whilst
the amount of gathering monsters slowly increase.
And you will die, but don't let that stop you. It's part of
the fun...
Graphically, the game has been frequently compared to either
old Quake or Heretic series.. And I do see why they'd say
that, the jaggedy polygonal graphics with pixelated meshes
does invoke some feelings of Quake and to some extent Doom and
Hexen.
However, even as that graphical style does give the game an
unique aesthetic. It does cause enemies in large packs or
far-away, appear as an almost solid mass of muddy pixels.
Which does irk me to an extent, I would like an option to have
an high-res pack, for the sake of player-convenience.
That's the only minus point that I have to give for this game.
Apart from the obvious caveat that this is purely an arcade-
game, purely single-player and not multiplayer.
Devil Daggers is an enjoyable fast-paced arcade-game. Easy to
pick up, however not so easy to master. It does cause you
stress, as much as the feeling of accomplishment as you slowly
climb up the leaderboards.

First, let me say that Conan Exiles is an excellent tribute to Robet E. Howard's Conan Universe. Anyone who is a fan of the Conan movies, books, or games is definitely going to like this one.
IMO Conan Exiles has a lot to offer; beautiful graphics, an interesting backstory (which is revealed through exploration), dungeons, siege warfare, a strong modding community. It posesses some very unique mechanics like climbing and the upcoming sorcery system, as well as a lot more on the way.
Furthermore, to address a common complaint, the melee combat is a lot like Skyrim at the moment. With simple light and heavy attacks the combat is nothing exraordinary, BUT is going to be revamped very shortly and will feature an in-depth combo attack system. Each weapon type will have its own unique combo sets (yes, multiple combo sets for every weapon type) and effects (cripple, bleed, knockdown, etc.), somewhat like the Age of Conan melee system.
In regard to online play; there are a wide variety of server settings if you want to run your own server (or play single player), similar to what ARK offers. However, there are plenty of private and official servers available to play on. Funcom has a quite a few server types to choose from on their official servers, but it basically boils down to PVP and PVE with varying degrees of roleplaying and XP/resource gain. The player limit on the official servers is 40 people, which is too low to be honest, as people tend to flock to the most crowded servers when the one they were playing on fills up, causing annyoing queue times.
PVP servers allow the destruction of player buildings, which I think is great. It does take a lot to destroy buildings above tier 1 and if you're good at building and find a decent spot to build in, you won't have to worry about it too much. The truth of it is though, that every PVP server has its share of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who will go out of their way to destroy everything they can. If you don't want to deal with that, no big deal, play on a PVE server.
That said, the game does have some bugs, some of which are very annoying. Honestly though, nobody should be surprised by an early access game having bugs. The whole point of early access is to suppliment the developers' budget to finish the game after all.
Now, Funcom has a history of ruining good games (Age of Conan, Secret World, etc.), but to their credit Conan Exiles has a very hard working team that seems to truly care about creating a quality game and releases regular updates aimed at fixing said bugs, as well as adding a plethora of new content. It really has come a long way since it's early access launch (which wasn't that long ago), especially when compared to games like ARK, which has taken years to get to where it is now (and is still buggy).
In short, this is a great game which is only going to get better. However, if you can't live with some bugs then do yourself a favor and wait until the game is officially released instead of trash talking it now and making yourself look like an idiot. It saddens me greatly to see such an amazing game slapped with the "mixed reviews" label because of some impatient fools who don't understand the meaning of "early access".

The first thing you see is a dagger and your own outstretched hand.
Touch it, and the game begins.
It's just you, a dark platform, and an endless legion of horrifying skull monsters.
You have one weapon: your hand can fire  daggers. If you click, you get a shotgun pattern. Hold the button, and you fire a stream of daggers.
It's a game of spatial awareness and precision, above everything else. The platform has edges, so you have to find some way to speed around the platform dodging enemies while simultaneously avoiding the abyss. It's just as frantic and terrifying as the videos depict.
When you die, you see how you stacked up on the leaderboard (likely not even close to the top), and you can click to instantly try again. Fair warning: watching the #1 replay will give you several heart attacks and a swift ego check.
You will fail.
You will fail,
.
But it's an addictive kind of failure.
Someday, I may place somewhere less pitiful on the list.
For now, money well spent.

Sonic Mania is a return to form for the Sonic the Hedgehog franchise and the sequel to Sonic 3 & Knuckles we never got.
Sonic Mania is very accurate in it's replication of the original trilogy of Sonic games.  Emphasis is placed squarely on momentum-based speed and platforming.  Three playable characters, Sonic, Tails and Knuckles, each bring their own abilities to the table, offering replay value.  Sonic has a new Drop Dash ability, which allows him to enter an immediate Spin Dash upon landing from a spin attack, allowing him to maintain his speed.  Tails can fly (and carry Sonic while doing so) and swim.  And Knuckles can glide, climb walls and break certain walls.
Stages are multi-faceted, tiered, and nuanced.  They offer many routes, some unique to one or more of the characters.  The game features a healthy mix of new and old Zones.  Old Zones are very well done, incorporating the designs of both the original version's first and second Act mixed together, giving a new feeling.  And the second Act of old Zones are entirely new, featuring new gimmicks and spins on the original version's location.  Like Sonic 3 & Knuckles, Zone's Acts also transition from Act to Act usually, giving them a feeling of coherence.  Every Act also has a unique boss which are quite challenging and the series' best.
Special and Bonus Stages also return as does the hunt for the 7 Chaos Emeralds.  Special stages are entered by finding hidden Large Rings in the Acts and are reminiscent of Sonic CD's 3D special stages.  Collect all 7 for...?
All-in-all, gameplay is extremely solid.
Designed as the Sonic game we never got for the Sega Saturn, the game looks excellent for what it sets out to achieve.  The sprites are detailed and smooth.  Characters and enemies alike exhibit a certain charm in their expressions and movements, properly conveying attitude and feeling.  Take a look at the background of stages and you'll notice many small details that give the Zones life.  The sights are fantastic.
Any fan of the original games will be right at home.  Sounds are crisp and properly reflect games of the period during the release of the original Sonic trilogy.  Rings still make the same chime and item boxes and enemies make the same satisfying pop when jump on them.
The music is expertly composed by Tiago "Tee" Lopes whom is known for making video game music remixes.  I highly suggest you take a listen to his music
.  Remixes for remade stages are an amazing blend of old and new and the new stage's original songs are catchy.  Words cannot express the astounding music in this game.  Here's
.
This game has decent replay value.  Time trials mode is back, and allows you to instantly restart from the beginning of the stage at the press of a button, allowing you to make the most of speed-running practice.  Online leaderboards exist, so if that's your thing, you'll be able to compete with your friends and the world for the best time.
A competition mode also exists in the vein of Sonic 2 and 3, pitting you in a direct race against a second player, albeit, locally only.  And with 3 characters to play as, a large variety of stages, and seven Chaos Emeralds to collect, there's more than enough replay value to warrant the asking price of $19.99 USD.
Sonic Mania is an endearing trip to what made Sonic good, hitting all the right notes.  It doesn't do everything it absolutely could to go beyond just being a great game, but being a great game is an important foundation in a faltering franchise.  Definitely recommend this game at it's full price, it's quite worth it.

This game is one of my all time favourites, I love the personal scale of it and the stories that are created. I expected a high-class strategy game and got that, but also to my delight a game that revolves around story-telling, not in a verbal way of course but you get to play through and influence important decisions all through the life of generations. This is what is most memorable to me in the end, and I´d like to share one such story.
It is a story of a ill-fated marriage, playing as the king of Sweden one of my vassals and a distant relative, the duke of Norrland, got children late in life but was blessed with twins that both turned out to be good leader material. The brother was kind and a natural leader of men, the sister was charismatic and intelligent though a little too good at lying for her own good and far more interested in women than men. As their father died and the brother inherited I felt content that I could look forward to a long life as king with my loyal young vassal supporting me from the north. To further influence him I helped him secure a marriage with a good norwegian girl in my court, thinking that she was also kind and seemed generally nice and they would be happy together. I settled back feeling like I had made a good move, but a couple of weeks later I got a message from my spymaster warning me that he had caught wind of  a plot against the duke. I investigated and found out that it was his twin sister that was plotting, that the dukes norwegian bride had become the sisters lover and joined in the plot, and everything seemed utterly messed up. I had little time to think about what to do about it for the duke was brutally murdered in his sleeps shortly thereafter. This made me pretty upset, and while the murderous wife escaped to her relatives I ordered the arrest of the newly crowned duchess of Norrland. I felt that seducing you brothers wife and getting her to murder him in his sleep is just too foul a thing to accept, and I felt obliged to execute her for her crimes. Justice had been done, bitter as it was, but then I noticed that the rest of my vassals were furious with me. Turns out it was a really unpopular thing to do, they thought me a tyrant for imprisoning and executing a duchess who also happened to be a relative without what they considered proven justification. This chain of events turned my long reign from a peaceful stable time to one of turmoil and constant rebellions from vassals, getting thousand of people killed in useless battles with malcontents.
Things didnt turn out well, but along the way I hade choices that could have influenced events. I could have been quicker to threaten/bribe the sister to perhaps prevent the murder, I could have accepted the murder after the fact and pretended I didn´t know the dark truth, or I could have settled for just imprisoning the duchess and not executing her, and so on. This is part of the greatness of this game, the way your choices really makes a difference.
I would also like to write about Berserker-Bjorn, the faroese chiefs only son who was named in order to invoke favour from the gods, and who later in life did indeed become a berserker and warrior of such epic ferocity that he personally killed upwards of a dozen french noble characters on the battlefield, and continued leading the charge at the age of 65 despite being maimed in battle in his thirties, and still killing young men in single combat with ease. His tale is too long for now though so I leave you with that.

I'm a Sonic fan. I hold no regrets of being one. My starting point being Sonic Advance 2, I have been adoring Sonic more than I adore Mario. While I still love the calmer and more accessible games that Mario puts out, I always play a Sonic game when given the chance because of the edgier and faster games he stars in. Sadly, especially since 2005, SEGA's been taking really awkward design choices as well as business practices regarding their blue hedgehog. I don't believe I have to mention the hilariously weird Shadow the Hedgehog game, as well as the flooringly cataclysmic Sonic 06.
This game is a stark reminder, that, before all that bullsh*t, Sonic was a name worth remembering. Sonic Mania wastes no time to get right into business, even the cutscene before the gameplay starts takes like 10 seconds flat. After that, it smacks you right in the face with Green Hill Zone's both nostalgic as well as modern remix, as if to say "I might be 26 years old, but I still got it!", and god f*cking damn it, it shows.
Each and every zone, regardless of being remixes or originals, are masterfully brought to life with the vivid color schemes, smooth animations, delicious sound effects, energetic and atmospheric music, and that classic, nostalgic Sonic feel that resonated with people the most in the rascally but still loveable porcupine's heyday of early 90s.
I can't pinpoint the exact reason why I keep coming back to this game more than I come back to Sonic CD. Maybe because it's a game that's made by fans, officially sanctioned and done in conjuction with SEGA and Sonic Team? Maybe because it keeps rewarding you with more goodies the more medals you get in the signpost stages? Maybe because it's an actually good Sonic game? The one that pretty much everyone in unanimously waited for admist the pleathora of painfully mediocre titles, overall mediocre experiences with occasionally solid moments, or straight up bad games that are better left ignored?
The answer would be "all of the above". Whenever I boot this game up, I feel like a little kid again, each and every second of this game is filled with care, love, and passion put into it, the same effort that was put into Sonic 1, 2, 3 and Knuckles, CD, and more. I simply can't hate this game even with Denuvo in it. I just can't.
Sonic Mania, despite the admittedly disrespectful DRM fiasco, is a great Sonic game, a great game period. Of course I wouldn't call it the "best Sonic game", nor would I call it "the best game ever", because that's a topic up for debate, considering how many diverse opinions this world of ours possesses.
Whether you pirate it, get it on other consoles, or buy this version, I strongly urge you to play this game. There's a little something for everyone here, Sonic fans, SEGA enthusiasts, 2D platformer aficionados, even for people who just want to play a good game and have fun with it.
Undoubtedly, this is a game I'll keep coming back to for weeks, months... probably even years on end. Even with its shortcomings, it's a great game overall, and I heavily recommend it.
My closing statement is this.
To Christian Whitehead, Headcannon, and Pagoda West... thank you for your efforts with this title. I'm looking forward to other projects you guys will partake in, Sonic-related or not.
To SEGA... well, thank you guys too for allowing this game to exist, but seriously, if you removed Denuvo from it, it would've been fantastic. I mean, it's good that you released an offline patch and all, but, y'know... eventual destruction of Denuvo-enabled games when the servers go down... that includes this game, too, so...
It's good to have you back, Sonic.
See you in Forces.

I started playing Audition in 2009. Over the years, I've probably spent over 6000 hours that's not recorded by Steam. This is to justify that I enjoy this game. There are many music, game modes and fashion to explore in this game.
Most of the music in game are not mainstream and you cannot use your personal library of music. There is a good range of music available. Some are only available in certain game modes. Besides English music, there are some Korean as this game originated from South Korea.

Besides the music and game modes, in game characters' fashion is one of the biggest highlight. You can dress your character by purchasing clothes from the mall with in game currency (earned from playing) or purchase in game cash.
Although Redbana Audition is based in the United States, it is opened to players worldwide.
I bonded many friendships through this game and shared my interest with other like minds.

I was fairly skeptical of this game at first, I'll admit. Now as control methods for games are important for myself, I've used three different ones: Xbox One Controller, KB/M, and (the strangest to most) X-52Pro HOTAS. I don't possess a wheel to play the game with but have friends that do that absolutely love it for this game. KB/M was extremely touchy for driving itself. The wheel either turns left/right or doesn't at all, and by turn I mean it's all the way right and all the way left. Xbox One Controller surprisingly works well and is fairly customizable. Combo key presses with the controller didn't work at the time of testing the xbox controller, so that was a bit of a con. My HOTAS though is what I majorily play the game with and absolutely love it. Gameplay for ATS is fairly straightforward. You're a new driver when you start off wanting to build a trucking company but have no truck of your own. You can do jobs for companies with their equipment (truck and trailer) to start to gain enough cash and experience till you can buy your own truck. Sadly there's only two brands of truck available in game: Peterbilt and Kenworth. I'd consider it a con that there's only two, but hope that there's a plan to introduce other available truck brands and designs to the game. Trailers are provided for all hauling jobs, so there's no worry over buying your own trailers.
Garages are upgradable to where you can hire more NPC drivers and purchase trucks for them to drive. Once the NPC is assigned to a garage and has a truck assigned for them to drive they do delivery jobs for you within their skillset, which can be trained up as they perform jobs. So higher trained drivers will bring in more money.
Other garages can be purchased in other cities to open up more NPC driver slots and assign more trucks. Garages can also be used as Quick Travel points for the player to move to different areas instantly.
Majority of the game otherwise is exactly what the game looks to be. You take a job from companies that need stuff transported from A to B. Once this is done you can search the local area of B for a new job or Quick Travel back to a Garage you own and find another job heading to the same place or somewhere else. Traffic is sometimes a total pain, much in reality, but generally a non-issue once you hit the major highways. The trucks drive and feel fairly realistic when operating. There's simple controls and advanced controls for trailers, meaning it can be as easy as backing up to the trailer and hitching it, or up to several steps before being able to drive off once you've backed up to it.
You can free roam with just your truck bobtailing around exploring areas, so there are definitely some sights to see within the game itself and plenty of achievement to hunt and 5 hidden achievements to find.

To start with - Divinity Original Sin 2 is probably the best turn based RPG game on the market and it's modernly wrapped.
I'm the kind of person that can sit for several hours in character creation, thinking if Rouge would be better than Warrior, but do I really want to play any of them? Fear not! DOS2 gives you free hand in your character's customisation. You can change almost everything in any given time on your ship - talents, skills, attributes and appearance, which is huge for me as I enjoy testing different builds and no need to worry that I'm gonna mess my playthrough.
As for companions - you can choose from 6 of them. You can set their skills however you like it. The only thing that matters are their quests (each hero has 1 quest related to them, which motivates them). You can either create your fresh character or play as 1 of these 6.
On the other hand talking about some flaws in here, I wish there was more Skills and Talents to choose from and they'd be better balanced. There's no balance at all in some skills right now, but don't worry, mods will probably fix it.
Also these bloody companions. You know, It can get messy after a combat - this burning, poison there, traps here, barrels there. They don't care. These ♥♥♥♥♥ are going to try to get to you no matter what and sadly going through this mess, you know how it ends, right? But sometimes, sometimes they're just afraid of everything and even a drop of poison or oil will stop the entire party following you. You'll have to get each one of them by hand and pass with them. Little bugs, sometimes annoying, not much to worry about, hilarious from time to time ;)
One of these aspects that makes Divinity the game it is. Environmental combat shines. Blowing up barrels, comboing your spells is what makes combat spectacular. Fights are challenging and tactical mind is desired. The terrain around them is very well made, you can take different approaches, heights and covers that benefit your team.
As for worse things here, I wish there was some kind of preparation phase, where you could split up your characters, because sometimes you just end up as a pile of 4 bodies waiting for a sweet fireball to wipe you all. Then cheese combat joining - if your character is too far or weird bugs when my characters just skips a turn (happened few time in scripted fights). Although combat is super fun, especially when played with friends.
Main story is solid. It has its slowdowns, but I'd say both writing and idea are on point. You'll encounter plenty of side quests, longer and shorter, more and less serious, many of them affecting your ending summary. They often feel unique and there's a great humour in the lesser ones (often Pet Pals). Quests can be finished in few different ways, often forcing its consequences, affecting your team and even other quests, which adds replayability to the game. Also some of them offer riddles to solve, fun and original, requiring a bit of thinking. The game does not hold your hand, either you figure a quest out yourself or pass it. Key words - Decisions does matter.
Can't think of any flaws here.
Honestly - as for isometric game DOS2 is beautiful. I even stopped few times to enjoy how good this game is. Everything is well planned and there's no contingency. As for audio - I have to say I fell in love with a soundtrack, sometimes I wish there was more tracks to listen to. Right now Main theme and Amber Ale are my favorites. They really did a great job to tribute Kirill Pokrovsky. Another awesome thing is that it's fully voice acted. At first I felt like a reading narrator is a cool addition to the game, but later on I noticed how much of a quality It added. Every voice actor did a great job here (animals especially :p). Well done! I wish more RPGs had a narrator (looking towards PoE).
A tiny flaw of everything voice acted might be npcs repeating their lines over and over when idle, mostly noticable when shopping or during long conversations (HEAR YE, HEAR YE)

Sometimes I pick up a game because I want to feel like a real badass. There’s something very special about becoming someone incredible, capable of great feats worthy of epic ballads and text book immortalization. Expeditions: Viking was one of those games for me. I went from being another little nobody, eating cold pizza at my desk to commanding a party of skilled raiders. I pillaged and I plundered and at the end of the day I felt like a hero. That is what gaming is all about.
You play as the son/daughter of a fallen Viking thane. Your father left for the British Isles, returning home as a corpse. Now it's up to you to restore your clan to its former glory and protect against the looming threat of invasion. As the title suggests, you must set out on an epic expedition to the same land where your father died. There you can either gain the loyalty of a ruling power, take over the entire island or simply pillage and plunder until your longboat is full of treasure. I was somewhat inclined to play as a power hungry brute, but decided instead to be tactful and responsible. That means I didn't raid any villages and tried my best to do no harm.
During my epic voyage I recruited a handful of highly specialized party members. These included a witch's apprentice, a burly thug, a noble warrior and steadfast childhood friend. In addition, players can round out their crew with some hired hands. This gives you the opportunity to create a few heroes of your own with stats that complement your chosen play style. I ended up leaving the docks with Cannon Fodders 1-4, all proud sons of Tazer Face.
While traveling your progress can be interrupted by a number of random events. For example, you might run into a group of bandits, triggering a fight, or you may come upon an omen. At one point in my quest I encountered a man erecting a Nithing pole and was given the option of helping or not. It was these events which gave the game some spice. It felt more realistic and broke up the samey business of exploration into memorable events.
One of the biggest problems I had with Expeditions: Viking was the camera configuration. The game takes place in a 3D world where the camera is aimed down at a 45 angle from somewhere around 3 stories high. The problem arises from the fact that the camera is rotatable. This can be nice because it allows the developers to flesh out the landscape organically and more true to life. The problem, however, is that from so high up it can become really difficult to locate certain locations, items and characters. For example, in one of the major cities I was supposed to find the local church. When I reached the quest marker I ended up running around in circles for several minutes because I couldn’t find the door. It sounds like a minor inconvenience, but when you’re trying to comb over large areas looking for small details, it becomes tedious and frustrating having to constantly swivel the camera. Games like Diablo and Age of Empires dealt with the shortcomings of such a camera angle by having its direction fixed. As a result, all the visual information players need is focused in one direction where it’s easily visible. Imagine driving down a main road and seeing all the store fronts facing traffic so their wares and signage are clearly visible. In Expeditions: Viking the disorganized (although realistic) landscape ended up hindering game play. I should be fighting enemies, not the camera.
The playstyle is turn based combat. I have to admit, I haven’t played many games in this genre, so I don’t know exactly which features are standard. However, even as a novice I felt like the combat system was intuitive and well designed. There are no complex menus to wade through and all functions can be completed easily with the mouse (although there are keyboard shortcuts for more advanced players). During a fight each side takes turns moving combatants and performing actions. Once your turn is over and the enemy starts moving there's nothing you can do to defend yourself so anticipating your enemies' moves is crucial to survival.
Expeditions: Viking labels itself as an RPG which it certainly lived up to. As mentioned before, there are many possible avenues to take during the story. What I really enjoyed, however, was the customization and growth of my party members' stats and abilities. Players aren't trapped in a specific class (i.e. archer, mage, paladin). Instead, experience points are invested into different weapon classes. As a result, characters can be masters of archery while also being skilled with a dagger in the event of close combat. This diversity within individual characters encouraged truly strategic gameplay. For example, pike-men could be placed behind swordsmen at choke points to maximum effectiveness, but as soon as the battle field opened up the characters were free to switch to higher damage swords. In addition to weapons proficiency, players can also invest in special abilities such as battle-cries which reduce the blocking proficiency of nearby enemies or even an auxiliary attack that requires no action points (basically a second turn). Beyond combat, experience points could also be allocated to survival skills that came in handy during camping and exploration.
Unfortunately, the game also plays with a very dangerous double edged sword. I am referring to its use of detailed animations. While it may seem enthralling at first to watch individual warriors string their bows, patch each other’s wounds and run into cover, after about 10 hours of gameplay it can become exceedingly tedious. In battles involving 10 or more enemies you’ll be wishing for a fast forward button. It just takes forever to watch every little action. Sure it’s nice to see what the AI is doing, but once you get the gist, it’s not necessary to sit through the last 6 seconds of animation. Of course 6 seconds doesn’t sounds like a lot of time, but add that up across 10 or more NPCs during 8 or more turns and you’re talking about a considerable amount of time. I appreciate the realism, but I also want to get on with it and bash some skulls.
Overall, Expeditions: Viking offers an decently engaging campaign made memorable by its in depth combat and exploration systems. Every battle (excluding chance encounters on the road) offered unique challenges. Each party member was highly customizable, allowing for virtually any play style while also developing as characters within the narrative. I would strongly recommend the game to anyone who enjoys strategy, turned based combat or vikings/viking culture in general.

Do you know that feeling? That special, rare feeling? It's a feeling that watching Breaking Bad gave me. That feeling that what you're watching (or in this case, playing) is something that you're not going to see anything like for a very long time once it's over. That it's cut from a very rare, valuable cloth and stitched together with the utmost care. Kentucky Route Zero gives me that feeling.
The more I see of Kentucky Route Zero the more in awe I am of the developers, Cardboard Computer. That this game was made by an impossibly small team of only 3 people blows my mind, but makes so much sense the more I think about it. The world of KR0 couldn't possibly be made by a large team, all throwing in more and more ideas, diluting the original vision. This game feels personal and intimate, but it's slow to reveal it's secrets.
Act 1 will see you through a mostly grounded-in-reality Kentucky backdrop, looking for an address to make one final delivery. Everything feels frozen in time, like it's caught both in the past and some weird version of the present at the same time. People you swear you just talked to will vanish out of sight when you look away for a second. Walls melt away as the lead character, Conway, lets his thoughts drift toward the Zero, a mythical road supposedly where your final delivery is to be made. Your sense of reality will all but fade by the time Act 2 closes, and seem like a distant memory once Act 3 is done with you.
Kentucky Route Zero is determined to drip with atmoshpere and mood each and every second you play it, and succeeds in spades. Music is very sparse and is usually a low humming ambiance. What little noise there is is generally droning static of caves, engines, and wind. Each act features a song by composer Ben Babbit, however, and all 3 are just beautiful. There's going to be a lot of talk of both the "Long Journey Home" and "Too Late To Love You" scenes.
The game is played entirely with the mouse, and is almost boringly simplistic in it's interactions. Pointing and clicking is literally all you will ever do, and I like it that way. There are no puzzles to impede progress, no quick time events. There aren't even any branching story choices, which again is something I like. You are given many many dialog choices, but they serve more as a way for you to choose which snapshots you want of each character and environment rather than a big story choice. Picking dialog in KR0 feels more like stitching together a screenplay or a poem.
Kentucky Route Zero is doing so much that I've never seen before in a video game, and it feels like the game is smarter than me. It's so dense and detailed, and 3 acts in it feels like we're just now getting a peek at the larger picture. Part of me hopes that once this sleepy, sad, hopeful journey is over that we won't have all the answers. That there will always be some mystery to the Zero. Considering what Cardboard Computer has delivered thus far, I think I an trust them to do just that.

Expeditions: Viking has many good things going for it, and some flaws which, while being minor, manage somehow to be incredibly annoying. Many other reviews have already stated the good things, so I will talk briefly about the flaws:
- The game is insanely slow. Not slow in a "hey, I'm thinking here" way. Slow in a "hey, I'm falling asleep here". Combat is marred by useless, mediocre, unskippable animations, you can't give orders to a character before the previous one has finished moving, everything feels very sluggish.
- Exploration is both slow and boring, with environments being infested with lootable barrels and crates which contain nothing interesting, apart from crafting materials. Which you kinda need, so it's click click click everywhere. In every alley, every corner, every house. Click click click. I wonder what the hell were the devs thinking when they designed the maps this way.
- There is a good deal of totally useless fetch quests: bring me three flowers, find six trees in the forest, and the like. No mark on the map for those, so you have to trek around to find things. Again, slow and boring. When I feel like walking around without direction I take a stroll 'round the city park, which is equally boring but at least good for your health. I do not buy and play tactical RPGs for that.
So, that's it. Then, you could ask, why do I rate the game as recommended? Well, because the rest is good. Dialogues are good, combat mechanics are good, atmosphere is good, viking lore is fascinating. Overall, the game is a good purchase. But, if your gaming time is at a premium or you can't stand games having long boring streaks, you would be better served by going with more professionally made RPGs, like Pillars of Eternity.

This is an "okay" game. It really is. But I just can't recommend it.
It is deeply flawed. No ultra major glitches as some reviewers have reported, but pesky small bugs all the time, and they start building up on your nerves until you feel like you can't take it anymore. You can't loot occupied camps after you kill the occupiers. You hardly loot at all in this game and it is seldom worth it. It is heavily combat oriented, so a diplomatic approach seems unfeasible. Combat, however, is pretty straightforward and simple. Very little skills to use and, those available, can hardly make any difference at all.
It is unbelievably easy, even in insane difficulty. You max your weapon-wielding skils very soon in the game, and you can also create "utility mules" for your group and focus your fighting characters on... fighting.
Crafting is... okay. But there are some unbalances as well. You can pretty much get the best gear available very soon, so that by the time you reach around one third of your gameplay you'll have all your characters maxed out. From that moment on, the game offers very little in the sense of accomplishment, rewards and evolving. Also, deconstructing a fur hide armor and use its salvages to build a sword feels stupid.
The storyline is what makes this game playable. Dialogues, overall, are interesting, the story is rich and "accurate" by today standards. The quests are a little bland, though. They consist almost entirely of "fetch quests", meaning "go there and pick up...", "go there and kill... and bring me back..." etc etc etc.
If you are not a seasoned player on the genre and might be thrilled with an average gaming experience, you could enjoy this title. If you are a seasoned player on the genre and has run out of options like I do, this might pass your time. If you have experience and haven't played other more famous CRPG games, I recommend you go elsewhere.

Hasn't aged well at all. Stale.
This is an update to a 1997 game, which a) makes it
work on current systems, b) gives it a modern, usable menu and, most importantly, c) modern controls. Seriously, grab the old one somewhere (or the original Duke Nukem, it's the same engine) and try to play it. Do some typical maneuvres like a quick 180-turn or a strafe-jump. Pan the camera upwards, notice the distorted perspective. You'll feel the difference. FPS games have improved much in these 17, yes, SEVENTEEN years since its release (writing this in 2014). It's still a bit unstable, crashing on a quicksave sometimes, doesn't work in some resolutions, but generally serviceable.
But the humour, the one-liners and the blatant, silly racism is just so antiquated and cringeworthy today, Might have been funny back then, and might still be if you're 12. But I'm glad we moved past classifying this as actual entertainment.  For comparison, the original Duke Nukem is just as bad, but riffs on 80s action movies, so way less racism, way more machoism and sexism.
TLDR: play for research purposes only. Treat this as an excellent emulator of the original game, now a museum piece to be sampled and documented. Not played.

Sonic Mania is a 2d Sonic the Hedgehog title in which Sonic,Tails and Knuckles must blast through 12 Zones in order to stop the evil Dr.Eggman from using his newfound purple gem thingy for......well it's not really clear but I assume take over the world!
This game can best be described as a massive celebration of all things classic about sonic, as it features tonnes of old zones utterly reimagined and improved upon, alongside a couple of extra new Zones.
The old zones that have been ripped out of the old games generally take a lot of cues from their original counterparts, however the level design is completely new.
Green Hill Zone for example is no longer a small linear run to the end, it is now a massive area in which you have TONNES of routes to choose from and explore, much in a closer way to Sonic 3 & Knuckles.
In fact all of this games level design is utterly insane, with an extremely high level of complexity, every single zone has so many routes available to take it can honestly be a little overwhelming to some.
To add to the zone complexity also the game utilises the various shields that have been present in Sonic 3 in new and interesting ways in certain zones, for example the lightning shield will now attract to the magnets in Flying Battery, or the fire shield will destroy bridges in Green Hill. and the Bubble shield.....actually I don't think i've found anything interesting about that one tbh.
No new shields are added to this game sadly but, what is new is Sonic's drop-dash ability. This allows sonic to rev up in mid-jump to cause himself to spin dash off upon landing. when I first knew about this ability my initial thoughts were along the lines of "ehh I probably won't use this much".....I couldn't have been further from the truth. I use this new ability CONSTANTLY throughout, it's a fun and easy way to keep the flow moving in stages, no longer to I have to awkwardly stop to spindash. Now all I have to do it jump and blast off!
Of Course it's a lot weaker than the spindash so there's still utility in the spindash, so there are plenty of instances where I would elect to use that over this!
Tails and Knuckles don't really get many extra abilities on top of their movesets however. They are exactly as they were back in sonic 3 all those years ago.
"So are there any new power ups at all" you may ask, well not really. But the game does have the Combine Ring power up from Knuckles Chaotix return, which groups your rings up into larger clumps for easy retrieval!
The Chaos Emeralds also make a return here too folks, and are handled exactly as they were in Sonic 3. Within each Zone there are various Giant rings that you can find and  jump into, upon doing this you get warped to the Special Zone in which the gameplay style changes drastically!
These Special Zones are best described as a combination of all the Special Zones from Sonic 1-3, as you must chase down a UFO in a 3d plane like in Sonic CD all the while collecting blue spheres to increase your speed from Mach 1 up until 3 so you are able to catch up!
Within these stages are tonnes of rings too which are absolutely necessary to collect in order to successfully get the chaos emerald, as your rings serve to be a time limit, run outta time and you fail collecting the emerald and will need to try again a later time!
The Key to success here is focusing on collecting rings first and foremost, and then move on to learning each track and collect as many blue spheres as possible while trying to avoid obstacles and pits that lie in your way!
To put it bluntly I freaking adore these Special Stages, they are exceptionally fun to blast through, however the controls do take a little getting used to here, as your jumping also serves as the primary way to take tight corners. So first few times playing through the stages may give you trouble but once you adjust to things, these are fun as hell!
And yes, it goes without Saying that getting the Chaos Emeralds grant you the games good ending when playing as Sonic and also allow access to the True Final Boss as well as each of the characters Super Forms.
Though Sadly the True Final Boss can only be accessed as Sonic which is a shame. (The other characters can access the true final boss but only by special means and not as part of a normal run-through)
Aside from these Special Zones, Bonus Stages also make a reappearance in the form of Blue Spheres that are returning from Sonic 3. In these the objective hasn't been changed, grab all the blue spheres and ignore the red to clear the stage, if you are able to collect all the stages rings first then you will receive a perfect bonus!
Clearing these will reward you with Medallions, these come in either Gold or Silver depending on whether you "perfected" the stage or not and are what is used to get pretty much all of the games unlockables, such as extra moves and modes. Though it doesn't matter which medallion type you get so Gold is mainly for bragging rights!
Unfortunately the rewards you get can ONLY be accessed via no-save mode which while a little understandable I can see being rather saddening for some folk.
Graphically, everything here is bloody gorgeous to look at, with everything looking like it was ripped right out of the 32-bit era. The visuals on display here essentially would fit perfectly on the SEGA Saturn especially the Special Zones with that Low Poly character model!
There are also an absolute tonne of small touches that many Sonic fans would love to see too, Such as Sonic's goggles in the Tornado or Tails' headgear ripped right outta the Sonic OVA among many others that I won't spoil here.
On top of this the Soundtrack is without a doubt exceptional, all the classic zones tunes have been gloriously updated with all the new zone tunes fitting perfectly and feel right at home here.
The game itself however, while solid, is prone to a couple of bugs here and there, I have had audio glitches happen quite often, such as the music cutting out or the jumping sound effect getting replaced by the ring collecting sound. I even managed to glitch into the walls of a level twice, once of which forcing me to restart because I couldn’t get back out. These are pretty rare occurrences though and for the most part everything is stable.
Ultimately Sonic Mania is a classic Sonic fans dream game, with exceptional Art, Sound and Level Design with the only major gripe I have being the lack of new Zones in comparison to the old ones, but assuming this game is successful (which it damn well better be) I think it's safe to say a sequel with original content would be just around the corner!
Overall....Sonic Fan or not I HEAVILY recommend this game to everyone, the team has clearly put a lot of love and effort behind this game and have proven that they know just what makes these games tick!

Not to knock certain others which are also good. This game is thematically easy to adapt to. Naturally, things are in flux such as the density of NPCs and animals, the threat these represent, and how close they are to resources and the like. Still, it does not take much suspension of belief to become immersed in the game's environment.
The development team reacts to the ideas from the mod community rather well. I've seen multiple popular mods absorbed into the core game. I've seen additions to server and admin tools based on things the mod community is doing and suggestions made to them.
It is clear that the development team is large enough to both add to the game, as well as clean up the sawdust from having made the game, presenting a relatively polished Alpha experience.
Comparing this game to others in the genre clearly sees it matched with sister games like ARK: Survival Evolved and Rust, whom I expect this game has learned a great deal from.
The ability to build is rapidly becoming increasingly and satisfyingly complex offering greater and greater potential for some truly engaging environments to protect and even role-play within.
The combat still needs work and the dev team is actively doing so as I write this.
The ability to climb is an important thematic element to the setting and adds an important dimension to the game.
With the coming additions to the game, such as sorcery, mounts, and loads more buildable items I feel you will find what is already a strong contender vying convincingly for the position of the best survival sandbox game.

So, after playing it for about 4 hours and completing it (not 100%), I can finally write a proper review of it.
Quick note, I have not played any of the console versions of this.
What you see is what you get basically. It feels like the older Mega Drive games, both in feel and look. All levels are very well made and really fun to play. I enjoyed every single stage I played, except Flying Battery. Not sure what happened when making those, but those levels felt really bad with cheap deaths and overall bad level design. The boss for Flying Battery is also very questionable, as the hitbox for it almost feels bugged. The rest of the stages felt amazing though.
There were also a few minor things, like I felt like the Tails AI was really off and not at all like in the older games. Not sure if that's just me. Other than that though, it's great.
The special stages as well are really fun and challenging. There were a few times where I was unsure if a wall was something I could jump over or if I would just bump into it, but other than that it was fine. I don't really like the Sonic 3 bonus stages, but those are completely optional at least and doesn't really add anything, so that's nice at least.
Yea, almost thought something was wrong with my computer until I read that it's an actual issue.
Other than that odd issue, the controls are fine, but that's it. There were a lot of times where I felt like I didn't do anything wrong, but the controls were just against me. It's fairly minor though and might be because there's no proper controller support.
The soundtrack is just really awesome and fits the game really nicely. The remixes are great and the new tracks are awesome. The boss themes are also just perfect.
This is what really bothers me honestly. The 2 weeks the game was delayed was obviously not for optimization of the PC port, but the implementation of the DRM everyone seems to love to complain about. If it really was for optimization, then there would at least be proper controller support or an unlocked framerate...
So, overall, other than a few minor issues, this game is awesome. What you see is what you get, classic Sonic gameplay with awesome music, just like back in the day.
I'll try to update the if the issues gets fixed.

The Inner world takes place in Asposia, an inverted world of kind with the air and light being brought in by Wind Fountain and Fosfos's respectfully. In this new world we meet Robert, the adopted son of the Wind Monk to the last remaining Wind Fountain. In this world, the Basylians, wind gods, are angry with the people of Asposia and have begun to rampage and turn people into stone. Conroy, the last active wind monk, is the pope like figure in control over all of Asposia trying to save the people of this world by pleasing the Basylians to not turn the citezens into stone.  The story starts off by Robert polishing Conroy's most precious medallion, a stray pidgeon appears and Robert befriends the pidgeon but shoo's the pidgeon away as Conroy finishes his speach. Robert fearful of Conroy hands him his medallion only for the medallion to get stolen by the pidgeon. Robert wanting to please Conroy chases after the pidgeon. This is where we meet Laura, the owner of the pidgeon and wanted by the state for a multitude of crime. Laura catches Robert trying to steal the pidgeon, which belongs to her, and she grabs the pidgeon, whos name is now known as Peck, and runs off. Thus beginning the story of The Inner World.
Throughout the rest of the game you will meet interesting new characters each with thier own set of witty and humorous dialoges as well as an immensive world with many secrets to behold. Robert, being sheltered all his life enters this world much like the player giving a shared viewpoint through Robert. Robert, a very shy and honest character, has a magnetic personality that I found myself easily attaching myself to. His interactions with the world around him create humor at every corner.
The humor in this game goes beyond character to character interactions, the game does not take itself seriously. In a later part of the game there is a cooking book called "Cooking for Posers by Gor Dun Ramsee", when I found this book I nearly fell to the floor laughing due to the call back to reality the game pulled on me. The world is filled with hints and nods to pop culture and the game itself is highly meta in its own rights.
While the story itself is nothing necessarily 'original' in story arc and plot points, the story is creative enough to work. The pacing of the story starts off very slow, but it gradually speeds up over time with some portions being slower than they should be. But the explosion of the storyline fits into the story arc of the game. Though the pacing fluxuated at certain points I was still enjoying the game due to the great story and the world of Asposia making me want more. The end of the story left me wanting more of this fantasy world that I fell in love with and I hope that in the future there could be a sequal or a storyline expansion to quench my thirst for more Asposia.
To add onto this amazing and humorous storyline and characters, the world itself is a beauty to look at. The animations are well crafted, though I did have some issues but that was only due to hardware problems, and it ties all of the story telling elements in to create an amazing fanasty world.
I highly enjoyed playing through this entire game and I would play through it again to find the parts of the side story that I missed in my first playthrough. My only complaint is the games issues with AMD GPU's but that can be fixed by installing Adobe AIR. All in all this game is a very well rounded with an incredible story with meta humor splurged throughout the extraordinary world that is Asposia.

The inner world.
A game that has reminded me of one of my favourite gaming genres of all time. The point and click.
It is hard to find a game nowadays with quite as much charm as the PaC genre did. Characters were often very quirky and memorable, puzzles were often (OFTEN) quite logical and made you think about how your character would think around in the world. The enviroments were stunning and mystifing, and the music was very atmospheric.
The inner world, is no exception.
The hand drawn animations, may turn some people off, as it isnt utulising the hardware, and making the best possible visuals, but the art style is something that i have not seen before, and it fits the world around it like a glove.
The puzzles, while did have some symptoms of adventure game logic, still managed to appear solvable by anyone because everything you need is in the area. Only pixel hunt that i managed to find is an object, which is shown falling during a cutscene. If you still have trouble with a puzzle, the game offers a great hint system, which can either A: give you slight hints, to point you in the direction of what you are supposed to do, or after a fair number of these, B: Flat out give you the answer.
The characters in the world are very quirky, silly, and each have their own unique traits that make themselves memorable. You will find yourself getting the achievement "Blabbermouth" (talk to each NPC at least once) fairly easily. The characters, whilst not having a sweeping backstory which tells a vast ammount of detail to give the characters intresting stories, still manages to achieve this in the designs, and the dialoge. (Best example would be the barmaid, who can be seen in the second screenshot, is against the gods of the game, and sins often.)
The music is where the game becomes a bit weaker for me. Most of the tracks are fitting and add a lot to the atmosphere. However, there is nothing here that i would probably listen to outside of the game. However, the music is very charming and creative, like the rest of the game.
The story is also, a bit weaker than what i would have hoped. However, again it fits the world, the art style, and the gameplay well. For this i cant condemm it much further than i wish it were deeper behind the motives behind the main antagonist, and wish that i could learn a bit more about the world through hidden objects in the enviroments.
Also, this game is hilarious at points. The game allowes you to do things out of order, and not have the right answer straight away. For example, in most PaC, there is a solution, you need item X. To get item X, you combine X and Y, and use it on Z. In the Inner world, you combine X and Y, use it on story progresson before using it on Z, and you get a humerous clip showing what would happen. This is what most of the achievements in the game are for. The characters often have funny things to say, and the reactions that some characters have made me burst out laughing. "please, stop crying..."
"I CAN CRY WHENEVER I WANT! ):<"
Ah, PaCs. Wish there were more of these. The inner world, reminded me of how good they are. If you have never played a PaC before, i implore you to pick this up. Don't try and play some of the old PaCs before this. They are still great, in every sence of the word, and some are better than this, but a modern gamer will be very confuzed, as there is a massive mind shift between traditional games today, and that of the past 2 decades. The game puts you in a role of a philosopher responsible of challenging the greek gods. You gather the crowd of people with different roles and try to eliminate the enemies. The levels are split into rooms (think Binding of Isaac) with vendors in-between. At the end of every level, there’s a boss encounter. The gameplay is pretty simple: you move your main character (philosopher) with WASD and show where the crowd should move (or what to do) with your mouse. Essentially, you can issue 2 commands to the crowd: attack (damage enemies) or defend (preventing enemy burst-damage attacks). There are also 4 types of special items which you need to find first before using.
In case you love to micromanage stuff, I’d skip this game. Otherwise – I definitely think you’ll have fun playing it. The game is very unlock-based, meaning that it’s pretty easy to complete, but hard to unlock everything (you’ll need lots of walkthroughs and grinding in a good way).

I really don't have the words to express how much I love this game, on so many different levels. For one, I'm a sucker for beautiful visuals and ambience, which is exactly what this game delivers. It is, on the surface, a simple point-and-click adventure in which you navigate from one set piece to another. But that is where the writing of the game comes in, and why I fell head-over-heels for this game. As with so many popular titles these days, the story leans more towards ambiguity and 'draw your own conclusion' than straightforward storytelling; the game manages to create a visually-captivating world that is similar yet very different from our own, but I never felt like I was simply going from one batch of symbolism to the next. I didn't always quite understand all the events in the game, but before long I was immersed in the world and deeply attached to these characters, of whom I felt we knew so much with only a few words.
That brings me to another awesome point to the game which, for personal reasons, is so important to me. One of the two main characters of the game, whom you alternate in controlling, is a hispanic woman. I know that seems like a silly detail, but think about it: what other game character, much less protagonist, can you name that fits that description? Yet the game never felt heavy-handed or like it was trying to shove things in your face, going "See? See? Isn't this thing we did here awesome? Aren't we awesome for doing it?" All of the things it does right (of which there are many) are subtle details, inter-woven into the story in a way that just serves to enhance the entire experience.
Plus, you get to make choices. Not big, world-changing moral choices, ala Fable series. More along the line of what Telltale Games have been doing: little choices in action and dialogue, things that truly make you feel as if you're in control of the character. If you consider yourself someone who enjoys narratives, want a unique and interesting experience, or are just looking to pass the time with something engaging, then I highly recommend this game. Hell, I recommend it even if you don't fall into any of those categories! Missing this game is just doing a disservice to yourself.

For those who have not previously come upon it, Kentucky Route Zero is a five part point and click/text adventure hybrid described by its creators as a "magical realist adventure game about a secret highway in the caves beneath Kentucky, and the mysterious folks who travel it."
I often find Kentucky Route Zero a difficult game to describe. The narrative follows the final delivery of a driver whose company is undergoing financial difficulty, as he seeks out 5 Doogwood Drive, an address that isn't on Conway's maps. Stopping for directions, Conway is told that it can be found on the other side of the Zero, a mysterious underground highway that the game derives its name from. As a vague plot synopsis, that probably isn't immediately appealing, and yet Kentucky Route Zero manages to be one of the most engaging and interesting gaming experiences I've ever had.
Gameplay is a juxtaposed combination of traditional style point and click adventure mechanics in 3D scenes for key areas, and evocative text only sequences, punctuated by an exploration oriented "driving" interface represented as a stylised overhead map.
The choices the game presents you with rarely offer alternate outcomes. In contrast to more traditional point and click adventures, where progressing is a matter of chosing the correct dialogue options or performing the correct tasks, KR0 opts for a far more subtle and resonating style in which your choices define the tone of the game and the attitudes of its characters in response to the situations and predicaments they encounter. In some ways, it feels as though the player's actions control a shifting lens through which subsequent revelations are seen - an understated, yet powerful mechanic that somehow makes the player's actions feel more real and meaningful than one would usually find.
The characters in and around the Zero feel deep and rich. Even characters whose appearances seem bit parts carry a sense of life and believability. As the game progresses, Conway attracts a party of companions who join his search for 5 Dogwood Drive, each with their own outlooks and energies, motivations and troubles. Each new character shifts the dynamics of character exposition, bringing new aspects of familiar faces into relief with the flashlight of their own perspectives.
Visually, Kentucky Route Zero offers a deceptively simple style, and at first glance could be mistaken for 2D vector work. Instead, KR0's point and click scenes are entirely 3D, combining some great set design, fantastic lighting and some nice camera work with dynamic effects that work to enhance and support the game's aesthetics rather than define them (in particular, there's a super neat bit with some trees towards the end of Act II that creates an opportunity for two pairs of characters' contrasting experiences and enthusiasm to be presented at once in a way that is both interesting and in some ways moving).
From a sound design perspective, the game is equally striking, with the already atmospheric visual and narrative tone boosted further by the kind of immersive soundscapes that tend to not be directly noticed until highlighted, but as soon as you're aware, you can't help but admire them.
Kentucky Route Zero is a masterful work of interactive storytelling that is executed astoundingly well. For those who already know this, here are



which are worth checking out if you haven't come across them already.
If you're undecided or would like to see more examples of this team's narrative work, Cardboard Computer have so far released two free standalone interludes,
, and
, which take place between Acts I and II, and Acts II and III respectively.
