Good: combat mechanics, world, Map layout
Neutral: Setting interpretations, quests, story, reused assets
Bad: Lore, game is a soapbox for the developers religious views, disrespect of the Viking culture, use of Viking terms with zero explanation as to what they are (enjoy using google) hindering actual game play, some quests have only one outcome with the illusion of choice
Game has enjoyable and tense combat set in great maps, but ultimately the bugs and blatant bigoted undertones of the developer make for an unpleasant experience.
To other reviews I'll predominately leave the discussions regarding game play and feature. The primary purpose of this review will be to discuss the games more obnoxious feature: It's a soapbox for the developers religious and cultural anthropologic views.
To quickly touch on what those concerned with issues relating to mechanics, yes the game is buggy and will lock up during long load times. There are some basic duh solutions that are omitted from quest lines because to quote the developers: You can't please everyone (in game). Several quests present the illusion of choice, but if you explore each chat branch you will discover there was only one path to go.
One of the first things you will notice is several decisions will impact people with certain personality traits that are assigned to that character. This mechanic drives how much a character likes you and how happy they are. You'll have no clue as to what character possesses what trait until you happen to notice them in the stats menu (which I did on my second run). Largely choices start make logical sense, be greedy and your greedy characters approve while you're altruistic characters do not, lie and you're cunning players will approve while you're honor characters will disaprove, and so on.
Over the course of the game you'll notice a few choices that are kind of biased in their implementation. Free slaves and you're open minded characters are happy for example. Despite viking culture having a rather well implemented system of slavery that included manners by which slaves freed themselves through combat or through hard labor (the game explains this). Compared to that of other cultures where your life ranged from being an object (Africa) to your status is at the whims of your master (Greece/Rome). A petty grievance that such a decision should benefit freedom minded or independent individuals rather than open minded, when being against slaver is obvious a predetermined possition and is by definition not open minded.
Little things like this will pervade the game. Everything paranormal is superstitious and myth. Vikings are portrayed as a backward people who didn't understand disease (they did) and believe it is curses (they separated the two in real life, though believed curses could bring disease). Sometimes this has a nice twist to it, such as in an earlier quest that lacked flushing out and made for little sense when taken in context of how it is presented.
This wouldn't amount to much, annoyances that are petty depending on the frequency as they are sometimes sparse and sometimes frequently, but always in your face and obnoxious. Then you'll reach a point in game where Sage that is either a play on Merlin or Odin will start appearing at your camps. The first time he'll begin going on about how Gods are merely manifestations of human consciousness, simply out of nowhere does this soapbox rant come. I'll not discuss the merits of this argument here, but understand this comes from a pivotal character, a man in the known, as apposed to the other characters whom believe in gods and appear dimwitted and ignorant on the matter (including the heads of religion).
At first you'll assume that this was just a one off cringe inducing Easter Egg or character, until he continues to manifest  and go on his rants. At this juncture I do not know how many there are in game, but I've encounter enough to make me want to quit as they do not seem to have end. The finest example as seen here:

Where the developers go into a cultural anthropological rant that one would be hard pressed to find many Viking scholars to be in agreement with. Again pressing home the developers views that vikings were merely backward and primitive people. You'll see this time and time again when your character marvels at great buildings of stone thinking they're fortresses when Vikings were not unfamiliar with large stone structures. This makes little sense in context of the game that they would consider the Isle's coasts undefended, but think every cathedral that dots the coast is a great fortress.
Worse the developer say that your names are forgotten to history in the title description despite it being a historic fact in 793 Vikings invaded and conquered a great portion of England (they're not forgotten either) and then did so a second time in 1066 when William the Conqueror declared himself King of England.
The game claims: Step into the pages of history: In a beautiful and visceral telling of the Nordic history. Yet the entire time Vikings are depicted as backward, primitive, dimwitted, ignorant, yet somehow progressive in gender roles in ways that erase their achievements in real life, and replaces it with trite female warriors whom still manage to be awesome, but it is sad that is the extent the game went. The extent that you'll step into history is the use of a lot of period correct (I assume) names and titles (albeit spelled in old English) that'll leave it very difficult for you the player to track what is going on at several instances during the game. Google will become your best friend as you try to figure out some of the settlement mechanics or names. Once you do it's a rather enjoyable experience except you'll lose a mountain of relation with the events when you are trying to track down another family that doesn't even go by the name in the quest or conversations.
When the bugs are fixed, it'll be up to you if you want to purchase the game. Combat is fun and even with the flaws (outside lore, story, developer rants) the game can be enjoyable. Personally though I regret getting it, but it's too late for a refund. Historic inaccuracies come with fiction but when the game serves more as a personal soapbox for the developers to make their own commentary on Viking culture, religion, and the nature of the world (get ready for a nurture vs nature argumen to be ranted at you in game for absolutely no contexual reason) there is little enjoy ability to be had. Not when it's subtle and then forced down your throat, so hard you'll gag.

In the world of Kentucky Route Zero, you never know what will happen next. That, and the unique, wildly imaginative presentastion, are the only two constants. It's wonderful, and unsettling. Brilliant, and confusing. Soothing, and depressing. Magical, and realistic.
And best of all, I still haven't seen the last two acts! Keep working, boys, and please do not stop until you're quite pleased with them! I will be patiently hungry in the meantime.

The controls are so close, but still feel very early access-y.
Add that on top of iffy hit boxes for enemies and platforms and it makes for potentially
very frustrating times.
Cameras are a bit frustrating too since you can only partially control them.
You can control zoom in/out, but not pan or pitch, which is horrible on certain levels.
Miss any platform and you fall into oblivion. So on levels where the camera stays low,
its almost impossible to see where the holes are.
As a result its difficult to see where exactly you are in relation to enemies and platform edges.
Some interactive objects, that you need in order to get to certain areas, like wind pillars that are supposed to lift you up, don't always work.  Several times I would finally manage to get into them without just falling out the other side (because the character doesn't slow down once in) instead of lifting me up, i slowly float down helplessly...then fall out the other side.
Its too bad because my kids love it too, but they can't enjoy it for long before getting upset because of all the above.
And normally they hand the controller to me if something is too difficult.  I wish it were just a matter of it being too
difficult, but it's not. The game is not difficult. It just needs to function consistently.
Id love to recommend this game because of how close it is to being done. But until the dev puts in the effort to polish out all the major glitches and hitboxes and bad camera, I can't recommend it. And that is a shame.
It should still be considered Early Access. the low price can't save it. It just needs to be tweaked and finished.
If that happens I will gladly change my review.

Quickly to the point:
Pros:
- awesome story without dull moments
- sense of urgency will keep you on your toes and always working towards your goals
- plot changes depending on your own agenda
- combat is quite complex and doesn't seem to suffer from the whims of RNG
- exploration is key, campaign map is huge and varied
- quests usually have more than one way of handing things and generally stick to shades of grey when it comes to morality of your actions
- your actions have impact on both the world around you and your team
- not sure how historically accurate the game is but it feels pretty solid
Cons:
- many, many bugs - haven't encountered a game-breaking one yet, but there's dozens of smaller ones
- long loading times, SSD is a must (fortunately the game is quite light)
- lack of ability to skip/speed up animations - they do get pretty repetitive
- random events seem to pull from a fairly limited pool making it very easy to see repeats
Conclusion:
One of the best RPGs I've played in the recent years. If you can get over the slightly janky technical side of things you'll find a real gem here.
Edit: Reviewing my review for Steam Awards, the game is still great!

Shadow Warrior is a classic game and the perfect successor to Duke3D. The enhancements to not only gameplay but also presentation are staggering and for the time, breath-taking. Shadow Warrior is a polished high speed run and gun chock full of action, fun and humor. The presentation is boasted by some of the most beautiful 2.5D graphics of the time with silky smooth animation and tons of effects like interactive environments and the ability to use vehicles.
The action is just as good as the graphics and style though, as stated it is high speed run and gun with a good variety of interesting weapons, most styled after ones used in kung-fu/asian flicks or tropes, enemies are intelligent and have a good variety and it never gets old, jumping and dodging enemy fire as you riddle them with dual UZI fire, or lurking in the shadows until you slice a hapless enemy in half, blood spraying everywhere. If you loved Duke, you'll take some time to adjust but you'll feel just at home, because everything about its gameplay has been sped up and polished.
I want to also point out something about the game to potential buyers.
While it has never been explicitly stated to be satire, I think it is evident that Shadow Warrior is parody/satire. Besides from the obvious goofiness of the game's story, names, wording and characters that play from tropes, the entire game itself is a running gag using all kinds of tropes or cliches and misconceptions.
The game is lampooning ridiculous stereotypes while at the same time making them strangely endearing (Lo-Wang) and just letting you have fun♥♥♥♥♥time. There is absolutely no spite, no toxicity, and no racism to be found in Shadow Warrior; only satire that is intelligent enough to be silly and crazy.

I gave this game a serious go, but I really can't recommend it in its current state.  If steam let me, I'd give it a meh, but the gorgeous visuals, beautiful world design, and neat building system can't make up for how much of a grinder this game is.
+ Gorgeous world and visuals
+ "Recruiting" Thralls adds a nice touch and helps bring life to the building aspect.
+ There are bits of lore scattered around the map and item descriptions which really help bring the dark world of Conan to life
+ Workshop support with some cool stuff.
= The combat is pretty ok, though hit detection with some weapons is pretty weird and you end up having to aim to the left and below your target to score solid hits in third person mode.
= Some weapons are only good for PvP or PvE.
= nudity is a setting
= Your general goal is to travel north.  That's about it on directions.  Finding everything you need is a bit more complex and involves exporing all parts of the map which aren't lethal to you.
= Uses a hunger and thirst system.  I'm not a big fan since it's so easy to stay fed and hydrated, which kind of defeats the point.
- Punishing difficulty.  I'm not talking "boo hoo git gud."  I'm saying the heat system makes half of the iron you need unreachable, and the other half is guarded by monsters and animals who are somewhat dangerous to fight with stone weapons and rags.   You will die a lot just from enemy ambushes.  I fought and barely survived three spiders at once, just to have two more spiders appear.  As I was fleeing, three hyenas decided to join in and cripple me with their attacks, which made me lose all the iron I had managed to reach.
- Massive grindfest.  I set my harvest multiplier to x10, crafting time to x0.1, and still felt like it was a massive grind to progress.  If the resource requirements are lowered by 80% so that I'm not constantly fighting encumberment to gather 4000 stone, it would be more enjoyable.  (Workshop mods can alleviate the weight and inventory restrictions)

Shadow Warrior Classic Redux is like Duke Nukem 3D: Same engine, same genre, same gameplay. What makes it different is that instead of playing as Duke Nukem, it's Lo Wang, and instead of aliens who came to Earth, it's the supernatural lackeys of Zilla. Classic Redux includes not only the main game but also it's expansions, Wanton Destruction and Twin Dragon. Only difference between the Expansions is that one ties up the loose end (with some reskinned enemies) from the main game while the other has Lo Wang go against his own brother.
Pros: As said, it comes with the expansions
Plays like Duke Nukem 3D, in a first-person mode where its just gunning down bad-guys
Good variety weapons, from fist and sword to rocket launcher and a severed demon (or orc? It is green.) head.
Cons: In some levels, you might get lost, wondering where to go to next.
The final bosses can be disappointing, especially if you are familiar with the way they fight.
Might offend some due to the Asian stereotypes (One of the enemies in the expansions can offend some due to how they look and/or sound).
If you are partial to FPS games, especially those similar to Doom and Duke Nukem 3D, Shadow Warrior can give you a bang for your buck.

As one of the first people to review this masterpiece, I'd love to say what an absolutely fantastic job Taxman, Stealth, and PagodaWest did on Mania. I've already played this game to absolute death on the Switch, but I pre-ordered the PC version months ago, and I'm ready to revisit the game already.
Sonic Mania is a true callback to the original quadrilogy of Sonic games on the Genesis, and in my opinion far surpassing them in both quality and gameplay itself. The game feels like it picks up where Sonic and Knuckles left off, with nothing but quality of life improvements everywhere as far as gameplay goes. Amazed at how my default tank could easily take his on, and how all the fast-paced projectile-based action felt like Quake on wheels, I easily caught on and was soon mastering my default tank. After beating him in a few rounds and scoring 12 in-game coins, I took to purchasing various parts and constructing my tank. A high-speed, light armoured creation with a devastating sniper and two laser guns attached to the turret. My friend had built a medium-armoured tank with a revolver. We had a few more duels and then more players started to show up. I took this as a challenge, and started racing across the map and singling them out and picking them off like wolf unleashed upon a flock of legless chickens. It felt great.
But my friend had to go, so I decided to face the horrors of the unknown, and ventured
into a public server…
Round one went alright, and I landed in 1st place. I had noted how few coins I'd accumulated from this massive victory, and how much faster and easier I'd gained points during the private death matches.
Round two followed suite and so did the third, but by now I had noticed a few bugs that had cost me many kills and caused me many deaths… The following being the most common: After I spawned, my tank seemed to behave as though it had just woken up after a twelve-year coma. It moved sluggishly, while refusing to fire any weapons of mass-destruction until I'd asked it nicely enough and apologised for swearing at it so brutally. Also, it seemed that some sniper rounds were being replaced by blanks. That, or  they'd decided they had places to be and just disappeared after leaving the barrel of my sniper. Maybe they were upset because I still hadn't used that "High-Power Scope" the game so frequently reminded me was attached to my gun… Or they were jealous because every other ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with one was content to sit around on the other side of the bloody solar system playing with themselves under the safety of a cloak and occasionally glancing through the "High-Powered Scope" In order to murder whichever unlucky sod had the misfortune of dropping their controller or taking their hands off of the keyboard in order to sneeze… Infact, everytime one of
snipers showed up, they would take the lead because no-one but me could be arsed to murder them right back…
So I shall conclude this with a few hints to whichever dev reads this… Balance that out. Cloaks should NOT be so effective and should have a very limited charge. Perhaps they recharge while moving. The same should go for Snipers. More movement = more power and it should become less powerful when camping. Because people should witness the fight first-hand, not through a damned scope from another planet in a different solar system…

A fantastic game that's pretty much murdered by the user interface. However, if you have time to learn, and the willingness to put up with the interface, this is certainly one of the more interesting of the Paradox titles. It's is certainly NOT the place to start your first grand strat game, and it is most definitly not a 'conquer the world' map painter, as Europa Universalis is mostly affectionatly known. The whole game is meant to produce a story as much as anything of the ups and many (painful) downs over the generations. Yes, it is going to f**k up your plans of empire building, repeatedly and seemingly at random; carefully groomed heirs will be killed off and your kingdom will fall to pieces before your eyes. It can hurt at times. But that's what you are signing up for.
What I can't defend is the awful GUI. Panels pop up obscuring each other, every action needs several extra clicks just to arrive at a screen finally telling you that you can't do that anyway. Those extra clicks add up over an hours plus play and it's almost hard to believe that any thought or lessons have been implemented from subsequent titles. There have been plenty of chances. Look at that impressive DLC list, couldn't one of those addressed some of the issues.
Very much a niche market game this. If you struggle long enough there's a good chance this will become your favourite, but don't rely on it.

Awesomenauts is a MOBA for people who don't like other MOBAs.  Instead of an overhead RTS view, the game is presented as a 2D sidescrolling platformer with a Saturday Morning Cartoon aesthetic. In this new age of videogames beomcing a realm more and more devoted to content and story, this one stands a testament to the ability of the gaming world to become a powerhouse in both creativity and a medium of expression. Rarely does one find a method of storytelling as intricate and articulate as this one, even within novels or written works, and here in Kentucky Route Zero I believe we have found a masterpiece in the art of world construction. Not only does it play off of the decisions one makes, but it also leaves room for the player to wonder what exactly they missed. The game, I feel, is not so much drawn on by what one does, but what one might have missed. A stunning work of creative non-ficiton in gaming form. Let there be more works like this to recreate the image of gaming at large, drawing the stereotype away from violence and chaotic, negative influences, and towards the infinite possibilities of both art creativity that game design creates.

Woodle tree adventure has (at this point) surpassed more then just my excpectations, right now it is safe to say "woodle tree adventure" is the best game I've ever played. This review will cover everything that you need to know about this amazing platformer puzzle action adventure rpg extraviganza of a game.
Gameplay
the gameplay is spectacular having a very well paced game, woodle runs like sonic yet jumps like rosalina's up-b in smash, this may seem like an odd combo but it works perfectly and I love it. The game controls fluently to the point where I thought I was the character in the game (its just that good) and the combat is just as great, with fast-paced action packed battles where you must use your leaf of the heavens to shatter your opponents while avoiding their attacks, all while watcing out for citizens, this is a mechanic I love as, the more citizens you hit the more woodle becomes devistated it truly makes you feel for the little tree
soundtrack
the soundtrack, which was created by David Wise and Nobuo Uematsu is a delight to the ears, the songs mostly consist of amazing piano works with some sax on the side. The music is heart warming, it can be light and then switch to a heazy blast in a matter of seconds, its truly spectacular. Plus the amazing guest artists such as earth wind and fire, ween and drake really brought some amazing pieces to the already amazing soundtrack.
difficulty
the game is very challenging however it is always making sure that it was your fault that you died never the games. Lag? theres none of that. Bad controls? nope. The game can be compared to the likes of darksouls however much harder. You are always rewarded for figureing those tuff parts of levels out and it makes you feel awesome. For example when you fight the first boss in the game, the minotaur, seems impossible until you realize you must climb the ladder of faith to reach his horns then perform a takedown. The games challenge is great.
Camera
for some odd reason this is complained about by many, and honestly I dont know why. The camera shows dinamic angles that make you feel good about yourself while not screwing with gameplay. Ill keep this paragraph short by saying the camera is great and y do ppl complain m8 XDDDDDDD!!!!!!111!!!11111!!!1

final verdict
woodle tree adventure is spectacular and shows a great side to gaming. Where games like street fighter V and CS GO failed to perform this game excelled. Woodle tree adventure is something you should all pick up, try to get it at full price so the devlopers can get supported to make a second entry in the franchise. Expeditions: Vikings is an annoying game, but one you can stick around for. If you like a nicely written story with likeable characters with their own interests and needs, this may be the game for you.
I'll start with the cons, since I think they need to be clear before you start:
1. Right now, this game is buggy. As in Ubisoft new release buggy. The game seems to cripple itself while processing what's going on. If the game seems to stop responding (as in you get the notification window), just click x and wait. It'll load.
2. The rules aren't always clear, and I've played both of these Expedition games: The biggest issue I have is LOS. sometimes, it seems like there's literally nothing in the way, or the cover should be made unusable by a factor. It's not big enough a deal to make the game unenjoyable, but it's worth noting.
3. The first three hours are overwhelming. Again. I played the other game, and I felt this both times. You're thrust into a miriad of skills where you simply don't know the value of anything. There are guides to overcome this, and it gets easier, but you've been warned.
4. This game is prone to dominant strategy, and you end up relying heavily on archers to get your work done. You don't - have - to, but it is much more effective.
5. loading screens. All the time. Even for things that don't seem like they need loading screens. And the game crashes on loading screens.
Now, I'll stop being a debbie downer - here's the good stuff. Remember, I'm recommending this game so in my opinion, I think these pros outweigh those cons:
1. The characters are actually really, really likeable. You will fall in love with Ketill, and you'll really appreciate Gunnarr. Guy's a bro, I swear. You even kinda get where the villain is coming from.
2. The campaign gameplay is interesting and fun. Travelling the maps feels cool! There's lots to do on each map and there are a lot of details on each map.
3. When the map is clear, the combat is entertaining. Think of it like turn based resource management - it's good stuff.
4. Story seems to be within reach, and you really can do what you want. Don't wanna kill anyone? Don't. wanna be a trader? Be a trader? Wanna be an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥? They have an achievement for that. Only people you need to answer to is your crew, and it's not hard to get them to like you if you're not a♥♥♥♥♥♥
Again, this game is very solid. I'll give it a true 8/10. It's fun enough to keep my interest for forty hours (a hundred over the series), if you let it you'll enjoy it too.

Expeditions: Viking is an immensely frustrating game. Not because it's bad, but because it could be so much better; if ever there was a game for a "thumb in the middle", this would be it.
It's got a boatload of different, interesting mechanics, but none of them really come together that well. The combat has a lot of depth and promise, but is marred by bad AI, frustrating bugs and a host of small issues. None of them are individually enough to make you give up on the game, but put together it's like having a speck of sand in your eye. You'll be more and more irritated until finally you can't take it anymore.
Many of these issues could be patched away, but as it stands right now I would recommend Expeditions: Viking only to those who know they can put up with a lot of niggling problems to enjoy a game that has a lot of personality and charm.

Gameplay video:
I've played both American Truck Simulator and European Truck Simulator 2 outside of VR and think they are both good games. However when you add in a VR headset and a steering wheel controller, it goes from good to fantastically immersive! You really feel like you're in the cab of a truck, especially if you use a steering wheel controller along with the VR headset.
One of the strong points of the game is the steam workshop. Fans have added their own mods that change the way the game runs, so you can customise it exactly to your liking. Fines too high? There's a mod to fix that! Traffic lights change too quick? There's a mod to fix that too! There are also fun mods, like the 10000HP engine I download and end up using in the gameplay video above. Completely unrealistic, but fun and challenging.
Overall, great game both in VR and out. I do strongly suggest trying it in VR if you have a headset lying around.

(As of writing this review, the game is still in early access, but despite this I still greatly enjoy the game.
I hope the devs make the combat more interesting before the final release though. Right now the enemy AI makes combat kind of bland, and it encourages cheesy tactics, such as sitting on rocks with spears. Enemies just feel like damage sponges that you repeatedly punch while they deliver a terribly predictable and constant stream of attacks. Archers are particularly annoying as they continuously stream arrows at you with pinpoint accuracy at every range, not changing their tactics or suffering any drawbacks within melee range.
Melee fights for me have devolved into tanking hits and slamming potions while my character swings wildly at everything in range. Staggering enemies with a shield doesn't seem to really be worth the effort, and there doesn't seem to be any benefit to playing a light and agile character. I think shield staggers need to be more rewarding, and I think enemies should be less resistance to melee staggering. I don't want fights to be easy in any way, but combat just isn't rewarding or challenging.
Also, the devs mentioned greatswords... where the hell are my greatswords? I'd also like different armor classes to be available early on to help encourage build diversity... and more things in general to encourage build diversity. Dark Souls spoils me there though. More customization options would be cool too, more hair, face shapes, different sliders? I dunno, I've been drinking.
Despite all of this, I'd still recommend the game. Its fun, it has potential, and the devs seem to have some great features planned. I mean, I don't care much for the combat at all but I still burned over a hundred hours on it which I don't regret.)

I absolutely LOVE this game, especially with the Game of Thrones mod. This is tied with Tales from the Borderlands for my all-time favorite video game and I can not list off enough good things to say about it.
For one, the best part of this game is that I get to live out my Game of Thrones fanatasies in a way that no other game has captured. I always love creating a character like me and making myself Robert Baratheon's trueborn son since I have black hair and then marrying my favorite character from A Game of Thrones, Margaery Tyrell. We always fall in love early because we have similar traits, have about three kids, and when I become king, I get to live out my dream, that I've had since I was a child, of being a good king, which is sadly impossilble in reality. I am a very charitable king and everyone loves me and I have a sexy queen (I have the biggest crush on Natalie Dormer). Everything is perfect when you marry Margaery, I highly suggest doing it. I can play a similar scenario where I marry Daenerys Targaryen and have to try my best to hide her from Robert, which can be awkward when the King finds out his son and heir married a traitor girl who's father was a tyrant and brother kidnapped and killed his true love. In this scenario, Robert turned out to be a complete tyrnat, had my mother, Cersei executed, and Lord Tywin, my grandfather imprisoned, and I was forced to rally a rebellion against my own father. It turned into a complete Civil War and right when I was about to win the war and fix the kingdom as king, a Northern Army came out of no where and I was slain by Eddard Stark in battle (who I'd befriended, which was sad, but him and Robert were likely closer friends) and this war eventually tore apart Westeros until the son of Daenerys and I took the throne to inherit a shattered kingdom with no parents alive to guide him (he turned out to be a tyrant as well, very similar to Joffrey, except named Steffon after my dead grandfather). Another scenario I like is to play as the Young Griff, Aegon Targaryen, win the Iron Throne through pure military conquest and marry Sansa Stark who immediately falls in love with you. There's something weird about marrying Sansa in this game because, I kid you not, we had ten kids in this scenario. It was getting really hard deciding names after a while and a lot of the middle children kind of got neglected, but everything was great, Aegon was a good king, and Westeros was made whole again. I even re-named the place that Aegon starts out in this scenario, Aegon's Landing, and gave it to my second son, Daeron who married his sister, Visenya. In another scenario, I played as Lord Corwen Baratheon and I was married to Baela Targaeryen and the two were in love. She was even nicknamed "the laughing dragon" because I assume the two made eachother laugh a lot. Anyways, Corwen's family had supported Rhaenyra in the Dance of Dragons who died and lost the war. King Aegon II's reign was terrible, he was a tyrant, and the High Septon started a rebellion against him. I joined the rebellion and I let Baela fight in the miliatary too since she had a dragon. In one battle, however, Baela and King Aegon's dragons met in battle and Baela was killed. However, the rebellion was successful, although, Aegon and his family survived and went into hiding, and the High Septon was given the honor of choosing a new King. He could've given one of Rhaenyra's children the crown, but instead, he decided to make Corwen the king since he'd lost his wife for the rebellion and the Baratheon line is related to the Targaryens. Baela and Corwen only had one son named Jasper and Corwen treasured the boy throughout his reign. King Corwen's reign was good, however, as soon as he was King, he had Aegon and his family excomunicated and spent the next five years hunting down members of Aegon's family and executing them for killing his wife. Finally, I captured the former King Aegon, the last member of his family, excomunicated, and one of the most satisfying feelings I've ever had was clicking that execute button for King Aegon, who'd killed my wife, Baela, and escaped capture many times.
I could go on with the stories this game has given me, but instead, I suggest you get this game for yourselves, and make some tales of your own. Just remember, Winter is Coming.
PS. Marry Margaery Tyrell. Seriously. She's the best wife in the game.

If you have never played a Heroes of Might and Magic game, shame on you.  This series spans back to my early childhood.    The Heroes game I played the most  was WOG, a custom expansion for HoM&M3.  I loved this series and logged countless hours into these games.  They are indepth yet easy to pick up, hard most of the time unless you are a seasond vet.
Build up your town.  Recruit Troops (this version allows upto 7th level units). Upgrade your buildings to get bounses, like resorces, spells, or your creature dwelling. In HoMM5 you can select from 2 differant upgrades for each creature type.  You have a army that is lead by your hero(s).  On the map you will be just one person, but if you attack a creature stack or another player the map closes in and you switch to battle.  This is simalar to RPGs where u wander around a map and you trigger combat then cut screen, there is your party ready to kick some butt.
This game allows may differant types of combonations with town faction/hero selection/creature types/pre-gen maps/campain.
New Features include the single player campain where you play as the orcs, and i think the 'caravans' are new to this expainsion.  Caravans can be selected where you hire creatures and there u selecet where you want your guys from and the caravans will farry you troops from creature dwellings or even other towns.
I must also point out this game does have some flaws.  First I mention the AI, to be honest the AI in heroes games has never been the best and this game is no exception. Many people claim that the normal setting is "Comp doesn't even try" (Yes they will even not capture resorce nodes, and be crippled by larger maps).  Also people claim the hard setting is "Comp Cheats way to much". Don't be upset, they are fan made mods that tweeks the AI so its more cunning and less cheating.  The random map generator built into the game is poor compaired to previous games.  Lack of teams is the biggest issuse, for multi player games.  If your playing single player the random map gen is fine. NOTE: the time for the computer to move on random maps seems to take extreamly long time even with a 'newer' computer.  YET AGAIN, fans of the Heroes games shine through as I have found 2 other random map gens, I've only used one and it worked great, but the comp lag remaind.
The best things I like about this game, caravans (YAY), the gfx (not the best but better then earlyer Heroes), the camera controals(feels natural, smooth when combined with arrow keys), balance (like most heroes games there is no horrid balance issuses), and the community (you will have to resort to the web for forums,)
Heroes games have a place in my heart and this one is no exception.

Okhlos is a rogue-like game developed by Coffee Powered Machine (yes please!) and published by Devolver Digital. The game is fully, 100% chaotic - you rampage through eight linear stages with your mob, looking to strike down the Gods of Greece
A majority of the environment is destructible and your mob consists of various characters such as citizens, warriors, defenders, slaves, and philosophers. The philosophers lead in this revolution against the Gods and if your philosophers die, the game ends
You control a philosopher and the mob separately, but the mob can only walk within a certain range of the philosopher. You can command the mob to come together, spread out, attack, and defend. It's a very clever idea for a rogue-like game and is definitely worth picking up!
However, the game suffers with tons of repetition, with eight stages means you'll become very familiar with these environments very quickly. If you're not hooked on the gameplay, the chaos and the Greek setting or history won't make up for it, sadly
Okhlos is a very fun, hectic game however it won't last long if you play it in long bursts or don't like rogue-like games such as this...

Okhlos, for a lack of better words, is essentially Pikmin set in ancient Greece.
Collect your red, green, blue and white pik-- I mean, minio-- oh, what the hell, HUMANS-- and go for a rampage. It's a simple and effective concept.
An irreverent take on historical figures in the description adds to the fun. Assuming, of course, that you know your Greco-Roman history and mythology well enough to know about the heroes in the game. The tone is completely non-serious, and tongue-in-cheek fun is always lurking around every description in the game.
The graphics are pseudo 8-bit 2.5D, which may or may not appeal to everyone, but in my opinion is well-suited for the game's style.
Sound work is fairly spot-on, with the music changing its tone to match how well you are progressing in the game. It becomes low and somewhat depressing when you aren't doing so well, and it becomes frantic and manic when you are rolling over everything. Demolishing 8-bit buildings has never been so satisfying until you've paired it with the sound of rolling thunder-- I mean, your horde of minions punching the crap out of olympians. Or giant bronze men. Or centaurs.
Despite all the positives, there are of course some things that are somewhat lacking in the game. With a hard limitation on how many minions you can take with you, one would think that dismissing unwanted minions would be a necessary thing to implement. Unfortunately, no such thing exists, and thus your only recourse is to try and kill off a chunk of your minions and hope that you get rid of only those that you don't want.
Verdict:
Graphics: 4/5
+ Appropriate style for a roguelike irreverent game that parodies almost all of classical history
+ Smooth; no lag even under the heaviest load of hundreds of minions all punching the crap out of the enemies
- 8-bit may not appeal to everyone
Audio: 3/5
+ Dynamic music reflects well on how your game is going, and helps to keep you pumped
- May get repetitive over time
Gameplay: 3/5
+ Simple to get into
+ Fun when you don't feel like doing something complicated
- May lack replay value. Levels are procedurally generated, but many of the enemies are simple recolours with stronger attacks or additional abilities.
Overall: 3.3/5 ** GOOD **
Simple fun, easy to get into - but possibly could be fleshed out a bit more. Lack of replayability a concern, but is inexpensive for what you get.

Some older reviews did not recommend the game due to bugs and the campaign timer. Since then a lot of bugs seem to have been fixed, as I haven't encountered any yet, and the campaign timer not only has a bar to show you the time but also can be disabled if you want. So for those reviews:
From what I've seen of the game so far I can say the overall world and scene is incredibly detailed with good depth. People have realistic problems, personalities, and reasons for
. No character is a generic "guard" or "merchant" - everyone has a name, which is certainly something.
Combat is turn based and, frankly, it's amazing. The mechanics work very well, options are extremely varied, and it's very accessible. You'll be able to pick it up very quickly and spend a bit more time mastering it as you encounter new enemies with different weapons and styles. Some people say it's too easy and that some abilities or combinations are OP. That may be true, but it does sort of feel like you're a fearsome raiding party catching people unawares, which often is the narrative case too.
It's not all about the combat, of course, and you can often diplomatically work your way through encounters. If not, you have the option of incapacitating people or killing them on a case-by-case basis during a fight.
Whatever you're doing there's always
, which actually do have a lasting impact on the game world. Your relationship with factions will go up or down, people will get injured or killed, and your companions will react differently based on their own personal moral codes. There are multiple endings based on your actions.
Negatively, there are some minor late game bugs - graphical and sound glitches mostly. Some late game dialogues glitch and people say weird things. I estimate I saw a total of about 8 glitches, all in the last quater of the game, but none stopped me playing or had a particular effect on the gameplay.
Overall the game has great story, mechanics, graphics, and world. RPG elements are abundant throughout with meaningful choices. If you like turn based combat, RPG's in general, or are facinated with the Viking/Norse lore, it's definitely worth picking up at
price, no need to wait for a sale to feel the value!

Half RPG, half turn-based combat with a huge amount of dialog and storyline. This will absorb you into the Viking way of life, keeping you busy choosing dialog responses and tweaking a bazillion options to improve your chances of final glory.
The scene is set in Denmark, 789 AD. You play as Hjalli, the chieftain of a village, whose father had previously mounted a failed expedition (raid!) to England and now you are planning to honour his memory by putting together a party and plan a new expedition. In order to do this, there is a seemingly endless series of quests to accomplish, which you pick up as you interact with the people you meet (and fight).
There is an overall timer (number of days) that you must keep an eye on. If you fail to mount your expedition before the timer runs out, you lose the game and have to start again. There have been many complaints about this - it doesn't allow you to casually explore - so the devs have implemented a feature to allow you to disable the timer, although this also means disabling achievements. Anyway, if you do manage to beat the timer, the game continues after you set sail. I haven't yet got this far though.
The general premise of the game is to complete quests which involve a LOT of dialog. Let me repeat that. A LOTTTT! You are constantly reading and selecting responses, and your choices can often improve or diminish your reputation, group morale and that sort of thing, so it's not like most games where you eventually just end up clicking stuff to move it on, you really have to pay attention and make the right choices. You can make peaceful or political decisions or you can go all-out and attack everyone in sight as soon as you clap eyes on them. This also "forces" you to pay attention to the storyline, which I am often guilty of ignoring in other games. It's an interesting story, and the devs obviously have some historical knowledge of the period because every now and then there's an interesting snippet of info. There's also a fair amount of humour, like this:
"...by far his outstanding feature, however, is his beard. It's the sort of beard you might expect to find adorning the face of a Jotunn. It looks like a bear crawled onto his chin and died."
One point I would like to note is that there is occasional bad language, including F-bombs. The writing is very good and this feels out of place, unnecessary and frankly a bit lazy. There are more imaginative and entertaining exclamations/insults that could be used, and I know the writers are capable of it, considering their excellent humour.
There are a ton of things to consider. Every detail of the game has multiple options and you can tweak anything and everything. There is a tongue-in-cheek reference to this in one of the dialogs: "This is the repairing menu. It may be the only simple menu in the game - savour it." Indeed!
However, playing the game feels easy because of the care and attention that has been given to guiding the player. For example, when camping, instead of manually setting every item, you can simply click auto-arrange. Great for new (and lazy) players. I suspect that the further you get into the game, the more necessary it will become to tweak things manually, once you get used to everything, but that's exactly the way it should be. Also, you only occasionally have to wander around looking for things (when a quest specifically requires searching for something). The rest of the time you can select one of your active quests and then you see a pointer to the next event, it's great, just follow the arrow, and you can check each quest to see which events are nearby to do them more efficiently.
I played the game for a bit and then took a two week break. Normally in this situation I would have to start a game again from the beginning to learn all the controls etc. but here, despite the complexity, I was able to jump right back in without any problem. Everything feels intuitive and natural, from spinning the camera angle with right-drag, to clicking the prominent taskbar icons to reveal the options. Great job.
While half of the game is following quests and chatting to people, the other half is turn-based combat which happens very frequently, in response to dialog events. The screen turns to hex-tiles and then you're in combat mode. I've played various turn-based-combat games such as Pit People, XCOM2, Loot Rascals etc. but for me this is the best I've seen. You must pay careful attention to the positioning of each and every one of your team, taking into consideration weapon types, cover, opportunity attacks (enemy gets a free hit if you move away), flanking and all sorts of other tactics. Most of your team carry both melee and ranged weapons, and you can switch them as needed. You really do have to think about your moves, but again, it comes naturally and never feels confusing. The fight always feels fair.
Winning battles usually gives you points that you can spend to upgrade your fighters' weapons, armour etc. but you don't always win. You can end up being defeated and your team sustaining injuries which will need to be tended to at the campsite. Your situation evolves all the time and you're constantly "putting out fires" like this and improving bits and pieces little by little.
The artwork is fabulous. There must be hundreds of people wandering around, and they all have distinctive appearances and individual Nordic names. The snow-covered environment really absorbs you into the story. However, my GTX550Ti (in between minimum and recommended spec) does struggle a bit, even on 'fastest' graphics setting. The most annoying thing about it is when you 'push' your mouse to the edges of the screen to look around, the slight lag causes it to go too far, making it hard to control and causing you to have to readjust multiple times. I would recommend a beefy graphics card to play this. It would be nice if it went to 1920x1200 too, but I'm stuck with 1080p and black borders. Oh, and more zoom please.
[SHORTENED FOR STEAM]
Frequent loading screens can take up to 90 seconds
Random snippets of voice acting. Good, but rare.
As I've said, the complexity is masked by brilliant guidance. The game inevitably gets harder as you progress, but you can choose for yourself when to let go of the auto-arrange and start tweaking things manually. Combat also has a lot to think about, but you quickly get used to it and start using the proper tactics. I've won a few battles and lost a few, which means the game is nicely balanced.
Lots to think about, intuitive tools and popup hints to deal with it all.
There are 40 achievements and I'm surprised to see the generally high rate of completion on the global achievements list because you do have to play for quite a long time to start picking them up. It just goes to show that people do love playing this.
Some trading cards and Steam Cloud (but no Linux support for me to use it with unfortunately).
The price may look fairly steep but there is a ton and a half of content here of epic proportions. A single playthrough will take many hours, and there's endless replay value as you can choose different dialog options and have a completely fresh and new game each time. I would even go so far as to say it's cheap at this price.
It's a long, epic adventure with loads of story, quests galore and the best turn-based combat I've seen. I really can't fault the content of it. It's a shame about the performance nuisances, but I'm getting a more powerful graphics card next week and hopefully this will address most of my issues.

As of now, 76 hours played. Why would someone play the game for so long when he actually does not recommend it? Well, let me try to explain.
This game is kind of a masterpiece.
Writing is excellent and the balance between text and action is ingenious. Thus you have just enough text to read to get emotionally invested in the story, yet not too much text to suppress the action. The balance is there and it is excellent.
The music...oh the music. I love the vocals, I love the instrumentals, I could listen to it all day long. The atmosphere it creates is incredible.
I am no historian, but to me it looks like this game, like it's predecessor, is fairly historically accurate. And I appreciate this. I learned a lot from Conquistador. Not so much in Viking, but it is above average in gaming industry in this aspect too.
So many things to do. I love that. You build a village, manage your hird, while trying to win in whatever way you like - be it trading, helping one of the nations or just conquering them all. You have to manage your resources. Amazing, really.
Characters. They are so real it is crazy. The writing is outstanding. I got attached to everyone in my hird and I would go to hell for every each one of them. Their personalities are so diverse and deep. Fairly often when you hear them talk to each other, you will feel like you know each other for years. The feeling of unity is there.
There were also philosophical moments. And I appreciate that greatly as I love when game makes me think about my believes.
So why the hell, you might ask, you do not recommend the game?! This reads like "Game of the Year", decade maybe.
That is true. Those I think about this game as one of the best turn-based, rpg and text-heavy game of all time. I do. And I do love this game. But I have problems with it as well. Quite big ones - maybe not for you, but for me they definitelly are.
Writing is probably the only thing I can't say a bad word about.
While the music is...just...the way it is, one of the best game music, the are PLETHORA of silent spaces. They are so frequent. And there are not many background noises to cover for that. I love music, but I hate silence. And there is a lot of silence.
While it is visible they were aiming for historical accuracy, there are a lot of things that does not make much sense. Like all the honey in the cold outside etc. But this is not that big of a deal.
What IS a big deal is that fighting for campsites does not let you loot the enemies! And boy you will kill about hundred of them during you playthrough just on those campsites.
Also I played beta. It was a final stage of beta just before release and during the beta, I reported more than 50 bugs. And now, patch 1.0.4? A LOT of those already-reported-during-beta bugs are NOT fixed. I get it, there are more important bugs. They have limited human resources. That is all fine. But this is full fledged release. None if this should concern you. It is not beta anymore, it is finished product. But the problem is - while it is finished, it is far from polished. And seeing the same bugs in final release like in beta just kills me. It really does.
I did a lot of savescumming during beta. I played on medium and yet it was fairly challenging. And it was at the end of the beta I finally realized how the combat mechanics works! After 40 hours! Now? I played it on insane with literally no problem. I have lost two fights. One was agains wolves that started to escape during the second turn. So there are like 7 or 8 enemies and you have two turns before they start to flee. WTF? Just how? And the second one I do not remember, but I know I lost. It is so easy. Medium in beta was more difficult than Insane in final game. And although there is no ironman right now, I played it like that.
In the middle of the second part of the game, you probably have your 6 characters geared out. And I mean they have THE BEST gear there is. After that point, the fights are FAR from challenging. You just do not care and rush them as they hit you for like 20-30 while you have no problem almost one shotting them. The fights become a chore at this point. They are just delaying the story.
SO. MANY. BUGS. It is insane.
And I could go on. In good things, but mainly in bad things. But I do not want to. Because part of me loves this game like no other. I have a hard time enjoying it though. I will try to play it again and I will try to record every single bug I encounter to help them fix this game for others to enjoy. Because everyone needs to play this game. It is that good.
Just...do not play it right now. It is still a beta no matter what the Steam store page says. Wait till it gets fixed. Then I would and will recommend it.

Expedition: Viking is a standalone follow up to the old Conquistador game this company made.
To me, this is more of a RPG game and less survival but a lot of the old parts are still here. It is a turnbased viking game with a skillpoint system rewarded for doing tasks or finding things instead of levels gained and experience. Which makes you able to do some interesting builds. It is very based around builds and combos you can do. A shield wall and spears behind, a berserker flanking? Witches throwing dust in peoples eyes or the very powerful archer? You can play it in many ways and build your character in many different ways. It often leads to combat but being social and talking can sometimes render you free of a fight or able to take down a powerful opponent before it can do anything to hurt you.

There is a TL;DR at the bottom, as this is a rather long review.
Divinity has been a thoroughly enjoyable game for me, in my first campaign. I played on classic difficulty (what would equate to normal) and had some challenges, mainly at the start of the game when I lacked skills or equipment and at the end of the game, during a couple of fights throughout act 4 and the final fight of the game. Classic difficulty was quite casual though, as I feel that the challenge to it was mainly due to my inexperience with the game.
I very much enjoyed the open maps within each act, even if they did get a lot smaller in acts 3 and 4. The world generally felt well populated and there was often always something to do on your first explore of the area. A lack of respawns did make exploring towards the end of each act a bit more boring as there was no risk to it, getting into a fight was part of the fun, to me at least. Though I can understand it was done this way to stop people grinding levels as if you kill pretty much everything you have to and do at least most side quests, you end up at the correct level at the end of the game. The final fight consisted of level
enemies, and I finished the game at level
.
Acts 1 and 2 felt the most fleshed out in terms of quests and things to do, while act 3 was over pretty quick, you can understand it from a story perspective.
Act 4 felt as if Larian Studios created it quickly. The map is small,
there are few quests and it feels almost as if the game is trying to rush you towards the end. There's also not a real risk of anything as you can literally save whenever you want with quicksaves. Are you in the middle of a conversation and want the best result? Quicksave, if you mess up, reload and retry! Same with combat. You can save mid turn in case something bad happens, you can reload and continue as normal.
This, however, is generally the only real gripe I have with the game. The game as a whole has kept me almost addicted and I have often found myself thinking about it outside of playing.
The storyline is well written and the game is mostly bug free, having only a few issues here and there that aren't really game breaking. Quests also tend not to hold your hand with where to go and what to do. It's up to the player to explore and experiment to get results. Or simply fire up Google and find a walkthrough, though I honestly wouldn't recommend doing that... Despite I did once, twice or a dozen times.
Combat is very enjoyable, the part of the game I enjoy most, in fact. It's turn based, almost DnD style combat. Each character takes it in turn to move, attack, heal or anything inbetween. You have a wide variety of classes, ranging from the usual types to more hybrid and unique types. Each class can match a playstyle and it is also encouraged for you to branch out, not sticking to a single type.
While your spells and abilities can affect your allies and enemies, they can also affect the world around them, to an extent. You can change the surface on the ground for a variety of effects (cover it in water, blood, fire, ice, etc.) and each different surface type has it's benefits and weaknesses.
There are 6 "origins" characters, premade characters each with their own backstory, personality, goals, ideals, etc. and while they are fairly fleshed out characters, you can also create your own if you feel the desire. At the same time, if you'd prefer a backstory of one of the origins characters, you can change how they look during the creation process. That being said, the character creation is rather lacking. Each race gets 2 body models (male and female) and a varying amount of face and hair choices, depending on the race and gender chosen. Humans have the most, even if they look bland and elves (
) tend to have the least. Here's hoping either the modding community or Larian themselves address this.
Game master mode (a different "game" to the main campaign) allows you to create your own campaign, making your own maps, characters, enemies and story as a whole, which can be as long or as short as you want. I'll be honest, I've not played with it properly, but I can assume the creative types will be able to spend hundreds, if not thousands of hours within this mode.
All in all, I have personally found this game to deliver on what I've wanted from an RPG in a long time. A good story, characters you can enjoy, a fantastic combat system and a beautiful world to explore. It could do with a bit more fleshing out, but I can only hope either DLC will help with that... Or game master mode will come into play for new player created campaigns to play.
TL;DR - game is good, combat is great, and for those that are into it, you can play as an undead lizard wizard who can talk to crabs.

Another brilliant Paradox Grand Strategy game by a company seemingly incapable of putting out a bad one. I have gotten hundreds and hundreds of hours of gameplay out of this game, and every expansion brings me back for another hundred more it seems. Once you go Paradox, other strategy games just feel...meh. If you like strategy games, Paradox makes the best, and CKII and Hearts of Iron are my favorite of the lot.
Pros: Deep levels of immersion, very complex but engaging mechanics, Paradox adds new dlc with meaningful content for years after a game is released (including a lot of free content), endless replayability, a very well served modding community, and building alternative timelines is pretty much always fun.
Cons: VERY steep learning curve for beginners (GREAT tutorials on Youtube though), with tooltips that aren't always very good at explaining things if you aren't already familiar with Paradox games, there are /so many/ dlc that it's quite expensive to buy them up front (Though whatever price it is during a Steam sale will be /worth it/).

Very simply put, Shadow Warrior was made for the fans of Duke Nukem, so if old-school shooters float your boat and you'd always bet on Duke, then Shadow Warrior might just be the stuff you need when most 'modern' shooters are little more than one long sequence of quick-time events and have a "2DEEP4U" plot to drive them.

I fell in love with this game as soon as I laid my eyes on the intro cutscene: so cute, so lovely, and so funny. Unfortunately my heart was broken not too long after.
The good: main character is lovable and a great vehicle for humor; great artwork; original, quirky setting; adorable critters with criminally too little screentime, like Peck, and the Gorfs have a welcome Adams-esque touch; the voicework solid and the music very nice, although the wind theme is oddly reminiscent of Oldboy's waltz (not complaining); the built-in hint system is extensive (luckily!).
The bad: I'd be hard pressed to name another recent adventure game so badly affected by moon logic: the gameplay hardly ever takes off, probably an attempt to squeeze length out of the assets. It's a mobile port, mostly workable, but leaving a room/location brings up a loading screen which is unbelievably slow, like the transitions in the UI. The story is functional at best, giving most characters some sort of motive, but is ultimately weak. Playing as Laura, in Chapter 2, she's just so whingy! The animations are far from smooth and the cutscenes often are lacking in detail. The translation, by virtue of being generally of good quality, makes the dozen or so non sequiturs stand out.
Recommended? tough call. On one side, it would have maybe worked better as a short animated film, for (too) much of my playing time I just wished I had watched a Let's Play instead. That's how miserable the puzzles made me.
OTOH these folks clearly have talent, and I'd like them to make more games.

A fantastic game that's pretty much murdered by the user interface. However, if you have time to learn, and the willingness to put up with the interface, this is certainly one of the more interesting of the Paradox titles. It's is certainly NOT the place to start your first grand strat game, and it is most definitly not a 'conquer the world' map painter, as Europa Universalis is mostly affectionatly known. The whole game is meant to produce a story as much as anything of the ups and many (painful) downs over the generations. Yes, it is going to f**k up your plans of empire building, repeatedly and seemingly at random; carefully groomed heirs will be killed off and your kingdom will fall to pieces before your eyes. It can hurt at times. But that's what you are signing up for.
What I can't defend is the awful GUI. Panels pop up obscuring each other, every action needs several extra clicks just to arrive at a screen finally telling you that you can't do that anyway. Those extra clicks add up over an hours plus play and it's almost hard to believe that any thought or lessons have been implemented from subsequent titles. There have been plenty of chances. Look at that impressive DLC list, couldn't one of those addressed some of the issues.
Very much a niche market game this. If you struggle long enough there's a good chance this will become your favourite, but don't rely on it.

I know I'm rather late to this radioactive party, but I've finally revisted the Zone.
For those not in the know, Stalker is an FPS dystopic horror that is known for its open world exploration, scary mutants, and almost-RPG aspects.  This is the logical sequel to the first game, Shadow of Chernobyl, but you don't really need to have played the first to enjoy this one.
Call of Pripyat is set in a post-Chernobyl disaster area, the Exclusion Zone or just "The Zone".  Although it's forbidden for anyone to enter, fortune-seeking scavengers known as "Stalkers" regularly find their way in to this cess pool of rust, mutants, and otherwordly death-traps known as "Anomolies".  They do this mostly to dig up "Artifacts", strange new types of matter that display all manner of bizarre and potentially useful phenomenon, which fetch a high price in the scientific, black, and black scientific markets.
The gameplay mechanics are a good blend of open-world scavenger hunts and solid shooter mechanics.  There are a wide variety of traditional weapons to use that often feature multiple ammo types, fire modes, and optional attachments.  One would think that with new Artifact-based tech, you might find more exotic weapons as well, but other than a slight exception toward the end-game, you won't find any gravity guns or psy-grenades here.
I say that this game is an almost-RPG simply due to the fact that, despite not having attributes or XP points, there is still a "grind" flow to the gameplay and a sort of character progression through acquiring gear, artifacts, and equipment upgrades.
There is a main mission to follow, which I found mostly uninspired, and a few side missions, which I found much more intriguing.  However, most of your time will be spent simply heading out to points of interests to dig up artifacts and scavenge useful or valuable items from the dead.  Then you will head back to safety when you need to take shelter from the intermittent deadly storms called "Emissions" and/or to sell your loot.  Rinse, repeat.  Fortunately, the game is full of interesting environments, fun shooting mechanics, and a variety of enemies that use a lot of different tactics and abilities to kill you.
As a fan of the original, I loved this game and in my first run through I racked up about 60 hours.  I found that most of this time was spent hoarding gear and supplies I'd never really use, however.  Where some missions were rather difficult (such as getting through the tunnel to Pripyat without losing anyone), I found that the endgame seemed almost an afterthought.  There was little reason to explore most of the areas in Pripyat, with only a handful of missions actually requring that you do so.  With a complete arsenal of fully upgraded armor, kitted out weapons, and thousands upon thousands of rounds of the best ammo, I found finishing the last few missions an absolute breeze.  Although this was a bit of a let down, I still enjoyed the experience overall and enjoyed how the ending elaborated on the outcome of many of my choices througout the side-missions.
There are a couple of important mods for this game now-a-days.  At a minimum I'd suggest getting Call of Pripyat: Complete, which overhauls the graphics and makes other great changes to the base game while still keeping it mostly similar to the original experience.
If you really want to ramp of the difficulty and immersion, there is also the Misery Mod, which puts an emphasis on harsh survival and is probably the most popular mod for the game.

Okhlos is a roguelike from Devolver Digital, the same guys who published Enter the Gungeon. The game's main selling point is its chaotic gameplay - you rampage through 8 linear stages with your mob, looking to strike down the gods of Greece. A lot of the environment is destructible, making the game enjoyable on a weird, primal level. Your mob consists of various characters - citizens, warriors, defenders, slaves, and philosophers. The philosophers lead in this revolution against the gods - if your philosophers die, it's all over. You control a philosopher and the mob separately, but the mob can only walk within a certain range of the philosopher. You can command the mob to come together, spread out, attack, and defend. There are power-ups to collect and carry (via slaves), and traps to avoid. It's an innovative idea for a roguelike and absolutely worth picking up if you're a fan of the genre. The only major flaw is the repetition: 8 stages means you'll become very familiar with these environments very quickly. If you're not hooked on the core gameplay, the chaos and the Greek setting won't make up for it.
Okhlos is a gem, but it's a gem that might get dull if you stare at it for too long. Strongly reccomend to any roguelike fan; cautiously reccomend to anyone who isn't instantly excited by gameplay footage.

PROS
- Fun casual rhythm game that doesn't take too long to learn as long as you stick with slower songs at first
- Provides challenge at faster/harder songs once you get used to easier ones
- Tutorial is not too long and effectively gives you the basics
- Lots of people to play with
- Nice community for the most part, friendly people
- Lots of rooms for newbies most of the time, and it's easy to make your own room if there isn't
- Lots of fun game modes (Club Dance is one of my favorites so far)
- Lots of songs (there are a lot of songs about sex and drugs, but there are good songs in there as well, and most of them are at least catchy)
CONS
- Graphics are blocky and outdated and cause slight lag at times (not that bad or even frequent, though, but it does affect gameplay)
- Getting beats is slow, and you can't get much if you don't have a lot, can't complete missions, or can't afford Bana Cash
- Some people did ban me from a room without explanation
- Missions pop up randomly and often have strange conditions (10 perfects or LESS) and show up even for beginners who couldn't do them
Overall, this game has been very fun so far despite its shortcomings. It needs a graphical update and a revamp of the missions system, but that's about it. If you like casual rhythm games, I would check this out.

As a fan of classic CRPG, the last few years have been good. But Divinity: Original Sin 2 stands out even among other great games in the genre.
The game is dense with content and production values. There is plenty of dialogue and it feels like your choices (in the side quests at least) matter. I can't think of many other games that pull that off with fully voiced NPCs. And the voice actors are good!
Quests are generally interesting and there are often several way that you can complete them. The pacing and ratio between combat, puzzles and interaction feels just right. Some of the battles can get lengthy, but Larian has been careful to not throw too many fights at you. Most fights are tied to one or another quest, so it never feels like the fights are dragging on.
Each of the pre-made companion NPCs have their own personality, background and story quest. Their quests are among the more interesting ones and span most of the length of the game. I found it easy to get attached to them.
They have removed a lot of the busywork associated with the genre. You can respec your entire party anytime past Act 1. The inventory carrying capacity is ample, and you can send everything you can't carry to your storage. There are plenty of waypoint teleports, which load instantaneously. You also have access to Teleporter Pyramids that you can plop down anywhere.
That's not to say that the game is without issues.
* Quite a few of the side quests are (at the time of release) bugged, and you may not be able to complete some of them.
* There are also a few other bugs, not related to the quest progress.
* Unlike the side and companion quests, the main quest is very linear and a bit less interesting.
* The UI has several issues. The worst ones for me: 1. When choosing quest rewards, you can only see current gear of one party member. 2. You can not see properties of the item you want to craft until it's crafted (which led to me not crafting much).
* The gear scaling is a bit too steep for my taste. It wasn't a big issue while leveling, but at the end I leveled up quicker than I geared up, and had to go searching for gear because I felt underpowered.
* There is still some annoying busywork that they could have done away with. The health of characters isn't restored after combat, and you need to resurrect fallen comrades. You need to travel to a specific place to refill Source Points (the currency of the most powerful spells), which takes about 2 minutes with the use of Teleporter Pyramids. These things don't contribute anything and only slow the game down.
Despite these flaws, I would still strongly recommend D:OS2 to any CRPG fan. Larian has modernized the genre and turn based RPG combat, and made it approachable to newcomers without dumbing down.

At one point of Fallen Earth's lifespan it was truly a remarkable statement in an otherwise bland mix of MMO's. A massive open world with secrets not listed on the maps. And deadly creatures in every part of it. And the best part: No classes. You built your character EXACTLY how you wanted it, with almost no restrictions. The PvP aspect was mixed with several unique builds and players trying dozens of different ideas. The PvE had[well still has I suppose] hundreds, if not thousands, of quests to keep you occupied if that was your thing. Myself personally I enjoyed interacting with the market and just exploring the world. A truly open world with few restrictions.
Today it's a shell of it's former pride. What once had potential to be an astounding example of how MMO's should be quickly became an example of what not to do. The company 'supporting' Fallen Earth has pretty much given up on doing anything with the game. And bugs/glitches now run rampant with no proper team to fix them any longer. The market's gone ballistic with duplicated items and the difference between who has something in game and who doesn't makes the social divide in our world look like nothing.
I really wanted to believe, in the 7 years[as of writing] I had dedicated to this game, that the company supporting FE would've done something right. Kept telling myself it'll get better. But it seems all that GamersFirst can accomplish is letting a dying dog whine while it dies, and investing into products that aren't even half the quality this game was. It's honestly amazing this game company has stayed in the market for so damn long. But I guess stupid people will invest in stupid ideas, and a company of complete morons will continue 'developing' worthless products and letting them die once they've milked out every last dollar. I've seen better company response from EA when they were 'supporting' Star Wars Battlefront.
Welp enough of that rant. Whoever reads this probably won't care about all that info really. So let's get into the Pros and Cons:
Pros:
-Massive world
-Full control over character/class development. Build your class how you want to build it.[Ofc there's standard balances in place but overall the RPG builds you can accomplish here are pretty much limitless]
-Lots of quests. Though many can get repetitive but they have to compromise somewhere. A few thousand unique quests would take a lot of resources to accomplish.
-No Crafting limits. You see a shiny gun that someone else is donning you can build it. Every item besides microtransaction cosmetics are available to craft. It'll take time but the mounts/guns/armor/ etc etc. Can be assembled by you.
Cons:
-Lack Luster campaign. It's a vague story that just kind of throws you all over the place. But at the very least it explains character death and respawn in a moderately logical manner. So that's nice.
-Factions you can choose from in-game mean literally nothing in terms of useful items/gear in the end-game. Only reason to choose a side is for PvP purposes really. Or if you like the lore and RP for it.
-Community is almost non-existant.
-End-Game is a dead end. Besides the almost non-existant PvP community once you reach the end that's it!
-End-Game gear is a grind that's almost impossible due to a dead community. Acquiring the materials to build all the cool high end stuff is gonna cost you dearly. Or you're gonna spend hours on end acquiring it if you're lucky enough to find a few players willing to fight and gather the parts with you.
-No support from the main publishers. Something goes wrong you're SoL.
-Bugs and no pesticide to control them. There's bugs and glitches everywhere in the game and no developer in sight to fix it. Sorry kiddo~
And for now that's it. So as a final word thanks to the orignal developers who did make this game. They did a damn good job and I really respect them having worked with them since the alpha stages. But as of today the game is simply a waste of time.

One of the great retro FPSes, Shadow Warrior is somewhat similar in gameplay to Duke Nukem 3D. The game is definitely quite difficult, but the introduction of quicksaving and quickloading eases off the difficulty for newer players. Since much of the game's humor comes from he hilariously stereotypical protagonist Liu Wang, some players may find it racist, but it's all just in good fun. The game looks good for its time, and the sound assets are great.
Gameplay wise, the game plays great. The player can fight enemies with his fists, a katana, dual-weilding uzis, a rocket launcher with optional heat seeking missiles and even a nuke, a  heart that creates a clone of Liu Wang, and more. The stage design is usually a major strength in old FPSes, and Shadow Warrior is no exception. The huge, expansive stages are fun to explore and packed with secrets. Enemy variation is not the best, but there's definitely enough to keep the player entertained.
The port remains faithful to the original, but one of the new editions is a multiplayer mode. It works well, but I rarely use it. One of the multiplayer's greatest strengths is the ability to design stages and share them with full Steam Workshop Support.
It may not be as well known as Duke Nukem 3D or Doom, but it's definitely just as good. From veterans to new players alike, Shadow Warrior Classic Redux is a classic that's definitely still worth the price today.

Gameplay is... point&click-y, but what do you expect ? It's a point&click game, so are the puzzles, cuz they are puzzles imo, any good ? It'd say they fit nicely into the whole world that the game creates and are no push-over so they will pose a fair challenge. (not all of them, of course, but you get my "drift")
All in all it's a very pleasant game to sink a couple of hours into with likable/interesting characters, interesting world, fun dialogue, enjoyable puzzles (yes, enjoyable!). What more can I say ?
If the price tag is too much for you wait for a sale, but if you're into point&clicks games you, dear reader, should definitely check this one out.

Moving forward I'd have to say I'll likely play this game from time to time to play a few of my more favorite frames but theres little to no value to invest significantly more time into it since it's neither fun nor very rewarding since the only content I have left to unlock requires siginificantly boring or long playing and or is of poor quality (Atlas).
