NOTE: I've probably got around 200 hrs in Oblivion on my Xbox.
Ah, Oblivion. With the possible exception of Fallout: New Vegas, in the warm embrace of no other game have I ever spent more time. It's not that its gameplay is as refined as Skyrim's, or its role-playing as satisfying as Mass Effect's - it really boils down to the setting.
Let's face it: gaming is an escape. It accomplishes nothing constructive (apart from marginal enhancements to one's reflexes and cost-benefit analysis); it leaves no legacy apart from a few so-called "achievement" notices drifting forgotten upon the seas of cyberspace. No, it is but for a player to forget and enjoy.
There are many means by which games make themselves enjoyable. Some offer frantic fun, others head-scratching challenges, still others rich stories as though they were interactive books. But others, like Oblivion, can pull us into reverie through the game worlds themselves. The jungles, oceans, and savannahs of Far Cry; the bustling cities ripped from the past in Assassin's Creed; even the indefinable awe of Jade Empire's mythical China. But for me, none can be more eternally enchanting than the Cyrodiil of Oblivion. Trees and flowers, brooks and lakes, beaches and grasslands - from the snow-capped northern peaks to the brooding southern swamps and through all the pastoral forests in between, Cyrodiil never fails to enamor.
Make no mistake - Oblivion is a fine game in almost any sense. Its open exploration, dynamic combat, solid writing and voice acting, and let's not forget the flourishes of humor and grandiosity, work to meet the standards of all but the most demanding gamers. Granted, from this standpoint there are better RPGs, and certainly less flawed ones. If, however, you enjoy a game even that little bit more for its having an enjoyable setting for all of this action, Oblivion is for you.
Just be sure to have at least a half-decent video card if you want it to reach this potential - the engine isn't very streamlined. Enjoy!

As a former Dungeon Keeper and Fallout fan, overall, this is pretty cool. After reading previous reviews from old builds, it seems the game has come a long way. This is good for a game that has 2 developers. There are some balancing issues. I'll get to those later. Oddly enough, being a long time big RTS guy and hearing this was too easy, it was actually a challenge. Sandbox mode there was not 1 second where I wasn't clicking trying to keep my dwellers alive. So much so that I didn't have any time for a creative approach. One big open room with the essentials. Once I got there, I could slowly start building my vision of a well made vault. This was with aging turned off. With aging turned on, it was purely survival... no time for anything pretty except keeping your people alive. I don't care how good you are. This almost felt like "work", more than fun gameplay.
With over 20 hours on record so far, I know how to play the game how they've intended. It's not that complicated. So... balancing issues. Also, AI. A lot of them "slack off", won't do their jobs... won't go to the doctor when they should, get food when they should, or won't clean up garbage when they are just walking around. Clicking on the dweller themself, it often just says "walking", "lonely - going for a chat", "Slacking" etc. It's difficult to maintain a large population to account for all the people not actually doing their job. There's also not enough resources to account for the "glorious" looking vault you expect to create. Without serious diligence and changing around the settings (I only play Sandbox), your "vault" is going to look like unorganized crap trying to survive 50 cycles. Not very rewarding. Out of pure determination, I spent an entire Sunday and there's only enough resources (All 4 floors) to make one floor look like a serious vault. But I had to turn off aging.
I'm not sure where the improvements need to be made, but there's several nuances that if resolved, could result in a fantastic game rivaling Dungeon Keeper.
Personal thoughts: I wish the textures were a little less "cartoony" and the models a little less blocky. This is just pure immersion. Save the blocky models and low res textures for low quality graphic settings, and more Fallout looking realism for Ultra. Something to shoot for.
Also very sad there is no multiplayer feature - or at least co-op. I hear this won't ever be implemented. But it's fun to think about.
All that being said, great job for a team of 2! 20 hours of entertainment for 15$ isn't bad. Keep up the good work folks.
Update: Seems the game has started breaking. Filling in the last corner of the entire floor with a few farms and they are flashing no water and no power when several lines are running to it with plenty of power and water to spare. Oh well, it's been a fun run.

"Who-a want-a some-a Wang?"
I wanted Wang! Shadow Warrior is an old school FPS in the same vein as Duke Nukem 3D or Blood (without the fanbase of either unfortunately.) It is shorter than Duke Nukem 3D, but when it might fall short in length, it makes up for advanced actions (ladders, vehicles, turrets) and for being different. Yes, there is inspiration from Duke Nukem 3D and it's probably not AS good as Duke Nukem 3D, but it is different and doesn't feel like it's just a humongous expansion pack. While there isn't quite as many different enemies and the weapons aren't quite as unique as Duke Nukem 3D, they're all fun to use and don't get old. If any felt a little underwhelming, it might be the Riot Shotgun. I realize they had to nerf it a bit, but reloading after every 4 shots is a bit tedious. I would've prefered a different way of nerfing it. But it was still extremely useful. And all the other weapons feel just powerful enough. This game also gave birth to the ever popular Rail Gun. Yes, SW had a Rail Gun before Quake 2 even thought about it! The game (like Duke Nukem 3D) isn't that hard on normal or lower. It lets you just semi pay attention and just enjoy making your way through the level. But on hard or very hard, the game is down right challenging, even more than Duke Nukem 3D. On Very Hard it will push even the most Hardcore FPS players to their limits.
This is obviously the Classic Redux version of the game and for the sake of the review I played it through the redux version as opposed to Classic. And for the most part the package is pretty good. You're not getting quite as much content for your money as Duke Nukem 3D. As Duke is longer and has 3 expansions instead of just 2, but SWCR is definitely worth the $10 they're asking for it. And it has a few benefits over Duke 3D Megaton Edition. That being that there's an FOV option and you can play the expansions in classic. However besides that, SWCR is a bit inferior to DN3D:ME. For starters, Classic Redux is kind of buggy. I got 2 texture bugs during the Code of Honour Episode (forcing me to even replay a level one time) and I saw a few monsters on a level clipped into a wall where they couldn't fight back and just stood there as I shot away at them. I'm not sure if I was just unlucky or if these are common bugs. I really hope it isn't the latter. And theres also no multiplayer or workshop support. None of these personally bother me, but it would really just be nice to have them as bonuses. On the bright side though, these could easily be added within a single big update, so this con could easily be taken away in the near future.
The Classic Redux has another thing in common with Duke 3D: Megaton, where the expansions have also been remastered. SW has 2 so far and apparently a 3rd one trying to be brought back to life by some SW fans. The 2 expansions included are pretty good I guess. Wanton Destruction being a bit better, as it continues the story and features some new reskinned enemies. I personally don't think they're as different from the original game like Nuclear Winter or Duke Caribbean is to Duke 3D, but they are more original than Duke it out in D.C. for what it's worth. And like I said theres a 3rd expansion possibly on its way in the near future. I would love to see this even if it doesn't really add much new, it would just be fun to have more official content.
In the end, SWCR has a few features over DN3D:ME but also doesn't have multiplayer or workshop currently. However, the singleplayer is still flawless and if you're more lucky than me, there'll be nothing to stop you from enjoying this cult classic.

If you are looking for a faster pased version of World of Tanks, with more customizeability, this is it.
This game is extreemly well balanced, so don't be intimadated by the pay options. From the very start, even though they give you very basic parts, you have a fighting chance. With the beginning gun, you can knock out most enemys with a couple of direct hits.
There is a high skill ceiling though. Since there is no matchmaking that I am aware of, you might end up either joining a match and just get stomped or find an enjoyably evenly matched game.
Even after playing for a couple of matches you can unlock more interesting parts with in game currency. You earn this currency at the end of every match. Win or lose you will earn coins based on your performance, though you get a little more if you win.
There are a few issues that I have though.
All parts can be sold back, but no matter how expensive a part is, you are only refunded 1 coin. So if you grind out a few matches and finally unlock a part only to find you don't like how it works, you are SOL.
That brings me to my next complaint. There is no way to tell how a part will perform before you buy it. some parts sound very interesting, but they are not quite clear how they work. Like the parts that give you additional guns/turrets say that you cannot fire both at the same time, but I am still not sure how to manually switch between them(since they both seem to use the primary fire function).
Aside from wasting hard-earned coins on bad parts, I have had a fun time with this game and would caution you to research the parts before bying them.

So here's the deal. After the apocalypse, you're in charge of managing a bunch of humans underground. You have to keep an eye on a number of their needs such as their health, hunger, hygiene and fitness. You also have to monitor power, water, oxygen, ore and building supplies. You can also encounter creatures that will attack your humans on sight. To increase your population you have to incubate babies. To keep your bunker alive, you have to replace the people that die e.g. by old age, fighting creatures etc. Furthermore, when your people become old they 'retire'. The younger generation have to pick up their slack and it's a constant balance of trying to fill in for them and grow your population.
I only wish that there were more research options as it's pretty easy to have a scientist constantly working to rack up those reasearch points or scenarios as there are only three in the game.

Here is my full out review of Woodle Tree Adventures:
First off, what do you do in the game? You play as a little cute tree stump that walks around and picks up cherries and water drops. Not very hard to do, so the game keeps a casual style.
As for the actual visual appearance of the game, it is very fascinating. The graphics are cartoony, but still maintain a very beautiful and eye catching style! You can't find worlds that look like this in other games. The worlds themselves are very detailed, and unique from each other. They may be short, but you still have a lot to do.
In terms of unlockables, you can upgrade your leaf to have more range and power, as well as unlock a cool little headband that doesn't do anything but just generally looks cool on your head. Pretty fun extra feature!
The music is probably one of the best parts of the game. Its very beautiful, and suits the environments very well. It sticks in your head for a while and also has the tendency to really relax you and make you feel very good while you play the game.
And about the camera, it isn't really that big of a deal. The game is still very playable, and the camera is not a huge annoyance factor. I have no idea why people are complaining so much about it, I mean it could have been better but the game is still playable.
So overall, do I recommend the game? Definitely. Its such a good price for such a great game!
A good bit of entertainment, fairly addictive, but not much depth. Considering the price however, I would say this is a really solid game.

Below the short informative review video, you'll also find a written review, should you prefer reading to listening.
Gear Up tries to fit in the niche of shooters with huge customisation options, similarly to Loadout previously. Let’s find out if it succeeds. The art style invokes memories of micro machines, with the plastic look to your tanks as if they were toys on a playing field. The customisation works towards the same end here, allowing wacky choices of shark turrets, slimy goop instead of wheels, supporting wheels should you fall over or purely cosmetic nonsense like an umbrella. However, the art direction is not purely focused on aesthetic qualities. I personally really liked the precise colouring, clearly indicating friend or foe. On top of that, every tank detail on your own as well as the enemy’s, clearly displays what kind of upgrades are utilised, allowing you to adapt in your playstyle. Better not let the small running tank with huge flamethrowers come anywhere near you!
In terms of mechanics, the game gives you a whole bunch of fragments to play with in order to create the tank of your liking. If you are amongst the crowd using a pure free approach, your inventory space will soon run out though. You start with a total amount of eight slots and each time you level up, you’ll get another one. However, the level ups require an exponentially growing amount of experience. Therefore, while it takes only about two hours to reach level four, to reach level eight roughly ten to twelve hours of gameplay are required. Nonetheless, after that much time spent in a game, I feel that paying the measly amount of 10 dollars to unlock an unlimited amount of slots for vehicle parts is only fair game. Another 10 bucks on top unlocks all parts right from the get go. Overall, I would say that the model is fair enough, gives you plenty of breathing room to play around, test the game and evaluate if you would like to drop some money towards the game’s way.
The game is not without fault though. Games like these intrinsically have the problem that there is often a selection of ideal combinations. For example currently, there is a wide array of miniguns used, as it is an easy to use, fast-projectile weapon that barely requires you to aim properly. Now you could whine about it like a baby, or you could just man up, build something way more awesome like a tank shooting saw blades and haemorrhage the enemy out of the playing field. Why give in to what is quote unquote ideal, if you can do crazy nonsense and have way more fun alongside it! Who cares if you put out point one dps less? Your wife? Come on...
All in all, Gear Up is a fun arena shooter that could keep you occupied for several hours, especially if you bring some friends along with you. However it will require you to put some money into it after roughly ten to twelve hours of game time.

Pay no attention to negative reviews that are posted for any other reason than critiquing the quality of the game itself. Many of the recent negative reviews are a knee-jerk reaction by the pentulant portion of the gaming community in response to the publisher's pricing policies--which is not within the scope of reviewing a game's quality. This game is an excellent representation of medieval grand strategy with RPG elements. You have the choice of playing as nearly any character that existed from the early middle ages, through the high and late middle ages. If you are new to the series, I recommend you make use of the
; it will be your best resource for learning how to play the game. However, if I wanted to give this game the credit it deserves I would have to write a review far longer than this one. So to keep it brief: this game is a must have if you are a fan of the genre or similar genres.
If you are new to the genre: This is not an RTS. Think closer to Medieval 2: Total War but with far, far more depth and consideration for dynasty building but without the TW style battles. That is how I would describe this game to a new player who knows nothing about this particular genre--in as few words as possible. If this genre is even remotely "up your alley" then this game offer's a ton of content that will likely result in many many hours of engaging strategy, diplomatic intrigue, and meticulous character/dynasty building.

Another miss with this game is the lack of a life system. It felt like I was playing
more than a platforming game. On that same front, the respawn points were without precedent. You die from an enemy: back to the beginning of the stage. You fall off the map, you go back near where you fell. It was all over the place.
Despite all that, I still found
a little fun. For $0.59 on sale, it's worth a cheap thrill. At full price, I wouldn't touch it with the Deku Tree's stick.

How does one describe the greatest game ever made? is it the story? the world building? the game mechanics? the difficulty and responsibilities the game gives you to manage? the innumerable ways to play the game?  For all of those questions i would tell you to look no further than the Stalker franchise.  If ever a game was to be the flag ship of PC gaming THIS is the game that people should look at in reverence and awe.
Games of today hold your hand, coddle you and all but tube feed you because they dont trust you to anything intelligent  with their property....no mods, tutorials for everything and a streamlined experience so that nobody strays too far from the course like some sort of amusement park ride.  The Stalker games fly in the face of all of that and rewards you for being different and when everything that can go wrong does...finding your own way to survive in the Zone.
Finding secret stashes, managing your limited resources,  risking your life in Anomolies (elemental effects like acid, fire, wind and the like) and doing perilous quests that arent for the foolhardy.  You arent John Rambo and you dont run around with a fully automatic LMG shooting wildly like in most modern games. This game cements my love and facination with the true Survival Horror games like the original Resident Evil series before they started taking steroids.
You are just one man with fear in his heart, a deathgrip on your ♥♥♥♥♥♥ beaten up shotgun, a dream of seeing a rusted ship you call home and only a fistfull of shotgun shells to guide your way back in pitch black darkness.
This game is the most liberating feeling knowing that your life is in your hands and at any moment a mutant could two shot you from behind.....you live by the ability to stay level headed and just how many rounds you have left in your gun(s).   This game is my pride and joy please at least try playing it its well worth $20.

.
In summary then, especially for the price, it's definitely worth picking up at least for a try- I've no doubt you'd get your money's worth. It should work on just about any PC, and if you buy the 3 Pack you could guilt-trip some mates into playing with you!

Well I just clocked 666 hours on this game so I feel I'll use that as a milestone to do a review on this. I have played all parts of this game by now including the editor. The game it's self is a great concept and probably the best small scale battle sim out there when it comes to being somewhat physics based. I'm talking you don't just shoot a tank in the front a certain ammount of times to kill it. Actual tactical placement takes place here. Different ammunition and multiple Nations to choose from. Along with multiple campaigns and skirmish mode plus lan and online multiplayer, with multiple modes of skirmish and online catagories. Along with the game being semi realistic if you have the patients to get past the basic learning curve the game has and can bring your self to playing a different kind of squad based strategy game then it's great. I put this game on the so called "shelf" for about a year until I decided to give it another crack saying "it just isn't for me" and "the gas and ammo being a part of the game is really annoying" "too much micro managing" and "the graphics aren't the best" Also there's this thing called Direct Control where you basically press (E) and it allows you to take direct control of a certain unit making the game really dynamic in it's self. being able to shoot A.I directly and moving where you want to move is a great really fun option!!  You can access every units inventory meaning you can pick up items on the ground or out of vehicles to use or store in your selected units inventory or transfer to another unit or vehicle the ground or even into a dead units invetory. most crates are also accessible. Along with most buildings being destructible and or garrisionable. Craters make cover for men along with grass and blown over trees or rubble and or destroyed vehicles. Fixing vehicles is also a thing that can be done to not only your vehicles but the enemy ones as well.
When I tried the game out for a second time two MAJOR things saved it for me. The first being that the I realized this was a different type of strategy game, a game that requires realistic strategy, and has a combat system that is somewhat based off of what would happen in real life. Notice how I say "somewhat" yes tanks have some physical properties about them. Yes different rounds have different effects just like in real life. However this has it's limit just like in every other game so far. don't expect to buy this and be blown away by the amazing physical qualities. You can expect however that this game has a better and more realistic battle system for a strategy game then most others. Now the second thing that really takes the cake for saving this game not just for me but probably for most other people who play it aswell is the mod workshop!! I can not stress enough about how important the workshop is for this game. There are people who literally overhaul this entire game.The workshop adds everything you could possibly imagine for this game. Graphics, Guns, Skins, Missions, Campaigns hell even new nations! Making the base game entirely more interesting than it was.
I have played this game for so long it feels and because of the mod workshop alone is why I would recommend this game.
Pros:
Mod workshop!!
Great concept!
Direct control!
Moderate price! (I would wait for a sale to purchase)
Moderate community! (My review is really late the community is still there just not all the time as the game has aged since release.)
Probably the best or at least most fun battle sim startegy game out there in my opinion.

While playing FE, it truely does bring on the feeling of being in a post apocalyptic world. Not because the game is immersive and sucks you in, but due to the lack of a decent player base. 20-30 players online overnight and 50-75+ players at peak times. (US time)
"It's dead Jim"
Twice a week they have maintenance, and occasionally they will ban a few exploiters. But, that's as far as Gamers First gets involved. They are hoping some other company comes along and buys the game. The only reason they have the game is because it was a package deal when they bought APB.
There are no updates, improvements, or anything along those lines.
Regarding the exploiters: For some reason, GF fails to fix the issues, and the people they ban, just make new accounts (rerolls) and they continue to do what they do. So you get a jacked up economy in return. Mostly everything is way overpriced in the auction house. In retrospect, if you spend $10-$20 on credits and buy items from their online store to sell in game, you'll have more than enough currency(chips) to last until you quit or get bored. I was up to almost 90 million in chips before I decided to go crazy and buy whatever I wanted, all four of my toons have wardrobe unlocks, filled with various types of vehicles,costumes,ect...and my highest toon is only level 28.(55 is the highest level)
The game does have a decent crafting system, and this is where it pays to be a subscriber. Upon being a sub, your crafting Queue goes up to 20 slots, instead of 3 for freemiums (meaning they bought at least one item from the cash shop), and only 1 slot for f2p. But if crafting isn't your thing, then there really is no reason to sub.
PvP in FE is mainly at level 55. Ya, sure, you can ask someone for a duel before you reach that level, or go wonder into one of the pvp zones and hope someone shows up. Other than that, there's just not enough people leveling up to get in some proper pvp pre 55.
Leveling up can be achieved a few various ways. You can play the game normally, going town to town doing quests,killing mobs. You can craft, but I don't recommend this way to gain xp, very slow. Then there are a few spots that give good xp if your goal is to hit level 55 a.s.a.p. (plenty of guides on the net on where to go and what to kill)
There is no steap learning curve when it comes to FE,  that other reviewer is full of it. Or maybe I'm just to old to think there is one. You kill stuff, collect stuff, go from A to B, and then on to C.
Do I recommend you play this game? Well, if your playing on an old crappy pc such as I and your options are limited, or if your looking for something to do to kill some time, then sure, you may like the game enough to stick around.
If your pc is newer and far better, then I suggest you play many of the other newer games out there.

This top-down resource management/life simulator accomplishes its goal of appealing to the wish for godlike control over life that began with games like Spore, Civ and Dungeon Keeper. It is paced just right, allowing you to jump from super slow or even essentially turn-based all the way up to having years pass in minutes depending on what you want to accomplish. It is not for everyone, if you came looking for precision aiming and next-gen graphics then you're in the wrong place but if you enjoy arbitrary rules creating engaging strategy then enjoy your Life in Bunker.

The game is still in its early access phase, and it seems people don't realize that. For how new it still is (under a year), the game plays great! Is it perfect? Far from it, but the game is super fun and has a TON of potential. More than any other survival game on the market if you ask me.
Plus, with the recent delay (only a couple months), it just gives them more time to polish and add more features before the official launch. Not to mention the official launch won't be the end of support. You can expect to see this game supported for years.
If you like Ark, Rust, or any other survival games, give this one a shot hands down.

Great game if you can take things lightly. A really good, no-thinking-necessary party game with pure random goofiness.
Unfortunately, that is also the gargantuan issue with the game. Every roll is luck, and decks are shuffled together. That the odds of benefitting from using any kind of actual synergy are 1:4, so you can't realistically give yourself any kind of strategic advantage in singleplayer mode. Why is this a problem, you might ask?
Single player mode is always you vs 3 AI. No one is ever on your side, even during maps where your "team" has to stop a single enemy. Because card draws and dice rolls are all randomized, you have a rough 25% chance of winning any given map regardless of what you do.
...Is what I'd like to say, but that, too, is not the case. The game's difficulty setting, rather than making AI more intelligent (i.e. using teamwork against you, which they often do anyways), the game instead adds a modifier to all dice rolls, making your already fairly poor chance of winning worse than ever. The endboss canonically fudges the numbers, ensuring she virtually never rolls lower than a 5. More times than not she'll steamroll through the map and earn wins before you have any chance to even try to stop her, let alone net the win yourself, and in the few cases you manage to slow her down, one of the two friendly NPCs will generally win instead...which results in you losing anyways.
I hate to say I just can't recommend the game. The multiplayer can be great if you have people to play it with, but that's it. The novelty of dealing with coded-to-cheat AI in single player wears off incredibly fast and turns into nothing more than maxing out the frameskip while groaning through the constant 1v6 dicerolls you'll get every time an AI attacks you.

There's no shortage of games over the years that have been inspired by or just re-skinned versions of Oregon Trail.  There's not a great deal of complex gameplay and it mostly just boils down to basic management and decision making along with some dice rolls.  Orion Trail isn't necessarily a re-skin, but as the name implies, the game is quite similar.  You will still be making choices and you'll definitely be at the whim of dice rolls, but it ties it all together in an entertaining package that separates itself from other games with the same idea.
You may not have your fourth child dying of dysentery on this trip, but Orion Trail does deliver plenty of hazards for you to encounter and potentially (most likely) fail miserably in trying to overcome.  The game starts you out by selecting four crew members with various stats that, for most of the game, are added to a pool.  After you stock up on supplies including fuel, food, crew, and ship armor, you set out on your trip across one of the maps that unlock linearly – but each can be revisited for later runs.  Each map is longer than the last and has more stops you'll need to make to reach the goal.  At these stops, one of a number of events will trigger that requires you to pick one reaction.  Each reaction is associated with a particular stat and will give you a certain reward (usually resources) at the risk of another resource.  You have to decide whether to pick a reaction that gives you a resource you need, or doesn't risk a resource you're low on, as well as one that you have a high corresponding stat in.  When you reach the 'dice roll,' here presented as a “Probability Drive,” each stat point counts toward the chances of victory.  If the Probability Drive lands on one of those, you are successful.  This sort of gameplay makes up the bulk of the game.  At times you may reach a location that allows you to send an away crew comprise of one of your chosen four officers (usually the one with the best stats) and a portion of your crew.  These situations allow you to risk the officer and crew members to potentially get more resources and crew in the process doing the same choice/roll loop.  You can return to the ship and move on with enough resources to breeze through the rest of the map or lose practically everything and limp along until your inevitable failure.  Sometimes it's best just to skip them altogether... but where's the fun in that?
While the game is simple and enjoyable, it is reliant on a couple of core components that can be a bit annoying after a while.   The first is the RNG of it all.  I think in the past, gamers in general were more acceptant of RNG.  The original Oregon Trail was filled with it.  The difference being of course that you couldn't see it in front of your face like a roulette wheel.  However, no matter how you look at it, when you shift probability in your favor, it's hard to accept losing and suffering for it.  It makes it seem like the player has really limited control in a game centered around choices.  The other part that eventually let me down is that the number of events that I came across is limited.  On maybe the second or third trail I did, I even hit the same exact event twice in that run.  I've seen several things across the maps repeatedly.  If the gameplay was more compelling on its own and the writing of the game wasn't such a significant part of what made it interesting to play, I'd be able to look past something like this, but it does present a real drawback to the game.
Orion Trail isn't worth it's retail price of $8.  It is, however, worth the $2.50 I paid for it on sale.  It kept me entertained and got some laughs which is more than I can say for a lot of games that try to be funny.  Really though, if you were even a little interested in Oregon Trail, you'll find this just familiar enough to be worth a couple bucks or so.  It's not going to win any Game of the Year awards, but you can sit down and in 10-20 minutes knock out a run, and whether you win or lose, feel good about playing it.

A fun choose your own adventure style game that parodies Star Trek.
The idea is to reach the goal at the end of the system by picking the next location you will go to. You can't go backwards so picking certain paths will close off others. When you reach your destination a random event will occur based on what location you have visited. These often involved a skill check and both your captain and your 3 officers have their own stats that include such things as tactics, diplomacy and science. The different options you have are all themed around a specific skill and the more points your crew has culmitavely in that skill, the greater your chance of success so it's best to pick the choices that play to your strengths. You will sometimes have the option to send out an away team as well, which are basically a themed set of encounters. In this instance though, your skill checks are not  your crews culmitive skills, but just the skills of the officer you send to lead the expidition. The amount of situations you can encounter in this random encounters and away missions is quite varied and they will play out differently depending on what skills you choose to favour. The are often bizzare and humorous and the writing is quite good.
There is also some resource management and you will need to make sure you don't run out of your vital resources or you will face consequences. You will need to keep an eye on your food, fuel, number of crew and the condition of your hull. While running out of fuel can be a bit of a pain, running out of hull will destroy your ship and end your journey.
The game has a nice retro pixel art style to convey the events happening  in what is mostly text based encounters but the art has a lot of humour and really adds to the zany atmosphere of the whacky adventures your crew will have. The music is quite good too with catchy retro chiptunes.
All up a fun little story based game. There is a lot of luck involved in the skill tests the game makes during your encounters but if you play to your crews strengths you can normally offset that. Plus the adventures are short enough that failure is not a big deal and sometimes it's fun to fail, just to see what disaster is going to befall you when you do.
7/10

Little King's Story / Pikmin / The Wonderful 101 are all on my favorite games of all time list. I really can't get enough of micromanaging those tiny different classes of creatures all at the same time, that's why I was so excited two days ago when I was caught by surprise by this game.
I couldn't believe someone was smart enough to apply a similar mob mechanic to a "roguelite" sort of game. That's the dream I've always had and did not know about.
Does it deliver though? Maybe I'm writing this too prematurely, but Steam won't allow me to play the game much more while still qualifying for a refund. But short answer: I don't think so.
While the setting, different characters, general artstyle and theme choice all work pretty well, it pains me to admit that the game hasn't made a good job on showing diversity on gameplay.
Having basically four commands for leading your mob, those being attack, defend, run and stay together, it seems diverse enough on paper. However, the level design doesn't exactly put the player on situations in which those commands are used in interesting ways, the biggest offender being the "stay together" command. I'd think there would be situations in which controlling the chaos was necessary, but in reality most enemies are just going to die by holding the attack button, sometimes needing to identify the attack animation, but that's just a matter of quickly pressing the defense and proceed to spam the attack again.
Another big issue is that controlling each type of unit that goes in the mob seems to play a big roll into the strategy, the player soon figures out that it's almost impossible to control which type of unit is dying and being recruited during the huge chaos installed. At the end of each big square area full of the same enemies, the player is given an opportunity to exchange types of units to other types and even to unique heroes that promotes special abilities to the horde. That's easily the most enjoyable part of managing the mob, but you'll soon realize it's a big gamble, being very common for no/few exchanges being made possible simply out of luck.
Boss fights tend to be what I enjoy the most in every game, they are the opportunity to push a different gameplay idea and take it to the max in a matter of minutes. In Okhlos unfortunately the bosses while seeming very different from each other at first sight, I felt like most of what changed from one to another was the amount of HP and consequent time to beat it. Although in a lower level, they mostly suffer the same fate as regular enemies: same-ish strategy over and over.
Okhlos is definitely a game I want to love, but can't. I very much appreciate that it exists because what's there is very promising but unfortunately is not taken to the maximum. I feel like it became a half baked idea and caught myself thinking maybe it was in Early Access.
I definitely can understand if someone absolutely loves it because it is indeed very unique, but for now it's a refund for me.

This game is worth every penny and just barely isn't "overwhelmingly" positive because some language translations were delayed to post-release and a few minor bugs.
This game gives me the Neverwinter Nights/Baldur's Gate feel so much and reminds me of the ye olde rpgs of the 90s. Classic, hard, and the game won't hold your hand. You are not some overpowered character that can waltz around and do whatever you want without repercussions. You will get destroyed, even by trash mobs, on higher difficulties and sometimes even on classic. The game also requires you to use your own wit and critical thinking to figure out how you want to advance in the game, since it doesn't have modern games' trend of markers to advance quests
The game's combat rewards time, patience, and strategy over just brute forcing your way through. The story is slow-paced, but interesting enough to get you through. The side-quests feel important enough to feel like main-quests(and some can have impact later down the line), very similar to the Witcher 3 almost in how detailed they are.  Customization of your character and it's class is fair, but the game also allows you to decide what your companion's class will be, even if they don't appear to be efficient in it. Want Ifan to be a mage? Got it. Want Lohse to be a Knight? simple.
The game also has a co-op feature where you and 3 other players can play in the same game session, which also makes some of the side AND main quests pan out differently
I haven't seen quality in an RPG like this for a long time and Larian has shown to have busted their♥♥♥♥♥that this game has quality and replayability.

Okhlos is one of the better roguelite games out there, it isn't on the level of Binding of Isaac, Gungeon, Nuclear Throne or even Spelunky when it comes to depth of game play and presentation (everything is pixelated so it's actually a bit ugly/messy) BUT it comes through via the unique game play and humor. Unlike 99% of roguelites which are platformers, arena shooters or roguelikes, this is a pikmin style roguelite wherein you control a mob and wage war against the Gods and cause anarchy. The game play isn't really that deep in that you you only a couple of moves (attack, defend, use items), but it's fun to run around and mob people. Speaking of mobs there are differnet types of mobs you can collect including heroes which will give you a buff like setting enemies on fire or increasing mob size, so unlike say Gungeon wherein you have a limit on the powerups you have, in this case if you're good enough you can actually collect all the heroes and a super powered mob running around which makes for fun times.
As for the negatives, as I mentioned the I'm not really a fan of the art style I mean compare it to beautiful games like Gungeon, League of Explorers or Darkest Dungeon it looks really messy and pixelated, I can understand in some games why that happens but in this case there is no need for it, especially when you have big♥♥♥♥♥bosses that could easily have a lot of detail. Because the depth isn't really there you won't be able to sink hundreds or even dozens of hour into this game like you do with other roguelikes so IMHO the value for money isn't really there, I'm guessing you can already unlock everything and get the full experience after around 10-12 hours which is kinda low when you compare it to the gold standard of roguelikes/lites like FTL, Darkest Dungeon, Isaac, Gungeon etc. Finally, the biggest negative for me is that the hardest things in the game aren't the bosses or opponents, it's the environmental hazards like spikes, fires and poisoned meat. A lot of roguelikes/lite emphasize brutal but FAIR game play, essentially if you die you only have yourself to blame. This game is the opposite of that, most of the time what kills me are things I can't control like the whole arena being covered with spikes or a pathway blocked by poisoned meat. I'm controlling a mob of 40+ people how am I supposed to prevent them from getting burned, poisoned or pierced when I'm fighting? On the other hand, the opponents are immune to traps so they can just chill in the middle of the spike trap while I have to go to them and get pierced just to clear the level. I think that'extremely unfair gameplay and IMHO the devs should make the opponents affected by traps so they can see how dumb and how prevalent the traps are. I don't like dying to traps and hazards and I think it takes away from the experience, I'd rather have more difficult enemies that you can interact with than bear traps or spears you have to cross over.
With that said, I think this game is something you can come back to time and time again if you want to blow off some steam with some mindless fun and I really hope the devs add more content and tighten the mechanics a bit more. Overall, in the sea of roguelikes/lite games on Steam I think this shines due to its unique gameplay and crazy humor so I think it deserves a spot in your collection.
